Here, even descriptions of cities and so on that are without drinking and the like, if they please the minds of connoisseurs, that too is not a fault. For it is said—

“Kabbaṃ [M 0.0024] na dussataṅgehi, nyūnamapyatra kehici;

Bandhaṅgasampadā taññū, kāmamārādhayanti ce”ti.

A poem, though deficient here in some of its parts, is not flawed if the perfection of its compositional elements pleases the connoisseurs as desired.

Tassattho – atra imesu kabbaṅgesu majjhe kehici aṅgehi kehici avayavehi nyūnamapi ūnamapi, nisaddotratabbhāve. Kabbaṃ na dussati, taṃ pana adussanaṃ bandhaṅgasampadā racitapuravaṇṇanādiaṅgasampadā taññū kabbaññū jane kāmaṃ icchānurūpaṃ ce ārādhayanti, evaṃ sante bhavati. Punapi nāyakavaṇṇanāsu sapakkhanāyakaṃ vaṇṇetvā tena nirākaraṇabhāvampi. No ce, paccatthikaṃ vaṇṇetvā attano nāyakena tassābhibhavanampi vaṇṇetuṃ vaṭṭati. Vuttañhi –

Its meaning is this: `atra`, among these poetic elements; `kehici aṅgehi nyūnamapi`, though deficient or lacking in some parts or components—the prefix `ni` here is in that sense. `Kabbaṃ na dussati`, the poem is not flawed. But this non-flawing occurs if the perfection of the compositional elements—that is, the perfection of elements such as crafted descriptions of cities—pleases the connoisseurs, those who know poetry, as desired, that is, according to their wish. Thus it is. Furthermore, in descriptions of the hero, after describing the hero of one's own side, it is also fitting to describe the refutation of the opponent by him. If not, then it is also fitting to describe the enemy and his being overcome by one’s own hero. For it is said—

“Guṇato paṭhamaṃ vatvā, nāyakaṃ tena sattuno;

Nirākaraṇamiccesa, maggo pakatisundaro.

First, having spoken of the hero's virtues, and the refutation of the enemy by him—this path is naturally beautiful.

Vaṃsavīrasutādīni, vaṇṇayitvā ripussapi;

Tajjayā nāyakukkaṃsa-kathanañca sukheti no”ti.

Having described the lineage, heroic deeds, learning, and the like, even of the enemy, the narration of the hero's excellence through the conquest of that enemy also delights us.

8.

8.

Bandho ca nāma saddatthā, sahitā dosavajjitā;

Pajjagajjavimissānaṃ, bhedenā’yaṃ tidhā bhave.

And composition is words and meanings, united and free from faults. This becomes threefold by the distinction of verse, prose, and a mixture of both.

8. Evametehi sotujanasamussāhanaṃ dassetvā idāni kattumicchitabandhoti vuttaṃ bandhassa lakkhaṇaṃ kattumārabhate “bandho cā”tiādi. Dosavajjitā dosehi saddanissitehi, atthanissitehi ca virodhehi vajjitā pariccattā, te vā vajjitā yehi, saddatthā sahitā ekībhūtā. Vuttalakkhaṇā yehi te pubbācariyehi sahitā vuccanti. Sahitānaṃ bhāvo sahadayahilādakāraṇaṃ sādhyaṃ sāhiccaṃ. Iti dosavajjite sahite saddatthe pasiddhabhāvena anuvaditvā bandho nāma sabhāvavuttivaṅkavuttialaṅkāravuttivasena tividhopīti appasiddhaṃ bandhasarīraṃ vidhīyate yathā “yo kuṇḍalī, so devadatto”ti. Casaddovattabbantarassa samuccayo, kiñcīti attho.

8. Having thus shown encouragement to the listeners with these verses, he now begins to state the characteristic of composition—which was mentioned as 'the composition intended to be made'—starting with 'And composition...'. `Dosavajjitā` (free from faults) means abandoned by faults related to word and meaning, and by contradictions; or, those (words and meanings) by which those faults are avoided. `Sahitā` (united) means unified. Those (words and meanings) which possess the stated characteristics are called `sahitā` by the ancient teachers. The state of being `sahita` is `sāhicca`, which is to be accomplished and is the cause of delight for the discerning. Thus, having restated the well-known nature of words and meanings being `sahita` and free from faults, the body of composition, `bandha`, is firmly established as being threefold—by way of natural expression, figurative expression, and ornamental expression—just as 'He who has earrings, that is Devadatta' is established. The word `ca` (and) is an aggregation of something further to be stated; its meaning is 'something more'.

Tattha [M 0.0025] jātiguṇakriyādabbalakkhaṇo saddānamattho mukhyo catubbidho hoti. Mukhyassatthassa catubbidhattā tividhesu saddesu tabbācako catubbidho hoti jātisaddo guṇasaddo kriyāsaddo dabbasaddoti. Tividho hi saddo vācako lakkhaṇiko byañjakoti byāpārabhedena. Byāpāro ca nāma saddassa’tthappatītikārittameva. So hi tividho mukhyo lakkhaṇo byañjanasabhāvo ceti. Tattha jātyādinirantaratthavisayo saddabyāpāro mukhyo. Soyeva abhidhāti uccate. Taṃbyāpāravā abyavahitajātyādisakehi tamatthaṃ mukhyabhāvena yo vadati goādiko, so vācako. Saddantaratthavisayaniddiṭṭho saddabyāpāro lakkhaṇo. Sā duvidhā suddhā, upacāramissā ceti. Tattha suddhā yathā “go muccatu, mañcā ugghosenti, gaṅgāyaṃ ghoso”ti. Ettha gosaddena visesanaṃ gottasāmaññamevoccate, na tu gobyatti. Vuttañhi –

Herein, the primary meaning of words is fourfold, characterized by genus, quality, action, and substance. Because the primary meaning is fourfold, the word that expresses it is also fourfold: a genus-word, a quality-word, an action-word, and a substance-word. Indeed, a word is threefold by distinction of function: expressive, indicative, and suggestive. And function is simply the word's capacity to cause the understanding of meaning. This function is threefold: primary, indicative, and suggestive in nature. Among these, the word-function whose immediate object is a meaning such as genus is primary. This very function is called denotation (abhidhā). The word, such as 'cow,' which possesses that function and expresses that meaning—such as genus—directly and primarily, is called expressive (vācaka). The word-function that points to a meaning connected with its primary one is indicative (lakkhaṇā). It is twofold: pure and mixed with transferred usage. An example of the pure indicative is: 'May the cow be released,' 'The benches are shouting,' 'A village in the Ganges.' Here, by the word 'cow,' only the general class or genus is meant, not the specific animal. As it is said—

“Visesyaṃnābhidhā gacche, khīṇasatti visesane”ti kābyappakāse dutiyaullāse āgatanyāyo’yaṃ.

“Denotation does not extend to the specific, as its power is exhausted in the general.”

Sāmaññassa byāpakattā, asarīrattā ca. Tattha bandhanamocanāni na sambhavantīti attano nissayabhūtā gobyatti ākaḍḍhīyate, tathā mañcānamugghosanaṃ na sambhavatīti attano ugghosanakriyāsiddhyatthaṃ mañcasamaṅgino purisā ākaḍḍhīyanti. Tathā gaṅgāsaddavāccassa jalappavāhassa ghosappatyākaratā na sambhavatīti gaṅgāsaddo attanobhidheyyassodakappavāhassa nikaṭaṃ taṭaṃ lakkheti. Upacārassānekappakārattā upacāramissā lakkhaṇāpyanekadhā siyā. Yathā katthaci kāraṇe kārīyamupacariyate, yathā “āyu ghata”nti. Katthaci kāraṇakāriyānamabhedo yathā “āyuyeveda”nti. Katthaci [M 0.0026] upamāne upameyyamupacarīyate, yathā “go bāhiko”ti. Katthaci abhedo tesaṃ, yathā “goyevāya”nti. Katthaci tadādhāratāya tadatthatāya (ka.) taṃbyapadeso, yathā “padīpaṭṭhā kapallikā padīpo”ti. Katthaci taṃkammasambandhā taṃbyapadeso, yathā “avaḍḍhakīpi vaḍḍhakī aya”nti. Katthaci saṃsāmisambandhā, yathā “rājasambandhī puriso rājāya”nti. Katthaci avayave samudāyabyapadeso, yathā “paṭekadese paṭasaddo” iccādi.

Because the universal is pervasive and incorporeal, binding and releasing are not possible for it. Therefore, the individual cow, which is its basis, is drawn in by implication. Similarly, since the shouting of benches is not possible, men associated with the benches are drawn in by implication for the accomplishment of the shouting action. Likewise, since being the location of a village is not possible for the flow of water denoted by the word 'Ganges,' the word 'Ganges' indicates the bank, which is near its denoted object, the flow of water. Because transferred usage (upacāra) is of many kinds, indicative meaning mixed with transferred usage can also be manifold. For example, in some cases, the effect is figuratively superimposed on the cause, as in 'ghee is life.' In some cases, there is an identity of cause and effect, as in 'this is indeed life.' In some cases, the object of comparison is figuratively superimposed on the standard of comparison, as in 'the Bāhika is a cow.' In some cases, there is an identity between them, as in 'this is indeed a cow.' In some cases, something is referred to by its container, as in 'the dish holding the lamp is a lamp.' In some cases, something is referred to by its relation to an action, as in 'this non-carpenter is a carpenter.' In some cases, the relationship is based on that of owner and property, as in 'the man connected to the king is the king.' In some cases, the whole is referred to by its part, as in 'the word 'cloth' (paṭa) for a part of the cloth,' and so on.

Lakkhaṇāya nissayo saddo lakkhaṇiko. Byañjanasabhāvo pana parapariyāyo saddassa tatiyo byāpāro. Tassa nissayo saddo byañjanako. Iccetaṃ tiṇṇaṃ saddānaṃ vasena atthopi tividho hoti vācco lakkhaṇiyo byaṅgyoti. Tattha byaṅgyoyevattho bandhasatthā vuccate. Teneva padhānabyaṅgyo bandho uttamo, apadhānabyaṅgyo majjhimo, abyaṅgyo adhamo, byaṅgyena vinā bandho nijjīvo siyāti pubbācariyānaṃ pavatti, sabhāvavutti bandhopi tu nijjīvoti nāsaṅkanīyo. Yasmā kavīnaṃ lokavohārakosallaṃ sabhāvavuttiyeva gameti. Yo hi sakalalokaṭṭhitiṃ na jānāti, so kaviyeva na hotīti.

The word that relies on indicative meaning is indicative. The nature of suggestion, however, is the third function of a word, an indirect way of conveying meaning. The word that relies on it is suggestive. Thus, based on these three kinds of words, meaning is also threefold: expressed, indicated, and suggested. Herein, the suggested meaning alone is called the 'soul' of composition. Therefore, a composition with a primary suggested meaning is highest, with a secondary suggested meaning is middling, and without a suggested meaning is lowest. The tradition of the ancient teachers is that without suggested meaning, a composition would be lifeless. However, a composition with natural expression should not be suspected of being lifeless, for the poets' skill in worldly communication reveals precisely this natural expression. Indeed, one who does not understand all worldly conventions is not a poet.

Athettha tividhampi atthaṃ tādisajanāvabodhatthaṃ samudāharissāma “munindavadanambhoje”tyādi. Ettha vāṇīsaddassa saddhammasaṅkhāto attho vāccattho. Vāṇī nāma cetanā, tassaṃ yāva devatatthaṃ nāropyate, tāva tappatī attano manosampīṇanaāsīsanā na saṃgacchatīti vākyasāmatthiyāyeva vāṇiyaṃ sāyamocityabhedena devatāsaddassa āropitottho lakkhaṇiyo. Tathā vadanasaddassāpi mukhaṃ vāccattho. Ambhojasaddassa samāropitottho lakkhaṇiyo. Manosampīṇanassa tu aññathā anupapattiyā passaddhyādikkamena yathābhūtāvabodhasambhavā anāyāsena [M 0.0027] vicittānekasaddatthapaṭibhānena ganthaparisamattisaṅkhātā yathicchitatthanipphatti hoteva, ayaṃ byaṅgyattho. Tabbācakā saddā vācakalakkhaṇikabyañjakā hontīti evaṃ sabbattha saddatthavicāro gantabbo.

Herein, for the understanding of such discerning people, we shall set forth all three types of meaning, beginning with “munindavadanambhoje” (in the lotus-face of the Lord of Sages). In this context, the literal meaning of the word “vāṇī” is that designated as the good teaching (Saddhamma). Vāṇī means volition; until a divine meaning is superimposed upon it, it is not satisfying, for it does not accord with the aspiration to delight one’s own mind. Thus, by the power of the sentence itself, the superimposed meaning of the word “deity” is indicative, through the appropriate relation of similarity to “vāṇī.” Similarly, the literal meaning of the word “vadana” is “face,” while the superimposed meaning of the word “ambhoja” (lotus) is indicative. However, since the delight of the mind is otherwise inexplicable, and since the comprehension of reality can arise through the sequence of tranquility and so on, and through the effortless brilliance of diverse and manifold word-meanings, the accomplishment of the desired meaning, which is designated as the completion of the composition, certainly occurs; this is the suggested meaning. The words that express these are expressive, indicative, and suggestive. Thus, the analysis of word-meaning should be undertaken in this way everywhere.

Tamevaṃ yathāvuttabandhasarīraṃ katividhamiccāha “pajje”ccādi. Ayaṃ yathāvutto bandho bandhasarīraṃ tidhā bhave tippakārena siyā, nādhikaṃ nāpyūnaṃ. Kathaṃ? Pajjagajjavimissānaṃ bhedena pajjasabhāvādīnaṃ visesena tidhā bhaveti pakataṃ. Tattha pajjaṃ nāma amhehiyeva viracitavuttodayākhye chandasi nirūpitā vuttajātippabhedā catuppadikatthā nirūpito muttakādipi vuttajātippakāroyeva. Tenevettha tesamadassanaṃ. Tesu ekagāthā niṭṭhitatthā sappadhānā gāthantarānirapekkhā muttakaṃ, ekakriyādānena aññamaññasāpekkhā niṭṭhitatthā paccekaṃ aniṭṭhitatthā gāthā kulakaṃ, nānābhittiyo bhinnakiriyo sappadhānā gāthā koso viya ṭhapitā koso, ekabhittipadosādikaṃ vaṇṇetuṃ samudāyena pavattā bhinnakriyā gāthā saṅghāto, sopi catubbidho pajjappakāro yathāvuttasaggabandhovāti viññātabbaṃ. Gajjaṃ nāma pādasanniṭṭhānarahito syādyantatyādyantappabandho. Tassa tu dve pakārā ākhyāyikā, kathāti. Vimissaṃ pajjagajjamayaṃ nāṭakappakaraṇādi, campū jātakamālādikā ca.

Now, as to how many kinds the body of composition, as described, is, it is said, “pajje,” and so on. This composition, the body of composition as described, is threefold, in three ways, neither more nor less. How so? It is explained that it is threefold by the division of verse (pajja), prose (gajja), and mixed (vimissa), and by the distinction of their inherent natures. Herein, verse (pajja) refers to the varieties of meters, such as the four-lined verse with a complete meaning, and also the types of verse like muttaka, etc., which have been explained in the treatise on prosody called Vuttodaya, composed by ourselves. Therefore, they are not detailed here. Among these, a single verse that completes its meaning, has a primary subject, and is independent of other verses, is a muttaka. A group of verses that are mutually dependent through a single action to complete their meaning, but are individually incomplete in meaning, is a kulaka. Verses with various subjects and distinct actions, having a primary subject and arranged like a treasury, are a kosa. A group of verses with distinct actions, proceeding as a whole to describe a single subject, is a saṅghāta. This fourfold type of verse should also be understood as the aforementioned canto composition. Prose (gajja) is a composition devoid of the structure of metrical feet. It has two kinds: ākhyāyikā and kathā. Mixed (vimissa) consists of verse and prose, such as a nāṭaka, prakaraṇa, etc., and also a campū, jātakamālā, and the like.

8. Idāni sañjānanābhilāsīnaṃ alaṅkāranissitaṃ bandhasarīraṃ, sova bandhoti adhikataṃ, “yo kuṇḍalī, so devadatto”ti pasiddhakuṇḍalittānuvādena appasiddhassa devadattattavidhānaṃ viya dassento “bandho”ccādimāha. Tattha bandho nāma ca bandhanaṃ pana. Dosavajjitā saddatthanissitadosehi pariccattā, te vā vajjitā etehi tādisā. Sahitā aññamaññānurūpatthena sahabhāvaṃ gatā. Saddatthā saddo, [M 0.0028] attho ca. Evaṃpakārehi tu īdisasaddatthānaṃ viññūnaṃ tuṭṭhijanakaaññamaññānurūpaguṇasahitānaṃ bhāvoti vacanatthena “sāhicca”miti vadanti. Saddatthāti ettha saddatthānaṃ kiṃ nānākaraṇanti? Saddo pana atthappatītiyaṃ attano mukhyabyāpāraṃ lakkhaṇabyāpāraṃ byañjanasabhāvabyāpārañceti tividhaṃ byāpārabhedena. Kamato vācako lakkhaṇiko byañjanako ceti tividho. Tathā atthopi vācco lakkhaṇiyo byaṅgyo cebhi tividho. Atra tu vācako saddo attanā dīpetabbamukhyatthassa jātiguṇakriyādabbabhedena catubbidhattā sayampi jātiguṇakriyādabbasaddavasena catubbidho. Vācakasaddassa mukhyabyāpāro “abhidhā”ti ca voharīyati. So mukhyabyāpāro jātyādīhi abyavahitattheva vattate. Tathā hi “go nīlaṃ pācako visāṇi”ccādo goādisaddānaṃ mukhyabyāpāro gopiṇḍanīlapaṭapācakakattusiṅgīti dabbānaṃ visesanabhūtajātiguṇakriyādabbesveva pavattati, na pana jātyādīnaṃ nissayabhūtagopiṇḍādīsūti. Vuttaṃ hi–

8. Now, for those who desire understanding, the body of composition is based on embellishment. That itself is composition; thus it is taken up. He says “composition,” and so forth, illustrating it with the example “He who wears earrings is Devadatta,” where the well-known fact of wearing earrings is used to establish the previously unestablished fact of being Devadatta. Herein, “composition” (bandha) indeed means “binding” or “arrangement.” It is faultless, abandoned by faults dependent on sound and meaning, or such faults are avoided by them. United, they have attained a state of togetherness through their mutual suitability. Sound and meaning (saddattha) are sound and meaning. Thus, the wise call the state of such sound and meaning—united by mutually suitable qualities that generate delight in the learned—'sāhicca' (literature), by the meaning of the word. Here, regarding sound and meaning, what is the distinction between them? Sound, in conveying meaning, has a threefold function, by division of function: its primary function, indicative function, and suggestive-nature function. Respectively, it is threefold: the designator, the indicator, and the suggester. Similarly, meaning is also threefold: the designated, the indicated, and the suggested. Herein, the designating sound, because its primary meaning to be illuminated is fourfold by the divisions of genus, quality, action, and substance, is itself also fourfold as genus-sound, quality-sound, action-sound, and substance-sound. The primary function of the designating sound is also called “denotation” (abhidhā). And that primary function operates only in the direct meaning of genus, and so forth. For example, in the case of words such as 'ox', 'blue', 'cook', 'horned', the primary function of the words 'ox', etc., operates only in the genus, quality, action, and substance that serve as qualifiers for substances like the ox-individual, blue cloth, the agent of cooking, and the horned one, respectively; it does not, however, operate in the ox-individual and so forth, which are the bases of that genus, etc. As it is said—

“Visesyaṃ nābhidhā gacche, khīṇasatti visesane”ti kābyappakāse dutiyaullāse āgatanyāyo’yaṃ.

“Denotation does not reach the qualified, its power being exhausted in the qualifier.”

Tassattho – visesane visesanabhūtajātyādimhi khīṇasatti khīṇabyāpāravatī abhidhā mukhyabyāpārova visesyaṃ dabbaṃ na gacche na pāpuṇātīti.

Its meaning is this: Denotation (abhidhā), the primary function, its power and activity being exhausted in the qualifier—that is, in genus, etc., which serves as a qualifier—does not reach or attain the qualified substance (dabba).

Jātyādīnaṃ nissayagopiṇḍādikaṃ abhidhā na vadati ce, evañca sati “go gacchati, nīlaṃ nivāseti, pācako āgacchati, siṅgī dhāvati”ccādīsu jātyādivisiṭṭhagopiṇḍādīnaṃ goādisaddassa kathaṃ vācakattaṃ yujjatīti? Dabbādhīnajātiguṇādīsu vuttesu tabbisiṭṭhassa dabbassa pariyāyato vācakattā. Nippariyāyato pana suddhalakkhaṇabyāpārasseva visayo. Lakkhaṇabyāpāropi suddho upacāramissoti duvidho. [M 0.0029] Tattha suddho lakkhaṇabyāpāro jātyādivajjitatthavisayo. Tathā hi “go gacchati, nīlaṃ nivāseti, pācako āgacchati, siṅgī dhāvati, mañcā ugghosenti, gaṅgāyaṃ ghoso”tyādīsu jātiguṇakriyāsiṅgadabbamañcagaṅgādīnaṃ gamanādīhi yogāsambhavato jātiguṇādayo atikkamma yathākkamaṃ gamananivāsanaāgamanadhāvanaugghosanaghosādīnaṃ nissayabhūtagopiṇḍādayo parāmasati.

If denotation does not express the ox-individual, etc., which are the bases of genus, etc., then how, in phrases such as “the ox goes,” “one wears blue,” “the cook comes,” “the horned one runs,” etc., can the word “ox,” etc., function as a designator of the ox-individual, etc., as distinguished by genus, etc.? Because when genus, quality, etc., which are dependent on substance, are expressed, the substance distinguished by them is designated figuratively. In a non-figurative sense, however, it is the domain of the pure indicative function alone. The indicative function is also twofold: pure and mixed with metaphor. Therein, the pure indicative function has as its domain meanings devoid of genus, etc. For example, in phrases like “the ox goes,” “one wears blue,” “the cook comes,” “the horned one runs,” “the beds resound,” “a settlement on the Ganges,” etc., since a connection with going, etc., is impossible for genus, quality, action, the horned substance, the bed, the Ganges, etc., the meaning, surpassing genus, quality, etc., successively refers to the ox-individual, etc., which are the bases of going, wearing, coming, running, resounding, and the settlement, etc.

Misso tu upacārabhedena bahuvidho. Tathā hi katthaci kāraṇe kāriyamupacarīyate, yathā “āyughata”nti, ettha āyuvaḍḍhanakāraṇabhūte ghate kāriyabhūtaāyuno vohāro āropito hoti. Uparipi upacāro yathāyogaṃ yojetabbo. Ataṃsabhāve hi taṃsabhāvāropanaṃ upacāro. Katthaci kāraṇakāriyānamabhedo, yathā “āyuyeva ghata”nti. Katthaci upameyyaupamānopacāro, yathā “go bāhiko”ti. Katthaci upamānaupameyyānamabhedo, yathā “goyevāyaṃ bāhiko”ti. Katthaci tadādhāratāya tadūpacāro, yathā “padīpaṭṭhā kapallikā padīpo”ti. Katthaci kriyāsambandhena taṃbyapadeso, yathā “avaḍḍhakīpi vaḍḍhakī aya”nti. Katthaci saṃsāmisambandhena taṃbyapadeso, yathā “rājavallabhopi rājā aya”nti. Katthaci avayave samudāyabyapadeso, yathā “paṭo daḍḍho”ti. Iminā mukhena upacārabhedo daṭṭhabbo. Byañjanasabhāvabyāpāro eva “dhana”nti ca vuccati, tassa tatiyabyāpārassa visayo tādisavākyameva vāti daṭṭhabbo.

The mixed type, however, is of many kinds due to the varieties of metaphor. For instance, in some cases, the effect is metaphorically applied to the cause, as in the phrase 'life-ghee' (āyughata), where the usage of 'life' (āyu), which is the effect, is superimposed upon ghee (ghata), which is the cause of prolonging life. Furthermore, metaphor should be applied as is appropriate. For metaphor is the superimposition of the nature of one thing upon that which does not possess that nature. In some cases, there is an identification of cause and effect, as in the phrase 'ghee itself is life' (āyuyeva ghata). In some cases, there is a metaphorical application of the standard of comparison to the object of comparison, as in 'the Bāhika is an ox' (go bāhiko). In some cases, there is an identification of the standard of comparison and the object of comparison, as in 'this Bāhika is indeed an ox' (goyevāyaṃ bāhiko). In some cases, something is metaphorically referred to by its container, as in 'the lamp-stand is the lamp' (padīpaṭṭhā kapallikā padīpo). In some cases, something is designated by its associated action, as in 'though not a carpenter, this one is a carpenter' (avaḍḍhakīpi vaḍḍhakī ayaṃ). In some cases, something is designated by its relationship of proximity, as in 'though a king's favorite, this one is the king' (rājavallabhopi rājā ayaṃ). In some cases, the whole is designated by a part, as in 'the cloth is burnt' (paṭo daḍḍho). In this way, the varieties of metaphor should be understood. The function of a suggestive nature is also called 'dhvani' (suggestion), and it should be understood that the domain of this third function is precisely such a sentence.

Ettha byaṅgyatthaṃ bandhassa jīvitamiti ca, byaṅgyatthapadhānaṃ bandhamuttamanti ca, byaṅgyatthapadhānarahitaṃ majjhimanti ca, abyaṅgyabandhaṃ adhamamiti ca vadanti. Honti cettha –

Herein, they say that the suggested meaning is the life of composition, that composition in which the suggested meaning is predominant is the best, that which is devoid of a predominant suggested meaning is mediocre, and that composition without a suggested meaning is the lowest. And here are the verses:

Atthappatītiyaṃ sadda-byāpāro tividho bhave;

Mukhyo lakkhaṇabyañjana-sabhāvo cāti ettha tu.

In the conveying of meaning, the function of sound is threefold: namely, the primary, the indicative, and the suggestive nature, indeed, in this context.

Abhidhāparapariyāyo, [M 0.0030] byāpāro paṭhamo bhave;

Dhanantāparapariyāyo, byāpāro tatiyo puna.

The first function has the synonym 'abhidhā' (denotation); the third function, again, has the synonym 'dhvani' (suggestion).

Mukhyo nirantaratthesu, lakkhaṇā tu tirohite;

Atthe’taro tu vākyassa, attheyeva pavattati.

The primary function is in direct meanings, but indication (lakkhaṇā) is in a hidden meaning; the other, however, operates only in the meaning of the sentence.

Byāpārassa pabhedena, tidhā saddopi vācako;

Lakkhaṇiko byañjakoti, tadatthopi tidhā mato.

By the division of function, sound is also threefold: the designator, the indicator, and the suggester; and its meaning is also considered threefold.

Vācco lakkhaṇiyo byaṅgyo-ccevaṃ saddesu vācako;

Jātiguṇakriyādabba-bhedena so catubbidho.

The designated, the indicated, and the suggested—thus, among sounds, the designator is fourfold by the distinctions of genus, quality, action, and substance.

Vāccatthassa catuddhāva, bhinnattā jātiādito;

Jātyādīnaṃ pabhedena, tathā lakkhaṇiko mato.

Since the designated meaning is indeed divided in four ways, beginning with genus, similarly, the indicator is considered to be divided by the divisions of genus, etc.

Upacārabahuttena, bhede satipi tassa tu;

Byañjako tu anaññattā, visuṃ tehi na vuccatīti.

Although it has many divisions due to the abundance of metaphors, the suggester, however, due to its non-difference, is not spoken of separately from them.

Lakkhaṇato evaṃ veditabbaṃ – “munindavadanambhoje” tyādigāthāyaṃ vadanasaddassa mukhattho vāccattho, āropitaambhojattho lakkhaṇiyattho. Ambhojasaddassa padumattho vāccattho, upacaritamukhattho lakkhaṇiyattho. Vāṇisaddassa saddhammasaṅkhāto attho vāccattho, āropitadevatāattho lakkhaṇiyattho. Ettha āsīsanā nāma yathāvuttanayena puññātisayatā, tato idha abhimatatthabādhakākusalanivāraṇañca kusalānamanubalappadānañca tato kāyacittapīḷāvigamo ca tato sukhappaṭilābho ca tato cittasamādhānañca tatoyeva anekavidhatthāvabodho ca tato abhimataganthaparisamatti ca bhavatītyayaṃ vākyasāmatthiyato laddhattho byaṅgyatto. Taṃtaṃatthappakāsakā saddā vācakalakkhaṇikabyañjanakā nāma bhavanti. Evaṃ saddasaddatthavicāro veditabbo.

It should be understood by way of example thus: In the verse beginning 'munindavadanambhoje,' the designated meaning (vāccattho) of the word 'vadana' (face) is its literal meaning, 'face' (mukhattho), while its indicated meaning (lakkhaṇiyattho) is the superimposed meaning of 'lotus' (ambhoja). The designated meaning (vāccattho) of the word 'ambhoja' (lotus) is its literal meaning, 'lotus' (paduma), while its indicated meaning (lakkhaṇiyattho) is the metaphorical meaning of 'face' (mukha). The designated meaning (vāccattho) of the word 'vāṇi' (speech) is the meaning designated as 'true Dhamma' (saddhammasaṅkhāto attho), while its indicated meaning (lakkhaṇiyattho) is the superimposed meaning of 'deity'. Here, 'āsīsanā' (aspiration) means an abundance of merit in the manner previously explained. From this arises the removal of unwholesome states that obstruct the desired meaning here, and the strengthening of wholesome qualities; and from that, the cessation of bodily and mental affliction; and from that, the attainment of happiness; and from that, the concentration of mind; and from that very thing, the comprehension of various meanings; and from that, the completion of the desired text. This meaning, obtained from the power of the statement, is the suggested meaning (byaṅgyattho). The sounds that reveal these respective meanings are called the designator (vācaka), the indicator (lakkhaṇika), and the suggester (byañjanaka). Thus, the analysis of sound and its meaning should be understood.

Idāni [M 0.0031] pakāsitabandhassa bhedaṃ vadati “pajjā”dinā. Ayaṃ vuttalakkhaṇo bandho pajjagajjavimissānaṃ bhedena gāthācuṇṇiyatadubhayamissānaṃ vasena tidhā bhave. Saddo ca attho ceti ca, sahabhāvaṃ itā pattāti ca, dosehi vajjitā, dose vā vajjitā yehīti ca, pajjañca gajjañca vimissañceti ca viggaho. Iha pajjaṃ nāma muttakakulakakosakasaṅghātavasena catuppabhedaṃ chandasi niddiṭṭhavuttavisesaviracitaṃ catuppadikagāthābandhaṃ. Tattha muttakaṃ nāma niṭṭhitatthā sappadhānā ekā gāthā, kulakaṃ nāma paccekamaniṭṭhitatthā aññamaññasāpekkhā ekakriyādvārikā nānāgāthā, kosako nāma nānāvidhavaṇṇanābhūmikā bhinnakriyādvārappavattā sappadhānā gāthārāsi, saṅghāto nāma sañcyākālādiekavaṇṇanābhūminissitā bhinnakriyāsamudāyena pavattā gāthā. Gajjaṃ nāma aniyatapado ākhyāyikākathāvasena dvippabhedo syādyantatyādyanto vacanappabandho. Misso pana imehi dvīhi saṃmisso nāṭakapakaraṇādi ca jātakamālādicampū ca.

Now, he speaks of the division of the composition that has been explained, beginning with 'pajjā' (verse). This composition, as defined, is threefold by way of the divisions of verse (pajja), prose (gajja), and mixed (vimissa), that is, by way of gāthā (stanzas), cuṇṇiya (prose), and a mixture of both. The analysis (viggaho) is: 'sound and meaning' (saddo ca attho ca), 'having attained co-existence' (sahabhāvaṃ itā pattā), 'free from faults' (dosehi vajjitā), or 'those by which faults are avoided' (dose vā vajjitā yehi), and 'verse and prose and mixed' (pajjañca gajjañca vimissañca). Here, 'pajja' (verse) is fourfold by way of muttaka, kulaka, kosaka, and saṅghāta, being a four-lined verse composition crafted with specific meters as described in prosody. Among these: 'Muttaka' means a single verse with a completed meaning, being self-contained and principal. 'Kulaka' means several verses, each with an incomplete meaning, interdependent, unified by a single action. 'Kosaka' means a collection of verses with diverse descriptive themes, proceeding through different actions, yet self-contained and principal. 'Saṅghāta' means verses based on a single descriptive theme, proceeding from a collection of different actions. 'Gajja' (prose) refers to a composition with unrestricted lines, twofold by way of being a narrative (ākhyāyikā) or a story (kathā), a prose composition that is syādyanta or tyādyanta. 'Misso' (mixed), however, is a mixture of these two, such as dramas (nāṭaka) and treatises (pakaraṇa), as well as Jātaka garlands (jātakamālā) and campū compositions.

9.

9.

Nibandho cā’nibandho ca, puna dvidhā niruppate;

Taṃ tu pāpentya’laṅkārā, vindanīyatarattanaṃ.

Bound and unbound, again, it is classified in two ways; indeed, ornaments lead it to a state of greater delight.

9. Evaṃ tippakāraṃ bandhasarīraṃ vatvā idāni aññathāpi dassetumāha “nibandhocā’nibandho ca, puna dvidhā niruppate” iti. Puna bhiyyo yathāvutto pajjamayabandho dvidhā dvippakārena niruppate nicchīyate. Kathaṃ? Nibandho ca tadekadesabhūtehi muttakādīhi catūhi saggabandhādivasena bandho ca anibandho ca kevalaṃ muttakavasenāti evaṃ dvidhā niruppate iti pakataṃ. Nanu tassetassa yathāvuttavātimayassa sakkaṭaṃ pākataṃ apabbhaṃso pesācikaṃ missañceti pañcavidhattaṃ vatvā “sakkaṭaṃ nāma devatābhāsā. Pākataṃ catubbidhaṃ sakkaṭehi vaṇṇaññattamattena uppannattā [M 0.0032] mahindasindhavādi tabbhavaṃ, tassamaṃ hiriharakamalādi, mahāraṭṭhādidesapasiddhaṃ desīyaṃ, tabbhavādīhi sammissaṃ missaṃ. Ābhīrādīnaṃ vācā apabbhaṃso, so ca pākataṃ viya catubbidho, tividho ca nāgaraupanāgaravuddhabhedena. Pisācānaṃ vacanaṃ pesācikaṃ. Sabbesaṃ vasena missa”nti sakkaṭādīnaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Tathā “siṅgārappadhānanaccasaṅkhātalāsyādīnaṃ paṭipādakatthena lāsyādikamabhinayappadhānattā dassanīyaṃ, itaraṃ kabbaṃ savanīya”nti duvidhaṃ vuttaṃ, evaṃ pubbācariyehi bhāsābhedena vuttaṃ pañcavidhattaṃ, viniyogabhedena vuttaṃ duvidhattañca idha kasmā na vuttanti? Saccaṃ, tathāpi tadevamidhānupayogitāya na vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

9. Having thus spoken of the threefold body of composition, now, to show it in another way, he says: 'Bound and unbound, again, it is classified in two ways.' Furthermore, the aforementioned verse-composition (pajjamayabandho) is classified (niruppate) or determined (nicchīyate) in two ways, in two aspects. How? 'Bound' (nibandho) is a composition by way of the four elements such as muttaka, etc., which are parts of it, like a composition in cantos (saggabandha); and 'unbound' (anibandho) is solely by way of muttaka. Thus, it is classified in two ways—this is the subject at hand (pakataṃ). Now, is it not the case that, having stated that this aforementioned poetic form (vātimayassa) is fivefold—Sakkaṭa, Pākata, Apabbhaṃsa, Pesācika, and Missa—it is said: 'Sakkaṭa is the language of the gods. Pākata is fourfold: 'tabbhava' (derived), which arises merely from a change of letters from Sakkaṭa, like Mahinda, Sindhu, etc.; 'tassama' (same as), like Hiri, Hara, Kamala, etc.; 'desīya' (regional), well-known in countries like Mahāraṭṭha, etc.; and 'missa' (mixed), which is mixed with tabbhava and so on. The speech of the Ābhīras, etc., is Apabbhaṃsa; and it too is fourfold like Pākata, and threefold by the distinctions of Nāgara, Upanāgara, and Vuddha. The speech of Pisācas (demons) is Pesācika. 'Missa' is mixed by way of all these.' Thus, the characteristics of Sakkaṭa and so on are stated. Likewise, it is said: 'That which is primarily for presentation, such as lāsya, etc., which consists of dance dominated by erotic sentiment, is to be seen because performance is primary; the other, poetry (kabba), is to be heard'—thus, it is twofold. In this way, why are the fivefold division by linguistic distinctions and the twofold division by application, as stated by the ancient teachers, not mentioned here? It is true, but it should be understood that they are not mentioned here because they are not relevant for this purpose.

Evamalaṅkārādhiṭṭhānabhāvena paṭhamaṃ bandhasarīraṃ dassetvā idāni hārakeyūrādinā purisasarīramiva bandhasarīraṃ saddālaṅkāraatthālaṅkārehi vindanīyataraṃ hotīti dassetumāha “taṃ tu” iccādi. Tusaddo visesavacanicchāyaṃ. Taṃ bandhasarīraṃ tu alaṅkārā alaṅkariyati taṃ bandhasarīrametehīti pasādādayo saddālaṅkārā, sabhāvavutyādayo atthālaṅkārā ca vindanīyatarattanaṃ atisayena vindanīyabhāvaṃ assādanīyabhāvaṃ pāpenti nayanti. Sabbathā niddosabhūtānaṃ saddatthānaṃ aññamaññānurūpato sahitabhāvena paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgataṃ tādisapurisasarīramiva vindanīyampi samānaṃ alaṅkārehi pasādhite sati accantameva vindanīyaṃ siyāti adhippāyo.

Having first shown the body of composition (bandhasarīra) by way of its being the basis of adornment, now, to show that the body of composition, like a man's body adorned with necklaces and armlets, etc., becomes more delightful (vindanīyataraṃ) through sound-ornaments (saddālaṅkāra) and meaning-ornaments (atthālaṅkāra), he says: 'But that...' (taṃ tu iccādi). The word 'tu' (but) is for expressing distinction. That body of composition, indeed, the ornaments (alaṅkārā)—which adorn that body of composition, such as sound-ornaments like 'pasāda' (clarity) and so on, and meaning-ornaments like 'sabhāvavutti' (natural expression) and so on—lead (pāpenti) or bring (nayanti) it to a state of greater delight (vindanīyatarattanaṃ), a state of extreme delightfulness (atisayena vindanīyabhāvaṃ), a state of enjoyability (assādanīyabhāvaṃ). The intention is that a body of composition, which is in every way flawless in its sounds and meanings, endowed with supreme beauty due to their harmonious combination in mutual suitability, though already delightful like such a man's body, becomes utterly delightful when adorned with ornaments.

9. Punapi tasseva bandhassa bhedaṃ kathetuṃ “nibandho cā”dimāha. Puna nibandho ca muttakādīhi catūhi avinābhāvato mahākabbādisabhāvena nirantaraṃ katvā bandho ca anibandho ca kevalaṃ mahākabbādisabhāvena muttakattā anirantaraṃ katvā bandho cāti sova bandho dvidhā niruppate nicchīyate. [M 0.0033] Punapi so bandho sakkaṭapākataapabbhaṃ sapesācikamissabhāsābhedena pañcavidho. Siṅgārapadhānanaccasaṅkhātalāsyādīnaṃ dassanappadhānattā tādisaṃ naccaṃdassanīyaṃ, tadaññaṃ kabbaṃ savanīyamiti vaḷañjanabhedato duvidho ca hoti. So sabbopi payojanābhāvato iha na gahito. Tattha sakkaṭaṃ nāma devatābhāsā. Tato kehici akkharehi bhinnaṃ pākataṃ nāma. Taṃ pana tabbhavatassamadesiyamissavasena catubbidhaṃ hoti. Tattha sakkaṭato vaṇṇaññattamattena nibbattaṃ tabbhavaṃ nāma, taṃ mahindasindhavādi. Tassamaṃ hiriharakamalādi. Dese pasiddhaṃ desiyaṃ. Missaṃ nāma tabbhavādīhi sammissaṃ. Apabbhaṃso nāma gopālakādīnaṃ vācā, so ca tabbhavādīhi catubbidho, nāgaraupanāgaravuddhabhedena tividho ca hoti. Pisācānaṃ vacanaṃ pesācikaṃ. Tehi sakkaṭādīhi sammissaṃ missaṃ nāma hoti. Idāni īdisappabhedavantabandhassa alaṅkārena sobhanattaṃ vattuṃ “taṃ tu”ccādimāha. Taṃ tu taṃ pana vuttappakāraṃ bandhasarīraṃ alaṅkārā pasādādisaddālaṅkārā, sabhāvavutyādiatthālaṅkārā ca vindanīyatarattanaṃ atisayapasādanīyattaṃ pāpenti. Nirantaraṃ bandho nibandhoti ca, na nibandho anibandhoti ca, atisayena vindanīyo vindanīyataro, tassa bhāvo vindanīyatarattananti ca viggaho.

9. Again, to explain the division of that very composition, he says, beginning with 'nibandho ca' (bound). Again, that very composition is classified (niruppate) or determined (nicchīyate) in two ways: 'bound' (nibandho), which is a continuous composition (nirantaraṃ katvā bandho) by way of its inseparability from the four (types) such as muttaka, etc., having the nature of great poetry (mahākabba) and so on; and 'unbound' (anibandho), which is a discontinuous composition (anirantaraṃ katvā bandho) by way of being merely muttaka, having the nature of great poetry and so on. Furthermore, that composition is fivefold by way of the distinctions of Sakkaṭa, Pākata, Apabbhaṃsa, Pesācika, and Missa languages. Due to the prominence of presentation, such dance as lāsya, etc., characterized by erotic sentiment, is to be seen; while other poetry (kabba) is to be heard—thus, it is twofold by distinction of application (vaḷañjanabhedato). All of this is not taken up here due to its lack of purpose (payojanābhāvato). Therein, Sakkaṭa is called the language of the gods. Then, Pākata is that which differs by some letters. That, however, is fourfold by the divisions of tabbhava (derived), tassama (same as), desīya (regional), and missa (mixed). Therein, tabbhava is what arises merely by the transformation of letters from Sakkaṭa; that is Mahinda, Sindhu, etc. Tassama is like Hiri, Hara, Kamala, etc. Desīya is what is well-known in a region. Missa is what is blended with tabbhava and so on. Apabbhaṃsa is the speech of cowherds, etc.; and it too is fourfold by tabbhava and so on, and threefold by the distinctions of Nāgara, Upanāgara, and Vuddha. The speech of Pisācas (demons) is Pesācika. Missa is what is mixed with Sakkaṭa and so on. Now, to speak of the beauty of such a composition, possessing various distinctions, when adorned with ornaments, he says, beginning with 'taṃ tu' (but that). That very body of composition, as described, the ornaments—sound-ornaments like 'pasāda' (clarity) and so on, and meaning-ornaments like 'sabhāvavutti' (natural expression) and so on—lead it to a state of greater delight (vindanīyatarattanaṃ), a state of extreme pleasurableness (atisayapasādanīyattaṃ). The analysis (viggaho) is: 'continuous composition' (nirantaraṃ bandho) is 'bound' (nibandho); 'not bound' (na nibandho) is 'unbound' (anibandho); 'exceedingly delightful' (atisayena vindanīyo) is 'more delightful' (vindanīyataro); and 'the state of being more delightful' (tassa bhāvo) is 'vindanīyatarattanaṃ'.

10.

10.

Anavajjaṃ mukhambhoja-manavajjā ca bhāratī;

Alaṅkatāva sobhante, kiṃ nu’te niralaṅkatā?

The faultless lotus-face and faultless speech, when adorned, indeed shine; what then of them unadorned?

10. Tameva samattheti “anavajja” miccādinā. Anavajjaṃ aññamaññānurūpādhikatanettakaṇṇādiavayavena piḷakatilakakāḷakādyanāhatāya ca sundarabhāvato agarahitaṃ mukhambhojaṃ vadanāravindañca tathā anavajjā padādidosānabhibhūtāya sundarabhāvena agarahitā bhāratī ca vāṇī upacārato tappaṭipādanīyo attho cāti ete alaṅkatāva [M 0.0034] mukhaṃ tilakatāḍaṅkādinālaṅkārena, saddatthā saddālaṅkāraatthālaṅkārehi pasādhitā sajjitā eva, niralaṅkatā tathā apasādhitā asajjitā sobhante kiṃ nu, na sobhantevāti vitakkemīti attho. Nuiti vitakke.

10. He establishes that very meaning by 'anavajja' (faultless) and so on. A faultless lotus-face (mukhambhoja), that is, a lotus-like face (vadanāravinda), which is unblameworthy (agarahitaṃ) due to its beauty (sundarabhāvato) from having features like eyes, ears, etc., that are mutually suitable and prominent, and from being untouched by boils, moles, dark spots, etc. And similarly, faultless speech (bhāratī), that is, 'vāṇī', which is unblameworthy (agarahitā) due to its beauty (sundarabhāvena) from not being overcome by faults of words (pada) and so on, and by extension, the meaning conveyed by it (tappaṭipādanīyo attho). These, when adorned—the face with ornaments like tilaka and earrings, etc., and the words and meanings (saddatthā) embellished (pasādhitā) and decorated (sajjitā) with sound-ornaments and meaning-ornaments—do they shine (sobhante kiṃ nu) when unadorned (niralaṅkatā), that is, unembellished (apasādhitā) and undecorated (asajjitā) in that way? The meaning is: 'Surely, they do not shine' (na sobhanteva), thus I ponder (vitakkemīti). 'Nu' (nu iti) means 'in pondering' (vitakke).

10. Tameva “anavajja” miccādinā samattheti. Vaṇṇasaṇṭhānādiavayavasampattiyā ca piḷakatilakakāḷakādidosarahitattā ca aninditaṃ mukhambhojañca anavajjā padadosavākyadosaatthadosehi amissattā agarahitā bhāratī vāṇī ca abhedopacārena tappaṭipādanīyattho cāti ime alaṅkatāva kuṇḍalatilakādiābharaṇehi ca saddālaṅkāraatthālaṅkārehi ca sajjitā eva, niralaṅkatā tehi avibhūsitā sobhante kiṃ nu, na sobhanteti maññe. Natthi avajjamassāti ca, mukhameva ambhojamiti ca viggaho. Kimiti paṭisedhe, nuiti vitakketi.

10. He confirms that very meaning with 'blameless' and so on. A lotus-face, unreproached for the perfection of its features such as form and complexion, and being free from faults such as freckles, moles, and dark spots; and blameless speech, unmixed with faults in word, sentence, or meaning; and, by non-differentiated metaphorical usage, the meaning to be conveyed by it—these are indeed already adorned with ornaments such as earrings and tilaka, and embellished with verbal and meaningful ornaments. Would they shine if unadorned, unembellished by them? I think not. The analysis is 'that which has no fault' and 'the face is indeed a lotus'. 'Kim' is in the sense of negation, 'nu' is in the sense of deliberation.

11.

11.

Vinā gurūpadesaṃ taṃ, bālo’laṅkattumicchati;

Sampāpuṇe na viññūhi, hassabhāvaṃ kathaṃ nu so?

Without a teacher's instruction, a fool wishes to adorn it. How indeed would he not attain a state of ridicule from the wise?

11. Alaṅkaraṇañca tesaṃ vinā gurūpadesena karonto vinā pahāsaṃ nāparaṃ visesamadhigacchatīti dassetuṃ silesālaṅkāramāha “vinā”tiādi. Gurūnaṃ pasādhanopāyopadesakānaṃ, alaṅkārakāraṇopāyopadesakānaṃ vā upadesaṃ “ettha evaṃ kate sobheyyā”ti upadisanaṃ vinā pariccajja mukhassa, bandhassa ca alaṅkaraṇānabhiññatāya bālo aññāṇako yo koci puggalo taṃ mukhaṃ, bandhaṃ vā alaṅkattuṃ anurūpavasena sajjetuṃ icchati adhippeti, so tādiso aññāṇapuggalo viññūhi tabbidūhi paṇḍitajanehi hassabhāvaṃ avahāsaṃ kathaṃ kena [M 0.0035] pakārena na sampāpuṇeyya. “Kimidaṃ aññāṇapurisena kariyatī”ti hasantevāti adhippāyo. Nuiti vitakke.

11. To show that one who adorns them without a teacher's instruction achieves no other distinction beyond ridicule, he states the figure of speech of paronomasia (silesa), beginning with 'Without...'. Disregarding the instruction of teachers—those who teach the means of adornment or the methods of creating embellishments, instructing, 'If done thus in this case, it would be beautiful'—any foolish, ignorant person who, due to inexperience in adorning the face or the composition, wishes and intends to adorn that face or composition appropriately, how, in what way, would such an ignorant person not attain a state of ridicule, of derision, from the wise, from those who know that, from learned people? The intention is that they will indeed laugh, saying, 'What is this being done by an ignorant person?' 'Nu' is in the sense of deliberation.

11. Idāni padādidosarahitabandhasarīrassa alaṅkārehi bhūsanamapi gurūpadesasahitameva seṭṭhanti dassetuṃ “vinā gurūpadesa” miccādisilesālaṅkāramāha. Bālo mukhādisarīrālaṅkāre, bandhālaṅkāre vā asamattho yo koci gurūpadesaṃ vinā sarīrālaṅkārakaraṇassa, bandhālaṅkārakaraṇassa vā anurūpopadesamantarena taṃ sarīraṃ, bandhaṃ vā alaṅkattuṃ tilakatāḍaṅkādīhi, saddālaṅkāraatthālaṅkārehi vā sajjetuṃ icchati ce, so viññūhi tadubhayaññūhi hassabhāvaṃ avahasitabbataṃ kathaṃ na sampāpuṇe, pāpuṇātyeva, tasmā gurūhi sādarato uggaṇhitvā kattabbanti bhāvo.

11. Now, to show that even the adornment with ornaments of a body of composition free from faults of words and so on is best only when accompanied by a teacher's instruction, he states the figure of speech of paronomasia (silesa), beginning with 'Without a teacher's instruction...'. If any fool, incapable of adorning the body (such as the face) or of adorning a composition, desires, without a teacher's instruction—that is, without appropriate instruction for adorning the body or adorning a composition—to adorn that body or composition with tilaka, earrings, and so on, or to embellish it with verbal and meaningful ornaments, how would he not attain a state of ridicule, of being laughed at, from the wise, from those who know both? He would indeed attain it. Therefore, the meaning is that one should learn respectfully from teachers and then act.

12.

12.

Ganthopi kavivācāna-malaṅkārappakāsako;

Yāti tabbacanīyattaṃ, tabbohārūpacārato.

Even a composition, which reveals the adornment of a poet's words, attains the state of being expressible by that term, due to the figurative usage of that term.

12. Nanu saddagammā, atthagammā ca alaṅkārāti gantho kathanti āha “ganthopī”tiādi. Kavivācānaṃ kavippayogānaṃ samudāyarūpānaṃ, paṭipādanīyatāya tabbacanīyānañca atthānaṃ alaṅkārappakāsako alaṅkārānaṃ yathāvuttānaṃ vibhāvito ganthopi kiriyākappasaṅkhātaṃ satthampi tabbacanīyattaṃ tena alaṅkārasaddena vāccataṃ yāti upagacchati. Kinti āha “tabbohārūpacārato”ti. Tassa katavohārassa alaṅkārasaddassa, tasmiṃ vā maṇḍanavisese pavattassa alaṅkāravohārassa upacaraṇaṃ soyamityabhedena parikappanaṃ upacāro. Kasmā? Paṭipādanīyapaṭipādakānaṃ abhedavasena kāraṇe kārīyassa upacariyatoti adhippāyo.

12. Since ornaments are understood through sound and through meaning, how is a composition an ornament? To this, he says, 'Even a composition,' etc. A composition, which reveals the ornaments of poets' words—being the aggregate of poetic expressions—and also of meanings that are to be conveyed and are expressible by those words, and which manifests the aforementioned ornaments, even a treatise called 'kiriyākappa', attains the state of being expressible by that term, that is, the state of being denoted by the word 'ornament'. How so? He says, 'due to the figurative usage of that term'. The figurative usage (upacāra) is the imputation of non-difference, thinking 'this is that', regarding the established usage of that term 'ornament', or regarding the usage 'ornament' that occurs in a particular embellishment. Why? The intention is that due to the non-difference between what is to be conveyed and what conveys, the effect is figuratively applied to the cause.

12. Idāni [M 0.0036] saddālaṅkāraatthālaṅkāragantho kathamalaṅkāroti āha “gantho”ccādi. Kavivācānaṃ kavīhi vuttavākyasaṅkhātānaṃ, upacārato tappaṭipādanīyaatthasaṅkhātānañca kavippayogānaṃ alaṅkārappakāsako saddatthālaṅkārappakāsako ganthoapi kiriyākappasaṅkhātaṃ satthampi tabbohārūpacārato tassa alaṅkāroti katavohārassa alaṅkārasaddassa kāraṇe kārīyūpacārena tabbacanīyattaṃ tena alaṅkārasaddena vattabbataṃ yāti. Apisaddo alaṅkāramapekkhati. Alaṅkāre pakāseti, alaṅkārānaṃ vā pakāsakoti ca, tena vacanīyo, tassa bhāvoti ca viggaho. Ettha bhāvoti vāccavācakasambandho. Tassa saddādialaṅkārassa vohāroti ca, tabbohārassa alaṅkārasaddassa upacāroti ca vākyanti.

12. Now, as to how a composition on verbal and meaningful ornaments is itself an ornament, he says, 'Even a composition,' etc. A composition that reveals the verbal and meaningful ornaments of poets' words—that is, of statements made by poets, and figuratively, of poetic usages which express the intended meanings—even a treatise called 'kiriyākappa', attains the state of being expressible by that term, that is, the state of being denoted by the word 'ornament', by means of the figurative usage of that term, through the figurative attribution of the effect to the cause with respect to the established usage of the word 'ornament' as 'that is an ornament'. The particle 'api' refers to the ornament. The analysis is: 'it reveals ornaments' or 'it is a revealer of ornaments'; and 'it is to be spoken of by that', and 'the state of that'. Here, 'state' refers to the relationship between the denoted and the denoter. And 'the usage of that verbal and other ornament', and 'the figurative usage of the word 'ornament' for that usage'—this is the sentence construction.

13.

13.

Dvippakārā alaṅkārā, tattha saddatthabhedato;

Saddatthā bandhanāmāva, taṃsajjitatadāvali.

Ornaments are of two kinds, therein, by the distinction of sound and meaning. Sound and meaning are indeed what is named 'composition'; it is the sequence of them, adorned by them.

13. Idāni yathāvuttaalaṅkārānaṃ pabhedaṃ, tappasaṅkañca taṃbandhasarīrañca heṭṭhā vuttampi ekato sambandhetvā dassetuṃ “dvippakārā”di āraddhaṃ. Tattha tasmiṃ kiriyākappasaṅkhāte ganthe, tasmiṃ vā bandhālaṅkārādhikāre alaṅkārā yathāvuttā dvippakārā honti. Kathaṃ? Saddabhedato, atthabhedato ca, saddālaṅkārā atthālaṅkārāti alaṅkārā dvippakārā hontīti attho. Yesaṃ bhedena te dvippakārā, te saddā, atthā ca. “Bandho” iti vuttaṃ nāmaṃ yassā āvaliyā sā bandhanāmā eva. Taṃsajjitatadāvali tehi alaṅkārehi sajjitā pakāsitā taṃsajjitā, tesaṃ saddatthānaṃ āvali samudāyā, mahāvākyaṃ, antaravākyaṃ vā. Paripuṇṇo bandho mahāvākyaṃ, muttakādayovayavā antaravākyāni, taṃsajjitatadāvalikaṃ pasiddhabhāvena anuvaditvā appasiddhā saddatthā vidhīyante.

13. Now, to show the classification of the aforementioned ornaments, along with their context and that body of composition, which was previously mentioned, connecting them together, it begins with 'of two kinds'. Therein, in that treatise called 'kiriyākappa', or in that section on compositional ornaments, the aforementioned ornaments are of two kinds. How? By the distinction of sound and meaning; that is, ornaments of sound and ornaments of meaning—thus, ornaments are of two kinds, this is the meaning. Those by whose distinction they are of two kinds are sound and meaning. That sequence to which the name 'composition' is given is indeed what is named 'composition'. 'Taṃsajjitatadāvali' means: adorned by those ornaments, made manifest by them, and the sequence (āvali) of those sounds and meanings, which is a collection, a major sentence, or a minor sentence. A complete composition is a major sentence; its parts, such as individual verses, are minor sentences. Having restated 'taṃsajjitatadāvalikaṃ' as something well-known, the less prominent sound and meaning are prescribed.

13. Idāni [M 0.0037] yathāvuttaalaṅkārānaṃ avuttabhedañca tadādhārādhikataṃ yathāvuttabandhasarīrañca ekato dassetuṃ “dvippakāre”ccādimāha. Tattha tasmiṃ kiriyākappasaṅkhāte alaṅkāraganthe, no ce, alaṅkārādhikāre vā alaṅkārā vakkhamānālaṅkārā saddatthabhedato saddālaṅkāraatthālaṅkārabhedena dvippakārā honti, yesaṃ bhedena alaṅkārā bhinnā, te saddatthā bandhanāmāva. Taṃsajjitatadāvali tehi saddatthālaṅkārehi alaṅkatā, tesaṃ saddatthānaṃ mahākabbādisamudāyarūpā paṭipāṭibandhoti vuttaṃ hoti. “Bandho” iti nāmaṃ yasseti ca, tehi saddatthālaṅkārehi sajjitāti ca, tesaṃ saddatthānaṃ āvalīti ca samāso.

13. Now, to show the unstated divisions of the aforementioned ornaments, along with their underlying subject matter and the structure of composition as previously mentioned, connecting them together, he says, 'of two kinds,' etc. Therein, in that treatise on ornaments called 'kiriyākappa', or if not, in the section on ornaments, the ornaments to be spoken of are of two kinds by the distinction of sound and meaning, that is, by the division of verbal ornaments and meaningful ornaments. Those sounds and meanings, by whose distinction the ornaments are differentiated, are indeed what is named 'composition'. It is said that 'taṃsajjitatadāvali' means 'adorned by those verbal and meaningful ornaments', and is 'the structured arrangement of those sounds and meanings, in the form of a collection like a great poem'. And the compound analysis is: 'that to which the name "composition" is given', and 'adorned by those verbal and meaningful ornaments', and 'the sequence of those sounds and meanings'.

14.

14.

Guṇālaṅkārasaṃyuttā, api dosalavaṅkitā;

Pasaṃsiyā na viññūhi, sā kaññā viya tādisī.

Though endowed with qualities and ornaments, if marked by even a trace of fault, such a composition is not to be praised by the wise, just like such a maiden.

14. Evaṃ guṇena alaṅkārena sajjitāpi sā saddatthāvali appakenapi dosena saṃyuttā satī asamphusitabbāva viññūhi siyāti dassetumāha “guṇa” iccādi. Saddālaṅkārākhyena guṇena, atthālaṅkārena ca saṃyuttāpi visesena sajjitāpi saddatthāvali dosalavena dosalesenāpi aṅkitā abhilañchitā satī viññūhi guṇadosavibhāgavidūhi paṇḍitapurisehi na pasaṃsiyā neva pasaṃsitabbā. Kāviyāti āha “kaññā viyatādisī”ti. Yathā hi kaññā dasavassikā sannaddhayobbanābhimukhabhāvena jananayanamanovilubbhinīguṇena, ābharaṇavisesena cālaṅkatā kenaci kuṭṭhadosalesena aṅkitā viññūnaṃ asamphusanīyā siyā, pagevāparā, evameva saddatthāvalipi appakenapi saddarūpena, atthalakkhaṇena ca dosena kuṭṭhakappena vajjanīyā eva viññūnaṃ, pageva bahunāti vuttaṃ hoti.

14. Thus, to show that even if a sequence of words and meanings is adorned with qualities and ornaments, if it is associated with even a slight fault, it should be untouchable by the wise, he says, 'qualities,' etc. Even if that sequence of words and meanings is endowed with the quality called verbal ornament and with the ornament of meaning, and is especially adorned, if it is marked or tainted by even a trace of a fault, by even a slight blemish, it is not to be praised, it is indeed not praiseworthy, by the wise, by learned men who know the distinction between qualities and faults. As an illustration, he says, 'like a maiden,' etc. For just as a ten-year-old maiden, on the verge of burgeoning youth, captivating the eyes and minds of people with her qualities, and adorned with exquisite ornaments, if marked by even a slight blemish like a trace of leprosy, would be untouchable to the wise—how much more so another!—so too, a sequence of words and meanings, even with a slight fault in the form of the word or the characteristic of the meaning, which is like leprosy, should indeed be avoided by the wise—how much more so if with a great one! This is what is said.

14. Evaṃ [M 0.0038] saddatthānaṃ guṇībhūtehi alaṅkārehi sajjitā saddatthāvali kenaci padādidosena abhilakkhitā ce, appasatthāti dassento “guṇālaṅkāri”ccādimāha. Guṇālaṅkārasaṃyuttā api saddālaṅkārasaṅkhātaguṇena, atthālaṅkārena ca visesena yuttāpi sā saddatthāvali dosalavaṅkitā padadosādinā aṇumattenapi dosena aṅkitā yuttā sahitā tādisī guṇālaṅkārasaṃyuttāpi dosalavaṅkitā kaññā viya dasavassikā yobbanappattā vanitāva viññūhi guṇadosaparikkhakehi na pasaṃsiyā na pasaṃsitabbā. Yathā hi dasavassikā itthī piyasabhāvasaṇṭhitā manuññehi guṇehi, sobhanānurūpagīveyyādiābharaṇavisesehi yuttāpi dissamānena kenaci setakuṭṭhalavena yuttā samānā guṇadosaparikkhakehi dassanīyā na hoti, evaṃ vuttappakārāpi bandhapaddhati kuṭṭhatulyena kenaci padādidosena yuttā viññūhi assādanīyāti adhippāyo. Dosānaṃ lavo, tena aṅkitāti ca, sā viya dissatīti tādīsīti ca viggaho.

14. Thus, showing that even if a composition of words and meanings is adorned with embellishments that have become its qualities, if it is marked by some fault in a word or the like, it is not praiseworthy, he says, 'guṇālaṅkāri,' etc. Even if that composition of words and meanings is connected with qualities and embellishments, and especially endowed with the quality called 'verbal embellishment' and with the embellishment of meaning, yet if it is marked by a trace of a fault—marked, connected, or associated with even a minute fault such as a fault in a word—such a composition, though connected with qualities and embellishments, being marked by a trace of a fault, is like a ten-year-old maiden who has reached youth, and is not to be praised, not praiseworthy, by the wise who examine qualities and faults. For just as a ten-year-old woman, of a naturally pleasing disposition, endowed with charming qualities, and adorned with beautiful and suitable ornaments such as necklaces, if she is associated with even a visible trace of white leprosy, is not pleasing to those who examine qualities and faults, so too, a composition of the aforementioned kind, if associated with some fault in a word or the like, which is similar to leprosy, is not to be savored by the wise—this is the intention. The analysis is: 'a trace of faults' (dosalava), and 'marked by that' (aṅkitā); and 'appearing like her' (sā viya dissati), thus 'such' (tādīsī).

15.

15.

Tena dosanirāsova, mahussāhena sādhiyo;

Niddosā sabbathā sā’yaṃ, saguṇā na bhaveyya kiṃ.

Therefore, the removal of faults should indeed be accomplished with great effort; this, being entirely faultless, how could it not be endowed with qualities?

15. Yato evaṃ, tena tasmā kāraṇā mahussāhena mahatā vāyāmena dosānaṃ padadosādīnamanatthanimittānaṃ nirāsova satthadiṭṭhiyā satthappabhāvato pariccāgoyeva sādhiyo sādhetabbo, “viññūhī”ti seso. Evaṃ dosanirāse ko guṇo upalabbhatīti ce. Sabbathā sabbappakārena niddosā dosehi niggatā sāyaṃ saddatthāvali saguṇā saddālaṅkārasaṅkhātehi guṇehi sahitā na bhaveyya kiṃ, bhavatyeva, guṇarahitaṃ taṃalaṅkatamanupādeyyaṃ siyāti adhippāyo.

15. Since this is so, therefore, for that reason, with great enthusiasm and mighty effort, the very abandonment of faults—such as faults of words and other causes of disadvantage—should be accomplished according to the view of the treatises and by the power of the treatises; 'by the wise' is the remainder. If it is asked, 'What quality is obtained when faults are thus removed?'—this sequence of words and meanings, being in every way entirely faultless, free from faults, would it not be endowed with qualities, possessed of the qualities called 'verbal embellishments'? Indeed, it would. The intention is that what is adorned but devoid of quality would be unacceptable.

15. Tena [M 0.0039] yato dosayuttā viññūhi anupādeyyā, tasmā mahussāhena adhikavāyāmena dosanirāsova padadosādīnaṃ nirākaraṇameva sādhiyo anekasatthavisayāya paññāya viññūhi sādhetabbo, evaṃ sati sabbathā sabbākārena niddosā dosarahitā sā ayaṃ saddatthāvali saguṇā saddālaṅkārasaṅkhātehi guṇehi yuttā na bhaveyya kiṃ, guṇayuttā bhaveyyāti adhippāyo. Dosānaṃ nirāsoti ca, natthi dosā etissā, niggatā dosehi vāti ca, saha guṇehi vattamānāti ca viggaho.

15. Since that which is associated with faults is unacceptable to the wise, therefore, with great enthusiasm and increased effort, the very removal of faults—that is, the elimination of faults in words and so on—must be accomplished by the wise through wisdom concerning the subject matter of many treatises. This being so, when this sequence of words and meanings is in every way and in all aspects faultless, devoid of faults, would it not be endowed with qualities, that is, possessed of the qualities known as verbal embellishments? It would indeed be endowed with qualities—this is the intention. The analysis is: 'the removal of faults' (dosanirāso); 'there are no faults in this' or 'she has departed from faults' (niddosā); and 'existing together with qualities' (saguṇā).

16.

16.

Sā’laṅkāraviyuttāpi, guṇayuttā manoharā;

Niddosā dosarahitā, guṇayuttā vadhū viya.

Though devoid of embellishments, being endowed with qualities, she is captivating; faultless, free from blemish, like a bride endowed with qualities.

16. Kiṃkāraṇamevaṃbhūto dosapariccāgena guṇādānena bandhoti āha “sā’laṅkāre”ccādi. Sā saddatthāvali alaṅkārehi viyuttāpi satī niddosā sabbappakārena dosehi niggatā guṇehi saddālaṅkārasaṅkhātehi saṃyuttā janānamānandasandohābhisandanekahetutāya mano harati attano santikamākaḍḍhatīti manoharā hotīti. Tatthodāharaṇamāha “dosarahitā guṇayuttā vadhū viyā”ti. Yathā yena kenacipi dosena virahitā vadhū manāpacāritādīhi guṇavisesehi saṃyuttā satī kenaci ābharaṇena amaṇḍitā apasādhitāpi kinnāma madhurā kavīnaṃ pasādhanaṃ kinnāma manoharā hoti, evamayaṃ saddatthāvalipi manoharā hotīti attho.

16. Why is a composition of this nature, which involves abandoning faults and adopting qualities, so? He says, explaining the verse 'Though devoid of embellishments...,' etc. That sequence of words and meanings, even if devoid of embellishments, being faultless—completely free from all kinds of faults—and united with qualities known as verbal embellishments, captivates the mind, meaning it draws it to itself, by being the sole cause of an outpouring of abundant joy for people; thus it is 'captivating' (manoharā). Therein, he gives an example: 'like a bride free from faults and endowed with qualities.' Just as a bride, free from any fault whatsoever and endowed with special qualities such as pleasing conduct, even if not adorned or embellished with any ornament, is indeed sweet, an ornament for poets, and indeed captivating, so too this sequence of words and meanings is captivating—this is the meaning.

16. Idāni dosapariccāgena guṇādāne payojanaṃ dasseti “sā’laṅkāraviyutte”ccādinā. Sā saddatthāvali alaṅkārehi viyuttā satīpi niddosā sabbappakārena dosarahitā guṇayuttā tatoyeva guṇībhūtā saddālaṅkārena yuttā dosarahitā dubbaṇṇadussaṇṭhānādidosehi [M 0.0040] pariccattā guṇayuttā hadayaṅgamaguṇayuttā vadhū viya aṅganā viya manoharā sādhujane ārādheti.

16. Now, he shows the purpose of abandoning faults and acquiring qualities with the phrase 'though devoid of embellishments,' etc. That sequence of words and meanings, even while being devoid of embellishments, being faultless—in every way free from faults, endowed with qualities, and for that very reason having become possessed of quality, endowed with verbal embellishment, free from faults, rid of blemishes such as poor complexion and bad form, endowed with qualities, endowed with heart-pleasing qualities—like a bride, like a woman, is captivating and pleases good people.

17.

17.

Pade vākye tadatthe ca, dosā ye vividhā matā;

Sodāharaṇametesaṃ, lakkhaṇaṃ kathayāmya’haṃ.

The various faults that are considered to exist in the word, in the sentence, and in their meaning—I shall explain the characteristics of these along with examples.

17. Yato evaṃ guṇālaṅkārasaṃyuttāyapi dosalavaṅkitāya viññūnamanādaraṇīyatā, alaṅkāraviyuttāpi dosābhāvena guṇayuttāya manoharatā, evamanatthāvahassāpi dosassa pariharitabbatā satthadiṭṭhiyā, tasmā te dose dassetuṃ paṭijānāti “pade”tiādinā. Tesaṃ padānaṃ vākyānaṃ attho tadattho, tasmiṃ. Udāharīyati lakkhyabhāvenāti udāharaṇaṃ, saha udāharaṇehīti sodāharaṇaṃ. Lakkhiyati lakkhiyamanenāti lakkhaṇaṃ.

17. Since, even when endowed with qualities and embellishments, if marked by a trace of a fault, a work is not respected by the wise; and even without embellishments, by being free from faults and endowed with qualities, it is captivating; and since a fault, even one that brings disadvantage, must be avoided according to the view of the treatises—therefore, he undertakes to show those faults with 'in the word,' etc. The analysis of the terms is as follows: 'tadarthe' means 'in their meaning,' that is, the meaning of those words and sentences. An 'udāharaṇa' (example) is so called because 'it is cited as that which is to be defined.' 'Sodāharaṇaṃ' means 'with examples.' A 'lakkhaṇa' (characteristic, definition) is so called because 'that which is to be defined is defined by this.'

17. Evaṃ alaṅkārayuttāpi appakena dosena yuttabandhassa anupādeyyattā, alaṅkāraalaṅkaraṇe asatipi dosarahite viññūhi upādeyyattā ca mukhyassa dosaparihārassa avassaṃ kattabbattā idāni adhigatadose dassetuṃ paṭijānāti “pade vākye”ccādinā. Pade nāmādicatubbidhapade ca, vākye “syādyantatyādyantānaṃ cayo vākyaṃ sakārakakiriyā”ti vuttalakkhaṇe vākye ca, tadatthe ca tesaṃ padavākyānaṃ atthe ca vividhā anekappakārā ye dosā viññūhi dosabhāvena matā ñeyyā, etesaṃ padādidosānaṃ sodāharaṇaṃ udāharaṇasahitaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ ahaṃ kathayāmi. Ettha ca–

17. Thus, since a composition, even if endowed with embellishments, is unacceptable if it has even a minor fault, and since a faultless one is acceptable to the wise even when there is no adorning with embellishments, and since the avoidance of the principal faults must necessarily be done, he now makes a promise with 'in the word, in the sentence,' etc., in order to show the faults that are to be understood. 'In the word' means in the four kinds of words: noun, verb, preposition, and particle. 'In the sentence' means in a sentence with the characteristic defined as 'A sentence is a collection of words ending in nominal and verbal inflections, containing an agent and an action.' 'And in their meaning' means in the meaning of those words and sentences. The various and manifold faults which are considered by the wise to be faults are to be known. He says, 'I shall explain the characteristics of these faults of words, etc., with examples.' And in this regard:

“Padaṃ catubbidhaṃ vuttaṃ, nāmākhyātopasaggikaṃ;

Nipātakañca taññūhi, asso khalvābhidhāvatī”ti rūpabhiddhiṭīkāyaṃ nāmakaṇḍe.

A word is said to be of four kinds: noun, verb, prefix, and particle; this is known by the wise. For example: 'A horse indeed runs forth.'

Vuttaniyāmena padaṃ tāva daṭṭhabbaṃ. Udāharīyanti lakkhiyabhāvenāti udāharaṇānīti ca, saha udāharaṇenāti sodāharaṇanti [M 0.0041] ca, lakkhīyati lakkhiyamanenāti ca viggaho.

First, the word should be understood according to the stated rule. The analysis is: 'examples' are so called because they are cited as that which is to be defined; 'with an example' means together with an example; and 'definition' is that by which something is defined.

Padadosauddesa

Enumeration of Faults of the Word

18.

18.

Viruddhatthantarājhattha-kiliṭṭhāni virodhi ca;

Neyyaṃ visesanāpekkhaṃ, hīnatthakamanatthakaṃ.

Having a contradictory other meaning, superfluous meaning, being obscure, and contradictory; requiring inference, dependent on a qualifier, inferior in meaning, and meaningless.

Vākyadosauddesa

Enumeration of Faults of the Sentence

19.

19.

Dosā padāna, vākyāna-mekatthaṃ bhaggarītikaṃ;

Tathā byākiṇṇagāmmāni, yatihīnaṃ kamaccutaṃ;

Ativuttamapetatthaṃ, sabandhapharusaṃ tathā

Faults of words and sentences: redundancy, broken style; likewise, the disordered, the vulgar, that which is lacking proper pause, displaced in sequence, overstated, devoid of meaning, and also harsh in connection.

Vākyatthadosauddesa

Enumeration of Sentence-Meaning Faults

20.

20.

Apakkamo’cityahīnaṃ, bhaggarīti sasaṃsayaṃ;

Gāmmaṃ duṭṭhālaṅkatīti, dosā vākyatthanissitā.

Lack of sequence, lacking propriety, broken style, the ambiguous, the vulgar, and corrupted ornamentation—these are the faults dependent on sentence-meaning.

Padadosādiuddesavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Enumeration of Word-Faults, etc.

18-19-20. Idāni yathāpaṭiññāte dose uddisati “viruddhatthantara” iccādinā. Viruddhaṃ atthantaraṃ yassa taṃ viruddhatthantaraṃ. Kiṃ taṃ? Padaṃ. Evamuparipi yathāyogaṃ. Adhiko attho visesyassa yena taṃ adhyatthaṃ. Nīyati avutto hetu ettha ānīyatīti neyyaṃ. Dosā padānanti yehi dosehi padāni duṭṭhāni, te viruddhatthantaratādayo padānaṃ dosāti attho. Evamuparipi yathāyogaṃ. Vākyānaṃ dosāti sambandho. Bhaggā rīti kamo yasmiṃ taṃ bhaggarītikaṃ, vākyaṃ. Apakkamatādayo vākyatthadosā, vākyatthānaṃ dosato. Vākyaṃ duṭṭhaṃ siyāti vākyameva visesyate. Tena sabbattha napuṃsakaliṅgena niddeso.

Now, as promised, he enumerates the faults with 'contradictory meaning' and so on. That which has a contradictory other meaning is 'contradictory meaning.' What is that? A word. Likewise for the following, as is appropriate. That by which the meaning of the qualified is excessive is 'overmeaning.' The unstated reason is inferred here, hence it is called 'to be inferred.' 'Faults of words' means: those faults by which words are corrupted, such as 'contradictory meaning' and so on, are the faults of words. This is the meaning. Likewise for the following, as is appropriate. 'Faults of sentences' is the connection. That in which the style or sequence is broken is 'broken-style,' a sentence. 'Lack of sequence' and so on are faults of sentence-meaning, due to the faultiness of the sentence-meanings. A sentence may be corrupted—thus the sentence itself is specified. Therefore, everywhere the indication is given in the neuter gender.

18-19-20. Idāni kathetabbabhāvena paṭiññāte dose uddisanto “viruddha…pe… nissitā”ti āha. Kavīhi icchitatthato [M 0.0042] viruddho aññattho yassa padassāti taṃ viruddhatthantaraṃ nāma. Visesyassa adhikatthabhāvakaraṇato ajhatthaṃ nāma. Kavīhi icchitatthassāvīkaraṇe avisadattā kiliṭṭhaṃ nāma. Desakālakalādīnaṃ viruddhattā virodhi nāma. Aññamāharitvā vattabbato neyyaṃ nāma. Visesanaṃ patvāva sātthakabhāvappattito visesanāpekkhaṃ nāma. Visesyassa hīnatāpādanato hīnatthakaṃ nāma. Attharahitattā anatthakaṃ nāmāti ime aṭṭha padanissitattā padadosā nāma.

Now, in declaring the faults that are to be discussed, he says: 'Contradictory... dependent.' A word whose other meaning is contrary to what is intended by poets—that is called 'contradictory meaning' (viruddhatthantara). Because it causes the meaning of the qualified to be excessive, it is called 'overmeaning' (ajjhattha). Due to the lack of clarity in conveying the meaning intended by poets, it is called 'obscure' (kiliṭṭha). Because it contradicts place, time, art, and so on, it is called 'contradictory' (virodhi). Because it must be stated by bringing in something else, it is called 'requiring inference' (neyya). Because it achieves meaningfulness only after attaining a qualifier, it is called 'dependent on a qualifier' (visesanāpekkha). Because it causes the qualified to become inferior, it is called 'inferior in meaning' (hīnatthaka). Because it is devoid of meaning, it is called 'meaningless' (anatthaka). These eight are called 'faults dependent on words' (padadosā) because they are dependent on words.

Vuttatthasseva puna vacanato ekatthaṃ nāma. Bhinnakkamattā bhaggarītikaṃ nāma. Tathā sammohakāraṇattā byākiṇṇaṃ nāma. Visiṭṭhavacanavirahato gāmmaṃ nāma. Yatisampattivirahato yatihīnaṃ nāma. Padatthakkamato cutattā kamaccutaṃ nāma. Lokiyaṃ vohāramatikkamma vuttattā ativuttaṃ nāma. Samudāyatthato apagatattā apetatthaṃ nāma. Bandhapharusayuttattā bandhapharusaṃ nāma, tena sahitaṃ sabandhapharusanti ime nava vākyānaṃ tathā dosā nāma. Ettha tathāsaddo “dosā”ti padaṃ upasaṃharati.

The repetition of what has already been stated is called redundancy. Due to a broken sequence, it is called broken style. Likewise, because it causes confusion, it is called disordered. Lacking distinguished wording, it is called vulgar. Due to the absence of the accomplishment of caesura, it is called lacking caesura. Because of deviation from the sequence of word-meanings, it is called out of sequence. Because it is stated exceeding worldly convention, it is called overstated. Deviating from the collective meaning, it is called devoid of meaning. Being connected with harshness of composition, it is called harsh composition; that which is accompanied by that is 'with harsh composition.' These nine are likewise called faults of sentences. Here, the word 'tathā' brings in the term 'dosā'.

Apagatakkamattā apakkamaṃ nāma. Ucitabhāvassa parihīnattā ocityahīnaṃ nāma. Bhinnavibhattikkamattā bhaggarīti nāma. Saṃsayajananato sasaṃsayaṃ nāma. Duppatītikarattā gāmmaṃ nāma. Dūsitālaṅkārattā duṭṭhālaṅkati nāmātime cha vākyatthanissitattā vākyatthadosā nāma.

Due to the absence of proper sequence, it is called 'lack of sequence.' Due to the falling away from what is fitting, it is called 'lacking propriety.' Because of a broken sequence of grammatical cases, it is called 'broken style.' Since it generates doubt, it is called 'ambiguous.' Because it is difficult to accept, it is called 'vulgar.' Due to corrupted ornamentation, it is called 'corrupted ornamentation.' These six are called 'faults of sentence-meaning' because they are dependent on sentence-meaning.

Añño attho atthantaro. Viruddho atthantaro yassāti viggaho. Dosapakāsakapadampi dosato abyatirittattā doso nāma. Evaṃ santepi samāsena padassa gahitattā napuṃsakaṃ hoti. Esevanayo ito paresupi. Visesyassa adhiko attho yassa taṃ, kiliṭṭhaṃ viya kiliṭṭhaṃ. Yathā hi malaggahito ādāso attano kiliṭṭhattā [M 0.0043] mukhādīnaṃ pakāsane avisado hoti, evamadhippetatthappakāsane asamatthaṃ padaṃ kiliṭṭhaṃ nāma. Virodho assa atthīti virodhi. Nīyati avutto hetu etthāti neyyaṃ. Visesane apekkhā yassa taṃ. Hīno visesyassa attho yena taṃ. Natthi attho yassa tanti viggaho.

Another meaning is 'atthantara.' The analysis is: 'that which has a contradictory other meaning.' A term indicating a fault is also called a fault because it is not different from the fault. Even so, because the word is taken as a compound, it becomes neuter. This same method applies to the following as well. 'That which has an excessive meaning of the qualified.' 'Kiliṭṭha' (obscure) is like something defiled. For just as a mirror covered with dirt, due to its own defilement, is not clear in showing a face and so on, so too a word incapable of revealing the intended meaning is called 'defiled.' 'That which has opposition' is 'virodhi' (contradictory). 'That wherein an unstated reason is inferred' is 'neyyaṃ' (requiring inference). 'That which has dependence on a qualifier.' 'That by which the meaning of the qualified is deficient.' 'That which has no meaning'—such are the analyses.

Padadosānaṃ anaññattepi vikappanābhedato “padānaṃ dosā”ti vuttaṃ, yathā “silāputtakassa sarīra”nti. Vākyānaṃ dosāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Eko attho yassa taṃ. Bhaggārīti kamo yassa taṃ. Visuṃ visuṃ ākiṇṇaṃ byākiṇṇaṃ. Gāme bhavo gāmmo, abyattānaṃ vohāro. Tappakāsakapadampi upacārato gāmmaṃ nāma. Yati hīnā etthāti yatihīnaṃ. Kamato cutaṃ kamaccutaṃ. Atikkamma vuttaṃ ativuttaṃ. Atthato apetaṃ apetatthaṃ. Bandhe pharusaṃ pharusatā yattha taṃ. Apagato kamo yasmā taṃ. Ocityaṃ hīnaṃ yattha taṃ. Bhaggā rīti yattha taṃ. Saha saṃsayena vattatīti taṃ. Gāmmaṃ vuttanayameva. Duṭṭhā dūsitā alaṅkati alaṅkāro yattha taṃ. Vākyānaṃ attho, tannissitā vākyatthanissitāti viggaho. Ettha anatthakāpetatthadosadvayaṃ padavākyato bhinnaṃ, aññaṃ bhaggarītidosadvayaṃ, gāmmadvayaṃ, kamaccutaapakkamadvayañca vākyavākyatthato bhinnaṃ.

Although the faults are not other than the words themselves, it is said 'faults of words' due to a conceptual distinction, as in 'the body of the stone doll.' Here too, in 'faults of sentences,' this is the same method. 'That which has one meaning.' 'That which has a broken style or sequence.' 'Scattered separately.' 'Occurring in a village is gāmmo,' the speech of the uneducated; the word indicating that is also called gāmmaṃ by metaphor. 'That wherein the caesura is deficient.' 'Deviated from the sequence.' 'Said transgressively.' 'Departed from the meaning.' 'That wherein there is harshness in composition.' 'That from which the sequence has departed.' 'That wherein propriety is deficient.' 'That wherein the style is broken.' 'That which proceeds with doubt.' Gāmmaṃ is by the method already stated. 'That wherein the ornamentation is corrupted.' The analysis of vākyatthanissitā is: 'dependent on the meaning of sentences.' Herein, the pair of faults, anatthaka and apetattha, are distinguished between word and sentence. The other pairs—the two bhaggarīti faults, the two gāmma faults, and the kamaccuta-apakkama pair—are distinguished between sentence and sentence-meaning.

Padadosaniddesavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Exposition of Word-Faults

21.

21.

Viruddhatthantaraṃ tañhi, yassa’ññattho virujjhati;

Adhippete yathā megho, visado sukhaye janaṃ.

For that is of contradictory other meaning, of which another meaning conflicts with the intended; as in: 'the cloud, being clear (visado), gladdens the people.'

21. Athoddesakkamena padādidose udāharati “viruddhi” ccādinā. Hi yasmā kāraṇā, pasiddhiyaṃ vā hisaddo. Yassa padassa añño adhippetato aparo attho adhippete vattumicchite atthe virujjhatīti anuvaditvā tasmā [M 0.0044] taṃ “viruddhatthantara”nti vidhīyate. “Yathe”tyudāharati. Yathā idaṃ viruddhatthantaraṃ, tathā aññampi tādisaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Na tvidameveti yathāsaddassa attho. Megho visado sukhaye jananti. Visaṃ udakaṃ, taṃ dadātīti visado megho vārivaho janaṃ lokaṃ sukhaye sukhayatīti kavicchitattho. Visasaddo garaḷassa ca vācako siyāti garaḷado megho mārayati, na pana sukhayatīti “visado”ti visesanapadassa viruddhatā.

21. Now, following the order of the enumeration, he illustrates the faults of words and so on, beginning with 'contradiction.' The word 'hi' means 'for which reason,' or it is used in the sense of 'indeed.' Having repeated the meaning that 'when another meaning of a word, different from the intended, conflicts with the intended meaning that one wishes to express,' therefore it is defined as 'contradictory other meaning.' He gives an example with 'yathā' (as). Just as this is a contradictory other meaning, so too should other similar instances be understood. The meaning of the word 'yathā' is not that it is only this one. 'The cloud, being clear (visado), gladdens people.' 'Visa' means water; thus, 'visado' means 'giving water,' so the rain-bearing cloud gladdens the people—this is the poet's intended meaning. However, since the word 'visa' can also denote poison, a 'poison-giving' cloud would kill, not gladden. Thus, the qualifying word 'visado' has a contradictory nature.

21. Idāni uddiṭṭhānukkamena viruddhatthantarādīnaṃ salakkhaṇalakkhiyaṃ dassento “viruddhi”ccādimāha. Yassa padassa aññattho kavicchitatthato añño attho adhippete icchitatthe hi yasmā virujjhati, tasmā taṃ padaṃ viruddhatthantaraṃ nāma. Pasiddhiyaṃ vā hisaddo. Tathā hesa appasiddhaṃ viruddhatthantaraṃ “yassa aññattho adhippete virujjhatī”ti pakāsetvā tasmiṃ pakāsitatthavisaye vattati. “Taṃ hī”ti yojitattā “yassa aññattho adhippete virujjhatī”ti lakkhaṇaṃ pasiddhabhāvena anuvaditvā taṃ viruddhatthantaranti anuvaditabbaappasiddhaviruddhatthantaraṃ vidhīyate, yathā “yo kuṇḍalī, so devadatto”ti. Upari pasiddhānuvādena appasiddhavidhānameva daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Yathā…pe… jana”nti udāharaṇaṃ lakkhiyaṃ dasseti. Yathā “megho visado”ccādi viruddhatthantarassa udāharaṇaṃ, evamīdisamaññampi imassudāharaṇaṃ, na kevalaṃ “megho”ccādimeva bhavatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Yathāsaddo cettha ivasaddapariyāyatthepi udāharaṇattho daṭṭhabbo, uparipyevaṃ. Megho ambudharo visado visasaṅkhātaṃ jalaṃ dadanto janaṃ sukhaye sukhayatīti kavīhi adhippetattho. Ettha visasaddassa garaḷasaṅkhātasappavisavācakattā, “visaṃ dadātīti visado”ti ettha visassa udakavisānaṃ sādhāraṇattā visadāyako megho nāsetiyeva, na sukhayatīti kavinā [M 0.0045] adhippetassa sukhakāraṇassa meghavisesanavisasaddassa viruddhaaññatthatāti visapadaṃ viruddhatthantaradosena duṭṭhanti.

21. Now, following the order outlined, he states 'contradictory' and so on, showing the characteristic and that which is characterized for a contradictory other meaning and so forth. For, since another meaning of a word, different from the poet's intended meaning, conflicts with the intended meaning, therefore that word is called 'having a contradictory other meaning.' Or the word 'hi' is used in the sense of being well-known. Similarly, this unestablished contradictory other meaning, having been explained as 'that whose other meaning conflicts with the intended,' functions in the sphere of the meaning thus explained.
