Since it is connected with 'taṃ hi' (that indeed), having restated the definition 'that whose other meaning conflicts with the intended' as something well-known, that unestablished contradictory other meaning which is to be restated is established, as in 'He who wears earrings is Devadatta.' Hereafter, the establishment of the unestablished by restating the established should be understood. The example 'yathā…pe… jana' illustrates that which is characterized. It is said that just as 'the cloud is visado' and so on is an example of a contradictory other meaning, so too are other similar instances examples of this, not merely 'the cloud' and so on. Here, the word 'yathā' should be understood as an example, and also in a sense synonymous with the word 'iva' (like). So too hereafter. The cloud, the water-bearer, being 'visado,' giving water (visa), gladdens people—this is the meaning intended by the poets. Here, because the word 'visa' can denote poison, specifically snake venom, and because 'visa' in 'visaṃ dadātīti visado' (he who gives visa, thus 'visado') is common to both water and poison, a cloud that gives poison would destroy, not gladden. Thus, because the word 'visa,' a qualifier of the cloud intended by the poet as a cause of happiness, has a contradictory other meaning, the word 'visa' is flawed by the fault of having a contradictory other meaning.

22.

22.

Visesyamadhikaṃ yenā’-

Dhyatthametaṃ bhave yathā;

Obhāsitāsesadiso,

Khajjoto’yaṃ virājate.

By which the substantive is excessive, this becomes 'excessive meaning'; as in: 'Illuminating all directions, this firefly shines.'

22. Yena padena visesyaṃ visesitabbaṃ aparaṃ padaṃ atthavasena adhikaṃ bhavatītyanuvaditvā etaṃ ajhatthaṃ bhaveti vidhīyate. “Yathe”tyudāharati “obhāsite”ccādi. Evamuparipi suviññeyyaṃ. Obhāsitā dīpitā asesā nikhilā disāyena soyaṃ khajjoto virājate dippati. Ettha khajjotassākhiladisābhāgāvabhāsanamativuttīti adhikatthaṃ.

22. Having restated that 'by which word the substantive to be qualified becomes excessive in meaning,' it is established that 'this is adhyattha.' He gives an example with 'yathā' (as in), 'obhāsita' and so on. Similarly, this should be easily understood in the following cases as well. 'He by whom all, entire directions are illuminated, lit up'—that this firefly shines, gleams. Here, the firefly's illumination of all directions is an exaggeration (ativutti); hence, it is an excessive meaning (adhikatthaṃ).

22. Yena visesanapadena visesyaṃ visesitabbaṃ padaṃ atthavasena adhikaṃ hoti, etaṃ yathāvuttalakkhaṇopetaṃ padaṃ ajhatthaṃ bhave ajhatthaṃ nāma padadoso bhave. Yathā tassudāharaṇamevaṃ. Obhāsitāsesadiso jotitasabbadiso ayaṃ khajjoto ayaṃ jotiriṅgaṇo virājate dippati. Ettha visesyassa khajjotassa sakaladisobhāsanassa ajhatthattā atyuttattā (ka.) “obhāsitāsesadiso”ti visesanapadaṃ ajhatthapadadoso nāma. Obhāsitā asesadisā yenāti viggaho.

22. By which qualifying word the substantive, the word to be qualified, becomes excessive in meaning, that word, endowed with the aforesaid characteristic, becomes a word-fault called 'excessive meaning' (adhyattha). Its example is as follows: 'Illuminating all directions,' 'illuminating all directions'—this firefly, this glow-worm, shines, gleams. Here, because the illumination of all directions by the substantive, the firefly, is excessive, the qualifying word 'illuminating all directions' is called the word-fault of 'excessive meaning.' The analysis is: 'By which all directions are illuminated' (Obhāsitā asesadisā yena).

23.

23.

Yassa’tthāvagamo dukkho,

Pakatyādivibhāgato;

Kiliṭṭhaṃ taṃ yathā tāya,

So’yamāliṅgyate piyā.

That whose understanding of meaning is difficult,

Due to the analysis of root and so forth,

is 'obscure' (kiliṭṭha); as in: 'By that beloved, he is embraced.'

23. Pakatyādivibhāgatoti [M 0.0046] paccayā paṭhamaṃ karīyatīti pakati. Ādisaddena paccayādīnaṃ pariggaho. Pakatyādīnaṃvibhāgato vibhajanato, “ayaṃ pakati, ayaṃ paccayo, ayamādeso”tiādinā pakatipaccayavibhāgakappanatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Pīṇetīti pī, tāya piyā vallabhāya soyaṃ sāmī āliṅgyate silissate. Ettha “piyā”ti kiliṭṭhaṃ.

23. Regarding 'due to the analysis of root and so forth': 'pakati' (root) is so called because it is made before the suffix. By the word 'and so forth,' suffixes and the like are included. 'By the division of the root and so forth' means by the analysis; it is said to be by the determination of the division of root and suffix, such as 'this is the root, this is the suffix, this is the substitute,' and so on. The root 'pī' is from the verb 'pīṇeti' (to gladden); by that beloved (piyā), cherished one, this husband is embraced, is clung to. Here, 'piyā' is obscure.

23. Yassa padassa atthāvagamo atthāvabodho pakatyādivibhāgato “ayaṃ pakati, ayaṃ paccayo, ayamādeso”tiādinā pakatyādīnaṃ vibhajanajānanena, “pakatyādi nāma ki”nti gavesanato vā dukkho, taṃ kiliṭṭhaṃ nāma. Yathā tassudāharaṇamevaṃ. Tāya piyā vanitāya so ayaṃ vallabho āliṅgyate silissate. Paccayā paṭhamaṃ karīyatīti pakati. Sā ādi yesaṃ paccayānaṃ, tesaṃ vibhāgoti vākyaṃ. Pīṇetīti pī, nārī. Tāya piyā ettha piyāsaṅkhātāya vallabhāya kathane pīsaddassa avisadattā “piyā”ti padaṃ kiliṭṭhaṃ.

23. A word whose understanding of meaning, whose comprehension, is difficult due to the knowledge of the analysis of root and so forth—such as 'this is the root, this is the suffix, this is the substitute'—or due to investigating 'what is meant by root, etc.,' that is called 'obscure' (kiliṭṭha). Its example is as follows: By that beloved woman, this lover is embraced, is clung to. 'Pakati' (root) is that which is made before the suffix. The phrase means: 'the division of those suffixes of which it is the beginning.' From 'pīṇeti' (to gladden) comes 'pī,' meaning 'woman.' Here, in the expression 'tāya piyā' (by that beloved), which refers to the cherished one, because the word 'pī' is unclear, the word 'piyā' is obscure.

24.

24.

Yaṃ kiliṭṭhapadaṃ mandā-bhidheyyaṃ yamakādikaṃ;

Kiliṭṭhapadadoseva, tampi anto karīyati.

Whatever yamaka and so forth is an obscure word and has a meager meaning, that too is included within the fault of obscure words.

24. Idāni yamakādikamanadhippetampi kiliṭṭheyeva antogadhaṃ dassetumāha “ya”ntiādi. Tattha yanti aniyamavacanaṃ, tassa niyamavacanaṃ yamakādikanti. Yamakamādi yassa paheḷikājātassa taṃ yamakādikaṃ. Kīdisanti āha “kiliṭṭhapada”ntiādi. Kiliṭṭhāni appatītadosasabhāve ṭhitatāya malitānyavisadāni padāni yassa taṃ kiliṭṭhapadaṃ. Mando appako abhidheyyo attho yassa taṃ mandābhidheyyaṃ, tādisaṃ tampi yamakādikaṃ kiliṭṭhapadadoseyeva yathāvutte anto abbhantare karīyati vidhīyati [M 0.0047] tattheva pakkhipīyati, kiliṭṭhapadadosato na byatiriccatīti adhippāyo.

24. Now, to show that even yamaka and so forth, though not intended, are included within the 'obscure' fault, he says 'whatever' and so on. Therein, 'whatever' is an indefinite term, and 'yamaka and so forth' is its definite term. That class of riddle which begins with yamaka is 'yamaka and so forth.' He asks 'Of what kind?' and says 'an obscure word' and so on. 'An obscure word' is that which has words that are obscure, tainted, and unclear because they stand in the nature of an unpleasing fault. 'Meager in meaning' is that which has a meager, small meaning to be expressed. Such a yamaka and so forth is also included, established, and placed right there within the aforesaid fault of obscure words. The intention is that it is not distinct from the fault of obscure words.

24. Idāni anadhippetamapi yamakādiṃ kiliṭṭhadoseyeva antokaraṇabyājena āvīkaronto āha “yaṃ kiliṭṭhe”ccādi. Kiliṭṭhapadaṃ appatītadosena missakattā avisadapadaṃ mandābhidheyyaṃ appakābhidheyyaṃ yaṃ yamakādikaṃ yaṃ yamakappaheḷikājātamatthi, tampi kiliṭṭhapadadoseyeva yathāvuttakiliṭṭhapadadoseyeva anto karīyati abbhantare karīyati, kiliṭṭhapadadosato abyatirittanti adhippāyo. Kiliṭṭhāni padāni yassa, mando abhidheyyo yassa, yamakaṃ ādi yassa paheḷikājātassa, kiliṭṭhapadānaṃ dosoti viggaho.

24. Now, revealing even unintended yamaka and so forth under the pretext of including them within the fault of obscurity, he says 'whatever is obscure' and so on. Whatever yamaka and so forth, whatever class of yamaka-riddle exists, which is an obscure word, an unclear word because it is mixed with an unpleasing fault, and has a meager, small meaning—that too is included within the fault of obscure words as previously stated; it is placed within. The intention is that it is not distinct from the fault of obscure words. The analysis is: 'that which has obscure words,' 'that which has a meager meaning,' 'that class of riddle which begins with yamaka'—this is the fault of obscure words.

25.

25.

Patītasaddaracitaṃ, siliṭṭhapadasandhikaṃ;

Pasādaguṇasaṃyuttaṃ, yamakaṃ mata’medisaṃ.

Composed of pleasing sounds,

With smooth word junctions,

Endowed with the quality of grace—

Such a yamaka is esteemed.

25. Hotu kāmamanabhimatamedisaṃ yamakādikaṃ, kiñcarahi abhimatanti āha “patīti”ccādi. Attano vacanīyatthappatītavasena vācakāpi saddā patītāyeva nāmāti patītehi pasiddhehi saddehi pāṭipadikehi racitaṃ kataṃ patītasaddaracitaṃ. Siliṭṭhā aññamaññāliṅganena maṭṭhā padānaṃ syādyantādīnaṃ sandhayo sandhanā yassa taṃ siliṭṭhapadasandhikaṃ. Patītasaddaracitattāyeva pasādasaṅkhātena guṇena saddālaṅkārena saṃyuttaṃ sammadevopetaṃ edisaṃ yathāvuttaguṇāsayaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ yamakaṃ mataṃ abhimatanti attho.

25. Let such yamaka and so forth be undesired; but what then is desired? He says 'pleasing' and so on. 'Composed of pleasing sounds' means made with sounds and nominal stems that are pleasing, being well-known, by virtue of conveying their own expressible meaning. 'With smooth word-junctions' refers to that in which the junctions of words, such as their case endings and so forth, are smooth and polished by mutual connection. Precisely because it is composed of pleasing sounds, it is thus endowed with the quality called 'grace' (pasāda), which is an ornament of sound. Such a delightful yamaka, possessing the aforementioned qualities, is considered desirable. This is the meaning.

25. Idāni adhigatesu yamakesu īdisaṃ yamakamiṭṭhamiti sissānaṃ upadisanto āha “patīte”ccādi. Patītasaddaracitaṃ “imassatthassāyaṃ vācako”ti patītehi pasiddhehi saddehi racitaṃ pāṭipadikehi kataṃ siliṭṭhapadasandhikaṃ siliṭṭhā syādyantādipadānaṃ sandhayo yassa taṃ [M 0.0048] pasādaguṇasaṃyuttaṃ patītasaddaracitattāyeva pasādasaṅkhātena saddālaṅkāraguṇena saṃyuttaṃ īdisaṃ evaṃbhūtaṃ guṇādhikato ramaṇīyaṃ upari vakkhamānayamakasadisaṃ yamakaṃ mataṃ viññūhi abhimataṃ. Patītā ca te saddā ca, tehi racitaṃ, siliṭṭhā padānaṃ sandhayo yassa, pasādoti guṇo saddālaṅkāro, tena saṃyuttanti viggaho.

25. Now, instructing the students on the mastered yamakas, saying 'such a yamaka is agreeable,' he states 'patīte' and so on. A yamaka composed of well-known words, meaning 'this is the expression for this meaning,' formed with well-known and established words, made from nominal stems, having smooth word-junctures—that is, having smooth junctures of words ending in case endings and the like—endowed with the quality of lucidity; and by the very fact of being composed of well-known words, it is connected with the quality of sound-ornament known as lucidity. Such a yamaka, being of this nature, more delightful due to its superior qualities, similar to the yamaka to be explained later, is considered agreeable by the wise. The analysis is: 'well-known are those words, and it is composed with them'; 'that which has smooth junctures of words'; 'lucidity is a quality, a sound-ornament, and it is endowed with that'.

26.

26.

Abyapetaṃ byapeta’ñña-māvuttānekavaṇṇajaṃ;

Yamakaṃ tañca pādāna-mādimajjhantagocaraṃ.

Unseparated, separated, and other,

Born of many repeated syllables;

That yamaka, too, has its scope

In the beginning, middle, and end of the lines.

26. Idāni taṃ yathāvuttamabhimataṃ dassetumupakkamate “abyapete”ccādinā. Āvuttā adhivuttā punappunuccāraṇupetā anekesaṃ patirūpattā, bahuvaṇṇā sarabyañjanarūpā, na eko vaṇṇo tassānuppāsattā, tathā ca vakkhati “vaṇṇāvutti paro yathā”ti subodhālaṅkāra 127 gāthā, tehi jātaṃ yamakanti viññāyate. Katividhaṃ taṃ vikappīyatīti āha “abyapetaṃ byapetañña”nti. Tattha yaṃ vaṇṇantarābyavahitaṃ vaṇṇasamudāyena vuttaṃ. Tadabyapetaṃ yamakaṃ. Yaṃ tu byavahitaṃ, taṃ byapetaṃ. Yaṃ pana ubhayamissaṃ, taṃ aññaṃ aparaṃ abyapetabyapetanti tidhā yamakaṃ tāva vikappīyate. Tametaṃ tividhaṃ yamakaṃ visayavibhāganirūpanāyaṃ ādi ca majjho ca anto ca gocaro visayo yasseti ādimajjhantagocaraṃ viññeyyaṃ. Kesaṃ pādānaṃ? Paccekaṃ catunnaṃgāthāvayavānaṃ. Sāpekkhattepi samāso gammakattā.

26. Now, he proceeds to illustrate that aforementioned agreeable yamaka with 'abyapeta' and so on. 'Āvuttā' means repeatedly uttered, endowed with repeated utterance, suitable for many, having many syllables in the form of vowels and consonants—not a single syllable, due to its being alliteration (anuprāsa). And thus it will be said, 'as the repetition of syllables follows.' From these, yamaka is understood to arise. How many kinds is it classified into? He states: 'unseparated, separated, and other.' Herein, that which is spoken by a group of syllables without the intervention of other syllables is called 'unseparated yamaka'. That which is intervened is called 'separated'. And that which is a mixture of both is called 'other', or 'unseparated-separated'—thus, yamaka is classified into three kinds. This threefold yamaka, for the purpose of defining its scope, should be understood as having its scope (gocara) in the beginning, middle, and end. Of what? Of the lines (pādānaṃ), that is, individually, of the four parts of a stanza. Even though there is dependency, the compound is understood because it is comprehensible.

Tattha pādacatukkassa ādimajjhantabhāvīnaṃ yamakānaṃ yāvanto pakārā sambhavanti, te mūlā satta. Kathaṃ? Ekasmiṃyeva pāde kvaci ādiyamakaṃ, kvaci majjhayamakaṃ, kvaci antayamakaṃ, kvaci majjhantayamakaṃ, kvaci majjhādiyamakaṃ, kvaci ādyantayamakaṃ, kvaci sabbayamakanti. Evaṃ paccekaṃ mūlabhūtā sattāti [M 0.0049] catūsu aṭṭhavīsati honti. Pādādiyamakañca paṭhamapādādiyamakamabyapetaṃ tathā dutiyatatiyacatutthapādādiyamakamabyapetaṃ paṭhamadutiyapādādiyamakamabyapetaṃ paṭhamatatiyapādādiyamakamabyapetaṃ paṭhamacatutthapādādiyamakamabyapetantiādinā anekadhā pasaṃsanti. Yadā ca sabbatoyamakaṃ, tadā mahāyamakādayo vikappā jāyantīti veditabbaṃ.

Herein, the kinds of yamakas that can occur at the beginning, middle, and end of a four-line stanza are fundamentally seven. How? In a single line, there is sometimes an initial yamaka, sometimes a middle yamaka, sometimes a final yamaka, sometimes a middle-final yamaka, sometimes a middle-initial yamaka, sometimes an initial-final yamaka, and sometimes a complete yamaka. Thus, there are seven fundamental types in each line, making twenty-eight in the four lines. And the initial yamaka of a line, the unseparated initial yamaka of the first line, and similarly the unseparated initial yamaka of the second, third, and fourth lines; the unseparated initial yamaka of the first and second lines; the unseparated initial yamaka of the first and third lines; the unseparated initial yamaka of the first and fourth lines, and so on, are extolled in various ways. And when it is a complete yamaka, then great yamakas and other variations arise—this should be understood.

26. Idāni abhimatayamakaṃ dīpeti “abyapete”ccādinā. Āvuttehi punappunaṃ vuttehi anekavaṇṇehi samudāyarūpattā anekehi sarabyañjanasarīrehi vaṇṇehi jātaṃ yamakaṃ aññehi vaṇṇehi abyavahitattā abyapetaṃ, vaṇṇantarehi byavahitattā byapetaṃ, ubhayamissakattā tehi aññaṃ abyapetabyapetañcāti tividhaṃ hoti. Tañca yamakaṃ visayavibhāganiyamena gāthāpādānaṃ ādigocaraṃ majjhagocaraṃ antagocaramiti tividhaṃ hoti. Ettha casaddo vattabbantare pavattati, vattabbantaraṃ nāma yathāvuttaabyapetādibhedato aññaṃ vattabbatāya samukhībhūtaṃ pādānaṃ ādimajjhāvasānantaraṃ, upanyāso vākyārambhoti ca etasseva nāmaṃ. Visadisena vaṇṇena apetaṃ byapetaṃ. Tabbiparītamabyapetaṃ. Abyapetañca byapetañca aññañcāti samāhāradvando. Aneke ca te vaṇṇā ca, āvuttāyeva anekavaṇṇā, tehi jātaṃ, ādi ca majjho ca anto ca, te gocarā yassāti viggaho.

26. Now, he explains the agreeable yamaka with 'abyapeta' and so on. The yamaka arises from many syllables, which are repeatedly spoken, due to their collective nature, being many syllables in the form of vowels and consonants. Because it is unseparated by other syllables, it is 'unseparated' (abyapeta); because it is separated by intervening syllables, it is 'separated' (byapeta); and because it is a mixture of both, it is 'other', or 'unseparated-separated'—thus it is threefold. And that yamaka, by the rule of dividing its subject matter, is threefold in relation to the verse lines: having the initial scope, the middle scope, and the final scope. Here, the word 'ca' functions to introduce something else to be stated. 'Something else to be stated' refers to something other than the aforementioned divisions like 'unseparated', which is present as suitable to be stated, concerning the beginning, middle, and end of the lines. 'Upanyāsa' or 'the commencement of speech' is also a name for this. That which is separated by a dissimilar syllable is 'separated' (byapeta). The opposite of that is 'unseparated' (abyapeta). 'Abyapetañca byapetañca aññañcāti' is a collective dvanda compound. The analysis is: 'many and those syllables' (i.e., the many repeated syllables), 'born from them'; 'the beginning, the middle, and the end'—these are its scopes.

Tattha pādacatukkassa ādimajjhāvasānesu labbhamānayamakabhedā ekekasmiṃ pāde satta satta bhavanti. Kathaṃ? Pādādiyamakaṃ pādamajjhayamakaṃ pādantayamakaṃ majjhantayamakaṃ majjhādiyamakaṃ ādyantayamakaṃ sabbatoyamakanti evaṃ paccekaṃ satta satta katvā catūsu mūlabhūtayamakā aṭṭhavīsa [M 0.0050] bhavanti. Ettha pādādiyamakādikampi abyapetapaṭhamapādādiyamakaṃ tathā dutiyatatiyacatutthapādādiyamakamiti ca abyapetapaṭhamadutiyapādādiyamakaṃ tathā paṭhamatatiyapādādiyamakaṃ paṭhamacatutthapādādiyamakamiti ca abyapetadutiyatatiyapādādiyamakaṃ tathā dutiyacatutthapādādiyamakamiti ca abyapetatatiyacatutthapādādiyamakamiti ca evamabyapetapādādiyamakā dasa honti. Tathā byapetāpi dasāti vīsati, abyapetapaṭhamapādamajjhayamakaṃ tathā dutiyapādamajjhayamakamiccādinā majjhayamakampi vīsatividhaṃ hoti. Abyapetapaṭhamapādantayamakaṃ tathā dutiyapādantayamakamiccādinā antayamakampi vīsatividhaṃ. Saṃsaggabhedato pana anekavidhaṃ hoti.

Herein, the variations of yamaka obtainable at the beginning, middle, and end of a four-line stanza are seven in each line. How? The line-initial yamaka, the line-middle yamaka, the line-final yamaka, the middle-final yamaka, the middle-initial yamaka, the initial-final yamaka, and the complete yamaka—thus, with seven types in each, there are twenty-eight fundamental yamakas in the four lines. Here, the line-initial yamaka and so on include: the unseparated line-initial yamaka of the first line; and similarly the unseparated line-initial yamakas of the second, third, and fourth lines; the unseparated line-initial yamaka of the first and second lines; and similarly the first and third lines, and the first and fourth lines; the unseparated line-initial yamaka of the second and third lines; and similarly the second and fourth lines; and the unseparated line-initial yamaka of the third and fourth lines—thus, there are ten unseparated line-initial yamakas. Similarly, there are also ten separated ones, making twenty. Likewise, the middle yamaka is also of twenty types, such as the unseparated line-middle yamaka of the first line, and similarly of the second line, and so on. The final yamaka is also of twenty types, such as the unseparated line-final yamaka of the first line, and similarly of the second line, and so on. However, due to the difference in combinations, it becomes manifold.

Abyapetapaṭhamapādādiyamakavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Unseparated Yamaka at the Beginning of the First Line

27.

27.

Sujanā’sujanā sabbe, guṇenāpi vivekino;

Vivekaṃ na samāyanti, avivekijanantike.

The good and the bad, all, even if discerning by way of qualities, do not attain discrimination in the presence of undiscerning people.

27. “Sujanā”iccādi. Sujanā sajjanā, asujanā asajjanāti ete sabbe ubhayapakkhapātino visesā janā guṇena sīlādinā karaṇabhūtena, hetubhūtena vā vivekinopi sādhūsu labbhamānānamasādhūsvanupalabbhanato puthubhūtāpi avivekīnaṃ janānaṃ antike samīpe tesaṃ sannidhāne vivekaṃ vibhāgaṃ na samāyanti napāpuṇanti, vibhāgavijānanapaññāvekallena ca vivekinopi janā te ekato katvā passantīti. Idaṃ paṭhamapādādiyamakamabyapetaṃ.

27. 'Sujanā,' etc.: 'Sujanā' means good people, 'asujanā' means bad people. All these particular people, inclined to both sides, are discerning by way of qualities such as virtue, which serve as an instrumental cause or a causal condition. Even though they are distinct—because these qualities are found among the good but not found among the bad—they do not attain discrimination or distinctness in the presence, near, or proximity of undiscerning people. And due to a lack of wisdom that discerns distinctions, the undiscerning see even those discerning people as one group. This is an unseparated yamaka at the beginning of the first line.

27. Idāni abyapetapaṭhamapādādiyamakassa mukhamattaṃ dassetumāha “sujani”ccādi. Sujanā sādhujanā, asujanā asādhujanā ceti sabbe ubhayapakkhikā sīlādinā, pāṇātipātādinā guṇena hetunā vivekino api sādhūsu [M 0.0051] pāṇātipātādīnaṃ, asādhūsu sīlādīnaṃ appavattito guṇena puthubhūtāpi avivekijanantike vivekañāṇarahitānaṃ janānaṃ santike vivekaṃ vibhāgaṃ na samāyanti na pāpuṇanti. Viveko vinābhavanametesamatthīti vivekino. Ettha visayopacārena vivekoti paññā, na vivekinoti avivekino, teyeva janā, tesaṃ antikamiti ca viggaho. Idaṃ abyapetapaṭhamapādādiyamakaṃ.

27. Now, to show merely an outline of the unseparated yamaka at the beginning of the first line, it is said, 'Sujanā,' etc. Good people are virtuous people, and bad people are non-virtuous people. All these, belonging to both sides, are discerning by way of qualities—such as virtue, or killing living beings—as a cause. Even though they are distinct by way of these qualities, because killing living beings, etc., does not occur among the good, and virtue, etc., does not occur among the bad, they do not attain discrimination or distinctness in the presence of undiscerning people, that is, of people devoid of the wisdom of discernment. They are 'discerning' (vivekino) because they possess separation (viveko or vinābhavanaṃ). Here, by metaphorical transfer, 'viveka' means wisdom. The analysis of avivekijanantike is: na vivekino'ti avivekino (not discerning, thus undiscerning); te yeva janā (those very people); tesaṃ antikaṃ (their presence). This is an unseparated yamaka at the beginning of the first line.

Abyapetapaṭhamadutiyapādādiyamakavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Unseparated Yamaka at the Beginning of the First and Second Lines

28.

28.

Kusalā’kusalā sabbe, pabalā’pabalā’thavā;

No yātā yāva’hosittaṃ, sukhadukkhappadā siyuṃ.

Skillful and unskillful, all, whether strong or weak, as long as they have not reached the state of having been, they may be givers of happiness and suffering.

28. “Kusalā”iccādi. Pabalā āsevanappaṭilābhavasena balavanto ca. Athāti anantaratthe nipāto. Apabalā tadabhāvato dubbalā ca sabbe kusalākusalā dhammā yāva yattakaṃ kālaṃ ahosittaṃ vinā uppattimattaṃ phaladānāsambhavato kevalaṃ “ahosī”ti vacanīyatthanimittamattakammabhāvena ahosikammattaṃ no yātā na sampattā, tāva tattakaṃ kālaṃ sukhañca dukkhañca taṃ padantīti sukhadukkhappadā siyuṃ. Yāva saṃsārapavatti, tāva sukhadukkhadāyakā hontīti. Idaṃ paṭhamadutiyapādādiyamakamabyapetaṃ.

28. 'Kusalā,' etc. The strong are powerful by way of gaining through repeated practice. 'Atha' is a particle in the sense of immediacy. And the weak are feeble due to the absence thereof. All skillful and unskillful phenomena, for as long as they have not reached the state of being defunct kamma (ahosikammattaṃ)—that is, the state of 'having been' (ahosittaṃ), which, being without mere arising due to the impossibility of giving fruit, is merely an action that is a sign for the meaning to be called 'it was'—for that long they would be givers of happiness and suffering. As long as the cycle of existence continues, they are givers of happiness and suffering. This is the unseparated Yamaka beginning with the first and second lines.

28. Pabalā āsevanādipaccayalābhena balavanto vā atha apabalā tadabhāvena dubbalā vā sabbe kusalākusalā ahosittaṃ phaladānābhāvato pavattimattataṃ yāva yattakaṃ kālaṃ no yātā appattā, tāva tattakaṃ sukhadukkhappadā yathākkamaṃ sukhadukkhapadāyino siyuṃ bhavanti. Idaṃ abyapetapaṭhamadutiyapādādiyamakaṃ. Kusalapaṭipakkhā akusalā. “Ahosī”ti vattabbassa bhāvo ahosittaṃ. “Ehipassiko”tiādīsu viya kriyāpadatopi ṇādipaccayā honti.

28. The strong are powerful by gaining conditions such as repeated practice, or the weak are feeble due to the absence thereof. All skillful and unskillful phenomena, for as long as they have not reached the state of 'having been' (ahosittaṃ)—which is merely an occurrence due to the absence of fruit-giving—for that long they would be givers of happiness and suffering, respectively giving happiness and suffering. This is the unseparated Yamaka beginning with the first and second lines. The unskillful are the opposites of the skillful. The state of what can be called 'it was' is ahosittaṃ. Just as in terms like 'ehipassiko,' suffixes such as ṇa are found even derived from verbs.

Abyapetapaṭhamadutiyatatiyapādādiyamakavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Unseparated Yamaka Beginning with the First, Second, and Third Lines

29.

29.

Sādaraṃ sā daraṃ hantu, vihitā vihitā mayā;

Vandanā vandanāmāna-bhājane ratanattaye.

With reverence, may that homage destroy distress, / performed by me, truly beneficial; / homage to the Triple Gem, the receptacle of homage and honor.

29. “Sādara”miccādi. [M 0.0052] Vandanā dvārattayopadassiyamānā māno ca pūjā, tesaṃ bhājane ādhārabhūte ratijananādinā atthena ratanasaṅkhātānaṃ buddhādīnaṃ taye samūhabhūte ratanattaye sādaraṃ ādarasahitaṃ katvā mayā vihitā katā, vihitā alaṃsaṃsāradukkhavisaṭanirākaraṇato visesena hitā padhyā sā vandanā so paṇāmo daraṃ darathaṃ kāyacittapariḷāhaṃ hantu hiṃsatu. Mayāti vuttattā meti atthato viññāyati. Idaṃ pana paṭhamadutiyatatiyapādādiyamakamabyapetaṃ.

29. 'Sādara,' etc. Homage is that which is shown through the three doors; māna is honor and worship. To the Triple Gem—which is the receptacle and basis for these, a group of the Buddha and others, called 'jewels' due to the meaning of generating delight, etc.—having done so with reverence, it was performed by me. That homage is especially beneficial because it sufficiently removes the pervasive suffering of saṃsāra. May that homage, that bowing, destroy distress, agitation, and the fever of body and mind. Since 'mayā' is stated, 'of me' (me) is understood by meaning. This, however, is the unseparated Yamaka beginning with the first, second, and third lines.

29. Vandanāmānabhājane dvārattayena vidhiyamānapaṇāmapūjānaṃ ādhārabhūte ratanattaye ratijananādiatthena ratanasaṅkhātānaṃ buddhādīnaṃ taye mayā yā vandanā sādaraṃ ādarasahitaṃ vihitā katā, vihitā lokiya lokuttara sampattisādhanato visesena hitā sā vandanā daraṃ mayhaṃ kāyacittadarathaṃ hantu vināsetu. Idaṃ abyapetapaṭhamadutiyatatiyapādādiyamakaṃ. Saha ādarena vattamānaṃ sādaraṃ, kriyāvisesanaṃ. Ettha kriyā nāma vihitāsaddena niddiṭṭhakaraṇaṃ. Karaṇañhi vihitāsaddassa vuttakammattepi aññathānupapattilakkhaṇasāmatthiyato bhijjitvā vijjamānaṃ “akāsi”nti kriyāya sambandhamupentaṃ kammañca hoti, bhāve vihitassa yupaccayantassa napuṃsakattā napuṃsakañca, sattāya ekattā ekavacanañca tabbisesanattā sādarasaddopi napuṃsakadutiyekavacano hoti.

29. To the Triple Gem—which is the basis for the bowing and worship performed through the three doors, and which is a group of the Buddha and others called 'jewels' due to the meaning of generating delight, etc.—may that homage, which was performed by me with reverence and which is especially beneficial as a means to attain worldly and transcendent prosperity, destroy and eliminate the distress of my body and mind. This is the unseparated Yamaka beginning with the first, second, and third lines. 'Sādaraṃ' means 'that which proceeds with reverence'; it is an adverb. Here, the action is the 'doing' indicated by the word 'vihitā'. For this 'doing', although expressed as a past participle by the word 'vihitā', is, by virtue of its characteristic of being inexplicable otherwise, analyzed as being present and becomes the object connected with the verb 'akāsi' (did). And because the word 'vihita' ending in the 'yu' suffix in the sense of an abstract noun is neuter, it is neuter; and because it is one in substance, it is singular. And because the word 'sādara' is its adjective, it is also in the neuter accusative singular.

“Visesye [M 0.0053] dissamānā yā,

Liṅgasaṅkhyāvibhattiyo;

Tulyādhikaraṇe bhiyyo,

Kātabbā tā visesane”ti sambandhacinto 15 gāthā bhedacintā 194 gāthā.

“Those gender, number, and case endings which are seen in the qualified noun, should likewise be applied in the qualifying adjective when in apposition.”

Hi vuttaṃ. Evaṃ kriyāvisesane gahite sāmatthiyato “mayā”ti tatiyantassa paṭhamantattaṃ, “vandanā”ti paṭhamantassa chaṭṭhuntañca hoti. Vandanā ca māno ca, tesaṃ bhājanaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ samūho tayaṃ, ratanānaṃ tayanti ca viggaho.

For it is said. Thus, when the adverb is taken, by implication, the instrumental 'mayā' becomes nominative, and the nominative 'vandanā' becomes genitive. 'Homage and honor, their receptacle.' 'A group of three is tayaṃ,' and 'a group of jewels' are the analyses.

Abyapetacatukkapādādiyamakavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Unseparated Yamaka Beginning with All Four Lines

30.

30.

Kamalaṃ ka’malaṃ kattuṃ-vanado vanado’mbaraṃ;

Sugato sugato lokaṃ, sahitaṃ sahitaṃ karaṃ.

The lotus, to adorn the water; the cloud, a giver of water, adorns the sky; the Sugata, well-gone, making the world beneficial and whole.

30. “Kamala”miccādi. Kamalaṃ aravindaṃ kaṃ jalaṃ alaṅkattuṃ sajjanatthāya hoti, vikasitāravindasandohasambhāvitodakassa vāpādīsu tādisaramaṇīyattasampattisambhavato, avanaṃ rakkhaṃ dadāti sassasampatyādikāraṇabhāvenāti avanado. Vanaṃ jalaṃ dadāti na tucchoti vanado megho ambaraṃ ākāsaṃ jaladhārabhārabharitambarakuharassa dassanīyatāguṇayogato alaṃkattunti adhikataṃ. Sahitaṃ sampuṇṇaṃ hitaṃ abhivuddhiṃ karaṃ karonto suṭṭhu gadatīti sugato mañjubhāṇī pubbabuddhā viya nekkhammādinā kāmacchandādike pajahanto gantvā arahattamaggena savāsanasakalakilese samucchinditvā sobhanaṃ nibbānapuraṃ gatoti vā sugatoti vutto so mahāmuni attano aparimitapāramitāsimpakacagalitatilakabhāvena lokaṃ lokattayaṃ, sahitaṃ lokanti vā yojanīyaṃ alaṅkattuṃ alaṃkaraṇāyāti. Idaṃ pādacatukkādiyamakamabyapetaṃ.

30. 'Kamala,' etc. The lotus (kamala) is for adorning (alaṅkattuṃ) the water (kaṃ), for the purpose of decoration (sajjanatthāya); or because of the possibility of attaining such loveliness in ponds and so forth, whose water is enhanced by a multitude of blooming lotuses. It gives protection (avanaṃ = rakkhaṃ), thus it is an 'avanado' (protection-giver), being the cause of the attainment of crops and so forth. It gives water (vanaṃ = jalaṃ) and is not empty, thus it is a 'vanado' (water-giver), a cloud. It adorns the sky (ambaraṃ); 'to adorn' (alaṅkattuṃ) is understood, due to the quality of beauty of the sky's expanse when filled with the burden of streams of water. 'Sugato' (Well-spoken) is so called because he speaks excellently (suṭṭhu gadatī), being a sweet speaker (mañjubhāṇī), making (karonto) what is complete (sahitaṃ = sampuṇṇaṃ) and beneficial (hitaṃ) for growth (abhivuddhiṃ). Or, he is called 'Sugato' (Well-gone) because, like the former Buddhas, having abandoned sensual desires and so forth through renunciation, he went by the path of Arahantship, uprooted all defilements with their latent tendencies, and reached the splendid city of Nibbāna. That Great Sage, called 'Sugato', by way of his immeasurable perfections flowing like sesame oil from a pressed husk, adorns the world (lokaṃ), the triple world; or it should be construed as 'the world together with its inhabitants' (sahitaṃ lokaṃ). 'To adorn' (alaṅkattuṃ) is for the purpose of adorning (alaṃkaraṇāya). This is the unseparated Yamaka beginning with all four lines.

30. Kamalaṃ [M 0.0054] padumaṃ kaṃ jalaṃ alaṅkattuṃ pañcavidhapadumasañchannassa udakassa ramaṇīyattā sajjetuṃ hoti. Avanado kāle vuṭṭhisampadāya sassasampadādīnaṃ kāraṇattā ārakkhaṃ dento vanado megho ambaraṃ ākāsaṃ alaṅkattuṃ jaladhārabhārabharitambarakucchiyā dassanīyattā sajjetuṃ hoti, sahitaṃ sampuṇṇaṃ hitaṃ abhivuḍḍhiṃ karaṃ karonto sugato citrakathī sundaraṃ nibbānaṃ gato vā so sugato so tathāgato lokaṃ lokattayaṃ, sahitaṃ lokaṃ vā alaṅkattuṃ citrakathādikāraṇehi tādisassa aññassa ca lokarāmaṇeyyassābhāvā sajjetuṃ hoti. Sabbapadatthānaṃ sattābyabhicārittā hotīti gammaṃ. Tatoyeva sabbe paṭhamantabhavanakriyāya yujjantīti vadanti. Idaṃ abyapetacatukkapādādiyamakaṃ.

30. The lotus (kamalaṃ), a paduma, is for adorning (alaṅkattuṃ) the water (kaṃ), for beautifying (sajjetuṃ) it, due to the loveliness of water covered with the five kinds of lotuses. The 'avanado' (protection-giver), giving protection (ārakkhaṃ) by being the cause of the prosperity of crops through timely rain, and the 'vanado' (water-giver), the cloud, is for adorning the sky (ambaraṃ), for beautifying it, due to the beauty of the sky's expanse filled with the burden of streams of water. The Sugata, a charming speaker (citrakathī), making what is complete (sahitaṃ) and beneficial (hitaṃ) for growth (abhivuḍḍhiṃ), or that Sugata, that Tathāgata, who has gone to beautiful Nibbāna, is for adorning the world (lokaṃ), the triple world, or the world with its inhabitants (sahitaṃ lokaṃ), for beautifying it, because there is no other such worldly delight caused by charming discourses and so forth. It is understood that the meanings of all the words do not deviate from reality. Therefore, they say that all nominative nouns are connected with the verb 'to be'. This is the unseparated Yamaka beginning with all four lines.

31.

31.

Abyapetādiyamaka-sseso leso nidassito;

Ñeyyāni’māyeva disā-ya’ññāni yamakānipi.

This brief indication of the unseparated initial yamaka has been shown; other yamakas too are to be known in just this way.

31. Iccevamabhimatayamake abyapetapādādiyamakassa disāmattaṃ dassetvā upasaṃharati “abyapete”ccādinā. Abyapetassa abyavahitassa catunnaṃ pādānaṃ ādo, ādibhūtassa vā yamakassa eso yathāvutto leso kocideva bhedo nidassito vikappito. Aparānipi kiṃ na vikappiyantīticeti āha “ñeyyāni”ccādi. Imāya disāya iminā upāyena maggeneva aññāni vuttato aparāni dutiyapādādiyamakatatiyapādādiyamakacatutthapādādiyamakādīni abyapetānipi paṭhamadutiyapādādiyamakapaṭhamatatiyapādādiyamakānipi byapetāni, paṭhamacatutthadutiyatatiyapādādiyamakādīnipi abyapetabyapetāni, tathā majjhantapādayamakāni ñeyyāni jānitabbāni, viññūnaṃ tādisāya disāya dassitattāti. Tattha ca –

31. Thus, in this section on yamaka, having shown merely a direction for the yamaka beginning with unseparated lines, he concludes with 'abyapete,' etc. This brief indication as stated, a certain distinction, has been shown and analyzed for the beginning of the four lines of the unseparated, that is, uncontiguous, yamaka, or for the initial yamaka. Should one ask why others are not analyzed, he says 'ñeyyāni,' etc. By this direction, by this method and way, other yamakas different from those mentioned are to be known and understood—such as the unseparated yamakas beginning with the second line, third line, fourth line, and so forth; and the separated yamakas beginning with the first and second lines, or first and third lines; and the unseparated-separated yamakas beginning with the first and fourth, or second and third lines, and so forth; and similarly the yamakas of the middle and final lines—since such a direction has been shown by the wise. And therein—

“Guṇāguṇena [M 0.0055] saha te, sādhavo’sādhavo janā;

Vigāhante samaṃ nātha, cittaṃ citte kathaṃ nu te”.

“O protector, good and bad people, along with their virtues and faults, plunge in equally; how then is your mind in relation to their mind?”

Iccādinā dutiyapādādiyamakādīni abyapetāni,

By this and so forth are shown the unseparated yamakas beginning with the second line, etc.

“Piyena vacasā sabbe,

Piyena’ppiyabhāṇino;

Pādānate jinokāsi,

So dhammo hantu vo’ppiyaṃ”.

With pleasant speech towards all, even those who speak unpleasantly, the Conqueror made them bow at his feet. May that Dhamma destroy what is unpleasant for you.

Iccādinā paṭhamadutiyapādādiyamakādīni abyapetāni,

Thus, the uninterrupted first-and-second-foot initial yamakas and so forth.

“Sa’malaṃ samalaṃ kattuṃ, suciraṃsuci raṃjaye;

Suciraṃ suciraṃgaṃ taṃ, sa’malaṃ samalaṃbhi yo”.

To make the defiled self adorned, may one for a long time delight in that pure-bodied one, the one of beautiful rays, who attained peace.

Iccādinā paṭhamacatutthadutiyatatiyapādādiyamakādīni abyapetabyapetāni,

Thus, the uninterrupted-and-separated yamakas at the beginning of the first-and-fourth and second-and-third feet, and so forth.

“Manohara hara klesaṃ, jina cetobhavaṃ mama;

Nanu tvaṃ pāramīsārā-matabhāvitamosadhaṃ”.

O captivating one, O Conqueror, dispel my mind-born defilement; surely you are the deathless medicine cultivated from the essence of the perfections?

Iccādinā majjhapādayamakāni,

Thus, the middle-of-foot yamakas and so forth.

“Sādhunā raṃjaya jaya-ddhaninā’pūrayi mahiṃ;

Yo taṃ jinavaraṃ dhīra-matthakāmosi ce tuvaṃ”.

He who filled the earth with the righteous sound of victory—if you, O wise one, desire the goal of that supreme Conqueror, cause him to delight.

Iccādinā antapādayamakāni jānitabbāni.

Thus, the end-of-foot yamakas and so forth are to be known.

31. Evaṃ abhimatayamakena abyapetayamakānamupāyādīni nigamento āha “abyapeti”ccādi. Abyapetādiyamakassa visadisavaṇṇehi abyavahitādiyamakassa, abyapetapādādiyamakassa vā eso leso “sujani”ccādiko appakodāharaṇanayo nidassito niddiṭṭho. Aññāni yamakānipi imāyeva disāya iminā nayeneva ñeyyāni viññūhi ñātabbāni. Ādo yamakaṃ, ādibhūtaṃ vā yamakaṃ, abyapetañca taṃ ādiyamakañcāti vākyaṃ. Evaṃ dassitena [M 0.0056] iminā kamena abyapetadutiyapādādiyamakādayo ñātabbāti adhippāyo.

31. Thus, concluding the methods and so forth of the uninterrupted yamakas by means of the desired yamaka, he says “abyapeti” and so forth. This brief exposition, a method of giving few examples, such as “sujani” and so forth, has been shown and indicated for the uninterrupted initial yamaka, or for the initial yamaka unseparated by dissimilar syllables, or for the uninterrupted foot-initial yamaka. Other yamakas, too, are to be known by the wise in this very direction and by this same method. The phrase is “initial yamaka,” or “the yamaka that is the origin,” and “it is an uninterrupted initial yamaka.” The intended meaning is that, by this sequence thus shown, the uninterrupted second-foot initial yamakas and so forth are to be known.

Tattha abyapetadutiyapādādiyamakamevaṃ veditabbaṃ –

Therein, the uninterrupted second-foot initial yamaka is to be understood thus:

Guṇāguṇena saha te, sādhavo’sādhavo janā;

Vigāhante samaṃ nātha, cittaṃ citte kathaṃ nu te.

O protector, those good and bad people, with their virtues and faults, plunge equally into your mind. How then is your state of mind?

Bho nātha te tuyhaṃ citte sādhavo asādhavo te janā guṇāguṇena sakasakaguṇena aguṇena ca saha samaṃ ekajjhaṃ kathaṃ nu vigāhante, cittaṃ acchariyaṃ sujanadujjanesu samamettā acchariyāti adhippāyo.

O Lord, in your mind, how do those good and bad people, along with their respective qualities and lack thereof, plunge equally together? The mind is wondrous—the intended meaning is that equal loving-kindness towards good and bad people is wondrous.

Abyapetapaṭhamadutiyapādādiyamakamevaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ –

The uninterrupted first-and-second-foot initial yamaka is to be seen thus:

Piyena vacasā sabbe, piyena’ppiyabhāṇino;

Pādānate jinokāsi, so dhammo hantu vo’ppīyaṃ.

With pleasant speech towards all, even those who speak unpleasantly, the Conqueror made them bow at his feet. May that Dhamma destroy what is unpleasant for you.

Jino appiyabhāṇinopi sabbe jane piyena yena vacasā pādānate akāsi, so dhammo vo appiyaṃ hantu. Ettha apisaddapariyāyassa pisaddassa gahitattā yatibhaṅgo natthi.

The Conqueror, with that pleasant speech, made all people, even those who speak unpleasantly, bow at his feet. May that Dhamma destroy what is unpleasant for you. Here, since the word ‘pi,’ a synonym for the word ‘api,’ is understood, there is no breach of meter.

Paṭhamacatutthadutiyatatiyapādādiabyapetabyapetayamakamevaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ –

The uninterrupted-and-separated yamaka at the beginning of the first-and-fourth and second-and-third feet is to be seen thus:

Sa’malaṃ samalaṃ kattuṃ, suciraṃsuci raṃjaye;

Suciraṃ suciraṃgaṃ taṃ, sa’malaṃ samalaṃbhi yoti.

To make the defiled self adorned, may one for a long time delight in that pure-bodied one, the one of beautiful rays, who attained peace.

Ettha “samalaṃ samalaṃ, suciraṃ sucira”nti visadisavaṇṇehi abyavahitattā abyapetaṃ, “samalaṃ samala”nti pubbaparayugaḷaṃ pubbaparayugaḷadvayaṃ (ka.) “kattu”miti bhinnavaṇṇehi, “suciraṃ sucira”nti pubbaparayugaḷaṃ pubbaparayugaḷadvayaṃ (ka.) “jaye”ti bhinnavaṇṇehi ca byavahitattā byapetañca hoti. Suciraṃsuci sobhanaraṃsinā uci yutto yo jino saṃ [M 0.0057] santiṃ nibbānaṃ samalaṃbhi alabhi, alaṃ accantaṃ atisayena suciraṃgaṃ visuddhadehaṃ taṃ jinaṃ samalaṃ jallikāsaṅkhātena, rāgādikucchitasaṅkhātena vā malena sahitaṃ saṃ attānaṃ alaṃkattuṃ nimmalaṃ katvā sajjetuṃ suciraṃ sucirakālaṃ raṃjaye attani abhiramāpeyya.

Here, “samalaṃ samalaṃ” and “suciraṃ suciraṃ” are uninterrupted because they are not separated by dissimilar syllables. The former and latter pair “samalaṃ samalaṃ” is separated by the dissimilar syllables of “kattuṃ,” and the former and latter pair “suciraṃ suciraṃ” is separated by the dissimilar syllables of “jaye,” and thus it is also separated. The Conqueror who, endowed with beautiful rays, attained peace, Nibbāna—one should cause oneself to delight for a very long time in that Conqueror, who has an exceedingly pure body, in order to adorn oneself, who is with defilement, having made oneself spotless.

Pādamajjhayamakamevaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ –

The middle-of-foot yamaka is to be seen thus:

Manohara hara klesaṃ, jina cetobhavaṃ mama;

Nanu tvaṃ pāramīsārā-matabhāvitamosadhanti.

O captivating one, O Conqueror, dispel my mind-born defilement; surely you are the deathless medicine cultivated from the essence of the perfections?

Manohara jina mama cetobhavaṃ klesaṃ santāpaṃ hara apanaya, tvaṃ pāramīsārāmatabhāvitaṃ osadhaṃ dibbosadhaṃ nanu.

O captivating Conqueror, dispel, remove my mind-born defilement and distress. Surely you are the divine medicine, the deathless medicine cultivated from the essence of the perfections?

Pādantayamakamevaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ –

The end-of-foot yamaka is to be seen thus:

Sādhunā raṃjaya jaya-ddhaninā’pūrayi mahiṃ;

Yo taṃ jinavaraṃ dhīra-matthakāmosi ce tuvanti.

He who filled the earth with the righteous sound of victory—if you, O wise one, desire the goal of that supreme Conqueror, cause him to delight.

Yo jinavaro sādhunā jayaddhaninā veneyyajayaghosena mahiṃ āpūrayi, dhīraṃ taṃ jinavaraṃ tuvaṃ sappurisa ce atthakāmo asi, raṃjaya abhiramāpehi. Iminā niddiṭṭhayamakeheva avasesā tatiyapādādiyamakādayo viññeyyā.

The excellent Conqueror who filled the earth with the righteous sound of victory, that is, the cry of victory over those to be tamed—if you, O good person, desire the goal of that wise, excellent Conqueror, then cause him to delight, make him rejoice. By these indicated yamakas, the remaining third-foot initial yamakas and so forth are to be known.

32.

32.

Accantabahavo tesaṃ,

Bhedā sambhedayoniyo;

Tatthāpi keci sukarā,

Keci accantadukkarā.

Their divisions are exceedingly numerous, having their origin in combination; even among them, some are easy to make, while others are exceedingly difficult.

32. Kiṃ pana sākallena na vikappitānīti āha “accanti”ccādi. Tesaṃ vikappānaṃ sambhedo saṅkaro missattamuccāraṇappakāro yoni pabhavo yesaṃ te sambhedayoniyo, bhedā pakārā accantabahavo atisayena bahulā yathāvuttanayena sambhavanti, tatthāpi tesu vikappesupi keci vikappā sukhena karīyanti payujjantīti [M 0.0058] sukarā, tabbiparīto ca keci vikappā accantadukkarā. Iti dvidhā saṅgayhanti, tesu sukarānaṃ kesañci abhimatayamakānaṃ mukhamattaṃ dassitaṃ. Idāni dukkarānaṃ kesañci mukhamattaṃ na sabbamevaṃ veditabbaṃ.

32. But why are they not analyzed in their entirety? To this, he says “accanti” and so forth. Their variations are called `sambhedayoniyo` because their origin and source are combination, confusion, mixture, and manner of pronunciation. The divisions, the types, are exceedingly numerous, extremely abundant, arising in the manner described. Even among those variations, some are easily made and applied, thus they are `sukarā`; and conversely, some variations are exceedingly difficult. Thus, they are classified in two ways. Among them, the mere outline of some of the easy, desired yamakas has been shown. Now, of the difficult ones, a mere outline of some is to be understood, not all of them.

Samunnatena te satā,

Kathaṃ na te na te siyuṃ;

Yato natenatepi’to,

Siyuṃ na te nate subhā.

By you, the exalted one, how could the good people not be yours? Since even the lowly, not led by you, would not be yours, O beautiful one, nor those who are bowed.

Idaṃ pādacatukkamajjhayamakamabyapetabyapetamekarūpaṃ dukkaraṃ.

This is a difficult four-footed middle yamaka, uninterrupted-and-separated, and of a single form.

Na bhāsurā tepi surā vibhūsitā,

Tathāsurā bhūri surāparājitā;

Sabhāsu rājāpi tathā surājito,

Yathā surājanti surāvinissaṭā.

Not so radiant are those gods, though adorned, nor the many Asuras defeated by strong drink; nor is a king in assemblies so well-resplendent, as they shine forth who are released from strong drink.

Idaṃ catukkapādamajjhayamakamekarūpabyapetaṃ.

This is a four-footed middle yamaka, devoid of a single form.

32. Sabbamidamanuddisitvā lakkhaṇātidesena nigamanaṃ kimatthamiccāsaṅkāyamāha “accante”ccādi. Tesaṃ yamakānaṃ sambhedayoniyo pabheduppattikāraṇabhūtā bhedā uccāvacapakārā accantabahavo, tatthāpi tesupi keci yamakā sukarā susādhiyā, keci accantadukkarā atisayena dussādhiyā. Sambhedo yoni yesanti viggaho.

32. Having pointed out all this, to resolve the doubt as to what is the purpose of concluding with a definition by way of indication, it is said, 'because they are extremely numerous,' etc. The mixed origins of these yamakas—the divisions that are the causes of their arising in various forms—are extremely numerous, and even among them, some yamakas are easy and readily accomplished, while others are extremely difficult and exceedingly hard to accomplish. 'Those whose origin is mixture' is the analysis.

Iha sukarassa upadisitattā dukkarayamakapavesopāyamattamupadisīyate –

Here, since the easy one has been taught, only a method for entering the difficult yamaka will be taught—

“Manaṃ manaṃ satthu dadeyya ce yo,

Manaṃ manaṃ pīṇayata’ssa satthu;

Manaṃ manaṃ tena dadeyya ce na,

Manaṃ manaṃpa’ssa na sādhupujja”nti.

If one would give mind by mind to the Teacher, the Teacher's mind would delight that person's mind; if, therefore, one would not give mind by mind, even that person's mind would not be worthy of worship by the good.

Idaṃ pādacatukkādiyamakamekarūpaṃ abyapetabyapetaṃ.

This four-footed beginning yamaka, of single form, is unseparated and separated.

Yo [M 0.0059] puggalo manaṃ attano cittaṃ satthu jinassa manaṃ khaṇamattampi dadeyya ce, satthu munindassa manaṃ cittaṃ assa puggalassa manaṃ cittaṃ pīṇayati sampīṇeti, tena tasmā manaṃ manaṃ cittaṃ cittaṃ dadeyya ce na yadi no dadeyya, assa puggalassa manaṃ cittaṃ manaṃpi muhuttampi sādhupujjaṃ sādhūhi pūjitabbaṃ na bhavati.

If a person would give his own mind, his thought, even for a moment, to the Teacher, the Victor, the Teacher's, the Sage-King's, mind, his thought, delights that person's mind, his thought, and gladdens it. Therefore, if one would not give mind by mind, thought by thought, that person's mind, his thought, even for a moment, would not be worthy of worship by the good.

“Samunnatena te satā,

Kathaṃ na te na te siyuṃ;

Yato nate’natepi’to,

Siyuṃ na te nate subhā”ti.

By you, who are ever exalted and good, how could they not be yours? Since, whether bowed or unbowed, they would not be other than yours, O beautiful one.

Idaṃ pādacatukkamajjhayamakamekarūpamabyapetabyapetaṃ.

This four-footed middle yamaka, of single form, is unseparated and separated.

Yato yena kāraṇena te tuyhaṃ satā sobhanena samunnatena sammā unnatena hetunā natepi avanatepi anatepi anavanatepi te te subhā te te sobhanā na na siyuṃ, bhavanteva, ato tena kāraṇena te subhā te sobhanā nate avanate kathaṃ na siyuṃ, bhavanteva.

Since, for which reason—by your good, exalted, rightly exalted cause—whether bowed or stooped, or unbowed or not stooped, those beautiful ones, those splendid ones, would indeed be yours, they are indeed so. Therefore, for that reason, how could those beautiful, splendid ones, when bowed or stooped, not be yours? They are indeed so.

“Jinaṃ paṇāmonatasajjanaṃ janaṃ,

Guṇe nivesentamasajjanaṃ’janaṃ;

Veneyyanette guṇabhājanaṃ janaṃ,

Name mamentaṃ khalu sajjanaṃjana”nti.

I bow to the Victor, revered by good people, who establishes people in virtues without clinging or negligence, who is an ointment for the eyes of the teachable, a vessel of virtues, the good person who is truly devoted to me.

Idaṃ pādacatukkantayamakamekarūpamabyapetabyapetayamakaṃ dukkaraṃ.

This four-footed end yamaka, of single form, is an unseparated and separated yamaka, difficult.

Paṇāmonatasajjanaṃ paṇāmitukāmonatasādhujanavantaṃ janaṃ veneyyajanaṃ asajja pamādamakatvā guṇe sīlādiguṇe nivesentaṃ niyojentaṃ veneyyanette añjanaṃ añjanabhūtaṃ guṇabhājanaṃ guṇānamādhārabhūtaṃ sajjanaṃjanaṃ iminā kāraṇena sādhujanānaṃ añjanabhūtaṃ janaṃ sādhujanaṃ khalu ekantena mamentaṃ mamāyantaṃ naṃ jinaṃ name namāmi.

I bow to that Victor (`naṃ jinaṃ name namāmi`), who has good people bowed down and desirous of paying homage (`paṇāmonatasajjanaṃ`); who, without clinging (`asajja`) and without negligence (`pamādamakatvā`), establishes and directs the teachable person (`veneyyajanaṃ`) in virtues, such as morality (`guṇe...`); who is an ointment for the eyes of the teachable (`veneyyanette añjanaṃ`), a vessel and foundation of virtues (`guṇabhājanaṃ...`); who is a good person, like an ointment for good people (`sajjanaṃjanaṃ`); and who is truly (`khalu`) devoted to me (`mamentaṃ`).

“Sābhāsu [M 0.0060] sābhā bhuvane jinassa,

Sābhāya sā bhāsatiyeva jātu;

Sābhāya sā bhāti na ce kathaṃ na,

Sābhā sasābhānamaticca bhātī”ti.

Among the existing splendors in the world is the beautiful splendor of the Victor; by that existing splendor, it certainly shines forth. If that splendor, being greater than the existing splendor, does not shine, how could it not shine, surpassing the beautiful splendors of those who have their own splendors? It shines indeed.

Idaṃ pādacatukkādiyamakekarūpabyapetaṃ.

This four-footed beginning yamaka is devoid of a single form.

Bhuvane sattaloke sābhāsu vijjamānābhāsu jinassa sābhā sobhanā ābhā sābhāya vijjamānāya, sobhanāya vā ābhāya ābhāto jātu ekantena bhāsatiyeva dippateva, sā jinābhā sābhāya vijjamānābhāto adhikā hutvā ce na bhāti yadi na bhāsati, sasābhānaṃ vijjamānasobhanābhānaṃ brahmādīnaṃ sābhā sobhanābhāyo aticca atikkamma kathaṃ na bhāti, bhāsatiyeva.

`Bhuvane` means in the world of beings (`sattaloke`); `sābhāsu` means in the existing splendors (`vijjamānābhāsu`); the Victor's `sābhā` is his beautiful splendor (`sobhanā ābhā`). By that existing (`vijjamānāya`) or beautiful (`sobhanāya`) splendor, it certainly (`jātu ekantena`) shines forth, it gleams forth (`bhāsatiyeva dippateva`). If that splendor of the Victor, having become greater than the existing splendor, does not shine, how could it not shine, surpassing the beautiful splendors of those, such as Brahma and others, who have their own existing beautiful splendors? It shines indeed.

“Na bhāsurā tepi surā vibhūsitā,

Tathāsurā bhūri surāparājitā;

Sabhāsu rājāpi tathā surājito,

Yathā surājanti surāvinissaṭā”ti.

Not radiant are those gods, though adorned, nor the many Asuras defeated by strong drink, nor a king in assemblies so well-adorned, as those who shine, released from strong drink.

Idaṃ pādacatukkamajjhayamakekarūpabyapetaṃ.

This four-footed middle yamaka is devoid of a single form.

Surāvinissaṭā surāpānato apagatā janā yathā surājanti, tathā vibhūsitā visesena alaṅkatā tepi surā te devā api na bhāsurā sobhamānā na honti, tathā evaṃ surāparājitā surāpānahetu parājitabhāvaṃ pattā bhūri asurā bahavo vepacittiādayo asurāpi na bhāsurā na sobhanti, tathā evaṃ surājito suṭṭhu alaṅkato rājāpi sabhāsu na bhāsuro.

As people who are released from strong drink, who have departed from drinking strong drink, shine well, so too those gods, though specially embellished, are not radiant, they do not shine. Likewise, the many Asuras, such as Vepacitti, who have attained a state of defeat due to drinking strong drink, are not radiant, they do not shine. In the same way, a king, though well-adorned, does not shine in assemblies.

“Jināṇattiyaṃ [M 0.0061] yo’hitāsā sitāsā,

Avassaṃva te hontya’tāsā hatāsā;

Ato sabbapāpe satāsā vatāsā,

Karonteva santissitā sāmitāsā”ti.

Those who have placed their hope in the Conqueror's instruction, who are pure in hope, assuredly they will be fearless, with craving destroyed. Therefore, fearing all evil, desiring blameless conduct, they act, relying on peace, desiring mastery.

Idaṃ pādacatukkantayamakamekarūpabyapetaṃ.

This four-footed end yamaka is devoid of a single form.

Ye sappurisā jināṇattiyaṃ buddhassa vinayapaññattisaṅkhātāṇattiyaṃ ohitāsā avītikkamavasena patiṭṭhitaāsā honti sitāsā parisuddhāsā, te sādhavo hatāsā anukkamena hatataṇhā avassaṃva ekanteneva atāsā bhayarahitā yato honti, ato tasmā sabbapāpe sabbākusale satāsā bhayasahitā vatāsāva niravajjavatābhilāsavanto sādhujanā santissitā santinissitāyo sāmitāsā sāmibhāvāsāyo karonteva.

Those good people who have placed their hope in the Conqueror's instruction—that is, the instruction known as the Buddha's Vinaya-enactment—who are established in hope by way of non-transgression, who are pure in hope; those good ones, with craving destroyed, having gradually destroyed craving, are certainly fearless, without fear, since they are so. Therefore, those good people, fearing all evil, all unwholesome things, desiring blameless conduct, relying on peace, desiring mastery, act.

33.

33.

Yamakaṃ taṃ paheḷī ca, nekantamadhurāni’ti;

Upekkhiyanti sabbāni, sissakhedabhayā mayā.

That yamaka and riddle, not entirely sweet, were all disregarded by me, fearing the vexation of the disciples.

33. Nanu yamakaṃ nāma kavīnaṃ sāmatthiyavisesasūcakanti tattha taṃ sopayogaṃ, paheḷikā ca sopayogā kīḷāvinodane sambādhaṭṭhānamantane parabyāmohane paramabyāmohane (ka.), kābyādāsa 3.97 ca, tasmā tattha kathamupekkhā bhavatoti āha “yamaka”ntiādi. Taṃ yathāvuttaṃ yamakañca sukaradukkarappabhedaṃ. Paheḷikā pana pubbācariyehi soḷasa niddiṭṭhā samāgatāvañcitādikā. Tatthidaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ –

33. Is not yamaka indeed a special indicator of the skill of poets? Therefore, it is useful there. And riddles are useful for amusement, for confidential conversation, and for deceiving others. Hence, why should indifference arise there? Thus, it is said, 'yamaka,' etc. That yamaka, as stated, is divided into easy and difficult types. However, riddles have been defined by the ancient teachers as sixteen, such as samāgata and vañcita. Here is their characteristic—

Samāgatā nāma siyā, guḷhatthā padasandhinā;

Vañcitāññattha ruḷhena, yattha saddena vañcanā.

Samāgatā, it is said, may be obscure in meaning through the combination of words; Vañcitā is where there is deception by a word that is commonly known elsewhere.

Ukkantātibyavahita-ppayogā [M 0.0062] mohakārinī;

Siyā pamussitā yassā, dubbodhatthā padāvali.

Ukkantā is a deluder due to its application being excessively separated; Pamussitā may be that whose sequence of words has a meaning that is difficult to understand.

Samānarūpā’mukhyatthā-ropāhitapadā siyā;

Pharusā paccayādīhi, jātasaddā kathañcipi.

Samānarūpā may be that whose words have an imputed meaning that is not primary; Pharusā is a harsh word, somehow produced from suffixes and so on.

Saṅkhyātā nāma saṅkhyānaṃ, yattha byāmohakāraṇaṃ;

Aññathā’bhāsate yattha, vākyattho sā pakappitā.

Saṅkhyātā is where numbers are the cause of confusion; Pakappitā is where the meaning of the sentence appears otherwise.

Sā nāmantarikā yassā, nāme nānatthakappanā;

Nibhūtā’vaṭṭhitaññatthā, tulyatthasutihetuto.

Nāmantarikā is that where there is an imputation of diverse meanings to a name; Nibhūtā is that whose meaning is established elsewhere, due to hearing a similar meaning.

Samānasaddā sā iṭṭha-saddapariyāyasādhitā;

Sammuḷhā mūḷhatāyeva, niddiṭṭhatthāpi sādhukaṃ.

Samānasaddā is that which is accomplished by a synonym of a desired word; Sammuḷhā is simply confusion, even when its meaning is well-defined.

Yassā sambandhabāhulyā, nāmaṃ sā pārihārikī;

Ekacchannā bhave byañjā-dheyyaṃ nissayagopanā.

Pārihārikī is that whose name is due to an abundance of connections; Ekacchannā may be that where the expression conceals the meaning by its support.

Sā bhave ubhayacchannā, yassā ubhayagopanā;

Saṃkiṇṇā nāma sā yassā, nānālakkhaṇasaṅkaroti.

Ubhayacchannā may be that which has a twofold concealment; Saṃkiṇṇā is that which has a mingling of diverse characteristics.

Dosattepi cesaṃ sabbesaṃ ukkantādīsu dosabhāve nāropitabbā. Esā hi manasoti (ka.) “bahuguṇe paṇamati”ccādinā subodhālaṅkāra 44 gāthā vākyasaṃkiṇṇanāmena na vuttā, pakappitā ca saṃsayadosaparihārena “yāte dutiyaṃ nilaya”nti subodhālaṅkāra 112 gāthā ādinā niddiṭṭhā.

Even if there is a fault among them, the state of being a fault should not be attributed to all of them, such as in Ukkantā and others. For this is not stated by the name 'mixed sentence,' as in 'bows to one of many virtues,' etc., but it is contrived and designated with the avoidance of the fault of doubt, as in 'he goes to the second abode,' etc.

“Pabhavā’natavittiṇṇā, tavā’ṇā mahatī sati;

Cirāya jayataṃ nātha, pahutaphalasādhanī”ti.

Powerful, unbent, widespread, your command, being great and accomplishing abundant fruit; O Lord, may you be victorious for a long time.

Ayaṃ samāgatā.

This is the Samāgatā.

“Bhaddamevo’paseveyya, [M 0.0063] vidhūtamadakibbisaṃ;

Sampāpaye puraṃ khemaṃ, sa danto’ttanisevina”nti.

One should associate only with the good person, who is rid of intoxication and defilements; that self-controlled one would cause the one who attends to himself to reach the secure city.

Ayaṃ vañcitā.

This is the Vañcitā.

Pamussitādayo tu lakkhaṇānusārena, tatthodāharaṇānusārena ca veditabbā.

But Pamussitā and others should be understood according to the characteristics, and also according to the examples given therein.

Evaṃ pubbācariyehi parikappitā paheḷikā ceti etāni sabbāni ekantena niyamena na madhurāni attharasassa vā saddarasassa vā kassaci abhāvena assāditabbāni na hontīti iminā kāraṇena sissānamuppanno khedoyeva bhayaṃ tato tesaṃ khedato vā uppannabhayato mayā upekkhiyantīti sambandhanīyaṃ.

Thus, all these riddles devised by ancient teachers are not invariably sweet, as they are not to be savored due to the absence of any flavor of meaning or flavor of sound. For this reason, the weariness that arises in the students is itself fear; therefore, it should be understood that they are disregarded by me on account of that weariness or the fear that arises from it.

33. Evaṃ sukaradukkaravasena duvidhattaṃ vatvā kavīnaṃ sāmatthiyappakāsane sappayojanayamakānañca, kīḷāvinodane sambādhaṭṭhānasammantane parabyāmohane cāti imesu sappayojanānañca paheḷikānamavacane kāraṇaṃ niddisati “yamaka”miccādinā. Taṃ yamakaṃ yathāvuttaṃ sukaradukkarādibhedaṃ yamakajātañca paheḷi ca pubbācariyehi niddiṭṭhā samāgabhādikā paheḷikā ca iti imāni sabbāni ekantamadhurāni na iti assādetabbassa attharasassa, saddarasassa vā niyamato abhāvā ekantena amadhurāni, iti iminā kāraṇena ca sissakhedabhayā sissānaṃ asahanasaṅkhātāya asahanena jātāya vā bhītiyā ca mayā upekkhīyanti. Sissānaṃ khedoyeva bhayaṃ, sissakhedato uppannaṃ vā bhayaṃ, tatoti viggaho.

33. Having thus explained their twofold division based on ease and difficulty, he indicates the reason for not mentioning beneficial yamakas and riddles—which serve purposes such as displaying the poets' skill, amusement, deliberation in confined places, and confusing others—with the phrase 'yamaka,' and so on. That yamaka, as described, with its divisions of easy and difficult, and the varieties of yamaka, and the riddles indicated by the ancient teachers, such as the Samāgatā and other riddles—all these are not entirely sweet. Because there is necessarily an absence of a savor of meaning or sound to be relished, they are entirely unsweet. For this reason, and from fear of wearying the students—that is, from the fear characterized as, or born from, the students' inability to endure—they are disregarded by me. The analysis is: 'The students' weariness is itself the fear,' or 'the fear arisen from the students' weariness.'

Ettha paheḷikā evaṃ daṭṭhabbā –

Herein, the riddle should be seen thus:

Samāgatā ca vañcitu-kkantā pamussitāpi ca;

Samānarūpā pharusā, saṅkhyātā ca pakappitā.

The Samāgatā, Vañcitā, Ukkantā, and also the Pamussitā; the Samānarūpā, Pharusā, Saṅkhyātā, and Pakappitā.

Athopi [M 0.0064] nāmantarikā, nibhūtā ca paheḷikā;

Atho samānasaddā ca, sammuḷhā pārihārikī;

Ekacchannobhayacchannā, saṃkiṇṇāti ca soḷasāti.

Furthermore, the Nāmantarikā and the Nibhūtā riddle; also the Samānasaddā, the Sammuḷhā, the Pārihārikī; the Ekacchannā, the Ubhayacchannā, and the Saṃkiṇṇā—thus there are sixteen.

Tatridaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ –

Therein, this is the definition:

Samāgatā nāma siyā, guḷhatthā padasandhinā;

Vañcitāññattha ruḷhena, yattha saddena vañcanā.

A Samāgatā, by name, is that which has a hidden meaning through the joining of words. A Vañcitā is where there is deception by a word that is established in another sense.

Ukkantātibyavahita-ppayogā mohakārinī;

Siyā pamussitā yassā, dubbodhatthā padāvali.

An Ukkantā, causing delusion, has an application of excessively separated terms. It is a Pamussitā whose sequence of words has a meaning that is difficult to understand.

Samānarūpā’mukhyatthā-ropāhitapadā siyā;

Pharusā paccayādīhi, jātasaddā kathañcipi.

A Samānarūpā is one that has words imposed with a non-primary meaning. A Pharusā has words produced in some way by suffixes and so forth.

Saṅkhyātā nāma saṅkhyānaṃ, yattha byāmohakāraṇaṃ;

Aññathā’bhāsate yattha, vākyattho sā pakappitā.

A Saṅkhyātā, by name, is that wherein counting is the cause of confusion. That is a Pakappitā wherein the meaning of the sentence appears otherwise.

Sā nāmantarikā yassā, nāme nānatthakappanā;

Nibhūtā’vaṭṭhitaññatthā, tulyatthasutihetuto.

That is a Nāmantarikā in whose name there is the contrivance of various meanings. A Nibhūtā has a different meaning established on account of hearing a similar meaning.

Samānasaddā sā iṭṭha-saddapariyāyasādhitā;

Sammuḷhā mūḷhatāyeva, niddiṭṭhatthāpi sādhukaṃ.

That is a Samānasaddā which is accomplished through synonyms of the desired word. A Sammuḷhā is simply confusion, even though its meaning is well indicated.

Yassā sambandhabāhulyā, nāmaṃ sā pārihārikī;

Ekacchannā bhave byañjā-dheyyaṃ nissayagopanā.

That is a Pārihārikī whose name comes from an abundance of connections. An Ekacchannā is the concealment of the basis, having manifested that which is contained.

Sā bhave ubhayacchannā, yassā ubhayagopanā;

Saṃkiṇṇā nāma sā yassā, nānālakkhaṇasaṅkaroti.

That is an Ubhayacchannā which has the concealment of both. That, by name, is a Saṃkiṇṇā which is a mixture of various characteristics.

Ayaṃ panettha attho – padasandhinā padānaṃ sandhānato guḷhatthā apākaṭatthā samāgatā nāma siyā. Guḷhatthāti pasiddhānuvādena apasiddhā samāgatā vidhīyate. Ito parampi anuvādānuvādyabhāvo evaṃ veditabbo. Yattha paheḷikāyaṃ aññattha ruḷhena saddena aññasmiṃ atthe pasiddhena ruḷhisaddena vañcanā vañcitā nāma siyā.

Herein, this is the meaning: by 'the joining of words' is meant due to the connection of words; having a hidden meaning, an unmanifest meaning, it is called Samāgatā. By the phrase 'having a hidden meaning,' the unfamiliar Samāgatā is defined by means of a familiar reference. Henceforth, the relationship between the reference and the referent should be understood in this way. Where, in a riddle, there is deception by a word established in another sense—that is, by a conventional word well-known in another meaning—it is called Vañcitā.

Atibyavahitappayogā [M 0.0065] atisayena antaritapayujjamānapadayuttā tatoyeva mohakārinī sammohakārikā paheḷikā ukkantā nāma. Yassā paheḷikāya padāvali padapanti dubbodhatthā duranubodhābhidheyyā, sā pamussitā nāma.

Having 'excessively separated usage' means it is endowed with words used with extreme separation; for that very reason it is 'delusion-causing,' that is, bewildering. Such a riddle is called Ukkantā. A riddle whose sequence of words, or line of words, has a meaning that is difficult to understand, that is, whose denotation is difficult to comprehend, is called Pamussitā.

Amukhyatthāropāhitapadā appadhānatthe mukhyatthapakāsakasaddānaṃ kiñci sadhammaṃ nissāya āropanato upaṭṭhitapadayuttā samānarūpā nāma siyā. Paccayādīhi paccayādesādīhi kathañcipi yena kenaci pakārena jātasaddā nipphannasaddā pharusā nāma.

Having 'words imposed with a non-primary meaning' means it is endowed with words that are present due to the imposition—relying on some shared quality—of words expressing a primary meaning onto a non-primary meaning; this is called Samānarūpā. By 'suffixes and so forth' is meant by suffixes, substitutions, and the like; 'in some way' means by whatever means; having 'produced words' means having derived words; this is called Pharusā.

Yattha yassaṃ paheḷikāyaṃ saṅkhyānaṃ gaṇanaṃ vuttamapi byāmohakāraṇaṃ hoti, sā paheḷikā saṅkhyātā nāma siyā. Yattha yassaṃ paheḷikāyaṃ vākyattho samudāyattho aññathā aññena pakārena ābhāsate viññāyate, sā pakappitā nāma.

Wherein, in a riddle, counting, that is, enumeration, even when stated, becomes a cause of confusion, that riddle is called Saṅkhyātā. Wherein, in a riddle, the sentence meaning, that is, the collective meaning, appears, that is, is understood, otherwise, that is, in a different way, that is called Pakappitā.

Yassā paheḷikāya nāme payuttābhidhāne nānatthakappanā vividhābhidheyyakappanā sambhavati, sā paheḷikā nāmantarikā nāma. Tulyatthasutihetuto samānatthasaddānaṃ payogahetuyā avaṭṭhitaññatthā patiṭṭhitaaññatthā hoti, sā nibhūtā nāma.

A riddle in whose name, that is, in the applied designation, a contrivance of various meanings, that is, a contrivance of various denotations, is possible, is called Nāmantarikā. 'On account of hearing a similar meaning' means due to the use of words with similar meaning; it 'has a different meaning established,' that is, a different meaning is founded; this is called Nibhūtā.

Yā paheḷikā iṭṭhasaddapariyāyasādhitā icchitatthasaddassa vevacanehi nipphāditā hoti, sā samānasaddā nāma. Sādhukaṃ niddiṭṭhatthāpi dassitaatthayuttāpiyā mūḷhatāyeva sammohabhāvatthaṃ eva bhavati, sā sammuḷhā nāma.

A riddle that is 'accomplished through synonyms of the desired word,' that is, which is produced by synonyms for the word with the desired meaning, is called Samānasaddā. Even though its 'meaning is well indicated,' that is, even though it is endowed with a demonstrated meaning, it is 'simply confusion,' that is, it exists for the sake of bewilderment; this is called Sammuḷhā.

Yassā paheḷikāya viracane nāmaṃ dassiyamānaṃ nāmaṃ sambandhabāhulyā sambandhassa bahulabhāvato bhavati, sā pārihārikī nāma. Yassā ādheyyaṃ byañja abhibyañjiya pakāsetvā [M 0.0066] nissayagopanā ādhāragutti bhavati, sā ekacchannā nāma.

A riddle in the composition of which the name, that is, the name being shown, arises from an 'abundance of connections,' that is, from the state of having many connections, is called Pārihārikī. A riddle in which, 'having manifested the contained'—that is, having revealed and shown the denoted meaning—there is 'concealment of the basis,' that is, the hiding of the support, is called Ekacchannā.

Yassā payoge ubhayagopanā ubhinnamādhārādheyyānaṃ gopanā bhavati, sā ubhayacchannā nāma. Yassā nānālakkhaṇasaṅkaro samāgatādinānāvidhalakkhaṇānaṃ saṅkaro hoti, sā saṃkiṇṇā nāma siyā.

A riddle in the application of which there is 'concealment of both,' that is, the concealment of both the support and the contained, is called Ubhayacchannā. A riddle which has a 'mixture of various characteristics,' that is, a mixture of the various kinds of characteristics of the Samāgatā and so forth, is called Saṃkiṇṇā.

Idāni samāgatādīnaṃ lakkhiyaṃ kamena evaṃ ñātabbaṃ –

Now, the examples for Samāgatā and so forth should be understood sequentially as follows:

“Pabhavā’natavittiṇṇā, tavā’ṇā mahatī satī;

Cirāya jayataṃ nātha, pahutaphalasādhinī”ti.

Powerful, unbent, widespread, your command, being great and accomplishing abundant fruit; O Lord, may you be victorious for a long time.

Ayaṃ samāgatā.

This is the confluence.

Nātha tava pabhavato paṭṭhāya natavittiṇṇā oṇatavasena patthaṭā, evaṃ sati nadī viya dissati. Pabhava pakaṭṭhatta sobhāvanta. Bho nātha tava tuyhaṃ mahatī satī mahantī samānā āṇā ānatavittiṇṇā attani natesu janesu patthaṭā pahutaphalasādhinī bahulatthanipphādanī cirāya cirakālaṃ jayataṃ ukkaṃsabhāvena pavattatu. Ettha pabhavaānataitisandhinā attho guḷho.

O protector, from your source, bowed and spread out in submission, it thus appears like a river. The source is excellent and resplendent. O lord, may your great command, being great, spread out among those who are bowed to you, accomplishing abundant fruit and producing many benefits, prevail victoriously in excellence for a long time. Here, the meaning is hidden by the euphonic combination of 'pabhava-ānata'.

“Bhaddamevo’paseveyya, vidhūtamadakibbisaṃ;

Sampāpaye puraṃ khemaṃ, sa danto’ttanisevita”nti.

One should associate only with the excellent, who is rid of the stain of intoxication; that tamed one, being served by oneself, leads to the secure city.

Ayaṃ vañcitā.

This is the deception.

Vidhūtamadakibbisaṃ vināsitamadadosaṃ bhaddameva mandapiya pindapissa (ka.) – bhaddajātikesu hatthīsu bhaddajātikahatthimeva upaseveyyāti vuttaṃ viya dissati. Bhaddameva uttamapurisameva seveyyāti attho. Sevanaṃ kimatthanti ce? Hatthipakkhe danto sikkhito so hatthi attanisevitaṃ attānaṃ bhajitaṃ janaṃ khemaṃ nibbhayaṃ puraṃ nagaraṃ sampāpeti. Purisapakkhe pana [M 0.0067] danto damito so ariyapuggalo attanisevitaṃ attānamupasevitaṃ janaṃ khemaṃ niddukkhaṃ puraṃ nibbānapuraṃ pāpeti. Ettha kavicchitauttamatthato aññena hatthiatthe ruḷhena saddena vañcanā nāma.

'Rid of the stain of intoxication' means having destroyed the fault of intoxication. 'Only the excellent' appears as if it is said, 'one should associate only with an excellent-bred elephant among excellent-bred elephants.' The meaning is: one should associate only with a supreme person. If it is asked, 'For what purpose is association?' In the case of the elephant, that tamed, trained elephant leads the person who has served it, who has resorted to it, to a safe, fearless city. But in the case of a person, that tamed, disciplined noble individual leads the person who has served him, who has resorted to him, to the safe, sorrowless city—the city of Nibbāna. Here, this is called deception by means of a word commonly known in another sense—the meaning of 'elephant'—different from the excellent meaning intended by the poet.

“Bahuguṇe paṇamati, dujjanānaṃpyayaṃ jano;

Hitaṃ pamudito niccaṃ, sugataṃ samanussara”nti.

This person bows to the one of many virtues, and also to the wicked; always rejoicing in what is beneficial, remember the Sugata.

Ayaṃ ukkantā. Imassattho upari āgamissati.

This is the evasive. Its meaning will come hereafter.

Byākiṇṇadosatte satipi paheḷikāruḷhattā esā iṭṭhā. Vuttañhi “paheḷikāyamāruḷhā, na hi duṭṭhā kiliṭṭhatā”ti. Iha sambandhīpadānaṃ aṭṭhānaṭṭhāpanena byavahitattaṃ hoti.

Although the fault of being scattered is present, this is desirable because it is established as a riddle. For it is said: 'When established in a riddle, impurity is not indeed a fault.' Here, there is separation due to the placing of related words in the wrong place.

“Mukhaphullaṃ giṅgamakaṃ, niyuruggatthanunnataṃ;

Paṭaccarī varaṃ poso, bhīruyā dhārayantiyā”ti.

A face-blossom, a giṅgamaka ornament, a bracelet, a breast-cloth, and a high ornament; a man wearing rags is better than a timid woman wearing these.

Ayaṃ pamussitā.

This is the forgotten.

Mukhaphullaṃ tilakādiṃ giṅgamakaṃ evaṃnāmakaṃ pasādhanaṃ niyuruggatthanunnataṃ niyuraṃ valayaṃ, uggatthanaṃ payodharapaṭaṃ, unnataṃ nalāṭapaṭādikaṃ, mukhato unnatābharaṇañca dhārayantiyā bhīruyā itthiyā paṭaccarī jiṇṇavatthanivāsī poso puriso varaṃ uttamo. Ettha bahupayogarahitehi saddehi racitattā atthassa duravabodhatā.

A face-blossom (such as a tilaka), an ornament named giṅgamaka, and the compound 'niyuruggatthanunnataṃ' meaning a bracelet (niyuraṃ), a breast-cloth (uggatthanaṃ), a forehead-band and the like (unnataṃ), and an ornament raised from the face—a man wearing rags, clothed in old garments, is better, superior, than a timid woman wearing these. Here, because it is composed of words rarely used, the meaning is difficult to understand.

“Nava’ggaratanāna’smiṃ, dissanti ratanākare;

Purisānettha aṭṭhannaṃ, aṭṭhā’sādhāraṇā’para”nti.

In this mine of jewels, nine supreme jewels are seen. Herein, eight are uncommon to eight persons, and another is common.

Ayaṃ samānarūpā.

This is the similar in form.

Asmiṃ ratanākare aggaratanāni nava dissanti, ettha imesu ratanesu aṭṭha ratanāni aṭṭhannaṃ purisānaṃ asādhāraṇāni, aparaṃ ratanaṃ sādhāraṇaṃ. Imāni nava lokuttarāni cittīkatādiatthena “ratanānī”ti ca tappabhavo sammāsambuddho [M 0.0068]“ākaro”ti ca kappitoti amukhyatthesu ratanādisaddānamāropanaṃ hoti.

In this mine of jewels, nine supreme jewels are seen; among these jewels, eight jewels are uncommon to eight persons, and the other jewel is common. These nine supramundane qualities are conceived of as 'jewels' in the sense of being venerated and so forth, and the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, their source, is conceived of as the 'mine'—thus there is a superimposition of words like 'jewel' and so on in non-primary senses.

“Vindanti devagandhabbā, himavantamahātale;

Rasavante sare satta, na nāgāpi uposathā”ti.

Devas and gandhabbas find, on the great plateau of the Himavanta, seven pleasant lakes; not even the nāgas who observe the Uposatha find them.

Ayaṃ pharusā.

This is the harsh.

Himavantamahātale himālayassa matthake rasavante sodake satta sare anotattādike devagandhabbā vindanti sevanti, uposathā nāgāpi na vindanti. Ayamaparattho. Himavantamahātale candaraṃsiyutte mahāpāsādatale devagandhabbā kīḷamānā gandhabbā rasavante madhuraguṇayutte satta sare vīṇāya chajjādike satta sare vindanti, nāgāpi ariyāpi uposathāpi upavutthāpi na vindanti nānubhavanti. Ettha dibbantīti devā. Uposatho etesamatthīti uposathāti viggaho. Lakkhaṇakkamato pasiddhapacurapayogato aññadatthā yena kenaci lesena paccayādīnaṃ jātasaddassa atthitā.

On the great plateau of the Himavanta, at the summit of the Himalayas, devas and gandhabbas find and frequent the seven lakes, beginning with Anotatta, which are pleasant and have good water; not even the nāgas who observe the Uposatha find them. This is the other meaning. On the great plateau of the Himavanta, that is, on the moonlit floor of a great palace, devas (those who sport) and gandhabbas, while playing, find the seven notes of the vīṇā, beginning with chajja, which are pleasant and endowed with sweet quality. Not even the nāgas, nor the noble ones, nor those observing the Uposatha, nor those who have kept the fast, find or experience them. Here, 'devā' is from 'they sport' (dibbanti). 'Uposathā' is the analysis for 'they have the Uposatha.' By some pretext, deviating from the sequence of grammatical rules and from well-known and abundant usage, there is the existence of another meaning for a word formed from suffixes and so on.

“Gītasadde sarā dve dve, dve chajjaññatra chassarā;

Pañcavaṇṇaṃ yathā cakkhu, chabbaṇṇā nāsikā tathā”ti.

In the sound of song, there are two vowels, two. Apart from chajja, the six notes are two. As the eye is of five colors, so the nose is of six colors.

Ayaṃ saṅkhyātā.

This is the enumeration.

Gītasadde sarā dve honti, chajja’ññatra chajjato aññatra chajjaṃ vajjetvā usabho gandhāro majjhimo pañcamo dhevato nisādoti. Ettha yugaḷato dve dve chassarā chasaravanto. Yathā cakkhu pañcavaṇṇaṃ hoti, tathā evaṃ nāsikā chabbaṇṇā hoti, gītasadde īkāraakārasaradvayasabbhāvato ca chajjaṃ ṭhapetvā usabhādīsu sarānaṃ tividhattā ca “cakkhū”ti sarabyañjanavasena pañcavaṇṇānaṃ sabbhāvato ca “nāsikā”ti channaṃ sabbhāvato ca evaṃ vuttaṃ. Ettha vuttasaṅkhyāgītādisaddasanniṭṭhānato sammohakārinī hoti.

In the word 'gītasadda' (sound of song), there are two vowels. Apart from chajja—that is, excluding chajja—there are usabha, gandhāra, majjhima, pañcama, dhevata, and nisāda. Here, in pairs, there are two by two, having six notes. As 'cakkhu' (eye) is of five letters, so 'nāsikā' (nose) is of six letters. It is stated thus because of the existence of two vowels, ī-kāra and a-kāra, in the word 'gītasadda'; and because the notes beginning with usabha, setting aside chajja, are of three kinds; and because in the word 'cakkhu' there is the existence of five letters by way of vowels and consonants; and because in the word 'nāsikā' there is the existence of six. Here, the stated enumeration is bewildering due to the determination of words like 'gīta' and so on.

“Pātu [M 0.0069] vo udito rājā, sirimā rattamaṇḍalo;

Sakantigahanakkhatta-saṅghayutto sulakkhaṇo”ti.

May the arisen king protect you, glorious, with a red orb, endowed with his own bright and dense assembly of constellations, possessing auspicious marks.

Ayaṃ pakappitā.

This is the conceived.

Sirimā sirimanto rattamaṇḍalo anurattajanapadamaṇḍalo, anurattaamaccamaṇḍalo vā sakantigahanakkhattasaṅghayutto sakassa attano ante samīpe gahanehi aviraḷehi khattasaṅghehi khattiyasamūhehi yutto saṃyutto sulakkhaṇo pasatthapurisalakkhaṇo udito pasiddho rājā narindo vo tumhe pātu rakkhatūti ayaṃ anadhippetattho. Sirimā “lakkhiyā vāsaṭṭhānattā”ti vuttattā sirimanto rattamaṇḍalo uggamane rattamaṇḍalo sakantigahanakkhattasaṅghayutto kantisahitehi gahanakkhattatāragaṇehi yutto sulakkhaṇo suṭṭhu sasalakkhaṇo udito uggato rājā cando vo tumhe pātūti ubhayapakkhassa sādhāraṇaguṇaguṇīpadapariggahena idha vākyatthassa aññathā dissamānatā hoti.
