‘Glorious’ (sirimā), that is, possessed of glory; ‘with a red orb’ (rattamaṇḍalo), that is, with a circle of devoted countries, or a circle of devoted ministers; ‘endowed with his own dense assembly of khattiyas’ (sakantigahanakkhattasaṅghayutto), that is, united with dense, unseparated groups of warriors near himself; ‘possessing auspicious marks’ (sulakkhaṇo), that is, distinguished by the marks of an excellent man; the ‘arisen’ (udito), renowned king, the lord of men—‘may he protect you’—this is the unintended meaning. ‘Glorious’ (sirimā), that is, possessed of glory because it is said to be ‘the dwelling place of fortune’; ‘with a red orb’ (rattamaṇḍalo), that is, with a red orb at rising; ‘endowed with his own bright and dense assembly of constellations’ (sakantigahanakkhattasaṅghayutto), that is, united with dense groups of stars and constellations accompanied by brightness; ‘possessing auspicious marks’ (sulakkhaṇo), that is, well-marked with the sign of the hare; the ‘arisen’ (udito), risen king, the moon—‘may he protect you.’ Here, by adopting terms for qualities and the qualified that are common to both sides, the meaning of the statement appears differently.

“Vuccatā’do isitye’ko, sumahantopakāravā;

Sanātano ca na isi, na sakhā na sanātano”ti.

In the beginning, one is called 'isi' (sage), of very great benefit; and eternal, yet not an isi, not a friend, not eternal.

Ayaṃ nāmantarikā.

This is the name-riddle.

Eko ādo pubbe “isī”ti vuccati, sumahantopakāravā atimahantopakārasamannāgato sanātano ca sassato ca hoti, tathāpi na isi isi nāma na hoti, na sakhā mittopi na hoti, na sanātano sassatopi na hoti, ayaṃ gamyamānattho. Sumahā atimahanto eko ādo nāmādimhi isīti vuccati, anto majjhe pakāravā pa-kārena samannāgato, sanātano ca sassato ca hoti, isipi nāma na hoti, mittopi na hoti, so nātano tanaiti akkharadvayarahito na [M 0.0070] hoti. Ādimajjhānaṃ vuttattā anteti ñāyati, “isipatanavihāro”ti gahetabbaṃ. Tattha isipatananāmena isiādīnaṃ gamyamānatthattā nānatthakappanā hoti.

One is called 'isi' (sage) in the beginning, endowed with very great benefit, and is eternal and everlasting. Yet, it is not an isi, not a friend, and not eternal—this is the meaning to be understood. The great, immense one is called 'isi' at the beginning of its name; in the middle, it possesses 'pa', being endowed with the syllable 'pa'; and it is eternal. It is not called an isi, nor is it a friend. It is not 'nātano', that is, it is not without the two syllables 'tana'. Since the beginning and middle have been stated, the end is understood. 'Isipatanavihāra' should be taken as the answer. There, by the name 'Isipatana', because the meaning to be understood is that of the sages and so on, there is a contrivance of different meanings.

“Dhāvantaṃ udayā atthaṃ, muhuttaṃ na nivattati;

Na candamaṇḍalaṃ etaṃ, nāpi ādiccamaṇḍala”nti.

Running from rising to setting, it does not turn back for a moment; this is neither the orb of the moon, nor the orb of the sun.

Ayaṃ nibhūtā.

This is the concealed.

Udayā udayato pabhuti atthaṃ yāva atthaṃ dhāvantaṃ javantaṃ muhuttaṃ muhuttakālaṃ na nivattati na punāvattati. Etaṃ candamaṇḍalampi na hoti, ādiccamaṇḍalampi na hoti. Udayā paṭisandhito atthaṃ yāvacuti. Dhāvantanti āyukiccato āyucandādīnamatthānaṃ, tappakāsakasaddānañca tulyattā ettha patiṭṭhitacandādiatthantarānaṃ sambhavo.

From the rising, from the very rising, until the setting, running swiftly, hastening, it does not turn back for a moment, for a short time; it does not return again. This is neither the orb of the moon, nor the orb of the sun. From the arising, from rebirth, until the setting, until death. The word 'running swiftly' refers to the activity of life, to the end of the life-span, the moon, and so forth; and because the words that indicate them are similar, there is here the possibility of other established meanings pertaining to the moon and so on.

“Deviṃ kittimahīnāmaṃ, kaḷāratthavhayaṃ puriṃ;

Hitvā na sari so dhīro, karontopyu’yyamavhaya”nti karontomuttamavhayanti (ka.).

"Having abandoned the queen named Kittimahī, and the city called Kaḷārattha, that wise one did not remember them, though making the effort called 'Uyyama'."

Ayaṃ samānasaddā.

This is a homonymic riddle.

Kittimahīnāmaṃ kittimahīnaṃ dvinnaṃ nāmena samannāgataṃ deviṃ aggamahesiṃ kaḷāratthavhayaṃ puriṃ kaḷāraatthānaṃ dvinnaṃ nāmena samannāgataṃ puriṃ nagarañca so dhīro hitvā pariccajitvā uyyamavhayaṃ uyyamanāmena samannāgataṃ karonto api na sari sampattiṃ nānusari, yasodharādeviñca kapilavatthupuriñca hitvā vīriyasaṅkhātapadhānaṃ karonto mahāsatto sampattiṃ na sari, etthābhimatayasodharādisaddānaṃ pariyāyehi kittimahīsaddādīhi racitatā.

The queen, the chief consort, endowed with the two names Kittimahī and Kittimahīna; and the city called Kaḷārattha, a city endowed with the two names Kaḷāra and Attha—that wise one, having abandoned and renounced them, though making an effort called 'Uyyama,' endowed with the name Uyyama, did not remember prosperity, did not recall it. The Great Being, having abandoned Queen Yasodharā and the city of Kapilavatthu, while making the exertion known as energy, did not remember prosperity. Here, the intended words such as Yasodharā are constructed by means of synonyms with words such as Kittimahī.

“Catuddisāmukhā bandhā, cattāro sindhavā sayaṃ;

Paribhuñjanti nikkhittaṃ, tiṇaṃ majjhe yathāsukha”nti.

"Bound facing the four directions, four Sindhu horses of their own accord enjoy the grass placed in the middle, at their pleasure."

Ayaṃ sammuḷhā.

This is a bewildering riddle.

Sindhavā [M 0.0071] cattāro assā catuddisāmukhā yathā catuddisāsammukhā honti, tathā bandhā majjhe nikkhittaṃ tiṇaṃ sayaṃ yathāsukhaṃ paribhuñjanti, aññamaññaṃ piṭṭhiṃ katvā bandhā viya khāyati, te pana sammukhaṃ katvā bandhā honti. Ettha “catuddisāmukhābandhā”ti niddiṭṭhattā piṭṭhiṃ katvā bandhāti sammuḷhatā hoti.

The four Sindhu horses, bound so as to face the four directions, of their own accord enjoy the grass placed in the middle at their pleasure. It appears as if they are bound back-to-back, but they are in fact bound facing one another. Here, because it is specified as 'bound facing the four directions,' the bewilderment is that they are bound back-to-back.

“Jano jīvanajānanda-karabandhussa bhāsitaṃ;

Sakkarontova pappoti, puññārikkhayagocare”ti.

"By honoring the words spoken by the friend who brings joy to life, one attains to the sphere of the destruction of the enemies of merit."

Ayaṃ pārihārikī.

This is an enigmatic riddle.

Jīvanajānandakarabandhussa jīvanato udakato jātānaṃ padumānaṃ ānandakarassa sūriyassa bandhussa sammāsambuddhassa bhāsitaṃ vacanaṃ sakkaronto pūjento jano puññārikkhayagocare puññānaṃ paṭipakkhattā puññārisaṅkhātānaṃ akusalānaṃ khayassa nimittabhūtaṃ nibbānamārammaṇaṃ katvā uppanne maggaphale pappoti pāpuṇāti. Ettha jīvanajānaṃ ānandakarassa bandhusseti ca, puññārīnaṃ khayanimittaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavatteti ca iminā buddho maggaphalā ca pārampariyena sambandhena vuttāti sambandhānaṃ bāhullabhāvo.

A person who honors and reveres the words spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened One—who is the friend of the sun, the bringer of joy to the lotuses born from water (life)—attains the arisen path and fruit by taking as object Nibbāna, which is the sign for the destruction of the unwholesome states known as 'enemies of merit' because they are opposed to merit. Here, by the phrases 'the friend of the bringer of joy to that which is born of life' and 'proceeding by taking as object the sign of the destruction of the enemies of merit,' the Buddha, the path, and the fruit are spoken of through a successive connection; thus, there is an abundance of connections.

“Na gaṇhāti mahantampi, saddaṃ na ca vibhūsanaṃ;

Catuppadassa kassāpi, kaṇṇoyaṃ na kilāphalo”ti.

"It does not grasp even a great sound, nor an ornament. This ear of any four-footed creature is not indeed fruitless."

Ayaṃ ekacchannā.

This is a single-concealed riddle.

Kassāpi catuppadassa kaṇṇo mahantampi saddaṃ na gaṇhāti, ārammaṇaṃ na karoti, vibhūsanampi na gaṇhāti. Tathāpi ayaṃ kaṇṇo aphalo na kila, saphalato nipphalo na hoti kira. Assakaṇṇo rukkho. Ettha kaṇṇoti ādheyyaṃ katvā tadādhārassa avacanato nissayagutti.

The ear of any four-footed creature does not grasp even a great sound, does not take it as an object, nor does it grasp an ornament. Yet this ear is indeed not fruitless; it is not, it seems, without fruit in comparison to that which is fruitful. The Assakaṇṇa is a tree. Here, by making 'ear' the attribute, and by not stating its substrate, there is concealment of the basis.

“Alaṅkaronto [M 0.0072] bhuvanaṃ, sassiriko sadevakaṃ;

Kasmiṃ sañjātasaṃvaddho, ko kena nupalimpatī”ti.

"Adorning the world, glorious, together with its gods; in what is he born and nurtured? Who is not smeared by what?"

Ayaṃ ubhayacchannā.

This is a double-concealed riddle.

Sassiriko sadevakaṃ bhuvanaṃ alaṅkarontoti buddho viya khāyati. Bhuvanaṃ bhuvanasaṅkhātaṃ kaṃ jalaṃ sadā eva alaṅkaronto sassiriko lakkhiyasamannāgato kasmiṃ jale sañjātasaṃvaddho ko kataro kena jalena na upalimpati na limpati. Padumoti visajjanaṃ. Padumo hi puṃnapuṃsakaliṅgo. Iha jalapadumānaṃ dvinnampi chāditattā ubhayacchannā nāma.

'Adorning the world, glorious, together with its gods'—this appears like the Buddha. The meaning is this: Always adorning the water (kaṃ), which is also called 'world' (bhuvana); glorious, endowed with fortune; born and grown in which water; which one is not smeared, not stained, by which water? The answer is: the lotus. For the word 'lotus' (paduma) is of both masculine and neuter gender. Here, because both the water and the lotus are concealed, it is called 'double-concealed'.

“Ādo soyeva yo ante, majjhimassādi majjhimo;

Siddhantādīsu vattantaṃ, asaṅkhatapadaṃ vadā”ti.

"He who is at the end is the very one at the beginning; the middle one is the beginning of the middle. Speak of the unconditioned state, which exists in doctrines and the like."

Ayaṃ saṃkiṇṇā.

This is a mixed riddle.

Ante avasāne yo hoti, ādopi soyeva hoti, majjhimassa ādibhūto majjhimo eva hoti, siddhaṃ nipphannaṃ tādīsu ariyesu vattantaṃ asaṅkhatapadaṃ vada kathehīti ayamaparattho. Ādo ādimhi soyeva sakāro eva ante pariyosāne yo yakāroyeva, majjhimo majjhimavaṇṇo majjhimassa saddassa ādi makāro, siddhantādīsu matasamayakālādīsu vattantaṃ vācakabhāvena pavattantaṃ asaṅkhatapadaṃ saṅkhatato aññattā asaṅkhatabhūtaṃ paññattiṃ vada kathehīti. Samayasaddo hi nāmapaññatti. Ettha siddhantasaddena ādisaddassa saṅgahitattā tādiattho labbhatīti atthassa guḷhatāya samāgatālakkhaṇena ca “so”ti “yo”ti “asaṅkhatapada”nti aññattharuḷhasaddena vañcitattā vañcitālakkhaṇena ca samayasadde nānatthakappanato nāmantarikālakkhaṇena cāti tīhipi lakkhaṇehi missitoti. Sesesupi saṃkiṇṇattaṃ evameva [M 0.0073] veditabbaṃ. Tattha tattha vuttalakkhaṇānusāreneva samāgatādīnaṃ anvatthasaññatā veditabbā.

He who is at the end, at the conclusion, that very one is also at the beginning; the middle one itself is the beginning of the middle. Speak, declare the unconditioned state, which exists among such accomplished noble ones—this is the other meaning. At the beginning, at the very start, is that very 'sa' sound; at the end, at the conclusion, is that very 'ya' sound. The middle letter, 'ma', is the beginning of the word 'middle' (majjhima). Speak, declare the designation which, being other than the conditioned, is unconditioned, and which exists in doctrines, conventions, times, and so forth, prevailing as a term. For the word 'samaya' is a nominal designation. Here, because the meaning 'such' is obtained from the word 'doctrine' (siddhanta) being taken together with 'and so on' (ādi), there is the characteristic of 'convergence' due to the obscurity of the meaning. And because one is misled by words established with other meanings, such as 'so,' 'yo,' and 'asaṅkhatapada,' there is the characteristic of 'deception.' And because various meanings are assigned to the word 'samaya,' there is the characteristic of 'polysemy.' Thus, it is mixed with these three characteristics. The mixed nature of the remaining examples should be understood in the same way. In each case, the conventional names 'convergence' and so on should be understood according to the characteristics described.

34.

34.

Desakālakalāloka-ñāyāgamavirodhi yaṃ;

Taṃ virodhipadaṃ ce’ta-mudāharaṇato phuṭaṃ.

That which contradicts place, time, art, worldly convention, logic, and scripture, that is a contradictory term; and this is clear from the example.

34. “Desi”ccādi. Deso thalajaladesādi. Kālo rattindivo. Kalā naccagītādayo. Loko carācarabhūtappavatti. Ñāyo yutti. Āgamo idha buddhavacanaṃ. Aññattha tu sutidhammasaṃhitā, te ca. Tehi virodho assa atthīti desa…pe… virodhi. Yanti anuvaditvā. Taṃ virodhipadanti vidhīyate. Etañca padaṃ udāharaṇato lakkhiyato phuṭaṃ pākaṭaṃ. Yato jalajādīnaṃ thalādīsu pātubhāvādi, ratyādīsu sambhavantānaṃ kusumādīnaṃ divādīsu sambhavo ca, “naccagītādicatusaṭṭhiyā kalāsu bhinnachajjo nāma sattasaro”tiādinā kalāsatthābhihitalakkhaṇātikkamavirodho ca, “aggisītalo, nissāro khadiro”tiādinā lokasīmātikkamo ca, vuttāyapā’naruppattasamuppattiyā middhassa rūpabhāvāpādanādiñāyavirodho ca, yathāsakamāgamena virodho ca sukhena ca sakkā pākaṭattā viññātuṃ, tato sabbametaṃ nodāhaṭanti adhippāyo.

34. "Desa," etc. "Desa" refers to regions such as land and water. "Kāla" means night and day. "Kalā" refers to the arts, such as dance and music. "Loka" denotes the way of mobile and immobile beings. "Ñāya" means logic. "Āgama" here refers to the word of the Buddha. Elsewhere, however, it refers to the collections of sacred lore and treatises. That which has a contradiction with these is 'contradictory to place... etc.' Having repeated the word 'that which,' 'that is a contradictory term' is designated. And this term is clear and manifest from the example and the thing exemplified. Since the appearance of aquatic beings on land, the occurrence in the daytime of flowers that bloom at night, the contradiction of transgressing the characteristics stated in the treatises on the arts (such as 'in the sixty-four arts of dance and music, the seven notes are called bhinnachajjo'), the transgression of worldly convention (such as 'fire is cold' or 'the khadira tree is without pith'), the contradiction of logic (such as attributing the nature of form to torpor, which has been stated to be without such arising and origination), and contradiction with one's own scriptures can all be easily understood due to their obviousness, the intention is not to provide examples for all of them.

34. Evaṃ yamakapaheḷikānamadassane kāraṇaṃ vatvā idāni uddesakkamena sampattavirodhidosaṃ “desakāli”ccādinā vadati. Yaṃ padaṃ deso thalajalapabbatādi. Kālo rattindivo hemantādivasena tividho, vasantādivasena chabbidho. Kalā naccagītādicatusaṭṭhi. Loko thāvarajaṅgamabhūtapavattisaṅkhāto. Ñāyo yutti. Āgamo iha buddhavacanaṃ, aññattha pana sutidhammasaṃhito ca. Tehi virodho assa atthīti desa…pe… virodhi. Taṃ virodhipadaṃ nāma. [M 0.0074] Etaṃ virodhipadaṃ udāharaṇato lakkhiyato phuṭaṃ paribyattaṃ. Vassikajātisumanādīnaṃ jalajādibhāvo ca, padumakumudādīnaṃ thalajādibhāvo ca, rattiādīsu labbhamānānaṃ kumudādīnaṃ divādīsu sambhavo ca, naccagītādicatusaṭṭhiyā kalāsu “chajjo usabho gandhāro majjhimo pañcamo dhevato nisādo”ti dassitasattasarānamekadesassa chajjassa bhinnasattasaro chajjo nāmāti samudāyavasena vohārakaraṇādīhi satthāgatataṃ, lakkhaṇātikkamañca, “aggi sītalo, candanaṃ uṇhaṃ, khadirarukkho nissāro, eraṇḍo sasāro” iccādinā lokamariyādātikkamo ca, middhassa arūpabhāvupapattiyā vuttāyapi rūpabhāvasādhanasadisayuttivirodhikathanañca, yathāsakamāgamamatikkamma kathanañcāti sabbesaṃ viruddhasabhāvassa pākaṭattā udāharaṇaṃ na dassayissāmāti adhippāyo. Imesameva desādivirodhīnamaviruddhattaṃ ettheva virodhipadadosaparihāre “bodhisattappabhāvenā”ticcādinā dissati. Desa…pe… gamehi virodho, so assa atthīti desa…pe… virodhi. Nindāyaṃ ayamassatthīti vivacchitā.

34. Having thus explained the reason for not showing examples of riddles with double meanings, he now, following the order of exposition, points out the fault of contradiction that has arisen, by saying, “desakāli,” and so on. Place (desa) is land, water, mountains, and so on. Time (kāla) is threefold by way of night and day, winter, and so on; or sixfold by way of spring, and so on. Art (kalā) refers to the sixty-four arts such as dance and song. The world (loka) is reckoned as the occurrence of stationary and moving beings. Reason (ñāya) is logic. Scripture (āgama) here is the word of the Buddha; elsewhere, however, it is also the compilation of teachings that have been heard. If there is a contradiction with these, it is called a 'desa…pe… virodhi' (contradictory to place, etc.). That is called a contradictory term. This contradictory term is plain and clear from examples and characteristics. For instance: the aquatic nature of vassikā and sumanā flowers, etc.; the terrestrial nature of lotuses and lilies, etc.; the occurrence in the daytime of lilies, etc., that are found at night, etc.; and in the sixty-four arts of dance, song, etc., its being found in treatises through conventional usage based on the whole, etc., that 'bhinnasattasaro chajjo' is the name for a part of the note 'chajjo' among the seven notes shown as 'chajjo, usabho, gandhāro, majjhimo, pañcamo, dhevato, nisādo', and the transgression of the characteristic; and the transgression of worldly convention, such as “fire is cold, sandalwood is hot, the khadira tree is without essence, the eraṇḍa tree has essence”; and the statement that contradicts reasoning, similar to proving the existence of form for torpor, even though its arising as formless has been stated; and speaking beyond one’s own tradition—due to the obviousness of the contradictory nature of all these, the intention is not to show examples. The non-contradiction of these very contradictions of place, etc., is seen here in the remedy for the fault of contradictory terms, as stated in “by the power of the Bodhisatta,” and so on. Contradiction with place… village—if it exists, it is called 'desa…pe… virodhi.' This is intended to be said in censure.

35.

35.

Ya’dappatīta’mānīya, vattabbaṃ neyyamāhu taṃ;

Yathā sabbāpi dhavalā, disā rocanti rattiyaṃ.

That which is unclear and must be brought forth to be explained, they call 'that which is to be inferred'; just as all directions shine white at night.

35. “Ya”miccādi. Appatītaṃ saddato, atthato vā anadhigataṃ nahyaññathāvagamo ganthantarābhāvato. Vakkhati hi “dullabhāvagatī sadda-sāmatthiyavilaṅghinī”ti. Yaṃ kiñci padaṃ samānīya ānetvā vattabbaṃ, taṃ neyyamāhu. Yathetyudāharati. Sabbāpi sakalāpi disā pubbadisādayo dasa disā rattiyaṃ rajanyaṃ dhavalā ujjalā rocanti dippantīti ettake niddiṭṭhe candamarīcino ettha neyyattaṃ.

35. “Yaṃ,” etc. “Appatītaṃ” means unclear in sound or meaning, not grasped, for there is no other understanding due to the absence of other texts. For it will be said: “Rare is the understanding that transcends the power of words.” Whatever word must be brought forth and explained, they call 'neyya' (to be inferred). He gives an example: When it is stated that 'all directions, the ten directions such as the eastern direction, are white, radiant, shining, blazing at night,' here lies the inferability of the moon's rays.

35. Idāni neyyadosamudāharati “ya”miccādinā. Yaṃ padaṃ appatītaṃ padantarena, tenābhihitatthena vā “imassatthoya”miti [M 0.0075] aviññātaṃ ānīya vattabbaṃ, tatoyeva padantaramānīya vattabbaṃ hoti, taṃ neyyamāhu “neyyadoso”ti porāṇā āhu. Yathā tatthodāharaṇamīdisaṃ “sabbāpi dhavalā disā rocanti rattiya”nti. Sabbāpi disā pubbadakkhiṇādayo dasa disā dhavalā setā rattiyaṃ rajanyaṃ rocanti dippanti. Ettha disāya visesanaṃ dhavalaguṇaṃ kelāsakūṭasudhābhitticandaraṃsiādīsu kuto sañjātamiti anicchitattā aññanivattanatthaṃ candakiraṇādivācakapadaṃ ānetvā dhavalatā imineti vattabbattā dhavala padaṃ neyyadosena duṭṭhaṃ hoti. Patītaṃ viññātaṃ, na patītaṃ appatītaṃ. Ettha akāro pasajjapaṭisedhe.

35. Now, he illustrates the fault called “neyya” with “yaṃ,” and so on. A word that is unclear—whose meaning is not understood as 'this is its meaning' either through another word or through what is expressed by it, and which therefore must be explained by bringing in another word—they call 'neyya'; the ancients called it the 'fault of what is to be inferred' (neyyadosa). An example of this is: 'All the white directions shine at night.' Here, 'all directions' refers to the ten directions—east, south, and so on—which are white (dhavalā) and shine (rocanti) at night (rattiyaṃ). In this context, the qualifier 'white' (dhavalaguṇaṃ) for 'directions' is unclear—from where does this quality of whiteness arise, such as from snow-capped peaks, whitewashed walls, or moonbeams? Since it is not determined, to negate other possibilities, one must bring in a word expressing moonbeams, etc., and explain that 'whiteness' is due to that. Thus, the word 'white' (dhavala) is flawed due to the fault of 'neyya.' 'Patītaṃ' means understood; 'na patītaṃ' means 'appatītaṃ' (unclear). Here, the 'a-' prefix is for negation of a predicate (pasajjapaṭisedhe).

36.

36.

Nedisaṃ bahu maññanti, sabbe sabbattha viññuno;

Dullabhā’vagatī sadda-sāmatthiyavilaṅghinī.

All the wise everywhere do not esteem such a thing much; rare is the understanding that transcends the power of words.

36. Appatītaṃ nicchanti viññūti dassetumāha “ne”tiādi. Īdisaṃ anantare vuttappakāraṃ neyyaṃ sabbepi viññuno ñeyyavidū sabbattha gajjādike na bahu maññanti na sambhāventi nappayujjanti. Kiṃ na bahumaññantīti ce āha “dullabhā”tiādi. Tathā hi avagatī atthāvagamo saddaṃ vācakaṃ, sāmatthiyañca ñāyaṃ vilaṅghayati cajati anupadassanatoti saddasāmatthiyavilaṅghinī dullabhā na labhyate. Ñāyopattho vā saddopattho vā yottho na hoti. So nappatīyate yathā manasi avaṭṭhitamattenāti attho. Tasmā saddato, atthato vā patītabbamaneyyaṃ, tabbiparītaṃ neyyanti viññeyyaṃ.

36. To show that the wise do not approve of what is unclear, he says 'ne,' etc. All the wise, who are knowers of what is to be known, do not esteem, value, or employ such an inferential expression much anywhere, in prose, etc. If asked why they do not esteem it much, he says, “dullabhā,” etc. For understanding (avagatī), namely, the understanding of the meaning, which transcends the word as signifier and capacity as logic, abandoning demonstration, is difficult to attain, it is not found. That meaning which is not supported by logic or by words is not understood merely by being established in the author's mind—this is the meaning. Therefore, it should be understood that what is to be understood through words or meaning is not 'neyya' (to be inferred), while its opposite is 'neyya'.

36. Imaṃ appatītapadaṃ viññūhi nābhimatanti dassento āha “nedisa”miccādi. Īdisaṃ yathāvuttappakāraṃ neyyaṃ sabbe viññuno sabbattha gajjapajjādike na bahu maññanti na sambhāventi nappayojenti. Avagatī atthāvabodho saddasāmatthiyavilaṅghinī [M 0.0076] saddasaṅkhātavācakañca sāmatthiyasaṅkhātañāyañca atikkamma pavattinī dullabhā tādisapayogābhāvato dullabhā hoti. Yo attho saddāgato, ñāyāgato vā na hoti, so kattuno manasi patiṭṭhitamattena patīto na hotīti taṃ padaṃ neyyadosamiti sabbe kavino pariharantīti adhippāyo. Bahumānaṃ karontīti vākye bahumaññantīti nāmadhātu. Saddasāmatthiyaṃ vilaṅghayati sīlenāti saddasāmatthiyavilaṅghinī.

36. To indicate that this unclear term is not approved of by the wise, he says “nedisaṃ,” and so on. All the wise do not esteem, approve, or employ such an inferential expression of the aforementioned kind much anywhere, in prose, verse, etc. Understanding (avagatī), the comprehension of meaning, which proceeds by transcending the signifier designated as 'word' and the logic designated as 'capacity', is difficult to obtain because such usage is absent. A meaning that is not derived from the word or from logic is not understood merely by being established in the author's mind; thus, all poets avoid such a term as having the fault of being 'neyya'—this is the intention. In the sentence 'they show great esteem,' 'bahumaññanti' is a nominal verb. That which by nature transgresses the power of the word is 'saddasāmatthiyavilaṅghinī'.

37.

37.

Siyā visesanāpekkhaṃ,

Yaṃ taṃ patvā visesanaṃ;

Sātthakaṃ taṃ yathā taṃ so,

Bhiyyo passati cakkhunā.

That which becomes meaningful upon obtaining a qualifier may be dependent on a qualifier; just as: 'He sees further with the eye.'

37. “Siyā”iccādi. Yaṃ padaṃ visesanaṃ patvā atthena saha vattatīti sātthakaṃ. Nibbisesanantu vuttatthameva hoti. Taṃ visesanāpekkhaṃ siyā. “Taṃ yathe”tyādinā udāharati. “Passatī”ti vutte “cakkhunā”ti labbhateva.

37. “Siyā,” etc. A word that, having obtained a qualifier, exists together with a meaning, is 'meaningful' (sātthakaṃ). But without a qualifier, it has only its stated meaning. Such a word might be dependent on a qualifier. He illustrates with “Taṃ yathā,” etc. When 'sees' is said, 'with the eye' is indeed understood.

37. “Siyā”miccādi. Yaṃ padaṃ visesanaṃ patvā sātthakaṃ atthasahitaṃ, tadabhāve niratthakaṃ hoti, taṃ visesanāpekkhaṃ nāma siyā. Taṃ yathā tassodāharaṇamevaṃ “taṃ so bhiyyo passati cakkhunā”ti. So puriso taṃ purisaṃ bhiyyo yebhuyyasā cakkhunā passati. Ettha “passatī”ti vutteyeva “cakkhunā”ti ñāyati. Cakkhunāti visesyapadaṃ visesanaṃ laddhāva sātthakaṃ hoti. Visesane apekkhā assāti ca, saha atthena vattamānaṃ sātthakamiti ca samāso.

37. “Siyā,” and so on. A word that, when it obtains a qualifier, becomes meaningful, endowed with meaning, but without it is meaningless, may be called “dependent on a qualifier.” For example, it is like this: “He sees him more with the eye.” That person sees that other person more extensively with the eye. Here, even when “sees” is said, “with the eye” is understood. The word “with the eye,” a qualifying term, becomes meaningful only when it has obtained a term to be qualified. The compound 'visesanāpekkhaṃ' means ‘having a need for a qualifier,’ and 'sātthakaṃ' means ‘meaningful when it occurs with its sense’.

38.

38.

Hīnaṃ kare visesyaṃ yaṃ, taṃ hīnatthaṃ bhave yathā;

Nippabhīkatakhajjoto, samudeti divākaro.

That which makes the qualified term inferior becomes of inferior meaning; just as: the sun rises, having made the firefly lightless.

38. “Hīna”miccādi[M 0.0077]. Yaṃ visesanapadaṃ visesyaṃ visesitabbaṃ hīnaṃ lāmakaṃ kare kareyya, taṃ visesanapadaṃ hīnatthaṃ hīno attho yassa taṃ hīnatthaṃ nāma bhaveyya. “Yathā”ityādinā udāharati. Nippabhīkato khajjoto yena so divākaro pabhākaro samudeti upagacchatīti. Ettha khajjotappabhāpaharaṇe na thuti divākarassāti.

38. “Hīna,” and so on. A qualifying term that would make the qualified term, the one to be qualified, inferior or base—that qualifying term would be called “of inferior meaning,” that is, “that whose meaning is inferior.” He illustrates with “yathā,” and so on. The sun, the light-maker, rises, he by whom the firefly is made lightless. Here, in the removal of the firefly’s light, there is no praise for the sun.

38. “Hīnaṃ kare”ccādi. Yaṃ padaṃ visesyaṃ hīnaṃ karoti, taṃ hīnatthaṃ bhave. Yathā tatthodāharaṇamevaṃ “nippabhīkatakhajjoto, samudeti divākaro”ti. Pabhārahitakatā khajjotā yena so divākaro sūriyo samudeti uggacchati. “Nippabhīkatakhajjoto”ti iminā visesanena lāmakālokaladdhayuttassa khajjopanakassa abhibhavanappakāsanaṃ sahassaraṃsino nindāyeva, na thutīti visesyaṃ hīnatthaṃ hoti. Hīno attho yasseti ca, natthi pabhā etesanti ca, nippabhā katāti ca, nippabhīkatā khajjotā yenāti ca viggaho.

38. “Hīnaṃ kare” and so on. A word that makes the qualified term inferior becomes of inferior meaning. For example, the illustration there is thus: “The sun rises, having made the firefly lightless.” The sun, the day-maker, rises and ascends, he by whom the fireflies have been made devoid of light. By this qualifier, “having made the firefly lightless,” the manifestation of the overpowering of the firefly, which possesses but a faint light, is indeed a dispraise of the thousand-rayed sun, not a praise; thus, the qualified term has an inferior meaning. The analyses are: ‘that whose meaning is inferior,’ and ‘there is no light for these,’ and ‘made lightless,’ and ‘he by whom fireflies are made lightless’.

39.

39.

Pādapūraṇamattaṃ yaṃ, anatthamiti taṃ mataṃ;

Yathā hi vande buddhassa, pādapaṅkeruhampica.

That which is merely a filler for the metrical foot is considered meaningless. As, indeed: “I worship the Buddha’s lotus-feet, and also…”

39. Hi api casaddānaṃ pādapūraṇamattattā anatthakattaṃ. Visesanavisesyapadadoso.

39. The words ‘hi’ and ‘api ca’ are meaningless because they are merely fillers for the metrical foot. This is a fault of qualifier and qualified terms.

39. “Pādapūraṇi”ccādi. Yaṃ padaṃ pādapūraṇamattaṃ catutthaṃsasaṅkhātassa pādassa pūraṇamattameva hoti, taṃ anatthamiti mataṃ ñātaṃ. Yathāsaddo vuttattho. Buddhassa pādapaṅkeruhaṃ pādambujaṃ vandeti. Ettha hi apicāti imesaṃ samattanādiatthesu appavattito kevalaṃ pādapūraṇamattato anatthakattaṃ. Mattasaddo avadhāraṇe. Visesanavisesyapadadoso.

39. “Pādapūraṇi” and so on. A word that is merely a filler for the metrical foot, being just enough to complete the quarter-verse, is considered and known to be meaningless. The word ‘yathā’ has the meaning already stated. One worships the Buddha’s lotus-feet, his lotus-like feet. Here, ‘hi’ and ‘api ca’ are meaningless because they do not occur with the sense of summation and so on, but are merely fillers for the metrical foot. The word ‘matta’ is used in the sense of determination. This is a fault of qualifier and qualified terms.

Padadosaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of word-faults is concluded.

Vākyadosaniddesavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Exposition of Sentence-Faults

40.

40.

Saddato atthato vuttaṃ, yattha bhiyyopi vuccati;

Tamekatthaṃ yathā’bhāti, vāridovārido ayaṃ.

Where that which has been stated by sound or by meaning is stated yet again, that is of a single meaning. For example: “This water-giver, the water-giver, shines forth.”

40. “Saddato”iccādi. Saddato vācakena tasmiṃyevatthe tasseva saddassa puna payogato atthato abhidheyyena pubbapaṭipādikasseva vatthussāvisesena puna paṭipādanato vuttaṃ payuttaṃ yaṃ padattharūpaṃ yattha yasmiṃ vākye bhiyyopi vuccati punapi payujjate, tamekatthanti anuvaditvā “yathe”ccādinā vidhīyate. Vāriṃ dadātīti vārido. Ayaṃ vārido megho ābhāti dippatīti. Jaladānamattāpekkhāya idaṃ saddato ekatthaṃ.

40. “Saddato” and so on. By sound, through the repeated use of the same word in the same meaning; by meaning, through the re-presentation of the same object without any difference from what was previously presented—that form of word-meaning which is spoken and used, and which is repeatedly uttered in a sentence, is, after being referred to as ‘of a single meaning,’ illustrated by ‘yathā’ and so on. ‘Vārido’ means ‘one who gives water.’ This cloud, the water-giver, shines forth, gleams. With respect to merely the giving of water, this is ‘of a single meaning’ by sound.

40. Idāni uddiṭṭhakkamena vākyadosaṃ niddisati “saddato”ccādinā. Saddato vācakena atthato abhidheyyena vuttaṃ payuttaṃ yaṃ padattharūpaṃ yattha yasmiṃ vākye bhiyyopi punapi vuccati yujjate, taṃ vākyaṃ ekatthaṃ nāma doso. Udāharaṇaṃ “yathi”ccādi. Vārido jaladāyako ayaṃ vārido megho ābhāti dippati. Sampattisādhakaṃ “jaladāyako”ccādivisesanaṃ vinā jaladānamattassa vuttattā saddato ekatthaṃ nāma hoti.

40. Now, following the stated order, he indicates the sentence-fault with “saddato” and so on. When that form of word-meaning which is spoken and used by sound (the expressive word) or by meaning (the denotation) is stated or used again in a sentence, that sentence has the fault named ‘of a single meaning’. The example is ‘yathā’ and so on. ‘Vārido,’ the water-giver; this ‘vārido,’ the cloud, shines forth, gleams. Because merely the giving of water is stated, without a qualifier such as ‘water-giver’ that establishes a special quality, it is called ‘of a single meaning’ by sound.

Yathā ca

And for example:

41.

41.

Titthiyaṅkurabījāni, jahaṃ diṭṭhigatāni’ha;

Pasādeti pasanne so, mahāmuni mahājane.

Abandoning the seeds of heretical sprouts, the speculative views here, that Great Sage gladdens the great multitude who are already gladdened.

41. Titthiyasaṅkhātānaṃ aṅkurānaṃ bījāni uppattihetubhūtāni diṭṭhigatāni dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo jahaṃ jahanto dūrīkaronto so mahāmuni sammāsambuddho iha loke attani pasanne pasādabahule mahājane pasādetīti aparamudāharaṇaṃ. [M 0.0079] Pasādasaṅkhātassa atthassa “pasanne pasādetī”ti vuttattā idamatthato ekatthaṃ.

41. Abandoning, casting far away, the sixty-two views, which are the seeds, the causes for the arising of sprouts reckoned as heretics—that Great Sage, the Perfectly Enlightened One, in this world gladdens the great multitude who are gladdened towards him and full of faith. This is another example. Because the meaning designated as ‘gladness’ is expressed by ‘gladdens the gladdened,’ this is ‘of a single meaning’ by sense.

41. “Titthiyi”ccādi. So mahāmuni titthiyaṅkurabījāni titthiyasaṅkhātānaṃ aṅkurānaṃ uppattikāraṇabhūtāni diṭṭhigatāni sassatādibhedabhinnā dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhiyo jahaṃ jahanto apanento iha loke pasanne attani pasanne mahājane pasādeti. Pasannasaddena vuttappasādasaṅkhātassa atthassa pasādetīti kriyāpadenapi vuttattā sadde bhinnepi atthato ekanti atthato ekatthassudāharaṇaṃ. Titthiyā eva aṅkurāni, tesaṃ bījāni, diṭṭhīsu gatāni, diṭṭhiyo eva gatānīti vā viggaho.

41. “Titthiyi” and so on. That Great Sage, abandoning and removing the sixty-two views—which are the seeds of heretical sprouts, the causes for the arising of sprouts called ‘heretical,’ the views divided into various kinds such as eternalism—gladdens in this world the great multitude who are gladdened in him. Because the meaning designated as ‘gladness,’ expressed by the word ‘gladdened,’ is also expressed by the verb ‘gladdens,’ even though the words are different, the meaning is one; thus, it is an example of ‘of a single meaning’ by sense. The analyses are: ‘the heretics themselves are the sprouts,’ ‘their seeds,’ ‘gone into views,’ or ‘the views themselves are what is gone’.

42.

42.

Āraddhakkamavicchedā, bhaggarīti bhave yathā;

Kāpi paññā, kopi guṇo, pakatīpi aho tava.

From the interruption of the commenced sequence, a ‘broken style’ may arise, as when: “Some wisdom, some virtue, and your nature too—oh!”

42. Āraddho vattumupakkamanto, kamo vacanapaṭipāṭi. Tassa vicchedo bhaṅgo, tato. “Yathe”tiādinā udāharati. Avuttassapi pasādavasā ajjhāhāroti. Mahāmuni tava te paññā kāpi sātisayattā aniddhāritaṃ sabhāvavisesā kāciyeva, aho pavattamānāyapi vasabhāvassāniddhāritattā acchariyanti attho. Ettha kāpi kopīti sabbanāmapadakkamassa pakatīti ettha vicchinnattā bhaggarīti.

42. ‘Āraddho’ means ‘having commenced to speak,’ and ‘kamo’ is ‘the sequence of speech.’ Its interruption is a ‘break,’ hence the term. He illustrates with ‘yathā’ and so on. Even what is unstated is supplied by the force of the context. O Great Sage, your wisdom is ‘some kind’ because of its surpassing nature, its specific characteristic being undefined; oh, even as it manifests, its inherent nature remains undefined, which is astonishing—this is the meaning. Here, the sequence of pronoun-terms ‘kāpi’ and ‘kopi’ is interrupted at ‘pakati,’ hence ‘broken style’.

42. “Āraddhakkami”ccādi. Āraddhakkamavicchedā vatthumāraddhapadakkamassa vicchedahetu bhaggarīti bhave bhaggarītivākyadoso bhavati. Udāharati “yathi”ccādi. Mahāmuni tava tuyhaṃ paññā sātisayabhūtā paññā kāpi vacanavisayātikkantattā kāpiyeva. Guṇo sīlasamādhiādianaññasādhāraṇaguṇasamūho kopi pamāṇapariggahassa kenaci [M 0.0080] lesenapi kattumasakkuṇeyyattā kopiyeva. Pakatīpi acinteyyabhūtā pakatīpi evameva aho vijjamānānaṃyeva paññādīnaṃ sabhāvāvabodhassa dukkaratā acchariyā. Kāpi kopīti padakkamassa “pakatī”ti ettha suññattā rītibhaṅgo. Āraddhoyeva kamo, tassa vicchedo, bhaggā rīti assa, ettha vāti viggaho.

42. “Āraddhakkami” and so on. From the interruption of the commenced sequence, that is, because of the interruption of the sequence of words commenced concerning the subject matter, the sentence-fault of ‘broken style’ arises. He illustrates with ‘yathā’ and so on. O Great Sage, your wisdom, being extraordinary, is ‘some kind’ because it transcends the scope of words. Virtue, the collection of qualities such as morality and concentration, uncommon to others, is ‘some kind’ because it cannot be measured by any means whatsoever. Nature, too, is inconceivable—nature is just so. Oh, how astonishing is the difficulty of comprehending the inherent nature of such wisdom and so on, which truly exist. The sequence of words ‘kāpi’ and ‘kopi’ is empty at ‘pakati,’ hence there is a break in the style. The analyses are: ‘the sequence is commenced,’ ‘its interruption,’ ‘its style is broken,’ or ‘in this case’.

43.

43.

Padānaṃ dubbinikkhepā, byāmoho yattha jāyati;

Taṃ byākiṇṇanti viññeyyaṃ, tadudāharaṇaṃ yathā.

Where confusion arises from the misplacement of words, that should be understood as ‘disjointed’; its example is as follows.

43. “Padāna”miccādi. Yattha yasmiṃ vākye padānaṃ syādyantākhyātikānaṃ dubbinikkhepā duṭṭhapanato byāmoho saṃmuḷhatā jāyati uppajjati, taṃ vākyaṃ byākiṇṇanti viññeyyaṃ ñātabbaṃ. Tassa byākiṇṇassa udāharaṇaṃ lakkhiyaṃ “yathe”ti dasseti. Yathā idaṃ, tathā aññampīti attho.

43. “Padānaṃ” and so on. In whatever sentence, due to the misplacement or faulty arrangement of words—those with nominal endings and verbs—confusion or bewilderment arises, that sentence should be known and understood as ‘disjointed’. He shows the example, the illustration, of that ‘disjointed’ fault with ‘yathā’. The meaning is: ‘as this, so also others’.

43. “Padāni”ccādi. Padānaṃ syādyantatyādyantapadānaṃ dubbinikkhepā duṭṭhapanato yattha vākye byāmoho saṃmoho jāyati, taṃ byākiṇṇadosoti viññeyyaṃ. Tadudāharaṇaṃ tassa byākiṇṇadosassa lakkhiyaṃ yathā iminā vakkhamānanayena.

43. “Padāni” and so on. Where in a sentence confusion or delusion arises due to the misplacement or faulty arrangement of words—those with nominal endings and those with verbal endings—that should be understood as the ‘disjointed’ fault. Its example, the illustration of that ‘disjointed’ fault, is as follows, according to the method to be explained.

44.

44.

Bahuguṇe paṇamati, dujjanānaṃ pyayaṃ jano;

Hitaṃ pamudito niccaṃ, sugataṃ samanussaraṃ.

To the one with many virtues he bows, this person of wicked ones; beneficial, always joyful, recollecting the Well-Gone One.

44. Bahuanantattā bahubhūte guṇe sīlādike samanussaraṃ sammadeva uṭṭhāya samuṭṭhāya anussaranto guṇavisayasatiṃ paccupaṭṭhāpento teneva kāraṇena pamudito haṭṭhapahaṭṭho ayaṃ jano sabbopi loko dujjanānaṃ sujanetarānampi devadattādīnaṃ niccaṃ kālaṃ hitaṃ sugataṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ paṇamati namassatīti ayaṃ attho kavivañcito. Tattha “bahuguṇe paṇamatī”tyādi byavahitapadappayogā moho jāyatīti byākiṇṇaṃ.

44. The meaning intended by the poet is: ‘This person, indeed all people, recollecting the many and abundant virtues such as morality, properly arising and recollecting, establishing mindfulness regarding the sphere of virtues, and for that very reason joyful and exceedingly delighted, always bows down to and worships the Well-Gone One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, who is beneficial even to the wicked and those other than the good, such as Devadatta.’ There, due to the use of separated words, such as in ‘bahuguṇe paṇamati,’ confusion arises; hence, it is ‘disjointed’.

44. “Bahuguṇe”ccādi. [M 0.0081] Bahuguṇe anantattā bahubhūte sīlasamādhiādiguṇe samanussaraṃ visesato anussaranto pamudito tatoyeva pahaṭṭho ayaṃ jano sattanikāyo dujjanānampi asappurisānampi niccaṃ satataṃ hitaṃ mittabhūtaṃ sugataṃ sabbaññuṃ paṇamati vandati. Ettha padānaṃ aṭṭhānapayogato byākiṇṇattaṃ padatthānusāreneva gamyate.

44. “Bahuguṇe,” etc. Recollecting the many virtues, such as morality and concentration, which are endless and abundant, and especially reflecting upon them, this multitude of beings, delighted and elated thereby, constantly and always bows down to and venerates the Sugata, the All-Knowing One, who is a friend and benefactor even to the wicked and the unvirtuous. Here, the scattered nature of the words due to their inappropriate usage is understood only by following the meaning of the terms.

45.

45.

Visiṭṭhavacanā’petaṃ, gāmmaṃ’tya’bhimataṃ yathā;

Kaññe kāmayamānaṃ maṃ, na kāmayasi kiṃ nvi’daṃ.

Devoid of distinguished speech, it is deemed rustic, as for example: “O maiden, though I desire you, why do you not desire me? What is this?”

45. Visiṭṭhassa kassaci atthassa vacanato kathanato apetaṃ pariccattaṃ. Kaññeityāmantanaṃ. Ahaṃ taṃ icchāmi, tādisaṃ maṃ tvaṃ kasmā nicchasi, idaṃ kiṃ nu iti gāmikajanavacanattā “kaññi”ccādikaṃ gāmmaṃ.

45. It is devoid of, abandoned by, the expression of any distinguished meaning. “Kaññe” is a vocative. “I desire you, why do you not desire me, what is this?”—because such words are the speech of villagers, the phrase beginning with “kaññi” is rustic.

45. “Visiṭṭhe”ccādi. Visiṭṭhavacanāpetaṃ piyabhūtena uttivisesena visesitabbassa kathanato parihīnaṃ vākyaṃ “gāmmadosa”nti kavīhi abhimataṃ. Udāharati “yathi”ccādi. Kaññe he kaññe kāmayamānaṃ maṃ tuvaṃ icchayamānaṃ maṃ na kāmayasi tvaṃ na icchasi, idaṃ kiṃ nu. Īdise icchāvighāte vuccamāne evaṃ–

45. “Visiṭṭha,” etc. A sentence that is devoid of distinguished speech, lacking the expression of a special quality that should be emphasized by one who is dear, is deemed a “rustic fault” by poets. He gives an example with “yathā,” etc.: “O maiden, O maiden, though I desire you, you do not desire me—what is this?” When such a thwarting of desire is spoken of, it is thus:

“Yācanā madīyā tava kāraṇāyaṃ,

Dine dine nipphalataṃ upeti;

Dakkho sadā māninimānabhaṅge,

Sa manmathonyatra gato mato nu”iti viya.

“My entreaties on your account, day by day, are fruitless. Skilled always in breaking the pride of the proud, has Cupid gone elsewhere or is he dead?”—thus it is said.

Piyatthassa kathanābhāvato “kaññe”tyādikaṃ vacanaṃ milakkhukānaṃ vacanattā gāmmaṃ. Ettha kaññāsaddo dasavassikāya vattatīti niyamo natthi. Visiṭṭhassa atthassa vacanato apetanti vākyaṃ.

Because there is no expression of a pleasing meaning, the speech beginning with “kaññe” is rustic, being the speech of barbarians. Here, there is no rule that the word “kaññā” applies to a ten-year-old girl. The sentence is one that is devoid of the expression of a distinguished meaning.

46.

46.

Padasandhānato kiñci, duppatītikaraṃ bhave;

Tampi gāmmaṃtya’bhimataṃ, yathā yābhavato piyā.

If, from the connection of words, something should become difficult to understand, that too is deemed rustic, as for example: “yā bhavato piyā.”

46. “Pade”ccādi. Padasandhānato pubbāparānaṃ padānaṃ sandhivasena yaṃ kiñci vākyaṃ duṭṭhu asutisubhagaṃ patītimavabodhaṃ karotīti karaṃ bhave, tampi yathāvuttaṃ gāmmantyabhimataṃ. Yathātyudāharati. Bhavato yā kāci vanitā piyā hotīti ekottho. Yabha methune. Yabhanaṃ yābho. So vijjate yassa so yābhavā. Tassa yābhavato piyāityapi bhavati.

46. “Pade,” etc. If, from the connection of words, due to the linking of preceding and following words, any sentence should become poorly composed, unpleasant to hear, and cause difficulty in understanding, that too is deemed rustic as stated. He gives an example with “yathā.” “Whatever woman is dear to you”—this is one meaning. “Yabha” is in the sense of sexual intercourse. “Yabhana” is “yābho.” He who possesses that is “yābhavā.” Thus, “dear to one who is sexually active” is also a meaning.

46. “Padasandhāni”ccādi. Kiñci vākyaṃ padasandhānato pubbāparapadānaṃ ghaṭanato duppatītikaraṃ bhave asabbhabhūtaduṭṭhatthassa pakāsako hoti, tampi gāmmanti yathāvuttagāmmadosena dūsitanti duppasitanti (ka.) sabbehi kavīhi abhimataṃ ñātaṃ. Yathāti udāharati. Bhavato bhavantassa yā kāci itthī piyā bhavatīti ayaṃ kavinā icchitattho. Yābhavato methunavantassa piyātipi attho. “Yabha methune”ti hi dhātu. Yabhanaṃ yābho, so assa atthīti yābhavā, tassa yābhavatoti gahite asotabbattā duppatītikaratā. Duṭṭhāyeva patīti avabodho, taṃ karotīti viggaho.

46. “Padasandhāna,” etc. Any sentence which, due to the joining of preceding and following words, becomes difficult to understand and reveals an improper or distorted meaning, that too is considered rustic, known and deemed by all poets to be tainted by the aforementioned rustic flaw. He gives an example with “yathā.” “Whatever woman is dear to him”—this is the meaning intended by the poet. “Dear to one who is sexually active” is also a meaning. Indeed, the root “yabha” is in the sense of sexual intercourse. “Yabhana” is “yābho”; he who possesses it is “yābhavā.” When “tassa yābhavato” is taken, it is unpleasant to hear, hence the difficulty in understanding. “Duṭṭhā patīti” means a distorted understanding; the analysis is “that which causes it.”

47.

47.

Vuttesu sūcite ṭhāne, padacchedo bhave yati;

Yaṃ tāya hīnaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ, yatihīnanti sā pana.

In the places indicated in the texts, a word-break is a pause (yati). That which is deficient in it is called 'deficient in pause' (yatihīna).

47. “Vuttesvi”ccādi. Vuttesu chandosatthapariniddiṭṭhesu anuṭṭhubhādīsu sūcite ṭhāne “etthayatī”ti chandovicitiyā pakāsitaṭṭhāne padānaṃ syādyantānaṃ chedo vicchiti vibhāgo anuvādo yaṃ yati bhaveti vidhīyati. Tāya [M 0.0083] yatiyā hīnaṃ parihīnaṃ viruddhaṃ yaṃ vākyaṃ, taṃ yatihīnanti vuttaṃ, “yamanaṃ virāmo yati, sā hīnā etthā”ti katvā. Panāti visese, sā yati panāti sambandho.

47. “Vuttesu,” etc. In the places indicated in the texts on prosody, such as the anuṭṭhubha and others, in the place revealed by Chandoviciti as “here is the yati,” the division, separation, distinction, or explanation of words ending in syā, etc., is prescribed as a pause (yati). A sentence that is deficient, lacking, or contrary to that pause is called “yatihīna,” having made the explanation “cessation is pause, that is deficient here.” “Pana” is for emphasis; the connection is “that pause, indeed.”

47. “Vuttesva”ccādi. Vuttesu chandosatthe niddiṭṭhaanuṭṭhubhādīsu sūcite ṭhāne “ayamettha yatī”ti pakāsite ṭhāne padacchedo syādyantatyādyantādīnaṃ padānaṃ vicchedo yati nāma bhave, tāya yatiyā yaṃ vākyaṃ hīnaṃ abhimataṭṭhāne vaṇṇavicchedena parihīnaṃ, taṃ vākyaṃ yatihīnanti yatihīnadosena duṭṭhanti viññūhi vuttaṃ.

47. “Vuttesu,” etc. In the places indicated in the prosody texts concerning the anuṭṭhubha and other meters, in the place revealed as “here is the yati,” the word division, the separation of words ending in syā, tyā, etc., is called a pause (yati). A sentence that is deficient in that pause, impaired by a syllable break in the intended place, that sentence is called “yatihīna,” meaning flawed by the fault of lacking a proper pause, so it is said by the wise.

48.

48.

Yati sabbattha pādante, vuttaḍḍhe ca visesato;

Pubbāparānekavaṇṇa-padamajjhepi katthaci.

The pause occurs everywhere at the end of a line, and especially in the stated half-verse; sometimes also in the middle of a word with multiple syllables before and after.

48. “Yati”ccādi. Sabbattha pādante sabbasmiṃ catutthaṃsasaṅkhātānaṃ gāthāpādānaṃ ante avasāne ca visesato visesena ekantena vuttaḍḍhe ca vuttānaṃ pādadvayasaṅkhāte aḍḍhe ca, tadavasāne cāti adhippāyo. “Siyā”ti seso. Nanu “padacchedo”ti vuttattā padamajjhe yati na hotevāti ceti āha “pubba”iccādi. Katthaci kismiñci ṭhāne, na sabbattha. Pubbāparānekavaṇṇapadamajjhepi yatīti sambandho. Pubbe ca apare ca pubbāpare. Aneke vaṇṇā anekavaṇṇā. Pubbāpare anekavaṇṇā yassa taṃ tathā. Tañca taṃ padañca, tassa majjhepi.

48. “Yati,” etc. Everywhere at the end of a line, at the end of all verse-quarters, and especially, definitively, at the end of the stated half-verse, which consists of two lines—this is the intended meaning. “Siyā” (may be) is the remainder. But since “word-break” is stated, does that not mean a pause cannot occur in the middle of a word? To this, he says, “pubba,” etc. In some place, not everywhere, a pause occurs even in the middle of a word with multiple syllables before and after—this is the connection. “Pubbāpare” means before and after. “Anekavaṇṇā” means multiple syllables. That which has multiple syllables before and after is such. And in the middle of such a word.

48. Idāni yatimhi labbhamānaṃ sabbavisayaṃ dasseti “yati”ccādinā. Sā pana yati sabbattha pādante catutthaṃsasaṅkhātagāthāpādānaṃ ante ca visesato niyamato vuttaḍḍhe ca vuttānaṃ pādadvayasaṅkhāte aḍḍhe ca, tadavasāne cāti adhippāyo. Katthaci kismiñci ṭhāne pubbāparānekavaṇṇapadamajjhepi pubbāparabhūtaanekavaṇṇasamannāgatapadānaṃ majjhe [M 0.0084] ca siyā. Padacchedassa “yatī”ti vuttattā padamajjhe na hotīti saṅkāpariharaṇatthaṃ “pubbāparānekavaṇṇapadamajjhe”ti vuttaṃ. Ettha pādanto, vuttaḍḍho, padamajjhañca yatiṭṭhānanti. Padamajjheyeva labbhamānā yati katthaci hoti, dvakkharatyakkharapadamajjhe pana na hoti.

48. Now, he shows the full scope of where pauses are obtainable with “yati,” etc. That pause occurs everywhere at the end of a line, at the end of verse-quarters, and especially, definitively, at the end of the stated half-verse, which consists of two lines; this is the intended meaning, and at its conclusion. In some places, a pause may occur even in the middle of a word with multiple syllables before and after, that is, in the middle of words endowed with multiple syllables both before and after. Because “yati” is stated as word-division, to dispel the doubt that a pause does not occur in the middle of a word, it is stated, “in the middle of a word with multiple syllables before and after.” Here, the end of a line, the stated half-verse, and the middle of a word are places for pauses. A pause obtainable only in the middle of a word occurs in some cases, but it does not occur in the middle of a two- or three-syllable word.

Tatthodāharaṇapaccudāharaṇāni yathā –

There, examples and counter-examples are as follows:

49.

49.

Taṃ name sirasā cāmī-karavaṇṇaṃ tathāgataṃ;

Sakalāpi disā siñca-tīva soṇṇarasehiyo.

I bow my head to that Tathāgata, whose color is like gold; he seems to sprinkle all directions with golden essence.

49. Udāharīyatīti udāharaṇaṃ. Paṭipakkhamudāharaṇaṃ paccudāharaṇaṃ. Cāmīkarasseva suvaṇṇassa viya vaṇṇo yassa taṃ tathāgataṃ sirasā namāmi. Kīdisaṃ? Yo tathāgato sakalāpi disā sabbāyeva dasa disā soṇṇarasehi cāmīkaravaṇṇattā rasehi suvaṇṇarasehi siñcatīva siñcatīti maññe, taṃ tathāgatanti apekkhate. Ettha pubbapādante vuttaḍḍhe ca niyatā yati. Cāmīkarasaddo cettha caturakkharo. Tattha cāmīiti pubbabhāgo, karaiti paro. Ettha pubbāparānekavaṇṇapadamajjhe yati. Siñcatīti ettha pana pubbāparānekavaṇṇapadamajjhattābhāvā siñcaityatra yati duṭṭhāti. Idaṃ paccudāharaṇaṃ.

49. That which is cited is an example. A contrary example is a counter-example. I bow my head to that Tathāgata whose color is like that of gold itself. What is he like? I think that Tathāgata, because his color is like gold, sprinkles all directions, all ten directions, with golden essences, as it were; this refers to that Tathāgata. Here, the pause is fixed at the end of the first line and at the stated half-verse. The word “cāmīkara” here has four syllables. Of these, “cāmī” is the first part, and “kara” is the latter. Here, a pause occurs in the middle of a word with multiple syllables before and after. In “siñcatī,” however, because there is no middle of a word with multiple syllables before and after, a pause at “siñca” is incorrect. This is the counter-example.

49. Tattha pādantavuttaḍḍhesu yatiyā pākaṭattā tasmiṃ padamajjhe yatiyā udāharaṇapaccudāharaṇāni iṭṭhodāharaṇapaṭipakkhodāharaṇāni yathā. “Taṃ name”ccādi. Yo tathāgato sakalāpi disā soṇṇarasehi suvaṇṇarasadhārāhi siñcatīva siñcati maññe, ivasaddo vitakke. Cāmīkaravaṇṇaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇasadisachavivaṇṇaṃ taṃ tathāgataṃ sirasā name. Ettha “cāmīkaravaṇṇa”nti yatiyā cāmīti akkharadvayamatikkamma ṭhitattā antepi karaiti akkharadvayenānūnattā [M 0.0085] padacchedassa pubbāparavaṇṇānamanekattamitiṭṭhodāharaṇaṃ. Siñcatīti pade siñcāti vaṇṇadvayamatikkamma yatiyā dissamānattepi tiiti parabhāge ekavaṇṇattā anekavaṇṇābhāvoti paccudāharaṇaṃ. Ettha anekavaṇṇattaṃ padavaseneva ñātabbaṃ. Cāmīkarassa vaṇṇo viya vaṇṇo yassa soti viggaho.

49. There, because the caesura is evident at the end of the line and in the stated half-verse, examples and counter-examples of the caesura in the middle of a word are given, such as desired examples and contrary examples, as follows. “Taṃ name,” etc. I think that the Tathāgata sprinkles all directions, as it were, with golden essences, with streams of golden essence; the word “iva” indicates conjecture. I bow my head to that Tathāgata whose complexion resembles the color of refined gold. Here, “cāmīkaravaṇṇa” is a desired example because the caesura stands after passing over two syllables (“cāmī”), and at the end it is not less than two syllables (“kara”), so there is a multiplicity of syllables before and after the word-break. In the word “siñcatī,” even though a caesura is seen after passing over two syllables (“siñca”), because the latter part “ti” is a single syllable, there is an absence of a multiplicity of syllables; hence, it is a counter-example. Here, the multiplicity of syllables should be understood by the nature of the word itself. The analysis is: “He whose color is like the color of refined gold.”

50.

50.

Saro sandhimhi pubbanto, viya lope vibhattiyā;

Aññathā tva’ññathā tattha, yādesādi parādi’va.

A vowel at a junction, when an inflection is elided, is like the end of the preceding word; otherwise, however, it is different there, and a substitution like 'y' and so forth is like the beginning of the following word.

50. “Saro”ccādi. Vibhattiyā lope sati sandhimhi saṃhitāyaṃ katāyaṃ saro parapadādibhūto pubbanto viya pubbapadassa antabhūto yo saro, so viya hoti, anekavaṇṇattābhāvepi tato vihitayatiyā nevatthi bhaṅgoti adhippāyo. Aññathā tu vibhattiyā alope tu sati saṃhitāyaṃ katāyaṃ pubbapadantabhūto saro ce, aññathā aññena pakārena hoti, parapadassādisaro viya hotīti attho. Taṃ vibhattiyā saddhiṃ vihāya katayatiyā natthi bhaṅgoti adhippāyo. Tattha tassaṃ yatiyaṃ yādesādi ivaṇṇādīnaṃ kātabbo yakārādesādi parādiva parapadassa ādisaro viya hoti. Katayādesādisahitaṃ byañjanaṃ vihāya katāya yatiyā natthi bhaṅgoti adhippāyo.

50. “Saro,” etc. When an inflection is elided and sandhi is made, the vowel at the junction becomes like the end of the preceding word, that is, like the vowel that is the final part of the preceding word. The meaning is that even in the absence of a multiplicity of syllables, there is no break in the caesura prescribed after it. But otherwise, when there is no elision of the inflection and sandhi is made, if there is a vowel at the end of the preceding word, it becomes otherwise, in another way; the meaning is that it becomes like the initial vowel of the following word. The meaning is that there is no break in a caesura made by leaving that vowel along with its inflection. There, in that caesura, a substitution like 'y' and so forth, which is to be made for vowels like 'i', is like the beginning of the following word, that is, like the initial vowel of the following word. The meaning is that there is no break in a caesura made by leaving the consonant together with the substitution like 'y' that has been made.

50. Idāni heṭṭhā vuttassa viruddhattepi yatibhaṅgābhāvaṃ dassento āha “saro”ccādi. Vibhattiyā lope sandhimhi sati saro sandhisaro pubbanto viya pubbapadassa anto viya hoti, aññathā tu vibhattiyā alope saṃhitāyaṃ katāyaṃ aññathā hoti, pubbapadantabhūto saro parapadassa ādisaro viya hoti. Tattha yatiyaṃ yādesādi [M 0.0086] ivaṇṇādīnaṃ kattabbayakārādesādi parādiva parapadassa ādisaro viya hoti, pubbantasadisasaramatikkamitvāpi parapadādisarasadisavaṇṇamāgamma taṃ anatikkamitvāpi parapadādisarasadisayādesādimatikkamitvāpi yatiyā payuttāya sati anekavaṇṇattābhāvepi yatibhaṅgo na hotīti adhippāyo. Pubbassa antoti ca, yo ca so ādeso ca, so ādi yassa makārādinoti ca, parassa ādīti ca vākyaṃ.

50. Now, showing the absence of a break in the caesura even when it contradicts what was stated below, he says: “saro,” etc. When an inflection is elided and there is sandhi, the vowel, the sandhi vowel, becomes like the end of the preceding word, like the final part of the preceding word. But otherwise, when the inflection is not elided and sandhi is made, it is different; the vowel that is the final part of the preceding word becomes like the initial vowel of the following word. There, in the caesura, a substitution like 'y' and so forth, which is to be made for vowels like 'i', becomes like the beginning of the following word, that is, like the initial vowel of the following word. The meaning is that when the caesura is applied, even if it is after passing over a vowel similar to the end of the preceding word, or after reaching a sound similar to the beginning of the following word but not passing over it, or even after passing over a substitution like 'y' which is similar to the beginning of the following word, there is no break in the caesura, even in the absence of a multiplicity of syllables. And the phrases are: 'the end of the preceding,' and 'that which is the substitution,' and 'that of which it is the beginning, such as 'm' and so forth,' and 'the beginning of the following'.

51.

51.

Cādī pubbapadantāva, niccaṃ pubbapadassitā;

Pādayo niccasambandhā, parādīva parena tu.

Particles like 'ca', always dependent on the preceding word, are indeed like the end of the preceding word; but prefixes like 'pa', always connected with the following word, are like the beginning of the following word.

51. Niccaṃ anavarataṃ pubbapadaṃ sitā nissitā cādī cakārādayo nipātā pubbassa padassa antā avayavā viya honti, te anto katvā yati kātabbāti adhippāyo. Parena parapadena niccasambandhā satatayogino, tusaddo aṭṭhānappayutto, pādayo tu parādīva parapadassa ādī avayavā viya honti, taṃ vihāya pubbapadante yati kātabbāti adhippāyo.

51. The particles like 'ca' (cādī), that is, particles beginning with 'ca', being always and uninterruptedly dependent on the preceding word, are like the final parts of the preceding word. The meaning is that the caesura should be made by including them at the end. But prefixes like 'pa' (pādayo), being always connected and constantly joined with the following word, are like the initial parts of the following word. The word 'tu' is used in an inappropriate place. The meaning is that the caesura should be made at the end of the preceding word, leaving them out.

51. “Cādi”ccādi. Niccaṃ satataṃ pubbapadassitā pubbapadaṃ nissāya pavattā cādī cakārādinipātā pubbapadantāva pubbapadassa antā avayavā viya honti, parena parapadena niccasambandhā nirantarayogino pādayo tu pādiupasaggā pana parādīva parapadassa ādī avayavāviya honti. Cādayo āgamma te bahi katvāpi pādayo āgamma te anto katvāpi pavatto virāmo yatibhaṅgoti adhippāyo. Coādi yesanti ca, pubbapadaṃ sitāti ca, po ādi yesanti ca, niccaṃ sambandhāti ca viggaho. Ettha ca tagguṇasaṃviññāṇattā cakārapakārādīnampi pariggaho.

51. “Cādi,” etc. The particles like 'ca' (cādī), that is, particles beginning with 'ca', being always and constantly dependent on the preceding word and proceeding by relying on the preceding word, are indeed like the final parts of the preceding word. But the prefixes like 'pa' (pādayo), that is, prefixes beginning with 'pa', being always and uninterruptedly connected with the following word, are like the initial parts of the following word. The meaning is that a pause that occurs by treating the 'cādis' as external, or by treating the 'pādis' as internal, is a break in the caesura. And the analysis is: 'those of which 'ca' is the beginning,' and 'dependent on the preceding word,' and 'those of which 'pa' is the beginning,' and 'always connected.' And here, because this is a bahubbīhi compound denoting a quality, the inclusion of 'ca', 'pa', and so forth is also to be understood.

Sabbatthodāharaṇāni yathā

Examples in all cases are as follows:

52.

52.

Name taṃ sirasā sabbo-pamātītaṃ tathāgataṃ;

Yassa lokaggataṃ patta-sso’pamā na hi yujjati.

I bow my head to that Tathāgata, who has transcended all similes; for whom, having attained the world's highest state, no simile is indeed fitting.

53.

53.

Munindaṃ taṃ sadā vandā-mya’nantamati’muttamaṃ;

Yassa paññā ca mettā ca, nissīmāti vijambhati.

I always bow to that Lord of Sages, supreme and of boundless intellect; whose wisdom and loving-kindness expand exceedingly, being without limit.

52-53. Sabbatthāti [M 0.0087] pubbantasadisādīsu. “Nameta”ntiādigāthādvaye padattho pākaṭo, adhippāyo tu yato lokaggataṃ patto, tato sabbopamātīto, yato paññāmettā loke nirantaramiva vattanti, tato anantamati, uttamo cāti. Ettha “sabbā upamā”ti samāsaṃ katvā vibhattilope saṃhitāyañca katāyaṃ parapadādiukāro pubbapadantabbakāraṭṭhaakāro viya hotīti sabbo iccatra pādantayati. Pattassopamā iccatra yakārādesassa parādisadisabhāvo viya hoti, vibhattiyā alope saṃhitāyaṃ katāyaṃ savibhattiyā akāro parapadādi ukāro viya hotīti taṃvibhattiyā pasiddhaṃ vihāya pattaiccatra pādantayati. Tathā vandāmyanantaiccatra yakārādesassa parādisadisabhāvo vihitoti myasaddaṃ vajjetvā vandāiccatra pādantayati. Pubbapadassitānaṃ cādīnaṃ pubbapadantasadisatā vuttāti mettā cāti casaddato yati, aparapadasambandhā pādayo parapadādisadisā hontīti nissīmāti ettha nisaddaṃ vihāya tato ādimhi yati.

52-53. 'In all cases' means in cases such as being similar to the end of the preceding word, and so forth. In the two verses beginning with 'Name taṃ,' the word-meaning is clear. The intention, however, is this: since he has attained the highest state in the world, he is beyond all similes; and since his wisdom and loving-kindness pervade the world as if uninterruptedly, he is of boundless intellect and supreme. Here, in 'sabbopamā', having formed the compound from 'sabbā upamā', and with the elision of the inflection and the making of sandhi, the initial 'u' of the following word becomes like the 'a' located in the final syllable of the preceding word; thus, there is a caesura at the end of the line at 'sabbo'. In 'pattassopamā', when the inflection is not elided and sandhi is made, the 'a' with its inflection becomes like the initial 'u' of the following word; thus, leaving aside what is established by that inflection, there is a caesura at the end of the line at 'patta'. Similarly, in 'vandāmyananta', the substitution of 'y' is prescribed to be similar to the beginning of the following word; thus, omitting the syllable 'mya', there is a caesura at the end of the line at 'vandā'. It is stated that particles like 'ca', being dependent on the preceding word, are similar to the end of the preceding word; thus, in 'mettā ca', the caesura is placed after the word 'ca'. And since prefixes like 'pa', being connected to the following word, are similar to the initial part of the following word, here in 'nissīmā', leaving aside the word 'ni', the caesura is at the beginning of what follows.

52-53. Sabbattha yathāvuttapubbantasadisasarādīsu pañcasu udāharaṇāniyathā. “Name ta”miccādi, lokaggataṃ pattassa yassa buddhassa upamā na hi yujjati sakalapadatthānaṃ atikkamma ṭhitattā na hi yujjati. Sabbopamātītaṃ taṃ tathāgataṃ sirasā name namāmi. Sabboti ettha okārassa pubbapadantasarasadisattā tato parāya yatiyā ca ssopamāti parapadādisadisaṃ [M 0.0088] vaṇṇamanatikkamma ṭhitāya yatiyā ca udāharaṇaṃ.

52-53. Examples in all five cases, such as a vowel similar to the end of the preceding word as stated, are as follows. 'Name taṃ,' etc. For that Buddha who has attained the highest state in the world, no simile is fitting; because he stands having transcended the meaning of all words, no simile is indeed fitting. I bow my head to that Tathāgata, who has transcended all similes. Here, in 'sabbo', the 'o'-vowel is an example of being similar to the final vowel of the preceding word and of the caesura that follows it; and 'ssopamā' is an example of a caesura that stands without passing over a syllable similar to the beginning of the following word.

“Muninde”ccādi. Yassa sambuddhassa paññā ca mettā canissīmā anantasattaanantañeyyavisayakaraṇato sīmārahitā ativijambhati. Anantamatiṃ udayabbayasambhavepi ñeyyassānantattā visayimhi visayavohārena anantapaññāya samannāgataṃ uttamaṃ tato eva pavaraṃ taṃ munindaṃ sadā vandāmi, yādesassa parādisadisattā tamanāgamma yati bhavati. Mettācanissīmāti ettha cādīnaṃ pubbapadantasadisattāca pādīnaṃ parapadādisadisattā ca “cā”ti “nī”ti imesampi yati bhavati.

'Muninda,' etc. The wisdom and loving-kindness of that Fully Enlightened One expand exceedingly, being boundless, that is, without limit, because their scope encompasses infinite beings and infinite objects of knowledge. I always bow to that Lord of Sages, who is of boundless intellect, supreme, and for that very reason excellent, being endowed with infinite wisdom—this is stated by way of referring to the object in the subject, because the knowable is infinite, even amidst arising and passing away. Because the substitution of 'y' is similar to the beginning of the following word, the caesura occurs without reaching it. Here, in 'mettā ca nissīmā', because particles like 'ca' are similar to the end of the preceding word, and prefixes like 'pa' are similar to the beginning of the following word, a caesura occurs for these as well, namely after 'ca' and before 'nī'.

Cādipādīsu paccudāharaṇāni yathā

Counter-examples for particles like 'ca' and prefixes like 'pa' are as follows:

54.

54.

Mahāmettā mahāpaññā, ca yattha paramodayā;

Paṇamāmi jinaṃ taṃ pa-varaṃ varaguṇālayaṃ.

Great loving-kindness and great wisdom, in whom there is supreme flourishing; I bow to that Conqueror, the most excellent, the abode of noble qualities.

54. “Mahā”iccādi. Yatthāti yasmiṃ jine. Paramodayāti mahāmettādayo ukkaṭṭhābhivuḍḍhiyo. Tatoyeva varaguṇālayaṃ, teneva pavaraṃ uttamaṃ taṃ jinanti sambandho. Ettha pubbapadanissitaṃ cakāraṃ parapadādibhūtaṃ katvā tato pubbe katā yati ca, parapadādisambandhapakāraṃ pubbapadantabhūtaṃ katvā pakārato paraṃ katā yati ca viruddhāti ubhayattha paccudāharaṇaṃ.

54. “Mahā,” etc. “Yattha” means in which Conqueror. “Paramodayā” means the highest developments, such as great loving-kindness. For that very reason, he is the abode of noble qualities; therefore, he is the most excellent, the supreme Conqueror—this is the connection. Here, treating the particle “ca,” which is dependent on the preceding word, as the beginning of the following word and making the caesura before it; and treating the prefix “pa,” which is connected to the beginning of the following word, as the end of the preceding word and making the caesura after “pa”—both are contradictory. Hence, this is a counter-example in both cases.

54. Cādipādīsu visayabhūtesu paccudāharaṇaṃ yathā. “Mahāmetti”ccādi. Yattha yasmiṃ jine mahāmettā ca mahāpaññā ca imā paramodayā ukkaṭṭhābhivuḍḍhiyo honti. Varaguṇālayaṃ uttamaguṇākaraṃ pavaraṃ tatoyeva uttamaṃ taṃ jinaṃ paṇamāmi. Ettha cakāraṃ parapadādiṃ katvā pakāraṃ pubbapadantaṃ katvā yatiyā pavattattā “ca yattha, taṃ pā”tidvayamapi paccudāharaṇaṃ.

54. A counter-example concerning particles like “ca” and prefixes like “pa” is as follows: “Mahāmettā,” etc. In which Conqueror great loving-kindness and great wisdom are these supreme flourishings, the highest developments. I bow to that Conqueror, who is the abode of noble qualities, the mine of supreme qualities, and for that very reason, the most excellent. Here, because the caesura occurs by treating the particle “ca” as the beginning of the following word and the prefix “pa” as the end of the preceding word, both “ca yattha” and “taṃ pa” are counter-examples.

55.

55.

Padatthakkamato [M 0.0089] muttaṃ, kamaccutamidaṃ yathā;

Khettaṃ vā dehi gāmaṃ vā, desaṃ vā mama sobhanaṃ.

That which is devoid of the proper sequence of meaning is 'kamaccuta' (lapsed in sequence), as for example: Give me a beautiful field, or a village, or a region.

55. “Pada”iccādi. Padānaṃ atthakkamato muttaṃ gaḷitaṃ kamaccutamidanti vidhīyate. Khettaṃ vā iccādinā arucitoyaṃ yācanakkamo vattuno aviññutaṃ gameti. Yo hi khettampi dātuṃ nicchati, kathaṃ so gāmādikaṃ dassatīti.

55. “Pada,” etc. What deviates or slips from the sequence of word meanings is determined to be 'kamaccuta'. By 'a field or,' etc., this improper sequence of request conveys the speaker's lack of discernment. For one who is unwilling to give even a field, how would he give a village, etc.?

55. “Padatthi”ccādi. Padatthakkamato padānaṃ atthakkamato muttaṃ gaḷitaṃ idaṃ vākyaṃ kamaccutaṃ nāma. Udāharati “yathi”ccādi. Mama sobhanaṃ khettaṃ vā gāmaṃ vā desaṃ vā janapadaṃ vā dehi. Ettha khettamiccādi yācanakkamo vattuno aviññubhāvaṃ vinā ucitapadatthakkamaṃ nappakāseti, tathā hi khettamapi dātumanicchanto gāmanigamajanapadādiṃ kathaṃ dassatīti kamahāni.

55. “Padatthi,” etc. This sentence, which deviates or slips from the sequence of word meanings, is called 'kamaccuta'. He illustrates with 'yathā,' etc.: 'Give me a beautiful field, or a village, or a region, or a country.' Here, the request sequence beginning with 'a field' fails to express the proper sequence of meanings, thereby indicating the speaker's lack of discernment. For indeed, one who is unwilling to give even a field, how would they give a village, town, or country? Thus, there is a loss of sequence.

56.

56.

Lokiyattha’matikkantaṃ, ativuttaṃ mataṃ yathā;

Atisambādha’mākāsa-metissā thanajambhane thanajumbhane (sī.).

What has transcended worldly meaning is considered 'ativutta' (overstated), as for example: The space in the swelling of her breasts is excessively constricted.

56. “Loki”ccādi. Loke vidito lokiyo, taṃ lokiyatthamabhidheyyaṃ atikkantaṃ ananuvuttaṃ yaṃ taṃ ativuttaṃ matanti vidhīyate. Yathetyādinā udāharati. Etissā vanitāya thanānaṃ payodharānaṃ jambhane byāpane ākāsaṃ gaganaṃ atisambādhaṃ accantappakaṃ.

56. “Loki,” etc. What is known in the world is 'worldly'; that which has transcended or is contrary to that worldly meaning or denotation is determined to be 'overstated'. He illustrates with 'yathā,' etc.: In the swelling and expanding of this woman's breasts, her bosoms, the space, the sky, is excessively constricted, extremely small.

56. “Lokiyatthi”ccādi. Lokiyatthaṃ loke pasiddhamabhidheyyaṃ atikkantaṃ kathanākārena atikkamitaṃ vākyaṃ ativuttamiti mataṃ. Udāharati “yathi”ccādi. Etissā thanajambhane thanānaṃ vijambhane ākāsaṃ atisambādhaṃ anokāsaṃ. Ettha payodharānaṃ mahantattaṃ vadāmāti loke mahantanti [M 0.0090] pasiddhaṃ gaganamapi atikkantattā vākyamativuttadosena dūsitaṃ.

56. “Lokiyatthi,” etc. A statement that, by its manner of expression, surpasses a meaning well-known in the world is considered 'overstated'. He illustrates with “yathā,” etc. In the swelling and expansion of her breasts, the sky is excessively constricted, without space. Here, the statement, in seeking to declare the greatness of the breasts, is tainted by the fault of overstatement because it has surpassed even the sky, which is renowned in the world as vast.

57.

57.

Samudāyatthato’petaṃ, taṃ apetatthakaṃ yathā;

Gāviputto balībaddho, tiṇaṃ khādī pivī jalaṃ.

That which is devoid of collective meaning is 'apetatthaka' (devoid of meaning), as in: The son of a cow, a strong bull, ate grass and drank water.

57. “Samudāyi”ccādi. Samudāyassa pakaraṇato padasandhino vākyassa attho abhidheyyaṃ aṅgaṅgibhūtaṃ kriyākārakasambandhīvisesalakkhaṇaṃ saṃvohārikaṃ, tato apetaṃ apagataṃ suññaṃ, vinā na (ka.) padatthamattena tassa katthaci byabhicārābhāvato etādisaṃ yaṃ tamapetatthakanti vidhi. Na hi “gāviputto”ccādīsu samudāyattho sambhavati.

57. “Samudāyi,” etc. The meaning of a sentence, as a combination of words in context, is conventional, characterized by the specific relationships of action and agent that form an organic whole. That which is devoid of this, being departed and empty, is ruled to be 'apetatthaka'; this is apart from the mere meaning of the words, for that does not deviate anywhere. Indeed, in terms like “gāviputto,” a collective meaning is not possible.

57. “Samudāyi”ccādi. Samudāyatthato visesanavisesyabhūtakriyākārakasambandhehi yuttavākyasaṅkhātapadasamudāyassa sambandhapadattā vohārānurūpaatthato apetaṃ apagataṃ, avayavatthamattassa vā sabbattha labbhamānattā samudāyatthato suññaṃ, taṃ vākyaṃ apetatthakaṃ nāma. Yathiccādinā udāharati “gāviputto balībaddho usabho tiṇaṃ khādi, jalaṃ pivī”ti. Ettha avayavatthamattena vinā samudāyena gamyamānassa kassaci visesatthassa abhāvā samudāyatthato apagataṃ nāma hoti.

57. “Samudāyi,” etc. A sentence is called 'apetatthaka' which is devoid and departed from a meaning that accords with usage—that is, from the collective meaning of a group of words forming a sentence connected by qualifier-qualified and action-agent relationships—or which is empty of collective meaning because the meaning of the individual elements is found everywhere. He illustrates with “yathā,” etc.: “The son of a cow, a strong bull, an ox, ate grass and drank water.” Here, because there is an absence of any specific meaning conveyed by the collective beyond the mere meaning of the individual elements, it is called 'departed from the collective meaning'.

58.

58.

Bandhe pharusatā yattha, taṃ bandhapharusaṃ yathā;

Kharā khilā parikkhīṇā, khette khittaṃ phalatya’laṃ.

Where there is harshness in the composition, that is 'bandhapharusa' (harsh composition), as in: Rough, barren lands are exhausted; what is sown in the field yields abundantly.

58. “Bandhe”ccādi. [M 0.0091] Kharāiccādikaṃ bandhapharusaṃ sutisubhagattābhāvato kharā kakkasā khilā khāṇukādayo parikkhīṇā khayaṃ pattā yato, tasmā khette kedāre khittaṃ vuttaṃ alamaccantaṃ phalati nipphajjati. vākyadoso.

58. “Bandhe,” etc. The verse beginning with 'kharā' is 'harsh composition' because of the absence of pleasantness to the ear. Since rough, harsh, barren, stump-like things, etc., are exhausted, having reached destruction, therefore, what is sown and cast in the field or furrow yields and is produced abundantly, exceedingly. This is a sentence fault.

58. “Bandhe”ccādi. Bandhe bandhasarīre pharusatā sutisukhatābhāvato pharusabhāvo yattha vākye bhavati, taṃ vākyaṃ bandhapharusaṃ nāma hoti. Yathāti udāharati. Kharā kakkasā khilā khāṇukādayo parikkhīṇā yasmā khīṇā honti, tasmā khette khittaṃ vuttaṃ bījaṃ alaṃ atisayena phalati nipphajjati.

58. “Bandhe,” etc. Where harshness, a state of harshness due to a lack of pleasantness to the ear, occurs in a statement, in the body of the composition, that statement is called 'harsh composition.' He illustrates with 'yathā.' Since rough, harsh, barren, stump-like things, etc., are exhausted, having become worn out, therefore the seed sown and cast in the field yields and is produced abundantly, exceedingly.

Vākyadosaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the section on sentence faults is concluded.

Vākyatthadosaniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of the Faults of Sentence Meaning

59.

59.

Ñeyyaṃ lakkhaṇamanvattha-vasenā’pakkamādinaṃ;

Udāharaṇametesaṃ, dāni sandassayāmya’haṃ.

The characteristic of 'lapsed sequence,' etc., is to be known by way of its etymological meaning; now I shall present examples of these.

59. “Ñeyya”miccādi. Apakkamādīnaṃ yathāuddiṭṭhānaṃ lakkhīyati udāharaṇamanenāti atthena lakkhaṇaṃ anvatthavasena apagato kamo yattha taṃ apakkamantiādinā atthānugamanavasena ñeyyaṃ viññātabbaṃ. Idāni vākyadose niddisitvā avasarappatte imasmiṃ kāle etesaṃ apakkamādīnaṃ udāharaṇaṃ lakkhiyaṃ ahaṃ sandassayāmi pakāsessāmi.

59. “Ñeyya,” etc. The characteristic of 'lapsed sequence,' etc., as previously stated, is to be known and understood by way of its etymological meaning—by following the meaning of terms like 'apakkama is that in which the sequence has departed'—in the sense that it is that by which an example is indicated. Now, having pointed out the sentence faults, at this opportune time, I shall present and clarify the examples of these, which are to be illustrated.

59. Idāni uddiṭṭhānukkamena apakkamādiatthadosāni vibhāveti “ñeyya”miccādinā. Apakkamādīnaṃ apakkamocityahīnādīnaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ apakkamādivisayabuddhiyā aviparītavuttiyā pavattikāraṇaṃ anvatthavasena apagato kamo yatthiccādivacanatthānugatañāṇavasena ñeyyaṃ ñātabbaṃ, visuṃ lakkhaṇaṃ na vadāmāti vuttaṃ hoti. Idāni ahaṃ etesaṃ apakkamādīnaṃ udāharaṇaṃ lakkhiyaṃ sandassayāmi. Atthānugatamanvatthaṃ anvatthassa ñāṇassa vasoti viggaho.

59. Now, in the stated order, he explains the faults of meaning, such as 'lapsed sequence,' by means of “ñeyya,” etc. The characteristic of 'lapsed sequence,' etc.—such as 'lapsed sequence,' 'impropriety,' and so on—is to be known by way of knowledge that conforms to the etymological meaning of terms like 'that in which the sequence has departed,' this being the cause for the correct functioning of the mind regarding the subject of 'lapsed sequence,' etc. This means, 'I do not state the characteristic separately.' Now I shall present the examples of these, which are to be illustrated. The analysis is: 'anvattha' means 'conforming to the meaning'; it is 'by way of knowledge that conforms to the meaning'.

Tatthāpakkamaṃ yathā

Therein, an example of lapsed sequence:

60.

60.

Bhāvanādānasīlāni, sammā sampāditāni’ha;

Bhogasaggādinibbāna-sādhanāni na saṃsayo.

Meditation, giving, and virtue, rightly accomplished here, are means for wealth, heaven, and Nibbāna, without doubt.

60. “Bhāvanā”iccādi. [M 0.0092] Sammā alobhādihetusampattiyā sakkaccaṃ sampāditāni nipphāditāni. Ettha bhogasaggādinibbānānaṃ hetavo yathākkamaṃ dānasīlabhāvanāyo, na tu bhāvanādānasīlāni.

60. “Bhāvanā,” etc. 'Rightly' means accomplished and perfected with care through the attainment of causes such as non-greed. Here, the causes for wealth, heaven, and Nibbāna are, in respective order, giving, virtue, and meditation, not meditation, giving, and virtue.

60. Tattha tesu apakkamādīsu apakkamaṃ yathā apakkamassodāharaṇamevaṃ. Ocityahīnaṃ yathātyādīsupi evamattho veditabbo. “Bhāvani”ccādi. Iha imasmiṃ attabhāve sammā sampāditāni alobhādihetusampattiyā sakkaccaṃ sampāditāni rāsikatāni bhāvanādānasīlāni bhogasaggādinibbānasādhanāni upabhogaparibhogāni, sagguppattiāyuārogyādīni, nibbānañceti etesaṃ sādhakāni. Na saṃsayo sadisavisadisavipākadāne saṃsayo nāma natthi. Ettha bhogasagganibbānānaṃ hetubhūtā pana kamato dānasīlabhāvanāyo bhavantīti phalakkamassa hetukkamaṃ viruddhamiti kamāpetaṃ nāma hoti.

60. Therein, among those such as non-departure, the example of non-departure is thus. Likewise, the meaning should be understood in cases such as 'lacking propriety,' and so on. Regarding 'Bhāvani,' etc.: Here, in this very existence, meditation, giving, and virtue—rightly accomplished, carefully fulfilled through the attainment of causes such as non-greed, and accumulated—are the means for wealth, heaven, and Nibbāna. They are conducive to enjoyment and use, rebirth in heaven, longevity, health, and so forth, and to Nibbāna. There is no doubt; in the giving of similar and dissimilar results, there is indeed no doubt. Here, however, giving, virtue, and meditation are the causes for wealth, heaven, and Nibbāna respectively. Thus, the sequence of the causes contradicts the sequence of the effects, and so this is called 'contrary to sequence' (kamāpeta).

Ocityahīnaṃ yathā

Lacking propriety, as in:

61. Pūjanīyataro loke, aha’meko nirantaraṃ.

Mayekasmiṃ guṇā sabbe, yato samuditā ahuṃ.

61. I alone am continuously more worthy of veneration in the world, since all virtues have gathered in me alone.

61. “Pūjanīyi”ccādi. Yato yasmā kāraṇā sabbe guṇā sīlādayo ekasmiṃ kevale mayi eva samuditā rāsibhūtā ahuṃ ahesuṃ, tasmā kāraṇā imasmiṃ sattaloke eko kevalo ahameva nirantaraṃ satataṃ pūjanīyataro atisayena pujjoti. Evamattapasaṃsanamarucitaṃ sappurisassa.

61.
