Regarding 'Pūjanīyi,' etc.: Because—for which reason—all virtues, such as morality and so on, were gathered and accumulated in me alone, for that reason, in this world of beings, I alone am continuously and constantly more worthy of veneration, exceedingly revered. Such self-praise is unbefitting for a noble person.

61. “Pūjanīyatare”ccādi. [M 0.0093] Yato yasmā sabbe guṇā sīlādayo ekasmiṃ mayi adutiye mayi eva samuditā rāsibhūtā ahuṃ ahesuṃ, tasmā loke sattaloke eko adutiyo ahameva nirantaraṃ satataṃ pūjanīyataro atisayena pūjanīyo. Evaṃ attappasaṃsanato ucitatāya parihānīti ocityahīnaṃ nāma.

61. Regarding 'Pūjanīyatare,' etc.: Because all virtues, such as morality and so on, were gathered and accumulated in me alone, in me without a second, therefore, in the world of beings, I alone, without a second, am constantly more worthy of veneration, exceedingly worthy of veneration. Thus, from such self-praise, there is a decline from propriety; hence, it is called 'lacking propriety.'

Yathā ca

And as in:

62.

62.

Yācitohaṃ kathaṃ nāma, na dajjāmyapi jīvitaṃ;

Tathāpi puttadānena, vedhate hadayaṃ mama.

Having been asked, how could I not give even my life? Nevertheless, with the giving of my son, my heart trembles.

62. “Yācito”iccādi. Ettha “yadi yāciṃsu, jīvitampi yācakānaṃ dajjāmī”ti dassitodāratāyānucitaṃ puttadāne hadayapavedhanakathanaṃ vessantarassa yajjevamavoca.

62. Regarding 'Yācito,' etc.: Here, Vessantara’s statement about his heart trembling at the giving of his son is inappropriate to the generosity he demonstrated when he said, 'If they should ask, I would give even my life to the beggars.'

62. Yathā ca, evampi ocityahīnassa udāharaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ “yācito”ccādi. Yācito yācakehi yācito ahaṃ jīvitamapi kathaṃ nāma na dajjāmi, tathāpi evaṃ dānajjhāsaye satipi puttadānena mama hadayaṃ vedhate kampate. Ettha vessantarassa “yadi yāceyyuṃ, jīvitamapi yācakānaṃ dajjāmī”ti katapaṭiññāya puttadānena hadayakampanassa kathanaṃ cāgātisayayogasaṅkhātaudāraguṇassa ananucchavikanti ocityahīnaṃ.

62. And also, in this way, an example of 'lacking propriety' should be seen: Regarding 'Yācito,' etc. 'I, having been asked by beggars, how could I not give even my life? Nevertheless, even with such a disposition for giving, my heart trembles and quakes at the giving of my son.' Here, for Vessantara, who had made the vow, 'If they should beg, I would give even my life to the beggars,' the statement about his heart trembling at the giving of his son is unbefitting the noble quality known as the application of extreme generosity; thus, it is 'lacking propriety.'

Bhaggarīti yathā

Broken style, as in:

63.

63.

Itthīnaṃ dujjanānañca, vissāso nopapajjate;

Vise siṅgimhi nadiyaṃ, roge rājakulamhī ca.

Trust is not fitting in women and wicked people, nor in poison, a horned animal, a river, disease, and a royal family.

63. “Itthīna”miccādi. Nopapajjate na yujjati. Ettha sambandhe chaṭṭhiyā pariccāgena viseiccādinā ādhāre sattamīniddeso [M 0.0094] attharītiyā bhaṅgo. Ādo majjhe ca cakārapariccāgā saddarītiyā bhaṅgo, rītīnaṃ anantattā bhaṅgāpyanantā. Udāharaṇaṃ tu disāmattaṃ.

63. Regarding 'Itthīna,' etc.: 'Nopapajjate' means 'na yujjati' (it is not fitting). Here, by abandoning the genitive case in the sense of relation and indicating the locative case in the sense of location with 'vise,' etc., there is a breach of the style of meaning. By abandoning the particle 'ca' at the beginning and in the middle, there is a breach of the style of sound. Because styles are infinite, breaches are also infinite. The example, however, is merely an indication.

63. “Itthīna”miccādi. Itthīnañca dujjanānañca vissāso sahavāsādīhi vissāso nopapajjate anatthasaṃsayānivattikāraṇattā na yujjati. Vise garaḷe ca siṅgimhi siṅgavati mahiṃ sādo ca nadiyañca roge vaḍḍhamānake roge ca rājakulamhi ca vadhabandhanādikārake rājakule ca vissāso nopapajjate. Ettha ādo sambandhe chaṭṭhiyā ārabhitvā taṃ pahāya sattamiyā vuttattā attharīti ca, ādimajjhesu casaddapariccāgato saddarīti ca bhinnā. Casaddaṃ payuñjantena ādo eva vā ante eva vā paccekaṃ vā yojetabbaṃ hoti. Īdiso payogo rītibhaṅgo nāma hoti. Rītīnaṃ bahuttā rītibhaṅgadosāpi bahuvidhā. Idaṃ pana mukhamattanidassanaṃ.

63. Regarding 'Itthīna,' etc.: Trust in women and wicked people—trust through cohabitation and so on—is not fitting; because it is a cause for not averting harm and doubt, it is not appropriate. Trust is not fitting in poison and venom; in a horned animal, one possessing horns; in a buffalo; in a river; in a growing disease; and in a royal family that causes execution, imprisonment, and so on. Here, because having begun with the genitive case in the sense of relation, it abandons that and is expressed with the locative case, the style of meaning is broken; and from the abandonment of the particle 'ca' at the beginning and in the middle, the style of sound is broken. When using the particle 'ca,' it should be connected either only at the beginning, or only at the end, or with each item. Such usage is called a breach of style. Because there are many styles, the faults of breaching style are also of many kinds. This, however, is merely an introductory illustration.

Sasaṃsayaṃ yathā

Doubtful, as in:

64.

64.

Munindacandimāloka-rasalolavilocano;

Jano’vakkantapantho’va, gopadassanapīṇito.

A person whose eyes are eager for the delight in the light of the moon-like Sage-king, like one who has entered upon the path, is pleased by the sight of a 'gopada'.

64. “Munindi”ccādi. [M 0.0095] Candimā viya candimā, munindoyeva candimā, tassa ālokanaṃ dassanaṃ, āloko pakāso vā, tasmiṃ raso anurāgo, tena lolāni capalāni locanāni akkhīni yassa so jano avakkanto okkanto paviṭṭho pantho maggo yena avakkantapantho eva gunnaṃ raṃsīnaṃ, iṭṭhatthanipphattisūcakabhāvena gopadatthassa vā padassanena pīṇito muditoti ettha gorūpassa padassanenātipi viññāyatīti sandeho.

64. Regarding 'Munindi,' etc.: The Sage-king is like the moon; the Sage-king is the moon itself. His 'āloka' is seeing, or 'āloka' is radiance. 'Rasa' in that is attachment. He is the person whose eyes ('locanāni,' 'akkhīni') are made fickle ('lolāni,' 'capalāni') by that. 'Avakkantapantho' means one by whom the path ('pantho,' 'maggo') has been entered ('avakkanto,' 'okkanto,' 'paviṭṭho'). He is pleased ('pīṇito'), gladdened ('mudito'), by the sight of the rays of qualities, or by the sight of the meaning of 'cow's track' as an indicator of the accomplishment of a desired aim. Here, because it is also understood as 'by the sight of the form of a cow,' there is doubt.

64. “Munindi”ccādi. Munindacandimālokarasalolavilocano munindasaṅkhātassa candimassa āloke dassane pātubhāve vā rasena ālayena cañcalanetto jano avakkantapanthova otiṇṇamaggova buddhassa dassanatthāya maggamotiṇṇoti adhippāyo. Gopadassanapīṇito gosaṅkhātaraṃsipadassanena, abhimaṅgalasammatagopadassanena vā santuṭṭho hoti. Ettha gopadassanenāti ca atthassa gamyamānattā viññātuṃ saṃsayo uppajjatīti sasaṃsayaṃ nāma. Avakkanto pantho yenāti ca, gunnaṃ raṃsīnaṃ, gāvassa vā padassananti ca, gopadassanena pīṇitoti ca viggaho.

64. Regarding 'Munindi,' etc.: 'Munindacandimālokarasalolavilocano' means a person whose eyes are made restless by delight and attachment in the light, the sight, or the manifestation of the moon that is the Sage-king. 'Avakkantapantho' means one who has descended upon the path; the intention is that he has entered the path to see the Buddha. 'Gopadassanapīṇito' means he is satisfied by the sight of rays designated as 'go,' or by the sight of a cow, which is considered auspicious. Here, because the meaning 'by the sight of a cow' is also understood, a doubt arises in understanding; hence, it is called 'doubtful' (sasaṃsayaṃ). The analyses are: 'avakkanto pantho yena' ('the path has been entered by him'); 'gunnaṃ raṃsīnaṃ' ('of the rays of qualities'); 'gāvassa vā padassanaṃ' ('or the sight of a cow'); and 'gopadassanena pīṇito' ('pleased by the sight of a cow').

65.

65.

Vākyatthato duppatīti-karaṃ gāmmaṃ mataṃ yathā;

Poso vīriyavāso’yaṃ, paraṃ hantvāna vissami.

That which, from the meaning of the statement, causes difficult understanding is considered vulgar, as in: 'This man, full of energy, having slain the other, rested.'

65. “Vākya”iccādi. Paraṃ sattuṃ hantvāna paharitvā vīriyavā sūro soyaṃ poso puriso vissami vissattho. Ayamattho tāva na duppatīto. Paraṃ accantaṃ hantvāna vīriyavā ucitasambhavo soyaṃ poso vissamīti duppatītoyamattho.

65. Regarding 'Vākya,' etc.: 'Having slain the other, the enemy, having struck him, this man, this person, energetic and heroic, rested, confident.' This meaning, for now, is not difficult to understand. But the meaning, 'Having utterly slain the other, this man, energetic and of noble birth, rested'—this meaning is difficult to understand.

65. Anvatthavasena lakkhaṇassa apākaṭattā salakkhaṇaṃ lakkhiyamudāharati “vākyatthato”ccādinā. Vākyatthato duppatītikaraṃ viruddhappakāsakaṃ gāmmanti mataṃ. Yathāti udāharati. Paraṃ sattuṃ hantvāna māretvāna vīriyavā sūro so ayaṃ poso vissami vigataparissamo ahosi, ayamattho iṭṭho. Paraṃ atisayena hantvāna vītikkamaṃ katvā vīriyavā upacitasambhavo upacitasukko so ayaṃ puriso vāyāmena vissami vigatavāyāmo ahosīti. Imassatthassa asabbhārahattā gāmmattaṃ. Vīriyaṃ ussāho sambhavo vā assa atthīti viggaho.

65. Because the definition is not manifest according to its literal meaning, he illustrates the defined thing along with its definition, beginning with 'vākyatthato,' etc. That which, from the meaning of the statement, is difficult to understand and reveals a contradiction, is considered vulgar. He gives an example, saying 'as': 'Having slain the other, the enemy, having killed him, this man, energetic and heroic, rested, became free from exertion'—this meaning is desired. 'Having excessively slain another, having transgressed, this man, energetic, of accumulated prosperity and accumulated merit, rested through effort, became free of effort'—because this meaning is unworthy of good people, it is vulgar. The analysis is: 'He has energy (vīriya), exertion (ussāho), or prosperity (sambhava).'

66.

66.

Duṭṭhālaṅkaraṇaṃ [M 0.0096] tetaṃ, yatthālaṅkāradūsanaṃ;

Tassālaṅkāraniddese, rūpamāvībhavissati.

That is faulty ornamentation where there is a flaw in the ornament; its form will become manifest in the exposition of ornamentation.

66. “Duṭṭhā”iccādi. Yattha yasmiṃ vākye alaṅkārānaṃ dūsanaṃ vikaṭatā, etantu duṭṭhālaṅkaraṇaṃ duṭṭhālaṅkaraṇaṃ nāma, tassa duṭṭhālaṅkārassa rūpaṃ sarūpaṃ alaṅkāraniddese taṃnāmake paricchede āvībhavissati pakāsissati, tattheva taṃ dassayissāmīti adhippāyo.

66. Regarding 'Duṭṭhā,' etc.: Where, in a sentence, there is a flaw or distortion of the ornaments, that is called 'faulty ornamentation.' The form, the true nature, of that faulty ornamentation will become manifest and clear in the chapter named 'Exposition of Ornamentation.' The intention is, 'I will show it right there.'

66. “Duṭṭhālaṅkari”ccādi. Yattha vākye alaṅkāradūsanaṃ alaṅkārānaṃ virodho hoti, etaṃ vākyatthanissitaṃ etaṃ vākyaṃ duṭṭhālaṅkaraṇaṃ duṭṭhālaṅkāro nāma, tassa duṭṭhālaṅkaraṇadosopalakkhitavākyassa rūpaṃ sarūpaṃ lakkhiyaṃ alaṅkāraniddese alaṅkārānaṃ nidassanaṭṭhānabhūte paricchede āvībhavissati. Ettha vuttepi puna tatthāpi vattabbaṃ siyāti na vuttanti adhippāyo. Uddese “duṭṭhālaṅkatī”ti vatvā idāni “duṭṭhālaṅkaraṇa”nti vacanaṃ alaṅkati alaṅkaraṇaalaṅkārasaddānaṃ tulyatthattā na virujjhati.

66. ‘Faulty ornamentation’ and so forth. Where, in a sentence, there is a corruption of an ornament or a conflict among ornaments, that sentence, being dependent on the meaning of the sentence, is called ‘faulty ornamentation’ (duṭṭhālaṅkaraṇa) or ‘faulty ornament’ (duṭṭhālaṅkāra). The form, the true nature, and the example of a sentence characterized by the fault of faulty ornamentation will become manifest in the chapter on the exposition of ornaments, which is the place for demonstrating ornaments. The intention is that it is not stated here, as it would have to be stated again there. In the summary, having said ‘duṭṭhālaṅkatī,’ the word ‘duṭṭhālaṅkaraṇa’ is now used; since the words ‘alaṅkati,’ ‘alaṅkaraṇa,’ and ‘alaṅkāra’ have the same meaning, there is no contradiction.

67.

67.

Kato’tra saṅkhepanayā mayā’yaṃ,

Dosānamesaṃ pavaro vibhāgo;

Eso’va’laṃ bodhayituṃ kavīnaṃ,

Tamatthi ce khedakaraṃ parampi.

This supreme classification of these faults has been made here by me in a summary manner. This alone is sufficient to enlighten poets, and also concerning any other troublesome fault, should it exist.

Iti saṅgharakkhitamahāsāmipādaviracite subodhālaṅkāre

Thus, in the Subodhālaṅkāra composed by the venerable Great Elder Saṅgharakkhita,

Dosāvabodho nāma

The Understanding of Faults,

Paṭhamo paricchedo.

The First Chapter.

67. Evaṃ “sodāharaṇametesaṃ, lakkhaṇaṃ kathayāmyaha”nti katapaṭiññānurūpaṃ paṭipajja dāni “katotri”ccādinā nikkhipananayaṃ saṅkhipati. Atra imasmiṃ adhikāre, paricchede [M 0.0097] vā esaṃ yathāvuttānaṃ dosānaṃ padadosādīnaṃ pavaro uttamo vibhāgo vibhajanaṃ saṅkhepanayā saṅkhepakkamena, na vitthārato, yato aparisaṅkhyeyyānaṃ natthi pariyanto mayā kato niṭṭhāpito. Nanu “saṅkhepanayā”ti vuttattā purātanehi purātarehi (ka.) dīpitā santi bahū dosā, te pariccattā siyunti? Ettha vuccate, vitthārakkamassa anadhippetattā “saṅkhepanayā”ti vuttaṃ, na pana sabbathā pariccāgena. Tathā hi–

67. Thus, having proceeded in accordance with the pledge made, ‘I will explain their characteristics with examples,’ he now summarizes the method of concluding with ‘Kato’tra’ etc. Here, in this section or chapter, this supreme and excellent classification—the division of the faults mentioned earlier, such as word-faults and others—has been made and concluded by me concisely, by way of summary, not extensively, for there is no limit to the innumerable. Now, since it is stated ‘by way of summary,’ might it be that many faults pointed out by the ancients have been omitted? Here it is replied: Because extensive treatment was not intended, it was said ‘by way of summary,’ but not by complete omission. For indeed—

“Nihantu soyaṃ jalitaṃ, pataṅgo aripāvaka”ntiādīnaṃ

‘May this moth extinguish the blazing enemy-fire’ and so on.

Akkhamatthantarādikaṃ viruddhatthantarānugatanti ca. Ettha hi pataṅgasaddena jotiriṅgaṇasaṅkhātamatthantaramasamatthamicchitatthe “vacanti gaṇḍā”tyevamādikaṃ amaṅgalaapayuttapadādikaṃ kiliṭṭhe antogadhanti ca.

And [the fault of] an unsuitable different meaning and so forth is included under 'contradictory meaning.' For here, by the word ‘pataṅga,’ a different meaning, namely ‘firefly,’ is unsuitable for the intended meaning. And such things as ‘they speak of tumors,’ which consist of inauspicious and inappropriate words, are included in the ‘defiled’ category.

Gajahesādi sambandhadūsitaṃ lokavirodhi, sogatāgamādīsu pasiddhaṃ rūpakkhandhādikamaññatra vuttaṃ appatītaṃ nāma. Idaṃ āgamavirodhiiti, sambandhadūsitappatītādikaṃ virodhimhi paviṭṭhanti ca, ānetabbahetuttā hetvapekkhaṃ neyyato na byatiriccatīti ca.

What is tainted by association, such as ‘an elephant’s neighing,’ is contrary to worldly convention. What is well-known in the Buddhist scriptures and so on, such as the aggregate of form, but is stated in another context, is called ‘unestablished.’ This is contrary to the scriptures. And what is tainted by association, unestablished, and so forth, is included in the ‘contradictory’ category. And because it requires a reason to be brought in, what is dependent on a reason is not different from what is to be inferred.

“Devo voharatu klesaṃ, rāhukhinno divākaro”

‘May the king dispel affliction, the sun afflicted by Rāhu.’

Iccādikaṃ asāmatthyābhidheyyādikaṃ ocityahīne saṅgahitanti ca. Jigucchaasabbhasaṃsūcakaatthantarakañca gāmmaṃ duppatītikare saṅgayhatīti ca. ( ) (duruccāraṇaṃ)? Sabandhapharusameveti ca.

And this and so forth, which expresses incapability and the like, is included in the category of ‘lacking in propriety.’ And that which has another meaning indicative of disgust and unrefined speech, and what is vulgar, is included in the category of ‘difficult to understand.’ ... And it is indeed connected and harsh.

Ettha pana ocityahīnaduppatītikarānaṃ vākyatthadosattepi phandhapharusassa ca vākyadosatte padapadatthānaṃ dosato vākyameva duṭṭhaṃ siyā, vākyañca padehi viriccate, pade duṭṭhe vākyattho ca duṭṭho siyā. Padadosato vākyavākyatthānaṃ nānābhāvābhāvañāpanatthaṃ asāmatthiyābhidheyyādikaṃ padaṃ ocityahīnādivākyatthadosādīsu [M 0.0098] anto kathitaṃ. Tathā hi purātanehi viruddhatthantarādīhi padehi viracitaṃ vākyaṃ viruddhantiādinā bahūni duṭṭhāni vākyāni dassitāni. “Harisamānayī”ti ettha hapubbaṃ risa’mānayīti icchitatthā pari bhaṭṭhaṃ bhaṭṭhaṃ. Nānatthamappasiddhehi yuttaṃ guḷhaṃ, yathā “sakko sahassagū”ti. Iti bhaṭṭhaguḷhatthādayo pasādālaṅkāraviruddhāti ca.

Here, however, even when the sentence meaning is flawed due to lack of propriety and difficulty in comprehension, and when there is a sentence fault of harshness, the sentence itself may be faulty due to faults in words and word-meanings. And a sentence is distinct from its words; if the words are faulty, the sentence meaning may also be faulty. To show the presence or absence of various sentence and sentence-meaning flaws arising from word-faults, words such as those expressing inadequacy and the like are discussed within the categories of sentence-meaning flaws like lack of propriety, etc. Thus, the ancients have shown many faulty sentences composed of words with contradictory meanings, etc., labeling them as ‘contradictory’ and so on. In ‘Harisamānayī’, the intended meaning is utterly lost. What is obscure (guḷhaṃ) is that which is connected with multiple meanings or uncommon words, for example, ‘Sakko sahassagū’. Thus, flaws such as lost and obscure meanings, etc., are contrary to the ornament of clarity.

Vākyepi visandhikamihānupayogīti ca, vākyantaropagataṃ vākyaṃ vākyagabbhaṃ, vākyantarapadasammissaṃ “apāthyameso dissati, vejjaṃ khādatyanārata”miccādikaṃ vākyasaṃkiṇṇañca byākiṇṇe samohitanti ca.

And in a sentence, what is disconnected and useless here... A sentence included within another sentence is called an ‘embedded sentence’. And a sentence mixed with words from another sentence, such as ‘This appears unreadable, the doctor eats constantly,’ is called a ‘mixed sentence’, and is included in the ‘disordered’ category.

“Kācuyyāne mayā diṭṭhā, vallarī pañcapallavā;

Pallave pallave mudhā, yassā kusumamañcarī”ti.

‘In Kācuyyāna, I saw a creeper with five shoots; on each shoot, in vain, a cluster of flowers.’

Idamavācakaṃ paheḷikāya pamussitāsannissitanti ca, tattha ca kavinā uyyānasaddena gehaṃ, latāvācinā vallarīsaddena aṅganā, pallavasaddena karacaraṇadasanacchadā, mañcarīsaddena nakhasobhā dantakantiyo ca vattumicchitā, vākyatthepi paduminīnaṃ rattiyamunniddatādikaṃ viruddhaṃ virodhinilīnanti ca nātyanuññātā, na tu sabbathā pariccāgena. Esova evaṃ yathāvuttanayena niṭṭhāpito ayaṃ saṅkhepanayo eva kavīnaṃ paṇḍitajanānaṃ khedakaraṃ “kathaṃ nāma bandhepīdisaṃ sati santī”ti evamāsuhanopajanaṃ paraṃ padadose asādhusandiddhapariyāya ñeyyaappatītatthaappayojaka dubbodhadesiyādikaṃ, vākyadose adhikaūnabhaggacchandādikaṃ, vākyatthadose upakkamopasaṃhāravisamañceti iccevamādikamaparampi dūsanaṃ atthi ce yadi bhaveyya, tampi bodhayitumavagametuṃ alaṃ samatthaṃ yathāvuttadosānusārena buddhimantehi sakkā ūhitunti.

This is ‘unexpressive,’ relying on a riddle, on concealment and implication. Here, the poet intended to express ‘house’ by the word ‘garden,’ ‘woman’ by the word ‘creeper’ which denotes a vine, ‘hands, feet, and lips’ by the word ‘sprout,’ and ‘the beauty of nails and the luster of teeth’ by the word ‘cluster of flowers.’ And in the meaning of the sentence, the blooming of lotuses at night and so forth is contradictory, and [the fault] ‘concealed by the contradictory’ is not entirely permitted, yet not entirely rejected. This concise method, thus completed in the manner described, is indeed troublesome for poets and scholars, generating vexation, as they think: ‘How can such things be in the composition of a good poet?’ Furthermore, if there are other blemishes—such as word-faults like improper, ambiguous, synonymous, inferable, unestablished, useless, obscure, and provincial expressions; sentence-faults like redundant, deficient, or broken meter; and sentence-meaning faults like incongruity between the opening and conclusion—this exposition is sufficient to make even those understood, for they can be inferred by the intelligent in accordance with the faults already described.

Evaṃ [M 0.0099] vadato ca ganthakārassāyamadhippāyo – ye dosā vibhāgaso na vuttā, te mayā ganthagāravabhayā saṅkhepitā, lakkhaṇato tu saṅgahitā. Na hi tesamantaṃ ko jahāpeti.

And when the author speaks thus, his intention is this: those faults not mentioned in detail have been summarized by me out of fear of the burden of the text, but they are included by their characteristics. Indeed, who can bring them to an end?

Tattha saddasatthaviruddhamasādhu. Yaṃ kriyādinimittamupādāya atthantarepi vattate, taṃ saññābhāveneva payuttaṃ sandiddhaṃ, yathā “ravimhihimahā”ti, idaṃ pana visesanatthe sādhu hoti. Pasiddhasaññāsaddassa pariyāyantarena parikappitapadaṃ pariyāyañeyyaṃ, yathā “vaḷavāmukhene”ti ettha “assavanitānanena” iti. Yaṃ accantābyabhicārībhāvena visesyassa guṇaṃ vadati, taṃ appatītatthaṃ, yathā “kaṇhamasī”ti. Adhigatatthānupayogaṃ appayojakaṃ, yathā “atiphenilaṃ sāgaramalaṅghī”ti. “Manuññaddhanayo pāde, khādayo kani bhanti te” iccādiko dubbodho, kani kaññe khādayo gaggharikā. “Ime lāvaṇyatallā te, gallā lolavilocane”iccādiko desiyo, tallo jalāsayaviseso, gallo kapolo. “Saggasevīnaṃ ripūnamitthīnamakaṅkaṇo pāṇi. Nettamanañjana”ntiādikaṃ adhikaṃ. “Akaṅkaṇo pāṇī”tiādinā vedhabyassa gammamānattā “saggasevīna”nti adhikanti. Yattha vattabbassa ūnatā, taṃ ūnaṃ, yathā “tilokatilakaṃ muni”ntiādi. Ettha “vandāmī”ti ūnaṃ, chandobhaṅgānvitaṃ vaco bhaggacchandaṃ pākaṭaṃ. Ārambhāvasānena visamaṃ upakkamopasaṃhāravisamaṃ, taṃ pana āraddhakkamapariccāgenāparena nikkhipanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Herein, that which is contrary to phonetics is faulty. That which, by taking a sign such as action, also applies to another meaning, is ambiguous when used merely as a conventional term, as in 'ravimhihimahā' (in the sun, snow, great); this, however, is correct in the sense of a qualifier. A word devised as an alternative for a well-known conventional term is to be understood as a synonym, as in 'vaḷavāmukhena' (by the mare's mouth), where 'assavanitānanena' (by the horse-female's mouth) is used. That which, by being absolutely invariable, states a quality of the thing qualified, has an unperceived meaning, as in 'kaṇhamasī' (black ink). That which is useless for the intended meaning is irrelevant, as in 'he crossed the very foamy ocean' (`atiphenilaṃ sāgaramalaṅghī`). The verse beginning 'Manuññaddhanayo pāde, khādayo kani bhanti te' is difficult to understand; 'kani' means 'O maiden' (`kaññe`), and 'khādayo' means anklets (`gaggharikā`). The verse beginning 'Ime lāvaṇyatallā te, gallā lolavilocane' is provincial; 'tallo' is a type of pond, and 'gallo' means cheek. The verse beginning 'The hand of the wives of enemies who serve heaven is without bracelets; the eye is without collyrium' (`Saggasevīnaṃ ripūnamitthīnamakaṅkaṇo pāṇi. Nettamanañjanaṃ`) is redundant. Since widowhood is understood from 'the hand is without bracelets' (`akaṅkaṇo pāṇī`) and so forth, 'of those who serve heaven' (`saggasevīnaṃ`) is redundant. Where there is a deficiency in what is to be said, it is deficient, as in 'the sage, the ornament of the three worlds' (`tilokatilakaṃ muniṃ`). Here, 'I venerate' (`vandāmi`) is deficient. Speech endowed with a broken meter is 'broken meter' (`bhaggacchandaṃ`), which is obvious. Uneven in beginning and end is 'uneven in commencement and conclusion' (`upakkamopasaṃhāravisamaṃ`); this, however, should be understood as the abandonment of the commenced order and the taking up of another.

Iti subodhālaṅkāre mahāsāmināmikāṭīkāyaṃ

Thus, in the Subodhālaṅkāra, in the sub-commentary named Mahāsāmināmikā.

Dosāvabodhaparicchedo.

The Chapter on the Understanding of Faults.

67. Evaṃ “sodāharaṇametesaṃ, lakkhaṇaṃ kathayāmyaha”nti katapaṭiññānurūpaṃ sampādetvā idāni “katotre”ccādinā nigamento dose saṅkhipati. Atra imasmiṃ adhikāre, [M 0.0100] paricchede vā esaṃ dosānaṃ yathāvuttapadadosādīnaṃ pavaro lakkhaṇāvirodhalakkhiyato uttamo vibhāgo asaṅkarato vibhajanaṃ saṅkhepanayā vitthārāpaniyasaṅkhepakkamena mayā kato vutto esova yathāvutto eso saṅkhepakkamo eva kavīnaṃ viracayantānaṃ khedakaraṃ bandhasarīre īdisaṃ īdisappayogaṃ kathaṃ nāma karomīti evaṃ pavattakhedamuppādayantaṃ parampi asādhusandiddhādi aññampi dūsanamatthi ce, taṃ sabbaṃ bodhayituṃ bodhetuṃ alaṃ samattho hoti. Niyati avuttopi attho etenāti ca, saṅkhepo ca so nayo cāti viggaho.

67. Thus, having fulfilled the promise, 'I will state their characteristics with examples,' he now, concluding, summarizes the faults with the verse beginning 'katotra'. Herein, in this section or chapter, the excellent classification of these faults—such as the aforementioned faults of words—a division supreme because it is characterized by non-contradiction with the definitions and is free from confusion, has been made and spoken by me according to the method of summary, a concise procedure that avoids extensiveness. This very concise method, as stated, is indeed capable of making known all other faults as well, such as the faulty and the ambiguous, which cause weariness to composing poets who think, 'How indeed can I make such a usage in the body of the composition?' And the analysis is: 'meaning, even if unstated, is conveyed by this' (`niyati avuttopi attho etena`), and 'it is a summary and it is a method' (`saṅkhepo ca so nayo ca`).

Ihāniddiṭṭhaṃ

What is not stated here.

“Nihantu soyaṃ jalitaṃ, pataṅgo aripāvaka”ntiādikaṃ

The verse beginning, 'Let this moth destroy the blazing enemy-fire' (`Nihantu soyaṃ jalitaṃ, pataṅgo aripāvakaṃ`).

Akkhamatthantarādikaṃ viruddhatthantare anupatattā na vuttaṃ, ettha sūriyavācako pataṅgasaddo jotiriṅgaṇavācakopi hotīti vattumicchitaamittaggivināse asamatthaññattho hoti.

The fault of 'inability to bear another meaning' (`akkhamatthantara`) and so on is not stated because it is included under 'contradictory other meaning' (`viruddhatthantara`). Here, the word 'pataṅga', which denotes the sun, also denotes a firefly. Thus, with respect to the desired destruction of the enemy's fire, it has the other meaning of something incapable.

“Vacanti gaṇḍi”ccādikaṃ āgame appasiddhaṃ lakkhaṇamattena sādhiyaṃ. Appayuttapadādidoso kiliṭṭhapadadose antogadho hotīti na vutto.

The verse beginning 'They call it a gong' (`Vacanti gaṇḍi`) is not established in the treatises but is determinable merely by its definition. The fault of an unconventional word (`appayuttapada`) and so on is not stated because it is included within the fault of an obscure word (`kiliṭṭhapada`).

Gajahesāturaṅgakoñcanādādisambandhadūsitañca. Jināgamādīsu pasiddharūpakkhandhādikamaññatra payuttamappatītannāmātīdaṃ dvayaṃ yathākkamaṃ lokavirodhamāgamavirodhañca hotīti virodhipade antogadhaṃ hoti. Hetvapekkhaṃ ānetabbahetuttā neyye antogadhanti na vuttaṃ.

And that which is faulty due to connection with the sounds of elephants, horses, herons, and so on. A term well-known in the Jina's teachings, such as 'form-aggregate', when used elsewhere, is called 'unfamiliar' (`appatīta`). These two, respectively, constitute 'contradiction of the world' (`lokavirodha`) and 'contradiction of the teachings' (`āgamavirodha`), and are thus included under the term 'contradictory' (`virodhipada`). 'Requiring a reason' (`hetvapekkhaṃ`) is not stated because it is included in 'requiring inference' (`neyya`), as it is a reason that must be supplied.

“Devo voharatu klesaṃ, rāhukhinno divākaro”

The verse: 'May the god remove affliction, the sun afflicted by Rāhu' (`Devo voharatu klesaṃ, rāhukhinno divākaro`).

Iccādikaṃ asamatthābhidhāyiccādi ocityahīne antogadhanti na vuttaṃ. Ettha divākaro sayaṃ rāhugahito aññesaṃ kilesāpanayane [M 0.0101] asamatthoti tamasāmatthiyaṃ visesanabhūtena “rāhukhinno”ti padena ñāyati.

This and other examples of 'stating the incapable' (`asamatthābhidhāyi`) are not mentioned because they are included in 'lacking propriety' (`ocityahīna`). Here, the sun, being itself seized by Rāhu, is incapable of removing the afflictions of others; that incapacity is known from the qualifying word 'afflicted by Rāhu' (`rāhukhinno`).

Jigucchāvamaṅgalaasabbhānaṃ tiṇṇamaññatrassa jotakaṃ vācakaṃ vā atthantaraṃ vā gāmmaṃ duppatītikarattā vākyatthagāmmadoseyeva antogadhanti na vuttaṃ. Duruccāraṇabhūtalakkhaṇaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ bandhapharusato abyatirittanti na vuttanti. “Harisamānayī”ti vattabbe hapubbaṃ risa’mānayiiccādikaṃ icchitatthato paribhaṭṭhattā bhaṭṭhañca “sakko sahassagū”iccādikaṃ apasiddhavisaye pariyuttaguḷhañceti ime atthaguḷhādayo pasādālaṅkāraviruddhattā pasādaguṇādāneneva pariccattāti na vuttaṃ. Ettha hi sahassaṃ gāvo cakkhūni assāti sahassagūti sakkassa nāmaṃ guḷhaṃ nāma hoti.

A word or another meaning which suggests one of the three—disgust, inauspiciousness, or impropriety—or which is vulgar, is not mentioned because, being difficult to understand, it is included in the fault of 'vulgarity of sentence meaning' (`vākyatthagāmma`). 'Harshness' (`kaṭṭha`), characterized by being difficult to pronounce, is not mentioned as it is not distinct from 'harshness of composition' (`bandhapharusa`). 'Corrupted' (`bhaṭṭha`), such as using 'hapubbaṃ risa’mānayi' when 'harisamānayī' should be said, which has fallen from the intended meaning; and 'obscure' (`guḷha`), such as 'sakko sahassagū', used in an unestablished sense—these and other faults such as 'obscurity of meaning' (`atthaguḷha`) are not mentioned because, being contrary to the adornment of clarity, they are rejected simply by the adoption of the quality of clarity (`pasāda`). Here, 'sahassagū' is an obscure name for Sakka, meaning 'he who has a thousand cows (or) eyes'.

Vākyadosepi visandhivākyaṃ idha anupayogittā na vuttaṃ. Vākyamajjhapatitavākyayuttaṃ vākyagabbhañca, vākyantarapadasammissaṃ.

Among sentence faults, 'a sentence with faulty sandhi' (`visandhivākya`) is not stated here as it is not applicable. Also 'a sentence with an embedded sentence' (`vākyagabbha`), which has another sentence inserted in its middle; and 'mixed with words of another sentence' (`vākyantarapadasammissaṃ`).

“Apāthyameso dissati, vejjaṃ khādatyanārataṃ”

The verse: 'This one sees what is unsuitable; he eats the physician incessantly' (`Apāthyameso dissati, vejjaṃ khādatyanārataṃ`).

Iccādikaṃ vākyasaṃkiṇṇañca byākiṇṇe antogadhanti na vuttaṃ. Ettha eso bhisakko anārataṃ niccaṃ apāthyaṃ rogassa ahitaṃ dissati vadati. Eso rogī anārataṃ satataṃ apāthyaṃ ahitaṃ khādati. Vejjaṃ bhisakkaṃ dissati kujjhati. Evaṃ anekavākyehipi sandhivākyaṃ saṃkiṇṇaṃ nāma.

This and other examples of a 'mixed sentence' (`vākyasaṃkiṇṇa`) are not mentioned because they are included in 'confused' (`byākiṇṇa`). Here, [the verse can be construed as:] 'This physician (`eso bhisakko`) incessantly (`anārataṃ`) sees (i.e., prescribes) what is unsuitable (`apāthyaṃ`) and harmful for the disease.' 'This patient (`eso rogī`) incessantly (`anārataṃ`) eats what is unsuitable (`apāthyaṃ`) and harmful.' 'He is hostile towards (`dissati`, i.e., `kujjhati`) the physician (`vejjaṃ`).' Thus, a sentence whose words can be construed with multiple clauses is called 'mixed' (`saṃkiṇṇa`).

“Kācuyyāne mayā diṭṭhā, vallarī pañcapallavā;

Pallave pallave mudhā, yassā kusumamañcarī”ti.

The verse: 'In Kācu's garden I have seen a creeper with five shoots; on every shoot, in vain, is its cluster of blossoms' (`Kācuyyāne mayā diṭṭhā, vallarī pañcapallavā; Pallave pallave mudhā, yassā kusumamañcarī`).

Idamavācakaṃ paheḷikāsu pamussitāsannissitamiti na vuttaṃ. Nanu cettha attanā paheḷikāya adassitattā avācakassa pamussitāya antogadhakaraṇaṃ asiddhena asiddhasādhananti? Nayidamevaṃ, “upekkhiyanti sabbāni, sissakhedabhayā mayā”ti ca upari kiliṭṭhapadadosaparihāre “paheḷikāyamāruḷhā, na hi duṭṭhā kiliṭṭhatā”ti ceti iminā [M 0.0102] purātanehi niddiṭṭhasoḷasapaheḷikāyopi dassitāti siddhena asiddhasādhanaṃ hoti. Tattha kavinā uyyānasaddena gehañca latāpariyāyavallarīsaddena aṅganā ca pallavasaddena karacaraṇādharā ca mañcarīsaddena nakhadantakantiyo ca vattumicchitā.

This 'non-expressive' (`avācaka`) is not mentioned because in riddles it is included under 'relying on the forgotten' (`pamussitāsannissita`). Now, is it not the case that, since a riddle was not itself shown by him, the inclusion of 'non-expressive' under 'forgotten' is proving the unproven by means of the unproven? This is not so. Because it was stated above, in the section on avoiding the fault of an obscure word, 'All are overlooked by me for fear of wearying the student,' and also, 'When employed in a riddle, obscurity is not a fault,' by this it is shown that even the sixteen riddles indicated by the ancients are included. Therefore, it is a case of proving the unproven by means of the proven. Therein, the poet intended to express: by the word 'garden' (`uyyāna`), a house; by the word 'creeper' (`vallarī`), a synonym for vine, a woman; by the word 'shoot' (`pallava`), the hands, feet, and lips; and by the word 'cluster of blossoms' (`mañcarī`), the radiance of the nails and teeth.

Vākyatthadosepi paduminīnaṃ rattiyaṃ pabujjhanādikaṃ viruddhaṃ virodhipadeyeva antogadhattā na vuttanti dassetuṃ “katotra saṅkhepanayā”ti vuttaṃ, na pana tesaṃ sabbathā pariccattattāti. Ettha ocityahīnaduppatītikarānaṃ dvinnaṃ vākyatthadosatte sati bandhapharusassa vākyadosatte sati virodhino padadosatte sati “asamatthābhidhāyi”ādipadaṃ, “jigucchādittayapakāsakā”dipadaṃ, kaṭṭhapadaṃ, paduminīnaṃ rattiyaṃ phullatādi dunniddatādi (ka.) vākyatthañceti ime cattāro dosā bhinnajātikesu ocityādīsu kathaṃ saṅgahitāti? Saccaṃ, tathāpi padānaṃ duṭṭhatte sati vākyavākyatthānamaduṭṭhatā nāma natthīti padadosena sandhivākyavākyatthadosānamanaññattaṃ sissānaṃ ñāpanatthaṃ padadosādikaṃ vākyatthadosādīsu saṅgahitanti veditabbaṃ. Imināyeva purātanehi viruddhatthantarādipadehi vicaritaṃ vākyaṃ viruddhantiādinā duṭṭhāni bahūni vākyāni dassitānīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Even among the faults of sentence-meaning, the contradiction of lotuses awakening at night and so on is not stated because it is included within the contradictory word itself. To show this, it is said, 'what is done here is by way of summary,' not that they are entirely abandoned. Here, when there are two faults of sentence-meaning, namely 'lack of propriety' and 'difficult to understand,' and when there is 'harshness of composition' as a fault of the sentence, and 'contradiction' as a fault of the word, how are these four faults—the word 'incapable of expressing' and so on, the word 'indicating the three things such as disgust' and so on, the harsh word, and the sentence-meaning such as lotuses blooming at night—included in 'propriety' and so on, which are of different kinds? True, nevertheless, when words are faulty, there is no such thing as faultlessness of the sentence or sentence-meaning. Therefore, to make known to students the non-difference of the faults of sandhi, sentence, and sentence-meaning from the fault of the word, it should be understood that word-faults and so on are included in sentence-meaning faults and so on. By this very reasoning, it should be seen that many faulty sentences have been shown by the ancients, such as by the statement, 'a sentence containing words with contradictory meaning and so on is contradictory'.

Imāyeva imissāyeva (ka.) gāthāya “tamatthi ce khedakaraṃ parampī”ti ettha parasaddenaasādhusandiddhapariyāyañeyyāppatītatthaappayojaka- dubbodhadesiyādipadadose ca adhikaūnabhaggacchandādivākyadose ca upakkamopasaṃhāravisamasaṅkhāte vākyatthadose ca pariggaṇhāti. Ettha saddasatthaviruddhamasādhu nāma. Kriyānipphattikāraṇamupādāya atthantare pavattanāmaṃ visesanatthena vinā saññābhājane payuttaṃ sandiddhaṃ nāma, yathā “ravimhi himahā”ti. Ettha himahā ravīti visesane kate doso [M 0.0103] natthi. Pasiddhasaññāsaddassa pariyāyanāmena kappitapadaṃ pariyāyañeyyaṃ nāma, yathā “vaḷavāmukhassa assavanitānana”nti. Atisayā vinā bhāvitatthena visesyassa guṇavācakaṃ padaṃ appatītatthaṃ nāma, yathā “kaṇhamasī”ti. Adhigatattānupayogipadaṃ appayojakaṃ nāma, yathā “atiphenilaṃ sāgaramalaṅghī”ti. Appasiddhavacanaṃ dubbodhaṃ nāma, yathā–

By this very verse, 'If there is anything distressing even in the other,' here, by the word 'other' (para), it encompasses the faults of words such as asādhu (ungrammatical), sandiddha (ambiguous), pariyāyañeyya (synonymous requiring interpretation), appatītattha (unapparent meaning), appayojaka (irrelevant), dubbodha (difficult to understand), and desiya (localism), and so on; as well as the faults of the sentence such as adhika (excessive syllables), ūna (deficient syllables), and bhaggacchanda (broken meter), and so on. It also includes the fault of sentence-meaning designated as upakkamopasaṃhāravisama (inconsistency between introduction and conclusion). Here, asādhu means what is contrary to grammar. Sandiddha is a word used in a different sense, without a qualifier, in a context where a specific term is expected, based on the cause of an action's completion—for example, 'in the sun, there is cold.' In this case, there is no fault if 'cold' is made a qualifier of 'sun.' Pariyāyañeyya is a word coined as a synonymous name for a well-known noun, such as 'the face of the horse-woman' for 'the mouth of the mare-faced fire.' Appatītattha is a word expressing a quality of the qualified subject, used without emphasis on its inherent nature, such as 'black ink.' Appayojaka is a word that, though understood, is useless, like 'he crossed the excessively foamy ocean.' Dubbodha is an uncommon expression, for example—

“Manuññaddhanayo pāde, khādayo kani bhanti te”ti.

On your feet, O maiden, anklets with charming sounds shine.

Kani he kaññe te tavapāde manuññaddhanayo manoharasaddasamannāgatā khādayo gaggharikā bhanti dibbantīti. Kismiñci deseyeva siddhanāmaṃ desiyaṃ nāma. Yathā–

‘Kani’ means ‘O maiden!’ ‘Te’ means ‘your.’ On your feet, anklets (khādayo, gaggharikā) endowed with charming sounds (manuññaddhanayo) shine (bhanti, dibbanti). A name established only in a certain region is called desiya (localism). For example—

“Ime lāvaṇyatallā te, gallā lolavilocane”ti.

O one with restless eyes, these your cheeks are pools of loveliness.

He lolavilocane te tava ime gallā kapolā lāvaṇyatallā manuññatallā jalāsayavisesā bhavanti. Kenaci lesena pakāsitamatthamupādāya payuttamadhikaṃ nāma. Yathā–

O one with restless eyes, these cheeks of yours are special pools of loveliness and charm. A word used by taking up a meaning revealed by some hint is called adhika (superfluous). For example—

“Tvayi rājati rājinda, ripūnaṃ saggasevinaṃ;

Thīnaṃ akaṅkaṇo pāṇi, siyā nettamanañjana”nti.

O king of kings, while you reign, of the women of your enemies who now enjoy heaven, the hand is without a bracelet, and the eye without kohl.

Ettha “akaṅkaṇo pāṇi, nettamanañjana”nti imināyevathīnaṃ vidhavattaṃ gamyamānaṃ hotīti tappakāsanatthaṃ payuttaṃ “saggasevina”nti idaṃ adhikaṃ nāma. Vattabbayuttato ūnaṃ vākyaṃ ūnaṃ nāma. “Tilokatilakaṃ muni”nti ettha “vandāmī”ti vattabbassa avuttattā ūnaṃ. Chandohānisaṃyuttaṃ bhaggacchandaṃ nāma. Idaṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ chandānaṃ akkharagaṇanato ūnādhikavasena pākaṭaṃ hoti. Ādyantato visamaṃ upakkamopasaṃhāravisamaṃ nāma. Idaṃ āraddhakkamaṃ pariccajitvā kamantarena niyamanti veditabbaṃ.

Here, by the very phrase 'a hand without a bracelet, an eye without kohl,' the widowhood of the women is understood. Therefore, the word 'enjoying heaven' used for its clarification is called adhika (superfluous). A sentence that is deficient in what ought to be stated is called ūna (deficient). In 'the sage, the ornament of the three worlds,' because 'I pay homage,' which should be said, is not said, it is ūna. That which is connected with a loss of meter is called bhaggacchanda (broken meter). This becomes manifest through deficiency or excess in the counting of syllables of the respective meters. That which is inconsistent from beginning to end is called upakkamopasaṃhāravisama (inconsistent in introduction and conclusion). This should be understood as abandoning the sequence that was begun and being regulated by another sequence.

Iti subodhālaṅkāranissaye

Thus in the commentary on the Subodhālaṅkāra.

Paṭhamo paricchedo.

The First Chapter.

2. Dosaparihārāvabodhaparicchedavaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Chapter on Understanding the Removal of Faults.

68.

68.

Kadāci kavikosallā, virodho sakalopya’yaṃ;

Dosasaṅkhyamatikkamma, guṇavīthiṃ vigāhate.

Sometimes, all this contradiction, by the skill of the poet, surpasses the enumeration of faults and enters the path of virtues.

69.

69.

Tena vuttavirodhāna-mavirodho yathā siyā;

Tathā dosaparihārā-vabodho dāni nīyate.

Therefore, the understanding of the removal of faults is now set forth, so that there may be non-contradiction in the aforementioned contradictions.

68-69. Iccevaṃ [M 0.0104] dosavibhāgaṃ paricchijja idāni yathāvuttadosaparihārakkamamupadisitumāha “kadācī”tyādi. Sakalopi ayaṃ virodho viruddhatthantarādikato na koci eko eva dosesu, dosānaṃ vā saṅkhyaṃ gaṇanaṃ dosabhāvaṃ atikkamma paricchijja guṇānaṃ vīthiṃ padaviṃ guṇasabhāvataṃ vigāhate abbhupagacchati kadāci, na sabbadā. Kavino payujjakassa kosallā tādisavisayapariggahalakkhaṇanepuññakāraṇā, na tu yathā tathā ceti. “Tene”ccādi. Yenevaṃ, tena kāraṇena vuttānaṃ viruddhatthantarādīnaṃ virodhānaṃ yathā yena pakārena avirodho niddosatā siyā bhaveyya, tathā tena pakārena dosānaṃ parihāro dūrīkaraṇaṃ avabujjhati ñāyati etenāti avabodho, tassa avabodho, tannāmiko paricchedo idāni nīyate ānīyate vuccateti attho.

68-69. Having thus determined the classification of faults, now, to teach the method of removing the aforementioned faults, he says, 'Sometimes,' etc. All this contradiction, arising from contradictory meaning and so on, is not just any single one among the faults; rather, having transcended the enumeration of faults and the state of being a fault, it sometimes—not always—enters and accepts the path of virtues, the way of virtues, the very nature of virtue. This is due to the skill of the poet, the composer, a skill characterized by the cleverness of grasping such a subject, and not just haphazardly. 'Therefore,' etc. Since it is so, for that reason, in whatever way there might be non-contradiction, faultlessness, of the stated contradictions such as contradictory meaning and so on, in that same way, the chapter named 'Understanding'—because by it the removal, the distancing, of faults is understood or known—is now set forth, brought forth, spoken. This is the meaning.

68-69. Evaṃ dosavibhāgaṃ paricchinditvā idāni yathāvuttadosānaṃ parihāratthamārabhanto “kadācī”tyādimāha. Sakalopi ayaṃ virodho padadosādiko dosasaṅkhyaṃ dosānaṃ, dosesu vā gaṇanaṃ dosabhāvaṃ atikkamma kadāci kavikosallā kavino byākaraṇābhidhānachandoalaṅkatiādīsu paricayalakkhaṇena paññāpāṭavena yato guṇavīthiṃ guṇapadaviṃ kevalaṃ guṇasabhāvaṃ vigāhate abbhupagacchati, tena kāraṇena vuttavirodhānaṃ yathāvuttapadadosādivirodhānaṃ avirodho aviruddhatā yathā [M 0.0105] siyā yena pakārena bhaveyya, tathā tena pakārena dosaparihārāvabodho yathāvuttapadadosādisambandhino pariharaṇakkamassa avabodhakāraṇattā tannāmikaparicchedo idāni laddhāvasare nīyate vuccate. Yathāvuttadosā kavisāmatthiyena niddosattaṃ bhajanti, tassa sāmatthiyassa upadesaṃ dassāmāti adhippāyo.

68-69. Having thus determined the classification of faults, now, beginning for the sake of removing the aforementioned faults, he says, 'Sometimes,' etc. All this contradiction, such as word-faults and so on, transcends the enumeration of faults, or the reckoning among faults, the state of being a fault. This is because sometimes, due to the poet's skill—that is, due to the sharp wisdom characterized by familiarity with grammar, lexicon, metrics, embellishments, and so on—it enters and accepts the path of virtues, the way of virtues, the very nature of virtue. For that reason, so that there may be non-contradiction of the stated contradictions, the aforementioned contradictions of word-faults and so on, in whatever way possible; in that same way, the chapter named 'Understanding the Removal of Faults'—so named because it is the cause for understanding the procedure of removing what is related to the aforementioned word-faults and so on—is now, the opportunity having arisen, set forth and spoken. The intention is: 'The aforementioned faults attain faultlessness through the poet's competence; I will show the instruction for that competence'.

Padadosaparihāravaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Removal of Word-Faults.

Tattha viruddhatthantarassa parihāro yathā –

Therein, the removal of contradictory meaning is as follows:

70.

70.

Vindantaṃ pākasālīnaṃ, sālīnaṃ dassanā sukhaṃ;

Taṃ kathaṃ nāma megho’yaṃ, visado sukhaye janaṃ.

To a person who finds happiness from the sight of fine, ripening rice, how indeed could this clear cloud bring happiness?

70. “Vindanta”miccādi. Pākena pariṇatabhāvena sālīnaṃ yuttānaṃ, manuññānaṃ vā sālīnaṃ rattasāliādīnaṃ sālijātīnaṃ dassanā sukhaṃ cetasikaṃ somanassaṃ vindantaṃ taṃ janaṃ visado ayaṃ megho ambudo kathaṃ nāma sukhayeti. Ettha tādisassa janassa asukhappadānaṃ garaḷassa meghassānurūpanti viruddhatthantaratā parihaṭā.

70. 'Vindanta,' etc. How indeed could this clear cloud, a rain-cloud, bring happiness to that person who experiences mental happiness and joy from the sight of rice fields endowed with ripeness, or of delightful varieties of rice such as red rice and so on? Here, the giving of unhappiness to such a person is fitting for a poisonous cloud; thus, the contradictory meaning is removed.

70. Tattha viruddhatthantarassa parihāro yathā evaṃ. “Vindanti”ccādi. Pākasālīnaṃ pariṇāmena yuttānaṃ, manuññānaṃ vā sālīnaṃ rattasāliādīnaṃ dassanā dassanahetu sukhaṃ cetasikasomanassaṃ vindantaṃ anubhontaṃ taṃ janaṃ taṃ kassakajanaṃ visado jaladāyako ayaṃ megho kathaṃ nāma sukhaye, na sukhayateva. Tādisassa janassa dukkhadānaṃ garaḷadāyakassa meghassāpi anurūpamiti viruddhaññattho apanīto hoti. Pākena sālinoti viggaho. Sukhaṃ karotīti sukhayeti nāmadhātu.

70. Herein, the avoidance of a contradictory meaning is as follows. 'Vindanti,' and so on. How indeed could this clear, water-giving cloud bring happiness to that person, that farmer, who experiences mental joy and happiness from the sight, on account of seeing, rice endowed with ripeness, or delightful rice such as red rice and other varieties? It certainly does not bring happiness. The giving of suffering to such a person is fitting even for a cloud that gives poison—thus the contradictory meaning is removed. The analysis is: rice with ripeness. 'It makes happy,' thus 'sukhayati' is a denominative verb.

Yathā vā –

Or as—

71.

71.

Vināyakopi [M 0.0106] nāgosi,

Gotamopi mahāmati;

Paṇītopi rasāpeto,

Cittā me sāmi te gati.

You are Vināyaka, and also a nāga; you are Gotama, and also of great wisdom; you are Paṇīta, and also devoid of taste; O Lord, your course is marvelous to me.

71. “Vināyakopi”ccādi. Vīnaṃ pakkhīnaṃ nāyako, garuḷo, satte vinetīti vināyako, vuddho, bhagavā ca. Tattha yadā vināyako garuḷo, tadā tu nāgo pannagosīti viruddhaṃ, pakkhantare tvaviruddhaṃ bhagavato āgussa rāgādino abhāvato. Imesaṃ gunnaṃ atisayena go gotamo hīnapasu, gotamavaṃsāvatiṇṇattā gotamo bhagavā ca. Hīnapasu ca tvaṃ mahāmati asīti viruddhaṃ accantahīnapasuno mahatiyā paññāya abhāvato. Pakkhantare tu na byāghāto. Paṇīto madhuro raso, uttamo ca sugato. Tattha madhurarasato apeto apagatosīti virujjhati, bhagavato tu rasehi siṅgārādīhi apetoti yujjati. Me mama. Sāmīti āmantanaṃ. Te tava gati pavatti cittā abbhutāti. Ettha viruddhatthantaraṃ virodhālaṅkāraṃ silāghanīyanti tena taṃ parihaṭaṃ.

71. 'Vināyakopi,' and so on. The leader of birds, the garuḍa; and one who disciplines beings, thus 'Vināyaka,' the Buddha, the Blessed One. Here, when 'Vināyaka' is the garuḍa, then 'nāga' as serpent is contradictory; but in the other sense, it is not contradictory, due to the Blessed One's absence of fault, such as lust and so on. 'Gotama' can mean a lowly animal, an ox; and the Blessed One is Gotama due to descending from the Gotama lineage. 'You are a lowly animal, yet of great wisdom' is contradictory, because an utterly lowly animal lacks great wisdom. In the other sense, however, there is no conflict. 'Paṇīta' means a sweet taste, and also supreme, the Well-Gone One. Here, 'devoid of sweet taste' is contradictory; but for the Blessed One, 'devoid of flavors such as the erotic and so on' is fitting. 'Me' means 'my.' 'Sāmi' is an address. 'Te' means 'your.' 'Gati' means 'course' or 'conduct.' 'Cittā' means 'marvelous' or 'wonderful.' Here, the contradictory meaning, which is the figure of speech 'virodhālaṅkāra,' is praiseworthy—thus it is removed by that.

71. Yathā vā uttadosassa parihāro īdiso vā. “Vināyako”ccādi. He sāmi tvaṃ vināyakopi garuḷopi nāgosi pannago asi. No ce, vināyakopi satte vinento eva nāgosi nikkileso asi. Gotamopi pasutamopi mahāmati mahāpaññavāsi. No ce, gotamopi gottato gotamoyeva mahāmati mahāpaññavāsi. Paṇītopi madhuropi rasāpeto madhurarasato apagatosi. No ce, paṇītopi uttamo eva rasāpeto siṅgārādirasato apagatosi. Te tuyhaṃ gati pavatti me mayhaṃ cittā acchariyā. [M 0.0107] Ettha garuḷassa nāgattañca pasutamassa paññavantattañca paṇītassa nirasattañca viruddhaṃ, tathāpi aññapakkhassa aviruddhattā viruddhatthantaradoso pasatthena viruddhālaṅkārena nirākato. Vīnaṃ pakkhīnaṃ nāyako, garuḷo. Satte vinetīti vināyako, buddho. Natthi āgu ago (ka.) etassāti nāgo, buddho. Gunnamatisayena gotamo, pasu. Mahatī mati assāti mahāmati, buddho. Padhānattaṃ nīto paṇīto, madhuro raso. Rasato apetoti rasāpeto, buddhoti viggaho.

71. Or, the avoidance of the aforementioned fault is as follows. 'Vināyaka,' and so on. O Lord, you are Vināyaka, a garuḍa, and also a nāga, a serpent. Or else, as Vināyaka, one who disciplines beings, you are a nāga, one free from defilements. As Gotama, the best of animals, you are of great wisdom, greatly discerning. Or else, as Gotama by lineage, you are indeed Gotama, of great wisdom, greatly discerning. As Paṇīta, sweet, you are devoid of taste, departed from sweet taste. Or else, as Paṇīta, supreme, you are indeed devoid of taste, departed from flavors such as the erotic and so on. Your course and conduct are marvelous and wonderful to me. Here, for a garuḍa to be a nāga, for the best of animals to be wise, and for the refined to be tasteless are contradictory; yet, because in another sense they are not contradictory, the fault of a contradictory meaning is removed by the excellent figure of speech, 'virodhālaṅkāra.' The leader of birds is the Garuḍa. He disciplines beings, thus 'Vināyaka,' the Buddha. He for whom there is no fault, thus 'Nāga,' the Buddha. The best of oxen is Gotama, an animal. He whose wisdom is great, thus 'Mahāmati,' the Buddha. Brought to prominence, thus 'Paṇīta'; also, a sweet taste. Departed from taste, thus 'Rasāpeta,' the Buddha—this is the analysis.

Ajhatthassa yathā –

Regarding excessive meaning, as follows—

72.

72.

Kathaṃ tādiguṇābhāve,

Lokaṃ toseti dujjano;

Obhāsitāsesadiso,

Khajjoto nāma kiṃ bhave.

How can a wicked person, devoid of such qualities, please the world? A firefly that has illuminated all directions—what indeed could it be?

72. “Katha”miccādi. Dujjano tādino guṇā lokaṃ tosenti, tādīnaṃ guṇānaṃ attani abhāve sati lokaṃ sattalokaṃ kathaṃ toseti, na tosetīti attho. Vuttamevatthantarena sādheti “khajjoto nāma obhāsitā dīpitā asesadisā yena tathāvidho kiṃ bhave, na bhaveyya tādino guṇassa abhāvato”ti. Ettha khajjotassa adhikatthabhāvena sito obhāsitāsesadisattadoso “kathaṃ tādiguṇābhāve”tiādivacobhaṅgiyā parihaṭo.

72. 'How?' and so on. The virtues of such a one please the world. A wicked person, when such qualities are absent in himself, how can he please the world, the world of beings? The meaning is that he does not please. He establishes the same meaning with another instance: 'A firefly, one by whom all directions are illuminated and lit up—what could such a one be? It could not be, due to the absence of such a quality.' Here, the fault of ascribing to the firefly the quality of illuminating all directions, which is an excessive meaning, is removed by the turn of phrase beginning, 'how, in the absence of such qualities...'

72. Ajhatthassa yathāti ettha parihāro ajjhāhāro, evamuparipi. “Kathi”ccādi. Dujjano guṇahīnajano tādiguṇābhāve santosajananakāraṇānaṃ tādisānaṃ sīlādiguṇānaṃ [M 0.0108] attani avijjamānatte sati lokaṃ sattalokaṃ kathaṃ toseti, na tosetiyeva, tathā hi khajjoto nāma obhāsitāsesadiso kiṃ bhave, na bhavatyeva. Ettha khajjotassa sakaladisobhāsanasaṅkhātamadhikatthadoso “kathaṃ tādiguṇābhāve”ccādivākyalīlāya nirākato. Tādī ca te guṇā ceti viggaho.

72. Regarding 'of excessive meaning, as follows,' here the word 'avoidance' is to be supplied, and similarly above. 'How?' and so on. A wicked person, a person deficient in qualities, when such qualities as virtue and so forth, which are causes for producing satisfaction, are non-existent in himself, how can he please the world, the world of beings? He cannot please it at all. For thus, a firefly that has illuminated all directions—what could it be? It could not be at all. Here, the fault of excessive meaning, described as the firefly's illuminating of all directions, is rejected through the graceful phrasing of the sentence beginning 'how, in the absence of such qualities...' The analysis is: they are 'such' and they are 'qualities'.

73.

73.

Paheḷikāyamāruḷhā, na hi duṭṭhā kiliṭṭhatā;

Piyā sukhā’liṅgitaṃ ka-māliṅgati nu no iti.

Defilement, when employed in a riddle, is not indeed a fault. As in: 'Whom, indeed, does an embrace by a beloved with happiness not embrace?'

73. “Paheḷikāyaṃ”iccādi. Kiliṭṭhatā kiliṭṭhapadadoso paheḷikāya visaye āruḷhā sahī na hi no duṭṭho siyā. Kīdisīti āha “piye”ccādi. Itīti nidassane. Piyā vallabhāya āliṅgitaṃ kaṃ janaṃ sukhaṃ kāyikaṃ cetasikañca no āliṅgati na saṃyujjati nu. Nuiti parivitakke nipāto. Ettha piyāti kiliṭṭhaṃ paheḷikāya samāropena parihaṭaṃ.

73. 'Paheḷikāyaṃ,' and so on. The fault of a defiled word, when employed in the context of a riddle, is indeed not a fault. What is it like? It says, 'piyā,' and so on. The word 'iti' is for illustration. An embrace by a beloved—what person does it not embrace, does it not connect with, physical and mental happiness? 'Nu' is a particle indicating deliberation. Here, 'piyā' is a defiled word, the fault of which is removed by its being employed in a riddle.

73. “Paheḷike”ccādi. Kiliṭṭhatā kiliṭṭhapadadosasaṅkhātā paheḷikāyaṃ visaye āruḷhā ce, na hi duṭṭhā duṭṭhā na hoti. Kimudāharaṇaṃ? Piyā sukhāliṅgitaṃ kamāliṅgati nu no iti, itisaddassa nidassanatthattā sesaudāharaṇānametamupalakkhaṇanti ñātabbaṃ. No ce, evaṃpakārānamudāharaṇānamapariggahetabbattā itisaddo pakāratthoti. Piyā vallabhāya āliṅgitaṃ upaguhitaṃ kaṃ nāma janaṃ sukhaṃ kāyikamānasikaṃ no āliṅgati nu, āliṅgatevāti. Ettha piyāti kiliṭṭhapadaṃ paheḷikāyamāropanena nirākataṃ hoti.

73. 'Paheḷike,' and so on. If a fault, described as the fault of a defiled word, is employed in the context of a riddle, it is not indeed faulty; it is not a fault. What is the example? 'An embrace by a beloved with happiness—whom does it not embrace?' The word 'iti' is for illustration, and this should be understood as indicating the remaining examples. Or else, since examples of this kind would not be fully encompassed, the word 'iti' signifies 'in this manner.' An embrace, a clasping, by a beloved—what person indeed does it not embrace with physical and mental happiness? It certainly does embrace. Here, 'piyā' is a defiled word, which is rejected by being employed in the riddle.

74.

74.

Yamake no payojeyya, kiliṭṭhapada’micchite;

Tato yamaka’maññaṃ tu, sabbametaṃmayaṃ viya.

One should not employ a defiled word in a desired yamaka; then, any other yamaka is as if entirely made of this.

74. “Yamake”ccādi. [M 0.0109] Tato aññanti icchitayamakato aññaṃ. Tuiti visesajotako. Etaṃmayaṃ viyāti etena kiliṭṭhapadena nibbattaṃ viya.

74. 'Yamake,' and so on. 'Other than that' means other than the desired yamaka. 'Tu' is a particle indicating a specific case. 'As if made of this' means as if produced by this defiled word.

74. “Yamake”ccādi. Kiliṭṭhapadaṃ icchite yamake iṭṭhayamake no payojeyya nappayujjeyya, tato iṭṭhayamakato aññaṃ sabbaṃ yamakaṃ pana etaṃmayaṃ viya iminā kiliṭṭhapadadosena kataṃ viya hoti. Ettha iṭṭhayamakaṃ vuttanayena ñātabbaṃ, etena nibbattaṃ etaṃmayanti viggaho.

74. 'Yamake,' and so on. One should not employ a defiled word in a desired yamaka, in an intended yamaka; one should not use it. Then, any other yamaka apart from the intended yamaka is entirely as if made of this, as if made by this fault of a defiled word. Here, the intended yamaka should be understood in the manner stated, and 'made of this' is the analysis: 'produced by this'.

Desavirodhino yathā –

Regarding the contradiction of place, as follows—

75.

75.

Bodhisattappabhāvena, thalepi jalajānya’huṃ;

Nudantāni’va sucirā-vāsaklesaṃ tahiṃ jale.

By the Bodhisatta's power, even on land, water-born lotuses appeared, as if dispelling the weariness of long dwelling in that water.

75. “Bodhisatte”ccādi. Bodhisattassa māyādeviyā sutassa vakkhamānassa visesassa taduppannadine sambhavā pabhāvena puññappabhāvato jalajāni ambujāni thalepi ahuṃ ahesuṃ acintanīyattā puññappabhāvassa. Kiṃ pana vāpyādīsu kiṃ karontāva tahiṃ tasmiñca jale suciraṃ sabbadāva āvasanamāvāso tena jāto kleso taṃ nudantāniva dūrato jahantāniveti. Acintanīyattā puññappabhāvassa īdisampi acchariyamahosīti na desavirodho.

75. 'Bodhisatta,' and so on. By the power of the Bodhisatta, by the power of his merit, due to the arising of the special one—the son of Queen Māyā, who will be spoken of—on the day of his birth, water-born things, lotuses, appeared even on land, because the power of merit is inconceivable. Moreover, what were they doing in ponds and so on? As if dispelling, as if abandoning from afar, the weariness born from long, indeed perpetual, dwelling in that very water. Because the power of merit is inconceivable, such a marvel occurred—thus, there is no contradiction of place.

75. Bodhisattappabhāvena bodhisattassa acinteyyānubhāvena jalajāni jalajasadisattā tannāmakāni padumakeravādīni tahiṃ jale visayattena pasiddhe tasmiṃ udake sucirāvāsaklesaṃ aticiraṃ nivāsato jātaāyāsaṃ nudantāni iva cajantāni iva thalepi ahuṃ ahesuṃ, vāpiādīsu kā kathā. Ettha jalajānaṃ thaluppattikathanasaṅkhātaṃ desavirodhaṃ acinteyyapuññappabhāvena īdisānaṃ [M 0.0110] acchariyānaṃ pātubhāvato “bodhisattappabhāvenā”ti iminā nirākaroti. Bodhiyaṃ catumaggapaññāyaṃ sattoti ca, tassa pabhāvoti ca, suciraṃ āvāsoti ca, tena bhūto klesoti ca vākyaṃ.

75. By the power of the Bodhisatta, by the inconceivable potency of the Bodhisatta, water-born things—that is, things of a water-born nature, such as lotuses and water lilies—as if dispelling, as if abandoning the weariness born from dwelling for a very long time in that water, which is well-known as their domain, came to be even on dry land; what need be said of lakes and the like? Here, the contradiction of place, which consists of the statement of the arising of water-born things on dry land, is refuted by the phrase 'by the Bodhisatta's power,' due to the manifestation of such marvels through the inconceivable power of merit. The analysis of the phrases is as follows: 'attached to enlightenment, which is the wisdom of the four paths'; 'his power'; 'a long dwelling'; and 'the weariness produced by that'.

Kālavirodhino yathā –

As for a contradiction of time, as follows:

76.

76.

Mahānubhāvapisuno, munino mandamāruto;

Sabbotukamayaṃ vāyi, dhunanto kusumaṃ samaṃ.

The gentle breeze, proclaiming the great might of the Sage, blew, scattering evenly the flowers of all seasons.

76. “Mahā”iccādi. Mando mudubhūto māruto ayaṃ sabbotukaṃ sabbesu utūsu pupphanakaṃ kusumaṃ pupphaṃ samaṃ ekato katvā dhunanto vikiranto munino munisadisattā bhavissantamunibhāvena ca bodhisattassa, muninoyeva vā sammāsambodhisamadhigamasamaye mahānubhāvassa pisuno sūcako vāyi pavāyatīti. Ettha yadyapekadā sabbotukāsambhavo nānāutūsu nānākusumassa sambhavā, tathāpi bhagavato mahānubhāvapisunamīdisamekapadikaṃ sambhavatīti kālavirodho iminā parihaṭo.

76. “Great,” etc. This gentle breeze, mild in nature, gathering together and scattering evenly the flowers of all seasons—that is, flowers that bloom in every season—blew, announcing the great might of the Sage, who is the Bodhisatta by virtue of his sage-like qualities and his future state as a sage; or indeed, it was indicative of the Sage’s great power at the time of attaining perfect self-enlightenment. Here, although the simultaneous existence of flowers from all seasons is impossible, since different flowers arise in different seasons, nevertheless such a singular marvel, indicative of the Blessed One's great might, is possible. Thus, the contradiction of time is dispelled by this.

76. “Mahānubhāve”ccādi. Ayaṃ mandamāruto acaṇḍasamīraṇo sabbotukaṃ vasantādīsu sabbautūsu vikasantaṃ kusumaṃ pupphajātaṃ samaṃ ekato katvā dhunanto kampento munino ekantabhāvittā munisaṅkhātassa bodhisattassa, sammāsambodhisamadhigamasamaye bhūtattā munino sabbaññuno vā mahānubhāvapisuno mahantaṃ puññappabhāvaṃ pakāsento vāyi sampavāyīti. Ettha nānākāle sambhavantānampi kusumānaṃ ekakāle sambhavassa kālavirodhattepi bhagavato puññānubhāvo tādisamacchariyamekakkhaṇe janetuṃ samatthoti kālavirodhaṃ “mahānubhāvapisuno”ti iminā nirākaroti. Mahānubhāvassa, mahānubhāvaṃ vā pisunoti vākyaṃ.

76. “Of great might,” etc. This gentle breeze, not a fierce wind, gathering together and shaking evenly the flowers of all kinds that bloom in all seasons, such as spring, blew, proclaiming the great might—revealing the great power of merit—of the Bodhisatta, known as the sage due to his exclusive cultivation of solitude; or indeed, of the Sage, the Omniscient One, due to his having come to be at the time of attaining perfect self-enlightenment. Here, although the simultaneous existence of flowers that arise at different times constitutes a contradiction of time, the Blessed One’s power of merit is capable of producing such a wonder in a single moment. Thus, the contradiction of time is dispelled by the phrase “proclaiming great might.” The analysis of the phrase is: ‘proclaimer of the great might’ (genitive) or ‘it proclaims the great might’ (accusative).

Kalāvirodhino yathā –

As for a contradiction of art, as follows:

77.

77.

Nimuggamanaso [M 0.0111] buddha-guṇe pañcasikhassapi;

Tantissaravirodho so, na sampīṇeti kaṃ janaṃ.

Even for the five-crested one, whose mind is immersed in the Buddha’s virtues, that contradiction in the lute’s sound does not fail to gladden any person.

77. “Nimuggi”ccādi. Buddhassa guṇe sīlādike aparimāṇe nimuggaṃ ogāḷhaṃ manaṃ cittaṃ yassa tassa pañcasikhassa gandhabbadevaputtassapi vīṇāya tantiyā saro kiriyākālamānalakkhaṇavilambitadutamajjhabhedabhinno chajjādiko tassa virodho kalāsatthapariniddiṭṭhakamavesamaṃ kaṃ janaṃ na sampīṇeti, pīṇetiyeva. Sammāsambuddhassa lokiyaguṇānubandhabuddhīnaṃ vikkhepappavattipi tathāvidhaṃ pīṇetīti. “Buddhaguṇe nimuggamanaso”ti iminā kalāvirodho parihaṭo.

77. “Immersed,” etc. For Pañcasikha, the celestial musician, whose mind is immersed and absorbed in the immeasurable virtues of the Buddha, such as morality—even for him, the sound of the lute strings, differentiated by its sixfold and other divisions based on action, time, measure, characteristic, and slow, fast, and medium tempo, and its non-conformity with the order prescribed in the treatises on art, does not fail to gladden any person; it gladdens indeed. Even the occurrence of distraction for those whose minds are connected to the worldly virtues of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One gladdens in such a way. By the phrase “one whose mind is immersed in the virtues of the Buddha,” the contradiction of art is dispelled.

77. “Nimuggi”ccādi. Buddhaguṇe sabbaññuno vimhayajanakasīlādiguṇasambhāre nimuggamanaso otiṇṇacittassa pañcasikhassapi gandhabbadevaputtassāpi so tantissaravirodho vīṇāya tantiyā ghaṭṭanakiriyā, addhamattikādikālo, hatthādīnaṃ sannivesalakkhaṇo mānoti imehi tīhi lakkhaṇehi yuttassa mandasīghamajjhimappamāṇehi bhinnassa chajjādisattasarassa kalāsatthāgatakkamassa vināsasaṅkhāto virodho kaṃ janaṃ na sampīṇeti, sampīṇeti eva. Ettha akantiyā kāraṇabhūto kalāsatthāgatakkamabhaṅgo lokuttarabuddhaguṇānugatabuddhiyā jātoti so bhaṅgo “nimuggamanaso buddhaguṇe”ti vuttattā pītiyā kāraṇameveti na virodho. Nimuggo mano assāti ca, tantiyā saroti ca, tesaṃ virodhoti ca vākyaṃ.

77. “Immersed,” etc. For Pañcasikha, the gandhabba devaputta, whose mind is immersed, whose consciousness has entered into the virtues of the Omniscient One, into the collection of awe-inspiring qualities such as morality—even for him, that contradiction in the sound of the lute strings, which consists of the destruction of the sequence found in the treatises on art for the seven notes beginning with ‘chajja,’ differentiated by slow, fast, and medium measures, and endowed with three characteristics, namely, the act of striking the strings, timing such as a half-measure, and the measure characterized by the arrangement of the hand—what person does it not gladden? It gladdens indeed. Here, the breaking of the sequence found in the treatises on art, which would be a cause of unpleasantness, arises from an intelligence that follows the supramundane virtues of the Buddha. Therefore, because it is stated “one whose mind is immersed in the virtues of the Buddha,” that breaking is indeed a cause of joy, and thus not a contradiction. The analysis of the phrases is: ‘one whose mind is immersed’; ‘the sound of the strings’; and ‘their contradiction’.

Lokavirodhino yathā –

As for a contradiction of the world, as follows:

78.

78.

Gaṇaye [M 0.0112] cakkavāḷaṃ so, candanāyapi sītalaṃ;

Sambodhisattahadayo, padittaṅgārapūritaṃ.

He whose heart is set on perfect enlightenment could regard the world-system, though filled with burning embers, as cooler even than sandalwood.

78. “Gaṇaye”ccādi. Candanāya api sītalaṃ gaṇaye cintesi. Kintaṃ? Padittaṅgārapūritaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ. Ko so? Sambodhiyaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇe sattaṃ paribaddhaṃ hadayaṃ cittaṃ yassa so. Sabbaññutaññāṇānubandhabuddhino hi tādiso manobandhoti na lokavirodho.

78. “Could regard,” etc. He would regard it as cooler than even sandalwood. What is that? The world-system filled with burning embers. Who is he? He is one whose heart, whose mind, is attached and bound to perfect enlightenment, the knowledge of omniscience. Indeed, for one whose intelligence follows the knowledge of omniscience, such a state of mind is not a contradiction of the world.

78. “Gaṇaye”ccādi. Sambodhisattahadayo sabbaññutaññāṇe āsattacitto so bodhisatto padittaṅgārapūritaṃ ādittaṅgārehi paripuṇṇaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ cakkavāḷagabbhaṃ candanāyapi candanato api sītalaṃ atisītalaṃ katvā gaṇaye cinteyyāti. Iṭṭhatthaluddhassa cittappavattiyā īdisattā aggino candanatopi adhikasītattakappanā “candanaṃ sītalaṃ, aggi uṇho”ti pavattalokasīmāya viruddhā na hoti. Sambodhiyaṃ sattahadayaṃ yasseti ca, padittāni aṅgārānīti ca, tehi pūritanti ca viggaho.

78. “Could regard,” etc. That Bodhisatta, whose heart is set on perfect enlightenment, whose mind is attached to the knowledge of omniscience, would regard the world-system—the interior of the world-system—filled with burning embers, replete with blazing coals, as cooler than even sandalwood, as extremely cool. Because the mind of one who is intent on a desired goal functions in such a way, the conception that fire is cooler than sandalwood is not in conflict with the established convention of the world, which states, “sandalwood is cool, fire is hot.” The analysis is: ‘one whose heart is set on perfect enlightenment’; ‘burning embers’; and ‘filled with them’.

Ñāyavirodhino yathā –

As for a contradiction of logic, as follows:

79.

79.

Pariccattabhavopi tva-mupanītabhavo asi;

Acintyaguṇasārāya, namo te munipuṅgava.

Though you have relinquished existence, you have brought forth existence; homage to you, O chief of sages, whose essence is of inconceivable virtues.

79. “Pariccatte”ccādi. Munipuṅgava munīnaṃ uttama pariccatto visaṭṭho bhavo sugatiduggatisaṅkhāto yenāti pariccattabhavopi tvaṃ upanīto ānīto pavattito bhavo vuḍḍhi yenāti upanītabhavo asi. Tasmā kāraṇā acintyaguṇasārāya te namo atthūti seso. Īdisaṃ na ñāyaviruddhamevaṃvidhattā munipuṅgavassa.

79. “Relinquished,” etc. O chief of sages, supreme among sages, though you are one who has relinquished existence—meaning one by whom existence (bhava), known as good and bad destinies, is abandoned, given up—you are also one who has brought forth existence, meaning one by whom welfare (bhava, i.e., growth) is brought forth, led forth, and set in motion. For that reason, ‘homage be to you, whose essence is of inconceivable virtues’; the rest of the phrase is to be understood. Such a thing is not contrary to reason, this being the nature of the chief of sages.

79. “Pariccatte”ccādi. Munipuṅgava muniseṭṭha tvaṃ pariccattabhavopi apanītasugatiduggatibhavopi upanītabhavo lokassānītaabhivuddhiko asi bhavasi, acintyaguṇasārāya tato eva cintāvisayātikkantasāraguṇassa te tuyhaṃ namo atthūti sabbākārato bhavassa pariccattattā attani avijjamānaṃ [M 0.0113] sugatibhavaṃ lokassa detīti etaṃ ñāyāgataṃ na hotīti paṭibhāti, tathāpi ca sabbaññūnaṃ pavatti īdisāyevāti ñāyavirodho nirākato. Acintyā guṇasārā yasminti viggaho.

79. “Relinquished,” etc. O chief of sages, O best of sages, though you have relinquished existence, having eliminated the existence of good and bad destinies, you are one who has brought forth existence, having brought welfare and growth to the world. Therefore, homage be to you, whose essential qualities are inconceivable, whose essential qualities transcend the sphere of thought. It may appear illogical that, having abandoned existence in all its forms, you give to the world a happy existence that you yourself do not possess. Nevertheless, the way of the Omniscient Ones is precisely thus, and so the contradiction of logic is refuted. The analysis is: ‘he in whom the essential qualities are inconceivable’.

Āgamavirodhino yathā –

As for a contradiction of the scriptures, as follows:

80.

80.

Nevālapati kenāpi, vacīviññattito yati;

Sampajānamusāvādā, phuseyyāpattidukkaṭaṃ.

A monk converses with no one, yet through verbal intimation, on account of intentional false speech, he might incur an offense of wrong-doing.

80. “Neve”tiādi. Yatīti bhikkhu kenāpi saha nevālapati na vadatyeva, tathāpi vacīviññattito copanavācāsaṅkhātena vacīviññattihetunā pavattito sampajānantassa musāvādato kāraṇā āpattidukkaṭaṃ “sampajānamusāvādassa hotī”ti vuttadukkaṭāpatti phuseyya āpajjatīti. Ettha anālapato vacīviññattiyā kathaṃ musāvādoti abhidhammāpannavirodho natthi, aparavacanatthe tvīdiso virujjhatīti.

80. “‘Never,’ etc. A yati, that is, a bhikkhu, does not converse with anyone, nor does he speak at all. Nevertheless, by means of verbal intimation—which is known as prompting speech and arises from the cause of verbal intimation—he might incur an offense of wrong-doing for the reason of intentional false speech; this is the offense of wrong-doing stated as, ‘there is an offense for intentional false speech.’ Herein, there is no contradiction with the Abhidhamma regarding how false speech can arise from verbal intimation for one who is not conversing; such a contradiction arises only in the context of another statement.

80. “Nevi”ccādi. Yati samaṇo kenāpi kenaci saddhiṃ nevālapati no bhāsati, tathāpi vacīviññattito copanavācāsaṅkhātaviññattikāraṇā pavattanato sampajānamusāvādā sampajānantassa musābhaṇanato āpattidukkaṭaṃ dukkaṭāpattiṃ phuseyya āpajjeyyāti. Ettha anālapantassa vacīviññattito musāvādo kathaṃ sambhavatīti abhidhammāpannavirodho, “santiṃ āpattiṃ nāvikareyya, sampajānamusāvāda’ssa hotī”ti nidānuddese niddiṭṭhavacīdvāre akiriyasamuṭṭhānā dukkaṭāpatti hotīti āgamavirodho nirākato. Musābhaṇanaṃ vinā āpatti kathaṃ bhavatīti? Yathā kāle avassamānameghato sañjātadubbhikkhaṃ “meghakataṃ dubbhikkha”nti vattabbaṃ hoti, evaṃ kathetabbakāle akathanato sañjātā vacīdvāre akiriyasamuṭṭhānā dukkaṭāpattipi [M 0.0114] tato sañjātāti vattabbā hoti. Sampajānantassa musāvādoti ca, āpattiyeva dukkaṭanti ca vākyaṃ.

80. “‘Not even,’ etc. A yati, a recluse, does not converse or speak with anyone at all. Nevertheless, due to the occurrence of verbal intimation, from the cause of intimation known as prompting speech, he may incur an offense of wrong-doing through intentional false speech, that is, through knowingly speaking falsely. Herein, the contradiction with what is laid down in the Abhidhamma—‘How can false speech arise from verbal intimation for one who is not conversing?’—and the contradiction with the scriptures are refuted by the fact that in the Nidānuddesa it is stated, ‘Should he not declare an existing offense, there is an offense for intentional false speech,’ and that an offense of wrong-doing arises from non-action through the verbal door. How can an offense arise without speaking falsely? Just as a famine that arises from the clouds not raining at the proper time is to be called ‘a famine caused by the clouds,’ so too an offense of wrong-doing that arises from non-action through the verbal door, due to not speaking at a time when one ought to speak, is to be called ‘arisen from that.’ The clauses are: ‘for intentional false speech,’ and ‘the offense itself is one of wrong-doing.’”

Neyyassa yathā –

As for what is to be inferred, for example:

81.

81.

Marīcicandanālepa-lābhā sītamarīcino sitamarīcino (sī.);

Imā sabbāpi dhavalā, disā rocanti nibbharaṃ.

Through the gain of anointment with the sandalwood paste of the rays of the cool-rayed moon, all these directions, being white, shine forth intensely.

81. “Marīcī”tyādi. Sītamarīcino candassa marīciyo dīdhitiyo eva candanaṃ, tassa ālepo upadeho, tassa lābhena imā sabbāpi disā nibbharamatisayaṃ dhavalā setā rocantīti natthettha neyyatā marīciyā saddopāttatthāya tu.

81. “‘Rays,’ etc. The rays of the cool-rayed moon, its beams of light, are themselves the sandalwood; its anointment is the application. Through the gain of this, all these directions shine forth intensely, being exceedingly white. Thus, there is no need for inference here, for the meaning is conveyed by the word ‘rays’ itself.

81. “Marīci”ccādi. Sītamarīcino candassa marīcicandanālepalābhā marīcisaṅkhātacandanālepassa paṭilābhato imā sabbāpi disā nibbharamatisayaṃ dhavalā setā rocanti dibbantīti. Disānaṃ dhavalakāraṇassa “marīcicandanālepalābhā sītamarīcino”ti vuttattā neyyadoso na patiṭṭhāti, candanamiva candanaṃ, marīciyoyeva candanamiti ca, tassa ālepoti ca, tassa lābhoti ca viggaho.

81. “‘Rays,’ etc. Through the gain of anointment with the sandalwood paste of the rays of the cool-rayed moon—that is, from obtaining the sandalwood-paste anointment designated as ‘rays’—all these directions shine forth intensely, being exceedingly white, appearing divine. Since the cause of the directions’ whiteness is stated as ‘through the gain of anointment with the sandalwood paste of the rays of the cool-rayed moon,’ the fault of requiring inference does not stand. The analysis is: ‘sandalwood-like, thus sandalwood,’ ‘the rays themselves are the sandalwood,’ ‘its anointment,’ and ‘the gain of it.’”

Yathā vā –

Or as, for example:

81.

81.

Manonurañjano māra-ṅganāsiṅgāravibbhamo;

Jinenā’samanuññāto, mārassa hadayānalo.

The mind-delighting, seductive display of Māra's daughters, unapproved by the Conqueror, became Māra's heart-fire.

82. “Mano”ccādi. Manaṃ passantānamanussarantānañca cittaṃ anurañjetīti manonurañjano, māraṅganānaṃ siṅgārakato vibbhamo vilāso jinena asamanuññāto abbhupagato mārassa vasavattino hadayānalo hadayaggi jāto. Soko cettha analatthe niruppito tassa [M 0.0115] tādisatthānativattanato, kāraṇantupacārenāti. Ettha yajjapi māraṅganāparājayo na saddopāttattho, tathāpi “siṅgāravibbhamo mārassa hadayaggī”ti vutte sāmatthiyā māraṅganāparājayo gamyate, tathāvidhassa mārasokassa māraṅganāparājayābyabhicārato. Nevedisassa neyyatā, vaṅkavuttīdisī guṇoyeva bandhassa.

82. “‘Mind,’ etc. ‘Mind-delighting’ (manonurañjano) means it delights the mind of those who see and recollect it. The flirtatious display, the alluring charm, arising from the coquetry of Māra’s daughters, unapproved and not accepted by the Conqueror, became a heart-fire, a heart-flame, for Māra, the sovereign. Herein, sorrow is designated in the sense of ‘fire’ because it does not deviate from such a state; this is by way of a metaphor based on the cause. Although the defeat of Māra’s daughters is not explicitly stated, when it is said, ‘the seductive display became Māra’s heart-fire,’ the defeat of Māra’s daughters is understood by implication, since such sorrow for Māra is invariably linked to their defeat. For such as this, there is no fault of requiring inference; on the contrary, such oblique speech is a virtue of composition.

82. Vattabbassa ñāyopāttattā neyyadosaparihāratthamudāharati “mano”ccādi. Manonurañjano dassanasavanānussaraṇaṃ karontānaṃ janānaṃ cittamattani anurañjanto māraṅganāsiṅgāravibbhamo māravadhūnaṃ ratikīḷāhetubhūtakāmapatthanāsaṅkhātasiṅgārena katalīlā jinena jitapañcamārena satthunā asamanuññāto anabbhupagato asampaṭicchito mārassa vasavattino hadayānalo hadayaggi ahosīti. Analattena kappitakāriyabhūto soko māraṅganāsiṅgāravibbhamasaṅkhātakāraṇena saddhiṃ abhedakappanāya analattakappanāya (ka.) “guḷo semhaṃ, tipusaṃ jaro”tiādīsu viya tulyādhikaraṇabhāvena vutto hoti. Ettha kiñcāpi māraṅganānaṃ parājayavācako saddo natthi, tathāpi “siṅgāravibbhamo mārassa hadayānalo”ti vutte māraṅganāparājayaṃ vinā tādisasokuppattikāraṇassa anadhigatattā aññathānupapattilakkhaṇasāmatthiyena tāsaṃ parājayo pakāsito hotīti īdisavaṅkavuttiyā bandhaguṇattā neyyadoso nirākato hotīti. Mano anurañjetīti ca, māraṅganānaṃ siṅgāroti ca, tena kato vibbhamoti ca vākyaṃ.

82. To avoid the fault of requiring inference, since what is to be said is arrived at by reasoning, the example ‘mind,’ etc., is given. ‘Mind-delighting’ means delighting the mind of people who engage in seeing, hearing, and recollecting it. The graceful display created by the coquetry—designated as the longing for desire which is the cause of the amorous sport of Māra’s daughters—was not approved, not accepted, not received by the Conqueror, the Teacher who has conquered the fivefold Māra. It became the heart-fire, the heart-flame of Māra, the sovereign. Herein, sorrow, the effect which is imagined as fire, is spoken of in apposition with its cause, the seductive display of Māra’s daughters, by means of a conception of non-difference, just as in expressions like ‘molasses is phlegm, lead is fever.’ Although there is no word explicitly stating the defeat of Māra’s daughters, when it is said, ‘the seductive display became Māra’s heart-fire,’ their defeat is revealed by the power of implication, which is characterized by the impossibility of it being otherwise, since without their defeat the cause for such sorrow could not be found. Thus, because such oblique speech is a virtue of composition, the fault of requiring inference is refuted. The clauses are: ‘it delights the mind,’ ‘the coquetry of Māra’s daughters,’ and ‘the display created by that.’”

Visesanāpekkhassa yathā –

As in the case of requiring a qualifier, for example:

83.

83.

Apayātāparādhampi, ayaṃ verī janaṃ jano;

Kodhapāṭalabhūtena, bhiyyo passati cakkhunā.
