This hostile person sees that person—even though his offense has departed—all the more with an eye that has become pale-red with anger.

83. “Apayāte”ccādi. [M 0.0116] Ayaṃ verī jano apayātāparādhampi jananti sambandho. Apayāto apagato aparādho yassa taṃ, kodhena pāṭalabhūtena setarattena. Iminā visesanāpekkhadoso parihaṭo.

83. “‘Departed,’ etc. The connection is: ‘this hostile person sees a person even though his offense has departed.’ The analysis is: he from whom the offense has departed, gone away. ‘Become pale-red with anger’ means become pale-red. By this, the fault of requiring a qualifier is avoided.

83. “Apayāti”ccādi. Ayaṃ verī jano apayātāparādhampi apagatāparādhampi janaṃ kodhapāṭalabhūtena kodhena bhūtasetalohitavaṇṇayuttena cakkhunā bhiyyo yebhuyyena passatīti. “Passatī”ti vacanassa vijjamānattepi “cakkhunā”ti visesyavacanaṃ “kodhapāṭalabhūtenā”ti visesanassa labbhamānattā sātthakaṃ hotīti visesanāpekkhadoso nirākatoti. Apayāto apagato aparādho asmāti ca, kodhena pāṭalabhūtanti ca viggaho.

83. “‘Departed,’ etc. This hostile person sees another person—even one whose offense has departed, gone away—all the more, for the most part, with an eye that has become pale-red with anger, that is, endowed with a pale-red color. Although the word ‘sees’ (passati) is present, the word for the qualified noun, ‘with an eye’ (cakkhunā), is meaningful because the qualifier ‘having become pale-red with anger’ is thereby obtained. Thus the fault of requiring a qualifier is refuted. The analyses are: ‘the offense has departed, gone away from him,’ and ‘become pale-red with anger.’”

Hīnatthassa yathā –

As in the case of inferior meaning, for example:

84.

84.

Appakānampi pāpānaṃ,

Pabhāvaṃ nāsaye budho;

Api nippabhatānīta-

Khajjoto hoti bhāṇumā.

A wise person should destroy the power even of slight evils; for the sun, by which a firefly is brought to lightlessness, is still the radiant one.

84. “Appakāna”miccādi. Budho paṇḍitaposo appakānaṃ pāpānampi kimutamadhikānaṃ pabhāvaṃ ānubhāvaṃ nāsaye appavattiṃ pāpeyya. Taṃ atthantaranyāsena sādheti. Bhāṇumā sūriyo nippabhataṃ ānīto khajjoto yena tathāvidho api hoti. “Mandappabho aya”nti jotiriṅgaṇampi nopekkhati cakkavāḷakuharānucaritamahānubhāvopīti. Ettha apītyādinā vacobhaṅgiyā hīnatthadoso parihaṭo.

84. “‘Of slight,’ etc. A wise person, a prudent man, should destroy the influence and power even of slight evils—how much more so of greater ones—he should bring them to non-occurrence. He proves this by means of a corroborative example. The sun is one by whom a firefly is brought to lightlessness, even so. Though it is of great power, traversing the hollow of the universe, it does not disregard even a firefly, thinking, ‘This one is of feeble light.’ Herein, by the turn of phrase with ‘api,’ etc., the fault of inferior meaning is avoided.

84. “Appakāni”ccādi. Budho paññavā appakānampi atimandānampi pāpānaṃ akusalānaṃ pabhāvaṃ vipākadānasāmatthiyasaṅkhātānubhāvaṃ nāsaye ahosikammatāpādanena nāseyya, [M 0.0117] bahūnaṃ pāpānaṃ vattabbameva natthi. Tamatthamatthantaranyāsālaṅkārena samattheti apiccādi. Bhāṇumā sūriyo nippabhatānītakhajjoto api nippabhatamāpāditajotiriṅgaṇehi samannāgatopi hotīti. Hīnapabhāvo hoti khajjopanake pahāya attano ālokaṃ karonto na hotīti adhippāyo. Ettha api nippabhaticcādivacanavilāsavasena hīnapakkhaṃ gahetvāpi sūriyaudārattasseva positattā “nippabhatānītakhajjoto”ti visesanapadaṃ hīnatthadosaṃ na nissayati. Natthi pabhā yesanti ca, tesaṃ bhāvoti ca, taṃ ānītā khajjotā yeneti ca viggaho.

84. ‘Appakāni,’ etc. A wise, intelligent person should destroy the power—the capacity to give results—of even the slightest and weakest evils, of unwholesome deeds, by rendering them ineffective. What need is there to speak of many evils? That meaning is supported by the figure of speech, the setting forth of another meaning, as in ‘api,’ etc. The radiant sun, which has rendered glow-worms lightless, even if endowed with them, is so. The meaning is that it is not of diminished power, making its own light and outshining the glow-worms. Here, through the skillful expression of words like ‘api nippabhata,’ even though the inferior side is taken, the sun’s greatness is affirmed; therefore, the qualifying phrase ‘nippabhatānītakhajjoto’ does not incur the fault of inferior meaning. The analysis is: 'those who have no light'; 'their state'; and 'he by whom glow-worms are brought to that state'.

Anatthassa yathā –

As in the case of meaninglessness:

85.

85.

Na pādapūraṇatthāya, padaṃ yojeyya katthaci;

Yathā vande munindassa, pādapaṅkeruhaṃ varaṃ.

One should not join a word anywhere merely to fill up a line; as in: ‘I venerate the excellent lotus feet of the Lord of Sages.’

85. “Na pāde”ccādi. Ettha vandeiccādo heṭṭhā viya pādapūraṇassa kassaci abhāvena anatthābhāvo.

85. ‘Na pāde,’ etc. Here, in the example beginning 'vande,' unlike in an inferior example, the absence of any line-filling word shows the absence of meaninglessness.

85. “Na pādi”ccādi. Pādapūraṇatthāya gāthāpādānaṃ pūraṇasaṅkhātapayojanatthāya padaṃ nāmādikaṃ katthaci na yojeyya viññūti, yathā niratthakapadāyojane udāharaṇamevaṃ “munindassa varaṃ pādapaṅkeruhaṃ vande”ti. Heṭṭhā duṭṭhodāharaṇe viya pādapūraṇatthaṃ kassaci padassa ayojitattā sātthakapadehi niratthakadoso nirākatoti. Mudunimmalasobhādisādhāraṇaguṇayogato paṅkeruhasadisaṃ upacārato paṅkeruhaṃ nāma. Pādameva paṅkeruhanti viggaho. visesanavisesyapadadosaparihāro.

85. ‘Na pādi,’ etc. For the purpose of filling the verse lines, a word—such as a noun or the like—should not be employed anywhere by the wise; as in the example of not employing meaningless words: ‘I venerate the excellent lotus feet of the Lord of Sages.’ Unlike in the inferior, faulty example, because no word was employed for the purpose of filling a line, the fault of meaninglessness is refuted by meaningful words. Due to possessing common qualities such as softness, purity, and radiance, that which is like a lotus is conventionally called a lotus. The analysis is: ‘the foot itself is a lotus.’ The avoidance of the fault of qualifier and qualified words.

86.

86.

Bhayakodhapasaṃsādi-

Viseso tādiso yadi;

Vattuṃ kāmīyate doso,

Na tatthe’katthatākato.

If such a distinction as fear, anger, praise, and the like is desired to be stated, the fault of redundancy is not incurred there, which arises from a single meaning.

86. “Bhaye”ccādi. [M 0.0118] Bhayañca cittutrāso kodho ca doso pasaṃsā ca thuti, tā ādi yassa turitādino so tādiso viseso yadi vattuṃ kāmīyate icchīyate, tattha tasmiṃ bhayādivisese visaye ekatthatāya ekatthabhāvena kato doso natthi.

86. ‘Bhaye,’ etc. Fear is mental agitation, anger is aversion, praise is commendation—if such a distinction as these, beginning with haste and so on, is desired to be spoken, no fault arises there from the state of having a single meaning.

86. Idāni vākyadosaparihāratthamārabhati “bhayakodhe”ccādi. Bhayakodhapasaṃsādi cittutrāsapaṭighathutiādīhi samannāgato tādiso viseso vattuṃ yadi kāmīyate ce viññūhi icchīyate, tattha bhayakodhādike visese ekatthatākato ekatthabhāvena kato doso vākyadoso na bhavati. Bhayādivisese vattumicchite pubbuccāritapadassa punuccāraṇe ekatthadoso na hotīti adhippāyo. Bhayañca kodho ca pasaṃsā cāti ca, tā ādi yassa turitakotūhalaaccharāhāsasokapasādasaṅkhātassa atthavisesasseti ca viggaho. Tagguṇasaṃviññāṇaaññapadatthasamāsattā bhayādīsu kathitamapi gahetvā punappunaṃ kathanamavirodhaṃ. Eko attho yesaṃ padādīnaṃ te ekatthā, tesaṃ bhāvo ekatthatā, tāya katoti viggaho.

86. Now, to address the avoidance of faults in phrasing, it begins with ‘bhayakodhe,’ etc. If such a distinction—endowed with mental agitation, resentment, praise, etc.—is desired to be expressed by the wise, then in the context of such distinctions as fear, anger, and the like, no fault of phrasing arises there from having a single meaning. The intent is that when one desires to express distinctions like fear, the fault of redundancy does not occur in the repetition of a previously uttered word. The analysis of the distinct meanings is: 'fear, anger, and praise,' and that which has these as its beginning, namely excitement, curiosity, wonder, laughter, sorrow, and serenity. Because it is a compound that conveys its qualities through another word’s meaning, speaking again and again, even when it is said in relation to fear, etc., is not contradictory. The analysis is: those words, etc., which have one meaning are `ekatthā`; their state is `ekatthatā`; ‘made by that’.

Yathā –

As in:

87.

87.

Sappo sappo ayaṃ handa, nivattatu bhavaṃ tato;

Yadi jīvitukāmo’si, kathaṃ tamupasappasi.

‘A snake! A snake! This is it! Oh, may you turn back from there! If you wish to live, why do you approach it?’

87. “Yathe”tyudāharati “sappo”iccādi. “Ayaṃ sappo sappo”ti bhayenāmeḍitaṃ handāti khede tato tamhā ṭhānā, sappato vā bhavaṃ bhavanto nivattatu gatamaggābhimukho āvattatu. Taṃ ṭhānaṃ, sappaṃ vā. Natthettha ekatthatādoso bhayenāmeḍitappayogato.

87. ‘Yathā,’ it gives the example: ‘sappo,’ etc. ‘This is a snake! A snake!’ is a repetition due to fear. ‘Handa’ is an exclamation of distress. ‘Tato’ means from that place, or from the snake. ‘Bhavaṃ nivattatu’ means may you turn back, may you return facing the path you came from. ‘Taṃ’ refers to that place, or the snake. Here, there is no fault of redundancy because of the usage of repetition caused by fear.

87. “Sappo”ccādi. [M 0.0119] Handa naṭṭho vata, ayaṃ sappo sappo bhavaṃ tato ṭhānato, sappato vā nivattatu āvattatu yadi jīvitukāmo asi, taṃ ṭhānaṃ, sappaṃ vā kathamupasappasi kathamupagacchasīti. Bhaye āmeḍitavacanattā ekatthatādoso natthi, jīvitukāmosīti ettha bindulopo.

87. ‘Sappo,’ etc. Handa, alas, I am lost! This is a snake, a snake! May you turn back, return, from that place or from the snake, if you desire to live. That place, or the snake, how do you approach it? How do you come near it? In fear, due to the repetition of words, there is no fault of redundancy. In ‘jīvitukāmosīti,’ here the bindu is elided.

Padadosaparihāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Avoidance of Word-Faults is concluded.

Vākyadosaparihāravaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Avoidance of Faults in Sentences

Bhaggarītino yathā –

As in the case of a broken style:

88.

88.

Yo koci rūpātisayo,

Kanti kāpi manoharā;

Vilāsātisayo kopi,

Aho buddhamahodayo.

Whatever the surpassing form, whatever the delightful loveliness, whatever the exceeding grace—ah, the great magnificence of the Buddha!

88. “Yo”iccādi. Rūpassa anubyañjanehi anubyañjitabāttiṃsavarapurisalakkhaṇopasobhitassa byāmappabhāketumālāvirājitassa atisayo ādhikkaṃ vācāgocarabhāvātikkamena avacanīyattā yo kociyeva. Mano anekalokassa cittaṃ haratīti manoharā cittamavaharantī kanti sobhā kāpi avacanapathā kāpiyeva. Vilāsassa gatyādino atisayo vacanapathātikkanto kopiyeva, tasmā buddhassa mahanto udayo abhivuḍḍhi aho abbhutoti. Ettha kiṃsaddenāraddhā rīti na katthaci bhaggā.

88. ‘Yo,’ etc. The excellence of form—adorned with the thirty-two excellent marks of a great man which are themselves embellished with the minor characteristics, resplendent with the fathom-long aura and the ketumālā—this excellence or pre-eminence is indeed ‘whatever,’ because it is indescribable, transcending the scope of speech. ‘Manoharā’ means that which captivates the mind of many worlds; a certain beauty or loveliness that captivates the mind is indeed ‘whatever,’ being beyond the path of words. The surpassing grace of movement and so on is indeed ‘whatever,’ transcending the path of words. Therefore, the great arising and increase of the Buddha—ah, it is marvelous! Here, the style begun with the word 'what' is not broken anywhere.

88. “Yo koci”ccādi. Rūpātisayo suppahiṭṭhitapādatādidvattiṃsapurisalakkhaṇehi sobhitassa cittaṅgulitādiasītianubyañjanehi [M 0.0120] alaṅkatassa byāmappabhāketumālāhi ujjalassa rūpakāyassa ādhikyaṃ yo kociyeva manogocarabhāvaṃ vinā vacanavisayātikkantattā yo kociyeva. Manoharā lokassa cittaṃ harantī kanti sobhā kāpiyeva vacīvisayātikkantattā kāpiyeva. Vilāsātisayo visayabhūtapiyabhāvasaṅkhātassa gamanādivilāsassa ādhikyampi kopiyeva vuttakāraṇenevakopiyeva. Tato buddhamahodayo buddhassa mahābhivuddhisaṅkhāto udayo aho acchariyoti. Ettha sabbanāmikena kiṃ saddena vattumāraddhakkamo na katthaci bhinnoti bhaggarītidoso natthīti.

88. ‘Yo koci,’ etc. The excellence of form—the pre-eminence of the physical body, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man beginning with well-planted feet, embellished with the eighty minor characteristics beginning with beautiful fingers, shining with the fathom-long aura and ketumālā—is indeed ‘whatever,’ because it transcends the sphere of speech without being an object of mind, it is indeed ‘whatever.’ Delightful loveliness, captivating the mind of the world, is indeed ‘whatever,’ because it transcends the sphere of speech, it is indeed ‘whatever.’ The surpassing grace, the pre-eminence of the grace of movement and so on, which is known as the state of being a beloved object, is also indeed ‘whatever,’ for the very reason stated, it is indeed ‘whatever.’ Hence, the great rise of the Buddha, known as a great increase—ah, it is marvelous! Here, the sequence begun to be spoken with the pronominal word 'what' is not broken anywhere; thus, there is no fault of broken style.

89.

89.

Abyāmohakaraṃ bandhaṃ, abyākiṇṇaṃ manoharaṃ;

Adūrapadavinyāsaṃ, pasaṃsanti kavissarā.

The chief poets praise a composition that does not cause confusion, is unscattered, delightful, and has words placed not too far apart.

89. “Abyāmoha”iccādi. Natthi dūramesanti adūrāni, tāniyeva padāni, tesaṃ vinyāso yāthāvato ṭhapanaṃ yassa taṃ. Tatoyeva abyākiṇṇo asammisso ca. So abyākiṇṇatāya eva manoharo cāti abyākiṇṇaṃ manoharaṃ. Teneva “ayamettha attho ayaṃ vā”ti evaṃ byāmohaṃ na karotīti abyāmohakaro, taṃ. Pasādālaṅkārālaṅkitaṃ bandhaṃ. Kavīnaṃ issarā padhānā. Ye kaniṭṭhaṅguligaṇanāniṭṭhā, te pasaṃsanti thuvanti tādisabandhaguṇassātisayapasaṃsārahabhāvena.

89. ‘Abyāmoha,’ etc. ‘Adūrāni’ means that in which there is nothing far; this refers to the words. Their `vinyāsa` is their arrangement, their proper placement. The composition is that which has this. Therefore, it is unscattered and unmixed. Being unscattered, it is thus delightful; hence, 'unscattered and delightful.' For that reason, it does not create confusion, such as thinking 'is this the meaning here, or is this?'; hence, it is non-confusing, that composition. It is a composition adorned with the ornament of clarity. The lords of poets are the foremost ones. Those who are not satisfied with counting on the little finger praise and laud it, because of the worthiness for the highest praise of the surpassing qualities of such a composition.

89. “Abyāmohe”ccādi. Adūrapadavinyāsaṃ nāmādipadānaṃ vohārakāle adūrasambandho yathā siyā, tathā paṭipāṭiyā padaṭṭhapanena samannāgataṃ abyākiṇṇaṃ, tatoyeva aññasambandhīpadehi asammissaṃ manoharaṃ, tatoyeva viññūnaṃ cittamārādhentaṃ abyāmohakaraṃ “imassattho imassattho eso eso vā”ti saṃsayamanuppādentaṃ bandhaṃ pasādālaṅkārasaṃyuttaṃ bandhanaṃ kavissarā kavīnaṃ [M 0.0121] padhānā paṇḍibhajanā, kaniṭṭhaṅguliyā gaṇitabbā aggakavinoti adhippāyo. Pasaṃsanti thomenti. Byāmohaṃ na karotīti abyāmohakaro. Vi ākiṇṇo byākiṇṇo, na byākiṇṇo abyākiṇṇo. Natthi dūraṃ yesaṃ, tāniyeva padāni, tesaṃ vinyāso ṭhapanaṃ yassa bandhassāti viggaho.

89. 'Non-confusing,' etc. 'Arrangement of words not too far apart' means that, during usage, the connection of words, beginning with nouns, should not be too distant, so that the composition is endowed with the sequential placing of words. It is unscattered, and for that very reason, unmixed with words related to others. It is delightful, and for that very reason, it pleases the minds of the wise. It is non-confusing, not giving rise to doubt such as, 'Is this its meaning, or is that its meaning? Is it this one, or that one?' The chief poets praise and extol such a composition, endowed with the ornament of clarity. The chief poets are the foremost among poets, to be served by the wise; the intent is that they are the chief poets who can be counted on the little finger. They praise and extol. 'Non-confusing' is that which does not cause confusion. 'Scattered' is byākiṇṇa; 'not scattered' is abyākiṇṇa. The analysis of the compound is: 'that composition which has the arrangement, the placement, of those very words that are not distant from one another.'

Yathā –

As:

90.

90.

Nīluppalābhaṃ nayanaṃ,

Bandhukaruciro’dharo;

Nāsā hemaṅkuso tena,

Jinoyaṃ piyadassano.

His eyes are like blue lotuses, his lower lip beautiful like a bandhuka flower; his nose is a golden goad. Therefore, this Victor is pleasing to behold.

90. “Yathe”tyudāharati “nīluppalābha”miccādi. Yassa jinassa nayanaṃ nettaṃ nīluppalābhaṃ indīvaradvayanibhaṃ, adharo adharoṭṭho bandhukamiva bandhukakusumamiva ruciro kanto, nāsā nāsikā sayaṃ hemaṅkuso suvaṇṇaṅkusoyeva, tena kāraṇena ayaṃ jino piyaṃ madhuraṃ dassanamassāti piyadassano. Īdiso na byākiṇṇadoso, abyākiṇṇo pasādoyevāti.

90. 'As,' he exemplifies with 'blue lotus-like,' and so on. Whose eye, the eye of that Victor, is blue lotus-like, resembling a pair of blue lotuses; whose lower lip, the lower lip, is beautiful like the bandhuka flower, charming like the bandhuka blossom; whose nose, the nasal feature, is itself a golden goad, just like a golden goad. For that reason, this Victor is 'one whose sight is pleasing and sweet'—thus he is called 'Piyadassano.' Such a composition does not have the fault of being scattered; it is indeed unscattered clarity.

90. Idāni byākiṇṇadosaparihāraṃ pariharati “nīluppali”ccādinā. Nayanaṃ yassa nettayugaḷaṃ nīluppalābhaṃ nīluppaladalasadisaṃ, adharo adharoṭṭho bandhukaruciro bandhukapupphamiva manuñño, nāsā nāsikā hemaṅkuso suvaṇṇaṅkusoyeva, tena kāraṇena ayaṃ jino piyadassano manuññadassano hotīti. Ettha pasādālaṅkārena yuttattā na byākiṇṇadoso. Ābhāsaddo nibhāsaddo viya ivattho. No ce, pabhāpariyāyo vā hoti. Bandhukamiva ruciroti ca, piyaṃ dassanaṃ yasseti ca viggaho. Iha dassanassa kattubhūtasādhujanasambandhattepi visayatteneva [M 0.0122] jinasambandho hotīti aññapadatthena tathāgato gahitoti.

90. Now, he demonstrates the avoidance of the fault of being scattered with 'blue lotus,' etc. Whose eye, that pair of eyes, is blue lotus-like, resembling the petals of a blue lotus; whose lower lip, the lower lip, is beautiful like a bandhuka flower, charming like a bandhuka blossom; whose nose, the nasal feature, is a golden goad, just like a golden goad. For this reason, this Victor is pleasing to see, delightful to behold. Here, because it is endowed with the ornament of clarity, there is no fault of being scattered. The word 'ābha' is like the word 'nibha,' having the meaning of 'like.' If not, it is a synonym for 'brightness.' And 'beautiful like a bandhuka,' and 'one whose sight is pleasing'—these are the analyses. Here, even though the act of seeing is connected to virtuous people as the agent, the connection to the Victor is only as the object. Thus, the Tathāgata is understood by means of the meaning of another word (i.e., a bahuvrīhi compound).

91.

91.

Samatikkantagāmmatta-kantavācābhisaṅkhataṃ;

Bandhanaṃ rasahetuttā, gāmmattaṃ ativattati.

A composition composed with charming words that have completely transcended vulgarity, being the cause of relish, overcomes vulgarity.

91. “Samatikkanti”ccādi. Sammā atikkantaṃ niggataṃ. Gāmmassa bhāvo gāmmattaṃ. Yāsaṃ kantānaṃ madhurānaṃ vācānaṃ tāhi abhisaṅkhataṃ racitaṃ bandhanaṃ rasassa mādhuriyassa hetuttā kāraṇabhāvena gāmmattaṃ yathāvuttaṃ ativattati atikkamati.

91. 'Completely transcending,' etc. 'Completely transcended' means gone forth. The state of being rustic is vulgarity. The composition, composed with those charming, sweet words, being the cause of the sweetness of relish, overcomes and surpasses the aforementioned vulgarity.

91. “Samati”ccādi. Samatikkantagāmmattakantavācābhisaṅkhataṃ visesato atikkantagāmmabhāvāhi kantavācāhi racitaṃ bandhanaṃ muttakādibandhanaṃ rasahetuttā paṇḍitānaṃ pītirasassa kāraṇattā yathāvuttagāmmadosaṃ ativattati atikkamma pavattatīti. Sammā atikkantaṃ gāmmattaṃ yāsaṃ, tāhiyeva kantavācāhi abhisaṅkhatanti ca, rasassa hetu, tassa bhāvoti ca viggaho.

91. 'Completely transcending,' etc. 'Completely transcending vulgarity—constructed of charming speech' means a composition, such as a free composition, specifically constructed of charming speech that has transcended the state of vulgarity. Because it is the cause of relish, the cause of delightful flavor for the wise, it overcomes, transcends, and proceeds beyond the previously mentioned fault of vulgarity. The analyses are: 'constructed of those very charming words whose vulgarity is completely transcended,' and 'the cause of the flavor, its nature.'

Yathā –

As:

92.

92.

Dunoti kāmacaṇḍālo,

So maṃ sadaya niddayo;

Īdisaṃ byasanāpannaṃ,

Sukhīpi kimupekkhase.

The desire-outcaste torments me. O compassionate one, he, merciless, torments me. Why do you, though happy, neglect one fallen into such misfortune?

92. “Yathe”tyudāharati. Kāmāturā kāci vanitā attano piyaṃ patiṃ viravati “dunoti”ccādinā. Dayāya saha pavattīti sadayaiti anunayavasena piyassa āmantanaṃ, sānunayāmantanañhi tatonuggahābhikaṅkhāyamaccantamucitaṃ, so kāmo kandappo eva caṇḍālo akaṇḍo [M 0.0123] vā asayhopatāpāvahattā. Kāme caṇḍālattāropanañca ucitameva yatonena kayiramānamasahanamupatāpamasahamānā taṃ paribhavantaṃ vippalapati, niddayo nikkaruṇo, idamapi ucitamupatāpe nikkaruṇānaṃ tādisī gatīti. Maṃ dunoti adhikamupatāpeti niddayattā, na bhavantaṃ, teneva bhavaṃ sukhī. Iminā aññāsattataṃ tassa dīpeti. Yadi nāññāsattosi, nāhamekākinī bhavāmi. Asahāyānañhi paṭisattavo honti. Ekākittāyevāhamappaṭisaraṇattānena dusāmīti duññāmīti (?) tava kāmaṃ tvaṃ sukhī hosi. Sanāthānaṃ tādisī vuttīti evaṃ sukhīpi tvaṃ īdisaṃ byasanamāpannaṃ kiṃ kasmā upekkhaseti. Evamayaṃ vaṅkavuttiyā attano, taṃ visayamanubhavantassa ca vimukhattaṃ nidassetītīdisaṃ na gāmmaṃ.

92. 'As,' he exemplifies. A certain woman, tormented by desire, laments to her beloved husband with 'he torments me,' etc. 'Sadaya' (compassionate) is an address by way of entreaty to her beloved, meaning 'one who proceeds with compassion'; for such an affectionate address is entirely fitting when longing for his favor. That desire, Kandarpa, is indeed an outcaste, or without cause, because it brings unbearable suffering. And it is fitting to describe desire as an outcaste, for she, unable to endure the unbearable torment caused by it, reproaches him, speaking wildly. 'Merciless' means without compassion; this too is fitting, for such is the way of the merciless in causing suffering. 'He torments me' means 'he torments me excessively due to his heartlessness—not you, for you are happy.' By this, she reveals his attachment to another. 'If you were not attached to another, I would not be alone. For those without companions have adversaries. It is because I am alone and without refuge that I am tormented by him. As for you, you are happy.' Such is the way for those who have protectors. 'Though you are happy, why do you remain indifferent to one fallen into such misfortune?' Thus, through her indirect speech, she demonstrates her own state and his detachment from experiencing that object. Such a composition is not vulgar.

92. Gāmmadosaparihāre lakkhiyaṃ dasseti “dunoti”ccādi. Kāmataṇhābhibhūtā aṅganā attano vallabhaṃ nissāya evaṃ vilapati “sadaya he kāruṇika so kāmacaṇḍālo so anaṅganīco niddayo nikkāruṇiko maṃ dunoti pīḷeti, sukhīpi mama viya anāthabhāvābhāvato sukhitopi tvaṃ īdisaṃ byasanāpannaṃ evaṃ kāmacaṇḍālena akāruṇena kataasayhasantāpasaṅkhātabyasanamanuppattaṃ maṃ kimupekkhase kasmā udāsīnosī”ti. Attano dukkhāturattā dukkhadūrīkaraṇaṃ kāruṇikānaṃyeva visayanti “sadaye”ti anunayavasena āmantanucitaṃ attano dukkhāturataṃ posetuṃ pīḷākārake kāme caṇḍālattāropanañca niddayattakathanañca ucitameva attani upekkhakattā. Sukhīpīti iminā tassa paravisayāsattatāya aticāraṃ abbhupagameti. Evaṃ vaṅkavuttiyā attano vallabhe sānurāgattañca attani tassa tadabhāvattañca dassetīti. “Kaññe kāmayamānaṃ maṃ, na kāmayasi kiṃnvida”nti ettha viya iha gāmmadoso natthīti [M 0.0124] gāmmadosaparihāramidaṃ. Kāmoyeva caṇḍālo kāmacaṇḍālo, saha dayāya yo vattatīti ca, natthi dayā asseti ca, sukhamassa atthīti ca viggaho. Apisaddo akkhame.

92. To illustrate the avoidance of the fault of vulgarity, he points out the example 'he torments me,' etc. Overcome by craving for sensual pleasure, a woman, relying on her beloved, laments thus: 'O compassionate one, O pitiful one, that desire-outcaste, that base bodiless one, merciless and pitiless, torments and oppresses me. Though you are happy—being free from the state of being without a protector like me—why do you neglect me, who has fallen into such misfortune, who has met with suffering in the form of unbearable torment caused by that cruel, merciless desire-outcaste? Why are you indifferent?' Because she is afflicted by suffering, and because removing suffering is the domain of the compassionate, the address 'O compassionate one' by way of entreaty is fitting. To emphasize her own afflicted suffering, it is fitting to describe desire, the tormentor, as an outcaste and to speak of its heartlessness, because he is indifferent to her. By 'though you are happy,' she implies his transgression due to attachment to another. Thus, through indirect speech, she shows her own affection for her beloved and his lack thereof toward her. Unlike in the example, 'O maiden, you whom I desire, why do you not desire me?', here there is no fault of vulgarity; thus, this is an avoidance of the fault of vulgarity. The analyses are: 'desire itself is an outcaste' is 'desire-outcaste'; 'he who acts with compassion'; 'he who has no compassion'; and 'he who has happiness.' The particle 'api' is used in the sense of impatience.

93.

93.

Yatihīnaparihāro, na pune’dāni nīyate;

Yato na savanubbegaṃ, heṭṭhā yetaṃ vicāritaṃ.

The avoidance of defective caesura is not brought forward again now, because this has been discussed below, and because, when avoided, it causes no agitation upon hearing.

93. “Yati”ccādi. Vicāritanti “taṃ name sirasā cāmī-karavaṇṇaṃ tathāgata”ntiādinā heṭṭhā pakāsitanti attho.

93. 'Defective caesura,' etc. 'Discussed' means it was explained previously by the phrase 'I bow my head to the Tathāgata, whose color is like gold,' etc.

93. “Yatihīni”ccādi. Yato yasmā savanubbegaṃ “dosānamuddesakkamena dosaparihārakkamo na vutto”ti evaṃ viññūnamuppajjamānaṃ imassa ganthassa savanāsahanaṃ natthi, tato yatihīnaparihāro yatihīnadosassa pariharaṇavasena pavattamudāharaṇaṃ idāni puna na nīyate nāharīyateti. Iminādhigatamādo vuttatthameva samattheti. Heṭṭhā yetaṃ vicāritanti evaṃ yatihīnadosapariharaṇaṃ heṭṭhā anantaraparicchede vicāritaṃ “taṃ name sirasā cāmī-karavaṇṇaṃ tathāgata”ntiādinā pakāsitanti. Ādo yatihīnadosapātubhāveyeva parihārakkamassāpi dassitattā ihādassanepi ganthassa ūnatā natthīti adhippāyo. Yati hīnā ettheti ca, tassa parihāroti ca, savane ubbeganti ca viggaho.

93. ‘Yatihīni,’ etc. Because for the discerning there is no intolerance of hearing this text—an agitation upon hearing that might arise from thinking, ‘the method for removing faults has not been stated in the order of their enumeration’—therefore, an example proceeding by way of removing the fault of defective caesura is not brought forward again now. By this, he supports the very meaning stated at the beginning. ‘This has been discussed below’ means that the removal of the fault of defective caesura was discussed below in the immediately preceding chapter, explained by the phrase, ‘I bow my head to the Tathāgata, whose color is like gold,’ etc. The intention is that since the method of removal was shown at the very appearance of the fault of defective caesura at the beginning, there is no deficiency in the text even if it is not shown here. And the analysis is: ‘caesura is defective herein’ (yati hīnā ettha), ‘its removal’ (tassa parihāro), and ‘agitation upon hearing’ (savane ubbegaṃ).

Kamaccutassa yathā –

As for the fault of misplaced order, for example—

94.

94.

Udāracarito’si tvaṃ, tenevā’rādhanā tvayi;

Desaṃ vā dehi gāmaṃ vā, khettaṃ vā mama sobhanaṃ.

You are of noble conduct, and thus my request is made to you: Give me a region or a village, or a fine field of mine.

94. “Udāra”iccādi. Udāraṃ udārattaṃ cāgātisayasambandhato caritaṃ atiguṇapavatti yassāti viggaho. Ettha ucitattā [M 0.0125] desādīnaṃ yācanakkamassa kamaccutassa parihāroyaṃ.

94. ‘Udāra,’ etc. The analysis is: ‘generous’ (udāraṃ) means one whose conduct (caritaṃ) is an extraordinary course of good qualities (atiguṇapavatti) due to its connection with supreme generosity (cāgātisaya). Here, because of its appropriateness, this is the removal of the fault of misplaced order (kamaccuta) in the sequence of requesting a region, etc.

94. “Udāri”ccādi. Tvaṃ puññavanta udāracaritosi cāgātisayayogato visāradapavattiyuttosi, teneva tena kāraṇeneva ārādhanā mama yācanā tvayi hoti. Desaṃ vājanapadaṃ vā, no ce, gāmaṃ vā saṃvasathaṃ vā, no ce, sobhanaṃ khettaṃ vā kedāraṃ vā mama dehīti anupubbaṃ hīnapadatthayācanā dāyakassa dānassāpi yācakassa icchitatthapaṭilābhassāpi anurūpattā kamaccutadosamapaneti. Udāraṃ caritaṃ assāti viggaho.

94. ‘Udāri,’ etc. You, O meritorious one, are of generous conduct, endowed with confident conduct due to supreme generosity; therefore, for that very reason, my request is made to you. Give me a region or a district, or if not, a village or a settlement, or if not, a fine field or farmland of mine. This gradual request for items of lesser value, being appropriate for both the giver’s gift and the requester’s attainment of the desired object, removes the fault of misplaced order. The analysis is: ‘one whose conduct is generous’ (udāraṃ caritaṃ assa).

Ativuttassa yathā –

As for the fault of overstatement, for example—

95.

95.

Munindacandasambhūta-

Yasorāsimarīcinaṃ;

Sakalopya’yamākāso,

Nā’vakāso vijambhane.

For the rays, a mass of glory, born from the moon-like Sage-King, this entire sky has no space for their unfolding.

95. “Muninda”iccādi. Munindoyeva cando, tato sambhūtā pātubhūtā, yasorāsī eva marīciyo, tāsaṃ. Ayaṃ sakalo ākāsopi gaganameva, na tasseko padeso. Vijambhane byāpane nāvakāso tādisattā tāsaṃ marīcinanti nātivuttaṃ.

95. ‘Muninda,’ etc. The Sage-King is indeed the moon; from him are born, manifested, the rays which are masses of glory; for those rays. This entire sky, indeed the firmament, not even a single part of it, has no space for their expansion (vijambhane, byāpane) due to their suchness (tādisattā); thus, it is not an overstatement regarding those rays.

95. “Munindi”ccādi. Munindacandasambhūtayasorāsimarīcinaṃ munindasaṅkhātacandato pātubhūtānaṃ kittisamūhasaṅkhātakiraṇānaṃ vijambhane byāpane ayaṃ sakalopi ākāso nāvakāso na okāso hotīti. Hetuphalādiekekakāraṇenāpi appameyyānaṃ sabbaññuguṇānaṃ pavattiyā appameyyasāmaññabhūtākāsassa niravakāsassa iva kathanamucitanti ativuttadoso iha na bhavati. Cando iva [M 0.0126] cando, munindo eva cando, tato sambhūtānaṃyeva yasānaṃ rāsī ca tā marīciyo cāti viggaho.

95. ‘Munindi,’ etc. ‘For the rays, a mass of glory, born from the moon-like Sage-King’ means that this entire sky has no space, no room, for the expansion or pervading of the rays, which are a mass of fame manifested from the moon that is the Sage-King. Because the immeasurable qualities of the Omniscient One arise from each single cause, such as cause and effect, it is fitting to speak of the immeasurable, ordinary sky as if it were without space; thus, the fault of overstatement does not occur here. The analysis is: ‘The Sage-King is like the moon,’ ‘the Sage-King is indeed the moon,’ and ‘a mass of fame, and those rays born from him.’

96.

96.

Vākyaṃ byāpannacittānaṃ, apetatthaṃ aninditaṃ;

Tenu’mmattādikānaṃ taṃ, vacanā’ññatra dussati.

Speech of those with deranged minds, devoid of meaning, is blameless; therefore, it is considered faulty elsewhere than in the speech of the mad and the like.

96. “Vākya”miccādi. Byāpannaṃ naṭṭhaṃ ayathāpavattaṃ cittaṃ yesaṃ, tesaṃ. Vākyaṃ vākyalakkhaṇopetaṃ. Apeto apagato suñño attho abhidheyyaṃ saṃvohārikaṃ yassa, taṃ. Aninditaṃ ahīḷitaṃ. Tena yathāvuttena kāraṇena. Taṃ vākyaṃ ummatto dhātukkhobhādinā khittacitto, so ādi yesaṃ bālādīnaṃ tesaṃ vacanā asaṅgatāya vācāya aññatra aññasmiṃ abyāpannacittavisaye dussati duṭṭhaṃ jāyate, ummattādīnaṃyeva tathāvidhāya vācāya ucitattāti.

96. ‘Vākya,’ etc. ‘Of those with deranged minds’ means of those whose minds are ruined, improperly functioning. ‘Speech’ means endowed with the characteristics of a sentence. ‘Devoid of meaning’ means that from which the meaning—the designated, the conventional—is absent, gone, empty. ‘Blameless’ means unreviled. ‘Therefore’ means for the reason stated. That speech is faulty, becomes corrupt, elsewhere—in another domain, that of an undiseased mind—than in the unconnected speech of the mad (one whose mind is deranged by a disturbance of the elements, etc.) and others such as fools, because such speech is proper only for the mad and the like.

96. “Vākya”miccādi. Byāpannacittānaṃ viruddhabhāvamāpannacittānaṃ vākyaṃ syādyantatyādyantapadasamudāyarūpaṃ vākyaṃ apetatthaṃ apagatasamudāyatthaṃ aninditaṃ viññūhi garahitaṃ na hoti, tena kāraṇena ummattādikānaṃ ummattavedanaṭṭādīnaṃ vacanāññatra vacanaṃ vinā anummattādivacane taṃ samudāyatthasambandharahitaṃ vacanaṃ dussati dosaduṭṭhaṃ hoti. Byāpannaṃ cittaṃ yesanti ca, apeto attho assāti ca, ummatto ādi yesanti ca viggaho.

96. ‘Vākya,’ etc. ‘Speech of those with deranged minds’ (byāpannacittānaṃ), meaning of those whose minds have fallen into a state of opposition, refers to a sentence, a collection of words with initial and final terms, which is ‘devoid of meaning’ (apetatthaṃ), meaning lacking a collective meaning, and is ‘blameless’ (aninditaṃ), meaning not censured by the discerning. For that reason, apart from the speech of the mad and the like—those afflicted by madness, etc.—that speech, which lacks connection to a collective meaning, becomes faulty, becomes corrupted by fault, when spoken by those who are not mad, etc. The analysis is: ‘those whose minds are deranged’ (byāpannaṃ cittaṃ yesaṃ), and ‘that which lacks meaning’ (apeto attho assa), and ‘the mad and the like’ (ummatto ādi yesaṃ).

Yathā –

For example—

97.

97.

Samuddo pīyate so’ya-maha’majja jarāturo;

Ime gajjanti jīmūtā, sakkasse’rāvaṇo piyo.

This ocean is being drunk; today I am afflicted by old age. These clouds thunder; Airāvaṇa is dear to Sakka.

97. “Yathe”tyudāharati “samuddo”iccādi. Na hettha “samuddo pīyate”iccādino padasamudāyassa koci eko attho gayhati, yo so bandhattho siyā. Avayavatthā [M 0.0127] eva tu ayosalākākappāpaṭibhantīti īdisamapetatthamaninditaṃ viññeyyaṃ byāpannacittānaṃ.

97. He cites ‘As’ (yathā) with ‘The ocean,’ etc. Here, no single meaning is grasped from the collection of words ‘the ocean is drunk,’ etc., which would be a cohesive meaning. Rather, the individual meanings appear like disconnected iron rods. Such speech, devoid of meaning and blameless, should be understood as characteristic of those with deranged minds.

97. “Samuddo”ccādi. So ayaṃ samuddo pīyate yena kenaci pīyate, ahaṃ ajja jarāturo jararogābhibhūto, ime jīmūtā meghā gajjanti thanayanti. Sakkassa erāvaṇo piyoti. Idaṃ ninditāninditānaṃ dvinnamudāharaṇaṃ. Idaṃ vākyaṃ avayavatthamantarena samudāyato gamyamānatthassābhāvā apetatthaṃ nāma hoti. Īdisaṃ vākyaṃ ummattakādīhi vuttamappītikaraṃ na hoti, aññehi vuttaṃ pana kaṇṇe ayosalākā viya appītikaraṃ. Jarāya āturoti vākyaṃ.

97. ‘The ocean,’ etc. ‘This ocean is drunk’ (samuddo pīyate) means it is drunk by anyone. ‘Today I am afflicted by old age’ (ahaṃ ajja jarāturo) means overcome by the sickness of aging. ‘These clouds thunder’ (ime jīmūtā gajjanti) means they rumble. ‘Airāvaṇa is dear to Sakka’ (Sakkassa erāvaṇo piyo). This is an example of both what is blameworthy and what is not blameworthy. This statement, due to the absence of a meaning that can be understood collectively apart from the individual meanings, is called ‘devoid of meaning’ (apetatthaṃ). Such a statement, when spoken by the mad and the like, is not unpleasant; but when spoken by others, it is unpleasant like an iron spike in the ear. The analysis is: ‘afflicted by old age’ (jarāya āturo).

98.

98.

Sukhumālāvirodhitta-dittabhāvappabhāvitaṃ;

Bandhanaṃ bandhapharusa-dosaṃ saṃdūsayeyya taṃ.

A composition enhanced by the shining quality of non-contradiction with delicacy—may it destroy the harsh fault of composition.

98. “Sukhumāli”ccādi. Na virujjhati sīlenāti avirodhī, tassa bhāvo avirodhittaṃ. Sukhumālassa avirodhittaṃ yassa so dittabhāvo, tena pabhāvitaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ saṃyuttaṃ taṃ bandhanaṃ bandhapharusadosaṃ saṃdūsayeyya nāsayeti attho.

98. ‘Sukhumāli,’ etc. ‘Non-contradictory’ (avirodhī) means not conflicting with virtue; its state is non-contradiction (avirodhittaṃ). The shining quality (dittabhāva) is that which has the non-contradiction (avirodhittaṃ) of delicacy (sukhumāla); by that, that composition is enhanced, augmented, conjoined, and it would destroy (saṃdūsayeyya), that is, annihilate (nāsayeti), the harsh fault of composition (bandhapharusa-dosa)—this is the meaning.

98. “Sukhumāli”ccādi. Sukhumālāvirodhittadittabhāvappabhāvitaṃ “aniṭṭhurakkharappāye”ccādinā vuccamānasukhumālaguṇassa aviruddhabhāvasamannāgatena vaṇṇānaṃ aññamaññasaṅgabhilakkhaṇena dittabhāvena piyabhāvena anubrūhitaṃ taṃ bandhanaṃ bandhapharusadosaṃ bandhapharusasaṅkhātadosaṃ saṃdūsayeyya nāseyya, taṃ bandhapharusadosanti vā sambandhoti. Na virujjhati sīlenāti avirodhī, tassa bhāvoti ca, sukhumālassa avirodhittaṃ yassāti ca, soyeva dittassa bhāvoti ca, tena pabhāvitanti ca vākyaṃ.

98. ‘Sukhumāli,’ etc. ‘Enhanced by the shining quality of non-contradiction with delicacy’ (sukhumālāvirodhittadittabhāvappabhāvitaṃ) means that composition, which is augmented by the shining quality (dittabhāva) characterized by the mutual connection of sounds and by loveliness (piyabhāva), being endowed with a non-contradictory state, of the delicate quality (sukhumāla-guṇa) spoken of by ‘mostly non-harsh syllables,’ etc., would destroy (saṃdūsayeyya, nāseyya) the harsh fault of composition (bandhapharusa-dosa), the fault reckoned as harsh composition; or, the connection is ‘that harsh fault of composition.’ The analysis is: ‘it does not conflict with virtue’ (na virujjhati sīlena) means non-contradictory (avirodhī); and ‘its state’ (tassa bhāvo); and ‘that which has the non-contradiction of delicacy’ (sukhumālassa avirodhittaṃ yassa); and ‘that itself is the state of shining’ (so yeva dittassa bhāvo); and ‘enhanced by that’ (tena pabhāvitaṃ)—this is the statement.

Yathā –

For example—

99.

99.

Passantā [M 0.0128] rūpavibhavaṃ, suṇantā madhuraṃ giraṃ;

Caranti sādhū sambuddha-kāle keḷiparammukhā.

Seeing the splendor of form, hearing sweet speech, the virtuous wander in the Buddha’s time, averse to amusements.

99. “Yathe”tyudāharati “passantā”iccādi. Keḷiyā kīḷāya parammukhā vigatacchandā carantīti sambandho.

99. He cites ‘As’ (yathā) with ‘Seeing,’ etc. The connection is that they wander (caranti) averse to amusements (keḷi, kīḷā), devoid of desire for them.

99. “Passante”ccādi. Sādhū sajjanā sambuddhakāle sambuddhassa dharamānakāle rūpavibhavaṃ tassa rūpasampattiṃ passantā cakkhuṃ santappetvā olokentā madhuraṃ giraṃ tasseva bhagavato aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgataṃ madhuravacanaṃ suṇantā keḷiparammukhā kīḷāya vimukhā kīḷābhiratirahitā caranti gacchanti pavattantīti. Kevalaṃ pharusasithilavaṇṇehi vinā sukhuccāraṇīyavaṇṇehi sambhūtasukhumālaguṇāvirodhaaññamaññasaṅgatavaṇṇavisadappavattaguṇayuttattā ettha bandhapharusadoso natthi. Keḷiyā parāni parivattitāni mukhāni etesanti viggaho. Ettha kāloti kiriyā. Sā ca atthato tadākārappavattasambandhoyeva. Loko pana visuṃ eko padatthoyevāti voharati. vākyadosaparihāro.

99. ‘Seeing,’ etc. The virtuous, good people, in the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One, while the Perfectly Enlightened One was alive, seeing the splendor of form, his physical perfection, delighting their eyes by gazing, hearing the sweet speech, the sweet utterance endowed with eight qualities, of that Blessed One himself, wander, go about, and conduct themselves averse to amusements, turned away from play, devoid of delight in play. Here, there is no fault of harshness in composition because the words are composed solely of easily pronounced sounds, without harsh or loose sounds, being endowed with the quality of a clear flow of sounds, which are harmonious and non-contradictory to the delicate quality. The analysis is: ‘those whose faces are turned away from amusement.’ Here, ‘time’ refers to action. And in meaning, it is solely the connection with the occurrence of that mode. However, the world speaks of it as a separate word-meaning. This is the removal of faults in the sentence.

Vākyadosaparihāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the removal of faults in sentences is concluded.

Vākyatthadosaparihāravaṇṇanā

Explanation of Avoiding Faults in the Meaning of Sentences

Apakkamassa yathā –

As in the case of digression:

100.

100.

Bhāvanādānasīlāni, sammā sampāditāni’ha;

Nibbānabhogasaggādi-sādhanāni na saṃsayo.

Mental development, generosity, and virtue, rightly perfected here, are without doubt the means to Nibbāna, enjoyment, heaven, and so forth.

100. “Bhāvanā”iccādi. Ettha bhāvanādīni niddisitvā yathākkamaṃ nibbānādīnaṃ niddesena apakkamadoso parihaṭo.

100. ‘Mental development,’ etc. Here, having specified mental development and so forth, the fault of digression is avoided by specifying Nibbāna and so forth in due order.

100. “Bhāvane”ccādi. [M 0.0129] Iha manussaloke sammā sampāditāni kammaphalaṃ saddahitvā yathāvidhi sampāditāni attano santāne pavattāpitāni bhāvanādānasīlāni nibbānabhogasaggādisādhanāni yathākkamaṃ nibbānaupabhogaparibhogasampattisagguppattiādīnaṃ hetubhāvena sādhakāni honti, ettha sādhane na saṃsayo hotīti. Iha bhāvanādayo uddisitvā uddesakkamaṃ anatikkamma nibbānādīnamanuddesassa katattā apakkamavākyatthadosassa okāso na hoti.

100. ‘Mental development,’ etc. Here in the human world, mental development, generosity, and virtue, rightly perfected and established in one’s own continuum—having believed in the results of kamma and perfected them according to method—become the means to Nibbāna, enjoyment, heaven, and so forth, being causally effective for the attainment of Nibbāna, the enjoyment and consumption of prosperity, the arising of heaven, and so forth, respectively. In this regard, there is no doubt about the means. Here, having specified mental development and so forth, and without transgressing the order of specification, since the restatement of Nibbāna and so forth has been made, there is no room for the fault of digression in the meaning of the sentence.

101.

101.

Uddiṭṭhavisayo koci kopi (ka. sī.), viseso tādiso yadi;

Anuddiṭṭhesu anudiṭṭhesu (?) neva’tthi, doso kamavilaṅghane.

If there is some such distinction regarding a specified subject, there is no fault in transgressing the order among the unspecified.

101. “Uddiṭṭhe”ccādi. Uddiṭṭhā paṭhamaṃ yuttā atthā visayo gocaro yassa uddesānuddesasambandhavijānanalakkhaṇassa visesassa so tādiso koci viseso anuddiṭṭhesu yathākkamamuddesakamānamatikkamena puna atthantaranissayena parāmaṭṭhesu yadi bhaveyya, kamassa yathoddiṭṭhesu anukkamassa vilaṅghane atikkame doso nevatthi.

101. ‘Specified,’ etc. The meanings first stated, which are connected, are the subject and scope of that distinction characterized by understanding the connection between specification and restatement. If some such distinction were to exist among the unspecified, which are again referred to by relying on another meaning, by transgressing the order of specification in due sequence, then there is no fault in transgressing the sequence as stated.

101. “Uddiṭṭhe”ccādi. Uddiṭṭhavisayo paṭhamaṃ payuttatthavisayo tādiso koci viseso uddesānuddesānaṃ “idamassa pubbakathanaṃ, idamassa pacchākathana”nti evaṃ aññamaññāpekkhalakkhaṇasambandhaparijānanalakkhaṇo viseso anuddiṭṭhesu atthantaraṃ nissāya puna vuttesu yadi “bhaveyyā”ti seso. Kamavilaṅghane uddesānuddesānaṃ kamātikkame doso satthaññūnaṃ sutikāle asahanakāraṇaṃ nevatthīti. Uddiṭṭhā paṭhamuccāritā atthā visayo gocaro asseti ca, kamassa vilaṅghananti ca vākyaṃ.

101. ‘Specified,’ etc. The subject of what is specified, the subject of the meaning first applied, is some such distinction, a distinction characterized by fully understanding the connection of mutual dependence between specification and restatement, such as ‘this is its prior statement, this is its subsequent statement.’ If it ‘should be’ among the unspecified, which are again stated by relying on another meaning, this is what is to be supplied. In transgressing the order, in transgressing the order of specification and restatement, there is no fault that causes intolerance for the learned at the time of hearing. And the meanings first uttered are the subject and scope of this, and ‘transgressing the order’ is the phrase.

Yathā –

As:

102.

102.

Kusalākusalaṃ [M 0.0130] abyā-kata’miccesu pacchimaṃ;

Abyākataṃ pākadaṃ na, pākadaṃ paṭhamadvayaṃ.

Wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—among these, the last, the indeterminate, does not produce a result; the first two do produce a result.

102. “Yathe”tyudāharati “kusale”ccādi. Kusalaṃ kāmāvacarādikamekavīsatividhaṃ, akusalañca dvādasavidhaṃ, abyākataṃ vipākakriyāsaṅkhātamiti etesu tīsu pacchimaṃ abyākataṃ, pākaṃ vipākaṃ dadātīti pākadaṃ. Neti nipātapadaṃ. Paṭhamadvayaṃ kusalākusalaṃ pākaṃ dadātīti pākadanti. Ettha apākadattaṃ abyākatasseva, pākadattaṃ tesameva dvinnanti viseso daṭṭhabbo.

102. ‘As’ illustrates, ‘wholesome,’ etc. Wholesome is of twenty-one kinds beginning with the sense-sphere; unwholesome is of twelve kinds; and indeterminate is reckoned as resultant and functional. Among these three, the last is the indeterminate. The term 'pākadaṃ' means 'it gives a result (pākaṃ), a fruition (vipākaṃ)'. 'Na' is a particle. The first two, the wholesome and unwholesome, give a result, thus they are result-giving (pākadaṃ). Here, the distinction to be seen is that non-result-giving belongs only to the indeterminate, and result-giving belongs only to those two.

102. “Kusale”ccādi. Kusalaṃ kāmāvacarādiekavīsatikusalañca akusalaṃ dvādasavidhaṃ akusalañca abyākataṃ vipākakriyārūpanibbānavasena catubbidhamabyākatañca iccesu evametesu tīsu pacchimaṃ uddesakkamena pacchimamabyākataṃ pākadaṃ na vipākadāyakaṃ na hoti, paṭhamadvayaṃ kusalākusalaṃ pākadaṃ yathāsakaṃ vipākadāyakaṃ hotīti. “Yathāsaṅkhyamanudeso samāna”nti pāṇini 1.3.10 suttamidaṃ. anudissate iti anudeso, pacchā uccārito iccattho “samānaṃ”iti sambandhechaṭṭhī (katvabodhinī) vuttattā uddiṭṭhehi samānamanuddiṭṭhānameva samasaṅkhyāya labbhamānattā saṅkhyāyānatikkamo hoti. Ettha pana kusalādisabhāvato tividhattepi vipākadānādānavasena duvidhakusalākusalādivisayabhūtavisesassa pavattiyā vatticchāto paṭhamaṃ vattabbataṃ vinā kamena nissayanaṃ nāma natthīti apakkamadoso na hotīti.

102. ‘Wholesome,’ etc. The wholesome consists of twenty-one types beginning with the sense-sphere, the unwholesome consists of twelve types, and the indeterminate is fourfold, as resultant, functional, material, and Nibbāna—among these three, the last, the indeterminate, is not result-giving, it does not produce a fruition; while the first two, the wholesome and unwholesome, are result-giving, they produce a fruition according to their respective nature. Since it is said that ‘the restatement corresponds to the enumeration,’ there is no transgression of the count because an equal number is obtained for what is restated as for what is specified. Here, although there are three categories based on the nature of wholesome and so on, due to the occurrence of a specific distinction—which is the subject of the wholesome, unwholesome, etc., being twofold in terms of giving or not giving results—and due to the desire to speak, there is no reliance on sequence without first stating it; thus there is no fault of digression.

103.

103.

Saguṇānā’vikaraṇe, kāraṇe sati tādise;

Ocityahīnatāpatti, natthi bhūtatthasaṃsino.

In revealing qualities, when there is such a cause, there is no incurring of impropriety for one who speaks according to reality.

103. “Saguṇāna”miccādi. [M 0.0131] Sotūnaṃ attatthanipphādanādike tādise kāraṇe hetumhi sati bhūtaṃ yathāpavattaṃ atthaṃ attano caritalakkhaṇaṃ saṃsino vadantassa sassa attano, sānaṃ vā guṇānaṃ āvikaraṇe adhikāravasena “pūjanīyataro loke”iccādikathane ocikyahīnatāya āpatti pāpuṇanaṃ sambhavo natthi.

103. ‘Of those with qualities,’ etc. When there exists such a cause, such as accomplishing the listeners’ own benefit and so forth, for one who speaks the truth as it has occurred, the meaning which is the characteristic of one's own conduct, in revealing one's own qualities or their own qualities, by way of authority, in speaking such as ‘more worthy of veneration in the world,’ there is no possibility of incurring the fault of impropriety.

103. “Saguṇi”ccādi. Tādise kāraṇe sati sotūnaṃ attatthanipphādanādike tādise hetumhi vijjamāne bhūtatthasaṃsino attani vijjamānakāyādisaṃvaralakkhaṇaguṇasaṅkhātamatthaṃ “pūjanīyataro loke ahameko”iccādinā tādisāvasare vadantassa saguṇānaṃ sassa attano, sānaṃ vā sakānaṃ guṇānaṃ āvikaraṇe pākaṭīkaraṇe ocityahīnatāpatti ocityahīnasaṅkhātadosassāpatti natthīti. Sasaddassa attaattaniyavācakattā sassa attano guṇā se ca te guṇā ceti vā viggaho. Bhūtoyeva attho, taṃ saṃsati vadati sīlenāti viggaho.

103. ‘Endowed with qualities,’ etc. When such a cause exists, such a reason as accomplishing the listeners’ own benefit and so forth, for one who speaks the truth—declaring the meaning reckoned as the quality characterized by restraint of body and so forth, present in oneself, on such an occasion with words like ‘I alone am the most worthy of veneration in the world’—for such a person endowed with qualities, there is no incurring of impropriety, the fault consisting of impropriety, in revealing or making known one's own qualities or their own qualities. Because the word ‘sa’ denotes self and own, the analysis is ‘one’s own qualities’ or ‘those qualities, and those qualities themselves.’ The meaning is simply ‘true,’ and the analysis of 'bhūtatthasaṃsino' is ‘one who speaks that by way of habit.’

104.

104.

Ocityaṃ nāma viññeyyaṃ, loke vikhyātamādarā;

Tattho’padesapabhavā, sujanā kavipuṅgavā.

Propriety, indeed, is to be understood as that which is renowned in the world with respect. Therein, the wise and excellent poets are the source of instruction.

104. “Ocitya”miccādi. Loke sattaloke vikhyātaṃ pasiddhaṃ ābālajanaṃ ābālajanānaṃ (ka.) yathāsakamanurūpaṃ vijānanato ocityaṃ ucitabhāvo nāmeti pasiddhiyaṃ ādarā ādarena ussāhena tato paramādaraṇīyassābhāvato, na hi anucitaṃ kiñci kenāpyādaraṇīyaṃ sabbathā anassādanīyattā, viññeyyaṃ “sotūna”nti seso. Tattha tasmiṃ ocitye upadesassa paṭhamuccāraṇassa uggaṇhāpanavasena pavattassa pabhavā uppattiṭṭhānabhūtā sujanā suṭṭhujanā kavipuṅgavā uttamā, kaviuttamā (?) kaviseṭṭhāti vuttaṃ hoti.

104. ‘Propriety,’ etc. In the world, among beings, what is renowned and established, known by all, from the ignorant upwards, as suitable according to one's own capacity, is called ‘propriety’—the state of being proper—in common usage. With respect, with zeal, because there is nothing more worthy of respect than that, for nothing improper is ever worthy of respect by anyone, being utterly disagreeable in every way. It is to be understood, ‘for the listeners’ is to be supplied. Therein, in that propriety, the source, the place of origin, of instruction—which proceeds by way of causing the first utterance to be grasped—are the wise, the truly wise, the excellent poets, the foremost, that is to say, the best of poets.

104. “Ocitye”ccādi. [M 0.0132] Loke sattaloke vikhyātaṃ ābālapasiddhaṃ ocityaṃ nāma ādarā gāravena viññeyyaṃ viññūhi ñātabbaṃ hoti, tattha ocityavisaye upadesapabhavā paṭhamuccāraṇassa uppattiṭṭhānabhūtā sujanā sādhujanabhūtā kavipuṅgavā uttamakavayo bhavantīti, pasiddhaocityapadena yuttattā ettha nāmasaddo pasiddhiyaṃ. Upadesassa pabhavāti ca, pumāno ca te gāvo ceti ca, kavīnaṃ puṅgavāti ca vākyaṃ.

104. ‘Propriety,’ etc. In the world, in the world of beings, what is renowned and well-known even to the foolish as propriety, indeed, is to be understood by the wise with respect and reverence. Therein, in the sphere of propriety, good people, who are virtuous people, and excellent poets, who are supreme poets, become the source of instruction, the place of origin for the first utterance. Because it is associated with the well-known word ‘propriety,’ the word ‘nāma’ here is in the sense of renown. And ‘the source of instruction’ is the phrase, and ‘men and those cows’ is the phrase, and ‘the best of poets’ is the phrase.

105.

105.

Viññātocityavibhavo-

Cityahīnaṃ parihare;

Tato’cityassa sampose,

Rasaposo siyā kate.

One who has understood the splendor of propriety should avoid what lacks propriety. Then, through the fostering of propriety, the nourishment of aesthetic sentiment may be achieved in the composition.

105. “Viññāta”miccādi. Viññāto avabuddho yathāvuttakavivarapasādā ocityameva vibhavo sampatti yena so ocityahīnaṃ nāma dūsanaṃ parihare parivajjeyya. Tato tasmā parihārato hetuto ocityassa sampose suṭṭhu vaḍḍhibhāve vaḍḍhane kate rasassa assāditabbatāsaṅkhātassa mādhuriyassa samposo siyā bhaveyya.

105. ‘Understood,’ etc. He by whom it is understood and comprehended—through the grace of the aforementioned excellent poets—that propriety itself is splendor and accomplishment, should avoid, should shun, the fault called 'lacking propriety.' Then, from that avoidance, from that cause, when the thorough fostering and growth of propriety is done, there may be nourishment of aesthetic sentiment, which is reckoned as sweetness to be savored.

105. “Viññāte”ccādi. Viññātocityavibhavo tādisakavīnamanuggahena viññātaocityasaṅkhātasampattisamannāgato kavi ocityahīnaṃ nāma dūsanaṃ parihare nirākareyya, tato dosaparihārato ocityassa sampose upabrūhane kate sati rasaposo mādhuriyasaṅkhatassa assādetabbassa pūraṇaṃ siyā bhaveyyāti. Ocityameva vibhavoti ca, viññāto ocityavibhavo yeneti ca, rasassa poso puṭṭhabhāvo vuddhabhāvo (ka.) posetabbabhāvoti ca vākyaṃ.

105. ‘Understood,’ etc. A poet who has understood the splendor of propriety—being endowed, through the favor of such poets, with the accomplishment designated as understood propriety—should avoid and eliminate the fault called 'lacking propriety.' Then, from the avoidance of that fault, when the fostering and strengthening of propriety is done, the nourishment of aesthetic sentiment—the fulfillment of what is to be savored, designated as sweetness—would occur. And ‘propriety itself is splendor’ is the phrase, and ‘he by whom the splendor of propriety is known’ is the phrase, and ‘the nourishment of aesthetic sentiment is its nourished state, the state of being nourished’ is the phrase.

Yathā –

For example:

106.

106.

Yo [M 0.0133] mārasenamāsanna-māsannavijayussavo;

Tiṇāyapi na maññittha, so vo detu jayaṃ jino.

He, whose victory celebration was near, did not consider the nearby army of Māra even as grass; may that Victor grant you victory.

106. “Yathe”tyudāharati “yo”iccādi. Vijayo parābhibhavo āsanno vijayo eva ussavo abbhudayo nippaṭipakkhā pavatti yassa ediso yo āsannaṃ attano samīpamupagataṃ mārasenaṃ tiṇāyapi na maññittha tiṇampi na maññittha, tiṇatopi hīnaṃ maññittha, so jino māraji vo tumhākaṃ jayaṃ detūti vidadhātu. Ettha jayāsīsanā “jino”ti accantamucitaṃ, yo ajini pañcamāreti jino parābhibhavekaraso, tassa paresaṃ vijayappadāne sāmatthiyekayogo siyāti. “Mārasenamāsannaṃ tiṇāyapi na maññitthā”ti idaṃ panettha atisamucitaṃ yato samīpamupagatampi tādisaṃ mārasenaṃ tiṇatopi hīnaṃ maññi, tenassa paresaṃ vijayappadānekarasatā visesato yuttāti.

106. ‘As’ illustrates with ‘who,’ etc. Victory is overcoming. He for whom victory itself is a near celebration, a rise, an unopposed proceeding, is such a one. He who did not consider the army of Māra that had approached, that had come near him, even as grass—did not consider it even as grass, considered it inferior to grass—may that Victor, the conqueror of Māra, grant you victory. Here, for the blessing of victory, the word ‘Victor’ is exceedingly fitting. For he who conquered the five Māras is the Victor, whose sole essence is overcoming; his unique capacity for granting victory to others is fitting. ‘He did not consider the approaching army of Māra even as grass’—this is exceedingly fitting here, because he considered even such an army that had come near him to be inferior to grass. Therefore, his single-mindedness in granting victory to others is especially fitting.

106. Iha satthe sabbattha saṅkhepakkamamicchantopi ācariyo ocityaṃ nāma ādarena saggarūhi uggaṇhitvā payujjitabbamiccevaṃ vitthārena sisse anusāsitvā idāni ocityahīnapariharaṇatthaṃ “yo mārasenamāsanne”ccādinā lakkhiyamudāharati. Āsannavijayussavo adūrasattuvijayasaṅkhātaussavo, atha vā accāsannapaṭipakkhavirahappavattisaṅkhātaabhivuddhiyā samannāgato yo jino āsannaṃ anekappakārabhiṃsanakarūpena attano samīpamāgataṃ mārasenaṃ mārabalaṃ tiṇāyapi tiṇalavaṃ katvāpi na maññittha sallakkhaṇaṃ nākāsi, so jino so jitapañcamāro vo tumhākaṃ jayaṃ detūti. Ettha yo pañcamāre jitattā jino nāma hoti, so parābhibhavane asahāyakiccattā paresaṃ jayadāne sāmatthiyayuttoti “jayaṃ detū”ti kataṃ jayāsīsanamatiucitaṃ [M 0.0134] hoti, jayadāne sāmatthiyasseva posakattā. “Mārasenamāsannaṃ tiṇāyapi na maññitthā”ti idaṃ vattabbameva natthīti. Evaṃ accantaucitapayogena ocityahīnadoso nirākatoti. Vijayo eva ussavo, āsanno vijayussavo yasseti viggaho.

106. Here in this treatise, the teacher, though desiring a concise approach in all matters, having learned with respect from his own teachers what is called propriety and having instructed his disciples in detail that it should be applied, now, in order to avoid what lacks propriety, gives an example of the principle with ‘yo mārasenamāsannaṃ,’ etc. ‘Āsannavijayussavo’ means one whose celebration is the victory over a not-distant enemy; or, one endowed with prosperity characterized by the absence of any close adversary. The Victor who did not consider Māra’s army, the force of Māra, which had approached him in various terrifying forms, even as a blade of grass, and paid it no heed—may that Victor, the conqueror of the five Māras, grant you victory. Here, because he conquered the five Māras, he is called the Victor. Since his deed of overcoming is done without assistance, he is endowed with the capacity to grant victory to others. Thus, the blessing of victory made, ‘may he grant victory,’ is most fitting, as it fosters the very capacity for granting victory. As for ‘He did not consider the approaching army of Māra even as a blade of grass,’ there is nothing more to be said. Thus, by this exceedingly proper usage, the fault of lacking propriety is eliminated. The analysis is: ‘Victory itself is the celebration; he whose victory celebration is near.’

107.

107.

Āraddhakattukammādi-kamātikkamalaṅghane;

Bhaggarītivirodho’yaṃ, gatiṃ na kvāpi vindati.

In the transgression and violation of the sequence of agent, object, and so forth, which have been undertaken, this fault of broken style finds no acceptance anywhere.

107. “Āraddha”iccādi. Kattā ca kammañca tāni ādīni yesaṃ karaṇādīnaṃ āraddhāni vattuṃ paṭṭhapitāni kattukammādīni tesaṃ kamo tassa atikkamo pariccāgo tassa laṅghane sati, vattumāraddhakattukammādikamānatikkameti vuttaṃ hoti. Ayaṃ yathāvutto bhaggarītivirodho kvāpi katthacipi ṭhāne gatiṃ na vindati patiṭṭhaṃ na labhate.

107. ‘Āraddha,’ etc. The agent and the object, and others beginning with them, such as the instrument, are the agent, object, etc., which have been undertaken, established to be spoken of. When there is a violation of the transgression—that is, the abandonment—of their sequence, it is said to be a transgression of the sequence of the agent, object, etc., that were begun to be spoken of. This fault of broken style, as stated, finds no footing, no establishment, in any place whatsoever.

107. “Āraddhi”ccādi. Āraddhakattukammādikamātikkamalaṅghane vattumāraddhakattukammādīnaṃ kamapariccāgassātikkame ayaṃ yathāvuttabhaggarītivirodho kvāpi katthacipi ṭhāne gatiṃ patiṭṭhaṃ na vindati na labhateti. Āraddhāni ca tāni kattukammādīni yesaṃ karaṇādīnaṃ tesaṃ kamassa atikkamo tassa laṅghananti viggaho.

107. ‘Āraddha,’ etc. In the violation of the transgression of the sequence of agent, object, etc., that have been undertaken—that is, in the transgression of the abandonment of the sequence of agent, object, etc., that were begun to be spoken of—this fault of broken style, as stated, finds no footing, no establishment, in any place whatsoever. The analysis is: The violation of the transgression of the sequence of the agent, object, etc., which are undertaken, beginning with the instrument.

Yathā –

For example:

108.

108.

Sujanaññāna’mitthīnaṃ, vissāso no’papajjate;

Visassa siṅgino roga-nadīrājakulassa ca.

Trust is not fitting with good people and others, with women, with poison, a horned creature, disease, rivers, and royal families.

109.

109.

Bhesajje vihite suddha-buddhādiratanattaye;

Pasāda’mācare niccaṃ, sajjane saguṇepi ca.

In prescribed medicine, in the pure Triple Gem beginning with the Buddha, and also in good people and in those possessing virtue, one should always cultivate faith.

108-109. Ettha ca “sujana”miccādike “bhesajje”iccādike ca gāthādvaye chaṭṭhiyā, sattamiyā ca apariccāgena nāttharītiyā bhaṅgo, cakārassekassa katattā na saddarītiyā [M 0.0135] bhaṅgo. Bahūnamatthānañhi samuccayatthaṃ vākye eko vā cakāro kātabbo paṭipadaṃ vā.

108-109. Here, in the two verses beginning with ‘sujana’ and ‘bhesajje,’ there is no breach of semantic style (attharīti) due to the consistent use of the sixth and seventh cases respectively, and there is no breach of verbal style (saddarīti) because only one ‘ca’ particle has been used. For, to connect many meanings in a sentence, either a single ‘ca’ particle should be used, or one for each item.

108. “Sujane”ccādi. Sujanaññānaṃ sajjanehi aññesaṃ dujjanānañca itthīnañca visassa jīvitaharaṇasamatthassa siṅgino visāṇavato ca roganadīrājakulassa ca vissāso saṃsaggo na upapajjate kiñcikāle virujjhanato na yujjateti. Ettha āraddhassa chaṭṭhuntakkamassa sabbattha apariccāgato attharītibhaṅgo ca, yuttaṭṭhāne ekasseva cakārassa yuttattā saddarītibhaṅgo ca natthi. Casaddassa anekatthasamuccayattā “sujanaññānañcā”tiādimhi vā, iha vuttaniyāmena avasāne vā, sabbattha vā yojanamarahati.

108. ‘Sujana,’ etc. ‘Sujanaññānaṃ’ refers to good people and other wicked people. Trust or association with them, and with women, and with poison capable of taking life, and with a horned creature, and with disease, rivers, and royal families, is not fitting, for it is not suitable, as they can become hostile at any time. Here, because the sequence of the sixth case, once begun, is not abandoned anywhere, there is no breach of semantic style; and because only one ‘ca’ particle is used in the appropriate place, there is no breach of verbal style. Because the word ‘ca’ serves to connect multiple meanings, it is appropriate to apply it either at the beginning, as in ‘sujanaññānañcā,’ etc., or at the end according to the rule stated here, or with every item.

109. “Bhesajje”ccādigāthāyampi eseva nayo sattamīmattameva viseso. Vihite pathye bhesajje osadhe ca suddhabuddhādiratanattaye ca sajjane sādhujane ca api punapi saguṇe vijjamānaguṇe ca pasādaṃ attano cittapasādaṃ niccaṃ satataṃ ācare sappuriso kareyya seveyyāti.

109. The same method applies to the verse beginning with ‘Bhesajje,’ the only difference being merely the seventh case. A good person should always, constantly, practice, perform, and cultivate faith—one's own mental serenity—in prescribed and suitable medicine and remedy, in the pure Triple Gem beginning with the Buddha, in good and virtuous people, and also in those possessing virtue, those with existing qualities.

Sasaṃsayassa yathā –

An example of the ambiguous (sasaṃsaya) is as follows:

110.

110.

Munindacandimāloka-

Rasalolavilocano;

Jano’vakkantapantho’va,

Raṃsidassanapīṇito.

A person, whose eyes are eager for the aesthetic sentiment of the light of the moon that is the Lord of Sages, is delighted by the sight of rays, like one who has strayed from the path.

110. “Muninde”ccādi. Ettha raṃsisaddo sasaṃsayaṃ pariharati.

110. ‘Muninda,’ etc. Here, the word ‘raṃsi’ dispels the ambiguity.

110. Sasaṃsayaparihāralakkhiyabhūtā “munindi”ccādigāthā anantaraparicchede vuttatthāva. Raṃsisaddoyeva hi viseso, ettha raṃsisaddena suṇantānaṃ uppajjamānasaṃsayena sasaṃsayabhūtaṃ bandhadosamohatīti.

110. The verse beginning with “munindi,” which is characterized by the dispelling of ambiguity, has the meaning stated in the immediately preceding section. Indeed, the word ‘raṃsi’ is the distinguishing feature here, for by the word ‘raṃsi,’ the fault of composition, which has become ambiguous due to the doubt arising in the hearers, is removed.

111.

111.

Saṃsayāyeva [M 0.0136] yaṃ kiñci, yadi kīḷādihetunā;

Payujjate na doso’va, sasaṃsayasamappito.

If anything is used for the very purpose of ambiguity, for reasons such as play, it is not a fault, though endowed with ambiguity.

111. “Saṃsaye”ccādi. Kīḷādīti ādisaddena ākiṇṇasammantanādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti, kīḷādihetunā yaṃ kiñci saṃsayāyeva yadi payujjateti sambandho.

111. Regarding “Saṃsaye,” etc.: In ‘kīḷādi,’ by the word ‘ādi’ (etc.), it includes crowded discussions and so forth. The connection is: “if anything is used for the very purpose of ambiguity, for the sake of play, etc.”

111. “Saṃsayāyeve”ccādi. Kīḷādihetunā kīḷāsambādhasammantanādikāraṇena yaṃ kiñci saṃsayuppādanasamatthaṃ yaṃ kiñci padaṃ saṃsayāya eva sotūnaṃ uppajjamānasaṃsayatthameva yadi payujjate tasmiṃ bandhane vattārehi payujjate ce, sasaṃsayasamappito sasaṃsayadosasahito bandho na dosova aduṭṭhovāti. Sasaṃsayena samappitoti viggaho.

111. Regarding “Saṃsayāyeve,” etc.: If any word capable of producing ambiguity is used by speakers in that composition for the very purpose of ambiguity—for the ambiguity arising in the hearers—for reasons of play, crowded gatherings, discussions, or other causes, then that composition, though endowed with ambiguity and accompanied by the fault of ambiguity, is not a fault; it is not faulty. The analysis is: “endowed with ambiguity.”

Yathā –

For example:

112.

112.

Yāte dutiyaṃnilayaṃ, gurumhi sakagehato;

Pāpuṇeyyāma niyataṃ, sukha’majjhayanādinā.

When the teacher has gone to a second dwelling from his own home, may we surely attain happiness through study and so forth.

112. “Yāte”ccādi. Gurumhi ajjhāpake sakagehato attano mūlanilayato dutiyaṃ nilayaṃ dutiyaṃ gharaṃ yāte sati niyatamekantamajjhayanādinā sukhaṃ pāpuṇeyyāmāti ayamanicchitattho. Gurumhi surācariye suraccācariye (ka.) sakagehato attano jātarāsito dutiyaṃ nilayaṃ dutiyaṃ rāsiṃ yāte sati niyatamajjhayanādinā sukhaṃ pāpuṇeyyāmāti ayamettha icchitattho.

112. Regarding “Yāte,” etc.: When the teacher, the instructor, has gone to a second dwelling, a second house, from his own home, his original abode, that we may surely attain happiness through study, etc.—this is the unintended meaning. When Guru, the preceptor of the gods, has gone from his own house, his own native sign, to a second house, a second sign, that we may surely attain happiness through study, etc.—this is the intended meaning here.

112. “Yāte”ccādi. Gurumhi ācariye sakagehato attano vāsāgārato dutiyaṃ nilayaṃ dutiyaṃ gharaṃyāte sati, ayamanicchitattho. Gurumhi surācariye sakagehato attano jātarāsito dutiyaṃ nilayaṃ dutiyaṃ [M 0.0137] rāsiṃ yāte gate sati anukūlattā niyatamekantena ajjhayanādinā uggahaṇādinā sukhaṃ mānasikasukhaṃ, no ce sukhakāraṇaṃ ganthaparisamattiṃ pāpuṇeyyāmāti. Ubhayapakkhassāpi aparatthe attho sādhāraṇo hoti. Ettha ajjhayanasaddasannidhānena payuttagurusaddassa ācariyatthavācakattepi icchitatthagopanatthaṃ payuttattā aduṭṭhoti.

112. Regarding “Yāte,” etc.: When the teacher, the instructor, has gone to a second dwelling, a second house, from his own dwelling place, this is the unintended meaning. When Guru, the preceptor of the gods, has gone from his own house, his own native sign, to a second house, a second sign, then due to this favorability, we may surely and exclusively attain happiness—mental happiness—or else the cause of happiness, the completion of the text, through study, grasping, and so forth. The meaning of the other words is common to both interpretations. Here, although the word ‘guru’ is used in proximity to the word ‘study’ and thus denotes the meaning of ‘teacher,’ it is not faulty, since it is employed for the purpose of concealing the intended meaning.

113.

113.

Subhagā bhaginī sā’yaṃ, etassi’ccevamādikaṃ;

Na “gāmma”miti niddiṭṭhaṃ, kavīhi sakalehipi.

‘This sister of his is beautiful,’ and similar expressions, are not designated as ‘vulgar’ by any of the poets.

113. “Subhagā”iccādi. Iccevamādikaṃ bhaginīiccevamādikaṃ.

113. Regarding “Subhagā,” etc.: The phrase ‘and so forth’ refers to expressions such as ‘sister’.

113. “Subhage”ccādi. Etassa purisassa sā ayaṃ bhaginī subhagā sundarāti iccevamādikaṃ sakalehi kavīhi api na gāmmamiti gāmmadosena na duṭṭhamiti niddiṭṭhanti. Subhaṃ sundarabhāvaṃ gatāti “subhagā”ti aggahetvā bahubbīhisamāse kate labbhamānatthassa asabbhabhāvepi kavīnaṃ cittakhedaṃ na janetīti adhippāyo. Iti evaṃ ayaṃ pakāro ādi assa īdisassa vākyassāti vākyaṃ.

113. Regarding ‘Subhagā,’ etc.: ‘This sister of this man is beautiful,’ and so forth—such expressions are designated even by all poets as not vulgar, that is, not corrupted by the fault of vulgarity. The intention is that even if ‘subhagā’ is not taken as ‘one who has gone to beauty,’ but a bahubbīhi compound is formed, and even if the meaning thereby obtained is unrefined, it does not cause mental distress to the poets. Thus, this is a sentence of this kind, having this manner as its beginning.

114.

114.

Duṭṭhālaṅkāravigame, sobhanālaṅkatikkamo;

Alaṅkāraparicchede, āvibhāvaṃ gamissati.

When faulty adornments are removed, the proper application of beautiful adornments will become manifest in the section on adornments.

114. “Duṭṭha”iccādi. Duṭṭhālaṅkārassa dosadūsitassa alaṅkārassa vigame apagame sati.

114. Regarding “Duṭṭha,” etc.: When there is the removal, the disappearance, of a faulty adornment, an adornment tainted by a fault.

114. “Duṭṭhi”ccādi. Duṭṭhālaṅkāravigame dosaduṭṭhassa alaṅkārassa apagame sati sobhanālaṅkatikkamo pasatthānamalaṅkārānaṃ pavattiākāro alaṅkāraparicchede alaṅkārapakāsakattā tannāmake paricchede āvibhāvaṃ pakāsattaṃ gamissati pāpuṇissatīti. Paricchijjatīti paricchedo. Alaṅkārapakāsakattā tadatthena alaṅkāro ca so paricchedo ceti viggaho.

114. Regarding 'Duṭṭha', etc.: When there is the removal of a faulty adornment, that is, with the disappearance of an adornment tainted by fault, the application of beautiful adornments—that is, the manner of occurrence of praised adornments—will become manifest, will attain manifestation, in the section on adornments, that is, in the section so named because it is an expositor of adornments. A 'pariccheda' is that which defines. Because it is an expositor of adornments, the analysis is: it is an adornment and it is a section.

115.

115.

Dose [M 0.0138] parīharitumesa varo’padeso,

Satthantarānusaraṇena kato mayevaṃ;

Viññāyi’maṃ guruvarāna’dhikappasādā,

Dose paraṃ parihareyya yasobhilāsī.

This excellent instruction to avoid faults has been thus composed by me in accordance with other treatises. Having understood this through the abundant grace of excellent teachers, one who desires glory should then thoroughly avoid faults.

Iti saṅgharakkhitamahāsāmipādaviracite

Thus, in the work composed by the venerable Great Elder Saṅgharakkhita,

Subodhālaṅkāre

In the Subodhālaṅkāra,

Dosaparihārāvabodho nāma

Named “The Understanding of the Avoidance of Faults”

Dutiyo paricchedo.

The Second Section.

115. “Dose”iccādi. Dose yathāvutte padadosādike pariharituṃ pariccajituṃ eso varo uttamo upadeso satthantarānaṃ bahūnaṃ anusaraṇena anugamena anupagamena (ka.) mayā evaṃ kato nipphādito, imaṃ upadesaṃ guruvarānaṃ adhikappasādā mahatā pasādena na appakena, tathāvidhena tādisassa mahato atthassa apasijjhanato, viññāya jānitvā ādarato kareyya dose yathāvutte dose yaso parisuddhabandhanaṃ kriyālakkhaṇato ekantena kittihetuttā, taṃsabbhāvā kitti vā, taṃ abhilasati sīleneti yasobhilāsī paraṃ accantameva parihareyya dūrato kareyya.

115. Regarding 'Dose', etc.: To avoid, to abandon the faults as stated, such as faults of words—this is the supreme, excellent instruction, thus made and accomplished by me by following and adhering to many other treatises. Having understood this instruction with the abundant grace of excellent teachers—that is, with great faith, not with little, because with such little faith a great purpose like this would not be accomplished—and having known it, one who desires glory should then utterly avoid the aforementioned faults, keeping them far away. Glory is pure composition, which, from its characteristic of being an action, is entirely a cause of renown, or it is renown itself due to its very existence. One who by nature desires that is a ‘desirer of glory’.

Iti subodhālaṅkāre mahāsāmināmikāyaṃ ṭīkāyaṃ

Thus, in the Mahāsāmināmikā commentary on the Subodhālaṅkāra,

Dosaparihārāvabodhaparicchedo dutiyo.

The Second Section: The Understanding of the Avoidance of Faults.

115. “Dose”ccādi. Dose yathāvuttapadadosādike pariharitumapanetuṃ varo uttamo eso upadeso satthantarānusaraṇena bahūnaṃ bāhirasatthānaṃ anussatiyā mayā evaṃ anantaruddiṭṭhakkamena kato viracito, imaṃ upadesaṃ guruvarānaṃ adhikappasādā adhikappasādena viññāya sabhāvato ñatvā yasobhilāsī yasapaṭilābhakāraṇattā [M 0.0139] kāraṇe kāriyopacārena dosāpagamena parisuddhabandhanaṃ vā tādisabandhanahetu uppajjamānakittiṃ vā icchanto paññavā dose yathāvuttadose paraṃ atisayena parihareyya dūrato kareyyāti. Ettha pubbaddhena dosaparihāraparicchedassa pasatthabhāvo dassito, aparaddhena sissajanānusāsanaṃ dassitaṃ hoti. Tathā pubbaddhena karuṇāpubbaṅgamapaññākiccaṃ dassitaṃ, aparaddhena paññāpubbaṅgamakaruṇākiccaṃ dassitaṃ. Tathā pubbaddhena attahitasampatti, aparaddhena parahitasampatti dassitāti. Evamanekākāradīpikāya imāya gāthāya paricchedaṃ nigameti. Aññe satthā satthantarā, antarasaddo hi aññasaddapariyāyo. Yathā “gāmantaraṃ na gaccheyyā”ti. Yasaṃ abhilasati sīlenāti vākyaṃ.

115. Regarding 'Dose', etc.: To avoid and remove the faults, such as the faults of words mentioned previously—this is the supreme, excellent instruction, thus composed and created by me in the order just stated, by following other teachers, by recalling many external treatises. Having understood this instruction with the abundant grace of the excellent teachers, having known its true nature, a wise person who desires fame—that is, one who desires either pure composition through the removal of faults (which is a cause for gaining fame, a metaphorical use of the cause for the effect) or the renown arising from such composition—should exceedingly avoid the faults as described, keeping them far away. Here, the first half of the verse shows the praiseworthy nature of the chapter on avoiding faults; the latter half shows the instruction for disciples. Similarly, the first half shows the function of wisdom preceded by compassion; the latter half shows the function of compassion preceded by wisdom. Likewise, the first half shows the attainment of one's own welfare; the latter half shows the attainment of the welfare of others. Thus, he concludes the section with this verse, which is a lamp in many ways. ‘Other teachers’ are `satthantarā`; for the word `antara` is a synonym for the word ‘other,’ as in ‘one should not go to another village.’ The analysis is, ‘One desires fame through virtue.’

Iti subodhālaṅkāranissaye

Thus, in the Subodhālaṅkāra-nissaya,

Dutiyo paricchedo.

The Second Section.

3. Guṇāvabodhapariccheda

3. The Section on the Understanding of Qualities

Anusandhivaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Connection

116.

116.

Sambhavanti guṇā yasmā,

Dosāne’va’matikkame;

Dassessaṃ te tato dāni,

Sadde sambhūsayanti ye.

Since qualities arise precisely when faults are overcome, therefore, I shall now point out those which adorn words.

116. Evaṃ dosaparihāropadesaṃ dassetvā idāni dosaparihārā samupagataguṇaṃ upadassitumadhikāraṃ viracayanto āha “sambhavanti”iccādi. Dosānaṃ yathāvuttānaṃ padadosādīnaṃ evaṃ yathāvuttanayena atikkame sati guṇā dhammā [M 0.0140] saddālaṅkārasabhāvā pasādādayo yasmā kāraṇā sambhavanti sijjhanti, tañca “pasādo kiliṭṭhādīnaṃ vajjanā sambhavatī”tyādinā yathāyogaṃ viññeyyaṃ, tato tasmā kāraṇā ye guṇā sadde sambhūsayanti alaṅkaronti, te saddālaṅkārasaṅkhāte guṇe idāni dassessaṃ upadisissāmi.

116. Having thus shown the instruction for abandoning faults, now, composing the section to present the qualities that arise from the abandonment of faults, he says, ‘They arise,’ and so on. Since, when the aforementioned faults, such as faults of word, are overcome in the manner described, qualities—which are principles having the nature of ornaments of sound, such as clarity and so on—arise and are accomplished (and this should be understood appropriately, as in ‘Clarity arises from avoiding what is defiled,’ and so on), therefore, for that reason, I shall now show and instruct on those qualities that adorn sound, which are known as the ornaments of sound.

116. Evaṃ dosaparihārapavesopāyaṃ dassetvā idāni yathāvuttadosānaṃ parihārena “bandhanissitaguṇā ete”ti dassetuṃ pubbāparaparicchedānaṃ sambandhaṃ ghaṭento “sambhavanti”ccādigāthamāha. Dosānaṃ niddiṭṭhapadadosādīnaṃ evaṃ anantaraparicchede niddiṭṭhakkamena atikkame sati guṇā pasādādisaddālaṅkārasaṅkhātā pasādādayo saddadhammā yasmā sambhavanti, tato ye saddadhammā sadde sambhūsayanti sajjanti, te saddadhamme dassessaṃ pakāsissāmīti. Ettha kiliṭṭhadosabyākiṇṇadosaparihārehi pasādālaṅkāro sijjhati, sesāpi yathālābhato ñātabbā.

116. Having thus shown the means of entering upon the abandonment of faults, now, in order to demonstrate that ‘these qualities are dependent on composition’ by means of the abandonment of the aforementioned faults, and connecting the relationship between the preceding and succeeding sections, he speaks the verse beginning with ‘They arise,’ and so on. Since qualities of sound, known as ornaments of sound such as clarity, arise when the specified faults of word, etc., are overcome in the order explained in the immediately preceding section, therefore, I shall show and make known those qualities of sound that adorn sound. Here, the ornament of clarity is achieved by abandoning defiled faults and scattered faults; the remaining ones should also be understood as they are obtained.

Saddālaṅkārauddesavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Enumeration of the Ornaments of Sound

117.

117.

Pasādo’jo madhuratā,

Samatā sukhumālatā;

Sileso’dāratā kanti,

Atthabyattisamādhayo.

Clarity, vigor, sweetness,

Evenness, delicacy,

Cohesion, elevation, charm,

Clarity of meaning, and composure.

117.
