Idāni te vibhajati “pasādo”iccādinā pasatthi pasādo pakāsatthatā, ojo samāsavuttibāhullaṃ atthapāriṇatyañca, madhuratā saddānaṃ rasavantatā, samatā pajjāpekkhāya catunnaṃ pādānamekajātiyasambandhatā, gajjāpekkhāya tu padānaṃ, sukhumālatā apharusakkharabāhullaṃ, silesanaṃ sileso bandhagāravaṃ, udāratā ukkaṃsatā kenaci atthena sanāthatā visiṭṭhavisesanayuttatā ca, kanti sabbalokamanoharatā, atthabyatti siddhena [M 0.0141] ñāyena vā abhidheyyassa gahaṇaṃ, samādhi lokappatītyanusāriamukhyatthatā, tesu ojaudāratā saddatthaguṇā, samādhi atthaguṇo, atthānugāmittā ettha saddānaṃ, aññe tu saddaguṇāva.

117. Now he divides them, beginning with ‘Clarity,’ and so on. Clarity (pasāda) is praiseworthiness and distinctness; vigor (oja) is an abundance of compound expressions and maturity of meaning; sweetness (madhuratā) is the tasteful quality of sounds; evenness (samatā), in respect to verse, is the connection of the four lines to a single class, and in respect to prose, of the words; delicacy (sukhumālatā) is the abundance of non-harsh syllables; cohesion (silesa) is the gravity of composition; elevation (udāratā) is excellence, being endowed with some meaning, and being connected with distinctive special terms; charm (kanti) is delightfulness to all the world; clarity of meaning (atthabyatti) is the grasp of what is to be expressed through what is established or through reasoning; composure (samādhi) is the state of having a non-primary meaning that accords with worldly convention. Among these, vigor and elevation are qualities of sound and meaning; composure is a quality of meaning, the words here being in accordance with the meaning; the others, however, are qualities of sound alone.

117. Idāni “pasādojo”iccādinā te saddālaṅkāre kamena vibhajituṃ uddisati. Pasādo pasannaphaḷikāvali attani āvunitarattakambalasuttamiva saddānaṃ atthassa pasādanasaṅkhāto pasādālaṅkāro ca, ojo samāsavuttibāhulyaatthapāriṇatyasaṅkhato saddatthānaṃ guṇo ca, madhuratā saddānaṃ rasavantabhāvasaṅkhātakaṇṇamadhuratā ca, samatā pajje pādassa sutito sadisatā ca, gajje padānaṃ tatheva sadisatāti evaṃ pādānaṃ padānañca tulyaguṇatā ca, sukhumālatā vaṇṇānaṃ atipharusaatisithilabhāvaṃ vinā samappamāṇamuduguṇo ca, sileso ṭhānakaraṇādisambhūtasabhāgavaṇṇasutīhi acchiddaguruguṇo ca, udāratā ukkaṭṭhena kenaci atthena bandhassa sajjitabhāvo ca, visiṭṭhavisesanapadena yuttatā ca, kanti sabbesaṃ piyaguṇatā ca, atthabyatti icchitatthassa siddhena vā nyāyena vā supākaṭabhāvo ca, samādhayo lokappatītianatikkantaaññadhammāropanena amukhyatthatā cāti ime saddatthaguṇā dasa honti. “Samādhayo”ti tasseva bahuttaṃ dīpeti, imesu dasasu ojodāratāti dve saddatthaguṇā, samādhi atthaguṇo pariyāyena tadatthajotakasaddaguṇopi, sesā satta saddaguṇā eva, ete sabbepi alaṅkaronti bandhamanenāti vākyena alaṅkārā nāma.

117. Now, beginning with ‘Clarity, vigor,’ and so on, he enumerates those ornaments of sound in order to analyze them. Clarity (pasāda) is the ornament of clarity, characterized as the clarification of the meaning of sounds, like a red woolen thread woven through a string of clear crystals. Vigor (oja) is a quality of sound and meaning, characterized by an abundance of compound expressions and maturity of meaning. Sweetness (madhuratā) is pleasantness to the ear, characterized as the tasteful quality of sounds. Evenness (samatā) is the similarity of a verse’s feet in terms of sound, and similarly the similarity of words in prose; thus, it is the equality of qualities of both feet and words. Delicacy (sukumālatā) is the soft quality of syllables, being of proper measure without excessive harshness or looseness. Cohesion (silesa) is the weighty and seamless quality arising from the sound of syllables that share a nature due to their place of articulation, organ of articulation, etc. Elevation (udāratā) is the state of a composition being endowed with some excellent meaning, and being furnished with distinctive qualifying words. Charm (kanti) is the quality of being pleasing to all. Clarity of meaning (atthabyatti) is the very clear manifestation of the desired meaning, either through what is established or through reasoning. Composure (samādhi) is the use of a secondary meaning by imposing the properties of another thing without transgressing worldly convention. These are the ten qualities of sound and meaning. ‘Composure’ (samādhayo) in the plural indicates the multiplicity of that quality. Among these ten, vigor and elevation are two qualities of sound and meaning; composure is a quality of meaning, and by extension, also a quality of the sound that illuminates that meaning; the remaining seven are purely qualities of sound. All these adorn the composition; hence they are called ornaments (alaṅkārā) from the phrase, ‘by this, they adorn the composition.’

Saddālaṅkārapayojanavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Purpose of the Ornaments of Sound

118.

118.

Guṇehe’tehi sampanno, bandho kavimanoharo;

Sampādayati kattūnaṃ, kittimaccantanimmalaṃ.

Endowed with these qualities, a composition delightful to poets brings to its authors utterly pure fame.

118. “Guṇehi”ccādi. [M 0.0142] Etehiyeva vuttehi dasahi guṇehi dhammehi saddālaṅkārasabbhāvehi sampanno yutto samiddho vā kavīnaṃ mano harati savase vattetīti kavimanoharo kavihadayahilādakārī bandho kattūnaṃ bandhantānaṃ kavīnaṃ accantanimmalaṃ atisayaparisuddhaṃ aguṇalesenāpa’nālimpattā kittiṃ guṇaghosaṃ sampādayati nipphādeti.

118. ‘By qualities,’ etc. Endowed, furnished, or flourishing with just these ten stated qualities, these principles which are the very substance of the ornaments of sound, a composition captivates the minds of poets, keeping them under its sway—thus it is ‘delightful to poets,’ gladdening the hearts of poets. This composition brings forth, produces, for its authors—the poets who compose—utterly pure fame, exceedingly purified because it is untainted by even a trace of fault, which is the renown of their qualities.

118. “Guṇe”ccādi. Etehi guṇehi imehi saddālaṅkārasaṅkhātadasavidhasaddadhammehi sampanno samannāgato samiddho vā bandho pajjādibandho kavimanoharo attano niravajjattā kavīnaṃ cittaṃ pīṇento kattūnaṃ racayantānaṃ accantanimmalaṃ appakadosenāpi asammissattā atiparisuddhaṃ kittiṃ bandhanavisayabhūtayasorāsiṃ sampādayati nipphādetīti. Iminā kāraṇena bandhassa yathāvuttadasavidhaguṇapariggaho saussāhaṃ kātabboti adhippāyo. Mano haratīti manoharo, kavīnaṃ manoharo kavimanoharoti viggaho.

118. ‘By qualities,’ etc. Endowed, possessed, or flourishing with these qualities, with these ten kinds of principles of sound known as the ornaments of sound, a composition—a composition of verse, etc.—is ‘delightful to poets,’ gladdening the minds of poets because of its own faultlessness. It produces, brings forth, for its authors—those who compose—an utterly pure mass of fame, exceedingly pure because it is unmixed with even a minor fault, a mass of glory which is the domain of composition. For this reason, the acquisition of the aforementioned ten kinds of qualities for a composition should be undertaken with enthusiasm—this is the intention. ‘It captivates the mind’ (mano harati), hence ‘delightful’ (manoharo); ‘delightful to poets’ (kavīnaṃ manoharo), hence ‘delightful to poets’ (kavimanoharo)—this is the analysis.

Saddālaṅkāraniddesavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Exposition of the Ornaments of Sound

119.

119.

Adūrāhitasambandha-subhagā yā padāvali;

Supasiddhābhidheyyā’yaṃ, pasādaṃ janaye yathā.

That string of words, beautiful with a not-far-placed connection, whose meaning is well-established—may it generate clarity, as follows.

119. Idāni yathoddesānamesaṃ niddesaṃ sodāharaṇaṃ karonto āha “adūra”iccādi. Adūre āsanne adūrena vā adūrāhitakriyākattukammādipadavasena āhito ṭhapito kato sambandho anvayo, tena subhagā manoharā supasiddho suppakāso sugammo abhidheyyo attho yassā sāti tathā, na tu bhāvattho tassa sabhāvagambhīrattā. Vuttañhi –

119. Now, making an exposition of these according to their enumeration, with examples, he says, ‘not far,’ etc. ‘Not far’ (adūre) means ‘near’ (āsanne), or ‘by means of what is not far’ (adūrena). A connection (sambandho), or an arrangement (anvayo), is placed (āhito), established (ṭhapito), or made (kato) by means of words denoting action, agent, object, etc., that are not placed far away. By that, it is ‘beautiful’ (subhagā), ‘charming’ (manoharā). ‘Well-established’ (supasiddho) means ‘very clear’ (suppakāso), ‘easily understood’ (sugammo), whose ‘expressed meaning’ (abhidheyyo attho) is such. But it is not the inner meaning (bhāvattho), because of its naturally profound nature. For it has been said:

“Kavīna’dhippāya’masaddagocaraṃ,

[M 0.0143] Pade phurantaṃ mudukamhi kevalaṃ;

Visanti bhāvāvagamā katassamā,

Pakāsayantyā’katiyo tu tādisā”ti.

“The intention of poets, beyond the range of sound, flashing forth only in a gentle word; those accomplished in understanding the inner meaning enter into it, but such forms merely reveal it.”

Tādisā yā padāvali padapanti ayaṃ pasādaṃ tannāmakaṃ guṇaṃ janaye uppādayati. Yathāti tamudāharati.

Such a string of words, a line of words, generates, produces the quality called ‘clarity’ (pasāda). ‘As follows’ (yathā)—he gives an example of that.

119. Idāni uddesakkamena etesaṃ saddālaṅkārādīnaṃ niddesaṃ sodāharaṇaṃ dassento āha “adūrāhite”ccādi. Adūre āsannapadese tadupacārena āsanne vā āhito kriyāya, laddhakriyāyogakattukammādipadānaṃ vasena ca kato, no ce vinyāsavasena ṭhapito vā sambandho icchitatthapatītikkamena aññamaññāpekkhalakkhaṇakriyākārakayogo tena subhagā manoharā, supasiddho pasiddhatthavisaye saddapayogato atipākaṭo abhidheyyo saddattho yassā sā ayaṃ padāvali padapanti pasādaṃ pasādanāmakaṃ guṇaṃ janaye uppādayati. Yathāti lakkhiyaṃ dasseti. Adūre āhitoti vā, upacaritattā adūro ca so āhito cāti vā, so ca so sambandho ceti ca, tena subhagāti ca, su atisayena pasiddhoti ca, so abhidheyyo asseti ca vākyaṃ. Ettha supasiddho nāma saddattho, adhippāyattho pana pakatigambhīro. Vuttañhi –

119. Now, showing the exposition of these sound embellishments and so forth in the order of their enumeration, with examples, he says: “adūrāhite,” etc. Placed near (adūre) in a proximate place, or by extension close (āsanne), placed (āhito) by action, and made (kato) by means of words such as agent, object, etc., that have acquired a connection to the action, and not established (ṭhapito) by way of transposition—this connection (sambandho), which is the conjunction of action and agent characterized by mutual dependence, without transgressing the understanding of the desired meaning. By that, it is beautiful (subhagā), charming (manoharā). Well-known (supasiddho) means very clear (atipākaṭo) in the sphere of established meaning through the use of words. This string of words (padāvali), this line of words (padapanti), whose expressed meaning (abhidheyyo saddattho) it is, generates, produces, the quality called clarity (pasāda). “As” (yathā) indicates the example. Alternatively, the phrases are: “placed near” (adūre āhito); or “because of being used metaphorically, it is near and placed” (upacaritattā adūro ca so āhito cāti vā); and “that is the connection” (so ca so sambandho ceti ca); and “thereby beautiful” (tena subhagāti ca); and “very well-known” (su atisayena pasiddhoti ca); and “that is its expressed meaning” (so abhidheyyo asseti ca). Here, “well-known” refers to the meaning of the word, but the intended meaning is naturally profound. For it has been said:

“Kavīna’dhippāya’masaddagocaraṃ,

Pade phurantaṃ mudukamhi kevalaṃ;

Visanti bhāvāvagamā katassamā,

Pakāsayantyā’katiyo tu tādisā”ti.

The intention of poets, beyond the range of words, flashing forth only in a gentle word; the accomplished, by understanding its nature, enter it. But such forms reveal it.

Tassattho – asaddagocaraṃ saddassa avisayaṃ hutvā mudukamhi pade kevalaṃ visuṃ phurantaṃ cāpentaṃ kavīnadhippāyaṃ kavīnamajjhāsayaṃ [M 0.0144] katassamā saddatthavisaye kataparicayā paṇḍitā bhāvāvagamā padatthāvabodhena visanti pavisanti, tādisā ākatiyo tu saddasaddatthānaṃ ākārā pakāsayanti adhippāyatthaṃ jotentīti.

Its meaning is: “Beyond the range of words” (asaddagocaraṃ) means being not an object of words (saddassa avisayaṃ hutvā). “Flashing forth” (phurantaṃ) means moving (cāpentaṃ), distinctly (visuṃ), “only in a gentle word” (mudukamhi pade kevalaṃ). The “intention of poets” (kavīnadhippāyaṃ), the inner thought of poets (kavīnamajjhāsayaṃ)—the “accomplished” (katassamā), that is, the learned (paṇḍitā) who are familiar with the domain of words and meaning, “enter” (visanti), penetrate (pavisanti), into it “by understanding its nature” (bhāvāvagamā), that is, through the comprehension of the meaning of the words. “But such forms” (tādisā ākatiyo tu), that is, the aspects of the words and their meanings (saddā-saddatthānaṃ ākārā), “reveal” (pakāsayanti), illuminate (jotenti), the intended meaning.

120.

120.

Alaṅkarontā vadanaṃ, munino’dhararaṃsiyo;

Sobhante’ruṇaraṃsī’va, sampatantā’mbujodare.

Adorning the Sage's face, the rays from his lower lip shine like the rays of dawn falling into the heart of a lotus.

120. “Alaṅkarontā”iccādi. Munino sammāsambuddhassa vadanaṃ sabhāvamadhurapakatimukhaṃ alaṅkarontā sajjantā sobhayamānā adharānaṃ raṃsiyo supakkabimbaphalopamaoṭṭhayugaḷavinissaṭabahutarakanticchitābhā muninoti viññāyati sutattā. Ambujodare tā kālopanatapupphakāsaramaṇīye padumabbhantare sampatantā pavattamānā aruṇaraṃsīva bālasūriyaraṃsiyo viya sobhante virājanti.

120. “Adorning,” etc. The rays of the lower lips (adharānaṃ raṃsiyo), adorning, embellishing, beautifying the face (vadanaṃ) of the Sage (Munino), the Perfectly Enlightened One, whose face is naturally sweet—these rays are the splendor of the abundant radiance emanating from his pair of lips, which resemble ripe bimba fruits. It is understood that “of the Sage” (munino) is meant, because it is stated. Within the heart of the lotus (ambujodare), which is charming with its flowers blooming at the appropriate time, within the lotus (padumabbhantare), falling upon (sampatantā), occurring (pavattimānā), they shine (sobhante), they gleam (virājanti), like the rays of dawn (aruṇaraṃsīva), like the rays of the young sun (bālasūriyaraṃsiyo viya).

120. “Alaṅkaronte”ccādi. Munino vadanaṃ pakatisundaramukhaṃ alaṅkarontā sajjantā adhararaṃsiyo tasseva munino oṭṭhadvayato nikkhantakantisamūhā ambujodare vikasanānurūpakālābhimukhe padumagabbhe upaḍḍhavikasiteti vuttaṃ hoti. Sampatantā pavattamānā aruṇaraṃsī iva bālasūriyaraṃsīva sobhante dibbantīti. Ettha adūrasambandhaṃ pasiddhatthañca nissāya pasādaguṇo pākaṭo. Adhararaṃsīnaṃ munisambandho sutānumitasambandhesu sutasambandhassa balavattā sutānumitesu sutasambandho balavā (paribhāsendusere 112), kākakkhigoḷakanayena vā labbhatīti. Adhare raṃsīti ca, ambujassa udaranti ca vākyaṃ.

120. “Adorning,” etc. The rays of the lower lip (adhararaṃsiyo), which are the masses of radiance emanating from the Sage's (munino) pair of lips, adorning, embellishing his naturally beautiful face (pakatisundaramukhaṃ), fall upon (sampatantā), occur (pavattimānā), in the heart of the lotus (ambujodare), in the lotus core (padumagabbhe) which is facing the time suitable for blooming, meaning it is half-bloomed. They shine (sobhante), they gleam (dibbantīti), like the rays of dawn (aruṇaraṃsī iva), like the rays of the young sun (bālasūriyaraṃsīva). Here, relying on a not-distant connection and a well-known meaning, the quality of clarity (pasādaguṇo) is evident. The connection of the lower lip's rays to the Sage is obtained by the strength of the stated connection among stated and inferred connections, or by the maxim of the crow's eye. The phrases are: “rays on the lower lip” (adhare raṃsī) and “heart of the lotus” (ambujassa udaraṃ).

121.

121.

Ojo samāsabāhulya-

Meso gajjassa jīvitaṃ;

Pajjepya’nākulo so’yaṃ,

Kanto kāmīyate yathā.

Vigor is the abundance of compounds; this is the life of prose. Even in verse, this, being unconfused and pleasing, is desired, as for example:

121. “Ojo”iccādi. [M 0.0145] Samāsassa ekatthavuttiyā bāhulyaṃ bhiyyobhāvo ityanuvaditvā puna ojo vidhīyate, eso ojo samāsabāhullalakkhaṇo gajjassa vuttirūpassa jīvitaṃ hadayaṃ sāraṃ tappadhānattā gajjassa, na pajjassa, soyaṃ ojo anākulo agahano atoyeva kanto hadayaṅgamo, pajjepi na kevalaṃ gajje kāmīyate payujjate. Yathetyudāharati.

121. “Vigor” (ojo), etc. Having restated “abundance of compounds” (samāsabāhulyaṃ) as “the prevalence, the greater occurrence (bhiyyobhāvo), of compounds whose function is to express a single meaning (ekatthavuttiyā),” vigor is again defined. This vigor, characterized by the abundance of compounds, is the life, the heart, the essence of prose (gajja), which is in the form of prose (vuttirūpassa), because of its predominance in prose, not in verse. This vigor is “unconfused” (anākulo), not dense (agahano), and for that very reason “pleasing” (kanto), heart-winning (hadayaṅgamo); it is desired (kāmīyate), employed (payujjate), even in verse (pajje), not only in prose. He gives an example, saying “As” (yathā).

121. Idāni ojaguṇaṃ dasseti “ojo”ccādinā. Ojo nāma samāsabāhulyaṃ bhinnatthesu pavattasaddānaṃ ekatthapavattilakkhaṇassa samāsassa bahulatā, eso ojo gajjassa gajjabandhassa jīvitaṃ hadayaṃ, jīvitasīsena hadayasaṅkhataṃ cittaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. So ayaṃ ojo anākulo nibyākulo kanto tatoyeva viññūnaṃ piyabhūto pajjepi pajjabandhepi kāmīyate kavīhi payujjateti. Bahulassa bhāvo bāhulyaṃ, samāsassa bāhulyanti viggaho. Gajjabandhādhikārassābhāvā pajjavisayassa ojaguṇassa lakkhiyaṃ dasseti “yathe”ccādinā.

121. Now, he shows the quality of vigor (ojaguṇaṃ) with “vigor” (ojo), etc. Vigor (ojo) means the abundance of compounds (samāsabāhulyaṃ)—the prevalence of compounds characterized by the occurrence of a single meaning among words that express diverse meanings. This vigor is the life, the heart, of prose (gajja), of prose composition (gajjabandha); it should be understood that by “the head of life,” the mind, designated as the heart, is meant. This vigor, being unconfused (anākulo), unagitated (nibbākulo), is pleasing (kanto) and thus beloved by the wise; it is desired, employed by poets even in verse (pajje) and verse composition (pajjabandhe). The analysis is: the state of being abundant (bahulassa bhāvo) is abundance (bāhulyaṃ); the abundance of compounds (samāsassa bāhulyaṃ). Since there is no section on prose composition, he shows an example (lakkhiyaṃ) of the quality of vigor pertaining to verse with “as” (yathā), etc.

122.

122.

Munindamandasañjāta-hāsacandanalimpitā;

Pallavā dhavalā tasse-vekonā’dharapallavo.

Anointed with the sandalwood of the Sage-lord's gently arisen laughter, the shoots became white; yet his unique lower-lip-shoot was not white.

122. “Muninda”iccādi. Munindassa mandaṃ īsakaṃ sañjāto pavatto taṃsabhāvattā bhagavato hāsassa yasassa (ka.) hāso hasitaṃ sova candanamiva candanaṃ dhavalattarūpattā, tena limpitā upadehitā pallavā sabbāni kilasayāni “idameve”ti niyamābhāvato, dhavalā pakativaṇṇapariccāgena sukkā ahesuṃ gāhāpitattā saguṇassa tādisavisiṭṭhassa paṭilābhato, evaṃ santepi tassa munindasseva eko aññassa tādisassābhāvā adharapallavo na dhavalo [M 0.0146] dhavalo nāhosi. Accāsannadesiyopi bahumantabbo’ya’massānubhāvoti.

122. “Of the Sage-lord,” etc. The laughter (hāso), the smile (hasitaṃ), which arose (sañjāto), occurred (pavatto), gently (mandaṃ), slightly (īsakaṃ), from the Sage-lord (Munindassa), the Blessed One, due to the nature of his laughter—that laughter, like sandalwood (candanamiva), was sandalwood (candanaṃ) due to its nature of whiteness. By that, the “shoots” (pallavā)—that is, all defilements (sabbāni kilesayāni), because there was no restriction of “this alone”—were anointed (limpitā), smeared (upadehitā), and became white (dhavalā), pure (sukkā), by relinquishing their natural color, because they were made to grasp and attain such a distinguished quality. Even so, that Sage-lord’s “unique” (eko)—because there was no other like him—lower-lip-shoot (adharapallavo) was “not white” (na dhavalo), it did not become white (dhavalo nāhosi). The intention is: even though it was very close to the source, this power of his should be greatly honored.

“Pemāvabandhahadaye sadaye jinasmiṃ,

Tasmiṃ nu kiṃ kumatayo bhavatha’ppasannā;

Kiṃ tena vo na vihitaṃ hita’muggadugga-

Saṃsārasāgarasamuttaraṇāvasānaṃ”.

Since the Conqueror is compassionate, his heart bound by love, why then, O you of wrong view, are you displeased with him? What welfare has not been provided for you by him, culminating in the crossing over the terrible and perilous ocean of saṃsāra?

Iccaparamudāharaṇaṃ. Evametādiso anākulo kanto ojo jānitabboti. Nanu ca ya-tasaddānaṃ nicco sambandho, tasmā kathaṃ “tasseveko nādharapallavo”ti ettha yasaddābhāvoti? Saccaṃ, kintu pakkantavisayo, tathā pasiddhavisayo, anubhūtavisayo ca tasaddo yasaddaṃ nāpekkhate. Yathā –

This is another example. Thus, such an unconfused (anākulo) and pleasing (kanto) vigor (ojo) should be known. But is there not a constant connection between the ‘ya’ and ‘ta’ words? Therefore, how is it that in “yet his unique lower-lip-shoot was not white” (tasseveko nādharapallavo), the ‘ya’ word is absent? True, but when the topic has been previously mentioned (pakkantavisayo), and likewise when the topic is well-known (pasiddhavisayo), and when the topic is experienced (anubhūtavisayo), the ‘ta’ word does not depend on the ‘ya’ word. For example:

“Savāsane kilese so, eko sabbe nighātiya;

Ahu susuddhasantāno, pūjānañca sadāraho”.

He, alone, having destroyed all defilements together with their latent tendencies, became one of an utterly pure continuum, and was always worthy of veneration.

Iccādi. Ettha buddho “buddhānussatimādito”ti pakkanto.

And so forth. Here, the Buddha is the previously mentioned topic, as in “beginning with the recollection of the Buddha.”

Pasiddhavisayo yathā –

A well-known topic, for example:

“Aggiṃ pakkhanda’ atha vā, ‘pabbataggā pate’ti vā;

Yadi vakkhati kattabbaṃ, ñātakārīhi so jino”.

“Leap into the fire,” or “fall from a mountain peak”—if that Conqueror says it is to be done, it should be done by his dutiful kinsmen.

Iccādi.

And so forth.

Anubhūtavisayo yathā –

An experienced topic, for example:

“Atītaṃ nānusocāmi, nappajappāma’nāgataṃ;

Paccuppannena yāpemi, tena vaṇṇo pasīdati”.

I do not grieve for the past, nor do I long for the future; I maintain myself with the present, therefore my complexion is serene.

Iccādi.

And so forth.

Yasaddo tuttaravākyaṭṭho pubbavākye tasaddameva gamayati. Yathā –

The word ‘ya,’ however, when standing in the subsequent clause, refers to the word ‘ta’ in the preceding clause. For example:

“Bodhiṃ [M 0.0147] namāmi natibhājanamaccuḷāraṃ,

Puññākaraṃ bhuvanamaṇḍalasotthibhūtaṃ;

Yo cakkhusotasatigocarataṃ sameto,

Dosāridappamathane’karaso budhānaṃ”.

I bow to the Bodhi, the unsurpassed object of veneration, the source of merit, that which has become the welfare of the world-sphere; which, for the wise, is endowed with the range of eye, ear, and mindfulness, and is of a single essence in crushing the arrogance of the enemy, defilement.

Iccādi.

And so forth.

Pubbavākyopātto tu yasaddo uttaravākyetasaddopādānaṃ vinā sākaṅkhe vākyassa ūnattaṃ janeti. Ettha pakkantavisayo tasaddo.

But the word ‘ya’ occurring in the preceding clause, without the word ‘ta’ being taken up in the subsequent clause, creates incompleteness in the sentence, due to its being expectant. Here, the word ‘ta’ refers to a previously mentioned topic.

122. Munindassa mandaṃ īsakaṃ sañjāto pavatto hāsoyeva sitaṃ candanacuṇṇamiva tena limpitā ālepitā pallavā rukkhalatādīnaṃ pakatirattāni kisalayāni dhavalā saguṇapariccāgena setā ahesuṃ, tathāpi tasseva tathāgatassa eko atulo asahāyo vā adharapallavo dantāvaraṇasaṅkhātapallavo na raṃsisaṃsaṭṭhopi samīpaṭṭhopi dhavalo seto nāhosi. Evamettha agahanasamāsabāhulyaṃ dīpitaṃ hoti.

122. A faint, slight smile arose from the Lord of Sages. By this smile, as if by sandalwood powder, the naturally red tender leaves of trees and creepers, being smeared and anointed, became white, having abandoned their own quality. Yet even so, that very Tathāgata's single, incomparable lower lip—the lip known as the tooth-covering—was not whitened, not even when touched by the rays or when nearby. Thus, here, the abundance of non-difficult compounds is illustrated.

“Pemāvabandhahadaye sadaye jinasmiṃ,

Tasmiṃ nu kiṃ kumatayo bhavatha’ppasannā;

Kiṃ tena vo na vihitaṃ hita’muggadugga-

Saṃsārasāgarasamuttaraṇāvasāna”nti.

To the Conqueror, whose heart is bound by love, who is compassionate, why, O misguided ones, are you not devoted to Him? What good has He not done for you, which culminates in the crossing over of the vast and difficult-to-cross ocean of saṃsāra?

Aparamudāharaṇaṃ. Tassattho – kumatayo he aññāṇā! Pemāvabandhahadaye sabbesu tumhesu niccaṃ pavattitadaḷhapemānubandhacitte sadaye tatoyeva dayāsahite tasmiṃ jinasmiṃ visayabhūte kiṃ nu kasmā appasannā bhavatha, tathā hi vo tumhākaṃ tena jinena uggo dāruṇo ca, duggo gantumasakkuṇeyyo ca, soyeva saṃsārasāgaro tassa samuttaraṇaṃ pariyantappattiyeva avasānaṃ yassa taṃ na vihitaṃ akataṃ hitaṃ vuddhi nāma kiṃ hoti, na [M 0.0148] hoteva. Etthāpi samāsassa pākaṭattā ojo guṇo kanto hotīti.

Another example. Its meaning is: O misguided ones, O ignorant ones! Why, indeed, are you not devoted to that Conqueror, who is the object of devotion, whose heart is bound by love, whose mind is ever filled with strong bonds of affection towards all of you, and who is compassionate on that very account? For what good, what increase, has not been done by that Conqueror for you, which has as its culmination the attainment of the end, the crossing over of that very ocean of saṃsāra, which is dreadful and difficult to cross? Here too, because the compound is obvious, the quality of vigor is pleasing.

Nanu ya-tasaddānaṃ niccasambandhoti kathaṃ “tasseveko”ti ca “tasmiṃ nu kiṃ kumatayo”ti ca iccādīsu heṭṭhā vuttayasaddo natthīti? Saccaṃ, tathāpi pakkantatthavisayo, pasiddhatthavisayo, anubhūtatthavisayo vā tasaddo yasaddaṃ nāpekkhati. Tathā hi –

Is it not so that the words 'ya' and 'ta' are always connected? How is it then that in phrases like 'that very one' and 'to Him, why, O misguided ones?' and so forth, the previously mentioned word 'ya' is absent? True, nevertheless, the word 'ta' does not depend on the word 'ya' when it refers to a departed object, a well-known object, or an experienced object. For example:

“Savāsane kilese so, eko sabbe nighātiya;

Ahu susuddhasantāno, pūjānañca sadāraho”ti.

He alone, having struck down all defilements together with their latent tendencies, became one of perfectly pure continuum, and ever worthy of veneration.

Evamādīsu “so”ti niddiṭṭhatasaddo “buddhānussatimādito”ti ettha atītena buddhasaddena vacanīyavisayo hoti.

In such instances, the specified word 'so' refers to the object that is to be expressed by the word 'Buddha' which has passed, as in 'from the recollection of the Buddha, etc.'

“Aggiṃ pakkhanda’ athavā, ‘pabbataggā pate’ti vā;

Yadi vakkhati kattabbaṃ, ñātakārīhi so jino”ti.

If that Victor says, 'Plunge into fire!' or, 'Fall from a mountain peak!', that is what should be done by dutiful kinsmen.

Evamādīsu tasaddo ñātakārīhi kattabbattā pasiddhabuddhapadatthavisayo.

In such instances, the word 'ta' refers to the well-known meaning of the word 'Buddha', because it is what should be done by dutiful kinsmen.

“Atītaṃ nānusocāmi, nappajappāma’nāgataṃ;

Paccuppannena yāpemi, tena vaṇṇo pasīdatī”ti.

I do not grieve for the past, nor do I long for the future; I maintain myself with the present, therefore my complexion is serene.

Evamādīsu tasaddo ananusocananappajappanayāpanasaṅkhātavijānanavasena anubhūtatthavisayo, tasmā tīsupi ṭhānesu tasaddo yasaddaṃ nāpekkhate. Ettha pana pakkantavisayo tasaddo adhippeto. Apica uttaravākye ṭhito yasaddo pubbavākye tasadde asatipi tameva dīpeti. Tathā hi –

In such instances, the word 'ta' refers to an experienced object, by way of the understanding characterized by not grieving, not longing, and maintaining oneself. Therefore, in all three instances, the word 'ta' does not require the word 'ya'. Here, however, the word 'ta' referring to a departed object is intended. Moreover, the word 'ya' standing in a subsequent clause can indicate that very thing, even if the word 'ta' is not present in the preceding clause. For example:

Bodhiṃ namāmi natibhājanamaccuḷāraṃ,

Puññākaraṃ bhuvanamaṇḍalasotthibhūtaṃ;

Yo cakkhusotasatigocarataṃ sameto,

Dosāridappamathane’karaso budhānanti.

I bow to the Bodhi, the unsurpassed object of veneration, the source of merit, the good fortune of the world sphere. He who attained the state of being an object for the eye, ear, and mindfulness of the wise, is of a single essence in crushing the pride of the enemy defilements.

Yo [M 0.0149] budhānaṃ cakkhusotasatīnaṃ gocarataṃ visayabhāvaṃ sameto patto, tesaṃyeva dosārīnaṃ kilesapaccatthikānaṃ dappamathane dappamaddane ekaraso padhānakicco samiddhivanto vā hoti, taṃ bodhiṃ namāmīti sambandho. Pubbavākye payojito yasaddo uttaravākye tasaddopādāne asati saṃsayamuppādayamāno vākyassa ūnattaṃ karoti. Udāharaṇaṃ pana pākaṭaṃ.

He who has attained, has reached, the state of being an object, a sphere, for the eye, ear, and mindfulness of the wise, and who is of a single essence—having a principal function, or being successful—in crushing the pride, in subduing the arrogance, of those very enemies that are the defilements—to that Bodhi I bow: this is the connection. The word 'ya' employed in the preceding clause, if the word 'ta' is not used in the subsequent clause, creates doubt and renders the sentence incomplete. The example, however, is clear.

123.

123.

Padābhidheyyavisayaṃ,

Samāsabyāsasambhavaṃ;

Yaṃ pāriṇatyaṃ hoti’ha,

Sopi ojova taṃ yathā.

Whatever maturity is here, which has as its sphere the meaning denoted by words and arises from compounding and expansion, that too is vigor itself. For example:

123. “Padi”ccādi. Padassa abhidheyyo attho so visayo yassa. Yattha pacurasaddābhidheyyo attho saṃkhittapadehi vuccate, so samāso. Yatthappakehi padehi abhidheyyattho pacurapadehi vuccate, so byāso. Tato samāsabyāsato sambhavo yassa. Taṃ tathāvidhaṃ yaṃ pāriṇatyaṃ pariṇatabhāvo hotīti anuvaditvā sopi iha sasatthe ojovāti vidhīyate. Taṃ yathetyubhayampi udāharati.

123. 'Word,' etc. That which has as its sphere the meaning denoted by a word. Where a meaning denoted by many words is expressed by concise words, that is a compound (samāsa). Where a meaning denoted by few words is expressed by many words, that is expansion (byāsa). That which has its origin from compounding and expansion. Having explained that such a maturity (pāriṇatya) is the state of being ripened, that too is here declared in this treatise to be vigor. He illustrates both with 'as for example that'.

123. “Pade”ccādi. Padānaṃ bahūnaṃ appakānaṃ vā padānaṃ abhidheyyavisayaṃ vitthārasaṃkhittatthavisayavantaṃ samāsabyāsasambhavaṃ yathākkamaṃ saṅkhepavitthāradvayena nipphannaṃ nipphattivantaṃ vā yaṃ pāriṇatyaṃ kattūnaṃ ganthavisaye pariṇatippakāsako yo saddadhammo atthadhammo hoti, saddaguṇo atthaguṇoti vuttaṃ hoti, sopi iha subodhālaṅkāre ojo nāma saddaguṇo atthaguṇo. Taṃ yathāti dvīsu lakkhiyaṃ dasseti, padānaṃ abhidheyyo visayo yassa pāriṇatyasseti ca, samāso ca byāso cāti ca, tato sambhavanti ca, tato sambhavo assāti ca, pariṇatassa [M 0.0150] kattuno ganthassa eva vā bhāvoti ca viggaho. Kattu pāriṇatyapakkhe tappakāsakaganthassa tadatthena pāriṇatyaṃ siddhaṃ.

123. 'Words,' etc. That maturity (pāriṇatya)—which has as its sphere the meaning of many or few words, possessing the sphere of extensive or concise meaning, arising from compounding and analysis, produced or possessing completion respectively by means of conciseness and extensiveness; which is the revealer of maturity in the subject of an author's composition; which is the nature of the word and the nature of the meaning, said to be the excellence of the word and the excellence of the meaning—that too, here in the Subodhālaṅkāra, is called vigor (ojo), an excellence of the word and an excellence of the meaning. 'As for example that' shows the object of the definition in two ways: 'that maturity, the sphere of which is the meaning denoted by words'; and 'compounding and analysis'; and 'they arise from that'; and 'it has its arising from that'; and 'the state of the very text of a matured author'—this is the analysis. In the view that it is the author's maturity, the maturity of the text that reveals it is established by its meaning.

124.

124.

Jotayitvāna saddhammaṃ,

Santāretvā sadevake;

Jalitvā aggikhandho’va,

Nibbuto so sasāvako.

Having illuminated the true Dhamma, having ferried across beings together with the devas, having blazed like a mass of fire, He was extinguished along with His disciples.

124. “Jotayitvāne”ccādi. Iminā heṭṭhā pacurapadābhihito buddhavaṃso saṅkheparūpena vutto.

124. 'Having illuminated,' etc. By this, the Buddhavaṃsa, previously described with many words, is stated in brief.

124. “Jotayi”ccādi. So tathāgato saddhammaṃ sapariyattikaṃ navalokuttarasaddhammaṃ jotayitvāna ñāṇālokena obhāsetvā sadevake satte santāretvā saṃsārasāgarapariyantamupanetvā aggikhandhova mahātejena aggikkhandho viya jalitvā anaññasādhāraṇarūpakāyasampattiyā pajjalitvā ante sasāvako sāvakehi saha nibbuto khandhaparinibbānena parinibbutoti. Iminā sakalabuddhavaṃse bahūhi padehi vuttattho saṅkhepakkamena vutto. Sataṃ dhammo, santo saṃvijjamāno vā dhammoti ca, saha devehi vattamānāti ca, saha sāvakehi vattamānoti ca viggaho.

124. 'Having illuminated,' etc. That Tathāgata, having illuminated the true Dhamma—the Dhamma with its scriptures and the ninefold supramundane true Dhamma—by making it shine with the light of wisdom; having ferried beings together with the devas across and brought them to the end of the ocean of saṃsāra; like a mass of fire, having blazed with great power, having blazed forth with unsurpassed bodily perfection; and in the end, along with his disciples, he was extinguished, fully extinguished by the parinibbāna of the aggregates. By this, the meaning conveyed with many words throughout the entire Buddhavaṃsa is stated in a summary manner. The analyses are: 'the Dhamma of the good,' or 'the Dhamma that is real or existing'; 'existing together with the devas'; and 'existing together with the disciples.'

125.

125.

Matthakaṭṭhī matassāpi, rajobhāvaṃ vajantu me;

Yato puññena te senti sentu (ka.), jenapādambujadvaye.

May the bones of my head, even when I am dead, turn to dust; for by that merit, may they settle on the pair of lotus feet of the Conqueror.

125. “Matthakaṭṭhī”iccādi. Matassāpi maraṇamāpannassāpi me matthake muddhani aṭṭhī rajobhāvaṃ dhūlittaṃ vajantu pāpuṇantu. Kasmāti ce? Yato yasmā kāraṇā puññena kusalena kammena hetunā te rajā jinassa ime jenā, pādā, teyeva ambujāniva ambujāni, tesaṃ dvaye [M 0.0151] senti pavattanti, tathā hotu vā mā vā, paṇatigedheneva vadati. Ettha “kathamahaṃ bhagavato pāde niccaṃ sirasā paṇamāmī”tyadhippāyo vitthārena vutto.

125. 'The bones of my head,' etc. Even when I am dead, even having met death, may the bones in my head, on my skull, turn into the state of dust, attain dustiness. If you ask why? Because, for that reason, by merit, by the cause of wholesome action, those dust particles settle, they are present, on the pair of His feet, which are like lotuses—the Conqueror's (jinassa, jenā), His feet (pādā), they are like lotuses (ambujāni). Whether it happens so or not, he speaks out of sheer desire for prostration. Here, the intention, 'How may I always bow with my head to the Blessed One’s feet?' is expressed at length.

125. “Matthaki”ccādi, matassāpi me mayhaṃ matthakaṭṭhī muddhani aṭṭhīni rajobhāvaṃ atisukhumarajattaṃ vajantu pāpuṇantu. Kasmā āsīsanaṃ karotīti ce? Yato yasmā kāraṇā puññena mayhaṃ tathāvidhena kusalakammena hetunā te rajā jenapādambujadvaye jinapaṭibaddhacaraṇapadumayugaḷe senti pavattanti, buddhassa siripāde kiñcipi rajojallaṃ na upalimpateva, tathāpi vandanābhilāsena evaṃ vuttaṃ. Ettha “kathamahaṃ bhagavato siripāde muddhanā niccaṃ paṇamāmī”tyabhilāso vitthārena vutto. Matthake aṭṭhīti ca, rajaso bhāvoti ca, jinassa imeti ca, jenā ca te pādā ceti ca, teyeva ambujānīti ca, tesaṃ dvayanti ca viggaho.

125. 'Matthaka,' etc. Even when I am dead, may the bones of my skull, the bones on my head, become the state of dust, the state of extremely fine dust. If it is asked why he makes this aspiration, it is because by my merit, by such a wholesome action of mine as the cause, those dust particles settle and proceed on the pair of lotus feet of the Jina, on the twin lotus feet connected with the Jina. Not even a speck of dust or dirt clings to the Buddha’s glorious feet, yet this is said out of a longing for veneration. Here, the desire, 'How may I always bow with my head to the Blessed One's glorious feet?' is expressed in detail. The grammatical analysis is as follows: 'bones on the head,' 'the state of dust,' 'of the Jina,' 'those feet are of the Jina,' 'they themselves are lotuses,' and 'a pair of them.'

126.

126.

Iccatra niccaṃpaṇati-gedho sādhu padissati;

Jāyate’yaṃ guṇo tikkha-paññāna’mabhiyogato.

Here, a constant longing for prostration is clearly seen as good; this quality arises from the persistent effort of those with sharp wisdom.

126. Byāsattamevassa vivarati “iccatri”ccādinā. Iccevaṃ atra gāthāyaṃ paṇatiyaṃ paṇāme gedho adhikacchando sādhu sundaraṃ padissati viññāyate, ayaṃ yathāvutto ojo guṇo pariṇatabhāvasaṅkhāto tikkhapaññānaṃ sātisayamatīnaṃ evaṃ santepi abhiyogato punappunappavattitaparicayabalena jāyate uppajjati.

126. He explains its very attachment by 'iccatra' and so on. Thus, in this verse, the longing for prostration, the excessive desire for bowing, is seen and understood as good and beautiful. This quality of vigor, as stated, designated as the state of maturity, arises and is produced in those of sharp wisdom and exceedingly keen intellect through application, by the power of familiarity developed through repeated practice.

126. Idāni saṃkhittassatthassa vitthārena pakāsitabhāvaṃ “iccatra”iccādinā niddisati. Iti iminā anantaragāthāyaṃ vuttakkamena atra imissaṃ gāthāyaṃ niccaṃpaṇatigedho nirantarapaṇāme adhikakattukāmatākusalacchando sādhu vibhūto vibhūtaṃ vā padissati paññāyati, ayaṃ [M 0.0152] guṇo yathāvutto ayaṃ pariṇatabhāvasaṅkhāto ojo nāma saddatthaguṇo tikkhapaññānaṃ sukhumabuddhimantānaṃ abhiyogato ganthavisayabhūtena nirantarābhyāseneva jāyate sijjhati, vattu pāriṇatyeneva bhavanato yesaṃ kesañci yena kenaci pakārena na sijjhatīti. Niccaṃ pavattā paṇatīti ca, tassaṃ gedhoti ca, tikkhā paññā yesanti ca, abhi punappunaṃ yogo yuñjananti ca viggaho.

126. Now, by 'iccatra' and so on, he indicates that the condensed meaning has been explained in detail. Thus, according to the sequence stated in the immediately preceding verse, here in this verse, the longing for constant prostration, the wholesome desire which is the wish to do excessively in continuous prostration, is seen and known as good and manifest. This quality, as stated, this quality of sound and meaning named 'ojo' or vigor, designated as the state of maturity, arises and is accomplished for those of sharp wisdom and subtle intellect through application, that is, by continuous practice which is the subject of the text. It is not accomplished for just anyone by any means, as it arises only from the maturity of the author. The analysis is: 'niccaṃ pavattā paṇati' (constant prostration); and 'gedha' (longing) in that; and 'tikkhā paññā yesaṃ' (those whose wisdom is sharp); and 'abhi punappunaṃ yogo yuñjanaṃ' (repeated application, engaging).

127.

127.

Madhurattaṃ padāsatti-ranuppāsavasā dvidhā;

Siyā samasuti pubbā, vaṇṇāvutti paro yathā.

Sweetness is twofold, by means of proximity of words and alliteration. The former may be similarity of sound, the latter like the recurrence of letters.

127. Mādhuriyamavadhārayamāha “madhuratta”miccādi. Savanīyattena manoharattaṃ madhurattaṃ. Taṃ padāni vākyālaṅkārāni samānāni uttaruttarehi, tesaṃ āsatti ṭhānādināyathākathañci samasutīnaṃ āsannatā padāsatti, paṭhamappayuttassakkharassa pacchā pāso pakkhepo anuppāso, padāsatti ca anuppāso ca, tesaṃ vasena dvidhā hoti. “Kīdisā te”ti āha “siyā”tiādi. Pubbā paṭhamābhihitā padāsatti samā yena kenaci ṭhānamattāsaṃyogādinā padantarena suti vaṇṇo yassā sā siyā bhaveyya, paro pacchimo anuppāso tu vaṇṇassa sarabyañjanalakkhaṇassa āvutti punappunuccāraṇaṃ siyāti. Evaṃ katthaci bandhe samānapadāsatti katthaci anuppāso katthaci tadubhayaṃ, dvayena rahito viraso bandho nassādīyate kavīhi, tādisaṃ madhurattaṃ duvidhaṃ paṭipajjitabbaṃ, silesasamatānvitantuccantameva ramaṇīyaṃ siyāti lakkhaṇaṃ dassetvā “yathe”ti lakkhiyamubhayatthodāharati “yade”ccādinā, “munindi”ccādinā ca.

127. He defines sweetness, saying 'madhurattaṃ' and so on. Sweetness is charm by being pleasant to hear. Padāsatti is the proximity of words, phrases, or ornaments that are similar to subsequent ones, by means of place and so on, in whatever way, being a closeness of similar sounds. Anuppāsa is the throwing or placing of a previously used letter afterwards. It is twofold by means of proximity of words and alliteration. 'What are they like?' he asks, saying 'siyā' and so on. The former, the first mentioned proximity of words, may be such that its sound or letter is similar to another word by some means such as place, quantity, or conjunction. But the latter, alliteration, may be the repeated utterance of a letter, characterized by vowel and consonant. Thus, in some compositions, there is similar proximity of words; in some, alliteration; in some, both. A tasteless composition devoid of both is not enjoyed by poets. Such twofold sweetness should be practiced. Having shown the characteristic that it should be most delightful when endowed with punning and evenness, he illustrates the example in both cases with 'yade' and so on, and 'munindi' and so on.

127. Idāni madhuraguṇaṃ dasseti “madhuri”ccādinā. Madhurattaṃ savanīyabhāvato manoharattaṃ madhuraguṇaṃ, padānaṃ vākyāvayavasaṅkhātānaṃ syādyantādīnaṃ uparūparipadehi samānānaṃ [M 0.0153] āsatti ṭhānakaraṇādinā yena kenaci pakārena aññamaññaṃ āsannatā, anuppāso pubbuccāritavaṇṇānaṃ puna pakkhipanañcāti dvinnaṃ vasā vibhāgena dvidhā hoti. Tattha pubbā padāsatti samasuti siyā, pubbāparavaṇṇānaṃ ṭhānamattākaraṇādīhi āsannasutisaṅkhatavaṇṇavutti hoti, paro anuppāso pana vaṇṇāvutti sarabyañjanasabhāvānaṃ pubbuccāritavaṇṇānaṃ punappunuccāraṇaṃ siyāti. Yathāti dvīsu udāharaṇamādisati. Evaṃ katthaci bandhe padāsatti katthaci anuppāso katthaci tadubhayaṃ, dvīhi vinimutto pana bandho viññūhi assādanīyo na hoti. Upari vakkhamānāhi silesasamatāhi yuttaṃ madhurattaṃ pana visesato assādanīyaṃ hotīti. Madhurassa bandhassa bhāvoti ca, padānaṃ āsattīti ca, anu pacchā pāso pakkhepoti ca, padāsatti ca anuppāso cāti ca, tesaṃ vaso bhedoti ca, samā suti vaṇṇo yassāti ca, vaṇṇassa āvuttīti ca viggaho.

127. Now, he explains the quality of sweetness by 'madhuri' and so on. The quality of sweetness is the charm of being pleasant to hear. Padāsatti is the mutual closeness of words, enumerated as parts of sentences, such as those having case endings, which are similar to successive words, by means of place, articulation, etc., in whatever way. And anuppāsa is the re-placing of previously uttered letters. Thus, it is twofold by division based on these two. Therein, the former, proximity of words, may be similarity of sound; it is the occurrence of letters characterized by close sound due to place, quantity, articulation, etc., of preceding and succeeding letters. But the latter, anuppāsa, may be the recurrence of letters, the repeated utterance of previously uttered letters which are of the nature of vowels and consonants. By 'yathā,' he indicates an example in both cases. Thus, in some compositions, there is proximity of words; in some, anuppāsa; in some, both. But a composition devoid of both is not enjoyable to the wise. Sweetness endowed with punning and evenness, which will be spoken of later, is especially enjoyable. The analysis is: 'madhurassa bandhassa bhāvo' (the nature of sweet composition); and 'padānaṃ āsatti' (proximity of words); and 'anu' (after) 'pāso' (throwing) 'pakkhepo' (placing); and 'padāsatti' (proximity of words) and 'anuppāso' (alliteration); and 'tesaṃ vaso bhedo' (division by means of them); and 'samā suti vaṇṇo yassa' (that whose sound/letter is similar); and 'vaṇṇassa āvutti' (recurrence of letters).

128.

128.

Yadā eso’bhisambodhiṃ,

Sampatto munipuṅgavo;

Tadā pabhuti dhammassa,

Loke jāto mahussavo.

When that foremost of sages attained supreme enlightenment, from that time forth a great festival of the Dhamma arose in the world.

128. Eso munipuṅgavo yadā yato pabhuti abhisambodhiṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ sampatto samadhigato, tadā pabhuti tato ārabbha dhammassa catusatipaṭṭhānādibhedassa sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyasaṅkhātassa mahussavo mahanto abbhudayo nippaṭipakkhā pavatti loke tividhe jāto ahosīti. Iha kvaci dīghatākataṃ sadisattaṃ, kvaci ṭhānakataṃ, kvaci saṃyogakataṃ, kvaci aññathā, tenāha “siyā samasuti pubbā”ti.

128. When that foremost of sages attained and fully understood supreme enlightenment, the knowledge of omniscience, from that time forth, beginning from then, a great festival, a great arising, an unopposed proceeding of the Dhamma—designated as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, with divisions such as the four foundations of mindfulness—arose in the threefold world. Here, sometimes the similarity is created by length, sometimes by place of articulation, sometimes by conjunction, sometimes otherwise. Therefore, he said, 'The former may be similarity of sound.'

128. “Yadi”ccādi. [M 0.0154] Eso munipuṅgavo yadā abhisambodhiṃ sabbaññutaṃ sampatto sasantāne uppādanavasena sampāpuṇi, tadā pabhuti tato paṭṭhāya dhammassa kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānādipabhedassa sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyadhammassa mahussavo mahābhivuddhi loke kāmādilokattaye jātoti. Iha “yadā eso”ti dīghakālavasena āsannatā, “ya e”ti ṭhānavasena āsannatā, “abhisambodhiṃ sampatto”ti saṃyogavasena āsannatā, “bhi dhi”nti dhanitato āsannatāti iccādinā padāsatti daṭṭhabbā. Abhisambujjhati etāyāti ca, pumā ca so goceti ca, munīnaṃ puṅgavoti ca, mahanto ca so ussavo cāti ca viggaho.

128. By 'yadi' and so on. When this foremost of sages attained supreme enlightenment, omniscience, having fully attained it by way of producing it in his own continuum, then, from that time onward, from that point on, a great festival and great increase of the Dhamma—the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, with divisions such as the foundations of mindfulness beginning with contemplation of the body—arose in the world, in the triple world of desire and so on. Here, in 'yadā eso,' the proximity is by way of long vowels; in 'ya e,' the proximity is by way of place; in 'abhisambodhiṃ sampatto,' the proximity is by way of conjunction; in 'bhi dhi,' the proximity is due to aspiration—thus, proximity of words should be seen. The analysis is: 'abhisambujjhati etāya' (one fully awakens by this); and 'pumā ca so go' (he is a man and a bull); and 'munīnaṃ puṅgavo' (a bull among sages); and 'mahanto ca so ussavo' (it is a great festival).

129.

129.

Munindamandahāsā te, kundasandohavibbhamā;

Disanta’manudhāvanti, hasantā candakantiyo.

Those gentle smiles of the lord of sages, with the splendor of a cluster of jasmine flowers, pursue the directions, mocking the radiance of the moon.

129. Kundānaṃ kusumānaṃ sandoho samūho, tassa vibbhamo yesaṃ te, munindassa mandahāsā manuññā hasitāni candassa kantiyo sobhāyo hasantā viḍambayantā disantamanudhāvanti anuvicaranti. Iccatra nakārasahitassa dakārassa, takārassa cānuvattanaṃ.

129. A cluster, a collection of jasmine flowers; they are those whose splendor is that. The gentle, lovely smiles of the lord of sages, mocking and surpassing the radiance and beauty of the moon, pursue and wander through the directions. Here, there is a recurrence of the letter 'da' accompanied by 'na', and of the letter 'ta'.

“Indanīladaladvanda-sundaraṃ sirimandiraṃ;

Munindanayanadvandaṃ, vindati’ndīvarajjutiṃ”.

The pair of eyes of the Lord of Sages, beautiful like a pair of sapphire petals and an abode of splendor, obtains the radiance of blue lotuses.

Iccaparamudāharaṇaṃ.

This is another example.

129. “Munindi”ccādi. Kundasandohavibbhamā supupphitakundakusumarāsisadisalīlāvantā te munindamandahāsā buddhassa manuññā hasitā candakantiyo nimmalacandakiraṇe hasantā nindantā disantaṃ taṃ taṃ disaṃ, disāpariyantaṃ vā anudhāvanti vidhāvantīti. Ettha nakārasahitadakārassa, nakārasahitatakārassa ca āvutti daṭṭhabbā. Mandā ca te hāsā ceti [M 0.0155] ca, munindassa mandahāsāti ca, kundānaṃ sandohoti ca, tassa vibbhamo yesanti ca, disāyeva disantaṃ, disānaṃ vā antanti ca viggaho.

129. Regarding 'munindi,' and so forth. Those gentle, lovely smiles of the Buddha, possessing a grace like a heap of fully bloomed jasmine flowers, mocking and surpassing the moon's radiance and the pure moonbeams, pursue and run about in every direction, or to the ends of the directions. Here, the recurrence of the letter 'da' conjoined with 'na' and 'ta' conjoined with 'na' should be observed. The analysis is: 'mandā ca te hāsā ca' (and gentle are those smiles); and 'munindassa mandahāsā' (the gentle smiles of the Lord of Sages); and 'kundānaṃ sandoho' (a heap of jasmine flowers); and 'tassa vibbhamo yesaṃ' (those whose grace is that); and 'disantaṃ' is 'disā eva' (the direction itself), or 'disānaṃ antaṃ' (the end of the directions).

“Indanīladaladvanda-sundaraṃ sirimandiraṃ;

Munindanayanadvandaṃ, vindati’ndīvarajjuti”nti.

The pair of eyes of the Lord of Sages, beautiful like a pair of sapphire petals and an abode of splendor, obtains the radiance of blue lotuses.

Idampi nakārasahitadakāravaṇṇāvuttiyā aparamudāharaṇaṃ.

This too is another example of the recurrence of the letter 'da' conjoined with 'na'.

Tattha indanīladaladvandasundaraṃ indanīlamaṇisakalikāyugaḷamiva manoharaṃ sirimandiraṃ tatoyeva sobhāya nivāsaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ munindanayanadvandaṃ indīvarajjutiṃ nīluppalakantiṃ vindati anubhoti, indīvarajjutisamānāti adhippāyo.

Therein, 'beautiful like a pair of sapphire petals' means charming like a pair of sapphire gem fragments. 'An abode of splendor' means being the very dwelling place of glory. The pair of eyes of the Lord of Sages 'obtains the radiance of blue lotuses' means it experiences the luster of blue water lilies; the intention is that they are similar to the radiance of blue lotuses.

130.

130.

Sabbakomalavaṇṇehi, nā’nuppāso pasaṃsiyo;

Yathā’yaṃ mālatīmālā, linalolālimālinī.

Alliteration with all soft letters is not praised. For example: 'This jasmine garland, with its line of clinging, eager bees.'

130. Yehi kehici āvuttito anuppāsoti ce? Netyāha “sabba”iccādi. Sabbehi komalehi sukumārehi vaṇṇehi akkharehi anuppāso na pasaṃsiyo silāghanīyo na hoti silesavirodhittā. “Yathe”ti taṃ udāharati. Ayaṃ mālatīmālā jātikusumadāmaṃ linānaṃ byādhitānaṃ lolānaṃ [M 0.0156] kusumarasārabbha lolupānaṃ alīnaṃ bhamarānaṃ mālā panti sā assā atthīti linalolālimālinī.

130. If one were to ask, 'Is alliteration constituted by any recurrence whatsoever?' To this, he replies 'No' with the words 'sabba,' and so forth. Alliteration with all soft, delicate letters is not praised, not commendable, because it is contrary to cohesion (silesa). He illustrates this with 'yathā.' 'This jasmine garland' (mālatīmālā) means a garland of jasmine flowers (jātikusumadāmaṃ). It is 'linalolālimālinī' because it has (sā assā atthīti) a row (mālā, panti) of bees (alīnaṃ, bhamarānaṃ) that are clinging (linānaṃ), afflicted (byādhitānaṃ), greedy (lolānaṃ), and excessively desirous (lolupānaṃ) of the flower's nectar (kusumarasārabbha).

130. Vuttānuppāsopi sabbakomalavaṇṇehi viracito na pasaṃsiyoti dassetuṃ “sabbakomalavaṇṇehī”tiādimāha. Sabbakomalavaṇṇehi sabbehi sukumārakkharehi kato anuppāso vaṇṇāvuttilakkhaṇo na pasaṃsiyo silesālaṅkāraviruddhattā pasattho na hoti. “Yathā”ti tamudāharati. Ayaṃ mālatīmālā esā jātisumanamālikā linānaṃ byāvaṭānaṃ patantānaṃ lolānaṃ gandhaluddhānaṃ alīnaṃ bhamarānaṃ mālinī pantiyuttāti. Ettha lakārasseva punappunappayogena komalavaṇṇāvutti. Mālatīnaṃ mālāti ca, lolā ca te alayo cāti ca, linā ca te lolālayo cāti ca, tesaṃ mālāti ca, sā assa atthīti ca viggaho.

130. To show that even alliteration in verse (vuttānuppāsa), when composed with all soft letters, is not praiseworthy, he states, 'sabbakomalavaṇṇehi,' and so forth. An alliteration, characterized by the repetition of letters, made with all soft and delicate syllables, is not commendable, not excellent, because it is contrary to the literary ornament of cohesion (silesa). He illustrates this with 'yathā.' 'This garland of mālatī flowers' (ayaṃ mālatīmālā) means this wreath of jāti jasmine flowers (esā jātisumanamālikā), which is 'mālinī' (possessed of a line) or endowed with a row (pantiyuttā) of bees (alīnaṃ, bhamarānaṃ) that are clinging (linānaṃ), busy (byāvaṭānaṃ), alighting (patantānaṃ), eager (lolānaṃ), and greedy for fragrance (gandhaluddhānaṃ). Here, through the repeated use of the letter 'la,' there is a recurrence of a soft letter. The analysis is: 'mālatīnaṃ mālā' (a garland of mālatī); and 'lolā ca te alayo ca' (and they are eager bees); and 'linā ca te lolālayo ca' (and they are clinging and eager bees); and 'tesaṃ mālā' (their line); and 'sā assa atthīti' (it has that).

131.

131.

Mudūhi vā kevalehi,

Kevalehi phuṭehi vā;

Missehi vā tidhā hoti,

Vaṇṇehi samatā yathā.

With exclusively soft sounds, or with exclusively harsh sounds, or with mixed sounds—thus balance (samatā) is threefold, as will be shown.

131. Samataṃ sambhāveti “mudūhi”ccādinā. Kevalehi kevalaphuṭādibhāvāpavattehi sakalehi mudūhi catūsupi pādesu sajātiyehi asithilakomalehi vā kakārādīhi vā sithilakomalassa silesapaṭipakkhattā kevalehi phuṭehi vā adhimattasutīhi bhakārādīhi rāgādīhi (ka.) vā akicchavacanīye kicchavacanīyassa sukhumālavipariyayattā missehi vā majjhimasutīhi mudubhūtasaṃsaṭṭhehi vā vaṇṇehi akkharehi karaṇabhūtehi samatā tidhā hoti gajje pajje vā. “Yathe”ti tividhamudāharati.

131. He explains balance (samatā) with the words 'mudūhi,' and so forth. Balance, whether in prose or verse, is threefold, by means of letters or syllables as its instrument: (1) by exclusively soft letters, that is, all those devoid of harshness, etc., in all four feet of a verse, being of a similar class, either not loose and soft, such as 'ka' and so on, because what is loose and soft is contrary to cohesion (silesa); (2) or by exclusively harsh letters, which are highly audible, such as 'bha' and so on, because in a context where pronunciation should not be difficult, the difficult-to-pronounce is the opposite of subtlety (sukhumāla); (3) or by mixed letters, which are of medium audibility or are mingled with soft letters. He illustrates these three kinds with 'yathā'.

131. Idāni samataṃ vibhāvetuṃ “mudūhi”ccādimāha. Kevalehi phuṭamissehi aññattā sakalehi mudūhi sithilakomalehi vaṇṇehi kakārādīhi vā kevalehi phuṭehi kevalakomalavaṇṇarahitattā sakalehi akicchuccāraṇīyehi adhimattasutīhi bhakārādīhi vaṇṇehi vā missehi yathāvuttamuduphuṭasammissehi vaṇṇehi vā karaṇabhūtehi samatā gajje vā pajje vā tidhā hotīti. Yadi sithilakomalavaṇṇehi vicaritaṃ silesālaṅkārassa, kicchuccāraṇīyehi phuṭavaṇṇehi kataṃ sukhumālālaṅkārassa [M 0.0157] ca virujjhatīti. “Yathā”ti tividhamudāharati.

131. Now, to explain balance, he states, 'mudūhi,' and so forth. Balance, whether in prose or verse, is threefold, by means of letters as its instrument: (1) by all exclusively soft letters, distinct from the harsh and mixed, being loose and soft letters such as 'ka' and so on; (2) or by exclusively harsh letters, devoid of any soft letters, being all not difficult to pronounce, highly audible, such as 'bha' and so on; (3) or by mixed letters, which are a mixture of the aforementioned soft and harsh sounds. For if a composition is made with loose and soft letters, it is contrary to the ornament of cohesion (silesa); and if it is made with difficult-to-pronounce harsh letters, it is contrary to the ornament of subtlety (sukhumāla). He illustrates these three kinds with 'yathā'.

Kevalamudusamatā

Exclusively Soft Balance

132.

132.

Kokilālāpasaṃvādī,

Munindālāpavibbhamo;

Hadayaṅgamataṃ yāti,

Sataṃ deti ca nibbutiṃ.

Harmonious with the cuckoo's song, the graceful speech of the Lord of Sages becomes pleasing to the heart and gives peace to the virtuous.

132. “Kokile”ccādi. Kokilānaṃ karavīkasakuṇānaṃ ālāpo kūjitaṃ, taṃ saṃvadati pakāsati sīlenāti kokilālāpasaṃvādī, taṃsadisoti attho, munindassa ālāpo visaṭṭhādiaṭṭhaṅgiko saro tassa vibbhamo vilāso sataṃ sappurisānaṃ hadayaṅgamataṃ manonusāritaṃ madhurabhāvaṃ yāti, nibbutiṃ nibbānañca tesaṃ deti.

132. Regarding 'kokile,' and so forth. The speech, the cooing of cuckoos and karavīka birds—that which is by nature harmonious with and manifests this is 'harmonious with the cuckoo's song' (kokilālāpasaṃvādī); the meaning is that it is similar to that. The speech of the Lord of Sages is a voice possessing the eight qualities beginning with clarity; its grace and charm attain a state of being pleasing to the heart, agreeable to the mind, and sweet for the virtuous, and it gives them peace and Nibbāna.

132. “Kokili”ccādi. Kokilānaṃ karavīkasakuṇānaṃ ālāpaṃ nādalīlaṃ saṃvādī pakāsanasīlo, taṃsadisoti adhippāyo, munindassa sabbaññuno ālāpassa visaṭṭhādiaṭṭhaṅgikanādassa vibbhamo vilāso sataṃ sappurisānaṃ hadayaṅgamataṃ cittārādhitabhāvaṃ yāti ca, nibbutiṃ sutasambandhena tesaṃyeva sādhūnaṃ nibbānaṃ deti ca dentopi hotīti. Ettha kokilālāpasaddena nissite nissayavohārena līlā gahitā.

132. Regarding 'kokili,' and so forth. The speech of cuckoos and karavīka birds, a playful melody (nādalīlaṃ), is by nature harmonious and revealing (saṃvādī pakāsanasīlo); the intention is that it is similar to that. The grace and charm of the speech of the All-Knowing Lord of Sages, a sound endowed with the eight qualities beginning with clarity, attains a state of being pleasing to the heart and delighting the mind for the virtuous; and through the connection of hearing it, it gives Nibbāna to those very same good people, becoming a giver thereof. Here, by the word 'cuckoo's speech,' 'playfulness' (līlā) is understood through the figurative usage of the support for that which is supported.

Kevalaphuṭasamatā

Exclusively Harsh Balance

133.

133.

Sambhāvanīyasambhāvaṃ,

Bhagavantaṃ bhavantaguṃ;

Bhavantasādhanākaṅkhī,

Ko na sambhāvaye vibhuṃ.

Who, desiring the means to the end of existence, would not venerate the Lord, the Blessed One, whose very nature is worthy of veneration, who has gone to the end of existence?

133. “Sambhāvanīye”ccādi. [M 0.0158] Sambhāvanīyo ādaraṇīyo. Sadevake loke santo sobhano bhāvo adhippāyo yassa taṃ. Bhavantaṃ nibbānaṃ gatoti bhavantagu, taṃ vibhuṃ. Bhagavantaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ. Bhavassa saṃsārassa anto avasānaṃ nibbānaṃ, tassa sādhanaṃ sampādanamākaṅkhati sīlenāti bhavantasādhanākaṅkhī, ko nāma saṃsāravattijano. Na sambhāvaye ādaraṃ na kareyya, karotyevāti attho.

133. Regarding 'sambhāvanīye,' and so forth. 'Worthy of veneration' (sambhāvanīyo) means worthy of respect (ādaraṇīyo). 'Of an excellent nature' (sambhāvaṃ) refers to him whose nature or intention is good and excellent in the world with its gods. 'One who has gone to the end of existence' (bhavantagu) means he has gone to the end of existence, Nibbāna. That Lord (vibhuṃ), the Blessed One (bhagavantaṃ), the Perfectly Enlightened One. 'One who desires the means to the end of existence' (bhavantasādhanākaṅkhī) is one who by nature desires the means, the attainment, of that end of existence (bhavassa anto), which is the cessation of saṃsāra, Nibbāna. 'Who' (ko nāma) refers to any person revolving in saṃsāra. 'Would not venerate' means would not show respect; the meaning is that one certainly does.

133. “Sambhāvanīyi”ccādi. Sambhāvanīyasambhāvaṃ sadevakena lokena ādaraṇīyasobhanādhippāyaṃ bhavantaguṃ bhavassa antasaṅkhātaṃ nibbānaṃ gataṃ vibhuṃ pabhuṃ bhagavantaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ bhavantasādhanākaṅkhī nibbānasādhanābhilāsī ko katamo saṃsāravattijano na sambhāvaye ādaraṃ na kareyya, karotyeva. Santo ca so bhāvo cāti ca, sambhāvanīyo sambhāvo yasseti ca, bhavassa antanti ca, bhavantaṃ gatoti ca, tassa sādhananti ca, taṃ ākaṅkhati sīlenāti ca viggaho.

133. Regarding 'sambhāvanīyi,' and so forth. Which person revolving in saṃsāra (ko katamo saṃsāravattijano), desiring the means to the end of existence (bhavantasādhanākaṅkhī), longing for the attainment of Nibbāna (nibbānasādhanābhilāsī), would not venerate, would not show respect to the Lord (vibhuṃ), the Master (pabhuṃ), the Blessed One (bhagavantaṃ), the Perfectly Enlightened One, who has gone to Nibbāna, reckoned as the end of existence, and whose excellent intention is worthy of respect by the world with its gods (sambhāvanīyasambhāvaṃ)? Indeed, one certainly would. The analysis is: 'santo ca so bhāvo ca' (and that nature is good); and 'sambhāvanīyo sambhāvo yassa' (one whose nature is worthy of veneration); and 'bhavassa anto' (the end of existence); and 'bhavantaṃ gato' (gone to the end of existence); and 'tassa sādhanaṃ' (the means to that); and 'taṃ ākaṅkhati sīlena' (one by nature desires that).

Missakasamatā

Mixed Balance

134.

134.

Laddhacandanasaṃsagga-sugandhimalayānilo;

Manda’māyāti bhītova, munindamukhamārutā.

The Malayan breeze, made fragrant by contact with sandalwood, approaches slowly, as if in fear of the breath from the mouth of the Lord of Sages.

134. “Laddhi”ccādi. Laddho candanatarūnaṃ saṃsaggo paricayo tena sobhano gandho assāti sugandhī surabhi malayānilodakkhiṇapavamāno munindassa mukhamārutā bhītova tādisamuduttasītalattasugandhasampattiyā attano dūratarattā āyāti anuvattati. Mandanti āgamanakriyāvisesanaṃ.

134. ‘Laddhi’ etc. ‘Laddho candanatarūnaṃ saṃsaggo paricayo tena sobhano gandho assāti sugandhī surabhi malayānilodakkhiṇapavamāno’ means: ‘The association, the familiarity, with sandalwood trees was obtained, and by that, it has a splendid fragrance,’ thus it is fragrant, sweet, a southern breeze from Malaya. As if fearful of the wind from the Sage’s mouth, it comes and follows on account of its own great distance from such an abundance of gentle, cool, and fragrant qualities. ‘Mandaṃ’ is an adverb modifying the verb of coming.

134. “Laddhi”ccādi. [M 0.0159] Laddhacandanasaṃsaggasugandhimalayānilo paṭiladdhacandanatarusārasamavāyena sobhanagandhasamannāgato malayadesato āgacchamānamāluto munindamukhamārutā buddhassa mukhasurabhivāsitapavanato bhīto iva tādisamudusurabhisītalattassa attani asambhavato bhītova mandaṃ saṇikaṃ yāti abhimukhametīti. Candanānaṃ saṃsaggoti ca, laddho ca so candanasaṃsaggoti ca, sobhano gandho yassāti ca, laddhacandanasaṃsaggena sugandhīti ca, malayato āgato aniloti ca, munindamukhato nikkhanto mārutoti ca viggaho. Mandanti kriyāvisesanaṃ. Ettha tividhasamatāyaṃ “kokilālāpasaṃvādi”ccāditividhalakkhiyassāpi “mudūhi vā kevalehi”ccādinā dassitalakkhaṇattayena tulyatā supākaṭāvāti.

134. ‘Laddhi’ etc. ‘Laddhacandanasaṃsaggasugandhimalayānilo’ means: the Malayan breeze, fragrant from its association with sandalwood, endowed with an excellent fragrance through its contact with the essence of sandalwood trees, a wind coming from the Malaya region. As if fearful of the wind from the Sage’s mouth, of the breeze perfumed by the Buddha’s mouth, because of the impossibility in itself of such gentleness, fragrance, and coolness, it goes slowly, gently, approaching. The analysis is: ‘Candanānaṃ saṃsaggo’ (association with sandalwoods), and ‘laddho ca so candanasaṃsaggo’ (and that association with sandalwoods was obtained), and ‘sobhanagandho yassa’ (whose fragrance is splendid), and ‘laddhacandanasaṃsaggena sugandhī’ (fragrant by association with sandalwood), and ‘malayato āgato anilo’ (wind coming from Malaya), and ‘munindamukhato nikkhanto māruto’ (wind emerging from the Sage’s mouth). ‘Mandaṃ’ is an adverb modifying the verb. Here, in the threefold equality, the similarity of the threefold characteristic described by ‘kokilālāpasaṃvādi’ etc. with the three characteristics shown by ‘mudūhi vā kevalehi’ etc. is very clear.

135.

135.

Aniṭṭhurakkharappāyā, sabbakomalanissaṭā;

Kicchamuccāraṇāpeta-byañjanā sukhumālatā.

Mostly unharsh letters, entirely issuing from soft sounds, with consonants devoid of difficult pronunciation—this is delicacy.

135. Sukhumālatā kathīyati “aniṭṭhurakkhare”ccādinā. Aniṭṭhurāni apharusāni akkharāni vaṇṇāni pāyāni bahūni yassā sā tathā, “niṭṭhurāni appakānī”ti pāyaggahaṇena sūcitaṃ, tatoyeva sabbehi kevalehi komalehi sithilehi laghūhi akkharehi nissaṭā niggatā kicchena dukkhena uccāraṇā tato apetāni apagatāni byañjanāni yassā sāti anuvaditvā sukhumālatā vidhīyate.

135. Delicacy is described by ‘aniṭṭhurakkhare’ etc. ‘Aniṭṭhurāni apharusāni akkharāni vaṇṇāni pāyāni bahūni yassā sā tathā’ means: ‘that which has mostly unharsh, not rough, letters or sounds, that is, many of them.’ By the inclusion of ‘pāya’ (mostly), it is indicated that ‘harsh ones are few.’ Therefore, delicacy is defined by restating that it is that which has consonants that have issued or proceeded from entirely soft, loose, and light letters, and are devoid of, or removed from, difficult, painful pronunciation.

135. Idāni sukhumālataṃ dasseti “aniṭṭhure”ccādinā. Aniṭṭhurakkharappāyā akakkasavaṇṇabahulā sabbakomalanissaṭā aniṭṭhurakkharānaṃ yebhuyyaggahaṇatoyeva sakalasithilavaṇṇavirahitā kicchamuccāraṇāpetabyañjanā dukkhuccāraṇīyavaṇṇehi vigataakkharasamannāgatā sukhumālatā nāmāti. Aniṭṭhurāni akkharāni pāyāni bahūni yassanti ca, sabbe ca te komalā ceti ca, tehi nissaṭāti [M 0.0160] ca, kicchena uccāraṇāti ca, tehi apetānīti ca, tāni byañjanāni yassāti ca viggaho. Niggahītāgamo.

135. Now, delicacy is shown by ‘aniṭṭhure’ etc. ‘Aniṭṭhurakkharappāyā’ means: abundant in unharsh letters, abundant in non-harsh sounds. ‘Sabbakomalanissaṭā’ means: by the predominant use of unharsh letters, it is devoid of all loose sounds. ‘Kicchamuccāraṇāpetabyañjanā’ means: having consonants devoid of sounds difficult to pronounce, endowed with letters free from sounds difficult to pronounce—this is called delicacy. The analysis is: ‘Aniṭṭhurāni akkharāni pāyāni bahūni yassa’ (whose unharsh letters are many), and ‘sabbe ca te komalā ca’ (and all of them are soft), and ‘tehi nissaṭā’ (issuing from them), and ‘kicchena uccāraṇā’ (difficult pronunciation), and ‘tehi apetāni’ (devoid of them), and ‘tāni byañjanāni yassa’ (whose consonants are those). The addition of niggahīta.

136.

136.

Passantā rūpavibhavaṃ, suṇantā madhuraṃ giraṃ;

Caranti sādhū sambuddha-kāle keḷiparammukhā.

Seeing the splendor of forms, hearing sweet speech, the good wander, averse to play, in the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One.

136. Udāharati “passantā”iccādi. Rūpavibhavaṃ rūpasampattiṃ passantā madhuraṃ giraṃ vācaṃ suṇantā sādhavo keḷiparammukhā kīḷāya nicchantā carantīti sambandho. Katthāti āha “sambuddhakāle”ti.

136. It exemplifies with ‘passantā’ etc. The connection is that ‘sādhavo’ (the good), ‘passantā rūpavibhavaṃ rūpasampattiṃ’ (seeing the splendor of forms, the perfection of forms), ‘suṇantā madhuraṃ giraṃ vācaṃ’ (hearing sweet speech, words), ‘keḷiparammukhā kīḷāya nicchantā’ (averse to play, not desiring play), ‘caranti’ (wander). Where? It says: ‘in the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One.’

136. “Passanti”ccādinā lakkhiyamudāharati, taṃ vuttatthameva.

136. With ‘passantā’ etc., it exemplifies the characteristic; that is indeed the meaning already stated.

137.

137.

Alaṅkāravihīnāpi, sataṃ sammukhate’disī;

Ārohati visesena, ramaṇīyā tadujjalā.

Even unadorned, such delicacy becomes prominent before the virtuous; radiant thereby, it is especially delightful.

137. Visiṭṭhassāññadhammassa abhāvepimināvopādeyo bandhoti āha “alaṅkāre”ccādi. Alaṅkārehi vihīnāpi edisī sukhumālatā sataṃ paṇḍitajanānaṃ sammukhataṃ abhimukhabhāvaṃ vācāgocarattaṃ ārohati upagacchati, kimutaatthālaṅkārālaṅkitetyapisaddo. Tena sabhāvavutyādinā alaṅkārena ujjalā dittā pana visesenātisayena ramaṇīyā manuññāti.

137. To show that this composition is worthy of adoption even in the absence of another superior quality, it says ‘alaṅkāre’ etc. Even devoid of adornments, such delicacy comes into the presence of the good, the wise, meaning into their direct presence or within the scope of their speech. The word ‘api’ implies, how much more so when adorned with figurative embellishments. But when radiant, shining with that adornment by way of natural expression etc., it is especially and exceedingly delightful and pleasing.

137. “Alaṅkāre”ccādi. Edisī evaṃvidhā sukhumālatā alaṅkāravihīnāpi atthālaṅkāravirahitāpi sataṃ paññavantānaṃ sammukhataṃ abhimukhabhāvaṃ tesaṃ vacanavisayabhāvanti attho ārohati pāpuṇāti. Tadujjalā tena sabhāvavuttivaṅkavuttisambhūtena atthālaṅkārena jotamānā visesena atisayena ramaṇīyā manuññā hoti. Alaṅkārehi vihīnāti ca, tena ujjalāti ca viggaho.

137. ‘Alaṅkāre’ etc. Such delicacy, even devoid of adornments, even without figurative embellishments, comes into the presence of the good, the wise—the meaning is, it comes into their direct presence or becomes the object of their speech. Radiant thereby, shining with figurative embellishment born of natural and artful expression, it becomes especially and exceedingly delightful and pleasing. The analysis is: ‘Alaṅkārehi vihīnā’ (devoid of adornments), and ‘tena ujjalā’ (radiant thereby).

138.

138.

Romañcapiñcharacanā, [M 0.0161] sādhuvādāhitaddhanī;

Laḷanti’me munīmeghu-mmadā sādhu sikhāvalā.

Whose feather arrangement is like goosebumps, whose sound is produced by cries of ‘sādhu’, these good peacocks, intoxicated by the sage-cloud, play gracefully.

138. Tamudāharati “romañce”ccādinā. Romañcā lomahaṃsā iva romañcā eva vā, piñchāni barihāni parihārāni (ka.) tesaṃ racanā chattākārena vidhānaṃ yesaṃ te tathā, “sādhū”ti vādo vacanaṃ taṃsadisoyeva vā, āhito dhani kekāsaṅkhāto yesaṃ te tathā, munimeghena munisadisena munisaṅkhātena vā vāridena ummadā mattā sādhusadisā sādhu eva vā sikhāvalā mayūrā laḷanti līlopetā vicaranti, aññamaññaṃ ramantīti attho.

138. It exemplifies that with ‘romañce’ etc. ‘Romañcā’ means: like hair standing on end, or simply goosebumps. ‘Piñchāni’ means: tail feathers; ‘tesaṃ racanā chattākārena vidhānaṃ yesaṃ te tathā’ means: ‘whose arrangement is a display like a parasol.’ ‘Sādhu’ in ‘sādhuvāda’ means: an utterance, a word, or something similar to it. ‘Āhitaddhanī’ means: ‘whose sound is produced,’ referring to the peacock’s cry. ‘Munimeghena ummadā’ means: intoxicated, joyful, by the sage-cloud, which is like a sage or named a sage, or by a rain-cloud. ‘Sādhu sikhāvalā’ means: peacocks similar to the good, or simply good peacocks. ‘Laḷanti’ means: they move playfully, wander, enjoying one another—this is the meaning.

138. Atthālaṅkārayuttasukhumālatamudāharati “rome”ccādinā. Romañcapiñcharacanā lomahaṃsasadisā romā eva vā piñchānaṃ barihānaṃ racanā chattākārena vitthāravantā sādhuvādāhitaddhanī “sādhū”ti vacanasadisehi sādhuvādehi vā pavattakekāninnādehi samannāgatā munimeghummadā munisadisena munisaṅkhātena vā meghena sañjātamadā ime sādhusikhāvalā sajjanasadisā sādhuno eva vā mayūrā laḷanti līlopetā bhavantīti. Idaṃ asesavatthuvisayaṃ samāsarūpakaṃ amukhyapakkhe “romañcā viya sādhuvādo viya muni viya sādhavo viyā”ti ca, mukhyapakkhe “piñcharacanā viya āhitaddhanī viya megho viya sikhāvalā viyā”ti upacaritabbaṃ. Romañcā eva piñchānīti ca, tesaṃ racanā yesanti ca, “sādhu”iti vādoti ca, āhito ca so dhani ceti ca, sādhuvādo āhitaddhani yesanti ca, muni eva meghoti ca, tena ummadāti ca, sādhavo eva sikhāvalāti ca vākyaṃ. “Munīmegho”ti ettha dīghattaṃ chandānurakkhaṇatthaṃ.

138. It exemplifies delicacy endowed with figurative embellishment with ‘rome’ etc. ‘Romañcapiñcharacanā’ means: whose feather arrangement is like goosebumps, or whose hairs themselves are the feathers, the arrangement of tail feathers being spread out like an umbrella. ‘Sādhuvādāhitaddhanī’ means: endowed with sounds produced by cries like ‘sādhu’ or by the continuous cries of peacocks. ‘Munimeghummadā’ means: intoxicated by the sage-cloud, by a cloud that is like a sage or named a sage. ‘Ime sādhusikhāvalā laḷanti’ means: these peacocks, similar to good people or simply good peacocks, play gracefully. This is a compound metaphor that applies to all the objects mentioned. In the figurative sense, it should be interpreted as ‘like goosebumps, like a cry of sādhu, like a sage, like good people’; and in the literal sense, as ‘like the feather arrangement, like the produced sound, like a cloud, like peacocks’. The phrases are: ‘Romañcā eva piñchāni’ (goosebumps are the feathers), and ‘tesaṃ racanā yesaṃ’ (whose arrangement is theirs), and ‘“sādhu” iti vādo’ (the word ‘sādhu’ is the cry), and ‘āhito ca so dhani ca’ (and that sound is produced), and ‘sādhuvādo āhitaddhani yesaṃ’ (whose sound is produced by a cry of sādhu), and ‘muni eva megho’ (the sage is the cloud), and ‘tena ummadā’ (intoxicated by that), and ‘sādhavo eva sikhāvalā’ (the good people are the peacocks). Here, the lengthening in ‘Munīmegho’ is for the sake of preserving the meter.

139.

139.

Sukhumālattamattheva, padatthavisayampi ca;

Yathā matādisaddesu, kittisesādikittanaṃ.

Delicacy exists in meaning, and also in the domain of the word; just as when words like ‘dead’ are to be used, there is the mention of ‘one whose fame remains’ and so on.

139. Na [M 0.0162] kevalaṃ sukhumālatā saddeva, atthepīti dassetumāha “sukhumālatta”miccādi. Atthevāti vijjateva, taṃ tu anocityagāmmādivajjanā sambhavati. “Yathe”ti tamudāharati. Matādisaddesu vattabbesu kittisesādīnaṃ saddānaṃ kittanaṃ kathanaṃ.

139. To show that delicacy is not only in the word, but also in the meaning, it says ‘sukhumālatta’ etc. ‘Attheva’ means: it certainly exists; and that arises by avoiding impropriety, vulgarity, and so on. ‘Yathā’ exemplifies that. When words like ‘dead’ are to be spoken, it is the mentioning, the speaking, of words like ‘one whose fame remains’ and so on.

139. Ayaṃ sukhumālatā na kevalaṃ saddeva, atthepīti dassetuṃ āha “sukhumālatta”miccādi. Sukhumālattamattheva padatthavisayampi ca padābhidheyyagocarampi sukhumālattaṃ attheva, tañca ocityahīnagāmmadosaparihārena sijjhati. “Yathā”ti tamudāharati. Matādisaddesu vattabbesu kittisesādisaddānaṃ kittanaṃ kathananti. Mato itiādi yesaṃ “jīvitakkhayaṃ patto” iccādīnamiti ca, kittiseso itiādiyesaṃ “devattaṃ gato, saggakāyamalaṅkarī”tyādīnamiti ca viggaho.

139. To show that this delicacy is not only in sound but also in meaning, it is said, ‘sukhumālatta,’ and so forth. Delicacy exists in the meaning itself, also in the domain of a word's meaning, and also in the range of what words denote—delicacy certainly exists. And that is achieved by avoiding the faults of impropriety and vulgarity. ‘Yathā’ exemplifies that. When words such as ‘dead’ are to be spoken, it is the mentioning, the speaking, of words such as ‘one whose fame remains.’ The analysis is: ‘Mato,’ etc., refers to those [expressions] meaning ‘having reached the end of life,’ etc.; and ‘kittiseso,’ etc., refers to those meaning ‘having gone to the state of a deva, adorning the heavenly body,’ etc.

140.

140.

Siliṭṭhapadasaṃsagga-

Ramaṇīyaguṇālayo;

Sabandhagāravo so’yaṃ,

Sileso nāma taṃ yathā.

A repository of delightful qualities due to the cohesion of smooth words, possessing a firm bond—this is called Silesa, as for example.

140. Silesaṃ dasseti “siliṭṭhe”ccādinā. Siliṭṭhānaṃ bandhalāghavābhāvena aññamaññaṃ siliṭṭhānaṃ padānaṃ saṃsaggena ramaṇīyo manuñño guṇo tassa ālayo pavattiṭṭhānaṃ. Bandhassa racanāya gāravo asithilatā, saha tena vattatīti sabandhagāravoti anuvaditvā soyaṃ sileso nāmāti vidhīyate. “Taṃ yathe”tyudāharati. Yathā ayaṃ sileso, tathā aññopi tādiso daṭṭhabbo, na tvayameveti “taṃ yathā” saddassattho.

140. He shows Silesa with ‘siliṭṭhe,’ etc. ‘Siliṭṭhānaṃ’ means: a delightful, pleasing quality due to the cohesion of words that are mutually smooth because of the absence of looseness in their bond; it is the repository, the place of occurrence, of that quality. ‘Gāravo’ means: firmness in the composition of the bond, non-looseness. Having stated that it exists together with that, it is defined that this is called Silesa. ‘Taṃ yathā’ exemplifies that. The meaning of the expression ‘taṃ yathā’ is that just as this is Silesa, so too should others of the same kind be seen, not just this one.

140. Idāni silesaṃ niddisati “siliṭṭhe”ccādinā. Siliṭṭhapadasaṃsaggaramaṇīyaguṇālayo ṭhānakaraṇādīhi āsannavaṇṇānaṃ [M 0.0163] vinyāsahetu aññamaññanissitānaṃ padānaṃ samavāyena manuññaguṇassa pavattiṭṭhānabhūto sabandhagāravo bandhagāravasaṅkhātaracanāya asithilabhāvena saha pavatto so ayaṃ bandho sileso nāmāti. Sileso nāma bandhagāravo, tappaṭipādakabandhopyettha silesoti vuccati. Siliṭṭhā ca te padā ceti ca, tesaṃ saṃsaggoti ca, tena ramaṇīyoti ca, so eva guṇoti ca, tassa ālayoti ca, bandhassa guruno bhāvoti ca, tena saha pavattatīti ca vākyaṃ. Taṃ yathā “bālindu”iccādi.

140. Now, he defines compactness (silesa) with ‘siliṭṭhe,’ and so on. That which is the abode of delightful qualities arising from the cohesion of smooth words, being the locus for the arising of a pleasing quality through the combination of mutually dependent words, due to the arrangement of sounds close in place and manner of articulation, and which proceeds together with the firmness of the composition called ‘compactness’ (bandhagārava)—this bond is called compactness (silesa). Compactness (silesa) means firmness of the bond (bandhagārava); the bond that establishes it is also called compactness here. The analysis is: ‘smooth words,’ their ‘cohesion,’ ‘delightfulness’ because of that, ‘that very quality,’ its ‘abode,’ the ‘firmness of the bond,’ and its ‘proceeding together with that.’ For example, ‘bālindu,’ and so on.

141.

141.

Bālinduvibbhamacchedi-nakharāvalikantibhi;

Sā munindapadambhoja-kanti vo valitā’vataṃ.

May that beauty of the Sage’s lotus feet, endowed with the splendor of the rows of nails that sever the charm of the young moon, protect you.

141. “Bālindu”iccādi. Bālinduno pañcamī pañcamīcandassa (?) pañcadasakalassa vibbhamo manoharattaṃ, taṃ chindati sīlenāti bālinduvibbhamacchediyo pañcamīcandassa kalāsannibhānaṃ nakharānaṃ nakhānaṃ āvaliyo tāsaṃ kantibhi sobhāhi saha valitā saṃyuttā sā, munindassa padāniyeva ambhojāni padumāni tesaṃ kanti. Vo tumhe sāmaññena vadati. Avataṃ pālayatu.

141. ‘Bālindu,’ and so on. ‘Bālinduvibbhamacchediyo’ means that which by its nature severs the charm, the loveliness, of the young moon. The rows of nails resemble the digits of the fifth-day moon. That [beauty] is endowed, united, with their splendors, their radiances. That is the beauty of the Sage’s feet, which are themselves lotuses. ‘Vo’ refers to ‘you’ in general. ‘Avataṃ’ means ‘may it protect.’

141. Bālindu…pe… kantibhi taruṇacandavilāsavināsanasabhāvasamannāgatanakhapantisobhāhi saha valitā saṃyuttā sā munindapadambhojakanti sā sambuddhapādapadumasobhā vo tumhe avataṃ rakkhatūti. Bālo ca so indu cāti ca, tassa vibbhamoti ca, taṃ chindati sīlenāti ca, nakhānaṃ āvaliyoti ca, tāsaṃ kantīti ca, bālinduvibbhamacchediyo ca tā nakharāvalikantiyo cāti ca, munindassa padānīti ca, tāniyeva ambhojānīti ca, tesaṃ kantīti ca viggaho.

141. ‘Bālindu’... (and so on)... endowed with the splendor of the rows of nails, which possess the nature of destroying the charm of the youthful moon—that splendor of the Sage’s lotus feet, that splendor of the Fully Awakened One’s lotus feet—may it protect you.
