The analysis is: ‘the young one and that moon,’ and ‘its charm,’ and ‘that which severs it by its nature,’ and ‘the rows of nails,’ and ‘their splendor,’ and ‘the splendors of the rows of nails which are the severers of the young moon’s charm,’ and ‘the Sage’s feet,’ and ‘those very lotuses,’ and ‘their splendor.’

142.

142.

Ukkaṃsavanto [M 0.0164] yo koci,

Guṇo yadi patīyate;

Udāro’yaṃ bhave tena,

Sanāthā bandhapaddhati.

If any quality possessing excellence is perceived, by that, this becomes noble; the method of composition is well-supported.

142. Udārattamavadhārayamāha “ukkaṃsavanto”iccādi. Yo koci “idameve”ti niyamābhāvā guṇo cāgātisayādiko ukkaṃsavanto adhimatto yadi patīyate viññāyate bandheti viññāyati “bandhapaddhatī”ti vakkhamānattā, ayaṃ udāro bhaveti vidhi. Udāroyaṃ hotu, kiṃ tato siyāti āha “teni”ccādi. Tena ukkaṃsavatā guṇena bandhapaddhati racanakkamo nāthabhūtena udāraguṇena saha vattatīti sanāthā, sampadāvāti sampadāvatīti (?) vuttaṃ hoti.

142. Confirming nobility, he said: ‘possessing excellence,’ and so on. Any quality, such as exceeding generosity, which is exceedingly excellent—because there is no restriction of ‘only this’—if it is perceived and understood in the composition (since ‘the method of composition’ will be stated), this is the rule: it is noble. ‘Let this be noble. What would result from that?’ He said: ‘by that,’ and so on. By that excellent quality, the method of composition, the order of arrangement, exists together with the noble quality that acts as a protector; thus it is well-supported. Thus it is said to be an accomplishment.

142. Idāni udārattamuddisati “ukkaṃse”ccādinā. Ukkaṃsavanto atisayavā yokoci guṇo cāgātisayādiko saddāvaliyā paṭipādanīyo ānubhāvo yadi patīyate sace katthaci bandhe viññāyate, ayaṃ yathāvuttaguṇo udāro nāma bhave. Tena kiṃ payojananti ce? Bandhabandhati padāvali tena ukkaṃsavatā guṇena sanāthā sappatiṭṭhā hoti. Ukkaṃso assa atthīti ca, nāthena saha vattatīti ca, bandhassa paddhatīti ca viggaho.

142. Now, he indicates nobility with ‘excellence,’ and so on. Whatever quality possessing excellence and pre-eminence, such as supreme generosity, whose influence is to be expressed through a series of words, if it is perceived or understood in any composition, this quality, as described, is called noble. If one asks, ‘What is its purpose?’ the sequence of words in a composition becomes well-supported and firmly established by that excellent quality. The analysis is: ‘it possesses excellence,’ and ‘it proceeds with a protector,’ and ‘the method of composition.’

143.

143.

Pādambhojarajolitta-gattā yetava gotama;

Aho te jantavo yanti, sabbathā nirajattanaṃ.

O Gotama, those beings whose bodies are smeared with the dust of your lotus feet—ah, those beings attain in every way the state of being without defilement.

143. Tamudāharati “pāde”ccādinā. Gotamāti bhagavantaṃ gottena ālapati. Tava bhagavato pādambhojānaṃ rajāni reṇavo, tehi littāni upadehitāni gattāni yesanti viggaho. Ye janā te jantavo sabbappakārena rajolavenāpyanupalittattā rajehi kilesasaṅkhātehi [M 0.0165] niggatā nirajā, tesaṃ bhāvo nirajattanaṃ nikkilesabhāvaṃ yanti pāpuṇanti. Aho acchariyaṃ yato rajasā littā nāma saṃkiliṭṭhāyeva siyuṃ, bhavaṃ pana pādarajasā vilepane jane niraje karoti. Acchariyaṃ bhavato idanti attho.

143. He illustrates this with ‘pāde,’ and so on. ‘Gotama’ addresses the Blessed One by his clan name. The analysis is: ‘those whose bodies are smeared, anointed, with the dust, the particles, of your, the Blessed One’s, lotus feet.’ Those people, those beings, are free from defilement, having gone forth from the dust known as defilements, because in every way they are unstained even by a speck of that dust. They attain the state of being without defilement, the state of being without taints. Ah, how wonderful! For those smeared with dust would normally be defiled, but you, sir, make people free from defilement by anointing them with the dust of your feet. The meaning is: ‘This of yours is a wonder!’

143. Idāni udāharati “pādambhoje”ccādinā. Bho gotama ye sattā tava tuyhaṃ pādambhojarajolittagattā pādapadumareṇulittamatthakanalāṭādisarīrāvayavayuttā te jantavo sattā sabbathā kilesasaṅkhātarajojallehi anupalittattā sabbappakārena nirajattanaṃ vigatakilesarajobhāvaṃ yanti pāpuṇanti, aho acchariyaṃ. Rajolittā nāma saṃkiliṭṭhā siyuṃ, tvaṃ pana pādarajasā upalittepi satte niraje karosīti bhāvo. Iha bhagavato ukkaṃsaguṇo dīpito hoti. Pādāniyeva ambhojānīti ca, tesaṃ rajānīti ca, tehi littāni gattāni yesanti ca, rajehi kilesehi niggatāti ca, tesaṃ bhāvoti ca vākyaṃ.

143. Now, he illustrates with ‘pādambhoje,’ and so on. O Gotama, those beings whose bodies are smeared with the dust of your lotus feet—that is, whose heads, foreheads, and other bodily parts are covered with the pollen of your lotus feet—those beings, because they are entirely unsmeared by the dirt and dust known as defilements, attain in every way the state of being without defilement, the state where the dust of defilements is gone. Ah, how wonderful! The meaning is: ‘Those smeared with dust would normally be defiled, but you make beings free from defilement even when they are anointed with the dust of your feet.’ Here, the exalted quality of the Blessed One is illuminated. The analysis is: ‘the feet are themselves lotuses,’ and ‘their dust,’ and ‘those whose bodies are smeared by them,’ and ‘free from the dust which is defilements,’ and ‘their state.’

144.

144.

Evaṃ jinānubhāvassa, samukkaṃso’tradissati;

Paññavā vidhinā’nena, cintaye paramīdisaṃ.

Thus, the surpassing excellence of the Conqueror’s power is seen here; the wise one should contemplate other such supreme things by this method.

144. Ko panettha ukkaṃsavanto guṇo yena bandho sanātho siyāti ce? Āha “eva”miccādi. Evamiti jinānubhāvassa sammāsambuddhapabhāvassa samukkaṃso atisayo dissati padissate atra bandhe, tasmā jinānubhāvena ukkaṃsavatā guṇena bandho sanātho siyāti. Pakāramimamaññatrapiatidisanto āha “paññavā”tiādi. Paññavā paññāsampanno anena vidhinā iminā pakārena edisaṃ evarūpaṃ paraṃ aññaṃ cintaye vitakkeyya.

144. If one asks, ‘What, then, is the excellent quality here by which the composition might be well-supported?’ he says: ‘Thus,’ and so on. ‘Thus’—the surpassing excellence, the pre-eminence, of the Conqueror’s power, of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddha’s power, is seen, is evident, here in this composition. Therefore, by the excellent quality of the Conqueror’s power, the composition is well-supported. Extending this principle elsewhere too, he said: ‘the wise one,’ and so on. The wise one, endowed with wisdom, should by this method, by this manner, consider, reflect upon other such supreme things.

144. Idāni [M 0.0166] yathāvuttaguṇanidassanañca sissānusāsanañca dasseti “eva”miccādinā. Atra imissaṃ anantaragāthāyaṃ evaṃ yathāvuttakkamena jinānubhāvassa tathāgatappabhāvassa samukkaṃso ādhikkaṃ dissati padissate, tasmā jinānubhāvasaṅkhātena ukkaṃsavatā guṇena bandho sanātho bhaveyya. Paññavā pasatthañāṇavanto anena vidhinā iminā kamena īdisaṃ paraṃ aññaṃ cintaye kappeyya.

144. Now, with ‘Thus’ and so on, he shows both the demonstration of the qualities as stated and the instruction for disciples. Here, in this immediately following verse, the surpassing excellence, the pre-eminence, of the Conqueror’s power, of the Tathāgata’s power, is seen, is evident, in the way described. Therefore, the composition should be well-supported by the excellent quality designated as the Conqueror’s power. The wise one, possessing excellent wisdom, should by this method, by this manner, consider or reflect upon such another supreme matter.

145.

145.

Udāro sopi viññeyyo,

Yaṃ pasatthavisesanaṃ;

Yathā kīḷāsaro līlā-

Hāsa hāso (ka.) hemaṅgadādayo.

That too should be understood as noble, which is a praiseworthy distinction; just as a pleasure-pond, playful laughter, golden armlets, and so on.

145. Aparamudārappakāraṃ dassetumāha “udāro”iccādi. Yaṃ pasatthaṃ silāghanīyaṃ visesanaṃ upādiyati, sopi na pana yathāvuttova udāro viññeyyo. “Yathe”tyudāharati. Kīḷāya kīḷatthaṃ saro, līlāya yutto hāso, hemaṃ hemamayamaṅgadanti samāso, taṃ ādi yesanti bāhirattho. Ādisaddena kusumadāmamaṇimekhalādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Ayaṃ tu bandhapharusagāmmapariccāgā sambhavati.

145. To show another kind of nobility, he said: ‘noble’ and so on. That which takes on a praiseworthy, commendable distinction—that too should be understood as noble, not just as previously stated. He illustrates with ‘Just as’. A lake for play, laughter endowed with charm, ‘hemaṅgada’ is a compound meaning ‘golden armlet’—this is the external meaning of ‘and so on’. By the word ‘and so on’ are included flower garlands, jeweled girdles, and the like. This, however, arises from the relinquishment of harshness and vulgarity in composition.

145. Aññamapi udāraṃ dasseti “udāro”ccādinā. Yaṃ pasatthavisesanaṃ pasaṃsanīyavisesanaṃ hoti, sopi udāroti viññeyyo. “Yathā”ti tamudāharati. Kīḷāsaro kīḷāya kato saro. Līlāhāso līlāya yutto hāso. Hemaṅgadādayo suvaṇṇakeyūrāiccādayoti. Kīḷatthāya saroti ca, līlāya yutto hāsoti ca, hemaṃ hemamayaṃ aṅgadanti ca, līlāhāso ca hemaṅgadañcāti ca, tāni ādīni yesaṃ kusumadāmamaṇimekhalādīnanti ca viggaho. Ayamudāro bandhapharusagāmmādidosapariccāgena sijjhati.

145. He shows yet another noble quality, saying: ‘noble’ and so on. That which is a praiseworthy distinction, a commendable distinction, that too should be understood as noble. He illustrates that with ‘Just as’. A pleasure-pond is a pond made for play. Playful laughter is laughter endowed with charm. Golden armlets and so on are golden bracelets and the like. The analysis is: ‘a pond for the purpose of play’, and ‘laughter endowed with charm’, and ‘golden, made of gold, armlet’, and ‘playful laughter and golden armlet’, and ‘those of which these are the beginning, such as flower garlands, jeweled girdles, and the like’. This nobility is accomplished by abandoning faults like harshness and vulgarity in composition.

146.

146.

Lokiyatthānatikkantā,

[M 0.0167] Kantā sabbajanānapi;

Kanti nāmā’tivuttassa,

Vuttā sā parihārato.

Not surpassing worldly meaning, and pleasing to all people—that is called ‘beauty’ (kanti), which is said to arise from avoiding that which is overstated.

Yathā “muninda”iccādi.

As in ‘muninda’ and so on.

146. Kantiṃ kathayati “lokiyi”ccādinā. Loke vidito lokiyo, taṃ lokiyaṃ atthaṃ abhidheyyaṃ anatikkantā anatītā sabbesaṃ kavīnamitaresaṃ vā janānaṃ eva kantā manoharā kanti nāmāti vuccati. Ayaṃ pana saddaguṇo ativuttassa vākyadosassa pariccāgena sambhavati. Tenāha “ativuttassā”tiādi. Udāharaṇattho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva.

146. He describes beauty (kanti) with ‘lokiya’ and so on. ‘Lokiya’ means known in the world; that which does not surpass that worldly meaning, the subject matter, but is pleasing and charming to all, whether poets or other people, is called ‘kanti’. This quality of sound, however, arises from the relinquishment of the fault of excessive verbiage in a sentence. Therefore, he said: ‘of that which is overstated’ and so on. The meaning of the example has already been stated below.

146. Idāni kantiṃ dasseti “lokiyi”ccādinā. Lokiyatthānatikkantā loke pasiddhasaddatthamanatikkantā sabbajanānaṃ sakalakavīnaṃ kantā manuññā kanti nāma vuccate, sā ativuttassa ativuttadosassa parihārato vuttā dosaparihāraparicchede kathitā hoti. Ativuttadosaparihārato eva kantiyā siddhattā tassa lakkhiyo eva etissā hotīti adhippāyo. Loke viditoti ca, so ca so attho ceti ca viggaho. “Yathā”ti kantiyā udāharaṇaṃ dasseti “muninda”iccādi. Taṃ vuttameva.

146. Now, he shows kanti (beauty) with ‘lokiya’ and so on. That which does not transgress worldly meanings, which does not go beyond the well-known meaning of words in the world, and which is charming and delightful to all people and all poets, is called kanti. It is stated in the section on the elimination of faults as the avoidance of the fault of over-expression. Since kanti is achieved precisely through the avoidance of the fault of over-expression, that very avoidance is its characteristic—this is the intended meaning. The analysis is 'known in the world' and 'that very meaning'. With ‘Just as’, he shows the example of kanti with 'lord of sages' and so on. That has already been stated.

147.

147.

Atthabyattā’bhidheyyassā-

Neyyatā saddato’tthato;

Sā’yaṃ tadubhayā neyya-

Parihāre padassitā.

Clarity of meaning is the quality of the intended meaning not needing to be inferred, whether from the word or from the sense. This quality, arising from both, is shown in the avoidance of the obscure.

Yathā “marīci”ccādi ca, “manonurañjano”ccādi ca.

As in ‘marīci’ and so on, and ‘manonurañjano’ and so on.

147. Atthabyattiṃ [M 0.0168] byañjayati “atthabyattābhidheyyi”ccādinā. Abhidheyyassa sambandhaatthassa saddato atthato vā sāmatthiyato vā aneyyatā patīti aññathā vagamo gatyantarābhāvā, yato vuttaṃ “dullabhāvagatī sadda-sāmatthiyavilaṅghinī”ti. Tamanuvaditvā atthabyatti vidhīyate. Sā pana byākiṇṇaneyyādidosavajjanāya jāyate. Tadubhayā jātā sāyaṃ aneyyatā neyyaparihāre padassitā pakāsitā. Paṭhamadutiyodāharaṇassattho vutto.

147. He explains clarity of meaning with ‘clarity of meaning, of what is to be expressed’ and so on. The non-inferability of the connected meaning of what is to be expressed—whether from the word, from the sense, or from its power—is the intended understanding; otherwise, there is a different understanding due to the absence of another way. For it is said: 'Rare is the comprehension that transgresses the power of word and meaning.' Having stated that, clarity of meaning is prescribed. It arises from the avoidance of faults such as diffuseness, obscurity, and so on. This non-inferability, arising from both, is shown and revealed in the avoidance of the obscure. The meaning of the first and second examples has been stated.

147. Idāni atthabyattiṃ dasseti “atthabyatti”ccādinā. Abhidheyyassa atthassa saddato atthato atthasāmatthiyato ca aneyyatā tattheva vijjamānattā saddassa atthassa vā āharitvā vattabbassa abhāvo atthabyatti nāma, tadubhayā tehi dvīhi jātā sā ayaṃ aneyyatāsaṅkhatā atthabyatti neyyaparihāre neyyadosaparihārapadese padassitā pakāsitāti. “Dullabhāvagatī sadda-sāmatthiyavilaṅghinī”ti vuttattā atthapatīti pana vinā saddañca sāmatthiyañca aññathānupalabbhatīti iha “saddato atthato”ti vuttaṃ. Atthassa byatti patītīti ca, natthi neyyaṃ āharitabbaṃ assa abhidheyyassāti ca, tassa bhāvoti ca, te ca te ubho saddatthā cāti ca, te avayavā etissāti ca, neyyassa parihāroti ca vākyaṃ. Idāni “yathe”ccādinā dvippakārāya atthabyattiyā yathākkamaṃ udāharaṇamanussāreti “mari”ccādigāthādvayena, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva.

147. Now, he shows clarity of meaning with ‘clarity of meaning’ and so on. The non-inferability of the meaning to be expressed—whether from the word, from the sense, or from the power of the sense—which, due to its existing right there, is the absence of any need to bring forth and state the word or the meaning, is called 'clarity of meaning'. This clarity of meaning, designated as non-inferability, arising from both, from those two, is shown and revealed in the avoidance of the obscure, in the section on avoiding the fault of obscurity. Because it is said, 'Rare is the comprehension that transgresses the power of word and meaning,' and because the comprehension of meaning cannot be found otherwise, without the word and its power, it is here said, 'from the word, from the sense'. The analysis is: 'the clarity and comprehension of meaning'; 'there is nothing obscure to be brought forth for this intended meaning'; 'the state of that'; 'both those are word and sense'; 'those are its components'; and 'the avoidance of the obscure'. Now, with ‘as’ and so on, he recalls the examples in order for the two kinds of clarity of meaning with the two verses beginning with ‘marīci’, which has already been stated below.

Puna atthena yathā –

Again, by meaning, as follows:

148.

148.

Sabhāvāmalatā dhīra,

Mudhā pādanakhesu te;

Yato te’vanatānanta-

Moḷicchāyā jahanti no.

O wise one, the natural purity on your toenails is in vain, for the shadows of the crowns of the bowed-down Ananta do not abandon them.

148. Puna [M 0.0169] dutiye tu dhīrāti āmantanaṃ. Te tava pādanakhesu sabhāvāmalatā pakatiparisuddhatā mudhā tucchā. Kasmāti ce? Yato yasmā kāraṇā te pādanakhā avanatassa sannatassa anantassa nāgarājassa moḷino kirīṭassa avanatānaṃ vā naramarānaṃ anantānaṃ moḷīnaṃ chāyā chaviyo no jahanti na pariccajanti, sañchaviyo pana jahantīti. Ettha nakhesu sañchavittā pādanakhassa moḷīnaṃ nirantarappaṇāmābyabhicārānaramarādīnaṃ bhagavato pādāravindavandanaṃ sāmatthiyā phuṭaṃ gamyate.

148. Again, in the second verse, 'O wise one' is an address. The natural purity, the inherent cleanliness, on your toenails is in vain, empty. If you ask why: because the shadows and hues of the crown of the bowed-down, humble Ananta, the serpent king, or of the crowns of the infinite bowed-down men and gods, do not abandon your toenails, do not forsake them; rather, their own hues are abandoned. Here, from the fact that the nails have these hues, the worship of the Blessed One's lotus feet by men, gods, and others—whose prostration with their crowns before the toenails is constant and unfailing—is clearly understood by implication.

148. “Puna atthena yathā sabhāvi”ccādi. Dhīra te tava pādanakhesu sabhāvāmalatā pakatiparisuddhatā mudhā tucchā. Kasmāti ce? Yato yasmā te caraṇanakhā avanatānantamoḷicchāyā pādānatassa anantanāgarājassa kirīṭassa sambandhinī, avanatānaṃ vā anantānaṃ devamanussānaṃ moḷīnaṃ chāyā kantiyo no jahanti na vijahanti, pakativaṇṇaṃ pahāya kirīṭakantisadisā te honti, tasmā ettha candakiraṇasannibhānaṃ nakharaṃsīnaṃ samīpe moḷīnaṃ nakharaṃsīhi amadditasakakantiyuttabhāvamāpajjanaṃ tādisānaṃ nirantarappaṇāmābhāvābhāvato khattiyādīnaṃ munindapādāravindadvande nirantarappaṇāmo sāmatthiyā vibhūtaṃ gamyate. Sassa bhāvoti ca, tena amalāti ca, tesaṃ bhāvoti ca, paṭhamapakkhe avanato ca so ananto cāti ca, tassa moḷīti ca, tassa chāyāyoti ca, dutiyapakkhe anantā ca te moḷī ceti ca, avanatānaṃ anantamoḷīti ca, tesaṃ chāyāyoti ca vākyaṃ.

148. Again, by meaning, as in ‘natural state’ and so on. O wise one, the natural purity on your toenails, their inherent cleanliness, is in vain, empty. If you ask why: because your toenails are such that the shadows and splendors of the crown of the bowed-down Ananta, the serpent king, or the shadows and splendors of the crowns of the infinite bowed-down gods and humans, do not abandon them, do not forsake them; having abandoned their natural color, they become like the splendor of a crown. Therefore, here, because the crowns, though near the moonbeam-like rays of the nails, possess their own splendor undiminished by those rays—which is due to the very presence of constant prostration by such beings—the constant prostration of Khattiyas and others to the pair of lotus feet of the Lord of Sages is clearly understood by implication. The analysis is: 'its nature,' and 'thus stainless,' and 'their nature'; in the first interpretation, 'he who bows and is infinite,' and 'his crown,' and 'its shadow'; in the second interpretation, 'they are infinite and those crowns,' and 'the infinite crowns of those who bow,' and 'their shadow'.

149.

149.

“Bandhasāro”ti maññanti, yaṃ samaggāpi viññuno;

Dassanāvasaraṃ patto, samādhi nāma’yaṃ guṇo.

That which even all the wise consider 'the essence of composition'—this quality, called 'samādhi', has reached the occasion for its demonstration.

149. Samādhiphalaṃ kiccāha “bandhe”ccādi. Yanti yaṃ samādhiṃ bandhassa gajjapajjamissabhāvassa sāroti sabbassa jīvitaṃ [M 0.0170] tapparāyattā bandhassa samaggāpi viññuno sabbepi kavino maññanti cintenti jānanti, ayaṃ samādhi nāma samādhikhyo guṇo dassane pakāsane avasaraṃ okāsaṃ anottarattā parassa sampatto uddiṭṭhānukkamenāti.

149. Having stated the fruit of samādhi, he says 'in composition' and so on. That samādhi which all the wise and all the poets think, consider, and know to be the essence of composition—the state of being a mixture of prose and verse—and the life of all composition, because it depends on that; this quality, named samādhi, has attained the opportunity, the occasion, for manifestation and revelation, being unsurpassed by another, in the order stated.

149. Idāni samādhayo niddisati “bandhi”ccādinā. Samaggā api viññuno sabbepi kavayo yaṃ samādhiṃ “bandhasāro”ti pajjagajjavimissasaṅkhātassa bandhassa jīvitamiti maññanti, ayaṃ samādhi nāma guṇo dassanāvasaraṃ patto uddiṭṭhānukkamena dassanokāsaṃ patto hoti. Bandhassa sāroti ca, dassane avasaranti ca, taṃ pattoti ca viggaho.

149. Now he indicates the samādhis (excellences of composition) with 'composition' and so on. All the wise and all the poets, united, consider that samādhi to be 'the essence of composition'—the life of composition, known as the mixed form of verse and prose. This quality, called samādhi, has attained the opportunity for manifestation, has attained the occasion for manifestation in the order stated. The analysis is: 'the essence of composition,' and 'opportunity for manifestation,' and 'having attained that'.

150.

150.

Aññadhammo tato’ññattha,

Lokasīmānurodhato;

Sammā ādhīyate’cce’so,

Samādhīti niruccati.

A quality of another object, elsewhere from that primary object, due to conformity with worldly convention, is rightly applied; thus, this is called 'samādhi'.

150. Kathamayaṃ saddavohāro bandhe “samādhī”ti vuccatītyāha “aññe”ccādi. Aññassa vatthuno pakatāpekkhāya dhammo guṇo pasiddho, tato tasmā mukhyavisayā aññattha amukhye visaye lokasīmānurodhato lokappatītyanuvattanena sammā sādhu lokasīmānuvattanameveha sādhuttaṃ ādhīyate āropyate, iti iminā kāraṇena eso evaṃvidho dhammo “samādhī”ti niruccatītidha sammā ādhīyatīti evaṃ nīharitvā vuccatīti attho.

150. To the question, 'How is this verbal usage 'samādhi' employed in composition?', he says 'another' and so on. A quality, a property, of another object is well-known with respect to its original context. Therefore, from that primary domain, elsewhere in a secondary domain, due to conformity with worldly convention, by following worldly understanding, it is rightly and properly applied or imposed—this very conformity to worldly convention being the propriety here. For this reason, such a quality is called 'samādhi'; the meaning is that it is so called because it is explained thus: 'it is rightly applied here'.

150. “Samādhī”ti ayaṃ vohāro bandhavisaye kathaṃ pavattatīti āsaṅkāyaṃ paṭhamaṃ nibbacanaṃ dassetuṃ āha “aññi”ccādi. Yasmā aññadhammo samādhānassa visayabhūtaamukhyato aññassa mukhyavatthuno pasiddhaguṇo, tato [M 0.0171] mukhyavisayato aññattha amukhyavisaye lokasīmānurodhato lokavohāramariyādāvirodhabhāvena lokappatītyanuvattaneneva sammā ādhīyati ṭhapīyati, iti iminā kāraṇena eso yathāvuttaguṇo “samādhī”ti niruccati vuccatīti. Aññassa dhammoti ca, lokassa sīmāti ca, tassā anurodhoti ca viggaho.

150. To address the question of how this term 'samādhi' functions in the domain of composition, he first presents the derivation, beginning 'another' and so on. Because a quality of another—a well-known property of a primary object, different from the secondary object of application—is rightly applied and established in a secondary domain, different from the primary domain, due to conformity with worldly convention, by following worldly understanding and without conflicting with the established norms of worldly usage; for this reason, this quality as described is termed 'samādhi,' is so called. The analysis is: 'a quality of another,' and 'the world’s convention,' and 'conformity to it'.

Samādhiuddesa

Exposition of Samādhi

151.

151.

Apāṇe pāṇinaṃ dhammo, sammā ādhīyate kvaci;

Nirūpe rūpayuttassa, nirase sarasassa ca.

In the inanimate, the quality of the animate is sometimes rightly attributed; in the formless, that of what possesses form; and in the tasteless, that of what possesses taste.

152.

152.

Adrave dravayuttassa, akattaripi kattutā;

Kaṭhinassā’sarīrepi, rūpaṃ tesaṃ kamā siyā.

In the non-fluid, that of what possesses fluidity; even in a non-agent, agency; and even in the bodiless, the quality of the hard. Their examples should follow in order.

151-152. Samādhānavisayamāha “apāṇe”iccādi. Kvaci ṭhāne pāṇinaṃ pāṇavantānaṃ padatthānaṃ dhammo guṇo apāṇe pāṇavirahite vatthuni sammā lokapatītyanuvattanena ādhīyate āropyate, evamuparipi yathānurūpaṃ. Nirūpeti rūpavirahite vatthuni, kvacīti sabbattha anuvattati. Asarīre aghane asaṃhate vatthuni kaṭhinassa daḷhassa, tesaṃ yathāvuttānaṃ samādhīnaṃ rūpaṃ udāharaṇaṃ kamā uddiṭṭhānukkamena.

151-152. He states the domain of application with 'in the inanimate,' etc. In some places, the quality or property of animate beings, of things that have life, is rightly attributed or imposed upon an inanimate object, an object devoid of life, by conforming to worldly understanding. And similarly for the following, as is appropriate. 'In the formless' means in an object devoid of form; and 'sometimes' applies throughout. In a bodiless, non-solid, uncompacted object, the quality of the hard, the firm, is attributed. The illustration, the example, of these samādhis, as stated, follows in the order indicated.

151-152. Uddese “samādhayo”ti bahuvacanena niddiṭṭhānaṃ samādhīnaṃ visayamupadasseti “apāṇe”ccādinā. Kvaci kismiñci ṭhāne pāṇinaṃ dhammo indriyabaddhānaṃ guṇo apāṇe pāṇarahitavatthumhi sammā lokapatītianusārena ādhīyate āropyate, kvaci rūpayuttassa rūpavantavatthuno dhammo nirūpe rūparahitavatthumhi, kvaci sarasassa rasavantassa vatthuno dhammo nirase rasarahite ca, kvaci dravayuttassa dravavantavatthuno dhammo adrave dravarahite ca, [M 0.0172] kvaci kattutā kattuguṇo akattaripi, kvaci kaṭhinassa thaddhassa vatthuno dhammo asarīrepi sarīrarahitepi sammā ādhīyate. Tesaṃ channaṃ samādhīnaṃ rūpaṃ udāharaṇaṃ kamā “apāṇe pāṇina”nti uddiṭṭhānukkamena siyā bhaveyyāti. Na santi pāṇā asseti ca, rūpā niggatoti ca, rūpena yuttoti ca, rasā niggatoti ca, rasena saha vattamānoti ca, dravāaññoti ca, dravena dravabhāvena yuttoti ca, kattuto aññoti ca, kattuno bhāvoti ca, natthi sarīraṃ assāti ca viggaho.

151-152. In the summary, he indicates the domain of the samādhis, which were designated by the plural term 'samādhis', with 'in the inanimate' and so on. In some places, the quality of animate beings, the property of those bound by the faculties, is rightly attributed or imposed upon an inanimate object, an object devoid of life, according to worldly understanding. In some cases, the quality of an object possessing form is attributed to the formless, an object devoid of form. In some instances, the quality of an object possessing taste is attributed to the tasteless, that which is devoid of taste. In some cases, the quality of an object possessing fluidity is attributed to the non-fluid, that which is devoid of fluidity. In some places, agency, the quality of an agent, is attributed even to a non-agent. In some cases, the quality of a hard, rigid object is attributed even to the bodiless, that which is devoid of a body. The illustration, the example, for these six types of samādhi should be in the order indicated by 'in the inanimate, of the animate.' The analysis is: 'it has no life in it,' and 'devoid of form,' and 'endowed with form,' and 'devoid of taste,' and 'existing with taste,' and 'other than fluid,' and 'endowed with the state of fluidity,' and 'other than an agent,' and 'the state of an agent,' and 'it has no body'.

Samādhiniddesa

Exposition of Samādhi

Apāṇe pāṇinaṃ dhammo

The quality of the animate in the inanimate.

153.

153.

Uṇṇāpuṇṇindunā nātha, divāpi saha saṅgamā;

Viniddā sampamodanti, maññe kumudinī tava.

O Lord, I imagine that your water-lilies, from their union with the full moon that is your uṇṇā, rejoice greatly, unsleeping, even by day.

153. “Uṇṇā”iccādi. Nāthāti lokattayekapaṭisaraṇabhūtatāya bhagavantaṃ ālapati. Tava uṇṇāromadhātusaṅkhātena puṇṇindunā saha saṅgamā saṃyogena kumudinī kumudiniyo kumudākarā divāpi viniddā vigatasoppā sampamodanti maññe suṭṭhuyeva pamodantīti parikappemīti. Ettha pāṇidhammassa suratarūpassa saṅgamassa viniddāya sampīṇanassa ca apāṇini āropitapumbhāve uṇṇāpuṇṇindumhi, tathā āropitaitthibhāvāsu kumudinīsu lokasīmānurodhena samādhānato soyaṃ pasiddho dhammo “samādhī”ti vuccati. Tadabhidhāyī saddo ca upacārato atthānugāmittā saddikavohāraṃ dasseti, evamuparipi yathāyogaṃ.

153. 'Uṇṇā,' etc. He addresses the Blessed One as 'Lord' because he is the sole refuge of the three worlds. 'I imagine that your water-lilies, your lotus ponds, from union, from conjunction, with the full moon that is your uṇṇā-hair-relic, rejoice greatly, unsleeping, with sleep departed, even by day.' Here, the qualities of the animate—namely sexual union, wakefulness, and delight—are imposed upon inanimate things: upon the uṇṇā-full-moon, to which a masculine nature is attributed, and likewise upon the water-lilies, to which a feminine nature is attributed. Through this application in conformity with worldly convention, this well-known quality is called 'samādhi.' And the term expressing it, by metaphorical transfer and adherence to the meaning, illustrates the verbal usage. Similarly for the following, as appropriate.

153. Tesu pāṇidhammasamādhino udāharaṇamādisati “uṇṇā”iccādinā. Nātha tava tuyhaṃ uṇṇāpuṇṇindunā uṇṇāromamaṇḍalasaṅkhātapuṇṇacandena saha saṅgamā aññamaññasamavāyahetunā kumudinī keravākarasaṅkhātā kumudiniyo divāpi [M 0.0173] viniddā vikasitā sampamodanti maññe atisantuṭṭhā hontīti kappemīti indusampamodo sahasaddena ñāyate. Ettha pāṇidhammasaṅkhāto suratasaṅgamo ca niddāpagamo ca sampamodanañcāti tiṇṇaṃ uṇṇāpuṇṇindukumudinīsaṅkhātesu apāṇesu lokavohārānatikkamma buddhiyā āropanena pāṇidhammato pasiddhā tayo atthā idha samādhayo nāma, tappaṭipādakaganthopi atthānugāmittā tadupacārena samādhīti daṭṭhabbo. Puṇṇo ca so indu ceti ca, uṇṇā eva puṇṇindu cāti ca, vigatā niddā yehīti ca viggaho.

153. Among them, he gives the example of the samādhi concerning the quality of the animate, beginning with 'uṇṇā,' etc. 'O Lord, your water-lilies, also called keravākaras, from their union—by reason of mutual connection—with your full moon, which is the circle of the uṇṇā-hair, rejoice greatly, unsleeping and blooming, even by day; I imagine they are supremely satisfied.' The delight of the moon is understood from the word 'saha' (with). Here, three meanings known as qualities of the animate—namely, sexual union, the departure of sleep, and great rejoicing—are, by intellectual imposition that does not transgress worldly usage, attributed to the inanimate uṇṇā-full-moon and water-lilies. These three meanings, well-known from the qualities of the animate, are here called samādhis. And the text that expounds this should also be seen as 'samādhi' by metaphorical transfer, due to its adherence to the meaning. The analysis is: 'and that moon is full,' and 'the uṇṇā is indeed the full moon,' and 'those from whom sleep has departed'.

Nirūpe rūpayuttassa

In the formless, the quality of that which possesses form.

154.

154.

Dayārasesu mujjantā, janā’matarasesvi’va;

Sukhitā hatadosā te, nātha pādambujānatā.

O Lord, people who bow at your lotus feet, immersing themselves in the flavors of compassion as if in the flavors of nectar, are happy, their faults destroyed.

154. “Dayā”iccādi. Nātha te pādambujesu ānatā paṇāmavasena janā tilokakuharapavattino sattā amatarasesviva pīyūsarasesu viya dayārasesu karuṇārasesu guṇesu. “Siṅgārādo vise vīriye, guṇe rāge drave raso”ti amarakosa 3.3.226 hi nighaṇṭu. Mujjantā nimujjamānā hatā naṭṭhā dosā vātādayo amatapakkhe, aññattha tu hatā naṭṭhā dosā rāgādayo yesanti viggaho, tatoyeva sukhitā sukhaṃ kāyikacetasikasukhaṃ itā pattā gatāti attho.

154. 'Dayā,' etc. O Lord, beings proceeding in the hollow of the three worlds, people bowing down at your lotus feet, are immersed in the qualities that are the flavors of compassion, the flavors of loving-kindness, as if in the flavors of nectar, the flavors of ambrosia. For the lexicon states: 'Rasa is used for erotic sentiment, poison, energy, quality, passion, and liquid.' 'Immersing' means sinking down. The analysis of 'with faults destroyed' is: 'those whose faults are destroyed, annihilated.' In the case of nectar, the faults are bodily humors like wind; in the other case, the faults are defilements like lust. Therefore, 'happy' means having gone to, attained, or reached happiness, that is, bodily and mental happiness. This is the meaning.

154. Idāni rūpadhammasamādhino udāharaṇaṃ uddisati “dayā”iccādinā. Nātha te tava pādambujānatā caraṇapadume paṇatā janā devamanussā amatarasesu iva sudhājalesu viya dayārasesu anaññasādhāraṇakaruṇāguṇesu mujjantā nimujjamānā hatadosā vinaṭṭhavātapittādayo vinaṭṭharāgādidosā vā sukhitā tatoyeva ajarāmarasaṅkhātasukhaṃ [M 0.0174] itā pattāti. Ettha rūpayuttajale labbhamānaṃ mujjanaṃ nirūpe dayāguṇe āropitaṃ hoti. Dayā eva rasā guṇāti ca, amatā eva rasāti ca, hatā vātādayo rāgādayo vā dosā yesanti ca, pādāni eva ambujānīti ca, tesu ānatāti ca viggaho.

154. Now, an example of the samādhi of the quality of form is indicated, beginning with 'compassion.' 'O Lord, those people and devas bowing at your lotus feet, immersing themselves in the flavors of compassion—in the qualities of compassion which are without parallel—as if in the flavors of nectar or the waters of ambrosia, become happy, their faults destroyed. Their imbalances of wind, bile, and so on are destroyed, or their defilements of lust and so on are destroyed; and for that very reason, they attain the happiness known as the ageless and deathless.' Here, the act of immersion, which is found in water possessing form, is superimposed upon the formless quality of compassion. The analyses are: 'Compassion itself is the essence, the quality'; 'the deathless itself is the essence'; 'those whose faults—wind and so on, or lust and so on—are destroyed'; 'the feet themselves are lotuses'; and 'bowing to them.'

“Siṅgārādovise vīriye, guṇe rāge draveraso”ti amarakosa 3.3.226 ettha rasasaddo guṇajalesu vattati.

'Rasa means embellishment, poison, energy, quality, attachment, and liquid'—here, the word 'rasa' is used in the sense of qualities and liquids.

Nirase sarasassa

Of that with taste, in the tasteless.

155.

155.

Madhurepi guṇe dhīra, nappasīdanti ye tava;

Kīdisīmanaso vutti, tesaṃ khāraguṇānabho he (sī.).

O wise one, even in your sweet qualities, those who do not delight—what is the state of mind of them, who possess harsh qualities?

155. “Madhure”ccādi. Dhiyā īratīti dhīro, bho dhīra tava madhurepi manoharepi guṇe karuṇādike ye nappasīdanti pasādaṃ na karonti, khāraguṇānaṃ amadhuraguṇānaṃ tesaṃ janānaṃ manaso vutti cittappavatti kīdisīti kimiva dissati, na viññāyate “īdisī”ti. Yato tādisaguṇāvabodhaparammukhā mohandhakārasambandhitāti.

155. 'Sweet,' etc. One who is moved by wisdom is a wise one. O wise one, even in your sweet and delightful qualities, such as compassion, are those who do not become serene, who do not generate serenity. Of those people who possess harsh, unsweet qualities, what is the state of their mind, the course of their thought, like? It cannot be known as 'such and such,' because they are turned away from understanding such qualities, being connected to the darkness of delusion.

155. Idāni sarasadhammasamādhino udāharaṇamuddisati “madhuri”ccādinā. Bho dhīra tava te madhure api guṇe pakatisundare karuṇāpaññāguṇepi ye hīnādhimuttikā janā nappasīdanti, khāraguṇānaṃ amadhuraguṇānaṃ tesaṃ janānaṃ manaso vutti cittappavatti kīdisī kathaṃ ruhati. Dhiyā īrati pavattatīti ca, kā viya sā dissatīti ca, khārā guṇā yesanti ca viggaho. Ettha samādhi nāma rasahīne āropitarasayuttadhammabhūtaṃ madhurakhāraguṇadvayaṃ.

155. Now, an example of the samādhi of the quality of taste is indicated, beginning with 'sweet.' 'O wise one, even in your sweet, naturally beautiful qualities, even in the qualities of compassion and wisdom, there are those people of inferior inclinations who do not become serene. Of those people who possess harsh, unsweet qualities, what is the state of their mind, the course of their thought? How does it arise?' The analyses are: 'One who is moved by, who proceeds by, wisdom'; 'what does it appear like?'; and 'those whose qualities are harsh.' Here, samādhi is the name for the duality of sweet and harsh qualities—which are qualities possessing taste—superimposed on that which is devoid of taste.

Adrave dravayuttassa

Of that connected with fluidity, in the non-fluid.

156.

156.

Sabbatthasiddha [M 0.0175] cūḷaka-puṭapeyyā mahāguṇā;

Disā samantā dhāvanti, kundasobhāsalakkhaṇā.

O Sabbatthasiddha, your great qualities, to be drunk from a small vessel and marked by the splendor of kunda flowers, run in all directions.

156. “Sabbatthasiddhi”ccādi. Sabbatthasiddhassa mahāmunino cūḷakapuṭena peyyā pātabbā kundasobhāsalakkhaṇā kundakusumassa sobhāsavantā jutivijambhino mahāguṇā samantā parito disā disantāni dhāvanti.

156. 'Sabbatthasiddhi,' etc. Of Sabbatthasiddhi, the Great Sage, the great qualities—to be drunk from a small vessel, marked by the splendor of kunda flowers, possessing the splendor of kunda flowers, expanding with radiance—run everywhere, all around, in all directions and intermediate directions.

156. Idāni dravayuttasamādhino udāharaṇamuddisati “sabbatthi”ccādinā. Sabbatthasiddha sabbakicce parinipphanna, nipphannehi sabbatthehi vā samannāgata he tathāgata tava cūḷakapuṭapeyyā cūḷakapuṭena pātabbā kundasobhāsalakkhaṇā kundasobhāhi samānalakkhaṇā kundasobhāsadisā vā mahāguṇā saṅkhyāmahantattā ānubhāvamahantattā vā mahantā vā arahattādayo guṇā samantā samantato disā dasadisāsu dhāvantīti. Ettha dravayuttaguṇabhūto cūḷakapuṭapeyyabhāvo dravarahite guṇe āropito samādhi nāma hoti. Sabbe ca te atthā ceti ca, te siddhā yasseti ca, cūḷakameva puṭamiti ca, tena peyyāti ca, mahantā ca te guṇā ceti ca, kundānaṃ sobhāti ca, tāhi samānaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ yesanti ca viggaho.

156. Now, an example of the samādhi connected with fluidity is indicated, beginning with 'sabbatthi,' etc. 'O Tathāgata, Sabbatthasiddha—perfected in all duties, or endowed with all accomplished aims—your great qualities, to be drunk from a small vessel, marked by the splendor of kunda flowers, having characteristics similar to the splendor of kunda flowers, or resembling the splendor of kunda flowers—great either in number or in power, or the great qualities such as Arahantship—run everywhere, all around, in the ten directions.' Here, the state of being 'to be drunk from a small vessel,' which is a quality associated with fluidity, being superimposed on a quality devoid of liquid, is called samādhi. The analyses are: 'And all are those aims'; 'those are accomplished for whom'; 'a small vessel indeed is the container'; 'to be drunk by that'; 'and those are great qualities'; 'the splendor of kunda flowers'; and 'those whose characteristics are similar to them.'

Akattari kattutā

The state of an agent, in a non-agent.

157.

157.

Mārāribalavissaṭṭhā, kuṇṭhā nānāvidhā’yudhā;

Lajjamānā’ññavesena, jina pādānatā tava.

Hurled by the power of Māra the enemy, the various weapons, blunted, ashamed, and in another guise, bowed at your feet, O Victor.

157. “Mārā”iccādi. Māroyeva ari sattūti mārārī, tena, balena attano sattiyā, tassa vā balena senāya vissaṭṭhā abhimukhaṃ chaḍḍitā nānāvidhā anekappakārā [M 0.0176] āyudhā bhindivāḷādayo kuṇṭhā bheṇḍivālādayo (ka.) pariccattatikhiṇabhāvā tāyeva kuṇṭhabhāvappattiyā lajjamānā “lokappatītānubhāvānamamhākampi evarūpaṃ jāta”nti lajjantā aññavesena “kathaṃ nāma pare amhe na jāneyyu”nti attano āvudhavesaṃ parivattitvā kusumavesena, jināti āmantanaṃ, tava pādānatā pādesu sannatā.

157. 'Mārā,' etc. Māra himself is the enemy, thus 'Mārārī' (Māra-the-enemy). Hurled forth by him, by his power, by his own strength, or by the strength of his army, various kinds of weapons, such as spears, became blunted, having abandoned their sharpness. Ashamed at having attained that blunted state, thinking, 'Such a thing has happened even to us, whose power is renowned in the world!', and thinking, 'How can we prevent others from recognizing us?', they changed their weapon-form into a flower-form with another guise. 'Jina' is a vocative. 'Tava pādānatā' means bowed at your feet, prostrate at your feet.

157. Idāni kattudhammasamādhino udāharaṇamuddisati “mārāri”ccādinā. He jina mārāribalavissaṭṭhā mārasattunā attano sattiyā vissaṭṭhā, mārārino vā senāya vissaṭṭhā abhimukhe pātitā nānāvidhāyudhā anekappakārabhindivāḷaususattitomarādayo āvudhā kuṇṭhā atikhiṇā lajjamānā “kasmā evaṃ lokapasiddhānubhāvānamamhākampi īdisaṃ vippakāramahosī”ti lajjantā aññavesena “kathamamhe pare na jāneyyu”nti āvudhavesaṃ hitvā tadaññabhūtena pupphavesena tava pādānatā pādasamīpe natā ahesunti. Ettha kattudhammabhūtaṃ lajjanañca aññavesena parivattanañca ānatañceti ime lajjanādīnaṃ akattubhūtesu visayesu āropitā samādhayo nāma honti. Māro eva arīti ca, balena vissaṭṭhāti ca, mārārinā balavissaṭṭhāti ca mārārino balaṃ senāti ca, tena vissaṭṭhāti ca, nānā anekavidhā pakārā yesanti ca, aññesaṃ vesoti ca, añño ca so veso cāti ca, pādesu ānatāti ca viggaho.

157. Now, an example of the samādhi of the quality of an agent is indicated, beginning with 'mārāri,' etc. 'O Victor, the various kinds of weapons—such as spears, arrows, javelins, and lances—discharged by the enemy Māra with his own power, or discharged by the army of Māra-the-enemy, and cast down before you, became blunted and lost their sharpness. Being ashamed, thinking, "Why has such a misfortune befallen even us, whose power is renowned in the world?", and thinking, "How can we prevent others from recognizing us?", they abandoned their weapon-form for another guise, that of flowers, and bowed at your feet, prostrated near your feet.' Here, shame, transformation into another guise, and bowing—these qualities belonging to an agent, being superimposed on subjects which are not agents, are called samādhis. The analyses are: 'Māra is the enemy'; 'discharged by power'; 'discharged by Māra-the-enemy with power'; 'the power of Māra-the-enemy is his army'; 'discharged by that'; 'those of various, of many, kinds'; 'the guise of another'; 'and that guise is another'; and 'bowed at the feet.'

Kaṭhinassa asarīre

Of the solid, in the bodiless.

158.

158.

Munindabhāṇumā kālo-

Dito bodhodayācale;

Saddhammaraṃsinā bhāti,

Indamandhatamaṃ paraṃ.

The Sun that is the Lord of Sages, having risen at dawn on the Mountain of Enlightenment's Dawn, shines with the rays of the True Dhamma, splitting the uttermost darkness.

158. “Muninda”iccādi. [M 0.0177] Bodho sabbaññutaññāṇasadiso soyeva vā udayācalo udayapabbato tasmiṃ kāle rattipariyante abhinikkhantasamaye udito pātubhūto munindo munindasadiso soyeva vā bhāṇumā sūriyo andhatamaṃ andhakāraṃ mohaṃ vā paraṃ accantameva saddhammaraṃsinā saddhammasadisena saddhammasaṅkhatena vā raṃsinā bhindaṃ padālento bhāti sobhatīti.

158. 'Muninda,' etc. Enlightenment is like all-knowing wisdom, or it is itself the Mountain of Dawn, the Mountain of Sunrise. At that time, at the end of the night, at the moment of the great renunciation, the risen and appeared Lord of Sages—the Sun, who is like the Lord of Sages or is the Lord of Sages himself—shines and gleams, utterly splitting and destroying the supreme darkness, that is, ignorance, with a ray of the True Dhamma, that is, with a ray like the True Dhamma or designated as the True Dhamma.

158. Idāni kaṭhinadhammasamādhino udāharaṇamuddisati “munindi”ccādinā. Bodhodayācale sabbaññutaññāṇasadise sabbaññutaññāṇasaṅkhāte vā udayapabbate kālodito rattikkhaye māraparājitasamaye vā udito pātubhūto munindabhānumā munindasadiso munindoyeva vā sūriyo andhatamaṃ pakatighanandhakāraṃ bahalamohandhakāraṃ saddhammaraṃsinā saddhammasadisena saddhammabhūtena vā kiraṇena paramatisayena bhindaṃ padālento bhāti sobhatīti. Ettha thaddhadhammabhūtaṃ bhedanaṃ asarīrabhūte andhakāre buddhiyā āropitaṃ samādhi nāma hoti. Munīnaṃ indoti ca, soyeva bhānumāti ca, bodho eva udayācaloti ca, saddhammo eva raṃsīti ca viggaho.

158. Now, an example of the samādhi of the quality of solidity is indicated, beginning with 'munindi,' etc. On the Mountain of Enlightenment's Dawn—which is like all-knowing wisdom or is designated as all-knowing wisdom, the Mountain of Sunrise—the Sun that is the Lord of Sages, who is like the sun or is the sun itself, having risen at the proper time, at the end of the night or at the time of Māra's defeat, appeared. He shines exceedingly, splitting and dispelling the natural thick darkness, the dense darkness of delusion, with a ray of the True Dhamma, that is, with a ray like the True Dhamma or that is the True Dhamma itself. Here, the act of splitting, which is a quality of a solid object, being superimposed by the intellect on the formless darkness, is called samādhi. The analyses are: 'The lord of sages'; 'he himself is the sun'; 'enlightenment itself is the Mountain of Dawn'; and 'the True Dhamma itself is the ray.'

159.

159.

Vamanuggiranādye’taṃ, guṇavutyapariccutaṃ;

Atisundaramaññaṃ tu, kāmaṃ vindati gāmmataṃ.

This, such as vomiting and spitting out, when not deviating from its figurative usage, is exceedingly beautiful; but the other certainly obtains vulgarity.

159. Koci dhammo amukhyavisaye bandhe sobhate, na mukhyavisayeti dassanto āha “vamanaṃ”iccādi. Vamanañca uggiranañca, ādisaddena virecanādipariggaho. Etaṃ yathāvuttaṃ guṇā padhānetarā pasiddhavisayā visayantarapariggahalakkhaṇā vutti payogarūpā, tato apariccutaṃ aparigaḷitaṃ santaṃ amukhyabhūtaṃ atisundaraṃ accantamanoharamalaṅkārarūpattā, aññaṃ tu itaraṃ pana mukhyanti vuttaṃ hoti. Kāmaṃ ekantena [M 0.0178] gāmmataṃ asabbhasabhāvaṃ bandhe tassānucitabhāvato vindati paṭilabhati pasavatīti attho.

159. Showing that some phenomenon shines in a secondary context in a composition, but not in a primary context, he said 'vomiting' and so on. 'Vomiting' and 'expelling'; by the word 'ādi' (etc.), purgatives and so on are included. This, as stated, is a figurative usage, a mode of application characterized by the inclusion of other contexts, wherein the qualities are secondary and their own contexts well-known. Being not fallen from that, being untainted, and being secondary, it is exceedingly beautiful and utterly charming due to its ornamental nature. The other, however, is said to be primary. It certainly obtains, acquires, or produces a vulgar nature, an unrefined quality, due to its unsuitability in that composition—this is the meaning.

159. Idāni imesuyeva pāṇidhammādīsu koci dhammo amukhyavisaye payutto pasattho, mukhyavisaye payutto apasatthoti dassento “vamanuggi”ccādimāha. Etaṃ vamanuggiranādi vamanauggiranavirecanādikaṃ guṇavutyapariccutaṃ amukhyapayogato agaḷitaṃ amukhyabhūtaṃ atisundaraṃ sabbesaṃ atipiyaṃ hoti, aññaṃ tu uttato byatirekaṃ mukhyavisaye payuttaṃ vamanuggiranādikaṃ pana kāmaṃ ekantena gāmmataṃ sabhāvaappiyagāmmadosataṃ vindati sevatīti. Vamanañca uggiranañceti ca, tāni ādīni yasseti ca, guṇā appadhānā vuttīti ca, tato apariccutanti ca viggaho.

159. Now, showing that among these very phenomena of living beings and so on, some phenomenon, when applied in a secondary context, is praised, but when applied in a primary context, is not praised, he said 'vomiting and expelling' and so on. This 'vomiting and expelling' and the like—such as vomiting, expelling, and purgation—not fallen from figurative usage, untainted by secondary application, being secondary, is exceedingly beautiful, most dear to all. The other, however, distinct from this, namely 'vomiting and expelling' and the like when applied in a primary context, certainly and entirely obtains or serves a vulgar nature, an inherently unpleasant vulgar defect. The grammatical analyses are: 'vomiting and expelling'; 'those of which these are the first'; 'qualities are secondary usages'; and 'not fallen from that'.

160.

160.

Kantīnaṃ vamanabyājā, munipādanakhāvalī;

Candakantī pivantīva, nippabhaṃ taṃ karontiyo.

The rows of the Sage's toenails, on the pretext of vomiting forth their own radiance, seem to drink the moon's radiance, making it lustreless.

160. Udāharati “kantīna”miccādi. Munino sammāsambuddhassa pādanakhānaṃ āvalī seṇiyo kantīnaṃ attano nirantaraṃ nissarantīnaṃ sobhāvisesānaṃ vamanabyājā uggiranalesena candakantī candacchaviyo sabbattha patthaṭattā pivantīva pānaṃ karontīti takkemi. Kīdisī viyāti parikappanābījamāha “nippabha”ntiādi. Taṃ candaṃ nippabhaṃ pabhāvirahitaṃ karontiyo vidahamānā. Idañhi kappanābījaṃ yato nakhasobhāliṅganena candassa sobhāvato nippabhattaṃ passitvā mahattañca tassā nakhāvaliyo candakantī pivantīti parikappeti kantīnañca vamanabyājaṃ.

160. He gives an example with 'kantīnaṃ' and so on. I imagine that the rows, the lines, of the toenails of the Sage, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, on the pretext of vomiting forth, with the guise of expelling, their own constantly emanating surpassing radiance, as if drinking the moon's radiance, the moon's splendor, because it is spread everywhere. He states the seed of the imagination as 'nippabhaṃ' and so on, asking 'What is it like?' Making that moon lustreless, devoid of light. Indeed, this is the seed of the imagination, for having seen the moon's splendor become lustreless due to the embrace of the toenails' brilliance, and the greatness thereof, one imagines that the rows of nails are drinking the moon's radiance and that there is a pretext of vomiting forth their own radiance.

160. Iṭṭhavisaye payuttavamanuggiranādīnamudāharaṇamuddisati “kantīna”miccādinā. Munipādanakhāvalī munipādanakhaseṇiyo kantīnaṃ attano candamarīcisadisasobhānaṃ vamanabyājā uggiranalesena taṃ nimmalacandaṃ nippabhaṃ karontiyo attano sabbattha patthaṭattā nippabhaṃ karontiyo candakantī candaraṃsiyo [M 0.0179] pivanti maññe. Nakharaṃsīnaṃ sabbattha patthaṭattā sappabhassāpi candassa nippabhattañca nakharaṃsīnaṃ adhikattañca disvā candakantī pivanti iveti nakhāvalīnaṃ candakantipivanañca sakakantivamanañca pakati na hoti, byājamiti kavinā parikappitaṃ hoti. Ettha bhattasitthādimukhyavisayato aññakantisaṅkhataamukhyavisaye payuttaṃ vamanaṃ guṇavuttīti ñātabbaṃ. Vamanameva byājamiti ca, munino pādāti ca, tesu nakhāti ca, tesaṃ āvaliyoti ca, candassa kantiyoti ca, niggato pabhāhīti ca viggaho.

160. Examples of 'vomiting', 'expelling', and so on, applied in a desirable context, are indicated with 'kantīnaṃ' and so on. I imagine that the rows of the Sage's toenails, the array of the Sage's toenails, on the pretext of vomiting forth, with the guise of expelling, their own radiance which is like moonbeams, making that pure moon lustreless—and because they are spread everywhere, making it lustreless—drink the moon's radiance, the moon's rays. Because the nail-rays are spread everywhere, upon seeing the moon, though radiant, become lustreless, and seeing the superiority of the nail-rays, one imagines it is as if they are drinking the moon's radiance. Thus, the nail-rows' drinking of the moon's radiance and vomiting forth their own radiance is not natural; it is a pretext imagined by the poet. Here, it should be understood that 'vomiting', when applied in a secondary context designated as radiance—other than its primary context such as grains of cooked rice—is a figurative usage (guṇavutti). The grammatical analyses are: 'the vomiting itself is the pretext'; 'of the Sage, the feet'; 'on them, the nails'; 'of them, the rows'; 'of the moon, the radiance'; and 'radiance has gone out from it'.

161.

161.

Acittakattukaṃ rujha-miccevaṃ guṇakamma taṃ guṇakammakaṃ (sī.);

Sacittakattukaṃ pe’taṃ, guṇakammaṃ yadu’ttamaṃ.

Thus, that quality-action which has an unconscious agent is delightful; and this, which has a conscious agent, if it is a quality-action, is superior.

161. Yathāvuttaṃ nigameti “acitta”iccādinā. Iccevaṃ acitto kattā yassa taṃ acittakattukaṃ. Guṇo kammaṃ yassa taṃ guṇakammaṃ. Tañca vamanādi rujhamatimanoharaṃ bhavati bandhocitattā. Nakhāvaliyo hi acittakattāro, kantiyo guṇakammanti vamanamatrātisundaraṃ. Nedameva rujhanti āha “sacitta”iccādi. Etaṃ vamanādikaṃ sacittakattukampiyadiguṇakammaṃ, uttamaṃ seṭṭhaṃ bandhocitattā.

161. He concludes what was stated with 'acitta' and so on. Thus, 'that which has an unconscious agent' is that of which the agent is unconscious. 'Quality-action' is that of which a quality is the action. And that—vomiting and so on—becomes delightful and exceedingly charming because it is suitable for a literary composition. For the rows of nails are unconscious agents, and radiance is the quality-action; thus, vomiting in this context is exceedingly beautiful. To show that not only this is delightful, he says 'sacitta' and so on. This vomiting and the like, even when it has a conscious agent, if it is a quality-action, is superior and excellent because it is suitable for a literary composition.

161. Anantarodāharaṇassa pasatthattañca kammani guṇe sati sacittakattukavamanādikañca iṭṭhamiti dassento “acittakattuka”miccādimāha. Iccevaṃ iminā pakārena acittakattukaṃ nakhāvalisaṅkhātaaviññāṇakakattuvantaṃ guṇakammaṃ nakhakantisaṅkhātaappadhānakammavantaṃ vamanādikaṃ rujhaṃ racanāya ucitattā rucijanakaṃ hoti, etaṃ vamanādikaṃ sacittakattukampi saviññāṇakakattuvantampi yadi guṇakammaṃ amukhyakammaṃ ce, uttamaṃ visiṭṭhameva, “kantīna”nti bhāvasambandhe chaṭṭhiyā satipi vamanakriyāya kammattaṃ nātivattati. Natthi cittaṃ yesanti ca, acittā kattāro yassāti ca, guṇo kammaṃ yasseti ca, saha [M 0.0180] cittena vattamānoti ca vākyaṃ. Iti nidassane evaṃ pakāre nipāto, atha vā vacanavacanīyānaṃ vacanavacanīyādīnaṃ (ka.) nigamārambhe nipātasamudāyo.

161. To show the praiseworthiness of the immediately preceding example, and that even vomiting and the like with a conscious agent is desirable when it is a quality-action, he states, 'acittakattukaṃ' and so on. Thus, in this way, the quality-action, such as vomiting, which has an unconscious agent—that is, having an insentient agent designated as the 'row of nails'—and which has a secondary action—that is, having a subordinate action designated as 'nail-radiance'—is pleasing and delightful because it is suitable for composition. Even this action of vomiting, if it has a conscious agent, a sentient agent, and if it is a quality-action, a secondary action, then it is indeed excellent and distinguished. In the phrase 'kantīnaṃ', even though the sixth case (genitive) is used to show relation, it does not cease to be the object of the act of vomiting. The analyses are: 'they have no mind' (for acitta); 'that which has mindless agents' (for acittakattuka); 'that of which a quality is the action' (for guṇakamma); and 'existing with mind' (for sacitta). Thus, 'iti' is a particle of this kind in an illustration; or, it is a collection of particles at the beginning of the conclusion of what is said and to be said.

162.

162.

Uggirantova sa sneha-rasaṃ jinavaro jane;

Bhāsanto madhuraṃ dhammaṃ, kaṃ na sampīṇaye janaṃ.

The Supreme Victor, as if pouring forth the essence of affection among the people, while speaking the sweet Dhamma—what person would he not gladden?

162. Tadudāharati “uggirantovā”tiādinā. So jinavaro jane sakalasattanikāye sneharasaṃ attano pemasaṅkhātaṃ anurāgaṃ uggirantova vamanto viya madhuraṃ atipaṇītaṃ dhammaṃ bhāsanto kaṃ janaṃ na sampīṇaye, sabbameva sampīṇeti. Ettha jinavaro kattā sacitto, sneharaso guṇakammaṃ.

162. He illustrates that with the phrase 'uggirantova' and so on. That Supreme Victor, speaking the sweet and exceedingly refined Dhamma, as if pouring forth or vomiting out the essence of affection, his own love known as fondness, among the entire multitude of beings—what person would he not gladden? He gladdens all of them. Here, the Supreme Victor is the conscious agent, and the essence of affection is the quality-action.

162. Idāni sacittakakattupakkhe udāharaṇamuddisati “uggiranto”ccādinā. So jinavaro jane sakalasattanikāye sneharasaṃ attano pemasaṅkhātaanurāgaṃ uggiranto iva vamanto viya madhuraṃ ādikalyāṇādibhāvena paṇītaṃ dhammaṃ saddhammaṃ bhāsanto desento yathāsayaṃ vadanto kaṃ janaṃ kīdisaṃ puggalaṃ na sampīṇaye, pīṇeti evāti. Ettha uggiranaṃ jinavarasaṅkhatasacittakakattuvantampi sneharasasaṅkhātaamukhyakammayuttattā pasatthaṃ hoti. Sneho eva raso anurāgoti viggaho.

162. Now, he presents an example for the case of the conscious agent with the phrase 'uggiranto' and so on. That Supreme Victor, speaking, teaching, and speaking according to their disposition the sweet Dhamma, the true Dhamma, which is refined by being excellent in the beginning and so on, as if pouring forth or vomiting out the essence of affection, his own love known as fondness, among the people, among the entire multitude of beings—what person, what kind of individual, would he not gladden? Indeed, he gladdens them. Here, the act of pouring forth, even though it has the Supreme Victor as its conscious agent, is praised because it is connected with the secondary action designated as 'essence of affection.' The analysis is: 'Affection itself is the essence, which is fondness.'

163.

163.

Yo saddasatthakusalo kusalo nighaṇṭu-

Chandoalaṅkatisu niccakatābhiyogo;

So’yaṃ kavittavikalopi kavīsu saṅkhya-

Mogayha vindati hi kitti’mamandarūpaṃ.

He who is skilled in the science of grammar, skilled in lexicons, prosody, and rhetoric, and constantly applies himself—even if this one is deficient in poetic skill, by entering the count among poets, he certainly gains boundless fame.

Iti saṅgharakkhitamahāsāmipādaviracite

Thus, in the work composed by the venerable great Elder Saṅgharakkhita,

Subodhālaṅkāre

in the Subodhālaṅkāra,

Guṇāvabodho nāma tatiyo paricchedo.

the third chapter, named 'The Apprehension of Qualities'.

163. Ganthantarāhitavāsanāya, [M 0.0181] tadanubandhapaṭibhāne cāvijjamānepi sutena abhiyogabalena kavitā kitti ca tadanugatā samupalabbhatīti samanusāsati “yo”iccādinā. Saddasatthe byākaraṇe kismiñci “idameve”ti niyamābhāvā kusalo cheko nighaṇṭumhi abhidhānasatthe ca chandasi vuttijātippapañcapakāsakachandovicitisatthe ca alaṅkatisu alaṅkārasatthe ca kusalo na kevalaṃ saddasattheyeva, atha ca pana niccamanavarataṃ divā ca ratto ca kato abhiyogo vāyāmo racanāvisaye yassa soyaṃ kavittavikalopi bandhakaraṇasaṅkhātakaviguṇaparihīnopi kavīsu kaviguṇopetesu saṅkhyaṃ gaṇanaṃ ogayha paṭilabhitvā amandarūpaṃ atibahuṃ kittiṃ parisuddhabandharacanālakkhaṇaṃ tappabhavaṃ khyātaṃ vindati paṭilabhatevāti.

163. Even without an inclination imbued by constant study of texts and the associated insightful understanding, poetry and the fame that follows it can still be attained through the power of diligent application based on learning—so he instructs with 'yo,' and so on. One who is skilled and clever in the science of sound, that is, grammar, where there is no fixed rule stating 'this alone,' and is skilled in lexicography, the science of synonyms, and in prosody, the science that reveals the varieties of meter and class, and in poetics, the science of literary embellishments—and who, moreover, constantly and unceasingly, day and night, applies effort and exertion to composition—such a person, even if deficient in poetic ability or lacking the poetic quality known as composition-making, still, by entering into and obtaining a place in the count among poets endowed with poetic qualities, certainly obtains immense, very abundant fame, which is the mark of a pure composition and the renown arising therefrom.

Iti subodhālaṅkāre mahāsāmināmikāyaṃ

Thus, in the commentary on the Subodhālaṅkāra named after the Mahāsāmi.

Subodhālaṅkāraṭīkāyaṃ

In the Subodhālaṅkāra-ṭīkā.

Guṇāvabodhaparicchedo tatiyo.

The Third Chapter: The Apprehension of Qualities.

163. Idāni uddesakkamena saddālaṅkāre niddisitvā byākaraṇanighaṇṭuchandoparivārite imasmiṃ nirantarābhiyogo ihalokiyādimahantayasassa kāraṇamiti sissānamanusāsanto “yo saddasatthakusalo”ccādimāha. Yo theranavamajjhimesu koci saddasatthakusalo saddānusāsanabyākaraṇavisaye pakatipaccayādivibhāgakappanāya cheko nighaṇṭuchandoalaṅkatīsu abhidhānachandoalaṅkārasatthesupi kusalo taṃtaṃvibhāgabuddhīnaṃ paṭipādanena cheko niccakatābhiyogo dhāraṇamanasikāravasena niccaṃ katussāho hoti. So ayaṃ appamādī kavittavikalopi pakatisiddhakabbaracanaguṇarahitopi kavīsu saṅkhyaṃ kabbakattūsu gaṇanaṃ ogayha kabbakaraṇaṭīkākaraṇādipakārena ogāhetvā taṃ gaṇanaṃ pāpuṇitvā [M 0.0182] amandarūpaṃ anappakasabhāvaṃ atibahuṃ kittiṃ niddosaṃ sattharacanalakkhaṇaṃ puññasañcayaṃ, tappabhavaṃ pasiddhiṃ vā vindati labhatevāti. Yathāvuttasatthesu abhiyogo bandhassa ekantakāraṇameva. Vuttaṃ hi–

163. Now, having pointed out the ornaments of sound in the order of their enumeration, and instructing the disciples that in this treatise, which is encompassed by grammar, lexicography, and prosody, continuous application is the cause of great fame in this world and beyond, he says, 'One skilled in the science of sound,' etc. Whoever among the elders, new, or middling monks is skilled in the science of sound, clever in the field of grammar in arranging the division of bases, suffixes, and so on; skilled also in lexicography, prosody, and poetics—that is, in the treatises on synonyms, prosody, and figures of speech—and clever in presenting the understanding of their respective divisions; and who, by means of retention and reflection, has made constant application and is ever enthusiastic—this diligent person, even if deficient in poetic ability, even if devoid of the quality of naturally accomplished poetic composition, still, by means of composing poems, writing commentaries, and the like, enters into the count among poets, the reckoning among poetry-makers, and having reached that count, certainly obtains immense, not insignificant, and very abundant fame, which is the mark of a faultless composition of a master, an accumulation of merit, or the renown arising therefrom. Application in the aforementioned sciences is indeed the sole cause of composition. For it is said—

“Sābhāvikī ca paṭibhā,

Sutañca bahunimmalaṃ;

Amando cābhiyogo’yaṃ,

Hetu hoti’ha bandhane”ti kābyādāsa 1.103.

Natural insight, and much stainless learning, and this unflagging application, are the cause here in composition.

Tattha sābhāvikī sabhāvasiddhā paṭibhā ca paññā ca bahu nimmalaṃ anappakaṃ nijjaṭaṃ sutañca amando abhiyogo ca anappako abhyāso ceti ayameso sabbopi iha bandhane imissaṃ kabbaracanāyaṃ hetu hoti kāraṇaṃ bhavatīti. Sadde sāsati ettha etenāti imasmiṃ atthe tappaccayañca tassa thādesañca katvā saddasatthanti ñātabbaṃ, saddasatthe kusaloti ca, nighaṇṭu ca chando ca alaṅkati alaṅkārañceti ca viggaho, ettha alaṅkatisaddo satthāpekkhāya napuṃsako hoti, niccaṃ kato abhiyogo asseti ca, kavino bhāvoti ca, tena vikaloti ca, amandaṃ rūpaṃ sabhāvo yasseti ca vākyaṃ.

Therein, natural, inherently accomplished insight and wisdom; and much stainless, not insignificant, unentangled learning; and unflagging application and not insignificant practice—all this becomes the cause and reason here in composition, in this poetic composition. The term `saddasattha` (science of sound) should be understood as derived in the sense 'one instructs in sound by this,' by applying the `-tha` suffix and the substitution of `ā` for the root vowel. And the analysis is: 'skilled in the science of sound'; and 'lexicon and prosody and ornament and ornamentation.' Here, the word `alaṅkati` is neuter with reference to `sattha` (treatise). And the explanatory phrases are: 'one who has constant application'; 'the state of a poet'; 'deficient in that'; and 'one whose nature is not slight'.

Iti subodhālaṅkāranissaye

Thus, in the Subodhālaṅkāra-nissaya.

Tatiyo paricchedo.

The Third Chapter.

4. Atthālaṅkārāvabodhapariccheda

4. The Chapter on the Apprehension of the Ornaments of Meaning.

164.

164.

Atthālaṅkārasahitā, saguṇā bandhapaddhati;

Accantakantā kantāva yatoaccantakantāva (ka.), vuccantete tato’dhunā.

The method of composition, when accompanied by the ornaments of meaning and endowed with qualities, is exceedingly lovely, like a beloved woman; therefore, these are now spoken of.

164. Evaṃ [M 0.0183] saddālaṅkāre paricchijja sampatyatthālaṅkāraṃ bodhayitumāha “atthālaṅkāra”iccādi. Saguṇā yathāvuttehi pasādādīhi saddaguṇehi sahitā bandhapaddhati kabbaracanaṃ. Alaṅkarīyati kantiṃ nīyati bandho etehi sarīramiva hārādīhīti alaṅkārā, tehi atthālaṅkārehi jātyādilakkhaṇehi sahitā saṃyuttā satī saguṇā patibbatādiguṇopetā atthena dhanena alaṅkārena ābharaṇena sahitā yuttā kantāva aṅganā viya. Yato accantakantā atisayaramaṇīyā siyā, tato tena kāraṇena ye atthālaṅkārā avasaraṃ pattā, te adhunā idāni vuccante kathīyanti.

164. Having thus defined the ornaments of sound, now, to explain the ornaments of meaning, he says, 'atthālaṅkāra,' and so on. The method of composition, that is, poetic composition, is endowed with qualities, being accompanied by the aforementioned sound-qualities such as clarity. They are called 'ornaments' (alaṅkārā) because 'the composition is adorned, is brought to beauty, by them, just as the body is by necklaces and so forth.' Being united with those ornaments of meaning, which are characterized by genus and so on, and endowed with qualities, it is like a beloved woman endowed with qualities such as faithfulness, possessed of wealth and adorned with jewelry. Since it would be exceedingly lovely and exceptionally charming, for that reason, those ornaments of meaning that have now found their occasion are spoken of at this time.

164. Evaṃ saddālaṅkāravibhāgaṃ dassetvā idāni tannissayaṃyeva atthālaṅkārabandhamārabhanto “atthālaṅkāri”ccādimāha. Saguṇā yathāvuttapasādādisaddaguṇayuttā bandhapaddhati pajjagajjādipabhedā racanāvali atthālaṅkārasahitā sabhāvavuttivaṅkavuttisaṅkhātena atthālaṅkārena saṃyuttā saguṇā atthālaṅkārasahitā kantā iva patibbatādīhi guṇehi yuttā suvaṇṇarajatamaṇimuttādidhanehi gīveyyakaṭakanūpurādīhi ābharaṇehi ca yuttā aṅganāva accantakantā yato atisayena ramaṇīyā, tato tasmā te atthālaṅkārā adhunā dāni vuccante. Alaṅkaronti bandhaṃ sarīraṃ vā etehīti ca, atthassa alaṅkārāti ca, tehi sahitāti ca, guṇehi saha vattatīti ca, bandhassa paddhatīti ca, accantaṃ atisayena kantāti ca viggaho.

164. Having thus shown the division of the ornaments of sound, now, beginning the composition of the ornaments of meaning which is based upon them, he says, 'atthālaṅkāri,' and so on. The method of composition—a series of compositions of various types such as verse and prose—is endowed with qualities, being possessed of the aforementioned sound-qualities such as clarity. When accompanied by the ornaments of meaning, that is, united with the ornaments of meaning known as natural expression (sabhāvavutti) and figurative expression (vaṅkavutti), it is, like a beloved woman, endowed with qualities and accompanied by ornaments. She is a woman endowed with qualities such as faithfulness, possessed of wealth such as gold, silver, gems, and pearls, and adorned with jewelry such as necklaces, bracelets, and anklets. Since the composition is exceedingly lovely, being exceptionally charming, therefore these ornaments of meaning are now spoken of. The analysis is as follows: 'They adorn the composition or the body by these'; 'ornaments of meaning'; 'accompanied by them'; 'existing together with qualities'; 'the method of composition'; and 'exceedingly lovely'.

165.

165.

Sabhāvavaṅkavuttīnaṃ, bhedā dvidhā alaṃkriyā;

Paṭhamā tattha vatthūnaṃ, nānāvatthāvibhāvinī.

The embellishment is twofold, by the division into natural and figurative expression. The first among them is that which reveals the various states of things.

165. Katippabhedā te iccāha “sabhāva”iccādi. Sabhāvavutti vaṅkavuttīti imesaṃ bhedā pabhedena alaṃkriyā atthālaṅkārādvidhādvippakārā. [M 0.0185] Tesu sabhāvavutti kīdisīti āha “paṭhamā”tiādi. Tattha tāsu paṭhamā sabhāvavutti vatthūnaṃ padatthānaṃ jātiguṇakriyādabbasabhāvānaṃ nānā vicittā, na dvekāva avatthā avasarā vibhāvinī pakāsikā viññeyyā. Jātyādīnaṃ padatthānaṃ yathāsabhāvamanekappakāraṃ sammadeva vivarantī sabhāvaṃ padatthānaṃ vicittaṃ vadatīti sabhāvavutti nāmāti adhippāyo, sāva jātiyā padatthasarūpassa tathātathāpaṭipādakattena vuttiyā dattiyā (ka.) jātipi vuccati.

165. To the question, 'Of how many kinds are they?' he says, 'sabhāva,' and so on. By the division and subdivision of these, namely natural expression and figurative expression, the embellishment—the ornaments of meaning—is twofold, of two kinds. Among them, to the question, 'What is natural expression like?' he says, 'paṭhamā,' and so on. Therein, among them, the first, natural expression, should be understood as that which reveals and makes known the various and diverse—not just one or two—states and conditions of things, that is, of the meanings of words, which are the natures of genus, quality, action, and substance. The intention is that it is called 'natural expression' because it properly reveals the manifold nature of the meanings of words, such as genus, according to their own nature, and it speaks of the varied nature of the meanings of words. It is also called 'genus' (jāti) because of its function of setting forth the essence of the meaning of a word, such as genus, in its particular way.

165. Pasatthālaṅkārā pasatthādialaṅkārā (ka.) pabhedato ettakāti dassento “sabhāvi”ccādimāha. Alaṃkriyā atthālaṅkārā sabhāvavaṅkavuttīnaṃ bhedā pabhedato dvidhā dvippakārā honti. Tattha tāsudvīsu paṭhamā sabhāvavutti vatthūnaṃ jātiguṇakriyādabbalakkhaṇānaṃ padatthānaṃ nānāvatthāvibhāvinī anekappakārassa pakāsinī hoti. Ettha jātyādīnaṃ padatthānaṃ anekappakārasabhāvapakāsinī sabhāvavutti nāma. Esāva jāti guṇādicatubbidhapadatthānaṃ sarūpasaṅkhātajātiyā tehi ākārehi paṭipādanato upacārato jāti nāma hoti. Jātyādipadatthānaṃyeva yathāsabhāvaṃ hitvā vatthuparikappitaatisayopamārūpakādisarūpasaṅkhātaṃ vaṅkasabhāvaṃ pakāsentī vaṅkavutti nāma. Yabhāvo ca vaṅko cāti ca, tesaṃ vuttīti ca, alaṃkaronti etāhīti ca, nānā anekā ca sā avatthā cāti ca vākyaṃ.

165. To show that the praiseworthy ornaments are of such variety, he begins with 'natural,' and so on. The embellishment, meaning the meaning-ornaments, are divided into two kinds based on their distinctions: natural expression (sabhāvavutti) and figurative expression (vaṅkavutti). Among these two, the first, natural expression, reveals the various states of things—the meanings of terms characterized by genus, quality, action, and substance—displaying them in many ways. Here, natural expression is so called because it reveals the diverse inherent nature of the meanings of terms such as genus. This itself is called 'genus' by transference, due to its presentation of the fourfold meanings of terms such as genus and quality by means of their inherent nature, which is called 'genus'. Figurative expression (vaṅkavutti), on the other hand, abandoning the inherent nature of the meanings of terms such as genus, reveals a figurative nature, which is a contrived exaggeration of the subject matter, consisting of simile, metaphor, and so forth. The analysis is: 'what is natural' and 'what is figurative,' and 'their expressions,' and 'they adorn by these,' and 'various and many,' and 'that state'.

Yathā –

As:

166.

166.

Līlāvikantisubhago,

Disāthiravilokano;

Bodhisattaṅkuro bhāsaṃ,

Viroci vācamāsabhiṃ.

Graceful in movement, lovely to behold, gazing steadfastly in all directions; the Bodhisatta-sprout shone forth, uttering noble speech.

166. “Yathe”ti taṃ udāharati. Līlāya vilāsena vihitāya vikantiyā gamanena sattapadavītihārasaṅkhātena subhago sundaro disāsu dasasu thiramacalaṃ vilokanaṃ yassa so bodhisattaṅkuro tadahujāto mahābodhisatto āsabhiṃ vācaṃ “aggohamasmī”tiādikamuttamaṃ nibbhayavacanaṃ bhāsaṃ vadanto viroci visesena ramaṇīyattaṃ patto. Ayaṃ sabhāvavutti. Evaṃ jātisabhāvavutyādayopi parikappanīyā.

166. He cites that as an example, saying 'As.' The Bodhisatta-sprout, the Great Bodhisatta born on that very day, who is auspicious and beautiful by means of graceful movement, by a gait performed with charm, consisting of seven paces, and whose gaze is firm and unmoving in the ten directions, shone forth, uttering noble speech, the supreme fearless utterance such as 'I am the chief,' having attained exceptional loveliness. This is natural expression. In this way, natural expressions pertaining to genus and so forth should also be conceived.

166. Idāni sabhāvavuttiyā udāharaṇaṃ āha “yathā – līlāvikanti”ccādi. Līlāvikantisubhago vilāsagamanena sattapadavītihārena sundaro disāthiravilokano dasadisāsu acalaolokano bodhisattaṅkuro mahābodhisattaṅkuro āsabhiṃ vācaṃ “aggohamasmī”tiādinā abhītavacanaṃ bhāsaṃ vadanto viroci asobhīti. Iha bodhisattasaṅkhātassa dabbassa līlāvikantidisāthiravilokanavaconicchāraṇasaṅkhatānaṃ avatthānaṃ pakāsitattā dabbasabhāvavuttīti ñātabbā. Esāyeva dabbagatagatyādivicitrasarūpaṃ alaṅkaraṇato alaṅkāro nāma, dabbagatagatyādayo pana alaṃkiriyamānattā alaṃkiriyā nāma. Jātiguṇakriyāsabhāvavuttiyopi evameva daṭṭhabbā. Līlāya yuttā vikantīti ca, tāya subhagoti ca, disāsu thiraṃ vilokanaṃ yasseti ca, bodhiyā paññāya sattoti ca, soyeva aṅkuroti ca, usabhassa bhāvoti ca vākyaṃ. Usabhassa bhāvasaṅkhātā akampanīyā ṭhiti āsabhaṃ nāma, akampabhāvato tena samāpi vācā upacārato āsabhī nāma hoti.

166. Now, as an example of natural expression, he says, 'As – graceful movement,' and so on. The Bodhisatta-sprout, the great Bodhisatta-sprout, who is beautiful by means of graceful movement, by a charming gait and a seven-pace stride, whose gaze is steady in the ten directions, shone forth, uttering fearless speech such as 'I am the foremost,' and so on. Here, it should be understood as the natural expression of substance, because it reveals the states of the substance known as the Bodhisatta, consisting of graceful movement, steady gazing across the directions, and the uttering of words. This itself is called an 'ornament' because it adorns the diverse nature of the substance's gait and so forth, while the substance's gait and so forth are called 'the adorned' because they are being adorned. The natural expressions of genus, quality, and action should also be seen in the same way. The analysis is: 'movement endowed with grace,' and 'beautiful by that,' and 'whose gaze is steady in the directions,' and 'a being of wisdom for awakening,' and 'that same one is a sprout,' and 'the state of a bull.' The unwavering stability, which is the state of a bull, is called 'āsabha.' Speech similar to that, due to its unwavering nature, is conventionally called 'āsabhī'.

167.

167.

Vutti vatthusabhāvassa, yā’ññathā sā parābhave;

Tassā’nantavikappattā, hoti bījopadassanaṃ.

The expression of a thing's nature, which is otherwise, is figurative. Because of its endless variations, a presentation of the seed is given.

167. Dutiyamāha [M 0.0186] “vutti”ccādinā. Vatthuno jātyādirūpassa padatthassa sabhāvo yassaṃ avatthāyaṃ yādisaṃ rūpaṃ tassa aññathābhāvena tassa rūpassa tathetaṃ dabbāpanena vutti vacanaṃ. Parā bhave aññā vaṅkavutti nāma siyā. Kiṃ sā sākallena vattuṃ sakkāti āha “tassā”iccādi. Tassā vaṅkavuttiyā anantavikappattā aparimitabhedakattā bījassa kāraṇattā sakalabyattibyāpisāmaññarūpassa yato pare vicittālaṅkārā pasavanti, upadassanaṃ kathanaṃ hoti niravasesābhidhānassa kenāpyasakkuṇeyyattā.

167. He speaks of the second with 'expression,' and so on. The expression (vutti) is a statement that proceeds by altering the nature of the meaning of a term—which has the form of genus and so forth—from whatever form it has in a given state, by presenting that thing as such. It would be called 'figurative expression' (vaṅkavutti), being otherwise, in a different way. Can that be fully described? He says, 'of that,' and so on. Because of the endless variations of that figurative expression, its immeasurable distinctions, and its seed-like causal nature—a general form pervading all manifestation and non-manifestation, from which diverse ornaments arise—the presentation is a mere statement, since a complete articulation is impossible for anyone.

167. Idāni vaṅkavuttiṃ dasseti “vutti”ccādinā. Vatthusabhāvassa jātyādipadatthasambandhino tāsu tāsu avatthāsu yo sabhāvo vijjati, tassa sabhāvassa aññathā vijjamānākāraṃ hitvā vattuparikappitena atisayaupamārūpakādiaññapakārena yā vutti yaṃ kathanaṃ atthi, sā parābhave sabhāvavuttito aññā vaṅkavutti nāma siyā. Tassā vaṅkavuttiyā anantavikappattā appamāṇapakkhattā kathanena parisamāpetuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā nayato tassa anantapakkhassa pariggahaṇatthaṃ bījopadassanaṃ kāraṇamattassa nidassanaṃ hoti. Vakkhamānabhedato ekamekampi attanā sadisaṃ anantabhedapariggahajānanatthaṃ pahotīti adhippāyo. Vatthūnaṃ sabhāvoti ca, anantā vikappā yassa sabhāvasseti ca, tassa bhāvoti ca, bījassa upadassananti ca viggaho.

167. Now, he shows figurative expression with 'expression,' and so on. The expression (vutti), the statement, which exists by abandoning the actually existing form of the inherent nature of a thing's essence (connected with meanings like genus and so forth) that is found in various states, and instead by a contrived exaggeration, simile, metaphor, or other different manner, that would be called 'figurative expression' (vaṅkavutti), being different from natural expression, in a figurative sense. Because of the endless variations of that figurative expression, its immeasurable aspects, and the impossibility of completing its explanation by speaking, a presentation of a seed is merely an example of the cause, for the purpose of grasping its infinite aspects by way of method. The intention is that even a single one of the divisions to be discussed is sufficient, by analogy with itself, for understanding and grasping the infinite distinctions. The analysis is: 'the nature of things,' and 'the state of that which has infinite variations,' and 'the state of that,' and 'the presentation of a seed'.

Vaṅkavuttiatthālaṅkārauddesavaṇṇanā

Description of the Exposition of the Meaning-Ornament of Oblique Expression

168.

168.

Tatthā’tisayaupamā-

Rūpakāvuttidīpakaṃ;

Akkhepo’tthantaranyāso,

Byatireko vibhāvanā.

Herein are hyperbole, simile, metaphor, repetition, and illustration; objection, corroboration, distinction, and peculiar allegation.

169.

169.

Hetukkamo [M 0.0187] piyataraṃ, samāsaparikappanā;

Samāhitaṃ pariyāya-vuttibyājopavaṇṇanaṃ.

Causal sequence, the more pleasing, condensation, and conception; collectedness, circumlocution, and eulogy through pretext.

170.

170.

Visesa ruḷhāhaṅkārā,

Sileso tulyayogitā;

Nidassanaṃ mahantattaṃ,

Vañcanā’ppakatatthuti.

Distinction, established egoism; paronomasia, equal connection; exemplification, greatness; deception, and indirect praise.

171.

171.

Ekāvali aññamaññaṃ, sahavutti virodhitā;

Parivuttibbhamobhāvo, missa’māsī rasī iti.

Chain, reciprocity, co-existence, opposition; exchange, delusion, emotion, mixture, blessing, and sentiment.

172.

172.

Ete bhedā samuddiṭṭhā, bhāvo jīvitamuccate;

Vaṅkavuttīsu poseti, sileso tu siriṃ paraṃ.

These divisions are declared; emotion is called life. Among oblique expressions, paronomasia, however, nourishes supreme beauty.

168-172. Yathoddesaṃ niddisitukāmo uddisati “tatthe”ccādi. Tatthāti tassaṃ vaṅkavuttiyaṃ “ete bhedā samuddiṭṭhā”ti iminā sambandho. Samuddiṭṭhāti saṅkhepanayena vuttā. Atisayo upamā rūpakaṃ āvutti dīpakañca, samāso samāsavutti parikappanā ca, viseso ruḷhāhaṅkāro ca, jīvitamuccateti tadabhāve bandhassa chavasseva heyyattā vuttaṃ, sileso tu vaṅkavuttīsu sabhāvavuttiṃ hitvā vatthusabhāvato aññathā yathā tathā parikappanarūpāsu atisayādīsu vuttīsu paraṃ siriṃ kantiṃ poseti taṃ pūreti āvahatīti.

168-172. Wishing to explain them according to the exposition, he states 'therein' and so on. 'Therein' means the connection is made with 'these divisions are declared' in that oblique expression. 'Declared' means stated concisely. Hyperbole, simile, metaphor, repetition, and illustration; condensation, condensed expression, and conception; distinction and established egoism.
