'It is called life' means it is said because in its absence, the composition is contemptible, like a mere corpse. But paronomasia, in oblique expressions—that is, in expressions like hyperbole and so on, which are of the nature of imagining things otherwise than the subject's nature, having abandoned natural expression—nourishes supreme beauty and charm; it fulfills and brings it forth.

168-172. Bhedavantānaṃ padatthānaṃ sabhāvakathanaṃ uddesakkamena pākaṭaṃ hotīti vattamānehi alaṅkārehi uddisanto “tatthātisaya…pe… rasī”ti gāthācatukkamāha. Tattha tatthāti tissaṃ vaṅkavuttiyaṃ iti evaṃ ete pañcatiṃsa bhedā samuddiṭṭhā saṅkhepena vuttāti. Etesaṃ pana padānaṃ attho niddese āvibhavissati. Iminā bhāvo ca sileso ca atippasatthoti dīpeti. Bhāvo bhāvālaṅkāro jīvitaṃ bandhassa pāṇabhūtoti vuccate, [M 0.0188] bhāvarahitassa bandhassa chavasarīrassa viya anupādeyyattā, sileso tu silesālaṅkāro pana vaṅkavuttīsu atisayopamādivaṅkavuttīsu paramukkaṃsabhūtaṃ siriṃ sobhaṃ poseti pūreti.

168-172. Pointing out with the current ornaments of speech that the statement of the nature of the meanings of terms possessing divisions becomes clear in the order of exposition, he states the four verses beginning 'Therein, hyperbole...' and ending with '...sentiment.' Therein, 'therein' refers to that oblique expression; thus, these thirty-five divisions are stated concisely. But the meaning of these terms will become evident in the explanation. Through this, he indicates that both emotion and paronomasia are highly praised. Emotion, the figure of speech of emotion, is said to be the life of the composition, being its vital essence, because a composition devoid of emotion is as unusable as a corpse. Paronomasia, however, the figure of speech of paronomasia, fosters and completes the supreme and excellent beauty in oblique expressions, such as the oblique expressions of hyperbole and simile.

Niddesavaṇṇanā

Description of the Explanation

173.

173.

Pakāsikā visesassa,

Siyā’tisayavutti yā;

Lokātikkantavisayā,

Lokiyāti ca sā dvidhā.

That which reveals a distinction may be hyperbolic expression. It is twofold: that with a transcendent scope, and that which is worldly.

173. Tatthātisayavuttīnaṃ tāva niddisanto āha “pakāsikā”iccādi. Visesassa vatthugatassātimattassa pakāsikāyāti anuvaditvā sā atisayavutti siyāti vidhīyate, atisayassa vatthuno ukkaṃsassa paṭipādikā vutti atisayavutti. Sā ca duvidhāti āha “loka”iccādi. Lokaṃ lokappatītiṃ atikkanto visayo gocaro yassā sā lokātikkantavisayā ca loke bhavā lokaṭhitimanatikkantattāti lokiyā cāti atisayavutti dvidhā dvippakārā bhavati.

173. First, indicating hyperbolic expressions, he says 'revealing' and so on. Having restated it as 'that which reveals the excessive distinction pertaining to the subject', it is prescribed that this may be a hyperbolic expression. A hyperbolic expression is an expression that conveys the excellence, the superiority, of a thing. And that it is of two kinds, he says: 'world' and so on. That which has a subject matter transcending the world, exceeding worldly convention, is 'transcending worldly scope'; and that which exists in the world, not transcending the worldly condition, is 'worldly'. Thus, a hyperbolic expression is twofold, of two kinds.

173. Idāni uddesakkamena atisayavuttiṃ dasseti “pakāsi”ccādinā. Visesassa jātyādipadatthagataadhikavisesassa yā vutti pakāsikā, sā atisayavutti nāma siyā, sā atisayavutti lokātikkantavisayā ca jātyādipadatthānaṃ yathāsabhāvasaṅkhatalokaṭhityātikkantavisayattā lokātikkanta visayāti ca lokiyāti ca yathāvuttalokamanatikkamma pavattanato lokiyāti cevaṃ dvidhā dvippakārā honti. Vadatīti vutti, atisayassa vuttīti ca, lokaṃ atikkanto visayo etissāti ca, loke bhavāti ca viggaho. “Visesassa pakāsikā”ti pasiddhaguṇānuvādena [M 0.0189] sā atisayavutti siyāti apasiddhaṃ atisayavuttividhānaṃ karoti, yathā “yo kuṇḍalī, so devadatto”ti. Anuvādakaanuvādanīyabhedo uparipyevameva daṭṭhabbo.

173. Now, in the order of the exposition, he presents the hyperbolic expression with 'revealing' and so on. That expression which reveals the superior distinction pertaining to the meaning of terms such as birth, etc., may be called a hyperbolic expression. That hyperbolic expression is of two kinds: 'transcending worldly scope,' because its scope transcends the worldly condition designated as the natural state of the meaning of terms such as birth, etc., and therefore has a scope that transcends the world; and 'worldly,' because it operates without transcending the world as stated. Thus, they are of two kinds. The analysis is: 'that which speaks is an expression' (vutti); 'the expression of excellence'; 'that whose scope transcends the world'; and 'that which is in the world'. By the phrase 'revealing the distinction', through the restatement of a well-known quality, he posits the less-known hyperbolic expression, stating 'it may be a hyperbolic expression', just as one might say, 'He who wears earrings is Devadatta.' The distinction between the predicate and the subject of predication should be understood in the same way above as well.

174.

174.

Lokiyātisayasse’te,

Bhedā ye jātiādayo;

Paṭipādīyate tva’jja,

Lokātikkantagocarā.

These divisions, which are birth and so on, belong to worldly hyperbole; but today, the one with a scope transcending the world is to be set forth.

174. Ayaṃ dvippakārā atisayavutti sabhāvavutyādīhi bhinnāti ce? Āha “loka”iccādi. Jātiādayo yato padatthassa vicittaṃ sarūpaṃ vadatīti vicittasarūpapaṭipādikā sabhāvavuttipi alaṅkāro, alaṅkāriyaṃ tu vatthumattaṃ, tato sabhāvavutyādayo ye bhedā visesā, ete lokiyātisayassa bhedā, yathā sarīre yaṃ sahajaṃ sundarattaṃ, tassa posakāpi muttāvalippabhuti alaṅkāroti vuccati, evaṃ bandhepyalaṅkāriyavatthunimittaṃ dhammattaṃ yāya ukkaṃsīyati, sā ukkaṃsoti vuccati. Sā ca vutti alaṅkārasaddena vuccate. Sā pana atisayavuttiyeva. Tenevāha “lokiyātisayassete, bhedā ye jātiādayo”ti. Yato evaṃ, tato lokātikkantavisayā ca visuṃ dassanīyāti āha “paṭī”tiādi. Tusaddo bhede. Ajja tu idāni pana lokātikkantagocarā paṭipādīyateti sambandho.

174. If it is asked, 'Is this twofold hyperbolic expression distinct from natural expression and so on?', he says 'worldly' and so on. Because natural expression, which conveys the diverse nature of the meaning of a word (since birth and so on declare it), is also a figure of speech—while the object of embellishment is merely the thing itself—therefore, those distinctions, which are natural expression and so on, are divisions of worldly hyperbole. Just as with the innate beauty that exists in a body, its enhancers like pearl necklaces and so on are also called 'ornaments'; so too in a composition, that by which the quality pertaining to the object of embellishment is elevated is called 'excellence'. And that expression is called by the term 'figure of speech'. But that is indeed hyperbolic expression itself. Therefore he said, 'These divisions, which are birth and so on, belong to worldly hyperbole.' Since it is so, he states 'to be presented' and so on, meaning that the one with a scope transcending the world is to be shown separately. The word 'tu' indicates difference. The connection is: 'But now, however, the one with a scope transcending the world is to be set forth'.

174. Idāni esā dvippakārāpi atisayavuttisabhāvavutyādīhi anaññāti dassetuṃ “lokiye”ccādimāha. Jātiādayo jātiguṇādipadatthagatavicittasarūpassa pakāsanato nissayavohārena “jātyādayo”ti niddiṭṭhā jātisabhāvavuttiguṇasabhāvavutyādayo ye bhedā [M 0.0190] visesā, ete lokiyātisayassa lokiyātisayavuttiyāyeva bhedā avayavā. Tattha lokiyātisayavutti nāma jātisabhāvavuttiguṇasabhāvavutyādayoyevāti. Esāyeva vicitrarūpapaṭipādikā ukkaṃsāti ca vuccati. Evaṃ lokiyātisayavuttiyā “līlāvikantisubhago”ti udāharaṇassa gamyamānattā vakkhamānaṃ paṭijānāti “paṭipādīyate”ccādinā. Ajja tu idāni pana lokātikkantagocarā atisayavutti paṭipādīyate udāharaṇato nipphādīyati. Loke bhavoti ca, tassa atisayo ādhikkamiti ca vākyaṃ.

174. Now, to show that this twofold hyperbolic expression is not other than natural expression and so on, he says 'worldly' and so on. Those distinctions, which are the natural expression of birth, the natural expression of quality, and so on—indicated by 'birth, etc.' as a dependent designation because they reveal the diverse nature inherent in the meaning of terms like birth and quality—are the divisions, the parts, of worldly hyperbole, that is, of worldly hyperbolic expression. Therein, worldly hyperbolic expression is precisely the natural expression of birth, the natural expression of quality, and so on. This very expression, which conveys diverse forms, is also called 'excellence'. Thus, since the example 'charming with graceful gait' is understood to be of worldly hyperbolic expression, he announces what is to be said next with 'is to be set forth' and so on. But now, however, the hyperbolic expression that has a scope transcending the world is to be set forth, to be produced by way of example. The phrases are: 'that which is in the world' and 'its excellence is a surpassing'.

175.

175.

Pivanti dehakantī ye,

Nettañjalipuṭena te;

Nā’laṃ hantuṃ jine’saṃ tvaṃ,

Taṇhaṃ taṇhāharopi kiṃ.

Those who drink the radiance of your body with the cupped hands of their eyes— O Conqueror, though you are the remover of craving, why are you unable to destroy their craving?

175. Tamudāharati “pivanti”ccādinā. Jina te dehakantī sarīrasobhāyo ye janā nettañjalipuṭena attano nayanadvandasaṅkhātena añjalipuṭena pivanti, esaṃ janānaṃ taṇhaṃ pipāsaṃ lobhameva vā harati anupatati apanayati (?). Taṇhāharopi samāno tvaṃ hantuṃ nivattituṃ kiṃ nālaṃ kasmā asamatthosi. Taṇhāharā nāma taṇhameva nudanti. Atra hanantāmapiha sampanudati lokaṭhitiṃ atikkamma dehakantiyā bahuttanadhammo vutto.

175. He illustrates this with 'they drink' and so on. [The meaning is:] O Conqueror, as for the radiance of your body, the splendor of your form, which people drink with the cupped hands of their eyes—that is, with the cupped hands consisting of their pair of eyes—though you are the remover of craving, why are you unable, why are you incapable, to destroy or restrain the craving, the thirst or greed, of these people? 'Removers of craving' indeed dispel craving itself. Here, transcending the worldly condition, the quality of the body's radiance being abundant is stated.

175. Idāni paṭiññātānusārena paṭipādeti “pivanti”ccādinā. Bho jina te tuyhaṃ dehakantī sarīrasobhāyo ye janā nettañjalipuṭena nettasaṅkhātena hatthapuṭena pivanti, esaṃ sādhujanānaṃ taṇhaṃ pipāsaṃ lobhameva [M 0.0191] vā taṇhāharopi tvaṃ sabbesaṃ taṇhāvināsakopi hantuṃ nivāretuṃ kiṃ nālaṃ kasmā asamatthosīti. Ettha pivanaṃ nāma pipāsaṃ vinetīti lokasabhāvo. Taṇhaṃ hantuṃ nālamiti lokasabhāvamatikkantattho. Kantīnaṃ adhikapiyatā atisayadhammo, tassa vutti pana taṇhaṃ hantuṃ nālamiti lokātikkantaatthaṃ visayaṃ katvā pavatto hoti. Sā pana kathetumicchitaṃ kantīnaṃ adhikapiyataṃ taṇhāhanane asamatthaṃ vatvā dīpetīti vaṅkavutti nāma. Vuccamānānaṃ upamārūpakādīnampi vaṅkavuttitā icchitatthassa pakārantarena pakāsanatoyeva. Yathā nāma sarīrasahajaṃ pīnattādisundarattaṃ uddīpanākārena ṭhitā kaṭakauṇhīsahārādayo alaṅkārā nāma bhavanti, evaṃ bandhasarīrasaṅkhāte alaṅkaraṇīyavatthumhi vijjamānaatipiyatādimeva uddīpetvā alaṅkurumānā “taṇhāharosi tvaṃ esaṃ kantī pivantānaṃ taṇhaṃ hantuṃ nāla”miti vācābhaṅgī alaṅkāro nāma. Alaṅkāriyaṃ nāma alaṅkātabbakantipiyatāya bahuttanti. Uttaripi alaṅkāraalaṅkāriyavibhāgo ca anurūpato yojanakkamo ca evameva daṭṭhabbo. Dehe kantīti ca, añjalīyeva puṭoti ca, nettāniyeva añjalipuṭoti ca, taṇhaṃ haratīti ca viggaho.

175. Now, in accordance with the declaration, he sets it forth with 'they drink' and so on. [The meaning is:] O Conqueror, as for the radiance of your body, the splendor of your form, which people drink with the cupped hands of their eyes—that is, with the cupped hands designated as their hands—for these virtuous people, why are you, though the remover of craving, indeed the destroyer of craving for all, unable to destroy or restrain their craving, thirst, or greed? Why are you incapable? Here, that drinking removes thirst is the nature of the world. 'Unable to destroy craving' is a meaning that transcends the nature of the world. The excessive loveliness of the radiances is an extraordinary quality; its expression, however, proceeds by making the meaning 'unable to destroy craving' its subject, a meaning that transcends the world. But that is called an 'oblique expression' because it reveals the desired excessive loveliness of the radiances by stating an inability to destroy craving. The obliqueness of similes, metaphors, and so on, which are being mentioned, is precisely due to their revealing the desired meaning in a different way. Just as ornaments like bracelets, headdresses, and necklaces, which exist to enhance the natural beauty, such as fullness, inherent in the body, are called figures of speech; so too, in the object to be adorned, which is designated as the body of the composition, the turn of phrase 'You are the remover of craving, yet for those who drink the radiance, you are unable to destroy their craving' is called a figure of speech, as it enhances and thus adorns the extreme loveliness that is already present. The object of embellishment is the abundance of the loveliness of the radiance to be adorned. Further, the distinction between figure of speech and object of embellishment, as well as the appropriate sequence of application, should be understood in the same way. The analyses are: 'radiance in the body,' 'the cupped hands themselves are a receptacle,' 'the eyes themselves are the cupped hands,' and 'he who removes craving'.

176.

176.

Upamānopameyyānaṃ, sadhammattaṃ siyo’pamā;

Saddatthagammā vākyattha-visayāti ca sā tidhā.

A simile would be the common property of the standard of comparison and the object of comparison; and it is threefold: understood through word, understood through meaning, and having the meaning of the sentence as its scope.

176. Upamaṃ niddisati “upamāne”ccādinā. Upamīyate anenāti upamānaṃ, padumādikavatthu. Padumādiko tu saddo upamānavācako. Upamīyatīti upameyyaṃ, mukhādikavatthu. Mukhādiko saddo tu upameyyavācako. Tesaṃ upamānopameyyānaṃ padumādimukhādivatthūnañca. Sadhammattanti samāno dhammo kantimantatā yassa so sadhammo, tassa bhāvo sadhammasaddassa pavattinimittasamānena dhammena saha sambandho sadhammattaṃ [M 0.0192] upamānopameyyapatiṭṭhitaṃ upamā siyā, upamīyati yathāvutto sambandhoti katvā. Sā panālaṅkāriyassa dhammassātisayapaṭipādanappakāro. Katividhā sāti āha “sadda”iccādi. Saddo ca attho ca, tehi gammā patīyamānā saddatthagammā. Vākyaṃ padasamudāyo. Tassa attho visayo gocaro yassā vākyatthavisayāti ca sā upamā tividhā saddagammaatthagammavākyatthavisayāti tidhā hoti.

176. He indicates the simile with 'upamāna,' and so on. That by which something is compared is the standard of comparison (upamāna), an object such as a lotus. But a word like 'lotus' is a word denoting the standard of comparison. That which is compared is the object of comparison (upameyya), an object such as a face. But a word like 'face' is a word denoting the object of comparison. Of these—the standard of comparison and the object of comparison, that is, of objects such as the lotus and the face—the state of having a common quality (`sadhammattaṃ`), established in both, would be a simile. `Sadhammattaṃ` is the state of having a common quality; that which has a common quality (`samāno dhammo`), such as radiance, is `sadhammo`, and its state is `sadhammattaṃ`. This state of having a common quality, established in the standard and object of comparison, would be a simile, because the aforementioned connection is compared. Moreover, it is a method for expressing the excellence of the quality to be adorned. As to how many kinds it has, he says, 'sadda,' and so on. Conveyed by word (`saddagammā`) and conveyed by meaning (`atthagammā`). A sentence is a collection of words. That whose sphere or domain is the meaning of the sentence is `vākyatthavisayā`. Thus, that simile is threefold: conveyed by word, conveyed by meaning, and having the meaning of a sentence as its sphere.

176. Idāni upamālaṅkāraṃ niddisati “upamāno”ccādinā. Upamānopameyyānaṃ candanīluppaladalābhādīnaṃ ānananayanādīnañca padatthānaṃ sadhammattaṃ kantimantatāpīnatāditulyadhammasambandho upamā nāma siyā, sā alaṅkaraṇīyavatthuno ādhikkapaṭipādanappakārā upamā saddatthagammā saddagammā ca atthagammā ca vākyatthavisayā ca, iti evaṃ tidhā tippakārā hoti. Ettha upamānopameyyabhūtānaṃ candānanādipadatthānaṃ sadhammasaṅkhato aññamaññatulyakantimantatāpīnatādidhammayogo padatthānaṃ upamatthassa patiṭṭhitattā upaṭṭhānatāya upamā nāma hoti, tannissayacandādayo pana nissitavohārena upamā nāma hoti, upamānabhūtacandādiatthapaṭipādako candimādisaddopi tadatthena upamā nāma hoti, upameyyupameyyanissayatappaṭipādakānampi upameyyabhāvo evameva daṭṭhabbo. Upamīyate anenāti upamānanti katvā candādi upamānaṃ vuccati, upamīyatīti upameyyaṃ, ānanādi, upamānañca upameyyañcāti ca, samāno ca so dhammo ceti ca, tassa bhāvoti ca, saddo ca attho cāti ca, tehi gammāti ca, vākyassa atthoti ca, so visayo yassā upamāyāti ca vākyaṃ.

176. Now, he indicates the simile ornament with 'upamāna,' and so on. The state of having a common quality among the meanings of the words for the standard of comparison and the object of comparison—such as sandalwood, blue lotus petals, lustre, etc., and face, eyes, etc.—that is, the connection of similar qualities like loveliness, fullness, etc., is called a simile. That simile, being a method for expressing the excellence of the object to be adorned, is of three kinds: conveyed by word, conveyed by meaning, and having the meaning of a sentence as its sphere. Here, for the meanings of words which are the standard of comparison (like the moon) and the object of comparison (like a face), the union with mutually similar qualities such as loveliness, fullness, etc., known as the common quality, is called a simile, because the meaning of comparison is established and present in the meanings of the words. However, the moon, etc., which are its basis, are called a simile by dependent designation. The word 'moon,' etc., which expresses the meaning of the standard of comparison, is also called a simile by that meaning. The status of being the object of comparison should be understood in the very same way for the object of comparison itself, for that which is dependent on it, and for that which indicates it. Because 'that by which something is compared' is the standard of comparison, the moon, etc., are called the standard of comparison. 'That which is compared' is the object of comparison, such as a face. And the analyses are as follows: 'standard of comparison and object of comparison'; 'that which is a common quality'; 'the state of that'; 'word and meaning'; 'conveyed by them'; 'the meaning of the sentence'; and 'that whose sphere it is, for the simile'.

177.

177.

Samāsapaccayevādī, saddā tesaṃ vasā tidhā;

Saddagammā samāsena, munindo candimānano.

Compounds, suffixes, and words such as 'iva' are the 'words'; by their power, the simile conveyed by word is threefold. By means of a compound: 'The Lord of Sages is moon-faced.'

177. Tattha [M 0.0193] saddagammāpi tidhā siyāti dassetumāha “samāsa”iccādi. Samāso ca paccayo ca ivādi ca, te saddā nāma, saddasaddena samāsādayo vattumadhippetāti attho. Tesaṃ samāsādīnaṃ vasā saddagammā tidhā hoti samāsasaddagammā paccayasaddagammā ivādisaddagammāti, samāsena samāsasaddena gammā upamā vuccatīti seso. Udāharati “munindo candimānano”ti, candimā viya ruciramānanaṃ mukhaṃ yassa so candimānano. Ettha ca candimaṃ upamānaṃ, ānanaṃ upameyyaṃ, rucirattaṃ dhammo, candimānanānaṃ samānadhammasambandhijotako viyasaddo, tesu sādhāraṇadhammavācakassa viyasaddassa copamājotakassāppayogo samāseneva vuttattā, ettha pana viyasaddo candimāsaddena upamānavācakena sambandhamupagato candagatameva sadisattaṃ vadati, mukhagataṃ pana sāmatthiyā padīyate, evamīdisaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

177. Here, to show that the simile conveyed by word can also be threefold, he says, 'samāsa,' and so on. Compounds, suffixes, and words such as 'iva' are called 'words'; the meaning is that by the word 'sadda,' compounds and so on are intended to be spoken of. By the power of these compounds and so on, the simile conveyed by word is threefold: that conveyed by a compound word, that conveyed by a suffix word, and that conveyed by a word such as 'iva.' The rest to be supplied is: a simile conveyed by a compound is expressed by means of a compound word. He gives the example: 'munindo candimānano' (the Lord of Sages is moon-faced), meaning 'he whose face is lovely like the moon is moon-faced.' Here, the moon is the standard of comparison, the face is the object of comparison, loveliness is the common quality, and the word 'viya' is what indicates the connection of the common quality between the moon and the face. Among these, the word expressing the common quality and the word 'viya' which indicates the simile are not used, because their meaning is expressed by the compound itself. Here, however, the word 'viya,' being connected with the word 'candimā' which denotes the standard of comparison, expresses only the similarity pertaining to the moon; the similarity pertaining to the face, however, is understood by implication. It should be understood in this way.

177. Tesu yathāvuttesu saddagammassa tividhattaṃ dassetuṃ āha “samāse”ccādi. Samāsapaccayevādī samāso, āyādipaccayā, ivādayo ca saddā nāma, tesaṃ samāsādīnaṃ vasā bhedena saddagammā tidhā samāsasaddagammā paccayasaddagammā ivādisaddagammāti tividhā hoti. Samāsena samāsasaddena gammopamā vuccati “munindo candimānano”ti. Munindo sammāsambuddho candimānano candasamānamanoharamukhamaṇḍalena yutto hoti, samāso ca paccayo ca ivaiti idaṃ ādi yesaṃ vādīnanti ca, saddena gammāti ca, munīnaṃ indoti ca, candimā viya ruciraṃ ānanaṃ mukhaṃ yasseti ca viggaho. Ettha “candimā”ti upamānaṃ, “ānana”nti upameyyaṃ, rucirattaṃ upamānopameyyānaṃ sādhāraṇadhammo, “viyā”ti saddo candānanānaṃ dvinnaṃ ānanagatarucirattaṃ cande ca, candagatarucirattaṃ ānane ca atthīti samānadhammasambandhaṃ [M 0.0194] joteti, iha sādhāraṇadhammavācakassa rucirasaddassa, tulyadhammasaṅkhātopamājotakassa viyasaddassa ca appayogo tesaṃ atthānaṃ samāsena vuttattā. Ettha upamānavācakena candimāsaddena yutto viya saddo candagatasadisattaṃ joteti, mukhagatasadisattaṃ pana sāmatthiyā patīyate. Tathā hi mukhaṃ candasamānamāgacchantaṃ candassa mukhasadisattaṃ vinā na bhavatīti aññathānupapatti sāmatthiyanti.

177. Among these, to show the threefold nature of the simile conveyed by word as described, he says, 'samāsa,' and so on. Compounds, suffixes beginning with 'āya,' and words such as 'iva' are called 'words.' By the power of these compounds and so on, the simile conveyed by word is threefold, divided into that conveyed by a compound word, that conveyed by a suffix word, and that conveyed by a word such as 'iva.' A simile conveyed by a compound is expressed by means of a compound word, as in 'munindo candimānano.' The Lord of Sages, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is endowed with a lovely face-orb similar to the moon. And the analysis is: 'compound, suffix, and that which has "iva" as its beginning'; 'conveyed by word'; 'lord of sages'; and 'he whose face is lovely like the moon.' Here, 'candimā' is the standard of comparison, 'ānana' is the object of comparison, loveliness is the common quality of the standard and the object of comparison, and the word 'viya' indicates the connection of the common quality between the two, that is, that the loveliness pertaining to the face is in the moon, and the loveliness pertaining to the moon is in the face. Here, the word 'rucira,' which expresses the common quality, and the word 'viya,' which indicates the simile in the form of a similar quality, are not used because their meanings are expressed by the compound. Here, the word 'viya,' being connected with the word 'candimā' which denotes the standard of comparison, indicates the similarity pertaining to the moon, while the similarity pertaining to the face is understood by implication. For indeed, a face becoming similar to the moon cannot occur without the moon's likeness to the face; this impossibility of the contrary is what is meant by implication.

178.

178.

Āyādī paccayā tehi, vadanaṃ paṅkajāyate;

Munindanayanadvandaṃ, nīluppaladalīyati.

Suffixes beginning with 'āya' and so on. By them: 'The face becomes like a lotus; the pair of eyes of the Lord of Sages becomes like blue lotus petals.'

178. Idāni paccayasaddagammaṃ dasseti “āyādi”ccādinā. Āyādīti āyaīyakapaccayādayo paccayā paccayasaddā nāma, tehi paccayasaddehi gammā upamā vuccati. Udāharati “vadana”miccādi. Paṅkajamiva ruciramācarati paṅkajāyate. Etthāpi paṅkajamupamānaṃ, ācaraṇakriyāya kattubhūtaṃ ānanamupameyyaṃ, rucirattaṃ sadhammo, paṅkajānanānaṃ samānadhammasambandhajotako ivasaddo. Tattha rucira ivasaddānaṃ pubbe viyāppayogo paccayena vuttattāti sabbattha viññeyyaṃ. Evamuparipi.

178. Now, he shows the simile conveyed by a suffix word with 'āyādi,' and so on. 'Āyādi' means suffixes such as 'āya,' 'īya,' and 'ka'; these suffixes are called 'suffix words,' and a simile conveyed by these suffix words is expressed. He gives the example 'vadanaṃ,' and so on. 'Paṅkajāyate' means 'it acts beautifully like a lotus.' Here too, the lotus is the standard of comparison; the face, being the agent of the action of 'acting,' is the object of comparison; loveliness is the common quality; and the word 'iva' indicates the connection of the common quality between the lotus and the face. In this case, it should be understood everywhere that, as before, the words 'rucira' and 'iva' are not used, because their meaning is expressed by the suffix. And similarly for the next example.

178. Idāni paccayasaddagammopamaṃ nidasseti “āyādi”ccādinā. Āyādī “āya īya ka”itiādayo paccayā paccayasaddā nāma, tehi paccayasaddehi gammopamā vuccati “vadanaṃ…pe… dalīyatī”ti. Vadanaṃ mukhaṃ paṅkajāyate padumamiva ruciraṃ ācarati. Munindanayanadvandaṃ sabbaññuno nettayugaḷaṃ nīluppaladalīyati nīluppalapattamiva ruciramācarati. Āyo ādi yesaṃ īyādīnanti ca, paṅkajamiva ruciramācarati pavattatīti ca, munindassa nayanadvandamiti ca, nīluppalassa dalamiti ca, tamiva ruciramācaratīti ca vākyaṃ. Ettha “paṅkaja”miti ca “nīluppala”miti ca upamānaṃ, ācaraṇakriyāya kattubhūtaṃ vadanaṃ [M 0.0195] nayanadvandañca upameyyaṃ, rucirattaṃ upamānopameyyānaṃ sadhammo, upamānopameyyānaṃ samānadhammajotako ivasaddo, tesaṃ atthānaṃ paccayena vuttattā tesamappayogo. Evarūpesu aññesupi evameva veditabbo.

178. Now, he illustrates the simile understood by suffix-words with 'āyādi' and so on. 'Āyādi' means suffixes like 'āya', 'īya', 'ka', etc.; these are called suffix-words, and by these suffix-words, a simile understood is expressed, as in 'vadanaṃ… dalīyatī'. 'Vadanaṃ' (the face) means 'mukhaṃ' (face), and 'paṅkajāyate' means 'it behaves beautifully like a lotus'. The pair of eyes of the Muninda, the All-Knowing One, is 'nettayugaḷaṃ' (pair of eyes), and 'nīluppaladalīyati' means 'it behaves beautifully like a blue lotus petal'. And the analysis of the phrases is: 'those of which āya, īya, etc., are the beginning'; 'it behaves beautifully like a lotus and proceeds'; 'the pair of eyes of the Muninda'; 'the petal of a blue lotus'; and 'it behaves beautifully like that'. Here, 'paṅkaja' and 'nīluppala' are the standard of comparison. The face and the pair of eyes, which are the agents of the action of behaving, are the object of comparison. Loveliness is the common quality of the standard and the object of comparison. The word 'iva' indicates the common quality of the standard and the object of comparison. Their non-application is due to their meanings being expressed by the suffix. In other such cases, it should be understood in the same way.

179.

179.

Ivādī iva vā tulya-samāna nibha sannibhā;

Yathāsaṅkāsa tulita-ppakāsa patirūpakā.

Words beginning with 'iva': like, like, equal, similar, resembling, very similar; as, appearing like, compared, appearing as, resembling.

180.

180.

Sarīsarikkha saṃvādī, virodhī sadisā viya;

Paṭipakkhapaccanīka-sapakkho’pamito’pamā.

Similar, resembling, agreeing, opposed, similar, like; opponent, hostile, of the same side, compared, simile.

181.

181.

Paṭibimba paṭicchanna-sarūpa sama sammitā;

Savaṇṇā’bhā paṭinidhi, sadhammādi salakkhaṇā.

Reflection, concealed, similar in form, equal, compared; of the same appearance, substitute, having common qualities and so on, having the same characteristics.

182.

182.

Jayatya’kkosati hasati, patigajjati dūbhati;

Usūyatya’vajānāti, nindati’ssati rundhati.

He surpasses, abuses, laughs at, retorts, harms; he envies, disparages, blames, is jealous, obstructs.

183.

183.

Tassa coreti sobhaggaṃ, tassa kantiṃ vilumpati;

Tena saddhiṃ vivadati, tulyaṃ tenādhirohati.

He steals his good fortune, he plunders his beauty; he disputes with him, he ascends to his level.

184.

184.

Kacchaṃvigāhate tassa, tamanvetya’nubandhati;

Taṃsīlaṃ, taṃ nisedheti, tassa cānukaroti’me.

He challenges him on his own ground, he follows and pursues him; he is of his character, he restrains him, and he imitates him—these are the terms.

179-184. Ivādī ivādayo nāma imeti sambandho. Ivo ca vā ca tulyo ca samāno ca nibho ca sannibho cāti dvande iva…pe… sannibhā. Saddamapekkhiya pulliṅgatā. Evamuparipi yathāyogaṃ. “Sadhammādī”ti ādisaddena sādhāraṇasacchāyādīnaṃ pariggaho. Jayaticcādīsu kammaṃ.

179-184. The word `Ivādī` is connected with `ime` (these), meaning 'the words beginning with `iva`'. The phrase '`iva` and `vā` and `tulya` and `samāna` and `nibha` and `sannibha`' is a dvanda compound, [resulting in the form] `iva… sannibhā`. The masculine gender is used with reference to the word (`sadda`). And similarly for the above, as appropriate. In 'sadhammādī', by the word 'ādi', the inclusion of 'sādhāraṇa', 'sacchāyā', etc., is meant. In 'Jayati' and so on, the object is to be supplied.

179- 184. Ivādisaddagammopamādhikāre paṭhamaṃ tāva “ivādayo nāma ete”ti dasseti “ivādi”ccādinā. Ivādīti padassa chaṭṭhamagāthāya imeti iminā sambandho, tassa cāti casaddaṃ yujjanaṭṭhāne yojetvā sannibhā cātiādayo yojetabbā. “Sadhammādī”tiādisaddena sādhāraṇasacchāyādayo gahitā. Nindati issatīti padacchedo, ime [M 0.0196] dvepaññāsa ivādayo nāma. “Jayati akkosati hasati”iccādikaṃ taṃtaṃkriyāpadasaṅkhataanukāriyānaṃ anukaraṇanti katvā dvandoyeva, “sandhisamāsā addhassā”ti sandhisamāso tadaddhassāti (ka.) vuttattā sandhisamāsānaṃ gāthaddhassa vinā ubhayaddhamajjhe alabbhanato dūbhatipadato pubbeyeva samāso kātabbo, no ce, asamāsoti gahetabbo. Tassa coreti sobhaggamiccādikampi vākyānukaraṇanti katvā tattha samāso, vākye kevalapadānīti vā gahetabbo. Imesaṃ sabbesampi iva saddapariyāyattā sadisatthāti sabbattha bhāvattho, avayavattho pana pākaṭoyeva.

179-184. In the section on similes understood by words beginning with 'iva', it is first shown that 'these are the words beginning with `iva`' by the phrase 'ivādi' and so on. The word 'ivādī' is connected with 'ime' in the sixth verse, and the particle 'ca' should be applied where appropriate, and terms like 'sannibhā ca' and so on should be added. By the word 'ādi' in 'sadhammādi', terms like 'sādhāraṇa' and 'sacchāyā' are included. The word division is 'nindati issati'—these fifty-two are called 'ivādi' words. Phrases like 'jayati akkosati hasati' are treated as a dvanda compound because they are an imitation of the various things to be imitated, which are the verb phrases. Since it is said, 'sandhi and compounds belong to a half-verse,' and since they are not found in the middle of both halves without a half-verse, a compound should be formed just before the word `dūbhati`; if not, it should be taken as a non-compound. Phrases like 'tassa coreti sobhaggam' are also treated as a compound, being an imitation of a sentence, or they should be taken as individual words in a sentence. For all of these, since they are synonyms of the word 'iva' and have the meaning of 'similar', the abstract sense of similarity is everywhere implied, but the meaning of the component parts is evident.

185.

185.

Upamānopameyyānaṃ, sadhammattaṃ vibhāvihi;

Imehi upamābhedā, keci niyyanti sampati.

By these (words), which reveal the common quality of the standard of comparison and the object of comparison, some types of similes are now set forth.

185. Ivādīnaṃ viniyogavisayaṃ dassetvā upamābhedaṃ dassetuṃ paṭijānāti “upamāna”iccādi. Kecīti iminā apariyantattamesaṃ apariyantapabhedaṃ (ka.) dasseti. Tathā ca vakkhati “pariyanto vikappāna”ntiādi. Niyyanti udāharīyanti.

185. Having shown the scope of application of terms beginning with 'iva', he undertakes to explain the types of similes, beginning with 'upamāna' and so on. By 'some' (keci), he shows their limitlessness. And thus it will be said, 'there is no limit to the variations,' and so on. 'Niyyanti' means 'they are exemplified'.

185. Idāni ivādisaddagammopamaṃ dassetuṃ paṭijānāti “upamāno”ccādinā. Upamānopameyyānaṃ sadhammattaṃ samānadhammasambandho. Vibhāvihi pakāsakehi. Imehi ivādīhi saddehi jānitabbā keci upamābhedā apariyantattā sampati dāni laddhāvasare niyyanti udāharaṇamattena paṭipādīyanti.

185. Now, to explain the simile understood by words such as 'ivādi', he undertakes to do so with 'upamāna' and so on. 'Upamānopameyyānaṃ sadhammattaṃ' is the state of having a common quality between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison, meaning the connection of a similar quality. 'Vibhāvihi' means 'by those that reveal'. Some types of similes, which are to be understood by these words such as 'ivādi', are now, having obtained the opportunity, conveyed by way of example alone, because of their limitlessness.

186.

186.

Vikāsipadumaṃ’vā’ti-sundaraṃ sugatānanaṃ;

Iti dhammopamā nāma, tulyadhammanidassanā.

The exceedingly beautiful face of the Sugata is like a blooming lotus; thus is called a simile of quality, for it demonstrates a similar quality.

186. “Vikāsi”ccādi. Sugatānanaṃ munindassa vadanaṃ atisundaraṃ accantaramaṇīyaṃ. Kimiva? Vikāsipadumaṃva pabujjhamānapadumaṃviya. Iti ayamevaṃvidhā dhammopamā nāma hoti. Kasmā? [M 0.0197] Ānanapadumānaṃ samānassa dhammassa guṇassa sundarassa lakkhaṇassa nidassanā sundarattanti paṭipādanato.

186. 'Blooming' and so on. The face of the Sugata, the lord of sages, is exceedingly beautiful and most delightful. Like what? Like a blooming lotus, like an awakening lotus. Thus, a simile of this kind is called a simile of quality. Why? Because it demonstrates the beautiful characteristic, the common quality of the face and the lotus, by establishing it as beauty.

186. Udāharaṇamāha “vikāsi”ccādinā. Sugatānanaṃ bhagavato mukhaṃ vikāsipadumaṃva bujjhamānapaṅkajamiva atisundaraṃ hoti. Iti īdisā upamā tulyadhammanidassanā atisundaramiti samānaguṇadassanena dhammopamā nāma hoti. Padumānanānaṃ sādhāraṇaguṇassa pakāsanato atisundaramiti tulyadhammo nāma hoti. Ettha padumagatatulyadhammasambandhasaṅkhātāya upamāya ivasaddena jotiyamānattepi atisundaranti vuttattā yathāvuttopamāya dhammena yuttattā dhammopamā nāma hotīti adhippāyo.

186. He gives an example with 'blooming,' etc. The face of the Blessed One, the Sugata's face, is exceedingly beautiful, like a blooming lotus, like a lotus that is unfolding. Such a simile, demonstrating a similar quality, is called a simile of quality because it shows the similar quality as 'exceedingly beautiful'. Because it manifests the common quality of lotuses and faces, 'exceedingly beautiful' is called the similar quality. Here, even though the simile—described as the connection with the similar quality residing in the lotus—is indicated by the word 'iva', because 'exceedingly beautiful' is stated, the intention is that it is called a simile of quality because it is endowed with the quality as described.

187.

187.

Dhammahīnā mukha’mbhoja-sadisaṃ munino iti;

Viparītopamā tulya-mānanena’mbujaṃ tava.

“The face of the sage is like a lotus”—this is a simile devoid of quality. “Your lotus is equal to your face”—this is a reversed simile.

187. “Dhamma”iccādi. Munino sammāsambuddhassa mukhaṃ ambhojena padumena sadisaṃ samānaṃ. Iti ayaṃ dhammahīnopamā nāma sundarasaṅkhātassa guṇassa aniddiṭṭhattā, sā tu atthavasā gamyate. Kathamaññathā yujjatīti? Ettha pana sadisasaddo upameyyassa mukhassa visesananti mukhagatameva sadisattaṃ vadati, ambhojagataṃ tu sāmatthiyā gamyate. Evamīdisaṃ ñeyyaṃ. “Viparīte”ccādi. Munīti gamyate sutattā, bho muni tava ānanena mukhena ambujaṃ tulyanti ayaṃ viparītopamā. Dhammahīnattepi pasiddhivipariyayenābhihitattā tannāmeneva vuttā. Evamuparipi.

187. 'Dhamma' and so on. The face of the sage, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, is like a lotus. This is called a simile devoid of quality because the quality described as 'beauty' is not specified; however, it is understood by the force of the meaning. How else could it be appropriate? Here, the word 'sadisa' (like) is an adjective of the object of comparison, the face, and thus states the likeness residing in the face, while that residing in the lotus is understood by implication. Such is to be understood. 'Reversed' and so on. 'The sage' is understood because it has been heard—'O sage, a lotus is similar to your face'—this is a reversed simile. Even though it is devoid of quality, it is called by that name because it is expressed by a reversal of what is well-known. The same applies to the preceding cases.

187. “Dhammahīne”ccādi. “Mukhambhojasadisaṃ munino”tyayaṃ upamā. Dhammahīnā tulyadhammapakāsakasundarādisaddahīnattā dhammahīnā nāma. Vācakābhāve tulyadhammo kathaṃ patīyatīti ce? Munino mukhaṃ vadanaṃ ambhojasadisaṃ padumasadisamiti. Ettha mukhassa ambhojasamānattaṃ mukhambhojānaṃ sādhāraṇadhamme asati [M 0.0198] kathaṃ bhavatīti? Aññathānupapattilakkhaṇasāmatthiyāti, ivapariyāyo sadisasaddo mukhassa visesanaṃ yasmā hoti, tasmā mukhagatasadisattaṃ vadati, ambhojagatasadisattaṃ pana sāmatthiyā eva viññāyate. He muni tava tuyhaṃ ānanena ambhojaṃ tulyaṃ samānanti ayaṃ viparītopamā. “Ambujena ānanaṃ tulya”nti lokappasiddhiyā vipariyayena “ānanena ambujaṃ tulya”nti vuttattā dhammahīnatte satipi viparītopamā nāma hoti. “Sutānumitesu sutasambandho balavā”ti paribhāsendusekhara 112 vuttattā ettha “munī”ti avijjamānepi pubbaddhe “munino”ti sutattā labbhamāno “tavā”ti tumhasaddasannidhānena āmantanattho viññāyati. Ettha ivapariyāyo tulyasaddo ambujavisesanabhūto ambujagatasadisattaṃ vadati, ānanagatasadisattañca ambujānanānaṃ sādhāraṇadhammo ca sāmatthiyā ñāyaticcādikaṃ vuttanayena ñātabbaṃ. Uparipi pākaṭaṭṭhānaṃ yathārahaṃ yojetabbaṃ.

187. 'Dhammahīna', etc. 'The sage's face is like a lotus'—this is the simile. They are called 'devoid of quality' (dhammahīnā) because they are devoid of words such as 'beautiful' that express a similar quality. If there is no expressive word, how is the similar quality to be understood? It means, 'the sage's face is like a lotus'. Here, how can the similarity of the face to a lotus exist if there is no common quality between the face and the lotus? By the power of implication, which is characterized by the impossibility of it being otherwise. Since the word 'sadisa', a synonym of 'iva', is an adjective of the face, it expresses the similarity residing in the face, while the similarity residing in the lotus is understood only by implication. 'O sage, your lotus is equal to your face'—this is a reversed simile. Because it is stated as 'the lotus is equal to the face', reversing the common worldly expression 'the face is equal to a lotus', it is called a reversed simile even while being devoid of quality. Since it is said, 'Among what is heard and what is inferred, the connection to what is heard is stronger,' here, even though 'muni' is not present in the preceding half-verse, because 'munino' is heard, it is obtained, and by the proximity of the word 'tumha' in the form of 'tava', a vocative meaning is understood. Here, the word 'tulya', a synonym of 'iva', functioning as an adjective for the lotus, expresses the similarity residing in the lotus; and the similarity residing in the face and the common quality of the lotus and the face are understood by implication, and so on, which should be understood in the manner explained. In other clear instances above as well, this should be applied as is appropriate.

188.

188.

Tavānana’miva’mbhojaṃ, ambhoja’miva te mukhaṃ;

Aññamaññopamā sā’yaṃ, aññamaññopamānato.

Your face is like a lotus, a lotus is like your face; this is a mutual simile, because of mutual comparison.

188. “Tava”iccādi. Aññamaññopamānatoti aññamaññassa mukhassa ambhojassa ca aññamaññena taṃdvayena upamānato.

188. 'Tava', etc. 'Aññamaññopamānato' means 'because of mutual comparison'; that is, because of the comparison of the face and the lotus to each other, by that very pair.

188. “Tavānani”ccādi. “Ambhojaṃ tavānanamiva, te mukhaṃ ambhojamivā”ti ayamupamā. Aññamaññopamānato aññamaññassa upamānattā aññamaññopamā nāma hoti. Aññamaññassa upamāti ca, aññamaññassa upamānanti ca viggaho. Viggahadvayepi pubbavibhattilopo. Sabbādīnaṃ byatihāralakkhaṇena uttaravibhattilopo. Samāsalakkhaṇena aññatthassa apekkhāsiddhattā [M 0.0199] mukhāpekkhāya aññaṃ ambhojañca, ambhojāpekkhāya aññaṃ mukhañca kamena upameyyā nāma. Ambhojāpekkhāya aññaṃ mukhañca, mukhāpekkhāya aññaṃ ambhojañca upamānaṃ nāma.

188. 'Tavānana', etc. This is the simile: 'The lotus is like your face, your face is like a lotus.' Because of mutual comparison, and because each is the standard of comparison for the other, it is called a mutual simile. The analysis is 'aññamaññassa upamā' (the simile of each other) and 'aññamaññassa upamānaṃ' (the standard of comparison of each other). In both analyses, the prior case ending is elided. The subsequent case ending is elided due to the characteristic of reciprocity of the 'sabbādi' group of words. By the characteristic of compounding, since the dependence of one on the other is established, with reference to the face, the other—the lotus—and with reference to the lotus, the other—the face—are in sequence called the objects of comparison (upameyya). With reference to the lotus, the other—the face—and with reference to the face, the other—the lotus—are called the standard of comparison (upamāna).

189.

189.

Yadi kiñci bhave’mbhojaṃ,

Locanabbhamuvibbhamaṃ;

Dhāretuṃ mukhasobhaṃ taṃ,

Tave’ti abbhutopamā.

If there were any lotus possessing the charm of eyes and eyebrows, it could bear the beauty of your face—this is a marvelous simile.

189. “Yadi”ccādi. Locanāni ca bhamuyo ca, tāsaṃ vibbhamo yasmiṃ, taṃ, tādisamambhojaṃ kiñci kimapi yadi bhave. Tamīdisamambhojaṃ tava mukhasobhaṃ vadanakantiṃ dhāretuṃ nisijjhate. Kiṃ nvacchariyamīdisanti abbhutatthavibhāvanena vadanamambujenopamīyatīti ayamabbhutopamā ñātabbāti.

189. 'Yadi', etc. 'Eyes and eyebrows, the charm of which is in it'—if there were any such lotus at all, that such a lotus would be capable of bearing the beauty of your face, the radiance of your countenance. By expressing the meaning of marvel with 'What a wonder this is!', the face is compared to a lotus. Thus, this should be understood as a marvelous simile.

189. “Yadi”ccādi. Locanabbhamuvibbhamaṃ locanabhamūnaṃ līlāvantaṃ kiñci ambhojaṃ kiñci acchariyaṃ padumaṃ yadi bhave ce siyā, tamambhojaṃ tava mukhasobhaṃ vadanakantiṃ dhāretuṃ samattho hoti. Iti īdisī upamā abbhutopamā abbhutadhammapakāsakattā abbhutopamā nāma. Ettha avijjamānopi vijjamānattena parikappito padumagato locanabbhamuvibbhamasambandho ambhojavisesanena “locanabbhamuvibbhama”nti iminā jotito. Tasmā ambhojaṃ locanabbhamuvibbhamasambandhasaṅkhataupamāya jotakattā nissitavohārena upamā, mukhaṃ upameyyanti mukhagato locanabbhamuvibbhamasambandho yadi mukhe na bhaveyya, tādisaṃ mukhasobhaṃ dhāretuṃ kathaṃ samatthoti sāmatthiyā ñāyati. Locanabbhamuvibbhamasaṅkhātasādhāraṇadhammo pana “locanāni ca bhamuyo ceti ca, tāsaṃ vibbhamo yasmi”nti ca viggahe nipphannena [M 0.0200] bhinnādhikaraṇaaññapadatthasamāsena guṇībhūtassapi gahitattā viññāyati gahaṇassa viññāyamānattā (ka.).

189. 'Yadi', etc. 'Locanabbhamuvibbhamam' means possessing the grace of eyes and eyebrows. If there were any such wondrous lotus, any marvelous lotus, that lotus would be capable of bearing the beauty of your face, the radiance of your countenance. Such a simile is called a 'marvelous simile' because it expresses a marvelous quality. Here, the connection of the lotus to the charm of the eyes and eyebrows, though non-existent, is imagined as existing and is illuminated by this adjective of the lotus, 'locanabbhamuvibhama'. Therefore, the lotus, being the illuminator of the simile designated as the connection to the charm of the eyes and eyebrows, is the simile by dependent designation, and the face is the object of comparison. If the connection to the charm of the eyes and eyebrows were not present in the face, how could it be capable of bearing such beauty? This is understood by implication. The common quality, designated as the charm of the eyes and eyebrows, is understood because it is grasped, even though it is subordinated, by the bahubbīhi compound with different referents which is formed with the analysis 'eyes and eyebrows, the charm of which is in it'.

190.

190.

Sugandhi sobhasambandhi, sisiraṃsuvirodhi ca;

Mukhaṃ tava’mbujaṃve’ti, sā silesopamā matā.

Fragrant, connected with splendor, and opposing the cool-rayed one; your face is like a lotus—this is considered a simile of paronomasia.

190. “Sugandhi”ccādi. Tava mukhaṃ ambhojamiva sisiraṃsunocandassa virodhi paccanīkaṃ, mukhaṃ taṃsamānakantittā ambujañca tadudaye saṅkocabhajanato. Sobhasambandhi kantiyuttaṃ, mukhamambujañca. Sugandho assa atthīti sugandhi ca dvayamapīti evaṃ silesapariggahena mukhambujānaṃ upamāyogato sā yathāvuttā silesopamā matā.

190. 'Sugandhi', etc. Your face, like a lotus, is an opponent of the cool-rayed one, the moon: the face, because its radiance is equal to the moon's, and the lotus, because it contracts at the moon's rising. 'Sobhasambandhi' means endowed with radiance; both the face and the lotus are so. 'Sugandhi' means 'it has fragrance'; both are so. Thus, because the comparison between the face and the lotus is established through the device of paronomasia, it is considered, as stated, a simile of paronomasia.

190. “Sugandhi”ccādi. Tava mukhaṃ ambhojamiva sisiraṃsuvirodhi candassa viruddhaṃ hoti tulyattā. Padumaṃ pana candodayena attano saṅkocanattā tassa viruddhaṃ hoti. Sobhasambandhi ca anaññasādhāraṇamukhagatakantisambandhayuttañca hoti. Padumaṃ pana padumagatakantisambandhinā yuttaṃ hoti. Sugandhi ca catujjātisugandhavahanato …vamanato (ka.) sugandhi ca hoti. Ambujaṃ pana padumasugandheneva yuttaṃ hoti. Iti īdisī upamā silesopamā ekapadātihitaubhayatthalakkhaṇena silesavasena vuttattā silesopamā nāma hoti. Sisirā sītalā aṃsu kanti asseti ca, tassa virujjhati sīleneti ca, paccayasāmatthiyavasena dvinnaṃ dvinnaṃ atthānaṃ labbhanato silissati aparopi attho ettha alaṅkāreti ca, silesavasena vuttā upamāti ca viggaho. Ettha sugandho ca sotasambandho ca sisiraṃsuvirodhittañceti ime upamānopameyyānamambujamukhānaṃ tulyadhammo, tesu ambujagatatulyadhammasambandho sadhammattā upamā nāma hoti, sā ambujasambandhinā ivasaddena jotitā, [M 0.0201] mukhagatatulyadhammo pana assatthitassīlatthe katapaccaye satipi sāmatthiyāyeva gamyate.

190. 'Sugandhi', etc. Your face, like a lotus, is opposed to the moon because of its equal radiance. The lotus, however, is opposed to it because it contracts at moonrise. It is also connected with splendor, possessing a radiance unique to the face. The lotus, however, is endowed with the splendor belonging to a lotus. And it is fragrant, carrying the fragrance of the four kinds. The lotus, however, is endowed only with the fragrance of a lotus. Thus, such a simile is called a simile of paronomasia because it is expressed by way of paronomasia, which has the characteristic of both meanings being conveyed by a single word. The analysis is: 'sisiraṃsu' means 'it has cool (sisirā) rays (aṃsu)'; 'virodhi' means 'it opposes by nature (sīlena)'. Because two meanings are obtained for each word by the power of the suffixes, another meaning is embraced here as an ornament. And 'a simile expressed by way of paronomasia' is the analysis. Here, fragrance, connection with splendor, and opposition to the cool-rayed one—these are the similar qualities of the standard of comparison and the object of comparison, the lotus and the face. Among these, the connection of the similar quality residing in the lotus is called a simile because it is a shared quality, and it is illuminated by the word 'iva' connected to the lotus. The similar quality residing in the face, however, is understood only by implication, even when a suffix is used in the sense of 'possession' or 'nature'.

191.

191.

Sarūpasaddavāccattā, sā santānopamā yathā;

Bālā’vu’yyānamālā’yaṃ, sālakānanasobhinī.

Because it is expressed by a word of similar form, it is a 'continuous simile', as follows: This garden garland, resplendent with a grove of sāla trees, is like a young woman.

191. “Sarūpa”iccādi. Ayamuyyānamālā bālāva itthī viya. Kathaṃ? Sālakānanasobhinī bālā tāva sahālakena kesasannivesavisesena vattate sālakamānanaṃ tena sobhate. Sālakānanasobhinī uyyānamālāpi sālānaṃ rukkhavisesānaṃ kānanena gahanena sobhate, evarūpā sā tādisī santānopamā ākhyāyate, kasmā? Silesopamattasabhāvepi sarūpena sadisena saddena “sālakānanasobhinī”tvevaṃvidhena saddasantānena visesabhūtena vāccattā pakāsiyattā tassāiti gamyate. Yatheti nidassane.

191. 'Sarūpa', etc. This garden garland is like a young woman. How? The young woman is 'sālakānanasobhinī': she shines with a face (ānana) that has curls (sālaka). The garden garland is also 'sālakānanasobhinī': it shines with a dense grove (kānana) of sāla trees, a special kind of tree. Such a simile is called a 'continuous simile'. Why? Because, although its nature is that of a simile of paronomasia, it is understood to be expressed and manifested by a distinct, continuous stream of words of similar form, such as 'sālakānanasobhinī'. 'Yathā' indicates the example.

191. “Sarūpe”ccādi. Sarūpasaddavāccattā tulyasutiyā acchinnasambandhavacanamālāya vuccamānattā sā upamā santānopamā nāma hoti, silesatte satipi katasamāsehi padasantānehi vuccamānattā santānopamā nāma hotīti adhippāyo. “Yathe”ti udāharati. Ayaṃ uyyānamālā esā uyyānapanti sālakānanasobhinī alakasaṅkhātakesasannivesasahitena mukhena sobhamānā bālāva aṅganā iva sālakānanasobhinī sālavanehi sobhamānā hoti. Upamānopameyyānaṃ samānaṃ rūpaṃ yesanti ca, sarūpā ca te saddā ceti ca, tehi vāccā upamāti ca, tassā bhāvoti ca, santānena yuttā upamāti ca, uyyānānaṃ mālāti ca, saha alakena vattamānanti ca, tañca taṃ ānanañcāti ca, tena sobhati sīlenāti ca, sālānaṃ kānananti ca, tena sobhati sīlenāti ca vākyaṃ.

191. "Sarūpe" and so on. Because it is expressed by a word of similar form, due to the similarity of sound, and because it is spoken with an unbroken chain of words, that simile is called a continuous simile. The meaning is that it is called a continuous simile because it is expressed by continuous words forming compounds, even when there is paronomasia. It illustrates with 'Just as': This garland of parks, this row of parks, is adorned with a grove of sāla trees; like a young woman shining with a face endowed with a hair arrangement called alaka, it shines, adorned with sāla forests. The analysis is: 'They whose standard and comparand have the same form'; and 'they are words of similar form'; and 'the simile expressed by them'; and 'its nature'; and 'a simile connected by continuity'; and 'a garland of parks'; and 'existing together with alaka (curls)'; and 'that face'; and 'it shines by that nature'; and 'a forest of sāla trees'; and 'it shines by that nature'.

192.

192.

Khayī [M 0.0202] cando bahurajaṃ, padumaṃ tehi te mukhaṃ;

Samānampi samukkaṃsī-tya’yaṃ nindopamā matā.

The moon is waning, the lotus is full of pollen; your face, though similar to them, surpasses them. This is considered a simile of dispraise.

192. “Khayī”iccādi. Cando khayī khayo accayo yasseti, padumaṃ bahurajaṃ bahūni rajāni parāgāvayavā yasminti, tehi evaṃbhūtehi candapadumehi kantiādinā samānampi sadisampi santaṃ tava mukhaṃ samukkaṃsi paramukkaṃsavantaṃ, khayasaddassa ca rajassa ca dosepi vattanato, saddacchalena khayassa dosarūpassa bahurajattassa ca tatthābhāvatoti. Iti evarūpā ayaṃ nindopamā matā ninditena candādinā khayassopamitattā.

192. "Waning," and so on. The moon is 'waning' because it has waning and decline. The lotus is 'full of pollen' because it has much pollen, i.e., pollen particles. Your face, though similar and equal in beauty and so on to such a moon and lotus, surpasses them, being supremely excellent. This is because the words 'waning' and 'pollen' also refer to faults, and by a play on words, the fault-like nature of waning and the state of having much pollen are absent in the face. Thus, such a simile is considered a simile of dispraise (nindopamā) because it is compared to the moon and so on, which are dispraised due to their waning.

192. “Khayi”ccādi. Cando khayī pāṭipadato paṭṭhāya dine dine ekamekāya kalāya sūriyassa āsannahetu khīyanasabhāvayutto hoti, padumaṃ bahurajaṃ bahureṇusamannāgataṃ hoti, tehi candapadumehi samānampi kantisugandhādīhi sadisampi te mukhaṃ tavānanaṃ samukkaṃsi khayarajasaddehi dosassāpi vāccattā saddacchalehi gamyamānassa tādisassa dosassa mukhe avijjamānattā adhikukkaṃsaguṇavantaṃ hoti, iti īdisī ayaṃ upamā nindopamā ninditānaṃ candapadumānaṃ mukhassa upamitāti nindopamā nāma hoti, mukhavisesanena ivasaddapariyāyena samānasaddena mukhagatasadhammo jotito hoti, upamāsaṅkhatacandapadumagatasadhammopi dvīsu tulyadhammopi sāmatthiyā gamyate, apisaddo cettha vattabbantarasamuccaye, samukkaṃsoti vattabbantaro.

192. "Waning," and so on. The moon is 'waning' because, from the first day of the lunar fortnight, it is naturally inclined to diminish day by day, losing one digit due to its proximity to the sun. The lotus is 'full of pollen,' endowed with much pollen. Your face, though similar to that moon and lotus in beauty, fragrance, and so on, surpasses them. This is because faults are also expressed by the words 'waning' and 'pollen,' and such faults, though implied by a play on words, are non-existent in the face; thus it possesses a superior excellence. Therefore, such a simile is called a simile of dispraise (nindopamā) because the face is compared to the dispraised moon and lotus. By the word 'samāna' (similar), which is an equivalent of the word 'iva' (like), the common quality belonging to the face is illuminated. The common quality belonging to the moon and lotus, which are designated as the standard of comparison, and the quality that is equal in both, is also understood by capacity. Here, the word 'api' is for the accumulation of other things to be said, and 'surpassing' is another thing to be said.

193.

193.

Asamattho mukheni’ndu, jina te paṭigajjituṃ;

Jaḷo kalaṅkī’ti ayaṃ, paṭisedhopamā siyā.

O Conqueror, the moon is unable to contend with your face, for it is dull and blemished. This would be a simile of prohibition.

193. “Asamattho”iccādi. Jina te mukhena jaḷo sīto akusalo ca kalaṅko migalañchanalakkhaṇo doso [M 0.0203] assa atthīti kalaṅkī. Saddacchalena dosakathanaṃ. Tādiso indu cando paṭigajjituṃ vivadituṃ asamattho, mukhantu visadaṃ alaṅkatañceti kathamanenāyaṃ sadisoti nisedhadvārena sadhammatāva gammate, ayaṃ paṭisedhopamā siyā.

193. "Incapable," and so on. O Conqueror, the moon, being dull—that is, cold and unskilled—and having the blemish of a deer-mark, is blemished. This is stating a fault by a play on words. Such a moon is unable to contend or dispute. But the face is pure and adorned; how can it be similar to this? Thus, the common quality is understood through negation. This would be a simile of prohibition.

193. “Asamattho”ccādi. He jina te tuyhaṃ mukhena paṭigajjituṃ vivadituṃ jaḷo sītalo avisado kalaṅkī sasalakkhaṇo vā sadoso vā indu cando asamattho hotīti, ayaṃ edisī upamā paṭisedhopamā nāma. Kalaṅko assa atthīti vākyaṃ. Ettha visadena kalaṅkarahitena mukhena sītalo avisado sadoso cando samāno bhavitumasamatthoti evaṃ paṭisedhadvayena indamukhasaṅkhātānaṃ upamānopameyyānaṃ tulyadhammasambandhassa pakāsitattā satipi nindopamābhāve paṭisedhopamā nāma hotīti adhippāyo. “Paṭigajjitu”nti idaṃ candassa visesanattā candagatasadhammaṃ joteti.

193. "Unable" and so on. O Conqueror, the moon—being dull, that is, cold and impure, and blemished, either marked with a hare or flawed—is unable to contend or dispute with your face. Such a simile is called a simile of prohibition. The analysis is 'it has a blemish.' Here, the meaning is that even though it has the nature of a simile of dispraise, it is called a simile of prohibition because the connection of common qualities between the moon and the face, which are the standard and the comparand, is revealed through a twofold negation: that the moon, being cold, impure, and flawed, is unable to be equal to the pure and unblemished face. The word 'to contend' is a qualifier of the moon, illuminating the common quality belonging to the moon.

194.

194.

Kacchaṃ candāravindānaṃ, atikkamma mukhaṃ tava;

Attanāva samaṃ jāta-mitya’sādhāraṇopamā.

Your face, surpassing the realm of the moon and lotus, is born equal only to itself. Thus, this is an incomparable simile.

194. “Kaccha”miccādi. Candassa aravindassa ca kacchaṃ padaviṃ atikkamma avatthariya tesa’mavakaṃsato avatthuyatesamaṇaṃsato (ka.), tava mukhaṃ attano sarūpeneva samaṃ jātamiti evarūpā asādhāraṇatābhidhānena sadisattapatītiyā asādhāraṇopameti nigadyate.

194. "Realm," and so on. Your face, having surpassed the realm or position of the moon and the lotus, and having overcome their inferiority, is born equal only to its own form. Thus, such a simile is called an incomparable simile by the declaration of incomparability, through the understanding of similarity.

194. “Kaccha”miccādi. He muni tava mukhaṃ candāravindānaṃ lokapūjitānaṃ sasiambujānaṃ kacchaṃ padaviṃ avatthaṃ vā atikkamma attano atulyattena attanā eva samānattavatthuno abhāvā samaṃ jātaṃ, iti īdisā upamā asādhāraṇopamā [M 0.0204] atulyadhammabhāvassa pakāsanato asādhāraṇopamā nāma hoti. Iha upamābhūtānaṃ candāravindānaṃ mukhassa hīnabhāvapaṭipādanadvārena candāravindehi mukhaṃ tulyanti paññāpanato candāravindā asādhāraṇopamā nāma hoti. Samasaddo mukhagatassa sādhāraṇadhammaṃ joteti. Sesaṃ suviññeyyaṃ.

194. "Realm," and so on. O sage, your face, surpassing the realm, position, or state of the moon and lotuses—which are revered by the world—is born equal only to itself due to its matchless nature, there being no object that is equal to it. Thus, such a simile is called an incomparable simile because it reveals the state of having an incomparable quality. Here, this is called an incomparable simile because, by demonstrating the inferiority of the moon and lotuses (the standards of comparison) to the face, the comparability of the face with the moon and lotuses is made known. The word 'sama' (equal) highlights the common quality belonging to the face. The rest is easily understood.

195.

195.

Sabbambhojappabhāsāro, rāsibhūtova katthaci;

Tavā’nanaṃ vibhātīti, hotā’bhūtopamā ayaṃ.

Like a mass of the essence of the radiance of all lotuses, gathered somewhere, your face shines forth. Thus, this is a simile of the non-existent.

195. “Sabba”iccādi. Katthaci ekaṭṭhāne rāsibhūto sabbesamambhojānaṃ pabhāsārova tavānanaṃ vibhātīti evaṃbhūtā ayaṃ abhūtopamā hoti.

195. "All," and so on. Your face shines forth like a mass of the essence of the radiance of all lotuses, gathered in one place somewhere. Such is this simile of the non-existent.

195. “Sabba”miccādi. Katthaci ṭhāne rāsibhūto sabbambhojappabhāsārova sakalapadumānaṃ uttamakantipuñjo viya tavānanaṃ vibhāti visesena pabhāti, iti īdisī upamā abhūtopamā avijjamānavatthuno upamitattā abhūtopamā nāma hoti. Arāsi rāsibhūtoti viggaho. Ettha yojanāvibhūto tādisapabhāsārābhāvato avijjamānatthena parikappito.

195. "All" and so forth. In some place, your face shines forth distinctly, like a mass of the essence of the radiance of all lotuses, like a mass of the supreme beauty of all lotuses. Thus, such a simile is called a 'simile of the non-existent' (abhūtopamā) because it is a comparison to a non-existent thing. The analysis is: 'what was not a heap has become a heap' (arāsi rāsibhūto). Here, in the application, because of the absence of such an essence of radiance, it is conceived as non-existent.

196.

196.

Patīyate’tthagammā tu, saddasāmatthiyā kvaci;

Samāsappaccayevādi-saddayogaṃ vinā api.

However, a meaning-based simile is understood, sometimes by the power of words, even without the connection of words such as 'iva', or formations like compounds and suffixes.

196. Atthagammopamaṃ dasseti “patīyate”iccādi. Atthagammā tu’pamā kvaci kismiñci ṭhāne samāsādisaddānaṃ yogaṃ vinā api saddānaṃ payogavisesādigāḷhena aññathānupapattilakkhaṇena sāmatthiyena patīyate.

196. He explains the meaning-based simile with the verse beginning 'it is understood,' and so forth. However, a meaning-based simile, in some place, is understood through the power of words—which is characterized by the impossibility of being otherwise and is firmly established by a particular usage of words, etc.—even without the connection of words like compounds and so on.

196. Tividhaṃ saddagammopamaṃ dassetvā idāni atthagammopamaṃ dasseti “patīyate”tyādinā. Atthagammā tu atthagammopamā [M 0.0205] pana kvaci ṭhāne samāsapaccayevādisaddayogaṃ vināpi tesaṃ saddānaṃ sambandhaṃ hitvāpi saddasāmatthiyā sambandhe payuttāvasesasaddānaṃ atthasattiyā patīyate. Saddānaṃ sāmatthiyanti viggaho.

196. Having explained the threefold word-based simile, now he explains the meaning-based simile with the verse beginning 'it is understood,' and so forth. However, a meaning-based simile, in some instances, is understood by the power of words—that is, by the force of meaning of the remaining words used in the connection—even without the connection of words like compounds, suffixes, 'iva', etc., and even abandoning the connection of those words. The analysis is 'the power of words'.

197.

197.

Bhiṅgāne’māni cakkhūni, nā’mbujaṃ mukha’mevi’daṃ;

Subyattasadisattena, sā sarūpopamā matā.

These eyes are bees; this is not a lotus, this is indeed a face. Through the clear similarity, this is considered a simile of identity.

197. Udāharati “bhiṅge”ccādinā. Na bhiṅgā ete, kiñcarahi cakkhūnimāni, nambujametaṃ, kintu mukhamevidanti evarūpā sā sarūpopamā matā bhiṅgādīnamaviparītasarūpassa dīpanato. Tenāha “subyatte”tyādi. Subyattena bhiṅgacakkhūnaṃ ambujamukhānañca pariphuṭena sadisattena cañcalattakantyādilakkhaṇena tenevābhedasaṅkāpubbameva vivecitaṃ aññatra cakkhādīsu yaṃ bhiṅgādiññāṇamuppannaṃ, tassa paccakkhānato upamājotakānamivādīnamabhāvepi bhiṅgalocanādīnaṃ sadisattaṃ patīyate sāmatthiyato. Evamuparipi yathāyogaṃ.

197. It is illustrated by the verse beginning 'bees,' and so forth. 'These are not bees, but rather eyes; this is not a lotus, but indeed a face.' Such a simile is considered a simile of identity because it reveals the non-contrary nature of bees and so forth. Therefore, it is said in the verse beginning 'through clear,' and so forth. Through the clear and manifest similarity of bee-eyes and lotus-faces, characterized by restlessness, beauty, and so forth, the previously arisen perception of non-difference with respect to the eyes and so forth (i.e., the idea that they are bees), is resolved by its rejection. Even in the absence of simile indicators like 'like,' the similarity of bee-eyes and so forth is understood through their inherent capacity. The same applies hereafter as appropriate.

197. Idāni udāharaṇamāharati “bhiṅgāni”ccādinā. Imāni bhiṅgāni bhamarā na bhavanti, kiñcarahi cakkhūni. Ambujaṃ na idaṃ padumaṃ na hoti, kintu mukhamevāti. Īdisī sā upamā subyattasadisattena supākaṭena bhiṅgalocanānaṃ ambujamukhānañca tulyabhāvena sarūpopamā nāma hoti. Ettha samāsapaccayaivādisaddapayogābhāvepi “bhiṅgānemāni cakkhūni”ccādinā cakkhumukhesu bhiṅgaambujanti viparītapavattabuddhiṃ paṭisedhetvā cakkhumukhavidhānato cañcalattakantimattādīsu subyattaṃ tulyattaṃ vinā cakkhumukhesu bhiṅgambujabuddhiṃ kīdisamuppajjatīti aññathānupapattilakkhaṇasāmatthiyā upamānabhūtānaṃ bhiṅgambujānaṃ upameyyabhūtānaṃ cakkhumukhānañca sadisattaṃ ñāyati. Suṭṭhu byattaṃ pākaṭanti ca, tañca taṃ sadisattañcāti ca, samānaṃ rūpaṃ sabhāvo yassā upamāyāti ca, sā ca sā upamā cāti ca vākyaṃ.

197. Now an example is given by the verse beginning 'bees,' and so forth. These 'bhiṅgāni' are not bees, but rather eyes. This 'ambujaṃ' is not a lotus, but indeed, it is the face. Such a simile is called a simile of identity (sarūpopamā) because of the clearly manifest similarity and comparable quality between bee-eyes and lotus-faces. Here, even in the absence of the use of compounds, suffixes, or words like 'iva,' by rejecting the inverted perception (that eyes are bees and faces are lotuses) with respect to the eyes and faces through phrases like 'these eyes are bees,' and by establishing them as eyes and faces, [the logic is understood]: without a clear similarity in qualities like restlessness and beauty, how could the notion of bees and lotuses arise with respect to the eyes and faces? Thus, through the inherent capacity characterized by the impossibility of being otherwise, the similarity of the bees and lotuses (the standards of comparison) and the eyes and faces (the objects of comparison) is understood. The analysis of the terms is: 'suṭṭhu byattaṃ' (well-manifested) means 'pākaṭaṃ' (evident); and 'that similarity'; and 'a simile whose form or nature is the same'; and 'that simile'.

198.

198.

Mayeva [M 0.0206] mukhasobhā’sse-tyala’mindu vikatthanā;

Yato’mbujepisā’tthīti, parikappopamā ayaṃ.

Let the moon's boasting cease, 'The splendor of this face is mine alone!' Because that splendor exists even in the lotus—this is a simile of supposition.

198. “Mayevi”ccādi. Indu canda, assa munino mukhasobhā vadanajuti mayeva, nāññatrāti evarūpā vikatthanā atthapasaṃsanena alamiti paṭisedho. Kimiti? Yato yasmā kāraṇā sā mukhasobhā ambujepi na kevalamindumhi atthi, no natthīti asatopi tathā vikatthanassa parikappanato vadanamindunopamīyatīti evarūpā ayaṃ parikappopamā.

198. [The verse beginning] 'Mine alone,' and so forth. The moon (indu, canda) boasts, 'The splendor of this Sage's face, the radiance of his countenance, is mine alone, not elsewhere.' Such boasting with self-praise is refuted by the statement 'enough' (alaṃ). Why is that? Because that facial splendor exists not only in the moon but also in the lotus; since it does not exist in the moon alone, such boasting is a supposition of something non-existent. Therefore, the face is compared to the moon—such is this simile of supposition.

198. “Maye”ccādi. He indu assa imassa lokasāmino mukhasobhā vadanakanti ekake mayi eva, īdisī vikatthanā attasilāghena alaṃ nippayojanaṃ. Kasmāti ce? Yato sā mukhasobhā ambujepi atthi, tasmāti. Iti īdisā ayaṃ upamā parikappopamā nāma hoti. Yatoti aniyamaniddiṭṭhakāraṇaṃ pana ambujepi sā atthīti dassiyamānaṃ padumepi tassa atthittameva. Parikappanāya vuttā upamāti viggaho. Idha candassa avijjamānavikatthanassa vijjamānattena parikappanato sadhammajotakasaddantare asatipi upamānabhūtainduno ca upameyyabhūtamukhassa ca sadisattaṃ imesaṃ dvinnaṃ sadisattaṃ vinā vattuno tādisakappanā kathaṃ hotīti imāya atthasattiyā gamyate.

198. [The verse beginning] 'Mine,' and so forth. 'O moon, the splendor of this Lord of the World's face, the radiance of his countenance, is in me alone.' Such boasting, rooted in self-praise, is useless. Why is that? Because that facial splendor exists even in the lotus. Therefore, such a simile is called a simile of supposition. The reason indicated by 'because' (yato) is not specifically defined, but it is shown that it exists even in the lotus, meaning its existence in the lotus. The analysis is 'a simile stated by supposition.' Here, because the moon's non-existent boasting is supposed as existent, even in the absence of another word illuminating the common quality, [the logic is as follows]: how could such a supposition by the speaker arise without the similarity of the moon (the standard of comparison) and the face (the object of comparison), without the similarity of these two? This is understood through the force of meaning.

199.

199.

Kiṃ vā’mbuja’ntobhantāli,

Kiṃ lolanayanaṃ mukhaṃ;

Mama dolāyate citta-

Micca’yaṃ saṃsayopamā.

Is it a lotus with bees buzzing inside, or is it a face with restless eyes? My mind wavers—this is a simile of doubt.

199. “Kiṃ vā”iccādi. Anto bhantā alī bhamarā yasmiṃ, tamīdisamambujaṃ kiṃ vā. Lolāni capalāni nayanāni yasmiṃ, tādisaṃ vā. Jina tavedaṃ mukhaṃ kinti mama cittaṃ dolāyate [M 0.0207] dolevācarati. Evaṃ pakkhadvayapariggahena saṃsayatīti attho. Iccayamīdisī saṃsayavesena ambujamukhānamopamāvagamā saṃsayopamā.

199. [The verse beginning] 'What is it?' and so forth. Is it a lotus of such a kind, in which bees (alī, bhamarā) are buzzing inside? Or is it a face of such a kind, in which eyes are restless (lolāni, capalāni)? O Conqueror, as to your face, my mind wavers; it acts like a swing. Thus, by grasping both alternatives, one doubts—this is the meaning. Thus, such a simile is a simile of doubt, because the understanding of the simile between the lotus and the face arises through the guise of doubt.

199. “Kiṃ vā’mbuje”ccādi. Antobhantāli abbhantare bhamamānabhamaravantaṃ ambujaṃ kiṃ vā, tuyhaṃ lolanayanaṃ cañcalanettaṃ mukhaṃ kiṃ vāti mama cittaṃ dolāyate ubhayasambhamajananato dolā viya hoti. Iti ayaṃ evarūpā upamā saṃsayopamā dvinnaṃ sadisattassa saṃsayena pakāsitattā saṃsayopamā nāma hoti. Anto bhantā alī yasminti ca, lolāni nayanāni yasminti ca, dolā viya ācaratīti ca, saṃsayena vuttā upamāti ca viggaho. Ihāpi sadhammapakāsake saddantare asatipi yathāvuttavisesanadvayena visiṭṭhānaṃ dvinnaṃ ambujamukhānaṃ saṃsayanimitte tulyatte asati kathaṃ saṃsayo uppajjatīti iminā sāmatthiyeneva tulyadhammasambandho gamyate.

199. [The verse beginning] 'What, a lotus?' and so forth. Is it a lotus with bees buzzing inside (abbhantare bhamamānabhamaravantaṃ)? Or is it your face with restless eyes (lolanayanaṃ, cañcalanettaṃ)? Thus, my mind wavers, like a swing, because it generates confusion about both. Thus, such a simile is called a simile of doubt because the similarity of the two is revealed through doubt. The analysis is: 'in which bees are buzzing inside'; and 'in which eyes are restless'; and 'it acts like a swing'; and 'a simile stated by doubt.' Here too, even in the absence of another word illuminating the common quality, how could doubt arise if there were no equality—which is the cause of doubt—between the two, the lotus and the face, distinguished by the two qualities mentioned? Thus, through this very inherent capacity, the connection of similar qualities is understood.

200.

200.

Kiñci vatthuṃ padassetvā,

Sadhammassā’bhidhānato;

Sāmyappatītisabbhāvā,

Pativatthūpamā yathā.

Having presented some object, and by stating a common quality, because of the existence of the perception of similarity, it is a simile of counter-object, as follows.

200. “Kiñci”iccādi. Kiñci vatthumicchitaṃ sambuddhādikaṃ upadassetvā sadhammassa tena vatthunā kenaci ākārena sadisassa aññassa vatthuno abhidhānato sāmyassa tesaṃ dvinnaṃ sadisattassa patītiyā avasāyassa sambhāvā vijjamānattena pativatthūpamā vuccate. Pativatthunā tathāvidhenādhigatassa vatthuno tulyatā paṭipāditā. Yathetyudāharati.

200. [The verse beginning] 'Some object,' and so forth. Having presented some desired object, such as the Perfectly Enlightened One, and by stating another object that is similar in some aspect to that object, having a common quality, it is called a simile of counter-object because of the existence of the perception and understanding of the similarity of those two. By means of a counter-object, the equality of the object thus understood is demonstrated. It is illustrated by 'as follows'.

200. “Kiñci”ccādi. Kiñci vatthumicchitaṃ jinādikiñcipadatthaṃ upadassetvā paṭhamaṃ nidassetvā sadhammassa paṭipādanīyaatthena saha [M 0.0208] kiñci ākārena sadisabhāvassa kassaci vatthuno abhidhānato kathanato sāmyappatītisabbhāvā sadisatāsambandhino parijānanassa vijjamānattā pativatthūpamā vatthuno upaṭṭhitassa jinādipadatthassa tulyatthapakāsanato nāmena pativatthūpamā nāma. Samāno dhammo yassa vā pārijātādino iti ca, samānānaṃ tulyānaṃ upamānopameyyānaṃ bhāvoti ca, sāmyassa patīti ca, sāmyappatītiyā sabbhāvoti ca, pativatthunā vuttā upamāti ca vākyaṃ. Yathāti udāharati.

200. [The verse beginning] 'Some object,' and so forth. Having first presented and indicated some desired object, such as the Conqueror or any other entity, and by stating or describing some object that has a nature of resemblance in some aspect, along with the sense of conveying a common quality, it is a simile of counter-object because of the existence of the understanding of the connection of similarity, the perception of similarity. It is called a simile of counter-object by name because it illuminates a comparable meaning to the presented object, such as the Conqueror or other entities. The analysis is: 'that whose quality is the same,' or 'of the Pārijāta tree and so forth'; and 'the state of similar and comparable standards of comparison and objects of comparison'; and 'the perception of similarity'; and 'the existence of the perception of similarity'; and 'a simile stated by means of a counter-object.' It is illustrated by 'as follows'.

201.

201.

Janesu jāyamānesu,

Ne’kopi jinasādiso;

Dutiyo nanu nattheva,

Pārijātassa pādapo.

Among beings born, not one is like the Conqueror; indeed, there is no second tree like the Pārijāta.

201. “Janesu”ccādi. Jāyamānesu janesu majjhe ekopi jano guṇavā jinasādiso sammāsambuddhasamāno na vijjatītyekaṃ tāva vatthu upadassitaṃ, dutiyo iccādi pativatthūpamadassanaṃ, nanūtyanumatiyaṃ, pārijātassa dibbarukkhavisesassa dutiyo samāno pādapo nattheva. Pārijātoyeva rukkhajātīsu uttamo, tathā jino janesūti.

201. [The verse beginning] 'Among beings,' and so forth. Among beings born, not even one virtuous person is found who is like the Conqueror, equal to the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One—this is one object presented. The line beginning 'second,' and so forth, is an illustration of the simile of counter-object. The word 'nanu' (indeed) expresses agreement. There is indeed no second tree equal to the Pārijāta, a special divine tree. Just as the Pārijāta is supreme among tree species, so too is the Conqueror among beings.

201. “Janesu”ccādi. Jāyamānesu janesu ekopi jinasādiso sambuddhasadiso natthi, pārijātassa rukkhassa dutiyo tena samo dutiyo pādapo rukkho natthi eva nanu, nanūti anuññāyaṃ. Tena sabbaññuno aññena atulyabhāvaṃ anujānāti. Iha pārijātarukkhassa aññehi rukkhehi uttamattañca buddhassa aññesu sattesu uttamattañcāti idaṃ dvayaṃ upamānopameyyabhūtānaṃ dvinnaṃ vatthūnaṃ sāmyaṃ nāma, etaṃ sāmyaṃ vuttatthassa samatthanavasena pativatthubhūtapārijātassa rukkhehi asamānattakathaneneva jotitaṃ hoti.

201. “Among beings,” etc. Among beings who are born, not even one like the Conqueror, like the Perfectly Enlightened One, exists. Is it not true that there is no second tree, no second plant, equal to that Pārijāta tree? The word “nanu” implies assent. By this, the incomparable nature of the Omniscient One with others is acknowledged. Here, the supremacy of the Pārijāta tree among other trees and the supremacy of the Buddha among other beings—this pair is called the similarity of the two objects, the subject of comparison and the object of comparison. This similarity is illuminated precisely by stating the incomparability of the Pārijāta tree, which is the counter-object, among other trees, by way of corroborating the stated meaning.

202.

202.

Vākyattheneva [M 0.0209] vākyattho,

Yadi kocyu’pamīyate;

Ivayuttaviyuttattā,

Sā vākyatthopamā dvidhā.

If the meaning of a statement is compared with the meaning of another statement, then, due to being connected or disconnected with 'iva', that simile based on the meaning of a statement is twofold.

202. Vākyatthavisayopamaṃ dasseti “vākyatthenevi”ccādinā. Vākyattho kriyākārakasambandhaviseso, teneva, na padatthamattena vākyattho vuttalakkhaṇo koci vattumicchito koci yadi upamīyate sadiso kathyate, sā vākyatthopamā dvidhā bhijjate. Kathaṃ? Yuttā ca viyuttā ca yuttaviyuttā, ivena atthaniddesoyaṃ yuttaviyuttā upamā, tassā bhāvā kāraṇā dvidhāti adhikataṃ.

202. He explains the simile concerning the meaning of a statement with “by the meaning of a statement itself,” etc. The meaning of a statement is a particular relationship between action and agent. If some meaning of a statement with the stated characteristics, which one desires to express, is compared or spoken of as similar—not merely by the meaning of a word, but precisely by that (meaning of a statement)—then that simile based on the meaning of a statement is divided into two. How? Connected and disconnected, thus connected-and-disconnected. This connected-and-disconnected simile is an indication of meaning by means of 'iva'. Because of its nature, it is twofold—this is what is meant.

202. Idāni vākyatthavisayopamaṃ dasseti “vākyatthe”ccādinā. Vākyattheneva kriyākārakasambandhavisesasaṅkhatasamudāyabhūtena vākyatthena koci vattumicchito yo koci vākyattho vuttalakkhaṇo yadi upamīyate sadisabhāvena kathīyate, sā upamā vākyatthopamā nāma hoti. Ivayuttaviyuttattā ivayuttaviyuttavasena dvidhā dvippakārā. Ettha “ivā”ti ivādīnamatthassa gahitattā ivasaddopi tappariyāyasaddāpi gayhante.

202. Now, he explains the simile concerning the meaning of a statement, beginning with “vākyatthe.” If any meaning of a statement, which has the characteristics previously stated, is desired to be spoken of as similar, by means of the meaning of a statement which is a collection constituted by a specific relationship between action and agent, that simile is called a “simile based on the meaning of a statement.” Due to being connected or disconnected with 'iva', it is twofold, of two kinds. Here, by 'iva', because the meaning of 'iva' and similar terms is taken, the word 'iva' and its synonyms are also included.

Ivayutta

Connected with 'iva'

203.

203.

Jino saṃklesatattānaṃ,

Āvibhūto janāna’yaṃ;

Ghammasantāpatattānaṃ,

Ghammakāle’mbudo viya.

This Conqueror, manifest to beings scorched by defilements, is like a rain cloud in the hot season for those scorched by the heat.

203. Udāharati “jino”iccādi. Saṃklesehi dasavidhehi tattānaṃ santāpaṃ anuppattānaṃ janānaṃ ayaṃ jino sammāsambuddho [M 0.0210] āvibhūto katakiccattā sammāsambodhādhigamena loke pātubhūto. Ekaṃ tāva vākyamupameyyabhūtaṃ. Kimivetyāha “ghamme”ccādi. Ghammasantāpena tattānaṃ janānaṃ ghammakāle gimhānasamaye ambudo megho viyāti dutiyavākyamupamānabhūtamityayamivayuttā vākyatthopamā. Ettha pubbuttaravākyatthānaṃ visesyavisesanabhāvo ekavākyatthattāva veditabbo. Evamuparipi.

203. He gives an example with “the Conqueror,” etc. This Conqueror, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has become manifest for beings who have attained suffering due to being scorched by the ten kinds of defilements; he has appeared in the world through the attainment of perfect enlightenment, having accomplished what was to be done. This first statement is the subject of comparison. What is it like? He says “in the heat,” etc. Just as a rain cloud is to people scorched by the heat in the hot season, in the summer season—thus the second statement is the object of comparison. This is a simile based on the meaning of a statement, connected with 'iva'.
