Here, the relationship of qualified and qualifier between the meanings of the preceding and following statements should be understood as being a single meaning of a statement. The same applies in subsequent cases.

203. Udāharati “jino”ccādinā. Ayaṃ jino eso jitapañcamāro satthā saṃklesatattānaṃ anekappakāra kilesasantāpatattānaṃ janānaṃ āvibhūto katakicco hutvā sabbaññutaññāṇādhigamena loke upaṭṭhito. Kena santattassa kassaci kimiveti ce? Ghammasantāpatattānaṃ janānaṃ ghammakāle gimhasamaye ambudoviya megho iva. Iha uttaravākyattho bhedakattā visesanaṃ hoti, pubbavākyattho pana bhedyattā visesyo hoti. Evaṃ vākyabhede satipi vākyattho ekoveti daṭṭhabbo. Evamuttaratrāpi. Uttaravākye ivasaddo tasmiṃyeva guṇaguṇīpadatthānaṃ sadisattaṃ dīpeti, pubbavākye guṇaguṇīnaṃ sadisattaṃ pana uttaravākyatthassa pubbavākyena samānattaṃ vinā aññathānupapattiyā ñāyati. Saṃklesehi tattāti ca, ghammo eva santāpoti ca, tena tattāti ca, ghammo eva kāloti ca vākyaṃ.

203. He gives an example with “the Conqueror,” etc. This Conqueror, this Teacher who has conquered the five Māras, has appeared in the world, having accomplished his task by attaining omniscient knowledge, for beings scorched by the heat of defilements of many kinds. If it is asked, “Like what for someone scorched by what?” For people scorched by the heat in the hot season, in the summer season, like a rain cloud, like a cloud. Here, the meaning of the latter statement is the qualifier because it differentiates, while the meaning of the former statement is the qualified because it is to be differentiated. Thus, even when there is a division of statements, the meaning of the statement should be seen as one. The same applies hereafter. In the latter statement, the word 'iva' indicates the similarity of the quality and the possessor of the quality in that very statement; in the former statement, however, the similarity of the quality and the possessor of the quality is understood through the logical impossibility of it being otherwise without the equality of the meaning of the latter statement with the former statement. And the statements are: “scorched by defilements,” “the heat itself is the scorching,” “scorched by that,” and “the heat itself is the season.”

Ivaviyutta

Disconnected from 'iva'

204.

204.

Munindānana’mābhāti, vilāsekamanoharaṃ;

Uddhaṃ samuggatassāpi, kiṃ te canda vijambhanā.

The face of the Lord of Sages shines, uniquely charming in its grace; even when risen high, O moon, what is your boasting?

204. Dutiyamāha “muninda”iccādinā. Vilāsena ekamatulyaṃ manoharaṃ dutiyassa tādisassābhāvato munindānanaṃ [M 0.0211] ābhāti atisayena sobhateti ekaṃ tāva vākyamupameyyabhūtaṃ. Bho canda uddhaṃ gaganatalaṃ samuggatassāpi abbhuṭṭhitassāpi te tava vijambhanā sāhaṃkāraparibbhamanena kiṃ payojanaṃ na kiṃpi, taṃsadisasobhāsampattiyābhāvato. Asadisattaṃ munindānanassa tassa tatopi uddhamuggacchato vilāsamattameva piyāsamattameva (ka.) phalasambhavatoti dutiyavākyamupamānabhūtaṃ. Tathā hettha sabbathā sadisatāpatītiyā kariyamānānamuggamanavijambhanānaṃ paṭikkhepena kathañcipi mukhacandānaṃ sādhammapatīti upamāvagamoti ayamivaviyuttavākyatthopamā.

204. He states the second example with “Lord of Sages,” etc. The face of the Lord of Sages shines, is exceedingly beautiful, being uniquely charming and incomparable in its grace, because there is no second like it—this is the first statement, serving as the subject of comparison. “O moon, even though you have risen high into the sky, even though you have ascended, what purpose is there in your boasting, your proud wandering? There is none at all, because there is no attainment of beauty equal to that of the Buddha's face.” The second statement is the object of comparison, because it implies that due to the incomparability of the face of the Lord of Sages, for that moon, even when rising higher than it, only a mere semblance of its grace is the possible result. Thus, here, by rejecting the rising and boasting that are done with the supposition of complete similarity in every way, the understanding of the simile—the perception of a common property between the face and the moon—arises somehow. This is a simile based on the meaning of a statement, disconnected from 'iva'.

204. Idāni ivaviyuttavākyatthopamaṃyeva udāharati “munindānani”ccādinā. Vilāsekamanoharaṃ līlāya atulyaṃ tatoyeva manoharaṃ munindānanaṃ sabbaññuno vadanaṃ ābhāti atidibbati, tasmā he canda uddhaṃ uccaṃ nabhaṃ samuggatassāpi te tuyhaṃ vijambhanā ahaṃkārena paribbhamanena kiṃ payojanaṃ. Iha pubbavākyatthassa uttaravākyattho ivaviyuttopamā nāma hoti. Tathā hi “sabbathā mukhena sadiso bhavāmī”ti mānaṃ karontassa candassa gaganatalārohopi vijambhanañceti imesaṃ dvinnaṃ paṭikkhepena mukhacandānaṃ vilāsekamanoharattaṃ kantimattasaṅkhātasadisattaṃ ivādīnamabhāvepi viññāyatīti katvā uttaravākyattho pubbavākyatthassa upamā ca visesanañca hoti. Vilāsena ekamatulyanti ca, tañca taṃ manoharañcāti ca viggaho. Apisaddo sambhāvanattho.

204. Now, he illustrates precisely the simile based on the meaning of a statement, disconnected from 'iva', with “the face of the Lord of Sages,” etc. The face of the Lord of Sages, the countenance of the Omniscient One, shines exceedingly brightly, being uniquely charming in its grace, incomparable, and therefore lovely. Therefore, O moon, even though you have risen high, high into the sky, what purpose is there in your boasting, your proud wandering? Here, the meaning of the latter statement is called a simile disconnected from 'iva' in relation to the meaning of the former statement. For by rejecting these two—the moon’s ascent to the sky and its boasting, while the moon makes the proud claim “I am equal in all respects to the face”—the similarity between the face and the moon, which consists of unique charm and mere radiance, is understood even in the absence of 'iva' and similar terms. Therefore, the meaning of the latter statement serves as both a simile and a qualifier for the meaning of the former statement. And the analysis is: “uniquely incomparable in grace,” and “that which is that and is charming.” The particle 'api' has the sense of possibility.

205.

205.

Samubbejeti dhīmantaṃ, bhinnaliṅgādikaṃ tu yaṃ;

Upamādūsanāyā’la-metaṃ katthaci taṃ yathā.

That which is characterized by discordant gender and so forth, however, disturbs the wise; this suffices somewhere as a fault of the simile, as for example:

205. Dosaparicchede [M 0.0212] duṭṭhālaṅkatītimupamālaṅkāradūsanaṃ dassetumāha “samubbejeti”ccādi. Yaṃ bhinnaliṅgādikaṃ tu, ādisaddena bhinnavacanahīnatāadhikatādīnaṃ pariggaho. Tusaddo atthajotako, tathāpīti attho. Dhīmantaṃ medhāviṃ samubbejeti na pīṇeti, etaṃ bhinnaliṅgadikaṃ katthaci na sabbattha upamādūsanāya virodhatthaṃ alaṃ samatthaṃ. “Taṃ yathe”ti udāharati.

205. In the section on faults, to show the fault of the simile-ornament, which is a “corrupted ornament,” he says “disturbs,” etc. That which is characterized by discordant gender and so forth—by the word 'ādi' are included discordant number, deficiency, excess, etc. The word 'tu' illuminates the meaning; the meaning is “nevertheless.” It disturbs the wise, the intelligent; it does not please them. This, characterized by discordant gender and so forth, is adequate, is capable, somewhere, but not everywhere, for the fault of simile, for the purpose of contradiction. He gives an example with “as for example.”

205. Dosaparicchede dosānamanuddesāvasāne niddiṭṭhāya duṭṭhālaṅkatiyā dassetabbaudāharaṇe –

205. In the section on faults, at the end of the brief statement of faults, in the example to be shown of the corrupted ornament mentioned—

“Duṭṭhālaṅkaraṇaṃ tetaṃ, yatthālaṅkāradūsanaṃ;

Tassālaṅkāraniddese, rūpamāvibhavissatī”ti.

“That is a corrupted ornament, where there is a fault of the ornament. In the exposition of that ornament, its form will become manifest.”

Katapaṭiññānusārena idāni dassetumāha “samubbejeti”ccādi. Yaṃ bhinnaliṅgādikaṃ tu vakkhamānaṃ yaṃ bhinnaliṅgavacanādikaṃ pana dhīmantaṃ paññavantaṃ kaviṃ samubbejeti “evaṃ nāma vattabbaṃ siyā”ti ubbegaṃ janeti, etaṃ bhinnaliṅgādikaṃ upamādūsanāya yathāvuttaupamāvināsanatthaṃ katthaci “itthīvāyaṃ jano yāti”iccādivattabbavisayato aññattha alaṃ samatthaṃ. “Taṃ yathā”ti udāharati. Bhinnaṃ visadisañca taṃ liṅgañceti ca, taṃ ādi yassa visadisavacanādinoti ca, upamāya dūsanamiti ca vākyaṃ.

In accordance with the promise made, he now begins to explain with 'it agitates,' etc. That which is characterized by discordant gender and so forth, which is to be explained—that which is characterized by discordant gender, number, etc.—agitates the wise, the intelligent, the poet, generating anxiety with the thought, 'It should be expressed thus.' This fault of discordant gender and so forth is sufficient to corrupt the simile, for the purpose of destroying the simile as stated, elsewhere than in contexts where it should be said, such as, 'This person goes like a woman,' etc. He gives an example with 'As follows.' And the analysis of the phrases is: 'that gender which is discordant and dissimilar'; 'that which has dissimilar number, etc., as its beginning'; and 'the corruption of the simile'.

206.

206.

Haṃsīvā’yaṃ sasī bhinna-

Liṅgā’kāsaṃ sarāniva;

Vijātivacanā hīnā,

Sā’va bhatto bhaṭo’dhipe.

This moon is like a female swan—a discordant gender. The sky is like lakes—a discordant number. A warrior to his lord is like a dog to its food—an inferior comparison.

206. “Haṃsīvāya”nti ayaṃ sasī cando haṃsīva haṃsīsadiso. Bhinnaliṅgā bhinnaliṅgopamā. “Ākāsaṃ sarānivā”ti vijātivacanā visadisavacanopamā. “Bhaṭo adhipe sāmini sāva [M 0.0213] bhatto”ti hīnā hīnopamā kukkurassa hīnena jātyādinā adhikassa upamitattā.

206. 'Like a female swan' means this moon, the moon, is like a female swan, similar to a female swan. It is a simile of discordant gender. 'The sky is like lakes' is a simile of discordant number, a simile of dissimilar number. 'A warrior to a lord, a master, is like a dog to food' is an inferior simile, a base simile, because a superior person is compared to an inferior creature, a dog, which is lower in terms of birth and so forth.

206. “Haṃsi”ccādi. Ayaṃ sasī cando haṃsī iva haṃsidhenūva hoti. Iccādikopamā bhinnaliṅgā upameyyato bhinnaliṅgattā bhinnaliṅgopamā nāma hoti. Ākāsaṃ nabhaṃ sarānivāti ayaṃ vijātivacanā upameyyena visadisavacanattā vijātivacanopamā nāma hoti. Adhipe sāmini bhaṭo sevako sāva sunakho iva bhattoti ayaṃ hīnā jātihīnena sunakhena uttamassa purisassa upamitattā hīnopamā nāma hoti. Bhinnaṃ liṅgametissāti ca, vividhā jāti sabhāvo asseti ca, vijāti vacanaṃ assā upamāyāti ca viggaho.

206. 'Like a female swan,' etc. This moon, the moon, is like a female swan, like a she-swan. A simile such as this is called a simile of discordant gender because its gender is discordant with the subject of comparison. 'The sky, the firmament, is like lakes'—this is called a simile of discordant number because it has a number dissimilar to the subject of comparison. 'A warrior, a servant, to a lord, a master, is like a dog, a hound, to food'—this is called an inferior simile because a superior man is compared to one inferior by birth, a dog. And the analysis is: 'its gender is different'; 'it has diverse kinds and natures'; and 'this simile has a number of a different kind'.

207.

207.

Khajjoto bhānumālīva,

Vibhātītyadhikopamā;

Aphuṭṭhatthā balambhodhi,

Sāgaro viya saṃkhubhi.

A firefly shines forth like the sun—this is an excessive simile. The army-ocean surged like the sea—this is a simile of unexpressed meaning.

207. “Khajjoto”iccādi. Khajjoto bhānumālīva sūriyo viya vibhātītyadhikopamā adhikena hīnassa upamitattā. Balambhodhi senāsāgaro sāgaro viya saṃkhubhīti aphuṭṭhatthopamā “balambhodhī”ti rūpakena senāya mahantattāvagamato puna “sāgaro viyā”ti upamāya kassaci visesatthassa asaṃphuṭṭhattā.

207. 'A firefly,' etc. 'A firefly shines forth like the sun'—this is an excessive simile because an inferior is compared to a superior. 'The army-ocean, the army-sea, surged like the sea'—this is a simile of unexpressed meaning because the greatness of the army is understood from the metaphor 'army-ocean,' and thus the simile 'like the sea' does not express any special meaning.

207. “Khajjoto”ccādi. “Khajjoto bhānumālīva vibhātī”ti ayaṃ adhikopamā adhikāya upamāya upamitattā adhikopamā nāma hoti. “Balambhodhi senāsamuddo sāgaro viya saṃkhubhī”ti ayaṃ aphuṭṭhatthā senāya mahattaṃ “balambhodhī”ti tirobhūtaupamāyeva avagataṃ, [M 0.0214] tasmā puna “sāgaro viyā”ti upamāya phusitabbatthassābhāvā aphuṭṭhatthopamā nāma hoti. Aphuṭṭho attho etissāti ca, balaṃ eva ambhodhīti ca vākyaṃ.

207. 'A firefly,' etc. 'A firefly shines forth like the sun'—this is called an excessive simile because it is a comparison with a superior standard of comparison. 'The army-ocean, the army-sea, surged like the ocean'—this is called a simile of unexpressed meaning because the greatness of the army is already understood from the concealed simile 'army-ocean' itself; therefore, due to the absence of a meaning to be expressed by the simile 'like the ocean,' it is called a simile of unexpressed meaning. And the analysis of the phrases is: 'its meaning is unexpressed,' and 'the army is indeed an ocean'.

208.

208.

Cande kalaṅko bhiṅgove-

Tyu’pamāpekkhinī ayaṃ;

Khaṇḍitā keravākāro,

Sakalaṅko nisākaro.

A blemish on the moon like a bee—this is a simile requiring another. The moon with its blemish, resembling a water-lily—this is a broken simile.

208. “Cande”iccādi. Kalaṅko bhiṅgo viyātyayamupamā “cande kusumagacchasadise” ityupamantaramapekkhateti yato cande bhiṅgo na sambhavati, pupphagacche tu sambhavatīti ayamupamā upamāpekkhinī. Sakalaṅko sasalakkhaṇo nisākaro cando keravākāro kumudasannibhoti khaṇḍitopamā keravassa antokaṇhattaṃ paṭipādetuṃ “sabhiṅgakeravākāro”ti vattabbattā.

208. 'On the moon,' etc. The simile 'a blemish is like a bee' requires another simile, namely, 'on the moon, which is like a flowering tree,' because a bee is not found on the moon but is found on a flowering tree; thus, this is a simile requiring another. 'The moon with its blemish, the night-maker with its mark of a hare, resembling a water-lily, like a white water-lily'—this is a broken simile, because to convey the inner darkness of the water-lily, it should have been said, 'like a water-lily with a bee'.

208. “Cande”ccādi. “Cande kalaṅko bhiṅgo ivā”ti ayaṃ upamāpekkhinī candassaupamābhūtapupphagacchakādiapekkhanato upamāpekkhinī nāma hoti. Cande bhiṅgapavattiyā abhāvato tassa visayabhūtapupphagacchakādi candassa upamattena gahetvā avuttattā duṭṭhāti adhippāyo. Sakalaṅko kalaṅkasahito nisākaro cando keravākāro kumudasadisoti ayaṃ khaṇḍitā candagataṃ kaṇhattaṃ pakāsetuṃ “sabhiṅgakeravākāro”ti vattabbe bhiṅgopamābhāvassa khaṇḍitattā khaṇḍitopamā nāma hoti. Upamaṃ apekkhatīti ca, khaṇḍaṃ itā gatāti ca, khaṇḍena itā yuttā vāti ca, keravassākāro asseti ca, saha kalaṅkena vattatīti ca vākyaṃ.

208. 'On the moon,' etc. 'A blemish on the moon is like a bee'—this is called a simile requiring another because it requires something like a flowering tree, which serves as the standard of comparison for the moon. The meaning is that it is flawed because, since bees do not occur on the moon, it is not stated that the moon is being compared to their proper domain, such as a flowering tree. 'The moon, the night-maker, together with its blemish, resembling a water-lily, like a white water-lily'—this is called a broken simile because, to reveal the darkness on the moon, it should have been said 'like a water-lily with a bee,' but the simile of the bee is broken off by its absence. And the analysis of the phrases is: 'it requires a simile'; 'it has gone to a broken state' or 'it is joined with a broken part'; 'it has the form of a water-lily'; and 'it exists together with a blemish'.

209.

209.

Iccevamādirūpesu, bhavanti vigatādarā;

Karonti cā’daraṃ dhīrā, payoge kvacideva tu.

Thus, in forms such as these, the wise are without regard; but in certain applications, they do show regard.

209. Vuttaṃ [M 0.0215] nigameti “icceva”mādinā. Rūpesu payogesu. Vigato apagato ādaro sambhāvanā yesaṃ tathā bhavanti. Kiṃ bhinnaliṅgādikaṃ niyamenānādaraṇīyameva, aniyameneti niyameneti (ka.) ce gayhūpagampi atthīti āha “karonti”ccādiṃ. Kvacideva tu payoge dhīrā kavayo ādaraṃ karonti cāti. Casaddo vattabbantaratthaṃ samuccinoti.

209. He concludes what has been said with 'thus,' etc. 'In forms' means in usages. They are such that regard and esteem have departed from them. Are faults like discordant gender, etc., invariably to be disregarded, or is it without a fixed rule? If the latter, there is also that which is acceptable—thus he says, 'they do,' etc. But in certain usages, the wise poets also show regard. The word 'ca' (and) includes another meaning to be stated.

209. “Icce”ccādi. Iti anantaraṃ niddiṭṭhesu evamādirūpesu payogesu dhīrā vigatādarā bhavanti. Imeyeva dhīrā kvacideva tu payoge bhinnaliṅgādike ādaraṃ karonti ca. Iti evaṃ ayaṃ pakāro ādi yesamiti ca, tāni ca tāni rūpāni ceti ca, vigato ādaro yesamiti ca viggaho. Casaddo vākyantarasamuccaye. Tasmā vigatādaratthena aññamādarakaraṇaṃ vuccamānakathāsantatiṃ ākaḍḍhati.

209. 'Thus,' etc. Thus, in the forms of usage such as these which were just pointed out, the wise are without regard. These very same wise ones, however, do show regard in certain usages involving discordant gender and so forth. And the analysis is: 'this kind is their beginning'; 'these are those forms'; and 'those from whom regard has departed.' The word 'ca' serves to include another sentence. Therefore, by the meaning of 'being without regard,' the mention of 'showing regard elsewhere' draws in the continuous narrative being spoken.

210.

210.

Itthīvā’yaṃ jano yāti,

Vadatyesā pumā viya;

Piyo pāṇā ivā’yaṃ me,

Vijjā dhanamiva’ccitā.

This person walks like a woman; she speaks like a man. This one is dear to me like life itself; knowledge is honored like wealth.

210. Udāharati “itthi”ccādi. Ayaṃ jano itthīva yāti kriyānuvattito. Esā itthī pumāva puriso viya vadati tādisassa pāgabbhiyayogato. Ettha liṅganānattamupamānopameyyānaṃ. Ayamicchito koci me pāṇā iva piyo iṭṭho, vijjā byākaraṇādayo dhanamiva accitā rāsikatāti vacanabhedo.

210. He gives an example with 'like a woman,' etc. 'This person walks like a woman' because of conforming to the action. 'This woman speaks like a man, like a man,' due to possessing such boldness. Here, there is a diversity of gender between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison. 'This desired one is dear to me, beloved, like life-breaths.' 'Knowledge, such as grammar and so forth, is honored, accumulated, like wealth.' This is a difference of number.

210. Idāni bhinnaliṅgānaṃ gahetabbavisayaṃ dasseti “itthīvā’ya”miccādinā. Ayaṃ jano itthīva avisadagamanena mahilā [M 0.0216] viya yāti. Esā itthī pumā viya tādisapāgabbhiyayuttattā puriso viya vadatīti. Iha dvinnaṃ upamānopameyyānaṃ liṅgabhede satipi kavayo ādaraṃ karonti. Ayaṃ puriso me mama pāṇā iva pāṇā iva jīvo iva (ka.) āyavova piyo. Accitā sañcitā vijjā byākaraṇanighaṇṭuādayo dhanamiva hontīti. Ettha upamānopameyyānaṃ vacanato visesatte satipi iṭṭhameva.

210. Now, with 'like a woman,' etc., he shows the domain where discordant genders are acceptable. 'This person walks like a woman,' with an unsteady gait, like a lady. 'This woman speaks like a man,' like a man, because she possesses such boldness. Here, even when there is a difference in gender between the two—the standard of comparison and the object of comparison—poets still show regard. 'This man is dear to me, to me, like life-breaths, like a vital breath.' 'Accumulated, collected knowledge, such as grammar, lexicons, and so forth, is like wealth.' Here, even when there is a distinction in the number of the standard of comparison and the object of comparison, it is still desirable.

211.

211.

Bhavaṃ viya mahīpāla, devarājā virājate;

Ala’maṃsumato kacchaṃ, tejasā rohituṃ ayaṃ.

O king, the king of gods shines like Your Honor. This one is capable, with his splendor, of ascending the path of the sun.

211. Hīnādhikamuttamudāharaṇamāha “bhavaṃ viyi”ccādi. Mahīpāletyāmantanaṃ, devarājā bhavaṃ viya virājate. Iti hīnenāpi hoti. Evaṃvidhe samucite visaye liṅgavacanabhedādikaṃ nopamaṃ dūsetīti dassetīti (ka.).

211. He gives an example concerning inferior and superior with 'like Your Honor,' etc. 'O king' is a vocative. 'The king of gods shines like Your Honor.' Thus, a comparison can also be made with an inferior. In such a fitting context, differences in gender, number, and so forth do not corrupt the simile.

211. “Bhava”miccādi. Mahīpāla bho rāja, devarājā sakko devarājā bhavaṃ viya virājateti. Ettha sakkamupādāya “bhavaṃ viyā”ti hīnattepi iṭṭhameva. Ayaṃ rājā aṃsumato sūriyassa kacchaṃ padaviṃ tejasā ārohituṃ pattuṃ alaṃ samatthoti. Ettha tejasā adhikopi sūriyo upamābhūto iṭṭhova, “kacchaṃ ārohitu”nti ivasaddapariyāyo. Īdisaṃ bhinnaliṅgādikopamādikaṃ upamādūsanaṃ na karoti.

211. 'Bhavaṃ,' etc. 'O Mahīpāla, O king, Sakka, the king of gods, shines like Your Honor.' Here, with reference to Sakka, 'like Your Honor' is indeed desirable, even in his inferiority. 'This king is capable of ascending to the path, the station, of the sun, Aṃsumat, with his brilliance.' Here, the sun, though superior in brilliance, serves as a desirable simile, and 'to ascend the path' is a synonym for 'iva' (like). Such a simile with differences in gender and so forth does not constitute a flaw in the comparison.

212.

212.

Upamānopameyyānaṃ, abhedassa nirūpanā;

Upameva upamāva (sī. ka.) tirobhūta-bhedā rūpakamuccate.

The establishment of non-difference between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison; the simile itself, with its distinction obscured, is called a metaphor.

212. Rūpakaṃ nirūpayati “upamāne”ccādinā. Upamānopameyyānaṃ yathāvuttānaṃ abhedassa nānattābhāvassa nirūpanā āropanena upamānopameyyānamabhedaṃ rūpayati dassetīti [M 0.0217] rūpakamuccate. Upamānassa upamānopameyyānamabhedāropanena tirobhūto apākaṭo bhedo nānattaṃ yassāti tādisī upameva yathāvuttalakkhaṇā rūpakamuccate “rūpaka”nti. “Padambuja”nti ettha padameva ambujasadisattā ambujaṃ rupyate. Ityupameyyopamānabhūtānaṃ padambujānamabhedāropanena upamānopameyyagatasādhammasaṅkhātāyapi upamāya bhedo vijjamānopi tirohito. Na tu āvibhūto abbhuto (ka.) “padaṃ ambujamive”ti. Sā copamā tathāvidhā upamānopameyyānamabhedamāyāti nāmāti rūpakamuccateti adhippāyo.

212. He defines metaphor with 'upamāna,' etc. The establishment of non-difference—the absence of distinction—between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison, as previously stated, is called a metaphor because it reveals the non-difference between them through superimposition. That very simile, having the aforementioned characteristics, whose distinction or difference is concealed and unmanifest due to the superimposition of non-difference upon the standard and object of comparison, is called a 'rūpaka' or metaphor. In 'padambuja' (foot-lotus), the foot itself, being similar to a lotus, is represented as a lotus. Thus, by superimposing non-difference upon the foot and the lotus, which are the object and standard of comparison, the distinction inherent in the simile—which is the common quality present in both—is concealed, even though it exists. It is not manifest, as in 'the foot is like a lotus.' And that simile, being of such a kind, is called a metaphor because it assumes the non-difference of the standard and object of comparison—this is the intended meaning.

212. Idāni uddiṭṭhakkamena rūpakālaṅkāraṃ dasseti “upamāno”ccādinā. Upamānopameyyānaṃ anantaraniddiṭṭhaupamānopameyyānaṃ abhedassa sabhāvato bhede satipi vibhūtasadisattaṃ nissāya “so eso, eso so”ti vattārehi parikappitassa abhedassa nirūpanā upamānopameyyapadatthesu buddhiyā āropanaṃ nissāya tirobhūtabhedā “padaṃ ambujamivā”ti evaṃ pākaṭanānattaṃ vinā “padambuja”nti tirohitabhedā upameva padatthānaṃ sādhammasaṅkhātā upamā eva rūpakaṃ iti vuccate. Vibhūtasadisattaṃ nissāya upamānopameyyavatthūni abhedena gayhanti. Tesamabhedaggahaṇeneva te nissāya pavattamānabhinnasādhammasaṅkhātāya upamāyapi bhedo tirohito hoti. Evaṃ tirobhūtanānattavantasādhammasaṅkhātā upamā eva vatthūnamabhedaṃ dīpetīti rūpakaṃ nāma hotīti adhippāyo. Tirobhūto bhedo yasseti ca, abhedaṃ rūpayati pakāsetīti ca vākyaṃ.

212. Now, according to the stated sequence, he explains the figure of speech 'metaphor' with 'upamāna,' etc. The establishment of non-difference between the standard and object of comparison—which were just indicated—is based on their manifest similarity, even though a natural distinction exists. This establishment of non-difference, conceived by speakers who say 'that is this, this is that,' is based on intellectual superimposition upon the meanings of the words for the standard and object of comparison. Thus, the simile itself—known as the common quality of the things signified—is called a metaphor when its distinction is concealed, as in 'padambuja' (foot-lotus), without the manifest distinction found in 'the foot is like a lotus.' Based on manifest similarity, the objects serving as the standard and object of comparison are grasped as non-different. Precisely by this grasping of their non-difference, the distinction within the simile itself—which arises from them and is known as a distinct common quality—also becomes concealed. Thus, the simile, known as a common quality possessing a concealed distinction, illuminates the non-difference of the objects, and for this reason it is called a metaphor—this is the intended meaning. The analysis is: 'that whose distinction is concealed,' and 'it forms or manifests non-difference'.

213.

213.

Asesavatthuvisayaṃ, ekadesavivatti ca;

Taṃ dvidhā puna paccekaṃ, samāsādivasā tidhā.

It is twofold: that which has the entire object as its scope, and that which is manifest in a single part. Each of these, in turn, is threefold, according to compounding and so forth.

213. Tassa [M 0.0218] bhedaṃ niddisati “asesa”iccādinā. Asesavatthu visayo yassa taṃ tathāvidhañca, ekadese avayave vivattatīti ekadesavivatti ceti taṃ rūpakaṃ dvidhā, puna paccekaṃ visuṃ visuṃ samāsādivasā upamānopameyyānaṃ katasamāsattā samāsarūpaka asamāsarūpaka samāsāsamāsarūpakavasena tidhā siyā.

213. He indicates its division with 'asesa,' etc. That metaphor is twofold: that which has the entire object as its scope, and that which is manifest in a part, a component, hence 'manifest in one part.' Again, each of these, separately, according to compounding and so forth, may be threefold based on the compounding of the standard and object of comparison: as compound metaphor, non-compound metaphor, and compound-non-compound metaphor.

213. “Asesi”ccādi. Taṃ rūpakaṃ asesavatthuvisayaṃ ekadesavivatti cāti dvidhā hoti, puna paccekaṃ taṃ dvayampi samāsādivasā samāsarūpakaṃ asamāsarūpakaṃ samāsāsamāsarūpakañceti imesaṃ bhedena tidhā hoti. Asesaṃ vatthu visayo asseti ca, ekadese vivattatīti ca, ekaṃ ekaṃ patīti ca, samāso samāsarūpakaṃ ādi yesamiti ca, tesaṃ vaso bhedoti ca, tīhi pakārehīti ca viggaho.

213. 'Asesa,' etc. That metaphor is twofold: having the entire object as its scope (asesavatthuvisaya) and being manifest in one part (ekadesavivatti). Again, each of these two, according to compounding and so forth, becomes threefold through the division into compound metaphor (samāsarūpaka), non-compound metaphor (asamāsarūpaka), and compound-non-compound metaphor (samāsāsamāsarūpaka). The grammatical analysis (viggaha) is as follows: for `asesavatthuvisaya`, 'the entire object is its scope'; for `ekadesavivatti`, 'it is manifest in one part'; for `paccekaṃ`, 'to each one'; for `samāsādi`, 'compound, etc.'; for `vasā`, 'according to'; and for `tidhā`, 'in three ways'.

Asesavatthuvisayasamāsa

Compound Metaphor Pertaining to the Entire Object

214.

214.

Aṅgulīdalasaṃsobhiṃ, nakhadīdhitikesaraṃ;

Sirasā na piḷandhanti, ke munindapadambujaṃ.

Adorned with finger-petals, with filaments of nail-radiance—who would not place upon their head the lotus-feet of the Sage-King?

214. Udāharati “aṅguli”ccādi. Aṅgulīhiyeva upamānagammattā siniddhatambāhi dalehi pattehi saṃsobhiṃ accantaṃ virocamānaṃ nakhānaṃ dīdhitiyo kiraṇā eva kesarāni yattha tādisaṃ munindassa padameva ambujaṃ sirasā muddhanā ke nāma janā na piḷandhanti pasādhanavasena na dhārentīti. Idamasesavatthuvisayaṃ samāsarūpakaṃ aṅgino padassa aṅgānamaṅgulyādīnamasesānaṃ rūpanato. Evamuparipi yathāyogaṃ.

214. He gives the example 'aṅguli,' etc. The lotus-foot of the Sage-King is exceedingly radiant, shining with petals that are the very fingers—smooth and reddish, a quality understood from the standard of comparison—and is such that the rays, the beams of the nails, are its very filaments. What people, indeed, would not place this upon their heads, would not wear it as an adornment? This is a compound metaphor pertaining to the entire object, due to the metaphorical identification of the principal object (the foot) and all of its parts (the fingers, etc.). So too in the following examples, as is applicable.

214. Idāni udāharati “aṅguli”ccādi. Aṅgulīdalasaṃsobhiṃ aṅgulisaṅkhatehi pattehi saṃsobhiṃ nakhadīdhitikesaraṃ nakharaṃsisaṅkhatakesaraṃ munindapadambujaṃ sirasā ke [M 0.0219] na piḷandhanti. Visesyabhūtaṃ caraṇaṃ visesanabhūtā aṅgulī nakhadīdhiti ceti imesaṃ upamābhūtehi ambujadalakesarehi abhedakappanāya ekattaṃ gahetvā samāseneva niddiṭṭhattā idaṃ asesavatthuvisayasamāsarūpakaṃ nāma. Aṅguliyo eva dalānīti ca, tehi saṃsobhīti ca, nakhesu dīdhitiyoti ca, tā eva kesarāni asseti ca vākyaṃ.

214. Now, he gives the example 'aṅguli,' etc. 'Aṅgulīdalasaṃsobhiṃ' means 'shining with petals designated as fingers.' 'Nakhadīdhitikesaraṃ' means 'having filaments designated as nail-rays.' Who would not place upon their head the lotus-foot of the Sage-King? This is called a compound metaphor pertaining to the entire object because the qualified subject (the foot) and its qualifiers (the fingers and nail-radiance) are taken as one with their standards of comparison (the lotus petals and filaments) through a conception of non-difference, and are expressed by a single compound. The analysis (vākya) is: 'The fingers are the very petals'; 'shining by means of them'; 'radiance in the nails'; and 'those are its very filaments'.

Asesavatthuvisayaasamāsa

Non-Compound Metaphor Pertaining to the Entire Object

215.

215.

Ratanāni guṇā bhūrī, karuṇā sītalaṃ jalaṃ;

Gambhīrattamagādhattaṃ, paccakkho’yaṃ jino’mbudhi.

His abundant qualities are jewels; compassion is cool water; his profundity, unfathomableness. This Conqueror is a manifest ocean.

215. “Ratanāni”iccādi. Ayaṃ jino sammāsambuddho, paccakkho na parokkho amhākaṃ ambudhi sāgaro. Kathaṃ? Ye tassa bhūrī bahavo guṇā mettādayo, te ratanāni atulyadullabhadassanādisādhammena. Yā tassa karuṇā, sā sītalaṃ jalaṃ sakalajanasantāpāpahattasādhammena. Yaṃ tassa gambhīrattamanuttānatā lābhādīsu, taṃ agādhattamakalalambhaso ambudhiṭṭhatāsādhammenāti idamasesavatthuvisayaṃ asamāsarūpakaṃ.

215. 'Ratanāni,' etc. This Conqueror, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is for us a manifest ocean, not a remote one. How so? His many abundant qualities, such as loving-kindness, are jewels, due to the common property of being incomparable, rare, difficult to see, and so forth. His compassion is cool water, due to the common property of removing the torment of all people. His profundity and imperturbability in regard to gain and so forth is unfathomableness, due to the common property of being like the ocean, not easily stirred. This is a non-compound metaphor pertaining to the entire object.

215. “Ratanāni”ccādi. Ayaṃ jino amhākaṃ paccakkho ambudhi sāgaro, tathā hi tassa bhūrī guṇā sīlasamādhiādayo ratanāni cittīkatādisādhammato ratanāneva, karuṇā anaññasādhāraṇakaruṇā sītalaṃ jalaṃ santāpavinodanasādhammena sītalajalameva hoti, gambhīrattaṃ lābhālābhādīsu ekākāratā agādhattaṃ gambhīratā eva hoti. Idaṃ asesavatthuvisayaasamāsarūpakaṃ. “Bhūrī”ti abyayaṃ.

215. 'Ratanāni,' etc. This Conqueror is a manifest ocean to us. For indeed, his abundant qualities, such as virtue and concentration, are jewels—truly jewels—from the common property of being prized, and so forth. His compassion, his unique compassion, is cool water—truly cool water—due to the common property of dispelling torment. His profundity, his uniformity in regard to gain and loss, is unfathomableness—truly profundity. This is a non-compound metaphor pertaining to the entire object. 'Bhūrī' is an indeclinable.

Asesavatthuvisayamissaka

Mixed Metaphor Pertaining to the Entire Object

216.

216.

Candikā [M 0.0220] mandahāsā te, muninda vadaninduno;

Pabodhayatya’yaṃ sādhu-manokumudakānanaṃ.

O Sage-King, your gentle smile is the moonlight of your face-moon; this awakens the forest of the mind-water-lilies of the virtuous.

216. “Candikā”iccādi. “Muninda”iccāmantanaṃ, te vadanameva indu vadaninduno iti samāsarūpakaṃ, ayaṃ mandahāsā candikā candakantiyo, asamāsarūpakaṃ. Sādhūnaṃ manāniyeva kumudāni keravāni, samāsarūpakaṃ. Tesaṃ kānanaṃ vanaṃ, pabodhayati vikāsayatīti idaṃ samāsāsamāsarūpakaṃ.

216. 'Candikā,' etc. 'Muninda' is a vocative. 'Your face is the very moon' (vadaninduno) is a compound metaphor. 'This gentle smile is moonlight' (candikā), the rays of the moon; this is a non-compound metaphor. 'The minds of the virtuous are the very water-lilies' (kumudāni keravāni); this is a compound metaphor. 'Their grove' (kānanaṃ) is a forest; 'it awakens' (pabodhayeti), 'it causes to blossom' (vikāsayatīti). This example, containing both types, is a mixed (compound and non-compound) metaphor.

216. “Candi”ccādi. He munindate tuyhaṃ vadaninduno mukhacandassa mandahāsā mandamihitabhūtā candikā candakantiyo, “aya”nti jātyekavacanena mandahāsacandikā niddiṭṭhā. Atha vā ayaṃ vadanindu. Sādhumanokumudakānanaṃ sappurisānaṃ cittasaṅkhātakeravakānanaṃ pabodhayati vikāsayati. “Candikā mandahāsā”ti asamāsarūpakaṃ. “Vadaninduno”ti ca “manokumudakānana”nti ca samāsarūpakaṃ. Tasmā idaṃ asesavatthuvisayasamāsāsamāsarūpakaṃ. Mandā ca te hāsā cāti ca, vadanameva indūti ca, sādhūnaṃ manānīti ca, tāniyeva kumudānīti ca, tesaṃ kānanamiti ca viggaho.

216. “Candi,” etc. O Sage-King, your gentle smiles, which are the gentle smiles of your moon-like face, are moonlight, the rays of the moon. By “ayaṃ” (this), in the singular of the class, the gentle-smile-moonlight is indicated. Or, this is the face-moon. It awakens, it causes to blossom, the grove of mind-lotuses of the virtuous, the grove of water lilies reckoned as the minds of good people. “Candikā mandahāsā” is a non-compound metaphor. “Vadaninduno” and “manokumudakānanaṃ” are compound metaphors. Therefore, this is a compound-non-compound metaphor pertaining to the entire object. The analysis (viggaha) is: “gentle and those smiles”; and “the face itself is the moon”; and “the minds of the virtuous”; and “those very lotuses”; and “their grove.”

217.

217.

Asesavatthuvisaye, pabhedo rūpake ayaṃ;

Ekadesavivattimhi, bhedo dāni pavuccati.

In a metaphor pertaining to the entire object, this is the subdivision. Now, the division is spoken of in a metaphor of partial superimposition.

217. Nigamayati “asesi”ccādinā. Dutiyassa pabhedaṃ vattuṃ paṭijānāti “eki”ccādinā.

217. It concludes with “asesi,” etc. To explain the second subdivision, it undertakes with “eki,” etc.

217. “Asese”ccādi. Asesavatthuvisaye rūpake ayaṃ “aṅgulīdalasaṃsobhiṃ”iccādikaṃ udāharaṇattayaṃ pabhedo hoti. Idāni ekadesavivattimhi rūpake bhedo viseso pavuccati.

217. “Asese,” etc. In a metaphor pertaining to the entire object, this set of three examples, beginning with “aṅgulīdalasaṃsobhiṃ,” constitutes the subdivision. Now, in a metaphor of partial superimposition, a specific division is explained.

Ekadesavivattisamāsa

Metaphor of Partial Superimposition in a Compound

218.

218.

Vilāsahāsakusumaṃ, [M 0.0221] rucirādharapallavaṃ;

Sukhaṃ ke vā na vindanti, passantā munino mukhaṃ.

Who, indeed, would not find joy seeing the Sage's face, a flower of charming smiles and a bud of lovely lips?

218. “Vilāsa”iccādi. Vilāsena yutto hāsoyeva kusumaṃ yassa. Ruciro manuñño adharoyeva pallavo yassa. Tādisaṃ munino mukhaṃ passantā ke nāma janā sukhaṃ na vindanti sabbepīti. Idaṃ aṅgāni hāsādīni rūpayitvā mukhamaṅgi na rūpitanti ekadesavivattisamāsarūpakaṃ. Evaṃ uparipi yathāyogaṃ.

218. “Vilāsa,” etc. That whose smile, endowed with charm, is indeed a flower. That whose lip, beautiful and delightful, is indeed a bud. Seeing such a face of the Sage, what people, indeed, would not find joy? All would. Here, the parts, such as the smile, are metaphorized, but the face, the whole to which the parts belong, is not metaphorized; thus, it is a metaphor of partial superimposition in a compound. Similarly, in what follows, apply this as appropriate.

218. “Vilāsi”ccādi. Vilāsahāsakusumaṃ līlāyuttahāsasaṅkhatapupphaṃ rucirādharapallavaṃ manuññaadharasaṅkhātakisalayaṃ munino mukhaṃ passantā ke vā ke nāma janā sukhaṃ na vindanti pītisukhaṃ nānubhonti, anubhavanteva. Visesanabhūtānaṃ hāsaadharānaṃ upamābhūtakusumapallavehi abhedaṃ dassetvā visesyabhūtassa mukhassa aññataraupamāvatthunā abhedena avuttattā abhedāropanaṃ ekadeseyeva vivattīti idaṃ ekadesavivattisamāsarūpakaṃ. Vilāsena yutto hāsoti ca, soyeva kusumaṃ asseti ca, ruciro ca so adharo ceti ca, soyeva pallavo asseti ca vākyaṃ.

218. “Vilāsi,” etc. Seeing the face of the Sage, which is a flower in the form of a charming smile (a flower consisting of a smile endowed with grace), and a bud in the form of a lovely lip (a tender shoot consisting of a delightful lip), what people, indeed, would not find joy and experience delight? They certainly do experience it. By showing the non-difference of the smile and lip, which are the qualifiers, with the flower and bud, which are the objects of comparison, and because the non-difference of the face, which is the qualified, is not stated with any other object of comparison, the superimposition of non-difference occurs only partially; thus, this is a metaphor of partial superimposition in a compound. The phrases are: ‘A smile endowed with charm,’ and ‘that very smile is its flower,’ and ‘that lip is beautiful,’ and ‘that very lip is its bud.’

Ekadesavivattiasamāsa

Metaphor of Partial Superimposition not in a Compound

219.

219.

Pādadvandaṃ munindassa, dadātu vijayaṃ tava;

Nakharaṃsī paraṃ kantā, yassa pāpajayaddhajā.

May the pair of feet of the King of Sages bestow victory upon you, whose supremely beautiful nail-rays are banners of victory over evil.

219. “Pāda”iccādi. Munindassa vijayino pādadvandaṃ tava vijayaṃ paṭipakkhaparābhavaṃ dadātu. Kīdisaṃ? Yassa paramaccantaṃ kantā manuññā nakharaṃsī pāpānaṃ lobhādīnaṃ jaye ussitā dhajā ketavoti. Idamekadesavivattiasamāsarūpakaṃ.

219. “Pāda,” etc. May the pair of feet of the victorious Sage-King grant you victory, the defeat of your adversaries. Of what kind? Whose supremely beautiful and delightful nail-rays are banners raised in the conquest of evils such as greed, etc. This is a metaphor of partial superimposition not in a compound.

219. “Pāde”ccādi.[M 0.0222] Yassa sambuddhassa paraṃ atisayena kantā manuññā nakharaṃsī caraṇanakhakantiyo pāpajayaddhajā pāpavijaye ussāpitadhajāyeva honti, tassa munindassa pādadvandaṃ caraṇayugaḷaṃ tava tuyhaṃ vijayaṃ paṭipakkhaparābhavaṃ dadātūti. Nakharaṃsīnaṃ upamābhūtadhajehi abhedamāropetvā “pādadvanda”miti anirūpitattā ekadesavivattiasamāsarūpakaṃ nāma. Pāpānaṃ jayoti ca, tasmiṃ dhajāti ca viggaho.

219. “Pāde,” etc. May the pair of feet of that Sage-King—whose nail-rays (the radiance of the toenails) are supremely and exceedingly beautiful and delightful, and are indeed banners raised in the victory over evil—may that pair of feet grant you victory and the overthrow of your adversaries. By superimposing non-difference of the nail-rays with the banners, which are the objects of comparison, and because the ‘pair of feet’ is not metaphorized, it is called a metaphor of partial superimposition not in a compound. The analysis is ‘victory over evils,’ and ‘a banner in that.’

Ekadesavivattimissaka

Metaphor of Partial Superimposition, Mixed

220.

220.

Sunimmalakapolassa, munindavadaninduno;

Sādhuppabuddhahadayaṃ, jātaṃ keravakānanaṃ.

By the Sage-King’s face-moon with its very pure cheeks, the well-awakened heart of the virtuous became a grove of water lilies.

220. “Sunimmala”iccādi. Sunimmalo kapolo yassa, tassa munindavadaninduno sādhūnaṃ pabuddhaṃ dhammāvabodhavasena vikasitaṃ hadayaṃ cittaṃ keravakānanaṃ jātanti ekadesavivattisamāsāsamāsarūpakaṃ.

220. “Sunimmala,” etc. He whose cheek is very pure—for that Sage-King whose face is the moon—the heart of the virtuous, awakened (blossomed by the understanding of the Dhamma), became a grove of water lilies; thus, it is a metaphor of partial superimposition, both in a compound and not in a compound.

220. “Sunimmali”ccādi. Sunimmalakapolassa munindavadaninduno sādhuppabuddhahadayaṃ sajjanānaṃ catusaccāvabodhena pasannamānasaṃ keravakānanaṃ kumudavanaṃ jātanti. Vadanahadayānaṃ upamābhūtehi indukeravehi abhedāropanaṃ katvā kapolassa maṇḍalādīhi upamāvisesehi anirūpitattā ekadesavivattisamāsāsamāsarūpakaṃ. Ettha samāso nāma vadanindūnameva. Asamāso nāma hadayakeravānamevāti. Tathā hi rūpakavisaye samāsāsamāsattaṃ upamānopameyyapadānaṃ dvinnamevāti. Suṭṭhu nimmaloti ca, so kapolo assāti ca, munindavadanameva indūti ca, pabuddhañca taṃ hadayañcāti ca, sādhūnaṃ pabuddhahadayamiti ca, keravānaṃ kānanamiti ca vākyaṃ.

220. “Sunimmali,” etc. For the Sage-King whose face is the moon with very pure cheeks, the heart of the virtuous, awakened (a mind delighted by the realization of the Four Noble Truths), became a grove of water lilies (a kumuda forest). By superimposing non-difference of the face and heart with the moon and water lilies, which are the objects of comparison, and because the cheek is not metaphorized with specific resemblances such as roundness, etc., it is a metaphor of partial superimposition, both in a compound and not in a compound. Here, the compound metaphor is only of the face and the moon. The non-compound metaphor is only of the heart and the water lilies. Thus, in the context of metaphor, the state of being in a compound and not in a compound applies to both the terms of the object of comparison and the subject of comparison. The phrases are: ‘Very pure,’ and ‘he has such a cheek,’ and ‘the Sage-King’s face is indeed the moon,’ and ‘that heart is awakened,’ and ‘the awakened heart of the virtuous,’ and ‘a grove of water lilies.’

221.

221.

Rūpakāni [M 0.0223] bahūnyeva, yuttāyuttādibhedato;

Visuṃ na tāni vuttāni, etthe’va’ntogadhāni’ti.

There are indeed many metaphors, distinguished by types such as appropriate and inappropriate; they are not stated separately, but are included within this very topic.

221.

221.

Ettakoyeva kiṃ rūpakabhedoti āha

“Rūpakāni”ccādi; Subodhaṃ; Tattha –

To the question of whether these are all the types of metaphors, it is said: “Metaphors,” etc. It is easily understood. In this regard—

“Sitapupphujjalaṃ lola-nettabhiṅgaṃ tavānanaṃ;

Kassa nāma mano dhīra, nākaḍḍhati manohara”nti.

‘Whose mind, O wise one, is not drawn by your charming face, resplendent with white flowers, with restless bee-like eyes?’

Yuttarūpakaṃ yuttattā pupphabhiṅgānaṃ, tadanusārena ayuttarūpakādipi viññeyyanti.

This is an appropriate metaphor because of the suitability of the flowers and bees. According to that, inappropriate metaphors, etc., should also be understood.

221. Rūpakāni punapi santīti dassetumāha “rūpakāni”ccādi. Rūpakāni yuttāyuttādibhedato yuttarūpakaayuttarūpakādibhedena bahūni eva honti, tāni rūpakāni ettheva rūpake antogadhāni. Iti tasmā kāraṇā tāni visuṃ na vuttāni. Anto majjhe gadhāni pavattānīti viggaho.

221. To show that there are still other metaphors, it is said: “Metaphors,” etc. Metaphors are indeed numerous, distinguished by types such as appropriate and inappropriate metaphors. Those metaphors are included within this very topic of metaphor. Therefore, for that reason, they are not stated separately. The analysis is: ‘included within’ means they exist in the middle.

“Sitapupphujjalaṃ lola-nettabhiṅgaṃ tavānanaṃ;

Kassa nāma mano dhīra, nākaḍḍhati manohara”nti.

‘Whose mind, O wise one, is not drawn by your charming face, resplendent with white flowers, with restless bee-like eyes?’

Ettha pupphabhiṅgānaṃ aññamaññayuttattā yuttarūpakaṃ nāma.

Here, because of the mutual suitability of the flowers and bees, it is called an appropriate metaphor.

He dhīra sitapupphujjalaṃ mandahasitasaṅkhātehi kusumehi vijotantaṃ lolanettabhiṅgaṃ manoharaṃ tavānanaṃ kassa nāma mano nākaḍḍhatīti. Imassa paṭipakkhato ayuttarūpakaṃ veditabbaṃ.

O wise one, whose mind, indeed, is not drawn by your charming face, resplendent with white flowers (that is, shining with flowers in the form of a gentle smile), and with restless bee-like eyes? From its opposite, an inappropriate metaphor should be understood.

222.

222.

Candimā’kāsapaduma-miccetaṃ khaṇḍarūpakaṃ;

Duṭṭha’mambhoruhavanaṃ, nettāni’ccādi sundaraṃ.

‘The moon is a sky-lotus’—this fragmented metaphor is flawed; but ‘a lotus grove, the eyes,’ etc., is beautiful.

222. Rūpakassa virodhāvirodho upamāyamivo’hituṃ sakkāti upalakkheti “candimā”iccādinā. Ettha ākāsassa taḷāke rūpite candassa padumattaṃ rūpakaṃ yuttanti etaṃ [M 0.0224] khaṇḍarūpakaṃ duṭṭhaṃ, “ambhoruhavanaṃ nettāni”ccādi tu vacanabhedepi sundaraṃ.

222. The compatibility and incompatibility of a metaphor can be understood, just as in a simile, as indicated by ‘the moon,’ etc. Here, if the sky were metaphorized as a pond, the metaphor of the moon being a lotus would be appropriate; however, this fragmented metaphor is flawed. But ‘a lotus grove, the eyes,’ etc., is beautiful, even with the difference in grammatical number.

222. Rūpake dosādosaṃ upamāyaṃ viya parikappetvā gahetabbanti upadisanto āha “candimi”ccādi. “Candimā cando ākāsapaduma”nti etaṃ khaṇḍarūpakaṃ ākāsassa taḷākattena anirūpitattā khaṇḍarūpakaṃ nāma. Duṭṭhaṃ khaṇḍitopamā viya dosaduṭṭhaṃ nāma. “Ambhoruhavanaṃ nīluppalavanaṃ nettānī”tiādikaṃ upamānopameyyānaṃ vacananānattepi sundarameva.

222. Advising that the faults and merits in a metaphor should be grasped by conceiving them as in a simile, he said: ‘the moon,’ etc. ‘The moon, the moon is a sky-lotus’—this is called a fragmented metaphor because the sky is not represented as a pond. It is flawed; it is called flawed by defect, like a fragmented simile. ‘A lotus grove, a blue lotus grove, the eyes,’ etc.—even with the difference in grammatical number between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison, it is indeed beautiful.

223.

223.

Pariyanto vikappānaṃ, rūpakasso’pamāya ca;

Natthi yaṃ tena viññeyyaṃ, avutta’manumānato.

There is no end to the variations of metaphor and simile; since that is so, what is unstated should be understood by inference.

223. Kimettakā evopamārūpakabhedā? Neti paridīpento avuttaṃ atidisati “pariyanto”iccādinā. Rūpakassa upamāya ca vikappānaṃ pabhedānaṃ pariyanto avasānaṃ natthi yaṃ yasmā kāraṇā, tena kāraṇena avuttaṃ ihānupātaṃ vikappajātaṃ sabbavikappabyāpakasāmaññalakkhaṇānugatarūpakavikappānusārena viññeyyaṃ. Kasmā? Anumānato yathāvuttavikappasaṅkhātaliṅgato avuttasesarūpakāvagamasaṅkhātena anumānañāṇenāti attho.

223. Are these all the types of similes and metaphors? Showing that they are not, he applies this principle to what is unstated with ‘there is no end,’ etc. Since there is no end or limit to the variations and distinctions of metaphor and simile, for that reason, the unstated types of variations not included here should be understood according to the variations of metaphor that follow the general characteristic encompassing all variations. Why? By inference; the meaning is, by inferential knowledge, which is the understanding of the remaining unstated metaphors, from the sign in the form of the stated variations.

223. Idāni imesameva upamārūpakānaṃ avuttānantabhedo vuttānusāreneva ñātabboti dassetumāha “pariyanto”iccādi. Rūpakassa ca rūpakālaṅkārassa ca upamāya ca upamālaṅkārassa ca vikappānaṃ vividhākārena kappitapakkhānaṃ pariyanto koṭi yaṃ yasmā natthi, tena kāraṇena avuttaṃ imasmiṃ subodhālaṅkāre avuttapakkhaṃ samūhaṃ anumānato anumānañāṇena viññeyyanti. Upamārūpakānaṃ sakalamavuttapakkhaṃ byāpetvā ṭhitaṃ sāmaññalakkhaṇaṃ anatikkamitvā vuttehi tehi tehi pakkhasaṅkhātehi liṅgehi [M 0.0225] siddhānumānañāṇena sāmaññalakkhaṇe antogadhānamanuttarūpakasaṅkhātānumeyyānaṃ avabodho sakkāti adhippāyo. Rūpakassa pana upamantogadhattā upamāya niddiṭṭhadosādosaṃ dvinnamapi uttānuttapakkhassa sādhāraṇaṃ hoti.

223. Now, to show that the endless unstated distinctions of these very similes and metaphors should be known by following what has been stated, he says: ‘there is no end,’ etc. Since there is no end or limit to the variations (aspects conceived in various ways) of metaphor and the rhetorical figure of metaphor, and of simile and the rhetorical figure of simile, for that reason, the unstated collection of aspects in this Subodhālaṅkāra should be understood by inference, through inferential knowledge. The intention is that the understanding of the unstated metaphors, which are inferable and included within the general characteristic, is possible through inferential knowledge established by those various stated instances called aspects, without transgressing the general characteristic that encompasses all unstated aspects of similes and metaphors. However, because metaphor is included within simile, the stated faults and merits of simile are common to both their stated and unstated aspects.

224.

224.

Punappunamuccāraṇaṃ, ya’matthassa padassa ca;

Ubhayesañca viññeyyā, sā’ya’māvutti nāmato.

The repeated utterance of a meaning, of a word, and of both, should be understood as that which is called ‘repetition’.

224. Āvuttimadhikiccāha “puna”iccādinā. Atthassa abhidheyyassa padassa saddassa ca ubhayesaṃ atthapadānañca punappunaṃ bhiyyo bhiyyo yaṃ uccāraṇaṃ, sāyaṃ tividhā nāmato āvutti viññeyyā, uccāraṇavasena ā punappunaṃ vattanamāvuttīti.

224. Concerning repetition, he says: ‘repeatedly,’ etc. That repeated utterance, again and again, of the meaning (the expressed object), of the word (the sound), and of both (meaning and word), should be understood as repetition of three kinds by name. Thus, repetition is the recurring again and again by way of utterance.

224. Idāni āvuttiṃ dasseti “punappune”ccādinā. Atthassa saddābhihitaatthassa ca padassa ca ubhayesaṃ atthapadānañca yaṃ punappunuccāraṇaṃ, sā ayaṃ tividhā nāmato āvutti iti viññeyyā. Punappuneti etadabyayaṃ kriyābāhulye vattate. Uccāraṇavasena ā punappunaṃ vattanamāvutti.

224. Now, he shows repetition with ‘repeatedly,’ etc. That repeated utterance of the meaning (the meaning expressed by words), and of the word, and of both (meaning and word), should be understood as this threefold repetition by name. The indeclinable ‘punappunaṃ’ occurs in the sense of abundance of action. Repetition is the recurring again and again by way of utterance.

Atthāvutti

Repetition of Meaning

225.

225.

Mano harati sabbesaṃ, ādadāti disā dasa;

Gaṇhāti nimmalattañca, yasorāsi jinassa’yaṃ.

This heap of glory of the Conqueror captivates the minds of all, seizes the ten directions, and grasps purity.

225. Udāharati “mano”iccādi. Jinassa ayaṃ yasorāsi sabbesaṃ janānaṃ mano cittaṃ harati, dasa disā ādadāti sabbadā sabbadhā (ka.) taṃvisayattā, nimmalattaṃ nimmalabhāvaṃ gaṇhāti, ettha gahaṇalakkhaṇassa dasagahaṇalakkhaṇassa (ka.) atthassa anekehi pariyāyavacanehi āvattitattā ayaṃ atthāvutti.

225. He illustrates with ‘mano,’ etc. This mass of glory of the Conqueror captivates the minds of all people, seizes the ten directions because they are always its domain, and grasps purity—the state of being stainless. Here, because the meaning characterized by ‘grasping’ is repeated through many synonymous terms, this is meaning-repetition.

225. Udāharati [M 0.0226] “mano harati”ccādinā. Jinassa ayaṃ yasorāsi sabbesaṃ sattānaṃ mano cittaṃ harati gaṇhāti, dasa disā ādadāti avisayaṭṭhānābhāvato gaṇhāti, nimmalattañca bhūtaparisuddhaguṇena nipphannattā gaṇhāti. Ettha “gaṇhātī”ti ekassevatthassa “harati, ādadāti, gaṇhātī”ti aññehi pariyāyavacanehi āvattitattā ayamatthāvutti nāma. Niggato malehīti ca, tassa bhāvoti ca, yasaso rāsiiti ca viggaho.

225. He illustrates with ‘mano harati,’ etc. This mass of glory of the Conqueror captivates and grasps the minds of all beings; it grasps the ten directions, as there is no place that is not its domain; and it grasps purity because it is produced by truly purified qualities. Here, because the single meaning of ‘grasping’ is repeated with other synonymous terms—‘harati,’ ‘ādadāti,’ and ‘gaṇhāti’—this is called meaning-repetition. The analyses are: ‘gone forth from stains,’ ‘the state of that,’ and ‘a mass of glory.’

Padāvutti

Repetition of Word

226.

226.

Vibhāsenti disā sabbā, munino dehakantiyo;

Vibhā senti ca sabbāpi, candādīnaṃ hatā viya.

The Sage's bodily radiances illuminate all directions; and all the splendors of the moon and so on are as if destroyed.

226. “Vibhāsenti”ccādi. Munino dehakantiyo sabbā disā vibhāsenti visesena dīpenti, yato evaṃ tasmā kāraṇā candādīnaṃ sabbāpi vibhā sobhā hatā pahatā viya senti pavattantīti padāvutti.

226. ‘Vibhāsenti,’ etc. The bodily radiances of the Sage illuminate all directions distinctly; for that reason, all the splendors and radiances of the moon and so on exist as if struck, as if destroyed. This is word-repetition.

226. “Vibhāsenti”ccādi. Munino dehakantiyo sabbā disā vibhāsenti yasmā visesena pakāsenti, tasmā candādīnaṃ sabbāpi vibhā kantiyo hatā pahatā viya senti pavattanti ca, “vibhāsentī”ti padasseva āvattanato ayaṃ padāvutti nāma. Dehe kantiyoti vākyaṃ.

226. ‘Vibhāsenti,’ etc. Because the bodily radiances of the Sage illuminate all directions distinctly, therefore all the splendors and radiances of the moon and so on are as if struck, as if destroyed. Because of the repetition of the word ‘vibhāsenti’ itself, this is called word-repetition. The phrase is ‘radiance in the body.’

Ubhayāvutti

Repetition of Both

227.

227.

Jitvā viharati klesa-ripuṃ loke jino ayaṃ;

Viharatyā’rivaggo’yaṃ, rāsībhūtova dujjane.

Having conquered the enemy of defilements, this Victor abides in the world; this host of enemies abides among the wicked as if heaped up.

227. “Jitvā”iccādi. Ayaṃ jino klesaripuṃ jitvā loke viharati pavattati, ayaṃ tena jito arivaggo sattusamūho [M 0.0227] dujjane rāsībhūto viya tato aladdhappatiṭṭhattā. “Viharatī”ti atthassa padānañca āvuttito ubhayāvutti.

227. ‘Jitvā,’ etc. This Victor, having conquered the enemy of defilements, abides, that is, proceeds, in the world. This group of enemies, the multitude of foes, conquered by him, is like a heap among the wicked, having found no foothold in him. Because of the repetition of both the meaning and the word ‘viharati,’ it is repetition of both.

227. “Jitvā”iccādi. Ayaṃ jino klesaripuṃ jitvā loke viharati, ayaṃ arivaggo klesaripusamūho dujjane rāsībhūtova viharatīti. Vāsasaṅkhatassa atthassa ca “viharatī”ti padassa ca puna punappunaṃ (?) uccāraṇato ayaṃ ubhayāvutti nāma hoti. Kleso eva ripūti ca, arīnaṃ vaggoti ca, arāsi rāsi abhavīti ca, kucchito janoti ca vākyaṃ.

227. ‘Jitvā,’ etc. This Conqueror, having conquered the enemy of defilements, dwells in the world; this host of enemies, the group of defilement-enemies, abides among the wicked as if heaped up. From the repeated utterance of the meaning of ‘dwelling’ and the word ‘viharati,’ this is called repetition of both. The phrases are: ‘Defilement itself is the enemy,’ ‘the host of enemies,’ ‘not being a heap, it became a heap,’ and ‘a contemptible person.’

228.

228.

Ekattha vattamānampi, sabbavākyopakārakaṃ;

Dīpakaṃ nāma tañcādi-majjhantavisayaṃ tidhā.

Though occurring in one place, it is helpful to the whole sentence; this is called the ‘illuminator,’ and it is threefold, its domain being the beginning, middle, and end.

228. Dīpakaṃ paridīpayamāha “ekatthe”ccādi. Ekattha vākyassādo majjhe ante vā vattamānampi kriyājātyādikaṃ sabbassa abhimatassa kassaci vākyassa kriyākārakasambandhābhidhāyino padasantānassa upakārakaṃ vākyatthānvayavasena dīpakaṃ nāma, dīpo viya ekadese vattitopi sakalapadatthavasena sabbavākyaṃ dīpayati pakāsetīti. Tañca dīpakaṃ ādi ca majjhañca antañca visayo gocaro yassa tādisaṃ tidhā ādidīpakaṃ majjhadīpakaṃ antadīpakanti tividhaṃ hotīti attho, tampi kriyādīnaṃ vasena paccekaṃ tividhaṃ hoti.

228. Explaining the Dīpaka, he says: ‘Ekattha,’ etc. A verb, class-noun, or the like, though occurring in one place—at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence—is called a Dīpaka, or ‘illuminator,’ when it is helpful to the whole of an intended sentence (a sequence of words expressing the relation between action and agent) by connecting with the sentence's meaning. For, like a lamp, though placed in one spot, it illuminates the entire sentence with respect to the meaning of all the words. And that Dīpaka, whose domain is the beginning, the middle, and the end, is threefold: initial Dīpaka, medial Dīpaka, and final Dīpaka. That, too, is threefold in each case, by way of verb and so on.

228. Idāni dīpakālaṅkāraṃ dasseti “ekatthe”ccādinā. Ekattha vākyassa ādimajjhāvasānesvekasmiṃ vattamānampi kriyājātiguṇattayaṃ sabbavākyopakārakaṃ vattumicchitakriyākārakasambandhappakāsakapadasantānasaṅkhātavākyassa vākyatthāvabodhavasena payojanaṃ dīpakaṃ nāma ekaṭṭhāne [M 0.0228] ṭhatvā visayībhūtasabbaṭṭhānagatadabbapakāsakapadīpasamānattā dīpakaṃ nāma hoti. Tañca dīpakaṃ ādimajjhantavisayaṃ vākyassa ādivisayaṃ majjhavisayaṃ antavisayañceti tidhā hoti. Etesu ekekamapi kriyājātiguṇabhedena punapi tividhaṃ hotīti viññeyyaṃ. Dīpetīti dīpo, padīpo. Paṭibhāgatthe kappaccayena dīpo viyāti dīpakaṃ. Vākyassa ādi ca majjhañca antañceti ca, taṃ visayo asseti ca vākyaṃ.

228. Now, the lamp figure of speech is illustrated with 'in one place' and so on. Even when a verb, genus, or quality occurs in one place—the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence—it is helpful to the whole sentence, being useful for understanding the meaning of the sentence, which is a sequence of words expressing the relationship between the intended action and agent. It is called 'dīpaka' because it is similar to a lamp that, standing in one place, illuminates substances in all places within its range. And that dīpaka is threefold according to its scope: initial, medial, and final, that is, at the beginning, middle, or end of the sentence. Each of these, again, should be understood as threefold according to the distinction of verb, genus, or quality. 'It illuminates,' therefore it is a lamp (dīpa), a light (padīpa). With the suffix 'ka' in the sense of similarity, it is 'like a lamp,' therefore it is dīpaka. The beginning, middle, and end of a sentence: that is its scope.

Ādidīpaka

The Initial Illuminator

229.

229.

Akāsi buddho veneyya-bandhūnamamitodayaṃ;

Sabbapāpehi ca samaṃ-nekatitthiyamaddanaṃ.

The Buddha brought about boundless prosperity for his trainable kinsmen, and the crushing of many heretics along with all evils.

229. Udāharati “akāsi”ccādi. Buddho veneyyā vinetabbāyeva bandhavo tesaṃ amitamaparimitaṃ udayamabhivuddhiṃ akāsi. Na kevalaṃ tameva, sabbapāpehi samaṃ ekato anekānaṃ titthiyānaṃ maddanañca akāsīti. Iha “akāsī”ti kriyāpadenādivattinā sabbameva vākyaṃ dīpayatīti kriyādidīpakametaṃ.

229. An example is given: 'He brought about' (akāsi), and so on. The Buddha brought about boundless, immeasurable prosperity and growth for his kinsmen, those who are to be trained. Not only that, but he also brought about the crushing of many heretics together with all evils. Here, the verb 'akāsi,' standing at the beginning, illuminates the entire sentence. Thus, this is a verbal initial illuminator.

229. “Akāsi”ccādi. Buddho veneyyabandhūnaṃ amitodayaṃ pamāṇarahitābhivuddhiṃ akāsi. Na kevalaṃ tameva, samaṃ ekakkhaṇe sabbapāpehi sahānekatitthiyamaddanañca akāsīti. Vākyādimhi kriyāya ṭhitattā idaṃ kriyādidīpakaṃ nāma. Amito ca so udayo ceti ca, anekā ca te titthiyā ceti ca, tesaṃ maddanamiti ca viggaho.

229. 'He brought about' (akāsi), and so on. The Buddha brought about boundless prosperity, growth without measure, for his trainable kinsmen. Not only that, but simultaneously, in a single moment, he also brought about the crushing of many heretics together with all evils. Because the verb stands at the beginning of the sentence, this is called the verbal initial illuminator. And the analysis is: 'that is boundless and that is prosperity,' and 'those are many and those are heretics,' and 'the crushing of them.'

Majjhedīpaka

The Medial Illuminator

230.

230.

Dassanaṃ munino sādhu-janānaṃ jāyate’mataṃ;

Tadaññesaṃ tu jantūnaṃ, visaṃ niccopatāpanaṃ.

The sight of the sage becomes the Deathless for good people; but for other creatures, it becomes poison, constantly tormenting.

230. “Dassana”miccādi. [M 0.0229] Munino dassanaṃ sādhujanānaṃ amataṃ nibbānaṃ nāma jāyate amatassa sādhanato, tehi sādhujanehi aññesaṃ jantūnaṃ niccamupatāpetīti niccopatāpanaṃ visaṃ jāyate, tasmiṃ manopadosassa visasadisattā nirayādidukkhāvahabhāvatoti. Kriyāmajjhadīpakametaṃ.

230. 'Seeing' (dassanaṃ), and so on. The sight of the sage becomes the Deathless, named Nibbāna, for good people, because it is the means to the Deathless. For creatures other than those good people, it becomes poison, constantly tormenting, because the corruption of mind in that regard is like poison, bringing suffering such as that of hell.

230. “Dassana”miccādi. Munino dassanaṃ sādhujanānaṃ amataṃ amatasaṅkhātanibbānassa ekantakāraṇattā kāriyopacārena amataṃ bhūtaṃ jāyate, tadaññesaṃ tehi sādhujanehi aññesaṃ jantūnaṃ tu niccopatāpanaṃ satatamupatāpakaraṇato visaṃ jāyate visatulyapaṭighakāraṇattā kāriyopacārena visaṃ bhavatīti. Idaṃ kriyāya majjhe ṭhitattā kriyāmajjhadīpakaṃ. Sādhavo ca te janā ceti ca, tehi aññeti ca vākyaṃ.

230. 'Seeing' (dassanaṃ), and so on. The sight of the sage becomes the Deathless for good people because it is the sole cause of Nibbāna, which is known as the Deathless; through figurative usage based on the effect, it truly becomes the Deathless. But for others, for creatures other than those good people, it becomes poison, constantly tormenting, because it constantly causes torment and is a cause of aversion comparable to poison; through figurative usage based on the effect, it becomes poison. Because the verb stands in the middle, this is a verbal medial illuminator. And the analysis is: 'those are good and those are people,' and 'others than them.'

Antadīpaka

The Final Illuminator

231.

231.

Accantakantalāvaṇya-candātapamanoharo;

Jinānanindu indu ca, kassa nā’nandako bhave.

The moon of the Jina's face and the moon itself, charming with supreme loveliness and moonlight—for whom would they not be a source of joy?

231. “Accante”ccādi. Accantaṃ kantaṃ manuññaṃ lāvaṇyaṃ piyabhāvo, tameva, tamiva vācandātapo candikā, tena manoharo jinānanindu indu cando ca kassa janassa ānandako na bhavatīti. Kriyāntadīpakaṃ.

231. 'Supreme' (accanta) and so on. 'Utterly lovely, delightful charm' (`accantaṃ kantaṃ manuññaṃ lāvaṇyaṃ`) is dearness (`piyabhāvo`). The compound `accantakantalāvaṇyacandātapo` means either 'by that very charm which is moonlight' (`tameva... candātapo`) or 'by moonlight which is like that charm' (`tamiva vā... candātapo`), where `candātapo` is moon's radiance (`candikā`). 'Charming by that' (`tena manoharo`), the moon of the Jina's face and the moon, that is, the celestial moon, for what person would they not be a source of joy? This is a verbal final illuminator.

231. “Accanti”ccādi. Accantakantalāvaṇyacandātapamanoharo atisayena manuññapiyabhāvasaṅkhātavilāsanāmakena candakiraṇena, no ce, atisayena manuññapiyatāsaṅkhātavilāsasadisena candakiraṇena manoharo jinānanindu sambuddhassa mukhacando ca indu ca pakaticando ca kassa ānandako na bhave. Idaṃ kriyāya ante ṭhitattā kriyāntadīpakaṃ nāma. Antaṃ atikkantanti ca, tañca taṃ kantañceti ca, [M 0.0230] lavaṇassa bhāvo lāvaṇyaṃ, madhurabhāvo, taṃsadisattā accantakantañca taṃ lāvaṇyañcāti ca, candassa ātapo kiraṇoti ca, accantakantalāvaṇyameva candātapoti ca, candapakkhe accantakantalāvaṇyamiva ca so candātapo cāti ca, tena manoharoti ca, jinānanameva indūti ca vākyaṃ. Iminā kriyādīpakattayeneva avuttajātidīpakaguṇadīpakānipi ñātabbāni.

231. 'Supreme' (accanta) and so on. 'Charming with supreme loveliness and moonlight' (`Accantakantalāvaṇyacandātapamanoharo`) means charming by the moon's rays, which are called grace (`vilāsa`) and are characterized by exceedingly delightful dearness; or, if not, charming by the moon's rays which are like grace, characterized by exceedingly delightful dearness. The moon of the Jina's face, that is, the Perfectly Enlightened One's face-moon, and the moon, that is, the natural moon—for whom would they not be a source of joy? Because the verb stands at the end, this is called a verbal final illuminator. And the analysis is: 'surpassing the end' (`accanta`); 'that which is lovely' (`kanta`); 'the state of saltiness (`lavaṇa`) is charm (`lāvaṇya`), the quality of sweetness'; 'because it is like that, it is exceedingly lovely charm'; 'the moon's heat (`ātapo`) is a ray'; 'exceedingly lovely charm is itself moonlight'; 'in the case of the moon, that moonlight is like exceedingly lovely charm'; 'charming by that'; and 'the Jina's face is itself the moon.' By this very threefold verbal illuminator, the unstated illuminators of genus and quality should also be understood.

Mālādīpaka

The Garland Illuminator

232.

232.

Hotā’vippaṭisārāya,

Sīlaṃ pāmojjahetu so;

Taṃ pītihetu, sā cā’yaṃ,

Passaddhādipasiddhiyā.

Virtue is for non-remorse; that is the cause of joy; that is the cause of rapture; and this is for the accomplishment of tranquility and so forth.

232. Ādidīpakādīsupi tesu payogakkamena pakārantaramatthīti vadati “hoti”ccādi. Sīlaṃ pañcasīlādikaṃ, avippaṭisārāya pacchānutāpābhāvāya hoti, so avippaṭisāro pāmojjassa uppannamattāya pītiyā hetu hoti, taṃ pāmojjaṃ pītiyā balavabhūtāya hetu hoti, sā cāyaṃ pīti passaddhādīnaṃ passaddhisukhādīnaṃ pasiddhiyā nipphattiyā hotīti yojanīyaṃ.

232. Regarding those initial illuminators and so on, he says that there is another type by way of the order of application, with 'is' (hoti), and so on. Virtue, such as the five precepts, is for non-remorse, for the absence of later regret. That non-remorse is the cause of joy, which is rapture as soon as it arises. That joy is the cause of rapture that has become strong. And this rapture is for the accomplishment, the fulfillment, of tranquility and so forth, such as tranquility and bliss—thus it should be construed.

232. Idāni navasu dīpakesu payogavisesena sādhetabbe aññappakāre dasseti “hoti”ccādinā. Sīlaṃ surakkhitaṃ pañcaṅgadasaṅgādisīlaṃ avippaṭisārāya hoti, so avippaṭisāro pāmojjahetu hoti uppannamattāya taruṇapītiyā kāraṇaṃ bhavati, taṃ pāmojjaṃ pītihetu balavapītikāraṇaṃ hoti, sā ayañca pīti passaddhādipasiddhiyā kāyapassaddhicittapassaddhiādīnaṃ siddhiyā hetu hoti. Na vippaṭisāro avippaṭisāro, nasaddo pasajjapaṭisedhe vattate. Pamuditassa bhāvoti ca, tassa hetūti [M 0.0231] ca, passaddhi ādi yesaṃ sukhādīnanti ca, tesaṃ pasiddhīti ca viggaho.

232. Now, he shows other types to be accomplished by means of specific applications in the nine illuminators, with 'is' (hoti) and so on. Well-guarded virtue, virtue consisting of the five or ten factors and so on, is for non-remorse. That non-remorse is the cause of joy, becoming the reason for fresh rapture as soon as it arises. That joy is the cause of rapture, becoming the reason for strong rapture. And this rapture is the cause for the accomplishment of tranquility and so forth, such as bodily tranquility and mental tranquility. 'Non-remorse' is what is not remorse; the word 'na' functions in the sense of prohibitive negation. And the analysis is: 'the state of being joyful,' and 'its cause,' and 'tranquility and so forth, such as happiness, of which these are the beginning,' and 'their accomplishment.'

233.

233.

Iccā’didīpakattepi, pubbaṃ pubbamapekkhinī;

Vākyamālā pavattāti, taṃ mālādīpakaṃ mataṃ.

Thus, even in being an initial illuminator, the garland of sentences proceeds, expecting each preceding one; that is considered a garland illuminator.

233. Kimidaṃ tava pakārantaramiccāha “iccādi”ccādi. Iccevamimaṃ yaṃ taṃ mālādīpakaṃ mataṃ. Nanu kriyādidīpakametamiccāha “ādidīpakattepī”ti. Yajjapyādidīpakametaṃ pubbaṃ pubbaṃ vākyaṃ “hotāvippaṭisārāya sīla”ntiādikaṃ apekkhinī apekkhamānā vākyānaṃ yathāvuttānaṃ mālā paramparā pavattāti. Taṃ yathāvuttaṃ mālādīpakaṃ mataṃ, nādidīpakanti.

233. He asks, 'What is this other type of yours?' with 'thus' and so on. Thus, this is considered a garland illuminator. He asks, 'But isn't this a verbal initial illuminator?' with 'even in being an initial illuminator.' Even if this is an initial illuminator, the garland, the succession of the aforesaid sentences, proceeds, expecting each preceding statement such as 'virtue is for non-remorse.' That is considered a garland illuminator as described, not an initial illuminator.

233. “Iccādi”ccādi. Ādidīpakattepi kriyādidīpakabhāve satipi vākyamālā anekavākyena sambajjhamānā paramparā pubbaṃ pubbaṃ “hotāvippaṭisārāyā”tiādikaṃ vākyaṃ apekkhinī pavattā. Iti idaṃ anantaragatappakāraṃ dīpakaṃ “mālādīpaka”nti matanti. Ādimhi dīpakamiti ca, visayopacārena ādi ca taṃ dīpakañcāti ca, mālā eva dīpakamiti ca vākyaṃ.

233. 'Thus' and so on. Even in being an initial illuminator, even when it is a verbal initial illuminator, the garland of sentences, a succession being linked by many sentences, proceeds, expecting each preceding statement such as 'for non-remorse.' Thus, this illuminator of the type that has an uninterrupted progression is considered a 'garland illuminator.' And the analysis is: 'an illuminator at the beginning,' and 'by figurative usage of the scope, the beginning is also that illuminator,' and 'the garland itself is the illuminator.'

234.

234.

Aneneva pakārena, sesānamapi dīpake;

Vikappānaṃ vidhātabbā-nugatī suddhabuddhibhi.

In this very manner, the understanding of the distinctions in the remaining illuminators should also be made by those of pure intellect.

234. Avutte dīpakavikappe atidisanto nigameti “aneni”ccādinā. Aneneva anantarā vuttena pakārena vidhinā dīpake dīpakavisaye dīpakavisese (ka.) sesānamavuttānaṃ vikappānaṃ jātyādidīpakādibhedānaṃ anugati avabodho suddhabuddhibhi parisuddhamatīhi kavīhi vidhātabbā kātabbāti.

234. Referring to the unstated distinctions of illuminators, he concludes with 'in this manner' and so on. In this very manner, by the method just described, regarding the subject of illuminators, the understanding of the remaining unstated distinctions—the divisions such as the class illuminator and so forth—should be made by poets with pure intellect, with purified minds.

234. Idāni avuttadīpakānipi atidisati “anenevi”ccādinā. Aneneva pakārena yathāvuttadīpakappakārena dīpake dīpakavisaye sesānaṃ api vikappānaṃ avuttajātidīpakaguṇadīpakasaṅkhātānaṃ [M 0.0232] pakkhānaṃ jātyādidīpakaguṇādidīpakādīnaṃ channaṃ mālādīpakānañca anugati avabodho suddhabuddhibhi kavīhi vidhātabbā vuttānusāreneva kātabbā. Visesato asaṅkarato kappīyantīti ca, suddhā buddhi yesanti ca vākyaṃ.

234. Now, he also refers to the unstated illuminators with 'in this very manner' and so on. In this very manner, by the method of the aforementioned illuminators, regarding the subject of illuminators, the understanding of the remaining alternatives—the aspects classified as the unstated class illuminator and quality illuminator, and of the six garland illuminators such as the class illuminator, quality illuminator, and so forth—should be made by poets with pure intellect, in accordance with what has been said. And the analysis is: 'they are determined specifically and without confusion,' and 'those whose intellect is pure'—this is the sentence.

235.

235.

Visesavacanicchāyaṃ,

Nisedhavacanaṃ tu yaṃ;

Akkhepo nāma so’yañca,

Tidhā kālappabhedato.

That which is a statement of denial, in the desire for a statement of distinction, is called 'akkhepa' (objection); and it is threefold by division of time.

235. Akkhepamupakkhipati “visesi”ccādinā. Visesassa yassa kassaci vacanicchāyaṃ yaṃ nisedhassa paṭisedhassa vacanaṃ vutti, so akkhepo nāma akkhipanaṃ paṭisedhoti katvā. Soyamakkhepo ca kālappabhedato atītādito tidhā tippakāro.

235. He introduces akkhepa (objection) with 'distinction' and so on. That which is a statement of denial or prohibition, in the desire for a statement of any particular distinction, is called akkhepa, taking it as 'rejection' or 'prohibition.' And this akkhepa is threefold, of three kinds, by division of time, such as past.

235. Idāni akkhepaṃ dasseti “visese”ccādinā. Visesavacanicchāyaṃ tu yassa kassaci padatthavisesassa kathanicchāya eva yaṃ nisedhavacanaṃ paṭisedhavacanaṃ atthi, so paṭisedho akkhepo nāma akkhepālaṅkāro nāma. Ayañca akkhepo kālappabhedato atītādikālavisesena tidhā hoti. Visesassa kassaci vacananti ca, tasmiṃ icchāti ca, nisedhassa paṭisedhassa vacanamiti ca, akkhipanaṃ paṭikkhipananti ca, kālassa kriyāya vā pabhedoti ca vākyaṃ.

235. Now, he shows akkhepa (objection) with 'visese' and so on. But when, in the desire for a statement of distinction, there is a statement of denial or prohibition, indeed in the desire to state any particular distinction of a word's meaning, that prohibition is called akkhepa; it is called the figure of speech akkhepālaṅkāra. And this akkhepa is threefold by division of time, by distinction of time such as past. And the analysis is: 'a statement of any distinction,' and 'the desire regarding that,' and 'a statement of denial or prohibition,' and 'rejection or opposing,' and 'a division of time or action'—this is the sentence.

236.

236.

Ekākī’nekasenaṃ taṃ, māraṃsavijayījino;

Kathaṃ ta’matha vā tassa, pāramībalamīdisaṃ.

Alone, how did the Jina, the victor, conquer that Māra with his vast army? Or rather, his power of perfections was such.

Atītakkhepo.

Past Objection.

236. “Ekāki”ccādi. So jino ekākī eko samāno anekasenaṃ taṃ māraṃ vijayi parājesi, taṃ kathaṃ yujjate. [M 0.0233] Atha vā kiṃ na yujjate, yato tassa jinassa pāramī samatiṃsavidhā pāramitā eva balaṃ īdisaṃ yādisaṃ tassa vijayakāraṇanti. Ettha ekākittakāraṇasāmatthiyā māravijayāyogabuddhi “sasenaṃ māraṃ vijitavāti kathaṃ yujjatī”ti evamākārā atītā akkhittāti atītakkhepoyaṃ.

236. "Alone," etc. That Victor, being alone and solitary, conquered that Māra who had a vast army—how is that fitting? Or, why should it not be fitting? For the strength of that Victor, namely the thirty kinds of perfections, was indeed such as to be the cause of his victory. Here, the thought of the unsuitability of conquering Māra due to the power of being alone—a thought of the form, 'How is it fitting that he conquered Māra with his army?'—is refuted. Since this thought concerns a past event, this is a past refutation.

236. Idāni udāharati “ekāki”ccādinā. Sa jino so sabbaññū ekākī asahāyo adutiyo anekasenaṃ taṃ māraṃ vijayī ajinīti, taṃ kathaṃ yujjati. Atha vā yujjateva, tassa jinassa pāramībalaṃ samatiṃsapāramībalaṃ samatiṃsapāramītāsaṅkhatasenā īdisamīdisāti. Buddhassa adutiyabhāvañca mārassa saparivārabhāvañca nissāya kassaci uppannā “ekākinā kathamanekaseno māro jito”ti viparītabuddhi atītamāravijayavisayattā atītā hoti, “tassa pāramībalaṃ īdisa”nti atthavisesassa kathanicchāya “atha vā”ti niddiṭṭhapaṭisedhavacanena akkhittanti atītassa akkhepanato atītakkhepo nāma.

236. Now, an example is given with 'alone,' etc. That Victor, that All-Knowing One, alone, without a companion, without a second, conquered that Māra who had a large army—how is that fitting? Or indeed it is fitting, for the strength of that Victor's perfections, the strength of the thirty perfections—the army consisting of the thirty perfections—was indeed such. Based on the Buddha's state of being without a second and Māra's state of having a retinue, the erroneous thought that arose in someone—'How could Māra with a large army be conquered by one alone?'—is considered past, because it pertains to a past victory over Māra. Since it is refuted by the statement of denial indicated by 'or indeed,' which is stated with the desire to express the specific meaning 'his strength of perfections was such,' this is called 'past refutation' because it is a refutation of a past matter.

237.

237.

Kiṃ citte’jāsamugghātaṃ,

Appatto’smiti khijjase;

Paṇāmo nanu soyeva,

Sakimpi sugate kato.

O mind, why do you fret, thinking, 'I have not attained the uprooting of agitation'? Is not that very reverence, even done once to the Well-Farer, itself the uprooting?

Vattamānakkhepo.

Present Refutation.

237. “Kiṃ citte”ccādi. Citta ejāya taṇhāya samugghātaṃ sabbathā appavattiṃ appattosmīti kiṃ khijjase, tuccho tava khedo. Sugate sakimpi ekavārampi kato paṇāmo soyeva taṇhāya samugghātoyeva nanu ekantakāraṇattā tassāti vattamānakkhepoyaṃ vattamānassa khedassākkhitattā.

237. "Why, O mind," etc. O mind, why do you fret, thinking, 'I have not attained the complete cessation, the eradication of agitation, of craving'? Your grief is futile. Is not that very act of reverence, even done once to the Well-Farer, itself the eradication of craving, being its sole cause? This is a present refutation because it refutes the present grief.

237. “Kiṃ citte”ccādi. [M 0.0234] He citta ejāsamugghātaṃ ejāsaṅkhatāya taṇhāya samucchedapahānaṃ appattosmīti kiṃ khijjase, tuccho tava khedo. Tathā hi sugate buddhavisaye sakimpi kato paṇāmo soyeva nanu taṇhāsamucchedassa ekantakāraṇattā kāraṇakāriyānamabhedabuddhiyā so ejāsamugghātoyeva kiṃ na bhavati, bhavatyeva. “Paṇāmo”tyādivisesakathanādhippāyena “kiṃ khijjase”ti cittassa vattamānakhedassa paṭisedhitattā ayaṃ vattamānakkhepo nāma. Ejāya samugghātoti vākyaṃ.

237. "Why, O mind?" and so on. O mind, why do you fret, thinking, 'I have not attained the uprooting of agitation, the complete abandonment of craving, which is designated as agitation'? Your vexation is pointless. For indeed, even a single act of reverence performed towards the Well-Farer, the Buddha, is, because it is the sole cause for the complete destruction of craving, and due to the understanding of the non-difference between cause and effect, is that very act not itself the uprooting of agitation? It certainly is. Because the mind's present vexation is refuted by the phrase 'Why do you fret?', which is spoken with the intention of stating the specific point 'reverence' and so on, this is called 'present refutation'. The analysis of the compound is: 'uprooting of agitation'.

238.

238.

Saccaṃ na te gamissanti, sivaṃ sujanagocaraṃ;

Micchādiṭṭhiparikkanta-mānasā ye sudujjanā.

Truly, they will not go to the blissful, the realm of the good—those very wicked ones whose minds are encompassed by wrong views.

Anāgatakkhepo.

Future Refutation.

238. “Sacca”miccādi. Sujanagocaraṃ sivaṃ santipadaṃ te saccaṃ niyataṃ na gamissanti. Ye micchādiṭṭhiyā sassatādikāya parikkantaṃ abhibhūtaṃ mānasaṃ cittaṃ yesaṃ tādisā suṭṭhu atisayena dujjanāti yojanīyaṃ. Ayamanāgatakkhepo bhāvino gamanassākkhittattā.

238. "Truth" and so on. Truly, certainly, they will not reach the blissful, peaceful state, the realm of the good. Those whose minds are encompassed and overcome by wrong views, such as eternalism, are to be understood as exceedingly wicked persons. This is a future refutation because their future going is refuted.

“Jīvitāsā balavatī, dhanāsā dubbalā mama;

Gaccha vā tiṭṭha vā kanta, mamāvatthā niveditā”ti kābyādāsa 2.139.

"My hope for life is strong, my hope for wealth is weak. Go or stay, beloved, my state has been made known."

Ayamanādarakkhepoti evamādayo tu tabbhedāyevāti upekkhitā.
