This is the indifference-refutation, and so on; but these are only varieties of that, and are therefore disregarded.

238. “Sacca”miccādi. Sujanagocaraṃ sādhūnaṃ visayagataṃ sivaṃ santipadaṃ te saccamekantena na gamissanti. Ke? Ye micchādiṭṭhiparikkantamānasā sudujjanā, teyevāti. “Micchādiṭṭhī”tiādivisesassa kathanādhippāyena “te na gamissantī”ti titthiyānaṃ bhāvino nibbānagamanassa buddhiyā paṭisiddhattā [M 0.0235] ayaṃ anāgatakkhepo nāma. Micchā viparītā ca sā diṭṭhi cāti ca, tāya parikkantaṃ mānasaṃ yesanti ca vākyaṃ.

238. "Truth" and so on. Truly, they will not at all reach the blissful, peaceful state, the realm of the good, accessible to the noble ones. Who? Those very wicked ones whose minds are encompassed by wrong views. With the intention of stating the specific characteristic of 'wrong view' and so on, the utterance 'they will not reach' refutes the belief held by adherents of other doctrines in a future attainment of Nibbāna; hence, this is called 'future refutation'. And the analysis is: 'wrong (micchā) means perverse (viparītā), and that is view (diṭṭhi)'; and 'those whose minds are encompassed by it'—this is the sentence.

“Jīvitāsā balavatī, dhanāsā dubbalā mama;

Gaccha vā tiṭṭha vā kanta, mamāvatthā niveditā” –

"My hope for life is strong, my hope for wealth is weak. Go or stay, dear one, my situation has been made known."

Tyādiko anādarakkhepopi dassitātītakkhepādīhi anaññattā visuṃ na vutto. Ayaṃ panettha attho – he kanta vallabha mama jīvitāsā balavatī hoti, dhanāsā dubbalā, tvaṃ gaccha vā tiṭṭha vā, mamāvatthā mama pakati niveditā viññāpitā. “Ettha mamāvatthā niveditā”ti visesassa kathanādhippāyena “gaccha vā tiṭṭha vā”ti iminā anādaravacanena attano vallabhassa vattamānassa anāgatassa vā gamanassa paṭisedhitattā vattamānakkhepo vā anāgatakkhepo vā hoti.

The indifference refutation, such as in the preceding example, is not stated separately because it is not distinct from the past refutation and others that have been shown. Here, this is the meaning: 'O dear beloved, my hope for life is strong, my hope for wealth is weak. Whether you go or stay, my state, my nature, has been declared, made known.' With the intention of stating the specific point, 'my state has been made known,' the present or future going of her beloved is refuted by this indifferent statement, 'Whether you go or stay'; therefore, it is either a present refutation or a future refutation.

239.

239.

Ñeyyo sotthantaranyāso,

Yo’ññavākyatthasādhano;

Sabbabyāpī visesaṭṭho,

Hivisiṭṭha’ssa bhedato.

The `atthantaranyāsa` is to be known, which establishes the meaning of another statement; it is universally applicable and of particular meaning, and its divisions are distinguished by 'hi'.

239. Atthantaranyāsaṃ nyāsayati “ñeyyi”ccādinā. Aññavākyatthasādhano aññassa vattumicchitassa kassaci vākyatthassa sādhano samatthako kassacideva atthassa parassa nyāso yo, so atthantaranyāso ñeyyo atthantarassa kassaci vatthuno nyāso payogoti katvā. Tassa bhedamāha “sabbe”ccādinā. Assa atthantaranyāsassa bhedato vikappato hivisiṭṭhā hisaddena visesitā sabbabyāpī ca visesaṭṭho cāti ime bhavanti. Nanu pativatthūpamāya imassa ca ko bhedoti? Saccaṃ, tathāpi ubhayattha atthantaranyāsamattena sadisattepi yattha mukhyato sāmyappatītisabbhāvo, sā pativatthūpamā. Yattha pana sādhanarūpassevatthantaranyāso, so atthantaranyāsoti pākaṭoyevubhinnaṃ bhedoti.

239. He explains the `atthantaranyāsa` with 'to be known,' and so on. That which establishes the meaning of another statement, that which is capable of proving the intended meaning of some other statement, the application of another meaning for some purpose—this is to be known as `atthantaranyāsa`, it being the application or use of another meaning for some subject matter. He states its divisions with 'all,' and so on. From the divisions and varieties of this `atthantaranyāsa`, there are these types: the universally applicable and the particular meaning; and these, when distinguished by the particle 'hi', also exist. Now, what is the distinction between this and the reciprocal simile (`pativatthūpamā`)? True, although in both cases there is a similarity in being merely an `atthantaranyāsa`, where there is primarily the perception of resemblance, that is the reciprocal simile. Where, however, there is the application of another meaning that is solely in the nature of a proof, that is the `atthantaranyāsa`. Thus, the distinction between the two is indeed clear.

239. Idāni atthantaranyāsaṃ dasseti “ñeyya”ccādinā. Yo aññavākyatthasādhano aññavākyatthassa sādhano hoti, aññavākyatthaṃ sādheti, so atthantaranyāso sādhiyavākyatthato aññatthassa ṭhapanaṃ kathanaṃ “atthantaranyāso”ti ñeyyo, assa atthantaranyāsassa bhedato pabhedena sabbabyāpī visesaṭṭho ca, eteyeva hivisiṭṭhā cāti cattāro bhavanti. Attho ca so antaro añño ceti ca, tassa nyāsoti ca, sabbaṃ byāpeti sīlenāti ca, visese padese tiṭṭhatīti ca, hisaddena visiṭṭhāti ca vākyaṃ.

239. Now, he shows the `atthantaranyāsa` with 'to be known,' etc. That which is the means of establishing the meaning of another statement, which establishes the meaning of another statement, is the `atthantaranyāsa`. The setting forth or stating of a meaning different from the meaning of the proposition being established is to be known as '`atthantaranyāsa`.' From the divisions and subdivisions of this `atthantaranyāsa`, there are the universally applicable and the particular meaning; and these themselves, when distinguished by 'hi', thus become four. And 'meaning' (`attho`) is that which is inner (`antaro`) and other (`añño`); and 'its placement' (`nyāso`); and 'it pervades all by its nature'; and 'it stands in a specific place'; and 'it is distinguished by the particle hi'—this is the phrasing.

Hi-rahitasabbabyāpī

Universally applicable without 'hi'.

240.

240.

Tepi lokahitāsattā, sūriyo candimā api candimārapi (sī.);

Atthaṃ passa gamissanti, niyamo kena laṅghyate.

Even they, attached to the welfare of the world, the sun and moon as well, will go to their setting. See! By whom can this law be transgressed?

240. Udāharati “tepi”ccādi. Lokassa hite abhivuddhiyaṃ āsattā abhirattā sūriyo candimā apīti te mahantāpi atthaṃ udayavipariyāsa’mabhāvaṃ gamissanti, na gamissantā puna (ka.) tatheva tiṭṭhanti, “passe”ti tamavabodhayati. Tathā hi niyamo “bhāvo nāma na pāyini. Sabbe saṅkhārā vayadhammino”ti ayaṃ niyati. Kena nāma vatthunā laṅghyate atikkamituṃ sakkāti. Ayaṃ hisaddarahito sabbabyāpī atthantaranyāso tādisassa niyamassa sabbagatattā.

240. He gives an example with, "Even they," and so on. Being attached and delighting in the welfare and prosperity of the world, even the sun and the moon—those great ones—will go to their setting, the state of non-being which is the opposite of their arising; they do not remain the same. By 'See!' he makes this understood. For such is the law: "Existence, indeed, does not endure. All conditioned things are of a nature to pass away." This is the fixed principle. By what thing indeed could it be transgressed, is it possible to overcome? This is a universally applicable `atthantaranyāsa` without the particle 'hi', due to such a principle being all-pervading.

240. “Tepi”ccādi. Lokahitāsattā lokābhivuddhiyaṃ laggā sūriyo api candimā api tepi mahānubhāvā atthaṃ vināsaṃ gamissanti, passa etesaṃ pākaṭaṃ vināsaṃ [M 0.0237] olokehi. Tathā hi niyamo “sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā”ti sabbapadatthamanatikkamma pavattaniyamo kena laṅghyate paccayasamuppannena kena padatthena atikkamyateti. Ayaṃ hisaddarahito atthagamanasaṅkhāto niyamo sabbattha gatoti sabbabyāpī atthantaranyāso. Pativatthūpamāya ca atthantaranyāsassa ca atthantaranyāsattena tulyattepi tattha sādhammapakāsattasabhāvo, ettha vuttatthassa sādhanasabhāvoti evamimesaṃ nānattaṃ subyattaṃ. Apīti sambhāvanāyaṃ, dutiyo apisaddo samuccaye.

240. "Even they," etc. Attached to the welfare of the world, engaged in the prosperity of the world, even the sun and the moon—those of great power—will go to their end, to destruction. See, observe their evident destruction. For this law, "All conditioned things are impermanent," is a law that proceeds without transgressing the meaning of any thing. By what is it transgressed? By what conditioned thing is it overcome? This law, designated as 'going to its end,' being present everywhere, is a universally applicable `atthantaranyāsa` without the particle 'hi'. Although the reciprocal simile (`pativatthūpamā`) and the `atthantaranyāsa` are similar in being an application of another meaning, in the former the nature is the illumination of a common property, while here it is the nature of proving the stated meaning. Thus, their distinction is very clear. 'Api' is in the sense of possibility; the second 'api' particle is for conjunction.

Hi-sahitasabbabyāpī

Universally applicable with 'hi'.

241.

241.

Satthā devamanussānaṃ, vasī sopi munissaro;

Gatova nibbutiṃ sabbe, saṅkhārā na hi sassatā.

The Teacher of gods and humans, he, the Master, the chief of sages, has also gone to Nibbāna; for all conditioned things are not eternal.

241. “Satthā”iccādi. Devamanussānaṃ devānañca manussānañca ukkaṭṭhaparicchedavasena satthā diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikehi paramatthehi yathārahaṃ anusāsatīti, vasī pañcahi vasitāhi atisayavasīhi vasippatto sopi munissaro nibbutiṃ khandhaparinibbānasaṅkhātaṃ gato pattoyeva, hisaddo samatthane. Sabbe saṅkhārā paccayasamuppannā na sassatā na niccā uppādavayadhammattā aniccā. Ayampi hisaddasahitasabbabyāpī atthantaranyāso aniccatāya sabbagatattāti.

241. "Teacher," and so on. The Teacher of gods and humans—that is, of both gods and humans by way of supreme distinction—is one who instructs them appropriately in ultimate matters pertaining to this life and the life beyond. The Master, having attained mastery through the five supreme masteries—he too, the chief of sages, has indeed gone to and attained Nibbāna, designated as the final passing away of the aggregates. The particle 'hi' is for corroboration. All conditioned things, arisen from conditions, are not eternal, not constant; being of a nature to arise and pass away, they are impermanent. This too is a universally applicable `atthantaranyāsa` with the particle 'hi', due to impermanence being all-pervading.

241. “Satthā”iccādi. Devamanussānaṃ ukkaṭṭhavasena satthā diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikatthehi yathārahamanusāsako vasī vuṭṭhānaadhiṭṭhānādīsu pañcasu vasibhāvesu sātisayaṃ issariyavā so munissaro api nibbutiṃ khandhanibbānaṃ gato eva. Hi tatheva, sabbe saṅkhārā sassatā na hontīti. Ayaṃ hisaddasahito aniccatāya sabbagatattā sabbabyāpī atthantaranyāso. Vaso assa atthīti vākyaṃ.

241. "Teacher," and so on. The Teacher of gods and humans, by way of supreme excellence, is the instructor in matters pertaining to this life and the next, as is fitting. He is the Master, possessing supreme sovereignty in the five states of mastery—in emergence, determination, and so forth. That chief of sages has also indeed gone to Nibbāna, the Nibbāna of the aggregates. 'Hi' means 'just so': all conditioned things are not eternal. This is a universally applicable `atthantaranyāsa` with the particle 'hi', due to impermanence being all-pervading. The phrasing is 'mastery is his'.

Hi-rahitavisesaṭṭha

Particular meaning without 'hi'.

242.

242.

Jino [M 0.0238] saṃsārakantārā, janaṃ pāpeti nibbutiṃ;

Nanu yuttā gati sā’yaṃ, vesārajjasamaṅginaṃ.

The Victor leads people from the wilderness of saṃsāra to attain Nibbāna. Surely this course is fitting for one possessed of confidence.

242. “Jino”iccādi. Jino saṃsāroyeva kantāro duggamattā, tato janaṃ sakalampi lokaṃ nibbutiṃ pāpeti. Nanu pasiddhiyamanumatiyaṃ vā. Sāyaṃ gati nibbutipāpanasaṅkhātā pavatti, vigato sārado bhayamassāti visārado, tassa bhāvo nibbhayatā nibbhayatāya (ka.) vesārajjaṃ, tena samaṅgīnaṃ yuttānaṃ. Yuttāti anurūpāti. Ayaṃ hisaddavirahito visesaṭṭho atthantaranyāso, vesārajjasamaṅgīnameva tathābhāvato na sabbabyāpī.

242. "Victor," etc. The Victor leads people, the entire world, from saṃsāra—which is a wilderness because it is difficult to traverse—to Nibbāna. 'Nanu' is used in the sense of what is well-known or of assent. This course is the proceeding designated as causing attainment of Nibbāna. One for whom timidity (`sārada`) or fear has departed is `visārado` (fearless); his state of fearlessness is `vesārajja` (confidence). For those endowed with this, it is fitting. 'Fitting' means 'appropriate'. This is a particular meaning `atthantaranyāsa` without the particle 'hi', because such a state belongs only to one endowed with confidence; hence, it is not universally applicable.

242. “Jino”iccādi. Jino janaṃ sattalokaṃ saṃsārakantārā nibbutiṃ pāpeti, sā ayaṃ gati pavatti vesārajjasamaṅgīnaṃ catuvesārajjaguṇasamannāgatānaṃ tathāgatānaṃ yuttā nanūti. Ayaṃ janānaṃ nibbānaṃ pāpanā vesārajjasamaṅgīnaṃyeva āveṇikattā visesaṭṭho hisaddarahito atthantaranyāso. Vigato sārado bhayaṃ asseti ca, kassa bhāvoti ca, tena samaṅginoti ca vākyaṃ. Nanūti pasiddhiyaṃ anumatiyaṃ vā vattate. Dvinnampi attho vuttanayena ñātabbo.

242. "Victor," etc. The Victor leads people, the world of beings, from the wilderness of saṃsāra to Nibbāna. Is this course, this proceeding, not fitting for the Tathāgatas, who are endowed with confidence, possessed of the qualities of the four confidences? This leading of people to Nibbāna, being unique to those endowed with confidence, is a particular meaning `atthantaranyāsa` without the particle 'hi'. The phrases are: 'Timidity, fear, is gone for him,' 'whose state is it?' and 'endowed with it.' 'Nanu' is used in the sense of what is well-known or of assent. The meaning of both should be understood in the way described.

Hi-sahitavisesaṭṭha

Particular meaning with 'hi'.

243.

243.

Surattaṃ te’dharapuṭaṃ, jina rañjeti mānasaṃ;

Sayaṃ rāgaparītā hi, pare rañjenti saṅgate.

O Victor, your very red lower lip delights the mind; for indeed, those who are themselves overcome by passion delight others upon encounter.

243. “Suratta”miccādi. Jina te tava surattaṃ bimbaphalasamānavaṇṇattā adharapuṭaṃ mānasaṃ passataṃ yesaṃ kesañci rañjeti pīṇetīti. Hi samatthane, tathā hīti attho. Sayaṃ [M 0.0239] yena kenaci rāgena rattavaṇṇena anurāgena vā parītā gatā saṅgate attanā saṃsaṭṭhe pare aññe rañjenti rattavaṇṇe anuratte vā karontīti sasileso sādhano. Ayañca hisaddasahito visesaṭṭho atthantaranyāso tathābhāvassa tathāvidhānameva sambhavato.

243. "Very red," etc. O Victor, your very red lower lip, being of a color similar to a bimba fruit, delights and satisfies the mind of whosoever sees it. The particle 'hi' is for corroboration; the meaning is 'for thus it is.' Those who are themselves overcome or pervaded by some `rāga`—either red color or attachment—when associated with, in contact with themselves, make others red or attached. This is a proof with a pun. And this is a particular meaning `atthantaranyāsa` with the particle 'hi', because such a state is possible only for those of that kind.

243. “Suratta”miccādi. Bho jina te tava surattaṃ adharapuṭaṃ oṭṭhayugaḷaṃ mānasaṃ passantānaṃ pasannacittaṃ (ka.) cittaṃ rañjeti pīṇayati. Hi tatheva, sayaṃ rāgaparītā rattavaṇṇena anurāgena vā yuttā saṅgate attanā saṃsaṭṭhe pare aññe rañjenti rattavaṇṇe anuratte vā karonti. Idaṃ tesaṃ sabhāvameveti. Ayaṃ īdisānameva āveṇikattā visesaṭṭho hisaddasahito atthantaranyāso. Puṭasadisattā adharo eva puṭamiti ca, rāgena parītā yuttāti ca viggaho.

243. "Suratta," etc. O Conqueror, your very red lower lip, the pair of lips, delights and satisfies the minds of those who see it. Indeed, just so, those who are themselves overcome by passion, endowed with red color or attachment, delight others with whom they are associated, making them red or attached. This is their very nature. This is an illustration by another meaning (atthantaranyāsa), a specific meaning accompanied by the word 'hi,' because it is unique to such cases. The analysis is: the lower lip is called 'puṭa' because it resembles a case; and 'overcome by passion' means 'endowed with it.'

244.

244.

Vācce gamme’tha vatthūnaṃ,

Sadisatte pabhedanaṃ;

Byatireko’ya’mapye’ko-

Bhayabhedā catubbidho.

Of objects, in their similarity, whether expressible or implied, the differentiation is Distinction. This, though one, is fourfold by the division into single and both.

244. Byatirekavikappamāha “vācce”iccādinā. Vatthūnaṃ vattumicchitānaṃ kesañci vatthūnaṃ sadisatte kathañci vatthūnaṃ tulyatte vācce saddena vācakena paṭipādite atha gamme asaddapaṭipādite sabbatthabalena pakaraṇādinā ñāte vā, na kevalaṃ saddapaṭipādite. Pabhedanaṃ tesameva vatthūnaṃ visesakathanaṃ byatireko byatirecanaṃ puthakkaraṇanti katvā. Ayaṃ byatirekopi ekobhayabhedā ekabyatireko ubhayabyatirekoti vāccagammānaṃ paccekaṃ visesena catubbidho.

244. He states the modes of distinction (byatireka) with 'vācce,' etc. When, regarding subjects intended to be spoken, in the similarity of some subjects or the equality of some subjects in some way, it is expressed by a word (vācce) or implied (gamme)—that is, not expressed by a word but known by the force of the entire context and so forth, not merely expressed by a word—the differentiation, the specific explanation of these very subjects, is called 'byatireka,' 'byatirecana,' or 'puthakkaraṇa' (separation). This distinction, too, is fourfold, being divided into single distinction (eka-byatireka) and double distinction (ubhaya-byatireka), specifically for each of what is expressible (vācca) and what is implied (gamma).

244. Idāni [M 0.0240] byatirekaṃ dasseti “vācce”iccādinā. Vatthūnaṃ vattumicchitānaṃ kesañci padatthānaṃ sadisatte yena kenaci ākārena samānatte vācce vācakasaddena paṭipādanīye atha puna gamme tasmiṃyeva sadisatte atthasattisaṅkhātasāmatthiyena gammamāne pabhedanaṃ tesaṃyeva vatthūnaṃ nānattakathanaṃ byatireko nāma. Ayampi byatireko ekobhayabhedā byatirecanasaṅkhātaputhakkaraṇasāmaññena abhinnopi vāccagammānaṃ dvinnaṃ paccekameva ekabyatireko ubhayabyatirekoti visesena catubbidho hoti. Sadisānaṃ bhāvoti ca, pakārena bhedanaṃ kathanamiti ca, byatirecanaṃ puthakkaraṇamiti ca, eko ca ubhayo cāti ca, tesaṃ bhedo visesananti ca viggaho.

244. Now, the distinction is shown with 'vācce,' etc. When, regarding certain concepts intended to be spoken, in their similarity or equality in some way, it is to be expressed by an expressive word (vācce), and then when implied in that very similarity by the capability called 'power of meaning' (gamme), the differentiation, the statement of the diversity of those very subjects, is called 'byatireka.' This 'byatireka,' though not different in the general sense of separation called 'byatirecana' or 'puthakkaraṇa,' is specifically fourfold due to the separate individual distinctions of 'vācca' and 'gamma,' being single distinction and double distinction. The analysis is: 'the state of similarity'; 'the statement of differentiation by way of kind'; '`byatirecana` means separation'; 'single and both'; and 'their division is a distinction.'

Vāccaekabyatireka

Expressible Single Distinction

245.

245.

Gambhīrattamahattādi-

Guṇā jaladhinā jina;

Tulyo tva’masi bhedo tu,

Sarīrene’disena te.

O Conqueror, with qualities such as depth and greatness, you are like the ocean; but the difference is your body, which is such.

245. Udāharati “gambhīra”iccādi. Tvaṃ gambhīrattaṃ agādhatā ajjhāsayavisiṭṭhatā ca mahattaṃ vepullaṃ guṇamahantatā ca taṃ ādi yassa upakāritādino, tasmā guṇā jaladhinā sāgarena tulyo. “Asī”tisaddapaṭipāditaṃ sadisattaṃ vuttaṃ. Bhedaṃ dasseti “bhedo tu”iccādinā. Bhedo tu viseso pana sāgarena saha īdisena dissamānena karacaraṇādimatā rucirena te sarīreneva hetunā, nāññathā, tassedisaṃ sarīraṃ natthīti. Sadisatte paṭipādite ekabyatirekoyaṃ ekasmiṃ jine vattamānena dhammena upameyyopamānabhūtajinasāgarānaṃ tassa bhedassa patīyamānattā.

245. He gives the example with 'gambhīra,' etc. You are equal to the ocean in qualities such as depth—profoundness and excellence of intention—and greatness—vastness and abundance of virtues—and others, of which helpfulness and so forth is the beginning. The similarity is stated, expressed by the word 'asi' (you are). He shows the distinction with 'bhedo tu,' etc. However, the difference, the distinction, with the ocean, is due to your body, which is such—visible, having hands and feet, etc., and beautiful—as the very reason; not otherwise, for such a body does not exist for it. When similarity is stated, this is a single distinction, because the difference between the subject of comparison (the Conqueror) and the standard of comparison (the ocean) is understood by means of a quality existing in the single Conqueror.

245. Idāni [M 0.0241] tamudāharati “gambhīratti”ccādinā. He jina tvaṃ gambhīrattamahattādiguṇā jaladhinā tulyo asi. Iminā vākyena jinasāgarānaṃ dvinnaṃ saddena vāccasadisattaṃ vuttaṃ. Bhedo tu sāgarena saha tava viseso pana te tuyhaṃ īdisena evarūpena dissamānahatthapādādiavayavayuttena sarīrena sarīrahetunā hoti. Dvinnaṃ vatthūnaṃ vattabbasadisattaṃ vatvā iminā vākyena “īdisena sarīrenā”ti ekasmiṃyeva jinapadatthe visesakathanena jaladhito jinapadatthassa visuṃ katattā sadisatte saddena vācce sati ayamekabyatireko nāma. Gambhīrassa gambhīraguṇayuttassa sāgarassa vā gambhīrajjhāsayasamaṅgino jinassa vā bhāvoti ca, mahato pakatiyā mahato sāgarassa vā guṇehi mahato jinassa vā bhāvoti ca, gambhīrattañca mahattañcāti ca, taṃ ādi yassa upakāritādinoti ca, so ca so guṇo ceti ca vākyaṃ.

245. Now, it is illustrated with 'gambhīratti,' etc. O Jina, you are like the ocean in qualities such as depth and greatness. By this statement, the expressible similarity by word between the two, the Jina and the ocean, is stated. However, your distinction from the ocean is by your body, which is such—of such a form, endowed with visible limbs like hands and feet—by reason of the body. Having stated the expressible similarity of the two objects, by specifying 'with such a body' in the single concept of the Jina, the concept of the Jina is distinguished from the ocean; thus, when the similarity is expressible by word, this is called single distinction (ekabyatireka). The analysis is: 'the state of being deep,' whether of the ocean possessing the quality of depth or of the Jina possessing profound intent; 'the state of being great,' whether of the ocean naturally great or of the Jina great in qualities; 'depth and greatness'; 'that of which helpfulness and so forth is the beginning'; and 'that quality'.

Vāccaubhayabyatireka

Expressible Mutual Distinction

246.

246.

Mahāsattā’tigambhīrā, sāgaro sugatopi ca;

Sāgaro’ñjanasaṅkāso, jino cāmīkarajjuti.

Both the ocean and the Sugata are great beings, exceedingly deep; the ocean is like collyrium, and the Jina has the radiance of gold.

246. “Mahā”iccādi. Sāgaro sugatopi cāti te ubho mahantā sattā makarādayo yattha sāgare, mahantaṃ vā sattaṃ sammappadhānaṃ yassa sugatassa, atigambhīrā atisayena agādhā iti. Sadisatābhedamāha “sāgaro”iccādinā. Sāgaro añjanasaṅkāso añjanena tulyo, kaṇhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Jino tu cāmīkarassa suvaṇṇasseva juti sobhā asseti cāmīkarajjuti. Vācce sadisatte ubhayabyatirekoyaṃ ubhayattha vattamānena guṇena ubhinnamupamānopameyyānaṃ bhedassa patīyamānattā.

246. ‘Great,’ etc. The ocean and the Sugata are both great beings: the ocean contains great beings such as makaras, or the Sugata possesses great being, that is, right effort; they are exceedingly deep, profoundly unfathomable. He states the distinction within similarity with ‘the ocean,’ etc. The ocean is like collyrium, similar to collyrium; thus it is said to be dark. But the Jina possesses the radiance of gold, the splendor of refined gold. In expressed similarity, this is a mutual distinction, because the difference between both the standard of comparison and the subject of comparison is understood through a quality present in both.

246. “Mahā”iccādi. [M 0.0242] Sāgaro sugatopi cāti ime dve mahāsattā kamena timitimiṅgalādimahāsattā ca, lābhālābhādīsu anaññasādhāraṇattā mahantatādibhāvasaṅkhātasadisattayuttā ca, atigambhīrā avagāhitumasakkuṇeyyattā ca, ajjhāsayagambhīrattā ca dvepi atigambhīrā honti. Tesu sāgaro añjanasaṅkāso, jino cāmīkarajjuti suvaṇṇasadisakantiyutto hoti. Ettha pubbaddhena dvinnaṃ vatthūnaṃ sadisattaṃ vatvā aparaddhena tadubhayavatthugatavisesena tesaṃ dvinnamaññamaññato visesitattā sadisatte saddena vattabbe sati ayaṃ ubhayabyatireko nāma. Mahantā sattā macchakacchapādayo yattha sāgareti vā, mahantaṃ sattaṃ samānabhāvo yassa sugatassāti vā, atisayena gambhīrāti ca, añjanena saṅkāso sadisoti ca, cāmīkarassa iva juti asseti ca vākyaṃ.

246. ‘Great,’ etc. The ocean and the Sugata are both great beings; sequentially, the one has great beings such as the Timitimiṅgala, and the other is endowed with a similarity reckoned as greatness due to uncommonness in gains and losses, etc. Both are exceedingly profound, the one because it is impossible to fathom, the other due to the profundity of its intention. Among them, the ocean is like collyrium, and the Jina has the radiance of gold, possessing a lustre similar to gold. Here, having stated the similarity of the two objects in the first half, and then, in the latter half, having distinguished them from each other by a particular quality residing in both objects, when similarity is to be expressed by word, this is called mutual distinction. The analysis is: ‘great beings such as fish and turtles dwell in the ocean,’ or ‘the Sugata, whose state is equal to a great being’; ‘exceedingly profound’; ‘similar to collyrium’; and ‘possessing radiance like that of gold.’

Gammaekabyatireka

Implied Single Distinction

247.

247.

Na santāpāpahaṃ nevi-cchitadaṃ migalocanaṃ;

Muninda nayanadvandaṃ, tava tagguṇabhūsitaṃ.

The eye of a deer does not dispel suffering, nor does it grant what is desired; O Lord of Sages, your pair of eyes is adorned with those qualities.

247. “Ni”ccādi. Migassa locanaṃ santāpaṃ kilesapariḷāhaṃ apahanati hiṃsatīti santāpāpahaṃ na bhavati. Neva icchitaṃ saggamokkhasampattiṃ dadātīti nevicchitadaṃ. Muninda tava nayanānaṃ dvandaṃ yugaḷaṃ tu tehi yathāvuttehi santāpāpahattaicchitadattaguṇehi bhūsitamalaṅkataṃ. Ettha pana migalocananayanānaṃ dīghattādinā sadisattaṃ patīyate. Gamme sadisatte ekabyatirekoyaṃ vuttanayena.

247. ‘Nor,’ etc. The eye of a deer does not dispel suffering, the fever of defilements; thus, it is not a ‘dispeller of suffering.’ Nor does it grant the desired, the attainments of heaven and liberation; thus, it is not a ‘granter of the desired.’ O Lord of Sages, your pair of eyes, however, is adorned and embellished with those qualities as described: dispelling suffering and granting the desired. Here, however, the similarity between the deer's eye and your eyes is implied through their length and other qualities. In implied similarity, this is a single distinction, in the manner stated.

247. “Na santā”iccādi. Migalocanaṃ migapotakacakkhuyugaḷaṃ santāpāpahaṃ kilesasantāpāpahaṃ na hoti. Icchitadaṃ lokehi patthitalokiyalokuttaratthānaṃ dāyakaṃ [M 0.0243] na hoti. He muninda tava nayanadvandaṃ pana tagguṇabhūsitaṃ janasantāpāpahānādiyathāvuttaguṇehi sobhitaṃ hoti, iha santāpāpahananādīnaṃ paṭisedhadvārena upamānopameyyabhūtaubhayalocanasaṅkhātavatthūnaṃ dīghaputhulatādisadisadhammaṃ sāmatthiyena pakāsetvā aparaddhena santāpāpahananādiguṇahetu jinanayanānaṃ visuṃ katattā sadisatte gammamāne ayamekabyatireko nāma. Santāpaṃ apahanati hiṃ satīti ca, icchitaṃ dadātīti ca, te ca te guṇā cāti ca, tehi bhūsitanti ca vākyaṃ.

247. ‘Not dispelling suffering,’ and so on. The eyes of a deer, a pair of eyes like those of a young deer, do not dispel the distress of defilements. They do not grant the worldly and supramundane attainments desired by beings. O Lord of Sages, your pair of eyes, however, is adorned with such virtues, made beautiful by the aforementioned qualities such as dispelling the distress of beings. Here, by negating the dispelling of suffering and so on, the similar qualities like length and breadth of the two objects—namely the eyes serving as the standard of comparison and the subject of comparison—are skillfully revealed. Then, in the latter part, because the Jina’s eyes are distinguished on account of qualities like dispelling suffering, while similarity is implied, this is called ‘single exclusion.’ The phrases are: ‘it dispels suffering,’ ‘it grants what is desired,’ ‘those very qualities,’ and ‘adorned with them.’

Gammaubhayabyatireka

Implicit Similarity with Mutual Exclusion

248.

248.

Munindānana’mambhoja-mesaṃ nānatta’mīdisaṃ;

Suvuttāmatasandāyi, vadanaṃ ne’disa’mbujaṃ.

The face of the Lord of Sages and the lotus—their difference is such: The face bestows the nectar of well-spoken words; the lotus is not like this.

248. “Muninda”iccādi. Munindānanaṃ ambhojañceti yāni vatthūni kantādinā patīyamānattā sadisatthāni, esaṃ nānattaṃ bhedo īdisaṃ. Kathaṃ? Vadanaṃ suvuttāmataṃ saddhammāmataṃ sandadātīti suvuttāmatasandāyi, ambujaṃ tu nedisanti. Iminā bhedena imesaṃ visadisattā “esa”ntyādināhu. Patīyamānena sadisānīti gamme sadisatte ubhayabyatirekoyaṃ vuttanayeneti.

248. ‘Muninda,’ etc. The face of the Lord of Sages and the lotus—these objects, which are similar because they are perceived as such through their beauty and so on, their difference is such. How so? The face bestows the nectar of well-spoken words, the nectar of the true Dhamma; thus it is called ‘bestowing the nectar of well-spoken words.’ But the lotus is not like this. By this distinction, their dissimilarity is stated with ‘their,’ etc. When similarity is implied, this is mutual exclusion in implied similarity, in the manner stated.

248. “Muninda”iccādi. Munindānanaṃ ambhojañceti imesaṃ dvinnaṃ nānattaṃ īdisaṃ. Kathanti ce? Esaṃ dvinnaṃ vadanaṃ suvuttāmatasandāyi suṭṭhu vuttattā suvuttasaṅkhātassa saddhammāmatassa dāyakaṃ hoti, ambujaṃ tu edisaṃ na īdisaṃ na hoti, tādisaṃ dhammāmataṃ na dadātīti adhippāyo. “Esaṃ nānattamīdisa”nti vacanena sugandhakantimattādīhi guṇehi dvinnampi bhedo natthīti gammamānattā taṃ pakāsetvā aparaddhena vadanato ambujassa, ambujato vadanassa visuṃ katattā sadisatte gammamāne ayamubhayabyatireko nāma. Nānā anekappakārānaṃ [M 0.0244] bhāvoti ca, sādhu vuttamiti ca, tameva amatanti ca, taṃ sammā deti sīlenāti ca vākyaṃ.

248. ‘Muninda,’ and so on. The distinction between these two—the face of the Lord of Sages and the lotus—is such. If it is asked how, of these two, the face bestows the nectar of well-spoken words; because it is well-spoken, it is the giver of the nectar of the true Dhamma, reckoned as well-spoken. But the lotus is not like this; it does not give such nectar of the Dhamma—this is the meaning. By the statement ‘their distinction is such,’ it is implied that there is no difference between the two in terms of qualities like fragrance and beauty. Having revealed that, then, in the latter part, because the face is distinguished from the lotus, and the lotus from the face, while similarity is implied, this is called ‘mutual exclusion.’ The phrases are: ‘nānā’ is the state of being of many kinds; ‘sādhu vuttaṃ’ is well-spoken; ‘that very nectar’; and ‘it rightly gives through virtue.’

249.

249.

Pasiddhaṃ kāraṇaṃ yattha, nivattetvā’ññakāraṇaṃ;

Sābhāvikatta’matha vā, vibhābyaṃ sā vibhāvanā.

Where a well-known cause is set aside and another cause is present, or where naturalness is to be discerned, that is vibhāvanā.

249. Vibhāvanaṃ sambhāveti “pasiddha”miccādinā. Yattha alaṅkatiyaṃ pasiddhaṃ lokappatītaṃ kāraṇaṃ kiñci nivattetvā nirasya aññaṃ kāraṇaṃ pasiddhakāraṇato aññaṃ nimittaṃ vibhābyaṃ avagamyate. Yattha kāraṇantaraṃ natthi, tattha kā gatīti āha “sābhāvikatta”ntiādi. Atha vā pakkhantare, sābhāvikaṃ sābhāvikattaṃ (ka.) dhammatāsiddhaṃ, tassa bhāvo sābhāvikattaṃ vibhābyaṃ, sā tādisī vibhāvanā viññeyyā, vibhāvīyate pakāsīyate kāraṇantaraṃ sābhāvikattaṃ vā etāyāti, etissanti vā katvā.

249. He explains vibhāvanā with ‘well-known,’ etc. Where, in a figure of speech, some well-known and worldly accepted cause, having been set aside and rejected, another cause—a different sign from the well-known cause—is to be understood. Where there is no other cause, what is the course? He says, ‘naturalness,’ etc. Or, in another case, naturalness, established by the nature of things—its state is naturalness—is to be discerned. Such a vibhāvanā is to be understood, thinking, ‘by this vibhāvanā another cause or naturalness is manifested or illuminated,’ or ‘in this vibhāvanā.’

249. Idāni vibhāvanaṃ dasseti “pasiddha”miccādinā. Yattha alaṅkāre pasiddhaṃ lokappatītaṃ kāraṇaṃ taṃtaṃguṇasādhanahetuṃ nivattetvā paṭisedhetvā aññakāraṇaṃ lokappasiddhakāraṇato aññaṃ kāraṇaṃ, atha vā no ce pasiddhakāraṇato aññakāraṇe labbhamāne sābhāvikattaṃ dhammatāsiddhaguṇaṃ vibhābyaṃ pakāsanīyaṃ hoti, sā vibhāvanā nāma hoti, kāraṇantaravibhāvanā sābhāvikavibhāvanāti duvidhā hotīti adhippāyo. Aññañca taṃ kāraṇañceti ca, sassa attano bhāvoti ca, tena sambhūtamiti ca, tassa bhāvoti ca, vibhāvīyati aññakāraṇaṃ sābhāvikattaṃ vā etāya vibhāvanāya, etissaṃ vibhāvanāyanti ca vāti viggaho.

249. Now, he explains vibhāvanā with ‘well-known,’ etc. Where, in a figure of speech, a well-known cause, accepted by the world, which is the means for establishing various qualities, is set aside and rejected, and another cause—a cause different from the well-known cause accepted by the world—is introduced; or if, when another cause is not found apart from the well-known cause, naturalness, a quality established by the nature of things, is to be discerned and manifested, that is called vibhāvanā. The meaning is that it is of two kinds: vibhāvanā of an alternative cause and vibhāvanā of naturalness. The analysis is: ‘and that other cause’; and ‘its own state’; and ‘produced by that’; and ‘its state’; and ‘another cause or naturalness is manifested by this vibhāvanā,’ or ‘in this vibhāvanā.’

Kāraṇantaravibhāvanā

The Exposition of an Alternative Cause

250.

250.

Anañjitā’sitaṃ [M 0.0245] nettaṃ, adharo rañjitā’ruṇo;

Samānatā bhamu cā’yaṃ, jinā’nāvañchitā tava.

O Conqueror, your eye is dark, though unadorned; your lower lip is red, though unrouged; and this brow of yours is perfectly arched, though unshaped.

250. Udāharati “anañjita”iccādi. Jina tava nettañca anañjitaṃ añjanasalākāya yavataṭṭhīnamaphuṭṭhameva asitaṃ kaṇhaṃ, adharo ca anañjitoyeva lākhārāgādinā aruṇo ratto, ayaṃ bhamu ca anāvañchitā ussāhena yena kenaci anāmitā samānā samānatā suṭṭhu ānatā, tato sabbaṃ lokiyaṃ taveti. Ettha pasiddhakāraṇamañjanādi, tannivattanepi kāraṇantaramatthādināvagamyate, tañca kammaṃ, kāriyassa akāraṇattāyogatoti kāraṇantaravibhāvanā’yaṃ.

250. He illustrates with ‘unadorned,’ etc. O Conqueror, your eye is unadorned—untouched even by a kohl-stick—and yet it is dark, black. And your lower lip, unadorned by lac-dye and so on, is red. And this brow of yours, unshaped by any effort, is even and beautifully arched. Therefore, all worldly beauty is yours. Here, the well-known cause, such as kohl, is negated; even with its negation, another cause is understood through implication, and that is kamma. Because an effect cannot be without a cause, this is an exposition of an alternative cause.

250. Idāni udāharati “anañji”ccādinā. He jina tava nettaṃ pakatimadhuraṃ nayanayugaḷañca anañjitaṃ vilocanānaṃ kaṇhattasādhanatthaṃ lokappasiddhaañjanehi anañjitaṃ samānaṃ asitaṃ bhavantarasiddhena kusalakammena nīlaṃ hoti, adharo ca arañjito kenaci rāgena arañjito samāno aruṇo rattohoti, ayaṃ bhamu ca anāvañchitā kenaci vāyāmena anāmitā samānā samānatā suṭṭhu ānatā hotīti. Ettha nayanaadharabhamūnaṃ kaṇharattakuṭilaguṇasādhane lokappasiddhāni añjanāni kāraṇāni paṭisedhetvā nettādīnaṃ asitādibhāvakathaneneva kāraṇavinimuttassa kāriyassa loke avijjamānattā atthappakaraṇādinā asitādibhāvassa kāraṇaṃ nāma pubbajātiyaṃ siddhakusalakammamevāti patīyamānattā ayaṃ kāraṇantaravibhāvanā nāma. Na añjitanti ca, na rañjitoti ca, na āvañchitoti ca vākyaṃ. Nasaddo pasajjapaṭisedhe vattate. Saṃ sammā ānatāti viggaho.

250. Now he illustrates with ‘unadorned,’ etc. O Conqueror, your eye is naturally sweet, and the pair of eyes, unadorned by the world-renowned collyriums used to darken the pupils, being unadorned, appears dark blue due to skillful deeds accomplished in past existences. And the lower lip, unrouged by any dye, being unrouged, appears crimson red. And this brow, unbent by any effort, remaining even, is beautifully arched. Here, by refuting the world-renowned collyriums that are causes for producing the dark, red, and curved qualities of the eyes, lower lip, and brows, and by merely stating the dark and other qualities of the eye and so on, it is implied that since an effect without a cause does not exist in the world, the cause for these dark and other qualities is indeed the skillful deeds accomplished in previous births, as understood from the context. This is called the exposition of an alternative cause. The phrases ‘na añjitaṃ’ (unadorned), ‘na rañjitaṃ’ (unrouged), and ‘na āvañchitaṃ’ (unbent) are used. The word ‘na’ (not) is used in the sense of absolute negation. The analysis of ‘samānatā’ is ‘sammā ānatā’ (perfectly arched).

Sābhāvikavibhāvanā

The Exposition of Naturalness

251.

251.

Na [M 0.0246] hoti khalu dujjanya-

Mapi dujjanasaṅgame;

Sabhāvanimmalatare,

Sādhujantūna cetasi.

Truly, wickedness does not arise, even in the company of the wicked, in the naturally very pure mind of good beings.

251. “Na hoti”ccādi. Dujjanehi saha saṅgame samāgame satyapi sādhujantūnaṃ sappurisānaṃ sabhāvena tādisena payogena vināva nimmalatare atisayena nimmale cetasi dujjanyaṃ sujanetarabhāvo na hoti tādisātisayasādhuttasamāyogatoti. Iha kiñcāpi sabhāvasaddena sabbathā hetunivattanaṃ kataṃ, tathāpi yonisomanasikārāditathāvidhanimittamattheva. Tathāpi loko tamanapekkhamāno, pasiddhañca kāraṇaṃ tādisamapassanto sābhāvikaṃ phalaṃ voharati, tadanusārena ca sābhāvikaṃ phalaṃ vibhābyateti, ayaṃ sābhāvikaphalavibhāvanā.

251. He illustrates with ‘Does not arise,’ etc. Even when there is association and mingling with wicked people, in the mind of good beings, of noble persons, which is naturally very pure, wickedness—the state of being other than a good person—does not arise, even without a specific effort, because of their endowment with such exceedingly excellent virtue. Here, although by the word ‘natural’ a complete negation of cause is implied, still, such conditions as wise attention and so on do indeed exist. Nevertheless, the world, disregarding that and not seeing such a well-known cause, speaks of a natural result, and in accordance with that, a natural result is to be discerned. This is the exposition of a natural result.

251. “Na hoti”ccādi. Dujjanasaṅgame api dujjanehi saha vāse satipi sādhujantūnaṃ sabhāvanimmalatare kiñci payogaṃ vinā pakatiyā eva atinimmale cetasi dujjanyaṃ dujjanaguṇaṃ khalu ekantena na hotīti. Iha cittanimmalahetubhūtānaṃ yonisomanasikārādīnaṃ vijjamānattepi lokena taṃ kāraṇaṃ anapekkhitvā aññampi pasiddhakāraṇaṃ cittanimmalakāraṇamadisvā sabhāvasiddhaṃ nimmalanti vohariyamānattāteneva lokavohārānusārena “sabhāvanimmalatare”ti sabbākārena kāraṇaṃ paṭisedhaṃ katvā sabhāvasiddhanimmalattasaṅkhātaphalassa pakāsitattā ayaṃ sābhāvikaphalavibhāvanā nāma. Dujjanānaṃ bhāvoti ca, sassa attano bhāvoti ca, tena nimmalataranti ca vākyaṃ.

251. He illustrates with 'does not exist,' and so forth. Even in association with the wicked, even when living with bad people, in the naturally very pure mind of good beings, without any effort, by its very nature exceedingly stainless, wickedness—the quality of the wicked—truly does not exist at all. Here, even though wise attention and other causes of mental purity exist, people disregard those causes and, not seeing another well-known cause for mental purity, declare it to be 'naturally pure.' Therefore, in accordance with worldly convention, by the phrase 'naturally very pure,' having negated cause in every way, the result known as natural purity is revealed. This is called the exposition of natural result. And the phrases are: 'the state of the wicked,' 'one's own state,' and 'thereby purer.'

252.

252.

Janako [M 0.0247] kārako (sī.) ñāpako ceti,

Duvidhā hetavo siyuṃ;

Paṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ tesaṃ,

Alaṅkāratayo’ditaṃ.

Generative and indicative—thus, causes are of two kinds. Their elaboration is declared to be an embellishment.

252. Hetuṃ niddisati “janako”iccādinā. Janako bhāvābhāvarūpassa nibbatyādikāriyassa kārako ñāpako vijjamānasseva kassaci sambandhato kutoci paṭibodhako cāti hetavo duvidhā siyuṃ. Nanu kimettha asanaṃ bhūsanaṃ (?), kevalaṃ “anenetaṃ karīyatī”ti sarūpakathanamatta, na tu (?) viseso tu na na tu (?) koci visesarūpo vācālaṅkāroti visesaṃ yojayati “paṭī”tiādinā. Tesaṃ kāriyuppādayogīnaṃ hetūnaṃ paṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ upabrūhanaṃ visiṭṭhabhāvena pariphuṭaṃ katvā yāthāvato kathanaṃ alaṅkāratāya bandhabhūsanarūpena uditaṃ abhihitaṃ visesarūpattā, na panetenetaṃ karīyatīti.

252. He indicates the cause with 'generative,' and so forth. The generative cause is the agent that brings about an effect, such as the arising of existence or non-existence; and the indicative cause is that which awakens understanding of something already existing through some connection from somewhere—thus, causes are of two kinds. But what is the embellishment here? It is merely a statement of the form, 'By this, that is done,' but there is no particular distinction, no special figure of speech. He connects the distinction with 'thorough,' and so forth. The elaboration—the strengthening and truthful statement, made clear in a distinguished manner—of those causes fit for producing effects, is declared and stated as an embellishment in the form of a binding adornment, because of its distinctive nature; it is not merely that 'by this, that is done.'

252. Idāni hetvālaṅkāraṃ dasseti “janako”ccādinā. Janako ca kassaci “sattā asattā”ti vuttassa bhāvābhāvasaṅkhātakāriyassa janakahetu ca ñāpako ca kassaci vijjamānattaṃ aññena kenaci sambandhena avabodhento ñāpakahetu cāti evaṃ hetavo duvidhā siyuṃ. Iha phalapakāsakahetumhi vuccamāne “iminā hetunā idaṃ phalaṃ jāta”nti sarūpakathanamattaṃ vinā visesarūpālaṅkāro idha natthīti āsaṅkiya alaṅkārasarūpaviseso esoti dassetumaparaddhamāha. Tesaṃ phalapakāsanakhamānaṃ hetūnaṃ paṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ visiṭṭhabhāvena pakāsaṃ katvā tatvato kathanaṃ alaṅkāratāya alaṅkārasabhāvena uditaṃ pasiddhaṃ hoti, kavīhi patthitaṃ vā hoti. Sāliaṅkurādīnaṃ sālibījādayo viya janyassa accantopakārako janakahetu [M 0.0248] nāma, vijjamānaaggiādīnaṃ dhūmādayo viya kassaci vijjamānattañāpako ñāpakahetu nāma. Alaṅkārassa bhāvo alaṅkāratā. Alaṅkāratayāti chandaṃ nissāya mattāhāni.

252. Now he shows the embellishment of cause with 'generative,' and so forth. The generative cause is the cause of an effect, designated as existence or non-existence, spoken of as 'being or non-being'; and the indicative cause is that which makes known the existence of something through some connection with another. Thus, causes are of two kinds. Here, when a cause that reveals an effect is spoken of, one might suspect that there is no special embellishment apart from the mere statement, 'by this cause, this effect arose.' To show that this is a special form of embellishment, he states the second half of the verse. The elaboration of those causes capable of revealing effects—revealing them in a distinguished manner and stating them truthfully—is declared or known as an embellishment by its very nature as an ornament, or it is desired by poets. Just as rice seeds and so forth are the generative cause that is of extreme benefit to what is generated, like rice sprouts, so smoke and so forth are the indicative cause that makes known the existence of something, like an existing fire. The state of an embellishment is ornamentation. The form `alaṅkāratayā` involves the loss of a mora due to metrical requirements.

253.

253.

Bhāvābhāvakiccavasā,

Cittahetuvasāpi ca;

Bhedā’nantā idaṃ tesaṃ,

Mukhamattanidassanaṃ.

By the power of the functions of existence and non-existence, and also by the power of wonderful causes, their distinctions are endless. This is merely an introductory indication of them.

253. Udāharati “bhāva”iccādi. Bhāvo sattā ca, abhāvo asattā ca, teyeva kiccāni tesaṃ vasena ca, cittā pasiddhahetuviparītā acchariyārahā hetavo tesaṃ vasenāpi ca bhedā hetuvikappā anantā anavaviyo anavadhayo (?), yato evaṃ tasmā tesaṃ hetūnaṃ idaṃ mukhamattanidassanaṃ, tasmā tammukhena sakkā hetuvisese pavisitunti.

253. He illustrates with 'existence,' and so forth. Existence is being, and non-existence is non-being; by the power of these functions, and also by the power of wonderful causes—which are contrary to well-known causes and worthy of admiration—the distinctions, the varieties of causes, are endless, without limit. Since this is so, this is merely an introductory indication of those causes. Therefore, through that introduction, one can enter into the specific distinctions of causes.

253. “Bhāvā”iccādi. Bhāvābhāvakiccavasā bhāvaabhāvasaṅkhatasattāasattākriyāvasena ca, cittahetuvasāpi ca pasiddhahetuno viruddhena acchariyahetūnaṃ pabhedena ca, bhedā hetuvisesā anantā yasmā apariyantā honti, tasmā idaṃ vakkhamānaṃ tesaṃ hetūnaṃ mukhamattanidassanaṃ avasesahetūnaṃ ogāhaṇadvāramattassa nidassanaṃ hoti. Bhāvo ca abhāvo cāti ca, teyeva kiccānīti ca, tesaṃ vaso bhedoti ca, cittā vicittā ca te hetavo cāti ca, tesaṃ vasoti ca, mukhameva mukhamattaṃ, mukhañca taṃ vā mattaṃ sāmaññañceti ca, tassa nidassanamiti ca vākyaṃ. Mattasaddo avadhāraṇe sāmaññe vā vattate.

253. He illustrates with 'existence,' and so forth. By the power of the function of existence and non-existence—that is, by the power of the action designated as being and non-being—and also by the power of wonderful causes—that is, by the variety of amazing causes contrary to well-known causes—the distinctions, the specific causes, are endless because they are boundless. Therefore, this which is about to be said is an introductory indication of those causes; it is an indication of a mere doorway for entering into the remaining causes. The phrases are: 'existence and non-existence,' and 'these very things are the functions,' and 'their power is distinction,' and 'they are wonderful and diverse causes,' and 'their power,' and 'the introduction itself is a mere introduction,' or 'it is an introduction and it is mere or general,' and 'the indication of that.' The word 'matta' is used in the sense of limitation or generality.

254.

254.

Paramatthapakāseka-

[M 0.0249] Rasā sabbamanoharā;

Munino desanā’yaṃ me,

Kāmaṃ toseti mānasaṃ.

Having the single essence of manifesting ultimate truth, all-captivating, this teaching of the Sage greatly satisfies my mind.

Bhāvakicco kārakahetu.

The operative cause whose function is existence.

254. Udāharati “paramattha”iccādi. Paramatthasabhāvassa nāmarūpādino pakāsoyeva ekaraso asahāyakiccaṃ yassā sā tādisī. Sabbesaṃ mano haratīti sabbamanoharā munino ayaṃ desanā me mānasaṃ cittaṃ kāmamekantena tosetīti ayaṃ bhāvakicco kārakahetu santosasattāya kāraṇato.

254. He illustrates with 'ultimate truth,' and so forth. She (the teaching) is such that her single essence, her unassisted function, is the very manifestation of the nature of ultimate reality, such as name-and-form. 'It captivates the minds of all,' thus it is 'all-captivating.' 'This teaching of the Sage greatly and completely satisfies my mind'—this is an operative cause with the function of existence, as it is the reason for the existence of contentment.

254. Idāni udāharati “paramattha”iccādinā. Paramatthapakāsekarasā nāmarūpakhandhaāyatanādiuttamatthānaṃ pakāsanasaṅkhāta asahāyakiccavatī sabbamanoharā vohārānurūpena visayabhāvūpagamanena sabbesaṃ manoharā munino ayaṃ desanā me mayhaṃ mānasaṃ kāmaṃ ekantena tosetīti. Buddhassa dhammadesanā pubbe avijjamānassa santosassa sattāsaṅkhātasamuppādaṃ karotīti kārakahetu nāma hoti. Sā ca desanā “mānasaṃ tosetī”ti ettakena adassetvā “paramatthapakāsekarasā”ti savisesanaṃ katvā vuttattā alaṅkāroti abhimatā. Eko ca so raso ceti ca, paramatthapakāsoyeva ekaraso ekakiccamasseti ca viggaho. Bhāvakicco bhāvasaṅkhātaṃ sattākiccaṃ katvā pavatto kārakahetu janakahetu.

254. Now he illustrates with 'ultimate truth,' and so forth. 'This teaching of the Sage, whose sole essence is the revelation of the ultimate truth'—that is, possessing the unassisted function designated as the revelation of the highest realities such as name-and-matter, aggregates, and sense bases—'all-captivating'—that is, captivating the minds of all by becoming an object of experience in accordance with convention—'greatly and completely satisfies my mind.' The Buddha’s teaching of the Dhamma brings about the arising, designated as existence, of a contentment that was previously non-existent; thus, it is called an operative cause. And that teaching is considered an embellishment because it is stated with the qualification 'whose sole essence is the revelation of the ultimate truth,' not merely by stating 'it satisfies the mind.' The analysis is: 'and it is one essence,' and 'the revelation of the ultimate truth is its single essence, its single function.' The operative cause with the function of existence is a generative cause, which proceeds by performing the function of being, designated as existence.

255.

255.

Dhīrehi saha saṃvāsā, saddhammassā’bhiyogato;

Niggaheni’ndriyānañca, dukkhassu’pasamo siyā.

Through association with the wise, through application to the true Dhamma, and through restraint of the senses, the calming of suffering may come to be.

Abhāvakicco kārakahetu.

The operative cause whose function is non-being.

255. “Dhīrehi”ccādi. [M 0.0250] Dhīrehi sappaññehi saha saṃvāsā saṃsaggena ca, saddhammassa sambuddhadesitassa abhiyogato abhyāsena ca, indriyānaṃ cakkhādīnaṃ niggahena visayappavattinirodharūpena vijayena ca hetunā dukkhassa pañcakkhandhasaṅkhatassa anuppādanirodhasaṅkhāto upasamo siyā bhaveyyāti ayaṃ abhāvakicco kārakahetu anuppādanirodhasaṅkhātassa abhāvassa kāraṇato.

255. 'With the wise,' and so forth. Through association and companionship with the wise, the discerning; through application to and practice of the true Dhamma taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One; and through the restraint of the senses, such as the eye—a victory in the form of preventing their engagement with objects—by these causes, may there be the calming of suffering, designated as the five aggregates, a calming designated as non-arising and cessation. This is an operative cause whose function is non-being, because it is the cause of non-existence, which is designated as non-arising and cessation.

255. “Dhīrehi”ccādi. Dhīrehi saha saṃvāsā samaggavāsena ca, saddhammassa buddhadesitassa abhiyogato nirantarābhyāsena ca, indriyānaṃ cakkhuādīnaṃ niggahena rūpādiārammaṇesu subhādiggahaṇassa nivāraṇena cāti imehi kāraṇehi dukkhassa khandhāyatanādikassa upasamo anuppādanirodho khandhaparinibbānaṃ vā siyāti. Abhiṇhaso yogoti viggaho. Abhāvakicco dukkhassa upasamasaṅkhātaṃ asattākiccaṃ katvā pavatto kārakahetu avijjamānasaṅkhātāya asattāya uppādanato janakahetu nāma. Abhāvo kiccamasseti ca, kārako ca so hetu cāti ca vākyaṃ. Bhāvakiccopi vuttabyatirekato ñāyati.

255. 'With the wise,' and so on. Through association with the wise and living in harmony, through devotion to and constant practice of the true Dhamma taught by the Buddha, and through restraint of the senses—preventing the grasping of the beautiful and so on in objects such as forms—by these causes, there may be the stilling of suffering, of the aggregates, sense-bases, and so on, the non-arising cessation, or the complete quenching of the aggregates. The analysis is 'frequent practice.' The operative cause whose function is non-existence, having performed the function of non-existence designated as the stilling of suffering, proceeds; because it produces a non-existence designated as non-being, it is called the generative cause. And the statements are: 'non-existence is its function,' and 'it is an operative cause.' The operative cause whose function is existence is also understood by way of contrast to what has been stated.

256.

256.

Muninda candasaṃvādi-kantabhāvopasobhinā;

Mukheneva subodhaṃ te, manaṃ pāpābhinissaṭaṃ.

O Chief of Sages, by your face, adorned with a charming beauty that rivals the moon, your mind, freed from evil, is easily understood.

Bhāvakicco ñāpakahetu.

The indicator cause whose function is existence.

256. “Munindi”ccādi. Munindeti āmantanaṃ. Te tava candasaṃvādinā candasadisena kantabhāvena upasobhinā sobhamānena mukheneva pāpehi rāgādīhi abhinissaṭaṃ byapagataṃ manaṃ cittaṃ subodhaṃ suṭṭhu viññāyatīti ayaṃ bhāvakicco ñāpakahetu avabodhasattāya ñāpanato.

256. 'O Chief of Sages,' and so on. 'O Chief of Sages' is a vocative. By your face, which is adorned with a charming beauty resembling the moon and shines with a moon-like loveliness, your mind—your consciousness, which has departed and gone forth from evils such as lust—is easily and well understood. This is an indicator cause whose function is existence, because it makes known the state of understanding.

256. “Muninda”iccādi. He muninda te tava candasaṃvādikantabhāvopasobhinā candakantabhāvasadisena kantabhāvena sobhamānena mukhena manaṃ tuyhaṃ cittaṃ pāpābhinissaṭaṃ rāgādīhi kilesehi nikkhantanti subodhaṃ suṭṭhu viññāyatīti. Iha mukhaṃ manakantabhāvasambandhena samannāgataṃ sayaṃ vijjamānameva kilesāpagamassa avabodhasattaṃ ñāpetīti bhāvakicco ñāpakahetu nāma jāto. Candena abhedopacārato candalāvaṇyena saṃvādī sadisoti ca, so ca so kantabhāvo ceti ca, tena upasobhitoti ca, pāpehi abhinissaṭanti ca vākyaṃ.

256. 'O Chief of Sages,' and so on. O Chief of Sages, your mind—your consciousness—which has gone forth from defilements such as lust and is thoroughly released from evil, is clearly and well understood because of your face, which shines with a charming beauty resembling the moon's loveliness. Here, the face itself, being naturally present and endowed with a beauty that captivates the mind, makes known the state of understanding the removal of defilements; thus, it becomes what is called an indicator cause whose function is existence. And the phrases are analyzed as: 'similar to the moon's loveliness due to a metaphorical identification with the moon,' and 'that very captivating beauty,' and 'adorned by it,' and 'thoroughly released from evil.'

257.

257.

Sādhuhatthāravindāni, saṅkocayatite kathaṃ;

Muninda caraṇadvanda-rāgabālātapo phusaṃ.

O Chief of Sages, how does the tender warmth of passion for your pair of feet, touching the lotus-like hands of the virtuous, cause them to close?

Ayuttakārī cittahetu.

The remarkable cause that performs what is unfitting.

257. “Sādhu”iccādi. Muninda te caraṇānaṃ dvandassa rāgo bālo ca so ātapo ceti rāgabālātapo taruṇakiraṇasamūho lohitattādinā sādhūnaṃ hatthāravindāni kantādinā phusaṃ visārittenā’masanto kathaṃ saṅkocayati makulayati, añjalipaṇāmabandhena ayuttametaṃ. Bālātapo hi padumānamummīlanahetu, ayaṃ tu apubbo bālātapo yo padumāni nimīletīti anucitakāriyakāraṇā ayuttakārī cittahetu, evaṃvidho viññeyyo bhāvakiccattepīti.

257. 'Virtuous,' and so on. O Chief of Sages, the tender warmth of passion for your pair of feet—which is analyzed as passion and tender warmth, a mass of young rays due to its redness—touching and caressing the lotus-like hands of the virtuous with its pervasive charm, how does it cause them to close and bud into the gesture of joined palms in homage? This is unfitting. For tender warmth is indeed the cause of lotuses opening, but this is an unprecedented tender warmth that causes lotuses to close; thus, because it causes an inappropriate action, it is a remarkable cause that performs what is unfitting. Such is to be understood, even while it is a cause whose function is existence.

257. “Sādhu”iccādi. He muninda te tava caraṇadvandarāgabālātapo pādayugaḷassa aruṇavaṇṇasaṅkhataabhinavasūriyakiraṇo sādhuhatthāravindāni sujanānaṃ karapadumāni phusaṃ attano sabbabyāpittā phusanto kathaṃ saṅkocayati karasampuṭarūpena makulayatīti. Bālātapo nāma padumavikasanaṃ vinā saṅkocanaṃ na karoti, eso ātapo acchariyo vicittoti gamyamānattā ayuttasaṅkocasattākaraṇato ayaṃ ayuttakārī cittahetu [M 0.0252] nāma. Ayuttaṃ karotīti ca, cittañca taṃ hetu cāti ca vākyaṃ.

257. 'Virtuous,' and so on. O Chief of Sages, how does the tender warmth of passion for your pair of feet—that is, the crimson-colored rays of the newly risen sun upon your pair of feet—touching the lotus-like hands of good people, caressing them with its all-pervasiveness, cause them to close in the form of cupped hands, making them into buds? Tender warmth, indeed, does not cause lotuses to close without their blooming; since this warmth is understood to be wondrous and varied, and because it brings about an unfitting state of closing, this is called a remarkable cause that performs what is unfitting. And the phrases are analyzed as: 'it performs what is unfitting,' and 'it is a remarkable cause.'

258.

258.

Saṅkocayanti jantūnaṃ, pāṇipaṅkeruhāni’ha;

Munindacaraṇadvanda-nakhacandāna’maṃsavo.

Here, the rays of the moon-like nails of the Chief of Sages' pair of feet cause the lotus-like hands of beings to close.

Yuttakārī cittahetu.

The remarkable cause that performs what is fitting.

258. “Saṅkocayanti”ccādi. Munindassa pādānaṃ dvande nakhā eva candā kantādinā tesaṃ aṃsavo kiraṇā iha loke jantūnaṃ sattānaṃ pāṇayo eva paṅkeruhāni kantādinā saṅkocayanti paṇāmakaraṇasampuṭarūpena milīyantīti milāyayantīti (?) yuttakārī cittahetu candato paṅkajasaṅkocassa ucitattā. Vuttanayepīti.

258. 'They cause to close,' and so on. On the pair of feet of the Chief of Sages, the nails are indeed moons due to their charm, and their rays—their beams—in this world cause the hands of beings, which are indeed lotuses due to their charm, to close, folding into the form of cupped hands for making homage. This is a remarkable cause that performs what is fitting, because it is appropriate for lotuses to close due to the moon. This is also in accordance with the method stated.

258. “Saṅko”iccādi. Munindacaraṇadvandanakhacandānaṃ sambuddhassa pādadvande nakhāvalisaṅkhātānaṃ candānaṃ aṃsavo raṃsayo iha loke jantūnaṃ pāṇipaṅkeruhāni saṅkocayanti karasampuṭākārena saṅkocayanti makulaṃ karontīti. Candakiraṇehi kattabbāya eva padumasaṅkocasattāya katattā ca, pakaticandakiraṇakattabbakiccassa candamarīcisamānaaññādiṭṭhapubbavicitraaṃsūhi katattā ca ayaṃ yuttakārī cittahetu nāma. Pāṇayo ca te paṅkeruhāni ceti ca, munindassa caraṇadvandamiti ca, tasmiṃ nakhānīti ca, teva candāti ca vākyaṃ.

258. 'Saṅko,' and so on. The rays—the beams—of the moon-like nails, reckoned as the row of nails on the Sambuddha's pair of feet, in this world cause the lotus-like hands of beings to close, making them into buds in the shape of cupped hands. And because the state of lotuses closing, which ought to be brought about by moonbeams, is accomplished, and because the function that ought to be performed by ordinary moonbeams is accomplished by these wondrous rays, similar to moonbeams and the likes of which have never been seen before, this is called a remarkable cause that performs what is fitting. And the phrases are analyzed as: 'they are hands and they are lotuses,' and 'the Chief of Sages' pair of feet,' and 'the nails therein,' and 'they are indeed moons.'

259.

259.

Uddiṭṭhānaṃ padatthānaṃ, anuddeso anudeso (?) yathākkamaṃ;

Saṅkhyāna’miti niddiṭṭhaṃ, yathāsaṅkhyaṃ kamopi ca.

The subsequent statement, in corresponding order, of items previously mentioned, is specified as 'enumeration,' 'in due order,' and also 'sequence.'

259. Kamaṃ vivaritumupakkamati “uddiṭṭhāna”miccādi. Uddiṭṭhānaṃ pubbe vuttānaṃ padatthānaṃ vatthūnaṃ kesañci yathākkamaṃ uddesakkamānatikkamena [M 0.0253] anuddeso puna atthantaraniddesanayena anukathanaṃ kathanaṃ (?) “saṅkhyāna”mityapi ca, “yathāsaṅkhya”mityapi ca niddiṭṭhaṃ vuttaṃ. Vidheyyattā tesaṃ padhānattamiti tadapekkhāya napuṃsakattaṃ, anuvaditabbattānuddesassāppadhānattamiti na pulliṅgapariggaho. “Kamo”iccapi niddiṭṭhoti liṅgavipariṇāmo.

259. He begins to explain 'sequence' with the words 'Of the stated,' and so on. The subsequent statement—a re-narration by way of indicating another meaning—of some previously stated items, in corresponding order and without transgressing the order of the original statement, is specified as 'enumeration' and 'in due order.' Because these terms are the predicate, they are primary, and with reference to them, the neuter gender is used for 'specified' (niddiṭṭhaṃ). Because the subsequent statement (anuddeso) is the subject, it is secondary, hence its masculine gender is not adopted for the verb. 'Sequence' (kamo) is also specified (niddiṭṭho); this is a change of gender.

259. Idāni kamālaṅkāraṃ uddisati “uddiṭṭhāna”miccādinā. Uddiṭṭhānaṃ paṭhamakathitānaṃ padatthānaṃ yathākkamaṃ uddiṭṭhakkamamanatikkamma anuddeso atthantaraṃ nissāya punakathanaṃ “saṅkhyāna”miti ca, “yathāsaṅkhya”miti ca niddiṭṭhaṃ, kamopi ca niddiṭṭho. Ettha pasiddhaṃ anuddesaṃ pubbaddhena anuvaditvā appasiddhaṃ kamampi kamapariyāyaṃ saṅkhyānayathāsaṅkhyadvayampi aparaddhena vidadhāti. Ettha vidhātabbaṃ dassetuṃ anuvādassa āhariyamānattā anuvādo appadhāno, vidhātabbo padhāno. Yañhi vidhātabbaṃ, taṃ padhānaṃ, itaramappadhānanti iminā kāraṇena vuccati. Tasmā “niddiṭṭha”nti “saṅkhyānaṃ, yathāsaṅkhya”nti dvayaṃ apekkhāya (tassa appadhānattā) idaṃ padadvayaṃ sīhaḷabyākhyāyaṃ na dissati napuṃsakaṃ hoti. “Kamo”ti apekkhāya “niddiṭṭho”ti pulliṅgo hoti. Appadhāno anuddesoti nāpekkhati. Kamamanatikkammāti ca, saṅkhyāya anabhikkamoti ca vākyaṃ.

259. Now he indicates the figure of speech 'sequence' (kamālaṅkāra) with the words 'Of the stated,' and so on. The subsequent statement (anuddeso)—a re-narration that relies on another meaning—of items first mentioned, in corresponding order and without transgressing the stated order, is specified as 'enumeration' and 'in due order'; and 'sequence' is also specified. Here, having reiterated the well-known subsequent statement (anuddesa) in the first half-verse, he establishes in the latter half the less-known 'sequence,' its method, and the pair 'enumeration' and 'in due order.' Here, since the subject (anuvāda) is introduced to show the predicate (vidhātabba), the subject is secondary and the predicate is primary. For it is said for this reason: 'What is to be predicated is primary; the other is secondary.' Therefore, 'specified' (niddiṭṭhaṃ) is neuter with reference to the pair 'enumeration' and 'in due order.' With reference to 'sequence' (kamo), 'specified' (niddiṭṭho) is masculine. The secondary subject (anuddeso) is not what the verb agrees with. And the phrases are analyzed as: 'without transgressing the sequence,' and 'without deviating from the enumeration.'

260.

260.

Ālāpahāsalīlāhi, muninda vijayā tava;

Kokilā kumudāni co-pasevante vanaṃ jalaṃ.

O Chief of Sages, your speech, laughter, and graceful movements are victories; cuckoos frequent the forest, and water lilies the water.

260. Tamudāharati “ālāpi”ccādinā. Muninda tava ālāpahāsā ca tesaṃ līlāhi, uddesoyaṃ. Vijayā kokilakumudānaṃ parābhavena kokilā karavīkā kumudāni ca, yathoddesamanuddesoyaṃ vuttāpekkhāya. Vakkhamānāpekkhāya tu ayampi uddesova, “kokilā vanaṃ, kumudāni jala”miti yathoddesamanuddesoyaṃ. Upasevante iva nissayanti maññe. Iti vatthuto eva sambhavo iveti [M 0.0254] parikappate. Yajjevaṃ parikappanāya kathaṃ yathāsaṅkhyanti ce? Atroccate – yatthālaṅkārantaramapi patīyate. Tatthuddesānurūpānuddesasambhave saṅkhyānamevālaṅkāro voharīyate tasseva mukhyato vattumicchitattā. Yatthālaṅkārantaraṃ na gamyate, tattha accantameva kamoti viññeyyaṃ.

260. He cites 'ālāpi' and so forth as an example. O Muninda, your speech and laughter with their grace—this is the uddesa. The victory over the cuckoos and water lilies; the cuckoos, karavīka birds, and water lilies—this is the anuddesa corresponding to the uddesa, in relation to what has been stated. But in relation to what will be stated, this too is an uddesa, and 'the cuckoos to the forest, the water lilies to the water' is the anuddesa corresponding to that uddesa. They seem to attend upon it, as if relying on it, I think. Thus, what is in reality a possibility is imagined with 'as if'. If it is thus by imagination, how then is it yathāsaṅkhya? Here it is said: where another figure of speech is also understood. There, when the anuddesa arises in accordance with the uddesa, the ordering itself is called the figure of speech, because that is what is primarily intended to be expressed. Where no other figure of speech is discerned, there it should be understood as being purely the sequence.

260. Udāharati “ālāpi”ccādinā. He muninda te tava ālāpahāsalīlāhi madhurasaralīlāhi saddhiṃ mandahasitalīlāhi sañjātā vijayā jayahetu kokilā karavīkā ca kumudāni keravāni ca vanaṃ jalañca kamena upasevante iva nissayaṃ karontīti maññeti. Ettha “ālāpahāsalīlāhī”ti uddeso, “kokilā kumudānī”ti vuttāpekkhāya anuddeso, “vanaṃ jala”nti vakkhamānāpekkhāya uddesova hoti, tatvato īdisavijayena kokilādīnaṃ vanādinissayakāraṇābhāvato ivasaddapayogena niddiṭṭho. Evaṃ sati ayaṃ parikappanā na bhavati. Kasmā? Nānālaṅkārasannipāte sati yo yo alaṅkāro vattunā icchito, tasseva mukhyato voharīyamānattā. Evaṃ parikappanālaṅkārasaṃsagge satipi uddesakkamena dassitassa anuddesassa mukhyattā ayaṃ kamālaṅkāro nāma. Īdisaññampi evameva daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ālāpo ca hāso ceti ca, tesaṃ līlāyoti ca viggaho.

260. He illustrates with 'ālāpi' and so forth. O Muninda, it is thought that the victory born from your graceful speech and laughter, along with your graceful sweet sounds and gentle smiles—a victory that is a cause of triumph—makes the cuckoos, karavīka birds, water lilies, and white lotuses gradually seek refuge in the forest and water, as it were. Here, 'ālāpahāsalīlāhi' is the uddesa; 'kokilā kumudāni' is the anuddesa in relation to what has been stated; and 'vanaṃ jalaṃ' is indeed an uddesa in relation to what will be stated. In reality, since such a victory is not a cause for the cuckoos and others to rely on the forest and so forth, this is indicated by the use of the word 'iva'. This being so, this is not the figure of imagination. Why? Because when various figures of speech are combined, whichever figure is intended by the speaker is the one that is primarily expressed. Thus, even when there is a combination with the figure of imagination, because the anuddesa shown in the sequence of the uddesa is primary, this is called the kamālaṅkāra. Other similar instances should also be understood in this way. The analysis is: 'ālāpo ca hāso ca' (speech and laughter), and 'tesaṃ līlāya' (with their grace).

261.

261.

Siyā piyataraṃ nāma, attharūpassa kassaci;

Piyassā’tisayene’kaṃ, yaṃ hoti paṭipādanaṃ.

That presentation of some meaning-form, which is exceedingly dear, may be called 'more beloved'.

261. Piyataramāharati “siyā”iccādinā. Atisayena piyassa kassaci attharūpassa abhidheyyasabhāvassa yaṃ paṭipādanamākhyānaṃ hoti, etaṃ piyataraṃ nāma siyā.

261. He introduces the 'more beloved' with 'siyā' and so forth. That presentation or explanation of the nature of an expressible meaning-form, which is exceedingly dear, may be called 'more beloved'.

261. Idāni [M 0.0255] piyatarālaṅkāraṃ dasseti “siyā”iccādinā, atisayena piyassa kassaci attharūpassa abhidheyyasabhāvassa yaṃ paṭipādanaṃ kathanaṃ hoti, etaṃ paṭipādanaṃ piyataraṃ nāma piyatarālaṅkāro nāma hoti. Atisayena piyanti ca, attho eva rūpaṃ sabhāvoti ca vākyaṃ.

261. Now, he explains the piyatarālaṅkāra with 'siyā' and so forth. That presentation or statement of the nature of an expressible meaning, which is some exceedingly dear meaning-form, that presentation is called 'more beloved' and is called the piyatarālaṅkāra. The analysis is 'atisayena piyaṃ' (exceedingly dear), and 'attho eva rūpaṃ sabhāvo' (the meaning itself is the form, the nature).

262.

262.

Pīti yā me samuppannā, santa sandassanā tava;

Kālenā’yaṃ bhave pīti, taveva puna dassanā.

The joy that has arisen in me, O peaceful one, from seeing you; may this joy arise again in time, from seeing you alone.

262. Udāharati “pīti”ccādi. Santa sappurisa mahāmuni tava sandassanā cakkhupathāpāthamattena madhurakathāsavanā yā pīti me mama samuppannā, ayaṃ pīti kālena īdisena sukhena sukhaṇane (?) taveva nāññassa kassaci, ko hi nāmoñño tavādisoti, puna dassanā bhaveyyāti.

262. He cites 'pīti' and so forth as an example. O peaceful one, noble person, great sage, the joy that has arisen in me from seeing you—merely by your coming into the range of my sight, or from hearing your sweet words—may this joy, in time, with such happiness, arise again from seeing you alone, and not anyone else. For who else, indeed, is like you?

262. “Pīti”ccādi. He santa sappurisa tathāgata tava sandassanā mama nette āpāthagamanato yā pīti me samuppannā, ayaṃ pīti kālena īdisakkhaṇena tayā sadisassa aññassābhāvā taveva puna dassanā dassanato bhaveti. Ettha pītiyā’tisayahetubhūtaṃ atiiṭṭhārammaṇañca dassane atigedhañca pakāsanena atipītīti padatthaṃ atipiyaṃ pībhipadatthaṃ (ka.), pakāsitaṃ hoti. “Ayaṃ pīti bhave”ti pubbakāle uppannapītiyā punāsambhavato taṃsadisāyeva pīti gahitā yathā “soyeva vaṭṭako vaddhako (sī. byākhyāyaṃ), tāniyeva osadhānī”ti.

262. ‘Pīti’ and so forth. O peaceful one, noble person, Tathāgata, the joy that has arisen in me from your coming into the range of my eyes—this joy, at such a moment, due to the absence of another like you, comes to be again only from seeing you. Here, the meaning of the term 'overwhelming joy' is expressed by revealing the exceedingly desirable object, which is the cause of the excess of joy, and the great eagerness for seeing. Regarding 'may this joy arise': since the joy that arose in the past cannot arise again, a joy similar to it is to be understood, just as in 'that very same quail, those very same herbs'.

263.

263.

Vaṇṇiteno’pamānena, vutyā’dhippetavatthuno;

Samāsavutti nāmā’yaṃ, atthasaṅkheparūpato.

When, by means of a praised simile, there is a statement of the intended subject, this is called 'concise expression', due to its nature of summarizing the meaning.

263. Samāsavuttiṃvattumāha “vaṇṇiteni”ccādi. Vaṇṇitena pasaṃsitena upamānena adhippetassa manasi nihitassa vatthuno atthassa vutyā kathanena ayaṃ vuttalakkhaṇā samāsavutti nāma. Kasmā? Atthassa vattumicchitassa saṅkhepo saṅkhipitvā [M 0.0256] kathanaṃ rūpaṃ sabhāvo, tasmā tatoyamanvatthasaññā saṅkhepavutti samāsavuttīti katvā. Kasmā? Ayaṃ guṇībhūtā sakatthā atthantaraṃ vidadhāti, na tu sakatthapadhānā.

263. To explain 'concise expression', he says 'vaṇṇitena' and so forth. This, with the characteristics stated, is called 'concise expression' by means of the statement or explanation of the meaning of the intended subject, placed in the mind, through a praised and esteemed simile. Why? Because its nature is the summary, the brief statement, of the meaning one wishes to convey. Therefore, from that, it has an etymologically fitting name, being called 'brief expression' or 'concise expression'. Why? Because this, its own meaning being subordinate, produces another meaning; it is not one where its own meaning is primary.

263. Idāni samāsavuttiṃ niddisati “vaṇṇite”ccādinā. Vaṇṇitena pasaṃsitena upamānena upamānavatthunā karaṇabhūtena adhippetavatthuno icchitatthassa vutyā kathanena atthasaṅkheparūpato vattumicchitatthassa saṅgaharūpattā ayaṃ yathāvuttalakkhaṇā samāsavutti nāma hoti. Ettha vattumicchitatthaṃ saṅgahetvā manasi katvā tassa upamābhūtatthassa vaṇṇanāya manasi katassa pakāsanato ayaṃ samāsavutti nāma. Etissā padābhihito sakattho appadhāno, gammamānattho pana padhāno hoti. Adhippetañca taṃ vatthu ceti ca, samāsena saṅkhepena vutti kathanamiti ca, saṅkhepoyeva rūpaṃ sarūpanti ca, atthassa saṅkheparūpanti ca viggaho.

263. Now, he defines 'concise expression' with 'vaṇṇite' and so forth. This, with the characteristics as stated, is called 'concise expression' because, by means of a praised and esteemed simile—the subject of comparison serving as the instrument—through the statement or explanation of the intended subject, the desired meaning, it is in the form of a summary of meaning, being a collection of the meaning one wishes to state. Here, having gathered the intended meaning and placed it in the mind, this is called 'concise expression' because it manifests what has been placed in the mind through the description of a meaning that serves as a simile. In this, the literal meaning denoted by the words is secondary, while the implied meaning is primary. The analysis is: 'adhippetañca taṃ vatthu ca' (that intended subject), 'samāsena saṅkhepena vutti kathanaṃ' (concise expression is a brief statement), 'saṅkhepoyeva rūpaṃ sarūpaṃ' (condensation itself is the form, the nature), and 'atthassa saṅkheparūpaṃ' (the form of a summary of meaning).

264.

264.

Sā’yaṃ visesyamattena, bhinnā’bhinnavisesanā;

Attheva aparāpya’tthi, bhinnābhinnavisesanā.

This [concise expression] is of one kind, having common qualifiers, where only the qualified is different. And there is indeed another kind, having both distinct and common qualifiers.

264. Tassā pabhedaṃ dasseti “sāya”miccādinā. Sā ayaṃ samāsavutti yaṃkiñci vatthu sāmaññākārappatītaṃ “īdisamidaṃ nāññathā”ti kutoci byavacchijjate kenaci guṇādinā vavatthāpīyate, taṃ visesyaṃ, tameva mattaṃ visesanabhedabyavacchedato, tena. Bhinnā atulyā avayavadhammassa samudāye vattanato. Abhinnaṃ tulyākāraṃ visesanaṃ yassaṃ sā abhinnavisesanāpi attheva. Aparāpyatthi, na kevalaṃ sāyeva. Kīdisī? Bhinnañca abhinnañca visesanaṃ yassanti bhinnābhinnavisesanā. Visesyaṃ tu bhinnanti.

264. He explains its divisions with 'sāyaṃ' and so forth. When any object whatsoever, understood in a general way, is differentiated from something else by some quality and so forth and thereby determined as 'this is like this, not otherwise', that is the qualified (visesya). By that [qualified] alone, due to the exclusion of difference in the qualifiers. It is 'distinct' (bhinnā), meaning dissimilar, because a property of a part applies to the whole. That which has a common (abhinna), i.e., similar, qualifier is indeed 'having common qualifiers' (abhinnavisesanā). There is also another, not only that one. What kind? That which has both distinct and common qualifiers is 'having distinct-and-common qualifiers' (bhinnābhinnavisesanā). But the qualified is distinct.

264. Idāni tassā samāsavuttiyā bhedaṃ dasseti “sāya”miccādinā. Sā ayaṃ samāsavutti visesyamattena guṇādisadisadhammena [M 0.0257] karaṇabhūtena kenaci upamānavatthunā manasi kataṃ “idaṃ upameyyavatthu īdisa”nti sāmaññāvatthato visuṃ katavisesyena bhinnā visuṃ jātā, tattakena atulyā vā, abhinnavisesanā tulyavisesanayuttā attheva bhinnābhinnavisesanā atulyatulyavisesanayuttā bhinnavisesyayuttā aparāpi atthi. Evaṃ samāsavutti dvidhā hoti. Visesyameva mattamiti ca, avayavena sambhavabhedasabhāvassa samudāyepi pavattattā bhinnāti vuttā. Abhinnāni visesanāni yassamiti ca, bhinnāni ca abhinnāni ceti ca, tāni visesanāni yassamiti ca viggaho.

264. Now, he explains the divisions of this 'concise expression' with 'sāyaṃ' and so forth. This 'concise expression' is 'distinct' (bhinnā), meaning having arisen separately, or dissimilar to that extent, by means of the qualified alone—which is made distinct from the general state by some subject of comparison serving as an instrument, such as a quality or similar characteristic, having mentally considered 'this subject of comparison is like this'. There is the type 'having common qualifiers' (abhinnavisesanā), endowed with similar qualifiers. And there is also another type, 'having distinct-and-common qualifiers' (bhinnābhinnavisesanā), endowed with dissimilar and similar qualifiers, and with a distinct qualified. Thus, 'concise expression' is twofold. The analysis is: 'visesyaṃ eva mattaṃ' (the qualified alone); and it is called 'distinct' (bhinnā) because the nature of having distinct parts also applies to the whole. And 'abhinnāni visesanāni yassaṃ' (that in which there are common qualifiers); and 'bhinnāni ca abhinnāni ca' (both distinct and common); and 'tāni visesanāni yassaṃ' (that in which there are those qualifiers).

Abhinnavisesana

Common Qualifier

265.

265.

Visuddhāmatasandāyī,

Pasattharatanālayo;

Gambhīro cā’ya’mambhodhi,

Puññenā’pādito puññenāsādito (sī.) mayā.

Pure, conveying the deathless, An abode of praised gems; Deep, indeed, is this ocean, Attained by me through merit.

265. Ubhayamudāharati “visuddha”iccādinā. Ayamambhodhi sāgaro puññena cirānucitakusalamūlena hetunā mayā āpādito patto, kīdiso? Visuddhaṃ lokavohārato devāsurānaṃ mathane visenāsammissattā amataṃ pīyūsaṃ sandadātīti visuddhāmatasandāyī, ambhodhi. Visuddhaṃ dosalesenāpyasamphuṭṭhattā accantanimmalaṃ amataṃ maraṇābhāvena amatasaṅkhātaṃ nibbānadhātuṃ sandadāti upadesakabhāvenāti visuddhāmatasandāyī, saddhammo. Pasatthāni niravajjattā ratanāni muttāmaṇiādīni, tesaṃ ālayo pavattiṭṭhānaṃ, ambhodhi. Pasatthāni buddhādīhi anekadhā, vaṇṇitāni ratanāni sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyadhammasaṅkhatāni, tesaṃ ālayo, saddhammo. Gambhīro ca agādhattā sāgaro [M 0.0258] saddhammo ca ayamāpāditoti pakataṃ. Ayaṃ visesyamattabhinnā abhinnavisesanā visesyassa ambhodhino vivacchitā saddhammā bhinnattā, visuddhāmatasandāyittādino ca visesanassa vuttena pakārenābhinnattāti.

265. He exemplifies both with 'pure' and so on. This ocean has been attained by me through merit, the cause being wholesome roots accumulated for a long time. What is it like? The ocean (ambhodhi) is 'pure, conveying the deathless' (visuddhāmatasandāyī) because, according to worldly convention, in the churning by gods and asuras, it bestows nectar unmixed with poison. The true Dhamma is 'pure, conveying the deathless' (visuddhāmatasandāyī) because it bestows the deathless element of Nibbāna—utterly stainless, untouched even by the slightest trace of defilements, and designated as deathless due to the absence of death—by way of instruction. The ocean (ambhodhi) is the abode, the place of origin, for excellent jewels, flawless, such as pearls and gems. The true Dhamma is the abode for the excellent jewels—praised in many ways by the Buddhas and others—which are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. Both the ocean and the true Dhamma are deep and unfathomable, as stated. This is the 'qualifier non-distinct, subject distinct' (abhinnavisesanā visesyamattabhinnā) because the intended Dhamma is distinct from the subject, the ocean, while the qualifier, such as 'pure, conveying the deathless,' is non-distinct in the way stated.

265. Idāni udāharati “visuddhā”iccādinā. Visuddhāmatasandāyī lokavohārato devāsurānaṃ samuddamathane visena amissattā visuddhabhūtapīyūsadāyako, upamābhūtasamuddavaṇṇanāya buddhiyaṃ vattamānassa saddhammassa pakāsanato visuddhāmatasandāyī kāmāmisādidosalavenāpi amissitattā atinimmalaṃ jarāmaraṇarahitaṃ nibbānaṃ upadesadānena veneyyānaṃ dāyako, pasattharatanālayo niddosattā pasatthānaṃ muttāmaṇiādīnaṃ ratanānaṃ pavattiṭṭhānabhūto samuddapakkhe, saddhammapakkhe pana pasattharatanālayo buddhādīhi pasatthānaṃ sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyadhammasaṅkhataratanānaṃ pavattidesabhūto, gambhīro pakatiyāyeva agādho, ekattanayādicatubbidhanayehi gambhīro ayaṃ ambhodhi ca eso samuddo ca, cittena gahitasaddhammo ca puññena bhavantaropacitakusalakammena mayā āpādito pattoti visesyabhūtassa ambhodhino vattumicchitasaddhammato bhinnattā ca, “visuddhāmatasandāyī”ti iccādikānaṃ visesanānaṃ ubhayavisesyepi yathāvuttanayena abhinnattā ca ayaṃ samāsavutti visesyamattena bhinnā abhinnavisesanā hoti.

265. Now he exemplifies with 'pure' and so on. In worldly terms, the ocean is 'pure, conveying the deathless' (visuddhāmatasandāyī) as it is a giver of pure nectar, unmixed with poison during the churning of the ocean by gods and asuras.
