The true Dhamma, revealed through the description of the ocean which serves as a simile, is 'pure, conveying the deathless' because, being unmixed with even a trace of defilements such as sensual pleasures, it bestows upon those to be trained the utterly pure Nibbāna, free from aging and death, by way of instruction. On the side of the ocean, it is an 'abode of praised gems' (pasattharatanālayo) as it is the place of origin for faultless, praised jewels such as pearls and gems. But on the side of the true Dhamma, it is an 'abode of praised gems' as it is the place of origin for the jewels designated as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, praised by the Buddha and others. It is deep and unfathomable by nature; this ocean is deep according to the fourfold method beginning with unity. And the true Dhamma, grasped by the mind, has been attained by me through merit, that is, wholesome kamma accumulated in other existences. And because the subject, the ocean, is distinct from the intended-to-be-spoken-of true Dhamma, and because the qualifiers, such as 'pure, conveying the deathless,' are non-distinct in relation to both subjects in the manner stated, this compound construction is one that is distinct only in its subject, with non-distinct qualifiers.

Bhinnābhinnavisesana

Distinct and Non-Distinct Qualifier

266.

266.

Icchitatthapado sāro,

Phalapupphopasobhito;

Sacchāyo’ya’mapubbova,

Kapparukkho samuṭṭhito.

Giver of desired benefits, excellent, Adorned with fruits and blossoms; With shade, this unprecedented one Has arisen like a wish-fulfilling tree.

266. “Icchite”ccādi. [M 0.0259] Ayamapubbova vuttaguṇayogena acchariyarūpattā kapparukkho samuṭṭhito, kīdiso? Icchitaṃ lokiyaṃ yaṃ kiñci atthaṃ padadātīti icchitatthapado, kapparukkho. Icchitaṃ lokiyalokuttaraṃ yaṃ kiñci atthaṃ padadātīti icchitatthapado, jino. Sāro seṭṭho, kapparukkho jino ca. Phalāni pupphāni, tehi upasobhito, kapparukkho. Saha chāyāya candasūriyālokavilomarūpāya vattate sacchāyo, kapparukkho. Jino tu pubbe vuttāya kāyakantādirūpāya chāyāya yuttoti sacchāyoti. Ayaṃ visesyamattabhinnā bhinnābhinnavisesanā jinato visesyassa kapparukkhassa bhinnattā, phalapupphopasobhitatthassa kapparukkheyeva sambhavā, icchitatthapadatthassa sāratāya sacchāyatāya ubhayattheva bhāvato vuttavidhināti.

266. With 'desired' and so on. This unprecedented one has arisen as a wish-fulfilling tree due to its connection with the stated qualities and its wondrous nature. What is it like? It grants any desired worldly benefit—thus, it is called 'giver of desired benefits' (icchitatthapado), the wish-fulfilling tree. It grants any desired benefit, whether worldly or transcendent—thus, it is called 'giver of desired benefits' (icchitatthapado), the Victor. It is excellent (sāro), the best—both the wish-fulfilling tree and the Victor. Adorned with fruits and flowers—the wish-fulfilling tree. Possessing shade (sacchāyo), it exists with shade that obstructs the light of the moon and sun—the wish-fulfilling tree. But the Victor is endowed with shade in the form of the previously mentioned bodily radiance and so on—thus, he is called 'possessing shade' (sacchāyo). This is a case of distinct subjects only, with distinct and non-distinct qualifiers (visesyamattabhinnā bhinnābhinnavisesanā), because the subject, the wish-fulfilling tree, is distinct from the Victor; because the state of being adorned with fruits and flowers applies only to the wish-fulfilling tree; and because the meanings of 'giver of desired benefits,' 'excellence,' and 'possessing shade' apply to both in the manner described.

266. “Icchitatthi”ccādi. Icchitatthapado sattehi icchitānaṃ lokiyaaviññāṇakavatthābharaṇādīnaṃ dāyako kapparukkhavaṇṇanāya citte patiṭṭhitassa jinapadatthassa kathetukāmatāya icchitatthapado sattehi patthitānaṃ lokiyalokuttarānaṃ sakalatthānaṃ anurūpavasena tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ dāyako, sāro rukkhesu īdisarukkhassābhāvato uttamo, sāro sadevakādisattalokesu tādisasattavisesābhāvato uttamo, phalapupphopasobhito kappaddumānurūpaphalehi pupphehi ca upasobhito, sacchāyo candasūriyālokehi āvaraṇīyarukkhacchāyāya samannāgato, sacchāyo nīlapītādichabbidharaṃsijālehi samannāgato, apubbo pubbe asañjāto ayaṃ kapparukkho eso paccakkho kappapādapo samuṭṭhito sattānaṃ puññānubhāvena loke pātubhūtoti. Vattumicchitatthajinapadatthato visesyassa kapparukkhassa [M 0.0260] bhinnattā ca, icchitatthadānasārabhāvasacchāyasaṅkhatānaṃ visesanānaṃ ubhayasādhāraṇattā ca, phalapupphopasobhitatāya rukkhasseva visesanattā ca ayaṃ samāsavutti visesyabhinnāva bhinnābhinnavisesanā hoti. Icchito ca so attho ceti ca, taṃ padadātīti ca, phalapupphehi upasobhitoti ca, saha chāyāya vattamānoti ca vākyaṃ.

266. With 'desired benefit' and so on. The term 'giver of desired benefits' (icchitatthapado) refers to the giver of desired worldly inanimate objects such as clothes and ornaments, as described for the wish-fulfilling tree. Due to the desire to speak of the meaning of the Victor's state, established in the mind through the description of the wish-fulfilling tree, 'giver of desired benefits' (icchitatthapado) refers to the giver of all benefits, worldly and supramundane, desired by beings, in accordance with their wishes. The excellent one (sāro) is the best among trees due to the absence of such a tree; the excellent one (sāro) is also the best among beings in the world with its gods, due to the absence of such a special being. Adorned with fruits and flowers, it is beautified by fruits and flowers suitable for a wish-fulfilling tree. Possessing shade (sacchāyo), it is endowed with the shade of a tree that can cover the light of the sun and moon; possessing shade (sacchāyo), it is endowed with a net of six-colored rays like blue and yellow. Unprecedented, not arisen before, this wish-fulfilling tree, this visible wish-fulfilling tree, has arisen in the world through the power of beings' merit. Because the subject, the wish-fulfilling tree, is distinct from the intended meaning of the Victor's state, and because the qualifiers—namely being the giver of desired benefits, excellence, and possessing shade—are common to both, and because the adornment with fruits and flowers is a qualifier unique to the tree, this compound construction is distinct in its subject and has distinct and non-distinct qualifiers (visesyabhinnāva bhinnābhinnavisesanā). The phrases are: 'And that desired object,' 'and that which gives it,' 'adorned with fruits and flowers,' and 'existing with shade'.

267.

267.

Sāgarattena saddhammo,

Rukkhatteno’dito jino;

Sabbe sādhāraṇā dhammā,

Pubbatrā’ññatra tu’ttayaṃ.

The true Dhamma is described by its oceanic nature, The Victor is described by his tree-like nature; All qualities are common in the former case, But in the latter, three are common.

267. Tadubhayaṃ vivarati “sāgaratteni”ccādinā. Saddhammo sambuddhabhāsito sāgarattena sāgaraguṇasadisattā sāgararūpena uditoti sambandho, kittitoti attho. Jino rukkhattena yathāvuttanayena udito taṃ patto anupekkhitassa kakkhavuttiyā ambhodhiādisaddānaṃ. Pakaraṇādinā tu tathā patītyudayo, aññathā kathaṃ ambhodhiādisaddānaṃ dhammādisacchāyakattaṃ siyā. Bhedo tu ayaṃ pubbatra “visuddhāmatasandāyi”ccādike sabbe ye keci tatropāttā visuddhāmatasandāyittādayo sādhāraṇā tulyā dhammā visesanāni ubhayatrāpi sambhavā, aññatra tu anantaravutta “icchitatthapado”iccādo pana tayaṃ sādhāraṇaṃ dvayaṃ sādhāraṇañca (ka.), asādhāraṇañca visesanaṃ vuttanayeneti.

267. He explains both with 'by its oceanic nature' and so on. The true Dhamma, spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened One, is 'described' (udito) by its oceanic nature (sāgarattena), that is, in the form of an ocean, because it resembles the qualities of an ocean; this is the connection, meaning it is praised. The Victor is described by his tree-like nature in the manner stated; this meaning is attained by one who disregards the coarse, literal application of words like 'ocean' and so on. However, through context and so on, such an understanding arises. Otherwise, how could words like 'ocean' and so on have the quality of reflecting the Dhamma and so on? The distinction here is this: in the former case, in the example beginning 'pure, conveying the deathless,' all the qualities mentioned there, such as being 'pure, conveying the deathless,' are common and equal distinguishing features, being possible in both cases. However, in the other case, in the immediately preceding example beginning 'giver of desired benefits,' three qualifiers are common, and one is uncommon, as explained.

267. Idāni tehi dvīhi samāsavuttehi vuttatthadvayaṃ pakāseti “sāgari”ccādinā. Sāgarattena sāgararūpena saddhammo sammāsambuddhena desitapariyattisaddhammo udito kathito, rukkhattena jino udito. Sāgarakapparukkhādisaddā attano abhidheyyabhūtasāgararukkhādike atthe mukhyabhāvena [M 0.0261] apavattitvā buddhiyaṃ pavattaatthassāpi sādhāraṇabhūtavisesanapariggahena gammamāne vattumicchitasaddhammajinapadattheyeva pakaraṇādito tādisaatthappatītiyāsambhavato mukhyabhāvena pavattantīti adhippāyo. Tathā hi yadi ete mukhyatthena na pavattanti, ambhodhikapparukkhasaddā saddhammajinapadatthe kathaṃ pakāsentīti tesu dvīsu udāharaṇesu pubbatra “visuddhāmatasandāyī”iccādipubbudāharaṇe sabbe dhammā “visuddhāmatasandāyī”ti sabbe visesanadhammā sādhāraṇā ambhodhisaddhammānaṃ samānā, aññatra tu “icchitatthapado”tiādike aññasmiṃ udāharaṇe pana tayaṃ “icchitatthapado, sāro, sacchāyo”ti visesanattayaṃ sādhāraṇaṃ. Phalapupphopasobhitabhāvo pana rukkhāveṇiko, “apubbo”iccādikaṃ visesanameva. Tathā hi iminā rukkhadhammabhūto koci viseso pakāsito na hotīti visesanattaṃ aññesuyeva vuttaṃ.

267. Now, with these two compound usages, the twofold meaning is shown by 'oceanic' and so on. The true Dhamma, the teaching proclaimed by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, is described by its oceanic nature, by its form as an ocean. The Victor is described by his tree-like nature. The words 'ocean,' 'wish-fulfilling tree,' and so forth, do not primarily function to denote their literal meanings like 'ocean' and 'tree.' Rather, their primary function is to denote the intended meanings of 'true Dhamma' and 'Victor,' because, through the inclusion of common distinguishing features, such an understanding arises from the context and so on, even for meanings present in the mind. The intention is that if these words did not operate primarily in that way, how could words like 'ocean' and 'wish-fulfilling tree' express the meanings of 'true Dhamma' and 'Victor'? In those two examples, in the former example, 'pure, conveying the deathless' and so on, all the qualities, all the distinguishing features, such as 'pure, conveying the deathless,' are common, shared by both the ocean and the true Dhamma. However, in the other example, 'giver of desired benefits' and so on, the three distinguishing features—'giver of desired benefits, excellent, possessing shade'—are common. But the state of being adorned with fruits and flowers is unique to the tree, while 'unprecedented' and so on are merely distinguishing features. Indeed, by this, no particular feature that is a property of the tree is expressed; thus, the quality of being a distinguishing feature is stated only of the others.

268.

268.

Vatthuno’ññappakārena, ṭhitā vutti tadaññathā;

Parikappīyate yattha, sā hoti parikappanā.

Where the state of an object, existing in one way, is conceptualized as otherwise, that is conceptualization.

268. Parikappanaṃ parikappeti “vatthuno”ccādinā. Vatthuno sajīvassa nijjīvassa vā vutti avatthā aññappakārena vattumicchitappakārāpekkhāya aññeneva rūpena ṭhitā, tasseva tato yathāvaṭṭhitappakārato aññathā aññena pakārena parikappīyate yattha vuttiyaṃ, sā parikappanā hoti, parikappīyate aññathā karīyate vatthuṭṭhiti etissanti katvā.

268. Conceptualization is defined by [the phrase] 'of the object,' and so on. The occurrence or state of an object, whether living or non-living, existing in one form—relative to the way one wishes to speak of it—is conceptualized in a way other than its actual state. That is conceptualization, because [the analysis is]: 'the state of the object is conceptualized, that is, made otherwise, by this'.

268. Idāni parikappanaṃ dasseti “vatthuno”iccādinā. Vatthuno yassa kassaci saviññāṇakaaviññāṇakapadatthassa vutti pavatti aññappakārena kappanīyappakārato aññena vijjamānappakārena ṭhitā pavattamānā, tadaññathā [M 0.0262] tato vijjamānappakārato aññenāvijjamānappakārena yattha vuttiyaṃ parikappīyate, sā parikappanā nāma hoti. Parikappīyate aññathā karīyate vatthuṭṭhiti etissamiti viggaho.

268. Now, conceptualization is shown by [the phrase] 'of the object,' and so on. The occurrence or state of any object, whether sentient or insentient, which exists and proceeds in a certain existing manner different from the way it is to be conceptualized, is conceptualized in that occurrence otherwise than that existing manner, in a non-existent manner. That is called conceptualization. The analysis is: 'The state of the object is conceptualized, that is, made otherwise, in this'.

269.

269.

Upamābbhantarattena, kiriyādivasena ca;

Kameno’dāharissāmi, vividhā parikappanā.

By way of simile's inclusion, and by way of action, etc., I shall gradually exemplify the various kinds of conceptualization.

269. Bhedaṃ tassā dasseti “upamā”iccādinā. Upamā abbhantare yassā, tassā bhāvo, tena ca, kiriyādivasena ca vividhā nānappakārā parikappanā idāni kamena udāharissāmi.

269. He shows its divisions by [the phrase] 'simile,' and so on. By the state of having a simile within it, and by way of action, etc., I will now gradually exemplify the various and diverse kinds of conceptualization.

269. Idāni tassa bhedaṃ dasseti “upamābbhantare”ccādinā. Upamābbhantarattena upamāya abbhantare vijjamānattā ca kiriyādivasena ca vividhā parikappanā kamena udāharissāmi. Upamā abbhantare assā parikappanāyeti ca, tassā bhāvoti ca, aneke vidhā pakārā yāsamiti ca viggaho.

269. Now, he shows its divisions by [the phrase] 'within a simile,' and so on. By way of simile's inclusion, that is, by its being present within a simile, and by way of action, etc., I will gradually exemplify the various conceptualizations. The analysis is: 'Simile is within this conceptualization,' and 'the state of that,' and 'those which have many kinds.'

Upamābbhantaraparikappanā

Conceptualization Including a Simile

270.

270.

Icchābhaṅgāturā’sīnā,

Tā’tiniccala’maccharā;

Vasaṃ nentīva dhīraṃ taṃ,

Tadā yogābhiyogato.

Afflicted by the breaking of desire, seated, those extremely motionless nymphs, as if leading that steadfast one under their sway, then through the application of yoga.

270. Udāharati “icchā”iccādi. Icchābhaṅgena “buddhaṃ bhagavantaṃ vase vattessāmā”ti bodhimūle katābhilāsavināsena āturā dukkhitā atiniccalasabhāvappattā atiniccalaṃ nāsikagge nayane katānatāvasena accantamakriyamāsīnā nisinnā tā accharā yoginisaṅkāsā māraṅganāti [M 0.0263] yathāvaṭṭhitāya sacetanānaṃ māraṅganālakkhaṇānaṃ māraṅganāvalakkhaṇānaṃ (ka.) vatthūnaṃ vutti vuttā, sāyamaññathā parikappīyate. Dhīraṃ devaṅganānampi siṅgārabhāvopacaritavilāsātisayenāpi akampattā. Taṃ bhagavantaṃ. Yogo mantānuṭṭhānaṃ, tattha abhiyogato yuñjanena vasamattano āyattabhāvaṃ tadā nentīva vahanti maññeti. Ettha iva saddasutiyā upamāsandeho na kātabbo, savasānayanamakubbantiyo māraṅganā vasaṃ nentīvāti parikappīyante. Hoti ca–

270. He exemplifies with 'desire,' and so on. Tormented and afflicted by the breaking of desire—that is, by the destruction of the wish made at the Bodhi-tree, 'We will bring the Buddha, the Blessed One, under our power'—those nymphs, Māra's daughters, resembling yoginīs, attained a state of extreme motionlessness. They sat extremely still and completely inactive, with their eyes cast down towards the tip of the nose. Thus, the state of the objects, characterized as the sentient Māra's daughters, is stated as it actually was; this is then conceptualized otherwise. 'Steadfast' (dhīraṃ) means unshaken even by the excess of charming gestures performed with amorous intent by celestial nymphs. 'That' (taṃ) refers to the Blessed One. 'Yoga' is the recitation of mantras. 'Through the application' to that, by engaging in it, 'at that time' they seemed to be bringing him 'under their sway,' into their own power. Here, one should not have a doubt that this is a simile just from hearing the word 'iva' (as if), for Māra's daughters, who were not bringing him under their sway, are conceptualized as 'as if bringing him under their sway.' And it is so:

“Vasaṃ nentīva dhīra”nti, nayane no’pamānatā;

Na hi kattukriyāya’tthi, upamānopameyyatāti.

'As if leading the steadfast one under their sway,' in this leading there is no simile. For there is no standard of comparison or object of comparison in the agent's action.

Kriyāparikappattepi ayamupamābbhantarā parikappanā, na kevalakriyāparikappanā māraṅganānamacalopavesanassa yogābhiyogena sāmyasandassanato, tathābhūtāya copavesanakriyāya dhīrassāpi tādisassa bhagavato avasānayanattanti parikappanatoti.

Even though it is a conceptualization of action, this is a conceptualization that includes a simile, not merely a conceptualization of action, because the motionless sitting of Māra's daughters is seen to be similar to the application of yoga, and because it is a conceptualization that such an act of sitting does not bring even such a steadfast one as the Blessed One under their sway.

270. Idāni udāharati “icchā”iccādinā. Icchābhaṅgāturā ajapālanigrodhamūle nisinnaṃ bhagavantaṃ “palobhessāmā”ti māraṅganā attanāyeva katāya icchāya anibbattiyā pīḷitā, atiniccalaṃ hutvā nāsikagge patitadiṭṭhehi samannāgatānaññavuttiyā kriyantaravirahato. Āsīnā jhāyamānā nisinnā tā accharā yoginisadisā taṇhāaratiragāsaṅkhātā māraṅganāyo dhīraṃ siṅgārādhippāyena katānekalīlāvilāsenāpi akampamānaṃ taṃ bhagavantaṃ yogābhiyogato mantajappanasaṅkhātayoge yuñjanena vasaṃ attano vasaṃ tadā attano parājitakāle nentīva pāpenti maññeti. Ettha pubbaddhena māraṅganāsaṅkhātasajīvapadatthānaṃ vijjamānappakāraṃ dassitaṃ. [M 0.0264] Puna aparaddhena tesameva avijjamānayogābhiyogena vasīkaraṇaṃ kappitaṃ. Māraṅganānaṃ niccalanisajjāya yoginīnaṃ mantajjhayanasadisattā māraṅganānaṃ yoginīnaṃ upamānopameyyattaṃ sāmatthiyā gamyateti esā upamābbhantaraparikappanā nāma. “Nenti ivā”ti payoge katepi kriyāparikappanaṃ na hoteva. Icchāya bhaṅgoti ca, tena āturāti ca, niggataṃ calaṃ calanaṃ asmā āsanasmāti ca, atisayena niccalanti ca, kriyāvisesanaṃ, yoge abhiyogoti ca vākyaṃ.

270. Now, he exemplifies with 'desire,' and so on. Māra's daughters, afflicted by the breaking of desire—that is, by the non-fulfillment of the desire they themselves had formed, 'We will tempt the Blessed One seated at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree'—became extremely motionless, endowed with gazes fixed on the tip of their noses, and devoid of any other activity. Seated, meditating—those nymphs, Māra's daughters, known as Craving, Discontent, and Passion, resembling yoginīs—imagined they were bringing that steadfast Blessed One, who was unshaken even by the many alluring gestures and amorous displays made with seductive intent, under their sway, into their own power, at that time of their own defeat, through the application of yoga, that is, by engaging in what is known as mantra recitation. Here, by the first half of the verse, the existing state of the sentient entities known as Māra's daughters is shown. Then, by the latter half, their subduing him through a non-existent application of yoga is conceptualized. Because the motionless sitting of Māra's daughters is similar to the mantra meditation of yoginīs, the status of Māra's daughters and yoginīs as object of comparison and standard of comparison is understood by implication; this is called conceptualization that includes a simile. Even when the phrase 'as if leading' is used, it is not a conceptualization of action. And [the phrases] 'breaking of desire,' and 'tormented by it,' and 'motionless' (meaning 'movement has gone out from this sitting'), and 'exceedingly motionless' are an adverbial qualifier; and 'application in yoga' is a phrase.

“Nenti ivā”ti idha ivasaddasutiyā upamājotanatthaṃ ceti saṃsayo na kātabbo, sādhammasaṅkhātaguṇavisesassa sambandhe asati kriyāmattassa upamābhāvato. Vuttaṃ hi–

Here, in 'as if leading', one should not have the doubt that the word 'iva' is for illuminating a simile just from hearing it, because in the absence of a connection with a specific quality known as a common attribute, it is a simile of mere action. For it was said:

“Vasaṃ nentīva dhīra”nti, nayena no’pamānatā;

Na hi kattukriyāya’tthi, upamānopameyyatāti.

'As if leading the steadfast one under their sway,' in this leading there is no simile. For there is no standard of comparison or object of comparison in the agent's action.

“Vasaṃ nentīva dhīra”nti ettha nayane gamyamāne pāpane upamānatā upamānabhāvo natthi, hi tatheva, kattukriyāya kattusambandhiyā kriyāya upamānopameyyatā upamānabhāvo upameyyabhāvo natthīti ayaṃ hetthattho.

In the phrase 'as if leading the steadfast one under their sway,' when 'leading' is understood as 'causing to reach,' there is no state of being a simile, no state of being a standard of comparison. For, just so, in the action of the agent, that is, in the action related to the agent, there is no state of being a standard of comparison and an object of comparison, no state of being a standard of comparison, and no state of being an object of comparison—this is the meaning here.

Kriyāparikappanā

Conjecture concerning Action

271.

271.

Gajaṃ māro samāruḷho, yuddhāya’ccanta’munnataṃ;

Magga’manvesati nūna, jinabhīto palāyituṃ.

Māra, mounted on an elephant exceedingly lofty for battle, surely seeks a path to flee, terrified of the Conqueror.

271. “Gaja”miccādi. Yuddhāya accantamatisayena unnatamuccaṃ gajaṃ hatthiṃ samāruḷho māro vasavattī taṃ jinātīti atthena jinato bhīto palāyituṃ kiñci nilīyanaṭṭhānaṃ maggaṃ pathaṃ anvesati nūna maññe. Iti kriyāparikappanā ārohanakriyāya maggamanvesanatthanti parikappitattā.

271. “Elephant,” etc. Māra, the Vasavattī, mounted on an elephant exceedingly high and lofty for battle, frightened of the Conqueror—in the sense that the latter conquers him—surely seeks some hiding place or path to flee, I think. Thus, this is the conjecture concerning action, because it is conjectured that the action of mounting is for the purpose of seeking a path.

271. “Gaja”miccādi. [M 0.0265] Yuddhāya yuddhatthaṃ accantaṃ atisayena unnataṃ diyaḍḍhasatayojanāyāmānurūpauccaguṇasamannāgataṃ gajaṃ girimekhalaṃ samāruḷho māro jinā bhīto palāyituṃ maggaṃ nibbhayaṃ pathaṃ anvesati nūna gavesati maññe. Yuddhatthaṃ kurumāno gajārohanaṃ maggānvesanatthamiti kavinā parikappitattā esā kriyāparikappanā nāma. Accantamiti asaṅkhya sasaṅkhyabhāvepi pakaraṇato ādhikke eva vattati.

271. “Elephant,” etc. Māra, having mounted the elephant Girimekhala, which is exceedingly, supremely elevated for battle, possessing qualities befitting a height of one hundred and fifty yojanas, terrified of the Conqueror, surely seeks a safe, fearless path to flee, I think. Because the poet has conjectured that the action of mounting the elephant for battle is for the purpose of seeking a path, this is called the conjecture concerning action. The word “exceedingly” (`accantaṃ`), even when referring to both countable and uncountable states, in this context refers only to excess.

Guṇaparikappanā

Conjecture concerning Quality

272.

272.

Muninda pādadvande te, cārurājīvasundare;

Maññe pāpābhisammadda-jātasoṇena soṇimā.

O Sage-lord, in your pair of feet, beautiful like a lovely lotus, I think the redness is due to the blood arisen from the crushing of evils.

272. Muninda te cāru ca taṃ rājīvaṃ padumañca tamiva sundaraṃ tasmiṃte pādadvande soṇimā lohitattaguṇo, iti yathāvaṭṭhitā acetanassa lohitattalakkhaṇassa vatthuno vutti vuttā, sāyamaññathā parikappīyate. Pāpānaṃ kilesārīnaṃ abhisammaddena atisayaṃ sampisanena jātaṃ soṇaṃ rudhiraṃ, tena jātoti maññe. Iti guṇaparikappanā pādadvandasannihitalohitattaguṇassa “pāpā…pe… soṇene”ti parikappitattā.

272. O Sage-lord, in your pair of feet, which are lovely and beautiful like that lotus, the redness is the quality of being blood-red. Thus, the account of the characteristic of redness, an inanimate thing, is stated as it actually is, but here it is conjectured otherwise. It is from the crushing, the exceedingly thorough grinding, of evils—the enemy defilements—that blood (`soṇaṃ`, i.e., `rudhiraṃ`) arises; 'I think' it is born from that. Thus, this is the conjecture concerning quality, because the quality of redness present in the pair of feet is conjectured as being 'from the crushing of evils... by the blood.'

272. “Muninde”ccādi. He muninda te tava cārurājīvasundare manuññapadumasundare pādadvande soṇimā rattavaṇṇaṃ pāpābhisammaddajātasoṇena maññe saparasantānagatapāpānaṃ sammaddanena jātena rudhirenāti maññe. Sabbaññuno pāde bhavantarasiddhapuññakammānubhāvena jātarattavaṇṇaṃ “pāpābhisammaddanenā”ti parikappitattā ayaṃ guṇaparikappanā nāma. Cāru ca taṃ rājīvañcāti ca, pāpānaṃ abhisammaddoti ca, tena jātañcāti ca, tañca taṃ soṇañcāti ca, soṇassa bhāvoti ca viggaho.

272. “O Sage-lord,” etc. O Sage-lord, in your pair of feet, which are lovely and beautiful like a lotus, delightful and beautiful like a lotus, I think the redness, the red color, is due to the blood arisen from the crushing of evils; that is, I think, by the blood arisen from the crushing of the evils present in one’s own and others’ continuities. Because the red color—arisen on the feet of the All-Knowing One through the power of meritorious actions accomplished in past existences—is conjectured as being ‘due to the crushing of evils,’ this is called the conjecture concerning quality. And the analysis (`viggaho`) is: ‘lovely and that lotus,’ and ‘the crushing of evils,’ and ‘born from that,’ and ‘that which is blood,’ and ‘the state of being red.’

273.

273.

Maññesaṅke [M 0.0266] dhuvaṃ nūna-miva’miccevamādihi;

Sā’yaṃ byañjīyate kvāpi, kvāpi vākyena gamyate.

By words such as ‘I think,’ ‘I suspect,’ ‘certainly,’ ‘surely,’ ‘as if,’ and so on, this conjecture is sometimes expressed, and sometimes understood by a statement.

273. Vohāratthaṃ parikappanāsūcake sadde dassento āha “maññe”iccādi. Iti evarūpo saddarāsi ādi yesaṃ “takkemi, parikappemi, cintayāmi, yathe”tyevamādīnaṃ, tehi sāyaṃ parikappanā kvāpi yathāvutte byañjīyate pakāsīyate, kvāpi katthaci pana vākyena gamyate maññeiccādīnamabhāvepīti.

273. To show the words indicating conjecture for the sake of conventional usage, he says ‘I think,’ etc. Thus, by such a collection of words, of which ‘I infer,’ ‘I conjecture,’ ‘I reflect,’ ‘as if,’ etc., are the beginning, this conjecture is sometimes expressed or revealed as stated; and sometimes, even in the absence of words like ‘I think,’ etc., it is understood somewhere by the sentence.

273. Vohārasukhatthaṃ parikappanāpakāsake sadde dasseti “maññe”ccādinā. Maññe, saṅke, dhuvaṃ, nūna, iva, evamādīhi saddehi sāyaṃ parikappanā kvāpi ettha viya katthaci byañjīyate pakāsīyate, kvāpi katthaci vākyena kriyākārakasambandhasahitapadasamudāyena gamyate ivādisaddayogābhāvepi kevalaṃ vākyasāmatthiyeneva ñāyate. “Maññe”ccādipadapañcakaṃdvandasamāsena niddiṭṭhaṃ. Iti evaṃ pakāro saddasamudāyo ādi yesaṃ “takkemi, parikappemi, cintayāmi, yathā”tiānīnanti viggaho.

273. For the ease of conventional usage, he shows the words that reveal conjecture with ‘I think,’ etc. By words such as ‘I think,’ ‘I suspect,’ ‘certainly,’ ‘surely,’ ‘as if,’ and so on, this conjecture is sometimes expressed or revealed, as here in some place; and sometimes, in some place, it is understood by a sentence—a collection of words together with the relationship of action and agent—and is known merely by the power of the sentence itself, even in the absence of the use of words like ‘as if.’ The five words beginning with ‘I think’ are indicated by a dvandva compound. And the analysis is: ‘Thus, such a collection of words, of which ‘I infer,’ ‘I conjecture,’ ‘I reflect,’ ‘as if,’ etc., are the beginning.’

Gammaparikappanā

Conjecture concerning the Understood

274.

274.

Dayāsañcārasarasā dayāsañjātasarasā (ka.), dehā nikkhantakantiyo;

Pīṇentā jina te sādhu-janaṃ sarasataṃ nayuṃ.

O Conqueror, the rays emanating from your body, sweet with the flow of compassion, delighting the good people, led them to a state of delight.

274. Udāharati “dayā”iccādi. Raso sineho, tena saha vattamāno saraso. Deho. Dayāya karuṇāya sañcāro dukkhitasattavisayā nirantarappavatti, tena saraso, tato. Jina te dehā sarīrato nikkhantakantiyo sādhujanaṃ pīṇentā tappentā tameva janaṃ sarasataṃ sapemataṃ nayuṃ pāpesuṃ, tādisaṃ tathāvidhadehanikkhantakantī naṃ sādhujanaṃ pīṇenti. Gammamānaparikappanāyaṃ yato kantiyo [M 0.0267] laddhasarasasarīrasaṃsaggā sayampi sarasā iva attānaṃ sevamānampi sādhujanaṃ sarasataṃ nentīti gamyate.

274. He illustrates with ‘compassion,’ etc. `Rasa` is affection (`sineho`); existing with that, it is `sarasa`. `Dehā` means from the body. The movement (`sañcāro`) of compassion (`dayā`) and pity (`karuṇā`) is a continuous proceeding towards suffering beings; because of that, it is `sarasa`; from that. O Conqueror, the rays emanating from your body (`sarīrato`), delighting (`pīṇentā`) and satisfying (`tappentā`) the good people, led (`nayuṃ`, `pāpesuṃ`) those very people to a state of delight (`sarasataṃ`), a state of affection (`sapemataṃ`). Such rays emanating from such a body delight the good people. This is an implicit conjecture because it is understood that since the rays have come into contact with a body full of essence, they themselves are as if full of essence and lead the good people who attend to them to a state of delight.

274. Vākyagammaparikappanamudāharati “daye”ccādinā. He jina te dayāsañcārasarasā dukkhitasattavisayāya karuṇāya savisaye nirantarappavattiyā sañjātasnehato dehā sarīrato nikkhantakantiyo dasadisāsu niggatā nīlādichabbaṇṇaraṃsiyo sādhujanaṃ katapuññaṃ uttamajanaṃ pīṇentā sarasataṃsasnehabhāvaṃ pemasahitattaṃ nayuṃ tameva sādhujanaṃ pāpesuṃ. “Sarasataṃ nayu”nti ettha “sādhujana”nti sutasambandhena ñāyati. Karuṇāsinehasommadehasaṃsaggato kantiyo sayampi nissayaguṇato sommabhūtā attānaṃ visayaṃ katvā pavattajanepi muduṃ karontevāti ivādīnaṃ abhāvepi vākyagammaparikappanā. Ettha acetanānaṃ kantivatthūnaṃ janapasādasaṅkhātavatthuṭṭhiti “dayāsañcārasarasā ivā”ti evamādiaññappakārena parikappito. Dayāya sañcāro punappunaṃ pavattīti ca, saha rasena snehena vattamānoti ca, dayāsañcārena sarasoti ca, nikkhantā ca tā kantiyo ceti ca, sādhu ca so jano ceti ca, sarasassa bhāvoti ca vākyaṃ.

274. He illustrates the conjecture implicit in the sentence with ‘compassion,’ etc. O Conqueror, from your body (`dehā`, i.e., `sarīrato`), the rays that emanated—the six-colored rays of blue and so on that went forth in the ten directions, sweet with the flow of compassion, that is, from the affection born from the continuous proceeding of compassion towards suffering beings as its object—delighting the good people, that is, meritorious and excellent people, led (`nayuṃ`, `pāpesuṃ`) those very good people to a state of delight (`sarasataṃ`), a state of affection (`sasnehabhāvaṃ`), a state of being endowed with love (`pemasahitattaṃ`). Here, in the phrase ‘led to a state of delight,’ the object ‘good people’ is known through contextual connection. Because of contact with the gentle body full of compassion and affection, the rays themselves, having become gentle due to the quality of their support, indeed soften even those people who proceed making them their object. Thus, even in the absence of words like ‘as if,’ this is a conjecture implicit in the sentence. Here, the state of the inanimate things, the rays, as the thing known as ‘the pleasing of people’ is conjectured in another way, such as ‘as if sweet with the flow of compassion,’ etc. The analysis is: ‘the repeated proceeding of compassion,’ and ‘existing together with essence, i.e., affection,’ and ‘sweet with the flow of compassion,’ and ‘those rays that have emanated,’ and ‘that person who is good,’ and ‘the state of being sweet.’

275.

275.

Ārabhantassa yaṃ kiñci, kattuṃ puññavasā puna;

Sādhanantaralābho yo, taṃ vadanti samāhitaṃ.

For one who undertakes to do anything, whatever attainment of another means there is, furthermore, by the power of merit, that they call ‘well-established.’

275. Samāhitaṃ samāharati “ārabhantassi”ccādinā. Yaṃ kiñci kāriyaṃ kattuṃ sattubhaṅgādikaṃ ārabhantassa sajjībhūtassa yassa kassaci pumuno puññavasā kusalabalena kāraṇena kusalasāmatthiyena puna sādhyate sādhiyamaneneti sādhanaṃ, tato tameva vā antaramaññaṃ, tassa lābho, aññakāraṇalābhoti attho. Taṃ samāhitaṃ vadanti, samādhānaṃ samāhitaṃ.

275. He explains ‘well-established’ (`samāhitaṃ`) with ‘for one who undertakes,’ etc. For any person who is prepared and undertakes to do any task, such as defeating enemies, by the power of merit—that is, by the strength of wholesome power or by means of wholesome ability—it is furthermore accomplished; that by which it is accomplished is the means (`sādhanaṃ`). Then, the attainment of that very thing, or another means—that is, the attainment of another cause—is the meaning. They call that ‘well-established’; `samāhitaṃ` is `samādhānaṃ` (accomplishment).

275. Idāni [M 0.0268] samāhitālaṅkāraṃ dasseti “ārabha”miccādinā. Yaṃ kiñci amittavijayādikaṃ kattuṃ ārabhantassa yassa puññavasā kusalabalena puna yo sādhanantaralābho tasseva kāriyasiddhiyā upakārakassa aññasādhanassa yo lābho atthi, taṃ kāraṇalābhaṃ samāhitaṃ vadanti tasseva kāriyassa samādhānattā patiṭṭhitattā samāhitaṃ iti kavino kathenti. Sādhyate sādhiyamaneneti ca, tañca taṃ antaramaññañceti ca, tassa lābhoti ca, samādhānamiti ca vākyaṃ.

275. Now he shows the figure of speech ‘well-established’ (samāhita) with ‘undertaking,’ etc. For one who undertakes to do anything, such as conquering enemies, by the power of merit, by the strength of the wholesome, whatever attainment of another means there is again—that is, the attainment of another aid that helps in the success of that very task—that attainment of a cause they call ‘well-established’; the poets declare it ‘well-established’ because that very task is settled and established. And the analysis is: ‘it is accomplished,’ and ‘that by which it is accomplished,’ and ‘that very other means,’ and ‘its attainment,’ and ‘settled.’

276.

276.

Mārāribhaṅgābhimukha-manaso tassa satthuno;

Mahāmahī mahārāvaṃ, ravī’ya’mupakārikā.

For that Teacher whose mind was intent on breaking Māra, the enemy, the great earth roared a mighty roar, as if helping.

276. Udāharati “māra”iccādi. Mārārino mārasattuno bhaṅge abhibhave abhimukhaṃ na parammukhaṃ manaṃ yassa tassa satthuno upakārikā āraddhamārabhaṅgakriyānuggāhikā mahāmahī ayaṃ mahārāvaṃ mārāridussahaṃ mahānādaṃ ravī akāsi. Idha mārāribhañjanaṃ kāriyamāraddhaṃ, tassa puññavaseneva mahīrāvo aparaṃ sādhanaṃ samāpannanti lakkhaṇaṃ yojanīyaṃ.

276. He illustrates with ‘Māra,’ etc. For that Teacher whose mind was intent—not turned away—on the breaking and overpowering of the enemy Māra, this great earth, helping and supporting the undertaken action of breaking Māra, made a mighty roar, a great sound unbearable to the enemy Māra. Here, the breaking of the enemy Māra is the task undertaken, and the characteristic to be applied is that the earth’s roar became another means of accomplishment solely by the power of merit.

276. “Mārāri”ccādi. Mārāribhaṅgābhimukhamanaso mārasaṅkhātassa sattuno maddane abhimukhacittassa tassa satthuno upakārikā āraddhamāravijayassa upatthambhikā ayaṃ mahāmahī mahārāvaṃ mārassa hadayavatthuṃ maddanto maddantī (?) viya sahitumasakkuṇeyyaṃ mahānādaṃ ravī akāsi. Ettha mārabhaṅgajananaṃ satthūhi āraddhakāriyaṃ, tasseva siddhiyā hetubhūtaṃ aññakāraṇaṃ nāma mahīrāvo. Māro eva ari sattūti ca, tassa bhaṅgoti ca, tasmiṃ abhimukhaṃ manaṃ yasseti ca, mahantī ca sā mahī ceti ca viggaho.

276. “Māra, the enemy,” etc. For that Teacher whose mind was intent on shattering Māra, the enemy, whose mind was directed towards crushing the foe called Māra, this great earth, aiding and supporting the undertaken victory over Māra, made a mighty roar, a great sound unbearable as if crushing Māra’s heart. Here, the generation of Māra’s breaking is the task undertaken by the Teacher, and the earth’s roar is another cause that serves as a reason for its success. And the analysis is: ‘Māra is indeed the enemy,’ and ‘his breaking,’ and ‘whose mind is intent on that,’ and ‘great, and that earth.’

277.

277.

Avatvā’bhimataṃ [M 0.0269] tassa, siddhiyā dassana’ññathā;

Vadanti taṃ pariyāya-vuttīti sucibuddhayo.

Not stating the intended meaning, but showing it otherwise for its accomplishment—that, those of pure wisdom call 'circumlocution'.

277. Pariyāyavuttiṃ paṭipādeti “avatvā”iccādinā. Abhimataṃ kiñci atthaṃ dhanadānādilakkhaṇaṃ avatvā añjasā vācakabyāpārena anākhyāya tassābhimatassatthassa siddhiyā nipphādanatthaṃ aññathā aññena pakārena tannibbattianuguṇena yaṃ dassanaṃ vacanaṃ, taṃ sucibuddhayo pariyāyavuttīti vadanti. Pariyāyena vacanaṃ pariyāyavuttīti.

277. He explains circumlocution with 'Not stating,' etc. Without stating some intended meaning, characterized by the giving of wealth and so on, and without declaring it directly through the function of speech, for the purpose of accomplishing that intended meaning, whatever showing or speech is made in another way, in a manner conducive to its realization—that, those of pure wisdom call 'circumlocution.' Speech by a circuitous route is circumlocution.

277. Idāni pariyāyavuttiṃ dasseti “avatvā”iccādinā. Abhimataṃ iṭṭhaṃ dhanadānādisarūpaṃ dhanadhaññādiṃ (sīhaḷabyākhyāyaṃ) yaṃ kiñci atthaṃ avatvā ujumakathetvā tassa abhimatatthassa siddhiyā nipphattiyā aññathā vattumicchitatthassānurūpenāññappakārena dassanaṃ yaṃ kiñci dassanaṃ kathanamatthi, sucibuddhayo pariyāyavuttīti taṃ vadanti. Pariyāyena vutti kathanamiti ca, suci buddhi yesamiti ca vākyaṃ.

277. Now, he illustrates circumlocution with 'Not stating,' etc. Without stating some desired meaning—agreeable and desirable—such as in the form of the giving of wealth, and without speaking straightforwardly, whatever showing or speech there is, expressed in another manner suitable to the intended meaning, for the success and fulfillment of that desired meaning, is what those of pure wisdom call 'circumlocution.' And the analysis is: 'circumlocution is speech by a circuitous route,' and 'those whose wisdom is pure.'

278.

278.

Vivaṭaṅgaṇanikkhittaṃ, dhana’mārakkhavajjitaṃ;

Dhanakāma yathākāmaṃ, tuvaṃ gaccha yadi’cchasi.

Wealth placed in an open courtyard, left unguarded; O wealth-seeker, go as you please, if you wish.

278. Udāharati “vivaṭaṅgaṇe”ccādi. Dhanaṃ vivaṭe kenaci anāvaṭattā aṅgaṇe pakāsappadese nikkhittaṃ atha ca pana ārakkhavajjitaṃ. Dhanaṃ kāmetīti dhanakāmāti āmantanaṃ. Tuvaṃ yadi icchasi gantuṃ dhanaṃ vā, yathākāmaṃ gaccheti dhanāvaharaṇamicchitamañjasā avatvā taṃsiddhiyā byājena vadati. Pariyāyavutti.

278. He gives the example with 'In an open courtyard,' etc. Wealth placed in an open courtyard—a visible place, not covered by anyone—and yet unguarded. 'He who desires wealth is a wealth-seeker'—this is a vocative address. 'If you wish to go, or for the wealth, go as you please'—thus, without directly stating the desired taking of the wealth, he speaks by way of a pretext for its accomplishment. This is circumlocution.

278. Udāharati “vivaṭa”miccādinā. Dhanaṃ muttāmaṇiādi vivaṭaṅgaṇanikkhittaṃ pākārādiparikkheparahitattā nirāvaraṇaṭṭhāne yena kenaci ṭhapitaṃ apica ārakkhavajjitaṃ. Bho dhanakāma tuvaṃ yadicchasi dhanaṃ gamanaṃ vā, yathākāmaṃ gacchāti [M 0.0270] cittenicchitadhanāvaharaṇavidhānaṃ “dhanamāharā”ti ujumavatvā evaṃ byājena vuttattā idaṃ pariyāyavutti nāma. Vivaṭañca taṃ aṅgaṇañceti ca, tasmiṃ nikkhittanti ca, ārakkhena vajjitamiti ca, dhanaṃ kāmetīti ca, kāmaṃ taṇhaṃ taṃsampayuttaṃ vā cittamanatikkammāti ca vākyaṃ.

278. He gives the example with 'Open,' etc. Wealth, such as pearls and gems, placed in an open courtyard—that is, in an unobstructed place free from any enclosure of walls and so on, set down by someone—and furthermore, unguarded. 'O wealth-seeker, if you wish for wealth or to depart, go as you please'—because this instruction for taking the wealth desired by the mind is spoken thus by way of a pretext, instead of directly saying, 'Take the wealth,' this is called circumlocution. And the analysis of the phrases is: 'open and that courtyard'; 'placed therein'; 'devoid of a guard'; 'he desires wealth' (for dhanakāma); and 'not transgressing desire, craving, or the mind associated therewith' (for yathākāmaṃ).

279.

279.

Thutiṃ karoti nindanto, viya taṃ byājavaṇṇanaṃ;

Dosābhāsā guṇā eva, yanti sannidhi’matrahi.

He offers praise as if finding fault—that is veiled praise. For here, what appear as faults are indeed virtues that come to the fore.

279. Byājavaṇṇanaṃ vaṇṇeti “thuti”miccādinā. Nindanto viya dosaṃ nidassento viya thutiṃ karoti vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati, taṃ byājathutilakkhaṇaṃ byājavaṇṇanaṃ nāma. Kathamettha guṇā patīyantīti āha “dosi”ccādi. Atra vuttivisese dosā viya ābhāsanti paṭibhanti. Tādisapadādinā dosābhāsā guṇā eva iddhimantatādayo na dosopi koci sannidhimavaṭṭhānaṃ yanti. Hīti avadhāraṇe atra byājavaṇṇanamevidaṃ, na nindakamiti.

279. He describes veiled praise with 'Praise,' etc. As if blaming, as if pointing out a fault, he offers praise, he speaks of virtue; that which has the characteristic of praise by pretext is called 'veiled praise.' As to how virtues are understood here, he says, 'What appear as faults,' etc. Here, in this particular mode of expression, they appear and shine forth as if they were faults. By means of such words, what appear as faults are indeed virtues, such as the possession of psychic power; not even a single fault is present or established. The particle hi is for emphasis, meaning: this is certainly veiled praise, not censure.

279. Idāni byājavaṇṇanaṃ dasseti “thuti”ccādinā. Nindanto viya dosaṃ dassento viya thutiṃ karoti vaṇṇanaṃ karoti, taṃ vaṇṇanākaraṇaṃ byājavaṇṇanaṃ nāma hoti. Nindāsabhāvena pavattathutittā nindā eveti ce? Atra asmiṃ vuttivisese dosābhāsā dosā viya paṭibhāsamānā guṇā eva tādisapadappayogena iddhimantatādayo guṇāva sannidhiṃ guṇasabhāvāvaṭṭhānaṃ yanti pāpuṇantīti. Byājena vaṇṇanamiti ca, dosā iva ābhāsanti paṭibhāsantīti ca vākyaṃ.

279. Now, he illustrates veiled praise with 'Praise,' etc. As if blaming, as if pointing out a fault, he offers praise, makes a description; that act of description is called veiled praise. (Objection:) Since it is praise that proceeds with the nature of blame, is it not simply blame? (Reply:) Here, in this particular mode of expression, what appear as faults—seeming like faults—are indeed virtues. Through the use of such words, virtues like the possession of psychic power attain presence, reaching a state of stability in their own virtuous nature. And the analysis of the phrases is: 'description by way of a pretext,' and 'they appear or shine forth as if they were faults.'

280.

280.

Sañcāletu’malaṃ tvaṃ’si, bhusaṃ kuvalayā’khilaṃ;

Visesaṃ tāvatā nātha, guṇānaṃ te vadāma kiṃ.

You are able, O Lord, to intensely shake the entire kuvalaya—the world, or the blue lotus. By that much, what can we say of the excellence of your virtues?

280. Udāharati “sañcāletu”miccādinā. Nātha tvaṃ akhilaṃ kuvalayaṃ uppalaṃ pathavīvalayañceti siliṭṭhaṃ sañcāletuṃ bhamayitumito [M 0.0271] cito ca bhusamaccantaṃ alaṃ samatthopi tāvatā taṃmattena te guṇānaṃ visesaṃ atisayalakkhaṇaṃ kiṃ kena kāraṇena vadāma. Iha uppalacālanasāmatthiyavibhāvanavasena nindati, tāva nikhilabhūmaṇḍalasañcālāvikaraṇato paramāya thutiyā saṃyojitoyaṃ bhagavā mahānubhāvaṃ vicitavāti bhuvanamaṇḍalasikhāmaṇīti. Byājavaṇṇanamīdisamaccantaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ, tadidañca sabbathā silesamupajīvati.

280. He illustrates with 'Able to shake,' etc. O Lord, you are fully capable of shaking the entire kuvalaya—which is a pun meaning both 'blue lotus' and 'the circle of the earth'—of spinning it intensely, exceedingly, here and there. Being capable to that extent, by that measure, what, and for what reason, shall we describe the surpassing excellence of your virtues? Here, he offers blame by way of revealing the ability to shake a lotus; yet, by making manifest the shaking of the entire globe of the earth, this Blessed One is connected to the highest praise, as one of great power and the crest-jewel of the world. Such veiled praise is exceedingly delightful, and it depends entirely on the pun.

280. Idāni udāharati “sañcāletu”miccādinā. Nātha tvaṃ akhilaṃ kuvalayaṃ nissesaṃ nīluppalavanaṃ pathavīmaṇḍalaṃ vā sañcāletuṃ kampetuṃ bhusamatisayena alaṃ samattho, tāvatā te guṇānaṃ visesamatisayaṃ kiṃ vadāma kathaṃ bhaṇāmāti. Kuvalayasaddassa uppalavisesavācakattā paṭhamaṃ nindāva, tasseva saddassa pathavīmaṇḍalavācakattā “iddhimato tava idaṃ kiṃ visesa”nti uttamaguṇavaṇṇanā katā hoti. Īdisā byājavaṇṇanā pasatthā, sā ca sabbathā silesaṃ nissāya pavattatīti. Kuyā pathaviyā valayaṃ maṇḍalamiti samāso.

280. Now, it illustrates with 'to shake,' and so on. O Protector, you are exceedingly capable of shaking the entire kuvalaya—that is, the whole forest of blue lotuses or the circle of the earth—of intensely stirring it. By that much, what can we say, how can we speak, of the surpassing excellence of your virtues? Since the word 'kuvalaya' denotes a type of lotus, at first it is like censure. But because that same word also denotes the circle of the earth, it becomes a description of supreme virtue, as if to say, 'For you who possess psychic power, what is so special about this?' Such dissembled praise is commendable, and it proceeds entirely by relying on paronomasia (silesa). The compound is formed from 'ku,' the earth, and 'valaya,' its circle or sphere.

281.

281.

Visesi’cchāyaṃ dabbassa, kriyājātiguṇassa ca;

Vekalladassanaṃ yatra, viseso nāma’yaṃ bhave.

Where, there being a desire for distinction concerning a substance, an action, a class, or a quality, a deficiency is shown, this may be termed 'Distinction'.

281. Visesavuttiṃ vatteti “visesicchāya”miccādinā. Visese atisaye kismiñcipi kāriyavisese icchāyaṃ dabbādīnaṃ yatra vekallassa abhāvassa dassanaṃ vacanaṃ, ayaṃ viseso nāma visesavutti nāma bhave.

281. He states the mode of 'Distinction' with 'a desire for distinction,' etc. Where, there being a desire for distinction, for excellence, or for any particular effect, there is a statement showing the deficiency or absence of substances and so forth, this may be called 'Distinction,' or the 'mode of distinction'.

281. Idāni visesālaṅkāraṃ dasseti “visesi”ccādinā. Visesicchāyaṃ atisaye kāriyavisese icchāyaṃ sati dabbassa ca kriyājātiguṇassa ca yatra yasmiṃ vuttivisese vekalladassanaṃ abhāvakathanamatthi, ayaṃ viseso [M 0.0272] nāma bhave visesavutti nāma siyāti. Vikalassa bhāvoti ca, tassa dassanamiti ca vākyaṃ.

281. Now, he shows the figure of speech 'Distinction' (visesālaṅkāra) with 'a desire for distinction,' etc. When there is a desire for distinction, for excellence in a particular effect, and where, in some special mode of expression, there is a showing of deficiency, a statement of absence, concerning a substance, an action, a class, or a quality, this may be called 'Distinction'; it may be the 'mode of distinction.' And the phrases are: 'the state of being deficient' (vikalassa bhāvo), and 'the showing of that' (tassa dassanam).

282.

282.

Na rathā na ca mātaṅgā, na hayā na padātayo;

Jito mārāri muninā, sambhārāvajjanena hi.

There were no chariots, nor elephants, nor horses, nor foot soldiers; yet the enemy of Māra was conquered by the Sage, indeed by adverting to the accumulations.

Dabbavisesavutti.

The mode of distinction concerning substance.

282. Udāharati “na rathā”iccādi. Subodhaṃ. Atra ca vijayopakaraṇacaturaṅgānīkalakkhaṇadabbābhāvena samatiṃsapāramitāsaṅkhatasambhārāvajjanasseva mārārivijayalakkhaṇo viseso vutto.

282. He illustrates with 'no chariots,' etc. This is easy to understand. And here, through the absence of the substance characterized as the fourfold army, the instrument of victory, a distinction is stated, characterized by the victory over Māra's enemy, which is precisely the adverting to the accumulations designated as the thirty perfections.

282. “Na rathā”iccādi. Rathā tayo antamaso saparivārānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ rathānaṃ anīkavohārato tādisā tayo rathā ca natthi. Mātaṅgā tayo vuttanayena anīkasaṅkhātā tayo mātaṅgā ca natthi. Na hayā tayo tādisā anīkasaṅkhātā tayo assā ca natthi. Padā na antamaso sāyudhānaṃ catunnaṃ purisānaṃ anīkavohārato tādisā cattāro purisā padā ca natthi. Tathāpi muninā sambhārāvajjanena hi samatiṃsapāramidhammānaṃ ābhogakaraṇeneva mārāri mārapaccattiko jito abhibhavito. Iha jayopakaraṇabhāvena ṭhitānaṃ rathānīkādīnaṃ dabbānaṃ vekallaṃ dassetvā sattuvijayasabhāvānaṃ sambhārānaṃ āvajjanavisesassa vuttattā esā dabbavisesavutti nāma. Ratho nāma catupurisaparivāro, tādisaṃ rathattayaṃ rathānīkaṃ nāma. Hatthī pana dvādasapurisaparivāro hoti, tādisaṃ hatthittayaṃ hatthānīkaṃ nāma. Asso tipurisaparivāro, tādisaṃ hayattayaṃ hayānīkaṃ nāma. Sāyudhā cattāro purisā padānīkaṃ nāma. Iha rathādīsu ṭhitā viya sīghaṃ pādabalena gantvā yujjhamānā purisā pādopacārena “pādā”ti vuttā. Rathādīnaṃ pamāṇaṃ tayoti anīkaṭṭhāne [M 0.0273] dassetvā purisapamāṇassāvuttepi antamaso cattāro purisā anīkaṃ nāma hontīti pakaraṇato cattāroti ñāyati. No ce? Sāvudhapurisavācakassa padātisaddassa “padātayo”ti bahuvacanena rūpasambhavato “rathā na, mātaṅgā na, hayā na, padātayo na” iti sambandho. Dabbavisesavutti dabbena dabbapaṭisedhanato visesakathanaṃ visesassa vuttīti ca, dabbena dabbapaṭisedhena visesavuttīti ca vākyaṃ. Kriyāvisesavutyādittayampi evameva daṭṭhabbaṃ.

282. 'No chariots,' etc. There are not even three chariots—since three chariots with their retinues are designated as an army unit—so there are no three such chariots. There are no three elephants, designated as an army unit in the way described. There are no three horses, similarly designated as an army unit. There are no 'feet' (padā), not even four armed men who are designated as an army unit. Nevertheless, the Sage, merely by bringing to mind the thirty perfections, indeed conquered and subdued Māra the adversary. Here, by showing the deficiency of the substances, the chariot units and so forth, which serve as instruments of victory, and by stating the special adverting to the accumulations, which have the nature of victory over the enemy, this is called the 'mode of distinction concerning substance.' A chariot has a retinue of four men; three such chariots are called a chariot unit (rathānīka). An elephant has a retinue of twelve men; three such elephants are called an elephant unit (hatthānīka). A horse has a retinue of three men; three such horses are called a horse unit (hayānīka). Four armed men are called a foot-soldier unit (padānīka). Here, men who fight by moving swiftly on the strength of their feet, as if they were standing on chariots, etc., are called 'pādā' (feet) by figurative usage. Although the number for chariots, etc., is shown in the section on army units as three, even though the number for men is not stated, it is known from the context that at least four men constitute an army unit. If not so, since the form 'padātayo' is possible as the plural of the word 'padāti' which denotes an armed man, the connection is 'no chariots, no elephants, no horses, no foot soldiers.' The phrase 'dabbavisesavutti' can be explained as: 'the statement of a distinction (visesakathanaṃ) through the negation of a substance by means of a substance (dabbena dabbapaṭisedhanato)'; or 'the mode of distinction (visesavutti) through the negation of a substance by means of a substance (dabbena dabbapaṭisedhena).'

283.

283.

Na baddhā bhūkuṭineva, phurito dasanacchado;

Mārāribhaṅgañcā’kāsi, munivīro varo sayaṃ.

A frown was not formed, nor did his lip quiver; yet the excellent Sage-Hero himself brought about the defeat of Māra's enemy.

Kriyāvisesavutti.

The mode of distinction concerning action.

283. “Na baddhā”iccādi. Bhūkuṭi bhamubhaṅgo kopajanito na baddhā na racitā, dasanacchado cādharo neva phurito neva kampito kopena. Tathāpi ca varo uttamo munivīro sayaṃ mārārino bhaṅgaṃ parājayaṃ akāsīti. Bhūkuṭibandhanādikriyāvigamena nibbikāravijayalakkhaṇo viseso dassito.

283. 'Not formed,' etc. The frown (bhūkuṭi), the knitting of the brows born of anger, was not formed, not created; and the lip, the lower lip, did not quiver, was not made to tremble by anger. Nevertheless, the excellent, supreme Sage-Hero himself brought about the breaking, the defeat, of Māra's enemy. Through the absence of the action of forming a frown and so on, a distinction characterized by an imperturbable victory is shown.

283. “Na baddhā”iccādi. Bhūkuṭi kopavikārabhūto bhamubhaṅgopi na baddhā na katā, dasanacchado dantāvaraṇo neva phurito na kampāpito. Tathāpi varo uttamo munivīro muniguṇavīraguṇayutto tathāgato sayaṃ mārāribhaṅgañca akāsīti. Ettha bhamubhaṅgaracanādikaṃ kriyaṃ akatvā nibbikārassa mārabhaṅgasabhāvavisesassa nibbikāramārabhaṅgassa (ka.) vuttattā esā kriyāvisesavutti nāma. Bhūnaṃ kuṭi vaṅkatāti ca, māro eva arīti ca, tesaṃ bhaṅgoti ca vākyaṃ.

283. 'Not formed,' etc. The frown (bhūkuṭi), the knitting of the brows which is a distortion caused by anger, was not formed, not made; the lip, the covering of the teeth, did not quiver, was not made to tremble. Nevertheless, the excellent, supreme Sage-Hero, the Tathāgata endowed with the qualities of a sage and a hero, himself brought about the breaking of Māra's enemy. Here, because a distinction is stated—the natural state of breaking Māra while being imperturbable—without performing the action of forming a frown and so on, this is called the 'mode of distinction concerning action.' And the phrases are explained as: 'the crookedness (kuṭi) of the brows (bhūnaṃ)'; 'Māra himself is the enemy (ari)'; and 'the breaking of them (tesaṃ bhaṅgo).'

284.

284.

Na [M 0.0274] disāsu byattā tatā (sī.) raṃsi,

Nā’loko lokapatthaṭo;

Tathāpya’ndhatamaharaṃ,

Paraṃ sādhusubhāsitaṃ.

No ray is manifest in the directions, nor is light spread throughout the world; yet the supreme, well-spoken word of the virtuous dispels the deepest darkness.

Jātivisesavutti.

The mode of distinction concerning class.

284. “Ni”ccādi. Disāsu dasasu byattā patthaṭā raṃsi na bhavati. Loke sakalasmiṃ patthaṭo vitthato ālokona bhavati. Tathāpīti visesanicchāyaṃ, tajjātikattābhāvepi sādhūnaṃ subhāsitaṃ saddhammasaṅkhātaṃ paramaccantameva andhatamaṃ iṭṭhāniṭṭhāvekallato paññācakkhussa andhakāraṃ mohandhakāraṃ haratīti andhatamaharanti. Raṃsiyā andhakārāpahārasamatthāya nivattiyā viseso subhāsitassa dassito.

284. 'Na,' etc. There is no ray, manifest and spread in the ten directions. There is no light, spread and extended throughout the entire world. The word 'nevertheless' serves to specify the distinction. Even though it does not belong to that class, the well-spoken word of the virtuous, designated as the good Dhamma, is 'that which dispels the deepest darkness' because it supremely and utterly dispels the deepest darkness—the darkness of delusion, which is darkness for the eye of wisdom due to the deficiency in discerning the desirable and undesirable. By the exclusion of the ray, which is capable of dispelling darkness, a distinction of the well-spoken word is shown.

284. “Na disāsu”iccādi. Disāsu byattā patthaṭā raṃsipi natthi, lokapatthaṭo ālokopi natthi. Tathāpi sādhusubhāsitaṃ saddhammo paramaccantaṃ andhatamaharaṃ atthānatthatīraṇakkhamassa paññācakkhussa andhakārakamohatamaṃ haraṃ hotīti. Idha andhakāraviddhaṃsane samatthaṃ raṃsijātyādikaṃ paṭisedhetvā subhāsitassa andhakārāpaharaṇasaṅkhātassa visesassa vuttattā ayaṃ jātivisesavutti nāma. Loke patthaṭoti ca, andhetīti andho moho, tamasadisattā andhoyeva tamoti ca, taṃ haratīti ca, sādhūnaṃ subhāsitamiti ca vākyaṃ.

284. 'Not in the directions,' etc. There is no ray, manifest and spread in the directions, nor is there light spread throughout the world. Nevertheless, the well-spoken word of the virtuous, the good Dhamma, is 'that which dispels the deepest darkness' because it supremely and utterly dispels the darkness of delusion, which makes blind the eye of wisdom that is capable of judging what is beneficial and what is not. Here, by negating the class of rays and so forth, which are capable of destroying darkness, and by stating the distinction of the well-spoken word, designated as the dispelling of darkness, this is called the 'mode of distinction concerning class.' And the phrases are explained as: 'spread in the world'; 'delusion is blinding (andho) because it makes one blind (andheti)'; 'it is darkness (tama) itself because it is like darkness'; 'it dispels that (taṃ harati)'; and 'the well-spoken word of the virtuous (sādhūnaṃ subhāsitaṃ).'

285.

285.

Na kharaṃ na hi vā thaddhaṃ, muninda vacanaṃ tava;

Tathāpi gāḷhaṃ khanati, nimmūlaṃ janatāmadaṃ.

Your speech, O Lord of Sages, is neither harsh nor rigid; yet it digs deep, completely uprooting the people's conceit.

Guṇavisesavutti.

The mode of distinction concerning quality.

285. “Na [M 0.0275] khara”miccādi. Muninda tava vacanaṃ na kharaṃ na lūkhaṃ, na thaddhaṃ vā kaṭhinañca na hi. Tathāpi tādisakharattādiguṇābhāvepi janatāya janasamūhassa madaṃ gāḷhaṃ daḷhaṃ taṇhaṃ (ka.) katvā nimmūlaṃ khanatīti. Ayosaṅkumhi pasiddhakharattādiguṇanisedhena munindavacanassa viseso āvikato.

285. 'Not harsh,' etc. O Lord of Sages, your speech is not harsh, not rough; nor is it indeed rigid or hard. Nevertheless, even in the absence of such qualities as harshness, it digs up forcefully and firmly, leaving no root, the conceit of the populace, the multitude of people. By negating the qualities of harshness and so on, which are well-known in an iron spike, the distinction of the speech of the Lord of Sages is made manifest.

285. “Na khara”miccādi. He muninda tava vacanaṃ kharaṃ kakkasaṃ na hoti, thaddhaṃ vā na hoti. Tathāpi janatāmadaṃ janasamūhassa jātyādiṃ nissāya pavattaṃ gabbaṃ gāḷhaṃ daḷhaṃ katvā nimmūlaṃ mūlamasesetvā khanatīti. Khaṇanakkhamaayosaṅkuādīsu labbhamānaṃ kharattādiguṇaṃ paṭisedhetvā buddhavacanassa madakhaṇanasabhāvasaṅkhātassa visesassa vuttattā ayaṃ guṇavisesavutti nāma hoti. Natthi mūlamassa khaṇanassāti ca, janānaṃ samūhoti ca, tāya madoti ca viggaho. “Gāḷhaṃ nimmūla”nti khaṇanakriyāya visesanattā gāḷhaṃ nimmūlaṃ khaṇanaṃ karotīti yojanā.

285. ‘Not harsh,’ and so on. O Lord of Sages, your speech is not harsh or rough, nor is it stiff. Nevertheless, it digs up the conceit of the multitude—the pride arising from birth and so on—making it firm and strong, and eradicating it, leaving no root. By negating the quality of harshness, etc., found in things capable of digging, like an iron stake, and by stating the special quality of the Buddha's speech, which is its nature of digging up conceit, this is called an expression of a special quality. The grammatical analysis is: ‘that digging of which there is no root’; ‘a multitude of people’; and ‘conceit by that.’ ‘Firmly and without root’ is an adverbial modifier to the action of digging; thus, the construction is: ‘it performs a firm and rootless digging.’

286.

286.

Dassīyate’tidittaṃ …tirittaṃ (ka.) tu,

Sūravīrattanaṃ yahiṃ;

Vadanti viññū vacanaṃ,

Ruḷhāhaṅkāramīdisaṃ.

Where heroism and valor are displayed as exceedingly brilliant, the wise declare such a saying to be ingrained conceit.

286. Ruḷhāhaṅkāraṃ vadanti.

286. They speak of ingrained conceit.

286. Idāni ruḷhāhaṅkāraṃ dasseti “dassīyate” iccādinā. Sūravīrattanaṃ sūrabhāvavīrabhāvaṃ atidittaṃ tu atisayena pana dittaṃ yahiṃ vākye dassīyate, īdisaṃ vacanaṃ viññū kavayo ruḷhāhaṅkāramiti vadantīti. Sūro ca vīro cāti ca, tesaṃ bhāvoti ca, ruḷho uggato ahaṅkāro ettha vuttiviseseti ca vākyaṃ.

286. Now, he points out ingrained conceit with the words ‘is seen,’ and so on. Where heroism and valor are displayed in a statement as exceedingly brilliant, the wise, the poets, declare such a saying to be ‘ingrained conceit.’ The grammatical analysis is: ‘a hero and a valiant one’; ‘their state’; and ‘in this specific expression, conceit has arisen, has sprung up.’

287.

287.

Dame [M 0.0276] nandopanandassa,

Kiṃ me byāpāradassanā;

Puttā me pādasambhattā,

Sajjā santeva tādise.

In the taming of Nandopananda, what is the use of my showing effort? My sons, devoted to my feet, are indeed ready for such a task.

287. Udāharati “dame”iccādinā. Nandopanandassa nāgarājassa appameyyamahānubhāvassa dame damane me mama niravadhisarantippameyyappabhāvānucaritakittinopi parassa byāpāradassanā payogapaṭipādanena kiṃ payojanaṃ, na kimpi, yato me pādasambhattā pādāvanatā tādise kammani sajjā baddhakacchā santeva vijjanteva, tatoti yojanīyaṃ.

287. He gives an example with ‘in the taming,’ etc. In the taming of Nandopananda, the Nāga king of immeasurable great power, what is the purpose for me—who possess limitless, continuous, and immeasurable power and a reputation that follows it—to show effort by undertaking an endeavor? None at all. Because my sons, devoted to my feet, bowing at my feet, are ready for such a task, with their loins girt, they indeed exist. Thus it should be construed.

287. “Dame”ccādi. Nandopanandassa nāgarañño dame damakaraṇe byāpāradassanā bhuvanattaye pavattamānaānubhāvena ca sampavattitakittisamūhena ca samannāgatassa mayhaṃ tādisapayogadassanena kiṃ payojanaṃ. Yasmā me pādasambhattā mayhaṃ caraṇāvanatā tādise kicce sajjā sannaddhā puttā bahavo santi eva, tasmāti. Cetovasitāya sūravīrabhāvo iha atiditto dassito hoti. Byāpārassa dassanamiti ca, pādesu sambhattāti ca vākyaṃ.

287. ‘In the taming,’ etc. In the taming, the subduing, of Nandopananda, the Nāga king, what is the purpose for me—who am endowed with power prevailing in the three worlds and with a great mass of accumulated fame—to show such an endeavor? Because my many sons, devoted to my feet, bowing at my feet, are ready and prepared for such a task, therefore... Here, the state of being a hero and valiant is shown as exceedingly brilliant through mastery of mind. The grammatical analysis is: ‘the showing of effort’; and ‘devoted at the feet.’

288.

288.

Sileso vacanā’nekā-

Bhidheyye’kapadāyutaṃ;

Abhinnapadavākyādi-

Vasā tedhā’ya’mīrito.

Paronomasia is a statement with many meanings connected to a single expression; by means of unbroken words, sentences, and so on, it is declared to be threefold.

288. Silesaṃ niddisati “sileso”iccādinā. Anekaṃ bhinnamabhidheyyattho yassātyanekābhidheyyaṃ. Ekena samānena padena sarūpena āyutamanvitaṃ yaṃ vacanaṃ vuttīti anuvaditvā so silesoti vidhīyate, yena kenaci [M 0.0277] rūpena upamānopameyyalakkhaṇatthānaṃ silesanato. Ayañcevaṃlakkhaṇo sileso tedhā īrito. Kathaṃ? Abhinnapadavākyādivasā abhinnamekaṃ padaṃ syādyantatyādyantarūpaṃ yatra, tameva vākyaṃ vākyalakkhaṇopetattā. Taṃ ādi yesaṃ, tesaṃ vasāti attho.

288. He defines paronomasia with ‘Paronomasia is,’ etc. ‘Having many meanings’ means that which has many different meanings. Having restated ‘whatever statement is connected, endowed with a single, similar word or form,’ it is then established as ‘that is paronomasia,’ because of the clinging together of the meanings characterized as the standard of comparison and the subject of comparison in some form or another. This paronomasia, so characterized, is declared to be threefold. How? By means of unbroken words, sentences, etc. This means where there is a single, unbroken word, in the form of a nominal or verbal inflection, and that itself is a sentence because it possesses the characteristics of a sentence. The meaning is: by means of those things of which that is the beginning.

288. Idāni silesālaṅkāraṃ dasseti “sileso”ccādinā. Anekābhidheyyaṃ ekapadāyutaṃ ubhayattha sādhāraṇattā tulyena saddarūpena yuttaṃ yaṃ vacanaṃ atthi, so sileso nāma. So pana yena kenaci sādhammarūpena upamānopameyyabhūtānamatthānaṃ siliṭṭhattā aññamaññaṃ phusitvā ṭhitattā sileso nāma. Ayaṃ vuttalakkhaṇo sileso abhinnapadavākyādivasā akatavikārānaṃ syādyantatyādyantapadasamannāgatānaṃ vākyalakkhaṇopetavākyānaṃ pabhedena tedhā īritoti. Anekamabhidheyyaṃ yasseti ca, ekañca taṃ padañceti ca, tena āyutanti ca, abhinnāni padāni yasminti ca, tañca taṃ vākyañcāti ca, taṃ ādi yesaṃ abhinnapadavākyānanti ca, tesaṃ vaso bhedoti ca vākyaṃ.

288. Now he shows the ornament of paronomasia with ‘Paronomasia is,’ etc. Whatever statement exists that has many meanings and is joined with a single word—that is, connected with an equivalent word-form that is common to both contexts—that is called paronomasia. It is called paronomasia because the meanings, which are the standard of comparison and the subject of comparison, are clung together, standing in contact with each other, through some common property. This paronomasia with the stated characteristic is declared to be threefold through the division of sentences possessing the characteristics of a sentence, which are endowed with undeclined nominal and verbal words, by means of unbroken words, sentences, etc. The grammatical analysis is: ‘that which has many meanings’; ‘and that is a single word’; ‘joined with that’; ‘wherein the words are unbroken’; ‘and that is a sentence’; ‘of which that is the beginning, of the unbroken words and sentences’; and ‘their division is the distinction.’

289.

289.

Andhantamaharo hārī, samāruḷho mahodayaṃ;

Rājate raṃsimālī’yaṃ, bhagavā bodhayaṃ jane.

The dispeller of blinding darkness, the charming one, has ascended the great eminence; this Blessed One, adorned with a garland of rays, shines forth, awakening the people.

Abhinnapadavākyasileso.

Paronomasia of unbroken words and sentences.

289. Udāharati “andhantami”ccādi. Ayaṃ bhagavā sūriyo mahāmuni ca. Tattha sūriyo tāva andhantamaharo pakatiyandhakāropahārī, mahāmuni tu andhakāramohatamāpahārī. Hārī manuñño sūriyo mahāmuni ca, sūriyo [M 0.0278] mahodayaṃ mahantaṃ udayaṃ pabbataṃ samāruḷho, mahāmuni tu mahodayaṃ mahantamabbhudayaṃ sammāsambodhisamadhigamarūpaṃ samāruḷho patto. Raṃsīnaṃ mālā, sā assa atthīti raṃsimālī, sūriyo mahāmuni ca. Jane bodhayaṃ niddāpagamanena kilesaniddāpagamanena vā pabodhayanto rājate dibbatīti. Abhinnapadavākyasileso bhaṅgena vinā yathāvaṭṭhānamubhayattha padayojanato.

289. He gives an example with ‘blinding darkness,’ etc. This Blessed One is the sun and the great sage. In this regard, the sun is the dispeller of blinding darkness, removing the natural darkness. The great sage, however, is the dispeller of the darkness of delusion. Charming and delightful are both the sun and the great sage. The sun has ascended the great eminence, the great Udaya mountain. The great sage, however, has ascended, has attained, the great eminence, the great success in the form of attaining perfect self-awakening. ‘A garland of rays, he has it,’ thus he is ‘garlanded with rays’—both the sun and the great sage. ‘Awakening the people’ means awakening them by dispelling sleep or by dispelling the sleep of the defilements, he shines, he is resplendent. It is a paronomasia of unbroken words and sentences because the words are applied in both cases as they stand, without being broken.

289. Idāni udāharati “andha”miccādinā. Mahodayaṃ mahantaṃ udayaṃ pabbataṃ, sabbaññupadavisaṅkhātamahābhivuddhiṃ vā samāruḷho āruḷho, sampatto vā, andhantamaharo cakkavāḷagabbhe patthaṭapakatighanandhakārassa, ñāṇalocanassa andhakaraṇato andhakāroti vuttamohassa vā viddhaṃsako, hārī teneva manuñño raṃsimālī attano raṃsimālāya samannāgato jane pakatiniddāya kilesaniddāya vā samannāgate satte bodhayaṃ bodhayanto ayaṃ bhagavā divākaro, chahi bhagadhammehi samannāgato buddho vā rājate dibbatīti. Dvīsu pakkhesu padānaṃ samānabhāvena ṭhitattā ayaṃ abhinnapadavākyasileso. Andho ca so tamo ceti ca, taṃ haratīti ca, mahanto ca so udayo pabbato cāti ca, mahanto ca so udayo abbhudayo abhivuddhi cāti ca, raṃsīnaṃ mālāti ca, sā assa atthīti ca, bhago sirī assa sūriyassa atthīti ca, bhago sirīkāmapayatanādippakāro assa satthuno atthīti ca viggaho. Abhinnapadavākyasaṅkhāto sileso. Aparopi attho ettha silissatīti sileso. “Bhinnapadavākyasileso”tiādikampi iminā nayena ñātabbaṃ.

289. Now, he gives an example with the word ‘blinding,’ and so on. ‘Having ascended the great eminence’: having ascended or attained the great Udaya mountain, or the great advancement known as the state of omniscience. ‘Dispeller of blinding darkness’: destroyer of the dense natural darkness spread within the cosmos, or of the delusion called darkness because it blinds the eye of wisdom. ‘Captivating’: thereby delightful. ‘Garlanded with rays’: endowed with his own garland of rays. ‘Awakening the people’: awakening beings who are in natural sleep or in the sleep of defilements. ‘This Blessed One’: the sun, or the Buddha endowed with the six blessed qualities, shines forth, is resplendent. Because the words stand equally in both interpretations, this is a paronomasia of unbroken words and sentences. The grammatical analyses are: ‘blind and that is darkness’; ‘he dispels that’; ‘great and that is the Udaya mountain’; ‘great and that is the rise, the advancement, the growth’; ‘a garland of rays’; ‘he possesses it’; ‘the sun possesses fortune and glory’; and ‘the Teacher possesses fortune, glory, desire, effort, and so on.’ This is the paronomasia known as that of unbroken words and sentences. Another meaning also adheres here, hence it is called paronomasia. ‘Paronomasia of broken words and sentences,’ and so on, should also be understood in this way.

290.

290.

Sāradāmalakābhāso, samānītaparikkhayo;

Kumudākarasambodho, pīṇeti janataṃ sudhī.

With spotless autumnal splendor, having brought decay to an end, and causing the lily-ponds to bloom, the wise one gladdens the people.

Bhinnapadavākyasileso.

Paronomasia of broken words and sentences.

290. “Sārade”ccādi. Sudhā assa atthīti sudhī, cando. Sobhanā sabbaññutaññāṇarūpaṃ buddhi assa atthīti sudhī, [M 0.0279] sammāsambuddho. Sārado saradakāle sambhūto amalako nimmalo ābhā sobhā yassa so, cando. Paresaṃ nibbānasāraṃ dadātīti sārado, amalako ābhāso, amalakassa hatthāmalakasseva vā ābhāso asesañeyyāvabodho yassa so, sammāsambuddho. Saṃ sammā kamenānīyamānattā ānīto parikkhayo kaṇhapakkho yena so, cando. Samaṃ vūpasamaṃ ānīto parikkhayo hāni kilesasattukato adhigatakkhayattā yenaso, sammāsambuddho. Kumudākarassa kumudassa raṃsiyā sambodhi vikāso yassa raṃsiyo sambodhi vikāsa’ssa (ka.) so, cando. Kuyā pathaviyā mudaṃ pītiṃ karotīti kumudākaro, sambodho catusaccāvabodho yassa so, sammāsambuddho, janataṃ janasamūhaṃ pīṇetīti. Ayaṃ bhinnapadavākyasileso vuttena vidhinā padānaṃ bhinnattā.

290. Sārada, etc. Sudhī means ‘one who has nectar’—the moon. Sudhī also means ‘one who has splendid wisdom’ in the form of the knowledge of omniscience—the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. Sārado means born in the autumn season, spotless, whose radiance and splendor are pure—the moon. Sārado also means ‘one who gives the essence’ of Nibbāna to others; he is the spotless radiance, or his comprehension of all that is to be known is like a myrobalan fruit in the hand—the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. Samānītaparikkhayo means the moon, by whom the waning of the dark fortnight is well and gradually brought to an end. It also means the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, by whom the destruction—the loss caused by the enemy defilements—is brought to calm and peace, as their destruction has been attained. Kumudākarasambodho means the moon, whose is the awakening, that is, the blossoming, of the water lilies by his rays. It also means the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, who creates joy (muda) for the earth (ku), thus he is Kumudākaro; his awakening (sambodho) is the comprehension of the four truths, and he gladdens the multitude of people. This is a pun of split words and sentences, because the words are split in the manner described.

290. “Sāra”iccādi. Sārado saradakāle sambhūto, veneyyānaṃ nibbānasāradāyako vā, amalakābhāso nimmalasobho, nimmalaketumālāsamannāgatattā tādisamatthakasobho vā, atha vā sāradāmalakābhāso saradakāle sañjātanimmalasobho, veneyyānaṃ nibbānasāradāyakanimmalasobho vā, atha vā sāradaāmalakaābhāso nibbānasāradāyakahatthāmalakasadisañeyyāvabodho. Samānītaparikkhayo kaṇhapakkhe suṭṭhu kamena ānīto parikkhayo paripuṇṇo vā cando, samasaṅkhatasantiṃ ānītakilesaparihānisaṅkhātaparikkhayo vā. Kumudākarasambodho kumudavikāsanena samannāgato, kusaṅkhātapathavīnissitānaṃ janānaṃ pītijananacatusaccāvabodhena samannāgato vā. Sudhī sudhāsaṅkhātaamatavantatāya [M 0.0280] tannāmako cando, sundarapaññavantatāya tannāmako sammāsambuddho vā. Janataṃ janasamūhaṃ pīṇetīti. Ubhayapakkhesu padaṃ bhinditvā atthassa yojanato ayaṃ bhinnapadavākyasileso. Sarade bhavo sārado, cando. Sāraṃ dadātīti sārado, bhagavā. “Sārado”ti idaṃ “ābhāso”ti padassa visesanaṃ hoti. Amalakonimmalo ābhāso assa candassāti ca, kamhi matthake ābhāsoti ca, amalo kābhāso assa satthunoti ca, sārado amalako ābhāso yassa candassa bhagavato vāti ca, sārado āmalakassa viya ābhāso ñeyyāvabodho assa bhagavatoti ca, saṃ sammā ānīto parikkhayo kalāhāni aneneti ca, samaṃ vūpasamaṃ ānīto parikkhayo hāni kilesasattuto yeneti ca, kumudānaṃ ākaroti ca, tesaṃ sambodho vikāso yasseti ca, mudaṃ pītiṃ karotīti mudākaro. Kuyā pathaviyā mudākaroti ca, so sambodho catusaccāvabodho yasseti ca, sudhā amataṃ assa candassa atthīti ca, su sobhanā dhī buddhi assa sambuddhassāti ca viggaho.

290. Sāra, etc. Sārado means born in the autumn season, or the one who gives the essence of Nibbāna to those who can be taught. Amalakābhāso means having a spotless splendor, or having such a splendor on the head, being endowed with a garland of spotless banners. Alternatively, sāradāmalakābhāso means a spotless splendor that arises in the autumn season, or the spotless splendor of one who gives the essence of Nibbāna to those who can be taught. Or, sāradaāmalakaābhāso means one whose comprehension of what is to be known is like a myrobalan fruit in the hand, who gives the essence of Nibbāna. Samānītaparikkhayo means the moon, whose waning in the dark fortnight is well and gradually brought about, or who is complete. Or, it means one whose destruction, which is the decline of defilements, is brought to a state of peace called ‘calm.’ Kumudākarasambodho means endowed with the blossoming of water lilies, or endowed with the awakening to the four truths which generates delight for the people who depend on the earth, designated as ‘ku.’ Sudhī refers to the moon, so named for possessing the deathless called ‘nectar,’ or the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, so named for possessing excellent wisdom. He gladdens the multitude of people. This is a pun of split words and sentences, because the meaning is applied by splitting the words in both cases. The analyses are as follows: ‘Born in autumn’ (sarade bhavo) is Sārado, the moon. ‘He gives the essence’ (sāraṃ dadāti) is Sārado, the Blessed One. The word Sārado qualifies the word ābhāso. And: ‘The moon has a spotless (amalako=nimmalo) radiance (ābhāso).’ And: ‘Whose radiance is on the head (kamhi=matthake)?’ And: ‘The Teacher has a spotless radiance (amalo ka-ābhāso).’ And: ‘The moon or the Blessed One has a spotless autumn radiance.’ And: ‘The Blessed One’s comprehension of what is to be known is a radiance like a myrobalan fruit.’ And: ‘By him the destruction, the loss of phases, is well brought about.’ And: ‘By whom the destruction, the loss from the enemy defilements, is brought to calm and peace.’ And: ‘A mine (ākara) of water lilies (kumuda).’ And: ‘Whose is their awakening (sambodho), their blossoming (vikāso).’ And: ‘He makes joy (mudaṃ), delight, thus he is mudākaro.’ And: ‘He is the joy-maker of the earth (ku).’ And: ‘His is that awakening (sambodho), the comprehension of the four truths.’ And: ‘The moon has nectar (sudhā), the deathless.’ And: ‘The Self-Enlightened One has good (su), splendid intelligence (dhī), wisdom.’

291.

291.

Samāhitattavinayo, ahīnamadamaddano;

Sugato visadaṃ pātu, pāṇinaṃ so vināyako.

Whose self is composed and disciplined, the crusher of the pride of snakes or of supreme beings; the Well-Gone One, may he clearly protect beings, he, the leader.

Bhinnābhinnapadavākyasileso.

A pun of split and unsplit words and sentences.

291. “Samāhite”ccādi. Saṃ sammā āhito patiṭṭhāpito attassa vinayo vinayanaṃ sabbattha savisaye appaṭihatacāravasena yassa so, garuḷo. Vinayanaṃ pavivittakāyacittappavattivasena damanaṃ yassa so, sammāsambuddho. Iti abhinnapadaṃ. Ahīnaṃ sappānaṃ inā nāyakā, tesaṃ madaṃ maddatīti ahīnamadamaddano, garuḷo. Ahīnānamuttamapurisānampi mahābrahmādīnaṃ madaṃ maddatīti ahīnamadamaddano, sammāsambuddho. Sundaraṃ gataṃ gamanaṃ samuddaṃ bhinditvā jalasaṅgamato paṭhamamevauggamanasāmatthiyayogato [M 0.0281] yassa so, garuḷo. Sundaraṃ gamanamassa nāgavikkantacārattā sugato, sammāsambuddho. Abhinnapadaṃ. So vīnaṃ pakkhīnaṃ nāyako, garuḷo. Visaṃ dadātīti visadaṃ pāṇinaṃ nāgalokaṃ pātu ahiṃsanavasena pālayatu, so vineti veneyyeti vināyako, sammāsambuddho. Pāṇinaṃ sakalasattalokaṃ visadaṃ asallīnaṃ pātu. Bhinnābhinnapadavākyasilesoyaṃ vuttanayena padānaṃ pana (ka.) ubhayamissattā.

291. Samāhite, etc. Whose discipline of self is well established by means of unimpeded movement in all his own spheres—he is Garuḷa. Whose taming is by means of the secluded activity of body and mind—he is the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. This is an unbroken expression. He crushes the pride of the leaders of snakes—he is Ahīnamadamaddano, Garuḷa. He crushes the pride of the not-inferior, the supreme beings, even the great Brahmās—he is Ahīnamadamaddano, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. Whose beautiful going is by the power of rising up first from the mass of water, having broken through the ocean—he is Garuḷa. Whose movement is beautiful due to his majestic, heroic gait—he is the Well-Gone One, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. This is an unbroken expression. He is the leader of birds, the winged ones—Garuḷa. As the poison-giver (visaṃ dadātīti visadaṃ), may he protect the nāga world for beings by means of non-harming. He trains the trainable, thus he is the leader (vināyako)—the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. May he protect all beings in the entire world of beings clearly and unshaken. This is a broken-unbroken word and sentence pun, because the words are a mixture of both types, in the manner described.

291. “Samāhite”ccādi. Samāhitattavinayo sammā āhitāya ṭhapitāya sarīrassa savisaye gatiyā samannāgato, sammā āhitena ṭhapitena cittadamanena samannāgato vā, ahīnamadamaddano nāgarājūnaṃ madamaddano, ahīnānaṃ uttamānaṃ bakabrahmādīnampi madamaddano vā, sugato pakkhavātavegena samuddajalaṃ dvidhā katvā tasmiṃ jale anekībhūteyeva nāgabhavanaṃ gantvā nāge gahetvā gamane samatthattā sundaragamano, samantabhaddakaanekappakāragamano vā, vināyako pakkhīnaṃ nāyako so garuḷarājā visadaṃ ghoravisattā visadāyakaṃ pāṇinaṃ nāgalokaṃ pātu ahiṃsanavasena pāletu. No ce, vināyako veneyye vinento so sammāsambuddho pāṇinaṃ sakalasattalokaṃ visadaṃ visāradaṃ katvā pātu ahitāpanayanahitopanayanena rakkhatūti. Ubhayapakkhesu “ahīnamadamaddano”iccādikehi bhinnehi ca “samāhitattavinayo”iccādikehi abhinnehi ca padehi samannāgatattā ayaṃ bhinnābhinnapadavākyasileso. Attassa vinayoti ca, samāhito attavinayo yassa garuḷassa tathāgatassa vāti ca, ahīnaṃ inā nāyakāti ca, ahīnānaṃ nāgarājūnaṃ madoti ca, hīnehi aññe ahīnā uttamā, tesaṃ madoti [M 0.0282] ca, taṃ maddatīti ca, vīnaṃ pakkhīnaṃ nāyakoti ca, veneyyajane vinetīti ca vākyaṃ. Dutiyapakkhe “visada”nti kriyāvisesanaṃ.

291. Samāhite, etc. Samāhitattavinayo means one who is endowed with the movement of his body in its own sphere, which is well-placed and established; or one who is endowed with a well-placed and established taming of mind. Ahīnamadamaddano means the crusher of the pride of nāga kings; or the crusher of the pride of the supreme, non-inferior ones, even Bakabrahmā and so forth.
