Sugato means one who is beautiful in going, being capable of going to the nāga abode and capturing nāgas by splitting the ocean water in two with the speed of the wind from his wings and remaining unmixed in that water; or whose going is of many kinds and universally auspicious. Vināyako, the leader of birds, that Garuḷa king, may he, despite his terrible poison, clearly protect the poison-giving nāga world for beings by means of non-harming. Otherwise, may that leader, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, while training the trainable, protect the entire world of beings by making them clear and confident, by removing what is harmful and providing what is beneficial. This is a broken-unbroken word and sentence pun, because it is endowed with both broken phrases like ahīnamadamaddano, etc., and unbroken phrases like samāhitattavinayo, etc., in both applications. The analysis of the phrases is: ‘discipline of self’; and ‘whose self-discipline is well-composed,’ referring to Garuḷa or the Tathāgata; and ‘the leaders of snakes’; and ‘the pride of the nāga kings’; and ‘others, different from the inferior, are the non-inferior, the supreme, and their pride’; and ‘he crushes that’; and ‘the leader of birds, the winged ones’; and ‘he trains the trainable people.’ In the second application, visada is an adverb.

292.

292.

Viruddhāviruddhābhinna-kammā niyamavā paro;

Niyamakkhepavacano, avirodhi virodhya’pi.

Actions may be opposed, unopposed, or mixed; one type has a rule, another does not. There is the statement of rule and exception, which may be non-contradictory or even contradictory.

293.

293.

Ocityasamposakādi, sileso padajādi’ti padajātipi (ka.);

Esaṃ nidassanesveva, rūpa’māvibhavissati.

Propriety, embellishment, and so on, and the word-born pun, and so on; in the very examples of these, the form will become manifest.

292-3. Silesabhedamaññathāpi dassetumāha “viruddha”iccādi. Viruddhāni cāviruddhāni ca aññamabhinnañca, tāniyeva kammāni kriyāni yesaṃ, te tayo silesā. Niyamo’vadhāraṇamasmiṃ atthīti niyamavā, paro añño silesopi. Niyamassa akkhepo nisedhanaṃ yassa, taṃ vacanamabhidhānaṃ yassa, tādisopi. Nāssa virodho atthītyavirodhi, sopi. Virodho asaṅgati ettha vijjatīti virodhi, sopi. Ocityaṃ samposetīti ocityasamposako, so ādi yassa alaṅkārantaragocarassa silesassa, so padato jātādisilesopi. Itite parepi silesabhedā santi. Esaṃ yathāvuttānaṃ nidassanesu payogesveva rūpaṃ sabhāvo lakkhaṇaṃ āvibhavissatīti.

To show the divisions of silesa in another way, he says: ‘opposing,’ etc. Opposing, non-opposing, and not different from each other—those whose actions and deeds are these very things, they are the three silesas. That in which there is restriction or determination is niyamavā ('possessing restriction'); this is another, different silesa. That which has the rejection or negation of restriction, that whose utterance is such, is also one. That in which there is no opposition is avirodhi ('non-opposing'); that is also one. That in which opposition or incongruity exists is virodhi ('opposing'); that is also one. That which nourishes appropriateness is ocityasamposako ('nourisher of appropriateness'); that which has this as its beginning, a silesa whose scope is another figure of speech, that is also a silesa born from a word, and so on. Thus, these are other divisions of silesa. Of these, as stated, their form, nature, and characteristic will become manifest in the examples and applications themselves.

292-3. Avuttasilesavisese dassetuṃ uddisati “viruddhā”iccādi. Viruddhāviruddhābhinnakammā api ubhayatthassa viruddhena ca aviruddhena ca abhinnena ca kammena samanvitā tayo silesā ca, paro añño niyamavāpi avadhāraṇena yuttasileso ca, niyamakkhepavacanopi avadhāraṇassa paṭisedhapakāsakābhidhānasileso ca, avirodhipi ubhayapakkhāvirodhisileso ca, virodhiapi ubhayatthassa [M 0.0283] virodhisileso ca, padajādi padena jāto vākyena jāto ocityasamposakādisilesopīti esaṃ silesānaṃ nidassanesveva nidassanasaṅkhataudāharaṇesveva rūpaṃ sarūpaṃ tesaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ vā āvibhavissati, nidassiyamānaudāharaṇeneva lakkhaṇassa gammamānattā visuṃ na kathessāmīti adhippāyo. Viruddhāni ca aviruddhāni ca abhinnañceti ca, tameva kammaṃ kriyā yesaṃ silesānamiti ca, niyamo avadhāraṇaṃ asmiṃ atthīti ca, niyamassa akkhepo paṭisedho assa atthīti ca, taṃ vacanaṃ abhidhānaṃ yassa silesassāti ca, nāssa virodho atthīti ca, ocityaṃ samposetīti ca, so ādi yassa upamāsilesādinoti ca, padato jātoti ca, so ādi yassa vākyassāti ca viggaho.

To show the distinctions of the unstated silesa, he indicates: ‘opposing,’ etc. And the three silesas with contradictory, non-contradictory, and non-different actions, endowed with action that is contradictory, non-contradictory, and non-different with respect to both meanings; and also the niyamavā (silesa endowed with restriction), endowed with determination; and also the niyamakkhepavacana (silesa with speech rejecting restriction), whose expression reveals the negation of determination; and also the avirodhi (silesa), which is non-opposing to both sides; and also the virodhi (silesa), which is opposing to both meanings; and also the silesa born from a word, born from a sentence, the nourisher of appropriateness, etc. Of these silesas, in the examples alone—that is, in the examples designated as illustrations—their form, true nature, or characteristic will become manifest. The intention is: ‘Since the characteristic is understood through the very examples being illustrated, I will not explain it separately.’ The analysis is: ‘And contradictory, and non-contradictory, and not different,’ and ‘that very action and deed belong to which silesas,’ and ‘restriction, determination, is present in this,’ and ‘the rejection, the negation, of restriction is present in this,’ and ‘that statement is the expression of which silesa,’ and ‘there is no opposition in it,’ and ‘it nourishes appropriateness,’ and ‘that is the beginning of which simile-silesa, etc.,’ and ‘born from a word,’ and ‘that is the beginning of which sentence.’

Viruddhakammasilesa

The Silesa of Contradictory Action

294.

294.

Savase vattayaṃ lokaṃ, akhilaṃ kallaviggaho kalaviggaho (sī.);

Parābhavati mārāri, dhammarājā vijambhate.

Making the entire world revolve under his power, he of pleasing form/conflict; the Foe of Māra is defeated, the King of Dhamma triumphs.

294. Tato kamena tedassīyanti “savase”iccādi. Akhilaṃ lokaṃ savase vattayaṃ mārāri dhammarājā ca, kallo manuñño viggaho kalaho yassa mārārino, viggaho sarīrasampadā yassa dhammarājassa, tesu mārāri parābhavati parābhavamapeti bodhiyaṃ paṭiladdhaparājayavasena, dhammarājā samantabhaddo tu vijambhate lokattayabyāpisamullapitavijayaddhanipavattivasena samaṃ bhavatīti ayaṃ viruddhakammasileso parābhavavijambhanānamaññoññavirodhato.

294. Then, in order, they are shown thus: ‘savase,’ etc. The Foe of Māra and the King of Dhamma, making the entire world revolve under their own power. The Foe of Māra is he whose conflict is pleasing and agreeable; the King of Dhamma is he whose form is bodily perfection. Among them, the Foe of Māra is defeated—he attains defeat—in the sense of the defeat obtained at the Bodhi tree. But the King of Dhamma, the All-Auspicious One, triumphs, in the sense that it truly comes to be through the rolling forth of the sound of the banner of victory proclaimed throughout the three worlds. This is a silesa of contradictory action due to the mutual opposition of 'being defeated' and 'triumphing'.

294. Idāni uddesakkamena udāharati “savase”iccādi. Akhilaṃ lokaṃ savase vattayaṃ anatthe yuñjanato attano vase vattayanto, no ce, sakalalokaṃ hite [M 0.0284] yuñjanato attano vase vattayanto kallaviggaho manuññakalaho, no ce, manuññasarīrasampattiyutto mārāri parābhavati bodhimūle laddhaparājayavasena parābhavaṃ pāpuṇāti, dhammarājā tathāgato pana vijambhate lokattaye patthaṭajayaghosavasena vijambhatīti. Parābhavanavijambhanakriyānaṃ aññamaññaviruddhattā ayaṃ viruddhakammasileso nāma. Sassa attano vaso issariyamiti ca, kallo manuñño viggaho vivādo deho vā yasseti ca vākyaṃ.

294. Now, following the order of the exposition, he gives the example: ‘savase,’ etc. Making the entire world revolve under his own power: by engaging it in what is unbeneficial, he makes it revolve under his own power; or else, by engaging the entire world in what is beneficial, he makes it revolve under his own power. He of pleasing conflict: he whose quarrel is pleasing; or else, one endowed with pleasing bodily perfection. The Foe of Māra is defeated: he attains defeat in the sense of the defeat obtained at the root of the Bodhi tree. But the King of Dhamma, the Tathāgata, triumphs: he triumphs in the sense of the proclamation of victory spread throughout the three worlds. Because the actions of being defeated and triumphing are mutually contradictory, this is called a viruddhakammasilesa. The analysis is: ‘Sa means one’s own; vaso means sovereignty’; and ‘kallo means pleasing; viggaho means dispute or body, of whom’.

Aviruddhakammasilesa

The Silesa of Non-Contradictory Action

295.

295.

Sabhāvamadhuraṃ puñña-visesodayasambhavaṃ;

Suṇanti vācaṃ munino, janā passanti cā’mataṃ.

Naturally sweet, arising from the emergence of special merit, people hear the Sage's speech and behold the Deathless.

295. “Sabhāve”ccādi. Sabhāveneva madhurā piyā vācā, madhuraṃ amataṃ, puññavisesassa udayo abhivaḍḍhi, tena sambhavo, yassa vā taṃ, munino vācaṃ saddhammasaṅkhātaṃ janā suṇanti, tassayaṃ amatañca tassa ca nissayaṃ amatanti (ka.) passantīti ayamaviruddhakammasileso savanadassanānaṃ aviruddhattāti.

295. ‘Sabhāvena,’ etc. Speech is naturally sweet and pleasing; sweet is the Deathless. The arising of special merit is its increase; from that it arises, or it is that to which it belongs. People hear the Sage's speech, reckoned as the True Dhamma, and they also see this Deathless. This is a silesa of non-contradictory action because hearing and seeing are not contradictory.

295. “Sabhāva”miccādi. Sabhāvamadhuraṃ “vācāmadhuraṃ karissāmī”ti kattabbapayogaṃ vināpi madhurattā pakatimadhuraṃ, no ce, kenaci paccayena anuppannattā saṅkharavisesaṃ vināpi pakatipaṇītaṃ, puññavisesodayasambhavaṃ puññavisesadesakassa munino kassaci kusalavisesassa abhivuddhiyā sambhūtaṃ, no ce, veneyyajanānaṃ nibbānādhippāyena katakusalavisesassa abhivuddhiyā ārammaṇattena paṭiladdhaṃ munino vācaṃ saddhammasaṅkhātaṃ suṇanti, amataṃ nibbānañca janā veneyyajanā passantīti. Savanadassanakriyānaṃ aññamaññāviruddhattā ayaṃ aviruddhakammasileso. Sassa attano bhāvoti [M 0.0285] ca, tena madhurā, madhuramiti ca, puññameva visesoti ca, tassodayoti ca, tena sambhavo yasseti ca viggaho.

295. ‘Sabhāva,’ etc. Naturally sweet: naturally sweet due to its sweetness even without the effort that should be made, thinking ‘I will make the speech sweet’; or else, naturally excellent even without special conditioning, because it has not arisen from any cause. Arising from the emergence of special merit: arisen from the increase of some special wholesome quality of the Sage who teaches special merit; or else, attained as an object due to the increase of a special wholesome quality performed by those to be trained with the intention of Nibbāna. People—those to be trained—hear the Sage's speech, reckoned as the True Dhamma, and see the Deathless, Nibbāna. Because the actions of hearing and seeing are not mutually contradictory, this is a silesa of non-contradictory action. The analysis is: ‘Sa means one’s own, bhāvo means nature’; and ‘by that it is sweet, it is sweet’; and ‘merit alone is special’; and ‘its arising’; and ‘that from which it arises’.

Abhinnakammasilesa

The Silesa of Non-different Action

296.

296.

Andhakārāpahārāya,

Sabhāvamadhurāya ca;

Mano pīṇeti dhinoti (sī. abhinavaṭīkā ca) jantūnaṃ,

Jino vācāya bhāya ca.

By his speech and by his radiance, which dispel darkness and are naturally sweet, the Conqueror delights the minds of beings.

296. “Andhakāre”ccādi. Andhakāraṃ mohasaṅkhātaṃ pakatiandhakāraṃ vā apaharatīti andhakārāpahārā, vācā, bhā ca. Tāya sabhāvabhāsāya, sobhāya ca jino jantūnaṃ mano cittaṃ pīṇetīti ayamabhinnakammasileso pīṇanalakkhaṇāyekāya kriyāya vācāya bhāya ca sampannoti.

296. ‘Andhakāra,’ etc. That which removes darkness—called delusion or natural darkness—is a ‘dispeller of darkness’; this refers to both speech and radiance. By that naturally radiant speech and by that splendor, the Conqueror delights the minds of beings. This is a silesa of non-different action, accomplished by a single action characterized by delighting, through both speech and radiance.

296. “Andhakārā”iccādi. Andhakārāpahārāya mohandhakāraṃ pakatiandhakāraṃ vā apaharaṇāya sabhāvamadhurāya ca sabhāvato kaṇṇasukhāya, sabhāvato nettābhirāmāya vācāya bhāya sarīrakantiyā ca jino jantūnaṃ mano cittaṃ dhinoti pīṇetīti. Pīṇayanasabhāvāya ekāya kriyāya saddhiṃ karaṇabhūtānaṃ dvinnaṃ vācābhānaṃ yojitattā ayaṃ abhinnakammasileso. Andhakāra’mapaharatīti ca, sabhāvena madhurāti ca vākyaṃ.

296. ‘Andhakārā,’ etc. For dispelling darkness—that is, for removing the darkness of delusion or natural darkness—and for being naturally sweet—that is, by speech naturally pleasing to the ear, and by radiance, or bodily beauty, naturally delightful to the eye—the Conqueror gladdens and delights the minds of beings. Because the two instruments, speech and radiance, are connected with a single action whose nature is to delight, this is a silesa of non-different action. The analysis is: ‘It dispels darkness,’ and ‘It is naturally sweet.’

Niyamavantasilesa

The Silesa with Restriction

297.

297.

Kesakkhīnaṃva kaṇhattaṃ, samūnaṃyeva vaṅkatā;

Pāṇipādādharānaṃva, munindassā’tirattatā.

Of the Lord of Sages, blackness belongs only to the hair and eyes; curvature, only to the eyebrows; excessive redness, only to the hands, feet, and lips.

297. “Kesi”ccādi. [M 0.0286] Kaṇhattaṃ kesakkhīnaṃyeva, na manasi, kaṇhattaguṇo pāpattañca siliṭṭhaṃ. Vaṅkatā bhamūnaṃyeva, na ajjhāsaye, vaṅkatānatattaṃ saṭhattañca siliṭṭhaṃ. Atirattatā pāṇipādādharānaṃyeva, na citte, atirattatāguṇo rāgo ca silissate. “Munindassā”ti “kaṇhatta”ntiādīsu sabbattha sambandhanīyaṃ. Niyamavā sileso kesakkhīnaṃvāti avadhāraṇappayogāti.

297. ‘Kesīnaṃ,’ etc. Blackness is only of the hair and eyes, not of the mind; here the quality of blackness and the state of evil are joined. Curvature is only of the eyebrows, not of the intention; here the quality of being curved and deceit are joined. Excessive redness is only of the hands, feet, and lips, not of the heart; here the quality of excessive redness and passion are joined. ‘Of the Lord of Sages’ is to be connected everywhere with ‘blackness,’ etc. It is a silesa with restriction because of the use of the emphatic particle in such phrases as ‘kesakkhīnaṃ’va’ (only of the hair and eyes).

297. “Kesakkhīna”miccādi. Munindassa kaṇhattaṃ kesakkhīnaṃ eva hoti, kaṇhattasaṅkhatamakusalaṃ na citte. Vaṅkatā bhamūnaṃyeva, najjhāsaye. Atirattatā pāṇipādādharānaṃ eva, na kesuci vatthūsūti. “Kesakkhīnaṃvā”tiādīsu niyamasaṅkhātaavadhāraṇapadassa vijjamānattā kaṇhabhāvena saddhiṃ pāpattassa ca, vaṅkaguṇena saddhiṃ sāṭheyyassa ca, rattaguṇena saddhiṃ rāgassa ca siliṭṭhattā ayaṃ niyamavantasileso nāma. Kesāni ca akkhīni ceti ca, kaṇhassa bhāvoti ca, vaṅkassa bhāvoti ca, pāṇayo ca pādāni ca adharāni cāti ca, atirattassa bhāvoti ca viggaho.

297. ‘Kesakkhīnaṃ’ etc. The blackness of the Lord of Sages is solely of the hair and eyes; unwholesome blackness is not in his mind. The curvature is solely of the eyebrows, not in his disposition. The excessive redness is solely of the hands, feet, and lips, not in any objects. In phrases like ‘Kesakkhīnaṃvā’ etc., because words denoting restriction, known as determination, are present, and because the state of blackness is punned with evil, the quality of curvature with deceit, and the quality of redness with lust, this is called the `niyamavantasilesa`. ‘Hair and eyes,’ ‘the state of blackness,’ ‘the state of curvature,’ ‘hands and feet and lips,’ and ‘the state of excessive redness’ are the analyses.

Niyamakkhepasilesa

Pun of Rejected Restriction

298.

298.

Pāṇipādādharesveva, sārāgo tava dissati;

Dissate so’ya’matha vā, nātha sādhuguṇesvapi.

In your hands, feet, and lips alone is ardor seen; or rather, O Protector, it is seen even in virtuous qualities.

298. “Pāṇi”ccādi. Nātha tava pāṇipādādharesveva sārāgo sobhano rattavaṇṇo dissati, na citte, sārāgo rattavaṇṇo chandarāgo cāti siliṭṭhaṃ. Ayaṃ niyamo akkhipyate. Atha vā kathaṃ niyamyate, yato so ayaṃ sārāgo sādhūnaṃ guṇesveva virāgalakkhaṇo dissate iti. Tasmā kathamavadhārīyatīti niyamakkhepavacano silesoyaṃ.

298. ‘Pāṇi’ etc. O Protector, your `sārāga`, which is a beautiful red color, is seen only in your hands, feet, and lips, not in your mind; `sārāga` is a pun on red color and passionate desire (`chandarāga`). This restriction is rejected. Or how can it be restricted, since this very `sārāga`, characterized by dispassion, is seen in the virtues of the good? Therefore, this is a pun that speaks of rejecting a restriction, asking, “How can it be determined?”

298. “Pāṇi”ccādi. [M 0.0287] He nātha tava sārāgo sobhano rattavaṇṇo pāṇipādādharesveva dissati, citte lobho pana na dissati. Atha vā so ayaṃ sārāgo kattukamyatākusalacchandabhūto sādhuguṇesvapi sajjanānaṃ sīlādiguṇesupi dissati. “Evā”ti dassitaniyamassa paṭisedhakena “atha vā”ti vacanena samannāgatattā rattavaṇṇasaṅkhātarāgena lobhassa siliṭṭhattā ca ayaṃ niyamakkhepavacanasileso. Saṃ sobhano rāgoti viggaho.

298. ‘Pāṇi’ etc. O Protector, your `sārāga`, which is a beautiful red color, is seen only in your hands, feet, and lips, but greed is not seen in your mind. Or rather, this `sārāga`, being a wholesome desire to act, is seen even in the virtuous qualities of good people, such as moral virtue and so on. Because it is accompanied by the phrase ‘atha vā,’ which negates the restriction indicated by ‘eva,’ and because of the punned connection of greed with the passion (`rāga`) known as red color, this is a pun that speaks of rejecting a restriction. The analysis is: `Saṃ`, a beautiful passion.

Avirodhisilesa

Non-contradictory Pun

299.

299.

Salakkhaṇo’tisubhago,

Tejassī niyatodayo;

Lokeso jitasaṃkleso,

Vibhāti samaṇissaro.

Possessing marks, supremely beautiful, radiant, of certain rising, Lord of the world, conqueror of defilements, the sovereign of ascetics shines forth.

299. “Salakkhaṇo”iccādi. Saha lakkhaṇena sasarūpena dvattiṃ savarapurisalakkhaṇena vā vattamāno salakkhaṇo, cando munindo ca, atisubhago so ca, tejassī sūriyo pabhāvisesayutto ca, niyato patidinamudayo pabhālakkhaṇo yassa so niyatodayo, sūriyo, niyato thiro udayo sammāsambuddho sambodhirūpo yassa so niyatodayo, munindo, lokeso brahmā munindo ca, jito saṃkleso jhānarativasena kāyacittābādho yena so, brahmā, jito saṃkleso dasavidho aggamaggaññāṇalābhā yena so. So maṇīnaṃ issaro upamaṇi uttamamaṇi (?), samaṇānaṃ issaro munindo vibhātīti yojjaṃ. Ayamavirodhisileso lakkhaṇasubhagādīnamubhayatthāpi abyavahitattā.

299. ‘Salakkhaṇo’ etc. ‘Salakkhaṇo’ (possessing marks) means existing with its own characteristic form or with the thirty-two excellent marks of a great man, referring to both the moon and the Lord of Sages; and ‘atisubhago’ (supremely beautiful) also refers to him. ‘Tejassī’ (radiant) refers to the sun, endowed with special splendor. ‘Niyatodayo’ (of certain rising) refers to the sun, whose daily rising is fixed and characterized by radiance; and it refers to the Lord of Sages, whose rising is steadfast, being the Perfectly Enlightened One whose nature is enlightenment. ‘Lokeso’ (lord of the world) refers to both Brahmā and the Lord of Sages. ‘Jitasaṃkleso’ (conqueror of defilements) refers to Brahmā, by whom bodily and mental afflictions are conquered through the delight of jhāna; and it refers to the Lord of Sages, by whom the tenfold defilements are conquered through obtaining the knowledge of the supreme path. It should be construed that he, the sovereign of gems and the sovereign of ascetics, the Lord of Sages, shines forth. This is a non-contradictory pun, as the qualities of possessing marks, being beautiful, and so on, apply to both meanings without conflict.

299. “Salakkhaṇo”iccādi. [M 0.0288] Salakkhaṇo lakkhaṇena sahito, atisubhago atisundarāya lakkhiyā samannāgato, no ce, dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇehi sahito ativiya sobhādīhi yutto, tejassī andhakāravidhamanasaṅkhatamahānubhāvena yutto, niyatodayo patidinaṃ pubbaṇhakāle niyamitagaganuggamano, no ce, nirantarapavattabuddhatejasā yutto thirasabbaññupadavisaṅkhātābhivuḍḍhiyā samannāgato, lokeso brahmabhūto, jitasaṃkleso jhānapītiyā vijitakāyacittadaratho, no ce, tilokassa issarabhūto catutthamaggaññāṇena hatadasavidhasaṃkileso, samaṇissaro so uttamo maṇi vibhāti sobhati, no ce, samaṇānaṃ issaro vibhāti dibbatīti. “Salakkhaṇo subhago”iccādikānaṃ dvinnaṃ padānaṃ aviruddhattā ca, paṭhamapāde candena dutiye sūriyena tatiye brahmunā catutthe maṇinā ca sabbaññupadatthassa siliṭṭhattā ca ayaṃ avirodhisileso nāma. Saha lakkhaṇena vattamānoti ca, atisobhano bhago sirī vā sirīkāmapayatanādiko vā assāti ca, tejo assa atthīti ca, niyato udayo asseti ca, lokassa iso issaroti ca, jito saṃkleso yeneti ca, maṇīnaṃ samaṇānaṃ vā issaroti ca vākyaṃ.

299. ‘Salakkhaṇo’ etc. ‘Salakkhaṇo’ means endowed with marks, and ‘atisubhago’ means endowed with extremely beautiful fortune; alternatively, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man and possessed of surpassing splendor and so on. ‘Tejassī’ means endowed with the great power that dispels darkness. ‘Niyatodayo’ means one whose ascent into the sky is fixed each day at dawn; alternatively, endowed with the uninterrupted radiance of a Buddha and possessed of the growth known as the steadfast state of omniscience. ‘Lokeso’ means one who has become Brahmā. ‘Jitasaṃkleso’ means one who has conquered bodily and mental distress through the bliss of jhāna; alternatively, one who has become the lord of the three worlds and has destroyed the ten kinds of defilements with the knowledge of the fourth path. ‘Samaṇissaro’ means that supreme jewel shines and is beautiful; alternatively, the sovereign of ascetics shines and is resplendent. Because the two terms ‘Salakkhaṇo subhago,’ etc., are non-contradictory, and because the meaning related to the state of omniscience is punned with the moon in the first line, the sun in the second, Brahmā in the third, and the jewel in the fourth, this is called the non-contradictory pun. The analytical phrases are: ‘one who exists with marks’; ‘he has a most beautiful fortune (`bhaga`), or splendor (`sirī`), or striving for the desire of splendor, etc.’; ‘he has radiance’; ‘his rising is certain’; ‘the lord and master of the world’; ‘by whom defilements are conquered’; and ‘the lord of jewels or of ascetics.’

Virodhisilesa

Contradictory Pun

300.

300.

Asamopi samo loke,

Lokesopi naruttamo;

Sadayopya’dayo pāpe,

Cittā’yaṃ munino gati.

Even though incomparable, he is equal in the world; even though Lord of the world, he is supreme among men; even though compassionate, he is without compassion towards evil; this is the astonishing way of the sage.

300. “Asamopi”ccādi. Natthi samo rājaguṇādīhi assāti asamo, koci rājādi, “asamo”ti lokekasikhāmaṇibhāvena [M 0.0289] muni. Tattha yadā asamo rājādi, tadā loke samoti viruddhaṃ asamattā tassa. Apisaddo virodhaṃ joteti. Pakkhantare tvaviruddhaṃ, loke devadattādīnaṃ virodhisattānaṃ rāhulādīnaṃ avirodhisattānañca samattā, tatoyevāyaṃ virodhābhāsānañcasā virodhoyeva. Lokeso brahmā muni ca. Tattha “brahmā naruttamo”ti viruddhaṃ dibbayonittā tassa. Pakkhantare tvabyāghāto uttamanarattā tassa. Dayo dānaṃ, saha dayenāti sadayo, koci puriso. Saha dayāya vattatīti sadayo, muni. Tattha puriso dāyako pāpe jane kathamadayoti virujjhati. Muni pāpe rāgādike adayoti virujjhati. Tasmā munino ayaṃ yathāvuttā gati pavatti cittā abbhutāti ayaṃ vuttanayena virodhisileso udāhaṭo.

300. ‘Asamopi’ etc. ‘Asamo’ means one who has no equal in royal qualities and so on, referring to some king; or ‘asamo’ means the sage, by being the single crest-jewel of the world. In the first case, when ‘asamo’ refers to a king, the statement that he is ‘samo’ (equal) in the world is a contradiction of his incomparability. The particle ‘api’ indicates the contradiction. In the alternative interpretation, however, there is no contradiction, because of his equality towards opposing beings like Devadatta and non-opposing beings like Rāhula. Therefore, this is an apparent contradiction which is indeed a contradiction. ‘Lokeso’ refers to both Brahmā and the sage. In that case, ‘Brahmā is the supreme among men’ is a contradiction due to his divine birth. In the alternative interpretation, there is no conflict, due to the sage’s being the supreme man. ‘Daya’ means giving. ‘Sadayo’ means ‘with giving,’ referring to some person. ‘Sadayo’ also means ‘acting with compassion,’ referring to the sage. In the first case, for a person who is a giver, how can he be ‘adayo’ (without giving) to a person in need? This is a contradiction. In the second case, for the sage, to be ‘adayo’ (without compassion) towards evils like lust is also a contradiction to his general compassion. Therefore, this aforementioned way and conduct of the sage is astonishing. Thus, this contradictory pun has been exemplified in the manner stated.

300. “Asamo”iccādi. Asamopi atulyopi koci rājādiko loke samo tulyo, no ce, sadisapuggalarahito eva rāhulabhadradevadattādisabbaloke anunayapaṭighābhāvena samo hoti. Lokesopi brahmabhūtopi naruttamo naravaro hoti, no ce, sakalalokādhipati hutvā eva naruttamo. Sadayopi yācakesu dayasaṅkhātena dānena yuttopi pāpe pāpiṭṭhe adayo dānarahito, no ce, dayāsahito eva akusale niddayo. Munino ayaṃ gati pavatti cittā vicittāti rājādino asamasamatā ca, brahmā hutvā uttamanarabhāvo ca, dānasahitassa kassaci purisassa dānarahitabhāvo ca viruddho hoti. Tasmā rājabrahmapurisehi munino siliṭṭhattā ayaṃ virodhisileso nāma. Pubbapubbapakkhe virodho aparāparapakkhehi nirākato hoti. Pubbapakkhe apisaddo virodhaṃ joteti, aparapakkhe avadhāraṇanti. [M 0.0290] Natthi samo yasseti ca, naro ca so uttamo ceti ca, saha dayena dayāya vā vattamānoti ca, natthi dayo dayā vā asseti ca viggaho.

300. ‘Asamo’ etc. Even though incomparable (`asamo`) or unequal (`atulyo`), some king is equal (`samo`, `tulyo`) in the world; alternatively, being one without a similar person, he is equal towards the entire world, including Rāhula, Bhadra, and Devadatta, by being devoid of attraction and aversion. Even though Lord of the world (`lokeso`), having become Brahmā, he is the supreme man (`naruttamo`); alternatively, having become the sovereign of the entire world, he is the supreme man. Even though compassionate (`sadayo`), being endowed with the giving (`daya`) towards beggars, he is without giving (`adayo`) towards the wicked; alternatively, being endowed with compassion (`dayā`), he is merciless (`niddayo`) towards the unwholesome. This way and conduct of the sage is astonishing (`cittā`) and varied (`vicittā`). The incomparability and equality of a king, the state of being the supreme man after having become Brahmā, and the state of being without giving for a person endowed with giving—these are contradictory. Therefore, because of the punned connection of the sage with a king, Brahmā, and a person, this is called the contradictory pun. In each former case, the contradiction is resolved by the latter case. In the former case, the particle ‘api’ indicates contradiction; in the latter, it indicates emphasis. The analyses are: ‘one who has no equal’; ‘he is a man and he is supreme’; ‘one who acts with giving or with compassion’; and ‘he has no giving or compassion.’

Ocityasamposakapadasilesa

Pun of a Word Fostering Appropriateness

301.

301.

Saṃsāradukkhopahatā-vanatā janatā tvayi;

Sukha’micchita’maccantaṃ, amatandada vindati.

The people, afflicted by the suffering of saṃsāra and bowed down before you, O Giver of the Deathless, obtain the happiness they exceedingly desire.

301. Udāharati “saṃsāre”ccādi. Saṃsāro abbocchinnaṃ vattamānā khandhapaṭipāṭiyeva dukkhaṃ dukkhamattādinā, tena upahatā pahaṭā janatā, amataṃ sukhaṃ amataṃ vā nibbānaṃ dadātīti amatandadāti āmantanaṃ, tvayi avanatā paṇāmavasena icchitamatimataṃ dukkhāpagamanibbattaṃ kāyikaṃ cetasikañca sukhaṃ accantaṃ vindati paṭilabhatīti. Ettha amataṃ sudhā nibbānañca, amatandado dukkhopahate sukhayatīti ucitanti “amataṃ dadātī”ti padamadhigate vatthuni ocityaṃ samposayatīti ocityasamposako padasilesoyaṃ. Ādisaddena “sugandhisobhāsambandhī”tyādyupamāsilesādayo saṅgahitāti.

301. He exemplifies with 'in saṃsāra' and so on. Saṃsāra is the uninterrupted succession of aggregates, which is suffering itself, by way of being suffering, etc.; by that, the people are afflicted and struck down. 'Amatandada' is a vocative, meaning 'he gives deathless happiness or deathless Nibbāna.' Bowed down to you, by way of reverence, they utterly obtain the physical and mental happiness desired by the mind, born from the cessation of suffering. Here, 'amata' is nectar and Nibbāna, and 'amatandada' makes those afflicted by suffering happy, thus it is fitting. Therefore, the phrase 'amataṃ dadāti' (gives the deathless), in the understood context, fosters appropriateness; this is a paronomasia that fosters appropriateness. By the word 'etc.,' similes involving paronomasia, such as 'related to fragrance and beauty,' and so on are included.

301. “Saṃsāra”iccādi. Saṃsāradukkhopahatā khandhadhātuāyatanānaṃ nirantarapavattisaṅkhātena dukkhena upahatā janatā, amatandada he sudhādāyaka no ce, nibbānadāyaka tathāgata tvayi avanatā paṇamanavasena onatā icchitaṃ abhimataṃ sukhaṃ kāyikacetasikasukhaṃ accantaṃ atisayena vindati sevatīti. Amatadāyakā dukkhite sukhite karontīti idaṃ ucitameveti ubhayatthassāpi vācakaṃ “amataṃ dadātī”ti padaṃ tādisajanassa sukhadāne ocityaṃ posetīti ayaṃ ocityasamposakapadasileso. Saṃsāroyeva dukkhanti ca, tena upahatāti ca, amataṃ sudhaṃ nibbānaṃ vā dadātīti ca vākyaṃ.

301. "Saṃsāra" and so on. The populace is afflicted by the suffering of saṃsāra—by the suffering characterized as the continuous occurrence of aggregates, elements, and sense bases. O giver of the deathless, O giver of ambrosia, or O Tathāgata, giver of Nibbāna, those bowing down to you in reverence obtain and experience their desired and cherished physical and mental happiness exceedingly. That givers of the deathless make the afflicted happy is indeed fitting. Thus, the phrase 'amataṃ dadāti' (gives the deathless), which denotes both meanings, fosters appropriateness in giving happiness to such a person; this is a paronomasia that fosters appropriateness. The sentences are: 'Saṃsāra is itself suffering,' and 'they are afflicted by it,' and 'he gives the deathless, ambrosia, or Nibbāna.'

302.

302.

Guṇayuttehi [M 0.0291] vatthūhi, samaṃ katvāna kassaci;

Saṃkittanaṃ bhavati yaṃ, sā matā tulyayogitā.

When a description of someone is made by equating them with objects endowed with qualities, that is considered Tulyayogitā.

302. Tulyayogitaṃ yojayati “guṇe”ccādinā. Guṇo dhammo sādhu asādhu vā, tena yuttehi vatthūhi saha samaṃ katvāna vatthuto asāmyepi tathābhāvamāropya kassaci purisādino thutinindatthaṃ yaṃ kittanamākhyānaṃ, sā tulyakkhaṇā tulyayogitā matā, vattumicchitena guṇena tādisānaṃ tulyayogitāpaṭipādanato tadatthiyena tulyayogitā tathā dvidhā vattati.

302. He applies 'Tulyayogitā' with 'guṇa' and so on. A quality (guṇa) is a property, whether good or bad; and having made objects endowed with that quality equal—even when they are unequal in reality—by imposing such a state of similarity for the purpose of praising or blaming some person or the like, that description or narration is considered 'Tulyayogitā,' having equal characteristics. Because it establishes the 'equal connection' for such things by means of the quality desired to be expressed, 'Tulyayogitā' thus functions in two ways, serving that purpose.

302. Idāni tulyayogitālaṅkāraṃ dasseti “guṇayuttehi”iccādinā. Guṇayuttehi sundarāsundarehi yehi kehici guṇehi yuttehi vatthūhi, samaṃ katvāna tatvato asamānesupi samānattabuddhiyā āropanaṃ katvā, kassaci purisādino thutiṃ nindaṃ vā nissāya yaṃ saṃkittanaṃ guṇāguṇakathanaṃ bhavati, sā tulyayogitāti matāti. Guṇehi yuttāti ca, tulyena guṇena saha yogoti ca, so etesaṃ raṃsimālībhagavantādīnamatthīti ca, tesaṃ bhāvo tulyaguṇasambandhoti ca viggaho. Ettha tulyaguṇayuttapadatthānaṃ tagguṇasambandhassa tulyayogitābhāvato tappaṭipādako uttiviseso tadatthiyena tulyayogitāti ñeyyā.

302. Now, he explains the figure of speech 'Tulyayogitā' with 'guṇayuttehi' and so on. By 'guṇayuttehi' (endowed with qualities) is meant objects endowed with any qualities, whether beautiful or ugly. Having made them equal, even though they are inherently unequal, by imposing the perception of equality, that narration of virtues or faults, which arises based on the praise or blame of some person or the like, is considered 'Tulyayogitā.' And 'endowed with qualities,' and 'connection with an equal quality,' and 'this exists for these, such as the radiant one and the Blessed One,' and 'their state is the connection of equal qualities'—these are the analyses. Here, since the connection with those qualities for things whose meaning is 'endowed with equal qualities' is the state of 'Tulyayogitā,' the special expression conveying that meaning should be known as 'Tulyayogitā' by virtue of its purpose.

303.

303.

Sampattasammado loko,

Sampattālokasampado;

Ubhohi raṃsimālī ca,

Bhagavā ca tamonudo.

The world has attained joy, has attained the wealth of light; both the radiant one and the Blessed One are dispellers of darkness.

303. Udāharati “sampatte”ccādi. Tamaṃ nudatīti tamonudo. Raṃsimālī sūriyo ca, atha vā sammāsambuddho cāti ubhohi karaṇabhūtehi hetubhūtehi vā [M 0.0292] loko sattaloko, sampatto sammado pīti yena tathāvidho ca, sampatto ālokassa sampadā yena tathāvidho cāpīti. Ettha pītidānādiguṇayuttena raṃsimālinā samaṃ katvā bhagavato thutivasena kittananti lakkhaṇaṃ yojanīyaṃ.

303. He exemplifies with 'sampatte' and so on. 'Tamonudo' means 'he dispels darkness.' The radiant one is the sun, or else the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. By both as instrumental causes or causal factors, the world, the world of beings, is such that it has attained joy and delight, and it has attained the wealth of light. Here, the characteristic of praise and glorification of the Blessed One should be applied by comparing Him to the radiant one, who is endowed with qualities like bestowing joy and so on.

303. Idāni udāharati “sampatti”ccādinā. Tamonudo andhakāraṃ paharanto raṃsimālī ca bhagavā ca ubhohi karaṇabhūtehi hetubhūtehi vā, loko sattaloko sampattasammado paṭiladdhapītiko ca sampattālokasampadā ca hotīti. Ettha pītidānālokakaraṇasaṅkhātaguṇayuttena sūriyena tulyaṃ katvā bhagavato thutivasena guṇakathanaṃ hoti. Sampatto sammado pīti yeneti ca, ālokassa sampadāti ca, sampattā ālokasampadā yeneti ca, tamaṃ nudatīti ca vākyaṃ. Udāharaṇe adassitepi asādhuguṇayuttena kenaci vatthunā samaṃ katvā kassaci kātabbanindāpi evameva daṭṭhabbā.

303. Now, he exemplifies with 'sampatti' and so on. The dispeller of darkness, the radiant one, striking away darkness, and the Blessed One—by both as instrumental causes or causal factors, the world, the world of beings, becomes one who has attained joy and delight, and has attained the wealth of light. Here, a description of the qualities by way of praise of the Blessed One is made by comparing Him to the sun, which is endowed with qualities characterized as giving joy and creating light. And the sentences are: 'one by whom joy and delight are attained,' and 'the wealth of light,' and 'one by whom the wealth of light is attained,' and 'he dispels darkness.' Even if not shown in the example, blame to be made of someone by comparing them with some object possessing unsuitable qualities should be understood in just this way.

304.

304.

Atthantaraṃ sādhayatā, kiñci taṃsadisaṃ phalaṃ;

Dassīyate asantaṃ vā, santaṃ vā taṃ nidassanaṃ.

When, by one accomplishing a different meaning, some result similar to that is shown, whether non-existent or existent, that is 'Nidassana'.

304. Nidassanaṃ padasseti “atthantara”miccādinā. Atthantaraṃ nidassetabbāpekkhāya aññaṃ kiñci ucitaṃ kāriyaṃ sādhayatā kenaci vatthunā hetubhūtena, tena atthantareneva sadisaṃ tulyaṃ phalaṃ kiñci asantaṃ aniṭṭhaṃ vā santaṃ iṭṭhaṃ vā dassīyate paṭipādīyate, taṃ evaṃlakkhaṇaṃ nidassanaṃ siyā.

304. He explains 'Nidassana' with 'atthantara' and so on. By some object serving as a cause, accomplishing some other appropriate action with respect to what is to be illustrated as a different meaning, some result similar or equivalent to that different meaning, whether non-existent (undesirable) or existent (desirable), is shown or conveyed; that which has such a characteristic is 'Nidassana'.

304. Idāni nidassanālaṅkāraṃ nidasseti “atthantari”ccādinā. Atthantaraṃ niddisitabbato aññaṃ ucitakāriyasaṅkhātamattaṃ ucitakicca… (ka.) sādhayatā sādhayantena kenaci vatthunā taṃsadisaṃ [M 0.0293] tena atthantarena samānaṃ asantaṃ aniṭṭhaṃ vā santaṃ iṭṭhaṃ vā kiñci phalaṃ dassīyate vatthūhi paṭipādīyate, taṃ tādisaṃ phalaṃ nidassanaṃ nāmāti. Attho ca so antaro añño cāti ca, tena atthantarena sadisamiti ca, nidassīyateti ca viggaho.

304. Now, he explains the figure of speech 'Nidassana' with 'atthantari' and so on. By some object accomplishing or establishing a mere appropriate action, which is different from what is to be indicated as a different meaning, some result similar to that, equal to that different meaning, whether non-existent (undesirable) or existent (desirable), is shown or conveyed by means of objects; such a result is called 'Nidassana.' And the analysis is: 'that meaning is different and other,' and 'similar to that different meaning,' and 'it is shown.'

Asantaphalanidassana

Illustration of a Non-Existent Result

305.

305.

Udayā samaṇindassa, yanti pāpā parābhavaṃ;

Dhammarājaviruddhānaṃ, sūcayantā dīpayantā (sī.) durantataṃ.

At the arising of the Chief of Ascetics, evils go to ruin, indicating the wretched end of those who oppose the King of Dhamma.

305. “Udayā”iccādi. Samaṇindassa mahāmunino udayā pātubhāvena pāpā lobhādayo parābhavaṃ nidhanaṃ yanti, parābhavantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Udayapubbakena pāpaparābhavanatthantarena sadisaṃ phalaṃ nidasseti. Kiṃ karontā? Dhammarājā dhammānapeto rājā, munindo cāti siliṭṭhaṃ, tena viruddhānaṃ, duṭṭho viruddho anto avasānaṃ yassa, tassa bhāvo, taṃ sūcayantāti dhammarājavirodhahetukaṃ asantaphalametaṃ nidassanaṃ parābhavassāniṭṭhattā.

305. "Udayā" and so on. With the arising, the manifestation, of the great sage, the Chief of Ascetics, evils such as greed go to ruin, to destruction; this means they are defeated. It illustrates a result similar to the other meaning, which is the destruction of evils preceded by the arising. What are they doing? The King of Dhamma is a king not separate from the Dhamma, and also the lord of sages—thus it is a paronomasia. Indicating the state of those opposed to him, whose end is wicked and hostile—this illustration is of a non-existent result caused by opposition to the King of Dhamma, due to the undesirability of ruin.

305. Idāni udāharati “udayā”iccādinā. Samaṇindassa munindassa udayā loke pātubhāvena pāpā lobhādayo dhammarājaviruddhānaṃ rājadhammehi samannāgatarājūhi, dhammādhipatinā munindena vā viruddhānaṃ durantataṃ aniṭṭhāvasānataṃ sūcayantā pakāsento parābhavaṃ parihāniṃ yanti pāpuṇantīti. Ettha pubbaddhena udayapubbako pāpaparābhavanasaṅkhāto atthantaro dassito, aparaddhena taṃsadisavirodhahetukaṃ durantasaṅkhātaṃ asantaphalaṃ dasseti. Dhammarājavirodhahetukaṃ asantaphalametaṃ parābhavassāniṭṭhattā. Samaṇānamindoti ca, dhammena yutto rājāti vā dhammesu rājāti [M 0.0294] vāti ca, tena viruddhāti ca, duṭṭho virūpo anto pariyosānaṃ yesamiti ca, tesaṃ bhāvoti ca vākyaṃ.

305. Now, it is illustrated with "Udayā" and so on. With the arising, the manifestation, in the world of the Chief of Ascetics, the Lord of Sages, evils such as greed—indicating and revealing the wretched end, the undesirable conclusion, of those opposed to the King of Dhamma (whether kings endowed with royal virtues, or the Lord of Dhamma, the Sage)—go to ruin, to decline, they attain it. Here, by the first half of the verse, another meaning is shown, namely, the destruction of evils preceded by the arising of the Buddha; by the latter half, an undesirable result, namely, a wretched end caused by similar opposition, is shown. This is an undesirable result caused by opposition to the King of Dhamma, due to the undesirability of ruin. And the grammatical analyses are: 'Chief of ascetics,' and 'a king endowed with Dhamma' or 'a king in the Dhammas,' and 'opposed to him,' and 'whose end, or conclusion, is wicked and perverse,' and 'their state.'

Santaphalanidassana

Illustration of a Desirable Result

306.

306.

Sironikkhittacaraṇo-

Cchariyāna’mbujāna’yaṃ;

Paramabbhutataṃ loke,

Viññāpeta’ttano jino.

This Victor, whose feet are placed on the heads of wondrous lotuses, makes known in the world his own supreme, wondrous nature.

306. “Siro”ccādi. Acchariyānaṃ bhagavato caraṇāravindadvandasampaṭiggahaṇatthaṃ pathaviṃ bhinditvā samuggatānamacchariyaguṇopetānamambujānaṃ sirasi matthake nikkhittā caraṇā yena so jino. Ambujoparicaraṇanikkhepalakkhaṇenatthantarena sadisaṃ phalaṃ dasseti. Attano paramacchariyabhāvaṃ viññāpeti. Santaphalamidaṃ nidassanaṃ jinabbhutatthadīpanassa iṭṭhattāti.

306. "Siro" and so on. The Victor is he whose feet were placed on the heads, the crowns, of wondrous lotuses—lotuses endowed with marvelous qualities that had broken through the earth and risen up to receive the Blessed One's pair of lotus-like feet. By another meaning, characterized by the placing of feet upon lotuses, it illustrates a similar result. He makes known his own supreme, wondrous nature. This illustration is of a desirable result, as the illumination of the Victor's wondrous meaning is desirable.

306. “Siro”iccādi. Ayaṃ jino acchariyānaṃ attano pādapaṭiggahaṇatthaṃ pathaviṃ bhinditvā uggatattā accharāpaharaṇayoggānaṃ ambujānaṃ sironikkhittacaraṇo matthake ṭhapitapādo loke sattaloke attano paramabbhutataṃ atiacchariyaguṇaṃ viññāpeti avabodhetīti. Ettha acchariyapadumānaṃ matthake caraṇanikkhepasaṅkhātena atthantarena paramabbhutataṃ viññāpetīti ayaṃ sadisasantaphalaṃ jinabbhutatthadīpanassa iṭṭhattā. Sirasi nikkhittāni caraṇāni yeneti ca, accharaṃ accharāsaṅghātaṃ arahantīti ca, paramo uttamo abbhuto guṇo asseti ca, tassa bhāvoti ca viggaho.

306. "Siro" and so on. This Victor, whose feet were placed on the heads of wondrous lotuses—lotuses worthy of a host of celestial nymphs, having broken through the earth and risen up to receive his feet—makes known, makes understood, in the world, in the realm of beings, his own supreme wondrous nature, his exceedingly wondrous quality. Here, by another meaning, characterized by the placing of feet on the heads of wondrous lotuses, he makes known his supreme wondrous nature; this is a similar desirable result, as the illumination of the Victor's wondrous meaning is desirable. And the grammatical analyses are: 'he by whom the feet were placed on the head,' and 'they are worthy of a host of celestial nymphs,' and 'his quality is supreme, highest, and wondrous,' and 'the state of that.'

307.

307.

Vibhūtiyāmahantattaṃ, adhippāyassa vā siyā;

Paramukkaṃsataṃ yātaṃ, taṃ mahantatta’mīritaṃ.

Greatness may be of manifestation or of intention; that which has reached supreme excellence is said to be greatness.

307. Mahantattamupadasseti [M 0.0295] “vibhūtiyā”iccādinā. Vibhūtiyā sampattiyā adhippāyassa vā ajjhāsayassa vā paramukkaṃsataṃ paramātisayabhāvaṃ yātaṃ upagataṃ mahantattaṃ nāma īritaṃ kathitaṃ.

307. He displays greatness with "vibhūtiyā" and so on. Greatness is said, is declared, to be that which has reached, has attained, the supreme excellence, the state of supreme superiority, of manifestation, of prosperity, or of intention, of aspiration.

307. Idāni mahantattālaṅkāraṃ dasseti “vibhūti” iccādinā. Vibhūtiyā sampattiyā vā adhippāyassa ajjhāsayassa vā paramukkaṃsataṃ atyukkaṃsabhāvaṃ yātaṃ yaṃ mahantattaṃ siyā, taṃ mahantattamiti īritanti. Mahato bhāvoti ca, paramo ukkaṃso atisayo yasseti ca, tassa bhāvoti ca vākyaṃ.

307. Now, he shows the figure of speech of greatness with "vibhūti" and so on. That greatness which may be, which has reached the supreme excellence, the state of exceeding excellence, of manifestation, of prosperity, or of intention, of aspiration, is said to be greatness. And the grammatical analyses are: 'the state of the great,' and 'whose excellence is supreme, surpassing,' and 'the state of that.'

Vibhūtimahantatta

Greatness of Manifestation

308.

308.

Kirīṭaratanacchāyā-nuviddhātapavāraṇo;

Purā paraṃ siriṃ vindi, bodhisatto’bhinikkhamā.

The Bodhisatta, whose parasol was suffused with the radiance of the crown-jewels, attained supreme glory before his renunciation.

308. Udāharati “kirīṭe”ccādi. Abhinikkhamā purā pubbe bodhisatto māyādeviyā putto paramukkaṭṭhaṃ anāññasādhāraṇaṃ siriṃ vibhūtiṃ vindi paṭilabhi. Kīdiso? Kirīṭe makuṭe ratanānaṃ chāyāhi sobhāhi anuviddho churito ātapavāraṇo setacchattaṃ yassa so tādisoti vibhūtiyā mahantattaṃ vuttaṃ “ātapavāraṇo ratanacchāyānuviddho”ti.

308. He illustrates with "kirīṭe" and so on. Before his renunciation, previously, the Bodhisatta, the son of Queen Māyā, attained, acquired, supreme, unparalleled glory and splendor. What was he like? He was such that his sunshade, his white parasol, was suffused, interwoven, with the radiance, the splendor, of the jewels in his crown, in his diadem. Thus the greatness of his manifestation is stated: 'his sunshade was suffused with the radiance of jewels.'

308. Idāni udāharati “kirīṭa”iccādinā. Bodhisatto antimajātiyaṃ mahābodhisatto abhinikkhamā abhinikkhamanato purā pubbe kirīṭaratanacchāyānuviddhātapavāraṇo moliratanaraṃsīhi rañjitasetacchatto paramukkaṭṭhaṃ siriṃ vibhūtiṃ vindi anubhavīti. Ettha moliratanakantiyā setacchattassa oviddhabhāvakathanena vibhūtiyā mahantattaṃ hoti. Kirīṭe ratanānīti ca, tesaṃ chāyāyoti [M 0.0296] ca, tāhi anuviddho churito ātapavāraṇo yasseti ca vākyaṃ.

308. Now, he illustrates with "kirīṭa" and so on. The Bodhisatta, the Great Bodhisatta in his final existence, before his renunciation, experienced, attained, supreme glory and splendor, being one whose sunshade was suffused with the radiance of the crown-jewels, whose white parasol was colored by the rays of the crest-jewel. Here, by stating that the white parasol was suffused by the luster of the crest-jewel, the greatness of his manifestation is shown. And the grammatical analyses are: 'jewels in the crown,' and 'by their radiance,' and 'he whose sunshade was suffused, interwoven, by them.'

Adhippāyamahantatta

Greatness of Intention

309.

309.

Satto sambodhiyaṃ bodhi-

Satto sattahitāya so;

Hitvā sneharasābaddha-

Mapi rāhulamātaraṃ.

That Bodhisatta, a being intent on enlightenment, for the welfare of beings, abandoned even Rāhula’s mother, though she was bound by the essence of affection.

309. “Satto”iccādi. Snehena piyabhāvena jātena rasena rāgena ābaddhamattani rāhulamātaraṃ bimbādevimpi, kimutaññaṃ yuvatijanaṃ, hitvā anapekkhitvā anāsatto hutvā sattānaṃ hitāya lokiyalokuttarāya vaḍḍhiyā bodhisatto siddhattho sambodhiyaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇeyeva satto āsatto, tattheva laggoti adhippāyo. Mahantattamukkaṭṭhaṃ tādisavanitāratanānāsajjanalakkhaṇamālakkhīyatīti.

309. “Satto”—and so forth. Having abandoned, disregarded, and become unattached to Rāhula’s mother, Bimbādevī herself, who was bound to him by affection, by love, by the essence born of fondness, by passion—how much more so to other young women—the Bodhisatta Siddhattha, for the welfare of beings, for their worldly and supramundane growth, was intent and attached solely to enlightenment, to omniscient knowledge; that is the intention. His greatness and excellence are discerned by the characteristic of not being attached to such a jewel among women.

309. “Satto”iccādi. So bodhisatto sneharasābaddhaṃ piyabhāvasaṅkhātarāgena ābaddhaṃ rāhulamātaraṃ api bimbādevimpi hitvā sattahitāya sattānaṃ lokiyalokuttaratthāya sambodhiyaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇeyeva satto laggoti. Tādisaitthiratanepi alaggatākathanena bodhisattassa ukkaṭṭhajjhāsayamahantattaṃ vuttaṃ hoti. Sammā bujjhati etāyāti ca, bodhiyaṃ satto laggoti ca, sattānaṃ hitamiti ca, snehena piyabhāvena jāto raso rāgoti ca, tena ābaddhāti ca viggaho.

309. “Satto”—and so forth. That Bodhisatta, having abandoned even Rāhula’s mother, Bimbādevī, who was bound by the essence of affection, by passion known as the state of dearness, was intent and attached solely to enlightenment, to omniscient knowledge, for the welfare of beings, for their worldly and supramundane benefit. By stating his non-attachment even to such a jewel of a woman, the greatness of the Bodhisatta's superior intention is declared. And the grammatical analyses are: “By this one rightly awakens,” and “he is attached to enlightenment,” and “it is for the welfare of beings,” and “the essence born from affection and dearness is passion,” and “bound by that.”

310.

310.

Gopetvā vaṇṇanīyaṃ yaṃ,

Kiñci dassīyate paraṃ;

Asamaṃ vā samaṃ tassa,

Yadi sā vañcanā matā.

If, having concealed something praiseworthy, something else is shown—whether unequal or equal to it—that is considered deception.

310. Vañcanaṃ [M 0.0297] vadati “gopetvā”iccādinā, vaṇṇanīyaṃ kiñci vatthuṃ gopetvā niraṃkatvā tassa vaṇṇanīyassa asamaṃ visamaṃ visadisaṃ paramaññaṃ yaṃ kiñci vatthu yadi dassīyate kavināti anuvaditvā sā vañcanā matāti vidhīyate.

310. He speaks of deception with “gopetvā” and so on. Having repeated that if a poet, having concealed and disregarded some praiseworthy thing, presents any other thing—unequal, uneven, dissimilar, or utterly different from that praiseworthy thing—it is considered deception, it is so defined.

310. Idāni vañcanālaṅkāraṃ dasseti “gopetvā”iccādinā. Vaṇṇanīyaṃ kiñci vatthuṃ gopetvā tassa vaṇṇanīyassa samaṃ sadisaṃ vā asamaṃ visadisaṃ vā paraṃ yaṃ kiñci vatthu yadi dassīyate kavinā, sā vañcanāiti matāti. Vañceti vaṇṇanīyaṃ etāya vuttiyāti vākyaṃ.

310. Now, he shows the figure of speech of deception with “gopetvā” and so on. If a poet, having concealed some object to be described, presents any other object—whether equal and similar, or unequal and dissimilar, to that object to be described—that is considered deception. The grammatical analysis is: “It deceives the object to be described by this expression.”

Asamavañcanā

Unequal Deception

311.

311.

Purato na sahassesu,

Na pañcesu ca tādino;

Māro paresu tasse’saṃ,

Sahassaṃ dasavaḍḍhitaṃ.

Before the Such One, Māra is not effective with thousands of arrows, nor with his five. Among others, his thousand arrows are increased tenfold.

311. Udāharati “purato”iccādi. Māro kāmo tādino lobhādīsu tādisattā munino purato sammukhe sahassaṃ isavo assāti sahassesu ca na hoti. Pañca isavo assāti pañcesu ca na hotīti vaṇṇanīyo mārotra gopyate. Tassa yo tibhuvanaṃ jayī. Paresu aññasattesu sarāgesu esamisūnaṃ dasavaḍḍhitaṃ dasahi guṇitaṃ sahassaṃ, kathamaññathābhuvanattayaṃ jayeyyāti māraṃ gopetvā dasasahassopalakkhitavatthantarassa dassitattā asamavañcanāyaṃ.

311. It illustrates by “before”—and so forth. Māra, who is desire, does not exist before the sage, the Such One, who is such with respect to greed and so forth, even among a thousand arrows, should there be a thousand; nor does he exist among five, should there be five. Thus, Māra, who is to be described, is concealed here. Of him who conquered the three worlds—for other beings who are lustful, this thousand of arrows is increased tenfold, multiplied by ten. Otherwise, how could he conquer the three worlds? Because Māra is concealed and another object, characterized by ten thousand, is shown, this is unequal deception.

311. Idāni udāharati “purato”iccādinā. Māro tādino lābhālābhādīsu avikārino tathāgatassa purato abhimukhe sahassesu ca sahassasaropi na hoti, pañcesu pañca isu ca tādise ṭhapetvā pañca isu na hoti. [M 0.0299] Paresu sugatasammukhe īdisesupi aññesu saṃkilesesu tassa tilokajetuno mārassa esaṃ sarānaṃ dasavaḍḍhitaṃ dasagaṇanāya vaḍḍhitaṃ sahassaṃ hoti dasasahassaṃ hotīti. Vaṇṇanīyaṃ māraṃ gopetvā dasasahassasaṅkhyāhi gaṇitassa aññassa sarasaṅkhātavatthuno dassitattā ayaṃ asamavañcanā nāma. Sahassaṃ isavo asseti ca, pañca isavo asseti ca, dasahi vaḍḍhitanti ca vākyaṃ.

311. Now, it illustrates by “before”—and so forth. Māra, before the Tathāgata, who is unchanging in gain and loss and so forth, is not even a thousand arrows among thousands, nor five arrows among five, leaving aside such a one. Among others, even in such defilements in the presence of the Sugata, for that Māra, the conqueror of the three worlds, this thousand of arrows is increased tenfold, multiplied by ten, becoming ten thousand. Because Māra, who is to be described, is concealed, and another object, namely arrows counted by the number ten thousand, is shown, this is called unequal deception. And the statements are: “A thousand arrows may be,” and “five arrows may be,” and “increased tenfold.”

Samavañcanā

Equal Deception

312.

312.

Vivāda’manuyuñjanto,

Munindavadanindunā;

Sampuṇṇo candimā nā’yaṃ;

Chatta’metaṃ manobhuno.

Engaging in dispute with the moon-like face of the Lord of Sages: “This is not the full moon; this is the umbrella of the mind-born one.”

312. “Vivāda”miccādi. Manobhunoti kāmassa. Samavañcanāyaṃ puṇṇacandaṃ niraṃkatvā chattassa dassitattā.

312. “Dispute”—and so forth. “Mind-born” means of Kāma (Desire). In this equal deception, because the full moon is rejected and an umbrella is shown.

312. “Vivāda”iccādi. Munindavadanindunā sabbaññuno mukhacandena vivādaṃ anuyuñjanto sampuṇṇo ayaṃ paccakkho candimā na hoti. Kiñcarahi etaṃ candamaṇḍalaṃ manobhuno anaṅgassa ubbhūtiyaṃ chattaṃ samussitasetacchattanti. Vaṇṇanīyaṃ candamaṇḍalaṃ ṭhapetvā tato aññassa candasadisassa chattassa dassitattā ayaṃ vutti samavañcanā nāma. Munīnaṃ indoti ca, tassa vadanamiti ca, indusadiso indu, munindavadanameva indūti ca, samantato puṇṇoti ca, manasi bhūtoti ca viggaho.

312. “Dispute”—and so forth. Engaging in dispute with the moon-like face of the Lord of Sages, the Omniscient One: “This visible moon is not complete. What then is this moon-disc? It is the umbrella, a raised white parasol, at the rising of the mind-born one, Anaṅga (Kāma).” Because the moon-disc, which is to be described, is set aside, and another umbrella similar to the moon is shown, this expression is called equal deception. And the analysis is: “Lord of sages,” and “his face,” and “moon-like is the moon,” and “the face of the Lord of Sages itself is the moon,” and “fully complete,” and “born in the mind.”

313.

313.

Parānuvattanādīhi, nibbindeni’ha yā katā;

Thutira’ppakate sā’yaṃ, siyā appakatatthuti.

That praise which is made here for the unachieved, by one disgusted with following others and so forth, that would be the Praise of the Unachieved.

313. Appakatatthutiṃ pakāseti “pari”ccādinā. Paresaṃ yesaṃ kesañci anuvattanaṃ sevā, tamādi yesaṃ tehi nibbindena virattena appakate asannihite buddhivisayeyeva iha kismiñci vatthumhi katā yā thuti saṃrādhanaṃ, sāyaṃ appakatatthuti siyā.

313. It explains the Praise of the Unachieved by 'para'—and so forth. Following any others whatsoever is service. By one who is disgusted and detached from those things which begin with that, the praise—that is, propitiation—which is made here for some object that is unachieved, not present, and existing only in the sphere of the intellect, that would be the Praise of the Unachieved.

313. Idāni appakatatthutiṃ dasseti “parānu”ccādinā. Parānuvattanādīhi aññassa yassa kassaci anuvattanādīhi nibbindena ubbegaṃ pattena appakate anadhigate buddhivisaye eva iha imasmiṃ kismiñci vatthumhi katā yā thuti saṃrādhanasaṅkhātā pasaṃsā atthi, sā ayaṃ appakatatthuti nāma siyāti. Paresamanuvattanamiti ca, taṃ ādi yesaṃ parapīḷādīnamiti ca, na pakatoti ca, rakāro sandhijo, appakate katā thutīti ca vākyaṃ.

313. Now, it shows the Praise of the Unachieved by 'parānu'—and so forth. By following others and so forth, that is, by following anyone else whatsoever, by one who has attained weariness and disgust, whatever praise—known as propitiation—is made here for some object that is unachieved, unattained, and existing only in the sphere of the intellect, that would be called the Praise of the Unachieved. And the statements are: 'Following others,' and 'that is the beginning of which things, such as the oppression of others,' and 'not achieved,' and 'the letter 'r' is from sandhi,' and 'praise made for the unachieved.'

314.

314.

Sukhaṃ jīvanti hariṇā, vanesva’parasevino;

Anāyāsopalābhehi, jaladabbaṅkurādibhi.

The deer live happily in the forests, not serving others, with effortlessly obtained water, dabba grass shoots, and so forth.

314. Udāharati “sukha”miccādi. Jalehi dabbaṅkurehi dabbatiṇuggamehi. Ādisaddena tarupallavādīhi. Kīdisehi? Anāyāsena sevāpariklesādinā vinā upalābhehi pāpuṇitabbehi. Paramaññaṃ kiñci na sevanti sīleneti aparasevino. Paracittārādhanabyasanaparammukhā hariṇā vanesu sukhaṃ nirākulaṃ jīvantīti. Ettha rājānuvattanaklesanibbindena sannihitā migavutti pasaṃsitāti.

314. It illustrates by 'happily'—and so forth. With water and shoots of dabba grass, that is, sprouts of dabba grass. By the word 'and so forth,' tree leaves and the like are included. Of what kind? Obtainable without effort, that is, to be acquired without the affliction of service and so forth. 'Not serving others' means they do not serve anyone else by nature. The deer, averse to the vice of pleasing the minds of others, live happily and undisturbed in the forests. Here, the livelihood of deer is praised by one disgusted with the affliction of serving kings.

314. Idāni udāharati “sukha”miccādinā. Hariṇā migā aparasevino vuttiṃ nissāya paraṃ asevamānā anāyāsopalābhehi parapariggahābhāvato parasevāparissamaṃ vinā labbhanīyehi jaladabbaṅkurādibhi udakadabbaṅkurarukkhalatāpallavādīhi vanesu icchiticchitāraññesu sukhaṃ jīvanti sukhajīvanaṃ karontīti. Ettha rājasevābyasanappattena kenaci anadhigatāpi migajīvikā pasaṃsitā hoti. Paraṃ na sevanti sīlenāti ca, abhāvo āyāsasseti ca, [M 0.0300] tena upalabhitabbāti ca, dabbānaṃ aṅkurānīti ca, jalañca dabbaṅkurāni ceti ca, tāni ādi yesaṃ pallavādīnamiti ca viggaho.

314. Now, it illustrates by 'happily'—and so forth. The deer, not serving others, relying on a livelihood of not serving another, live happily, making a happy life, in whatever forests they desire, with things obtainable without effort—that is, obtainable without the toil of serving others due to the absence of others’ possessions—such as water, dabba grass shoots, leaves of trees and creepers, and so forth. Here, the livelihood of deer, though unattained by one who has fallen into the vice of serving kings, is praised. And the analysis is: 'They do not serve another by nature,' and 'absence of toil,' and 'by that they are to be obtained,' and 'shoots of dabba grass,' and 'water and dabba grass shoots,' and 'those of which leaves and so forth are the beginning.'

315.

315.

Uttaraṃ uttaraṃ yattha, pubbapubbavisesanaṃ;

Siyā ekāvalī sā’yaṃ, dvidhā vidhinisedhato.

Where each subsequent term is a qualifier of each preceding one, that is a Single Chain, which is twofold through affirmation and negation.

315. Ekāvaliṃ kathayati “uttara”micchādinā. Yattha vuttiyaṃ uttaraṃ uttaraṃ upariṭṭhānamupariṭṭhānaṃ pubbassa pubbassa visesanaṃ vidhinisedhanavasena ekāvali nāma siyā. Ayaṃ ekāvali vidhinisedhato vidhivasena nisedhanavasena ca dvidhā.

315. It explains the Single Chain by 'subsequent'—and so forth. Where in an expression, each subsequent, higher-placed term is a qualifier of each preceding one by way of affirmation and negation, that would be called a Single Chain. This Single Chain is twofold through affirmation and negation, that is, by way of affirmation and by way of negation.

315. Idāni ekāvaliṃ dasseti “uttara”miccādinā. Yattha uttiyaṃ uttaraṃ uttaraṃ uparūparibhavaṃ padaṃ pubbapubbavisesanaṃ pubbapubbapadassa vidhinisedhanavasena visesanaṃ hoti, sā ekāvali nāma siyā. Ayaṃ ekāvali vidhinisedhato vidhinisedhavasena dvidhā hotīti. Uttaraṃ pubbanti ṭhānūpacārena ṭhānībhūtaṃ padameva vuccati. Pubbassa pubbassa visesanamiti ca, ekato āvaliyanti saṃvaliyanti padāni etāyāti ca, vidhividhānañca nisedho paṭisedho cāti ca vākyaṃ. Ettha “uttaraṃ uttara”nti ca “pubbassa pubbassa”iti ca kamena visesanavisesyaguṇena byāpanicchāyaṃ nibbacanaṃ, visesyaguṇaṃ gammamānameva.

315. Now, it shows the Single Chain by 'subsequent'—and so forth. Where in an expression, each subsequent, higher and higher word is a qualifier of the preceding word by way of affirmation or negation, that would be called a Single Chain. This Single Chain is twofold by way of affirmation and negation. 'Subsequent' and 'preceding' are said of the word itself, which is the basis, by way of metaphorical usage. And the statements are: 'Qualifier of each preceding one,' and 'by this, words are strung together in a line,' and 'affirmation is establishing, and negation is prohibition.' Here, 'subsequent, subsequent' and 'of the preceding, of the preceding' is an expression with the intention of showing the sequential relationship between qualifier and qualified, where the quality of the qualified is simply understood.

Vidhiekāvali

Affirmative Single Chain

316.

316.

Pādā nakhālirucirā,

Nakhālī raṃsibhāsurā;

Raṃsī tamopahāneka …pahāreka (sī.) -

Rasā sobhanti satthuno.

The feet are lovely with rows of nails; the rows of nails are radiant with rays; the rays, whose sole function is dispelling darkness, shine—of the Teacher.

316. Udāharati [M 0.0301] “pādā”iccādi. Sugammaṃ. Ettha pādādīnaṃ visesyānaṃ nakhālirucirattādividhānena visesanena visesitabbattā ayaṃ vidhiekāvali.

316. It illustrates with 'feet'—and so forth. This is easily understood. Here, because the qualified terms, such as 'feet,' are to be qualified by a qualifier that affirms their loveliness due to the rows of nails and so forth, this is an Affirmative Single Chain.

316. Idāni udāharati “pādā”iccādinā. Satthuno pādā nakhālirucirā nakhapantīhi manuññā nakhālī nakhapantiyo raṃsibhāsurā raṃsīhi dibbamānā raṃsī kantiyo tamopahānekarasā andhakāravidhamane asahāyakiccā hutvā sobhantīti. Ettha pādādīnaṃ pubbapadānaṃ nakhālirucirattādividhāyakehi uttarauttaravisesanehi visesitattā ayaṃ vidhiekāvali nāma. Nakhānaṃ āli pāḷīti ca, nakhālīhi rucirāti ca, raṃsīhi bhāsurāti ca, tamaso apahāro apaharaṇamiti ca, so eko raso kiccaṃ etāsaṃ raṃsīnamiti ca viggaho.

316. Now it illustrates with 'feet'—and so forth. The Teacher’s feet are lovely with rows of nails, charming with rows of nails; the rows of nails are radiant with rays, shining with rays; the rays, being splendors whose sole function is dispelling darkness, having an unassisted task in the dispelling of darkness, shine. Here, because the preceding terms, such as 'feet,' are qualified by successive qualifiers that affirm their loveliness due to the rows of nails and so forth, this is called an Affirmative Single Chain. And the analysis is: 'a line or row of nails,' and 'lovely with rows of nails,' and 'radiant with rays,' and 'dispelling or removal of darkness,' and 'that is the sole function or task of these rays.'

Nisedhaekāvali

Negative Single Chain

317.

317.

Asantuṭṭho yatī neva,

Santoso nā’layāhato;

Nā’layo yo sajantūnaṃ,

Nā’nantabyasanāvaho.

A discontented one is never an ascetic; one afflicted by craving is not contented; that which does not bring endless disaster to beings is not attachment.

317. “Asantuṭṭho”iccādi. Asantuṭṭho catupaccayasantosavasena yo koci yati nāma neva siyā. Ālayena taṇhāya āhato ca yo, so santoso nāma na hoti. Yo jantūnaṃ sattānaṃ anantabyasanāvaho na hoti, so ālayo nāma na bhavatīti. Asantuṭṭhādīnaṃ yatittādinisedhanavasena visesanānaṃ pavattiyā nisedhaekāvali ayaṃ.

317. “A discontented one,” etc. Any so-called ascetic who is discontent regarding contentment with the four requisites would certainly not be. And he who is afflicted by attachment, by craving, is not called 'contented.' That which does not bring endless disaster to beings, to sentient beings, is not called 'attachment.' Because of the occurrence of qualifiers such as 'discontented,' by way of negating the state of being an ascetic and so forth, this is a series of negations.

317. “Asantuṭṭho”iccādi. Asantuṭṭho cīvarādīsu catūsu paccayesu dassitadvādasavidhasantosānaṃ aññatarena asantuṭṭho [M 0.0302] yati na eva bhikkhu nāma na hoti. Ālayāhato taṇhāya pahato santoso na hoti. Yo jantūnaṃ anantabyasanāvaho na yo sattānaṃ apariyantapīḷāpāpako na hoti, so ālayo na hotīti. Asantuṭṭhādīnaṃ yatibhāvādipaṭisedhavasena visesanānaṃ pavattattā ayaṃ nisedhaekāvali nāma. Asantuṭṭhapadaṃ yatisahitasakalasattasamudāyassa sādhāraṇabhāvena ṭhitaṃ, yati na bhavatīti yatito aññesu sakalasattasaṅkhātesu avayavesu patiṭṭhāpanato “asantuṭṭho”ti visesyo, “yati ne”ti idaṃ visesanaṃ. Sesesupi visesanavisesyattaṃ vuttaniyāmena yathārahaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Na santussatīti ca, ālayena hatoti ca, natthi anto etesamiti ca, tāni ca tāni byasanāni ceti ca, tāni āvahatīti ca vākyaṃ.

317. “A discontented one,” etc. An ascetic who is discontent with any of the twelve kinds of contentment shown regarding the four requisites, such as robes, is certainly not called a monk. One afflicted by attachment, struck by craving, is not contented. That which does not bring endless disaster to beings, that which does not cause boundless affliction to sentient beings, is not attachment. Because of the occurrence of qualifiers such as 'discontented,' by way of negating the state of being an ascetic and so forth, this is called a series of negations. The word 'discontented' stands as a common factor for the entire aggregate of beings, including ascetics; but because 'is not an ascetic' establishes it in the constituent parts other than the ascetic—which are designated as all beings—'discontented' is the subject of qualification, and 'is not an ascetic' is the qualifier. In the remaining phrases also, the relationship of qualifier and qualified should be applied appropriately according to the stated principle. The analyses are: “He is not contented,” and “struck by attachment,” and “there is no end to these,” and “those are disasters,” and “it brings them.”

318.

318.

Yahiṃ bhūsiyabhūsattaṃ, aññamaññaṃ tu vatthunaṃ;

Vināva sadisattaṃ taṃ, aññamaññavibhūsanaṃ.

Where, of things, even without similarity, there is the state of being mutually adorned and adorning, that is mutual embellishment.

318. Aññamaññamāha “yahi”miccādinā. Yahiṃ sadisattaṃ vinā eva vatthunaṃ padatthānaṃ aññamaññaṃ bhūsiyabhūsattaṃ, taṃ aññamaññaṃ nāma vibhūsanamalaṅkāroti.

318. He speaks of mutual adornment with “where,” etc. Where, even without similarity, of things—of the meanings of words—there is the state of being mutually adorned and adorning, that is called mutual embellishment, an ornament.

318. Idāni aññamaññālaṅkāraṃ dasseti “yahi”miccādinā. Yahiṃ alaṅkāre sadisattaṃ vinā eva vatthunaṃ aññamaññaṃ tu bhūsiyabhūsattaṃ alaṅkāriyaalaṅkārattaṃ hoti, taṃ aññamaññavibhūsanaṃ hotīti. Bhūsiyañca bhūsā cāti ca, tāsaṃ bhāvoti ca, aññañca aññañceti ca viggaho. “Aññamañña”nti ettha chaṭṭhuntaasaṅkhyamabyayaṃ, sasaṅkhye ceti “bhūsiyabhūsatta”nti imassa visesanaṃ katvā vattabbaṃ. Alaṅkāriyamapekkhāya alaṅkāravatthu ca, tamapekkhāya alaṅkāriyavatthu ca aññamaññaṃ nāma. Tandīpakālaṅkāropi tadatthiyena tannāmako hoti.

318. Now, he shows the figure of mutual adornment with “where,” etc. Where, in a figure of speech, even without similarity between things, there is the state of being mutually adorned and adorning—that is, the state of being the adorned and the adorner—that is mutual embellishment. The analysis is: “The adorned and the adorning,” and “their state,” and “one and the other.” Here, 'aññamaññaṃ' is an indeclinable numeral with a genitive sense, and it should be stated as a qualifier of 'bhūsiyabhūsattaṃ' when a number is involved. The adorning object in relation to the object to be adorned, and the object to be adorned in relation to that, are called 'mutual.' The lamp-figure also is so named because it has that purpose.

319.

319.

Byāmaṃsumaṇḍalaṃ [M 0.0303] tena, muninā lokabandhunā;

Mahantiṃ vindatī kantiṃ, sopi teneva tādisiṃ.

The orb of fathom-rays attains great splendor by that sage, the kinsman of the world; and he too attains such splendor by that very orb.

319. Udāharati “byāmaṃsu”iccādinā. Subodhaṃ.

319. He gives an example with “the fathom-rays,” etc. It is easily understood.

319. Idāni udāharati “byāmaṃsu”iccādinā. Byāmaṃsumaṇḍalaṃ byāmapabhāmaṇḍalaṃ lokabandhunā tena muninā karaṇabhūtena mahantiṃ mahatiṃ pūjanīyaṃ vā kantiṃ sobhaṃ vindati sevati, sopi muni tena eva byāmaṃsumaṇḍalena tādisiṃ kantiṃ vindatīti. Aññamaññaṃ asadisānaṃ byāmaṃsumaṇḍalamunisaṅkhātānaṃ dvinnaṃ vatthūnaṃ byāmaṃsumaṇḍalaṃ paṭhamavākye alaṅkāriyaṃ hoti, munipadattho alaṅkāro hoti. Aparavākye ime dve vipallāsena alaṅkāriyaalaṅkārā honti. Aṃsūnaṃ maṇḍalamiti ca, byāmaṃ eva aṃsumaṇḍalamiti ca, loko bandhu asseti ca, sā viya dissatīti ca viggaho.

319. Now, he gives an example with “the fathom-rays,” etc. The orb of fathom-rays, the orb of fathom-light, through that sage, the Kinsman of the World, who is the instrument, attains and enjoys great, glorious, or venerable splendor and beauty. That sage, too, by that very orb of fathom-rays, attains such splendor. Of the two dissimilar things, designated as the orb of fathom-rays and the sage, which mutually adorn each other, the orb of fathom-rays in the first sentence is the object to be adorned, and the meaning of the word 'sage' is the adornment. In the next sentence, these two become the adorned and the adornment through inversion. The analyses are: 'a circle of rays'; 'the fathom-light itself is the circle of rays'; 'the world is his kinsman'; and 'it appears like that'.

320.

320.

Kathanaṃ sahabhāvassa, kriyāya ca guṇassa ca;

Sahavuttīti viññeyyaṃ, tadudāharaṇaṃ yathā.

The statement of the coexistence of an action and of a quality should be understood as co-occurrence; its example is as follows.

320. Sahavuttiṃ vadati “kathana”miccādinā. Subodhaṃ.

320. He speaks of co-occurrence with “the statement,” etc. It is easily understood.

320. Idāni sahavuttiṃ dasseti “kathana”miccādinā. Kriyāya guṇassa cāti dvinnaṃ sahabhāvassa sahattassa kathanaṃ sahavuttīti viññeyyaṃ. Tadudāharaṇaṃ yathā tassa udāharaṇaṃ evaṃ vakkhamānanayena daṭṭhabbanti. Saha saddhiṃ bhavanamiti ca, sahabhāvassa vutti kathanamiti ca, tassa udāharaṇamiti ca viggaho. Sahabhāvo candarasminakhaṃsuādīnaṃ padatthānaṃ. Evaṃ santepi tesaṃ taṃsahattaṃ yassaṃ kriyāyaṃ guṇe vā bhavatīti sahattaṃ kriyāguṇānaṃ hotīti katvā “kathanaṃ sahabhāvassa kriyāya ca guṇassa cā”ti vuttaṃ.

320. Now he shows co-occurrence with “the statement,” etc. The statement of the coexistence, the togetherness, of the two—that is, of an action and a quality—is to be understood as co-occurrence. As for its example, the example for it should be seen in the manner that will be explained. The analyses are: 'being together with'; 'the statement of coexistence'; and 'its example.' Coexistence pertains to the meanings of words such as 'moonbeams' and 'nail-rays.' Although this is so, since their togetherness occurs with respect to a certain action or quality, it is the togetherness of the action and quality. For this reason, it is said: “The statement of the coexistence of an action and of a quality.”

Kriyāsahavutti

Co-occurrence of Action

321.

321.

Jalanti [M 0.0304] candaraṃsīhi, samaṃ satthu nakhaṃsavo;

Vijambhati ca candena, samaṃ tammukhacandimā.

The Teacher's nail-rays blaze together with the moonbeams; and his moon-like face unfolds together with the moon.

321. “Jalanti”iccādi. Samanti saha, tassa satthuno mukhacandimā. Sesaṃ subodhaṃ. Ettha jalanavijambhanānaṃ ubhayasādhāraṇānaṃ kriyānaṃ sahabhāvo vihitoti kriyāsahavutti ayanti.

321. “Blaze,” etc. `Samaṃ` means 'together.' `Tassa satthuno mukhacandimā` means 'that Teacher's moon-like face.' The rest is easily understood. Here, since the coexistence of the actions of blazing and unfolding, which are common to both pairs, is set forth, this is co-occurrence of action.

321. Idāni yathāpaṭiññātaudāharaṇaṃ dasseti “jalanti”iccādinā. Satthu satthuno nakhaṃsavo nakhakiraṇā candaraṃsīhi samaṃ jalanti, tammukhacandimā ca candena samaṃ vijambhatīti. Ettha ubhayapadatthānaṃ sādhāraṇabhūtajalanavijambhanakriyānaṃ sahabhāvassa vuttattā esā kriyāsahavutti nāma. Candassa raṃsiyoti ca, nakhānaṃ aṃsavoti ca, tassa satthuno mukhanti ca, tameva candimasadisattā candimāti ca vākyaṃ. Samaṃiti sahapariyāyo nipāto.

321. Now he presents the example as promised, with “blaze,” etc. The Teacher's nail-rays, the rays from his nails, blaze together with the moonbeams, and his moon-like face unfolds together with the moon. Here, since the coexistence of the actions of blazing and unfolding, which are common to the meanings of both pairs of words, is stated, this is called co-occurrence of action. The analyses are: 'the rays of the moon'; 'the rays from the nails'; 'that Teacher's face'; and 'that very thing, being like the moon, is moon-like.' `Samaṃ` is a particle synonymous with 'together.'

Guṇasahavutti

Co-occurrence of Quality

322.

322.

Jinodayena malinaṃ, saha dujjanacetasā;

Pāpaṃ disā suvimalā, saha sajjanacetasā.

With the arising of the Victor, evil becomes defiled along with the minds of the wicked; the directions become immaculate along with the minds of the virtuous.

322. “Jinodayena”ccādi. Jinodayena karaṇabhūtena, hetubhūtena vā dujjanacetasā saha pāpaṃ malinaṃ kiliṭṭhaṃ, sajjanacetasā saha disā dasavidhāpi suvimalā accantanimmalā suvimalayasomālāvalayitattā sajjanaceto pāpāpagameneti. Ettha malinattassa ca suvimalattassa ñāyasambandhino sahabhāvo vuttoti ayaṃ guṇasahavutti.

322. “With the arising of the Victor,” etc. By the arising of the Victor, as the instrument or the cause, evil becomes defiled and tainted along with the minds of the wicked. Along with the minds of the virtuous, the ten directions become exceedingly pure and utterly stainless, being encircled by a garland of immaculate fame due to the departure of evil from the minds of the virtuous. Here, since the logically connected coexistence of impurity and extreme purity is stated, this is co-occurrence of quality.

322. “Jino”iccādi. Jinodayena jitamārassa bhagavato pātubhāvena, karaṇabhūtena hetubhūtena vā [M 0.0305] pāpaṃ lobhādidhammaṃ dujjanacetasā dujjanānaṃ cittena saha malinaṃ kiliṭṭhaṃ hoti. Imināyeva jinodayena disā dasa disāyo sajjanacetasā saha suvimalā sajjanacetasantānato pāpānaṃ apagamena kittimālāya bhuvanattaye patthaṭattā atinimmalāti ubhayapadatthānaṃ sādhāraṇabhūtamalinabhāvasuvimalabhāvasaṅkhātassa guṇassa sahabhāvassa vuttattā esā guṇasahavutti nāma. Jinassa udayoti ca, dujjanānaṃ cetoti ca, vigataṃ malaṃ etāhiti ca, su atisayena vimalāti ca, santo ca te janā ceti ca, tesaṃ cetoti ca vākyaṃ.

322. “The Victor,” etc. By the arising of the Victor—the manifestation of the Blessed One who has conquered Māra—as the instrument or the cause, evil, that is, states such as greed, becomes defiled and tainted along with the minds of the wicked. By this very arising of the Victor, the ten directions become exceedingly pure along with the minds of the virtuous, because of the removal of evil from the mental continuity of the virtuous and because garlands of fame are spread throughout the three worlds. Since the coexistence of the quality—designated as the common state of being defiled and being pure, which pertains to the meanings of both sets of words—is stated, this is called co-occurrence of quality. The analyses are: 'the arising of the Victor'; 'the mind of the wicked'; 'that from which defilement has departed'; '`su` means exceedingly pure'; 'they are peaceful people'; and 'their mind.'

323.

323.

Virodhīnaṃ padatthānaṃ, yattha saṃsaggadassanaṃ;

Samukkaṃsābhidhānatthaṃ, matā sā’yaṃ virodhitā.

Where the perception of an association between things of opposing meanings is for the purpose of expressing pre-eminence, that is considered opposition.

323. Virodhaṃ vibhāveti “virodhīna”miccādi. Virodhīnaṃ aññamaññaviruddhānaṃ kriyādīnaṃ yattha vuttivisese saṃsaggassa sannidhino dassanaṃ, kimatthaṃ? Samukkaṃsassa atisayassa abhidhānatthaṃ kathanatthāya, sā ayaṃ virodhitā virodhīti matā.

323. It explains opposition with ‘of the opposing’ and so on. Where, in a specific expression, the perception of an association or proximity of opposing things, such as actions that are mutually contradictory, occurs—for what purpose? For the purpose of declaring, that is, stating, pre-eminence or superiority; that is considered opposition.

323. Idāni virodhālaṅkāraṃ dasseti “virodhīna”miccādinā. Yattha uttivisese samukkaṃsābhidhānatthaṃ vaṇṇanīyavatthugataadhikakathanāya virodhīnaṃ aññamaññaviruddhānaṃ padatthānaṃ kriyāguṇādīnaṃ saṃsaggadassanaṃ sanniṭṭhānadassanaṃ sambandhadassanaṃ hoti, sā ayaṃ utti virodhitāti matāti. Virodho etesaṃ guṇādīnaṃ atthīti ca, saṃsaggassa sambandhassa dassanamiti ca, samukkaṃsassa adhikassa abhidhānanti ca, virodhīnaṃ bhāvo asaṅgahitoti ca vākyaṃ. Virodhitādīpakavutti tadatthena tannāmikā hoti.

323. Now the figure of speech of opposition is shown with ‘of the opposing’ and so on. Where, in a particular expression, the perception of an association, proximity, or connection of mutually contradictory things—such as actions and qualities—occurs for the purpose of expressing pre-eminence or for stating the superiority of the subject being described, that expression is considered opposition. The component phrases are: ‘there is opposition in these qualities and so on,’ ‘the perception of association or connection,’ ‘the expression of pre-eminence or superiority,’ and ‘the nature of opposing things is to be uncombined.’ The exposition that illuminates opposition is so named from that meaning.

324.

324.

Guṇā sabhāvamadhurā, api lokekabandhuno;

Sevitā pāpasevīnaṃ, sampadūsenti sampadūsanti (ka.) mānasaṃ.

Qualities, naturally sweet, even those of the World's Sole Kinsman, when attended to by evil-doers, utterly corrupt their minds.

324. Udāharati [M 0.0306] “guṇā”iccādi. Lokekabandhuno lokanāthassa sabhāvamadhurā sādhujanasampīṇanekacāturā api guṇā arahantatādayo sevitā pāpasevīhi tesaṃ pāpasevīnaṃ mānasaṃ sampadūsenti dosaduṭṭhāpādanavasenāvikaronti “tādiso guṇātisayo tassā”ti. Ettha guṇānaṃ sabhāvamadhurānaṃ pītivisesuppādanayoggānaṃ sampadūsanena saha virodhoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

324. It illustrates with ‘qualities’ and so on. The qualities of the World's Sole Kinsman, the World Protector—naturally sweet and skilled in variously delighting the virtuous—such as Arahantship and others, even when attended to by evil-doers, utterly corrupt the minds of those evil-doers, distorting them by way of producing corrupting defilements, making them think, ‘Such is his abundance of virtues!’ Herein, it should be seen that there is an opposition of the qualities—which are naturally sweet and fit to produce special joy—with that corruption.

324. Udāharati “guṇā”iccādinā. Lokekabandhuno buddhassa guṇā arahattādayo sabhāvamadhurā api pakatimadhurā api sevitā pāpasevīhi sevitā samānā pāpasevīnaṃ mānasaṃ sampadūsenti atisayena kopentīti. Evaṃ hīnādhimuttikehi sahitumasakkuṇeyyo tassa guṇātisayo vattati. Nanu sabhāvamadhuro guṇo pītiṃ vinā sampadūsanaṃ na kareyya, sampadūsanampi tādisasabhāvamadhuraṃ vinā na bhaveyyāti aññoññaviruddhānamesaṃ madhuraguṇasampadūsanakriyānaṃ saṃsaggaguṇādhikadassanatthanti lakkhaṇena yojetabbaṃ. Apisaddo virodhatthe vattate. Sabhāvena madhurāti ca, eko ca so bandhu cāti ca, lokassa ekabandhūti ca, pāpaṃ sevanti sīlenāti ca vākyaṃ.
