324. It illustrates with ‘qualities’ and so on. The qualities of the Buddha, the World's Sole Kinsman—such as Arahantship—though naturally and inherently sweet, when attended to by evil-doers, corrupt the minds of those evil-doers, provoking them excessively. Thus his surpassing excellence of virtue is unable to be endured by those of inferior inclination. Indeed, a naturally sweet quality should not cause corruption without first causing joy, nor would such corruption occur without such a naturally sweet quality. This association of mutually contradictory things—sweet qualities and the action of corrupting—should be connected by the characteristic for the purpose of showing the superiority of the virtue. The word ‘api’ functions in the sense of contradiction. The component phrases are: ‘sweet by nature,’ ‘he is the one kinsman,’ ‘the one kinsman of the world,’ and ‘they practice evil by habit.’

325.

325.

Yassa kassaci dānena, yassa kassaci vatthuno;

Visiṭṭhassa ya’mādānaṃ, parivuttīti sā matā.

The acceptance of a superior thing, which occurs by means of giving any object whatsoever to any person whatsoever, is considered exchange.

325. Parivuttiṃ pavatteti “yassa”iccādinā. Yassa kassacīti paṭiggāhakaṃ dasseti. Visiṭṭhassa yaṃ ādānanti sambandho. Sesaṃ subodhaṃ.

325. It introduces exchange with ‘of any’ and so on. ‘Of any person whatsoever’ indicates the recipient. The connection is ‘the acceptance of a superior thing.’ The rest is easily understood.

325. Idāni parivuttiṃ dasseti “yassa kassaci”ccādinā. Yassa kassaci vatthuno khuddakavatthuno yassa kassaci paṭiggāhakassa dānena hetubhūtena visiṭṭhassa uttamavatthuno [M 0.0307] yaṃ ādānaṃ gahaṇaṃ atthi, sā parivuttīti matāti. Dānaggahaṇaparivuttattā parivutti nāma.

325. Now, it explains exchange with ‘of any person whatsoever’ and so on. Where there is the acceptance or taking of a superior, excellent object, by means of the giving—which is the cause—of some small object to any recipient whatsoever, that is considered exchange. Because it is an exchange of giving and receiving, it is named exchange.

326.

326.

Purā paresaṃ datvāna, manuññaṃ nayanādikaṃ;

Muninā samanuppattā, dāni sabbaññutāsirī muninda samanuppattā, dāni sabbaññutāsiriṃ (ka.).

Having formerly given pleasing eyes and so forth to others, the Sage has now attained the glory of omniscience.

326. Udāharati “purā”iccādi. Subodhaṃ. Ettha nayanādidānena sabbaññutāsiriyā ādānanti parivutti ayaṃ.

326. It illustrates with ‘formerly’ and so on. This is easily understood. Herein, this is an exchange: the acquisition of the glory of omniscience by means of the giving of eyes and so forth.

326. Idāni udāharati “purā”iccādinā. Muninā purā pubbe paresaṃ manuññaṃ nayanādikaṃ datvāna idāni sabbaññutāsirī sabbaññutāsaṅkhātā anaññasādhāraṇā sirī samanupattāti. Iha yassa dinnaṃ tato eva gahaṇe parivuttisaddassa niruḷhattā nayanādīnaṃ dānena sabbaññutāsiriyā ādānato, dānābhāve ādānābhāvato ca paṭiggāhakajane avijjamānepi sabbaññutā vijjamānattena parikappitāti parivutti hoti. Teneva daṇḍiyaṃ–

326. Now it illustrates with ‘formerly’ and so on. The Sage, having in the past, previously, given pleasing eyes and so forth to others, has now attained the glory of omniscience, a glory called omniscience, unique and not shared by others. Here, although the word ‘exchange’ is established in meaning for taking from the very one to whom something was given, it is nevertheless an exchange because the glory of omniscience is acquired through the giving of eyes and so on, and because in the absence of giving there is an absence of acquisition, and because omniscience, though not existing among the recipients, is conceived of as being present for the exchange. Therefore, it is said in the Daṇḍin:

“Satthappaharaṇaṃ datvā, bhujena tava rājunaṃ;

Ciraṃ citābhaṭo tesaṃ, yaso kumudapaṇḍaro”ti kābyādāsa 2.356.

‘Having given the striking of weapons to the kings with your arm, their glory, white as a water lily, was for a long time amassed and taken.’

Imasmiṃ udāharaṇe paccatthikānaṃ āyudhappahāraṃ datvā tava bāhunā tesaṃ rājūnaṃ ciraṃ rāsikato keravanimmalo yaso ābhaṭoti. Dadāti kammayuttato eva ādānaṃ dassetvā parivuttiphuṭā katā. Nayanāni ādīni yassa uttamaṅgādinoti ca, sabbaṃ jānātīti ca, tassa bhāvoti ca vākyaṃ.

In this example: ‘Having given the striking of weapons to the enemies with your arm, the glory of those kings, pure as a water lily, was for a long time amassed and taken.’ By showing the taking from the very one connected with the act of giving, the exchange is made clear. The component phrases are: ‘eyes and so on, meaning the head and other principal parts,’ ‘he knows all,’ and ‘the state of that.’

327.

327.

Kiñci disvāna viññātā,

Paṭipajjati taṃsamaṃ;

Saṃsayāpagataṃ vatthuṃ,

Yattha so’yaṃ bhamo mato.

Where a perceiver, having seen something, apprehends another object similar to it as being free from doubt, that is considered confusion.

327. Bhamaṃ [M 0.0308] sambhāveti “kiñcī”tiādinā. Viññātā puriso kiñci disvā ujjalanādikaṃ disvāna taṃsamaṃ tassa pure dissamānassa padatthassa sadisamaññaṃ vatthuṃ saṃsayāpagataṃ asannidhiṃ katvā paṭipajjati jānāti yattha visese, sāyaṃ bhamo mato.

327. It explains confusion with ‘something’ and so on. A knowing person, having seen something—such as brightness—and then perceiving another object similar to that previously seen thing, apprehends it as free from doubt, disregarding its non-proximity; where this occurs in a specific case, it is considered confusion.

327. Idāni bhamālaṅkāraṃ dasseti “kiñci”iccādinā. Yattha uttivisese viññātā avabodhakārako kiñci disāvilocanādikaṃ disvāna taṃsamaṃ vatthuṃ tena dissamānavatthunā tulyamaññaṃ vatthuṃ saṃsayāpagataṃ nissaṃsayaṃ katvā paṭipajjati jānāti, so ayaṃ alaṅkāro bhamoti matoti. Tena tassa vā samanti ca, saṃsayo apagato etasmāti ca, bhamanaṃ anavaṭṭhānaṃ vatthūnanti ca viggaho. Saṃsayāpagatanti kriyāvisesanaṃ.

327. Now the figure of speech of confusion is shown with ‘something’ and so on. Where, in a particular expression, a perceiver—the one who causes understanding—having seen something, such as a glance in a direction, apprehends another object similar to the object seen, making it free from doubt and without hesitation, this figure of speech is considered confusion. The etymological analyses are: ‘similar to that’ or ‘similar to it’; ‘doubt has departed from this’; and ‘confusion is the instability of things.’ ‘Saṃsayāpagataṃ’ is an adverb.

328.

328.

Samaṃ disāsu’jjalāsu, jinapādanakhaṃsunā;

Passantā abhinandanti, candātapamanā janā.

Seeing the directions equally bright from the radiance of the Conqueror’s toenails, people, thinking it is moonlight, rejoice.

328. Udāharati “sama”miccādi. Jinassa pādesu nakhaṃsunā disāsu sabbāsu samaṃ ekato ujjalāsu sajotīsu tā ujjalā disā passantā janā, candātapoti mano yesaṃ te tathāvidhā. Abhinandanti santussantīti.

328. It illustrates with ‘equally’ and so on. By the radiance of the nails on the Conqueror’s feet, all directions are at once equally bright and shining. People seeing those bright directions, whose minds think, ‘It is moonlight,’ are of that kind. They rejoice, that is, they are satisfied.

328. Idāni udāharati “sama”miccādinā. Jinapādanakhaṃsunā karaṇabhūtena disāsu dasasu samaṃ ekakkhaṇe ujjalāsu tā ujjalā disā passantā janā candātapamanā candātapoti pavattacittā abhinandantīti. Vijjamānanakhamarīciyaṃ buddhimakatvā candātape buddhiyā pavattāpanato bhamo nāma. Samanti asaṅkhyaṃ. Candātapoiti mano yesanti vākyaṃ.

328. Now it illustrates with ‘equally’ and so on. By means of the radiance of the Conqueror’s toenails, which is the instrument, the ten directions being equally bright in a single moment, people seeing those bright directions rejoice, their minds proceeding with the thought, ‘It is moonlight!’ Because the perception of moonlight is made to arise without forming a perception of the existing nail-rays, it is named confusion. ‘Samaṃ’ means ‘countless.’ The component phrase is ‘candātapo iti mano yesaṃ,’ meaning ‘those whose minds think, “It is moonlight!”’

329.

329.

Pavuccate [M 0.0309] yaṃ nāmādi,

Kavīnaṃ bhāvabodhanaṃ;

Yena kenaci vaṇṇena,

Bhāvonāmā’ya’mīrito.

That which is called ‘name’ and so forth, which is the poets' means of conveying intention, is declared by whatever mode of description; this is called Bhāva.

329. Bhāvaṃ bhāveti “pavuccate”ccādinā. Kavīnaṃ bhāvo adhippāyo, taṃ bodhetīti bhāvabodhanaṃ yaṃ nāmādi. Ādisaddena visesanavākyānaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Yena kenaci nisedhanarūpena ākārena pavuccate, ayaṃ bhāvo nāma īritoti.

329. He explains Bhāva with ‘is called’ and so on. The poets' ‘bhāva’ is their intention (adhippāya); that which makes known this intention is ‘bhāvabodhana,’ namely ‘name’ and so on. By the word ‘ādi’ is meant the inclusion of descriptive phrases. It is declared by whatever mode, even in the form of negation; this is called Bhāva.

329. Idāni bhāvālaṅkāraṃ dasseti “pavuccate” iccādinā. Kavīnaṃ vattūnaṃ bhāvabodhanaṃ adhippāyapakāsakaṃ yaṃ nāmādi nāmapadavisesanapadādi yena kenaci vaṇṇena ākārena sāgarādiatthantaraṃ paṭisedhetvā vā no vā pavuccate, ayaṃ bhāvo nāmāti īritoti. Nāmaṃ ādi yassa visesanavākyadvayasseti ca, bhāvaṃ bodhetīti ca vākyaṃ. Kavīnaṃ adhippāyasaṅkhātabhāvapakāsako uttiviseso tadatthena bhāvo nāma, tassa nissayabhūtaṃ nāmādipadasantānaṃ iha nissitopacārena bhāvo nāmāti īritaṃ.

329. Now he explains the 'bhāvālaṅkāra' (ornament of intention) with 'pavuccate' and so on. That which is the poets' means of conveying their intention (bhāva), which reveals their aim, namely 'name' and so on, such as nouns and qualifying words, by whatever description or mode, whether by negating another meaning like 'ocean' and so on, or not, is declared. This is called 'bhāva', so it is said. The phrase 'nāmaṃ ādi yassa visesanavākyadvayassa' means 'of which two qualifying phrases 'name' is the beginning', and the phrase 'bhāvaṃ bodhetīti' means 'it makes known the intention'. The specific expression of the poets, which reveals the intention understood as 'bhāva', is called 'bhāva' in that sense. The sequence of words like 'name' and so on, which serves as its basis, is here metaphorically called 'bhāva'.

330.

330.

Nanu teye’va santā no,

Sāgarā na kulācalā;

Manampi mariyādaṃ ye,

Saṃvaṭṭepi jahanti no.

Surely, those are not oceans, nor are they family mountains;

Rather, they are the virtuous, who do not abandon their boundary

even slightly, even in dissolution.

330. Udāharati “nanu”ccādi. Manampīti īsakampi. Mariyādanti attano ācārasīmaṃ, saṃvaṭṭepi palayakālepi. Sesaṃ subodhaṃ. Ettha na ime pakatisamuddādayo samuddādayo honti, ye palayakāle attano velānullaṅghanasaṅkhātaṃ acalattasaṅkhātañca mariyādaṃ pariccajanti. Kiñcarahi [M 0.0310] santā evete samuddādayo, ye yadi palayakālepi samāpateyyuṃ, tadāpi attano mariyādaṃ na muñcanti. Koci vipattiṃ patto niratisayaṃ dhīrattamattanovabodhetīti aññanisedhena kathitaṃ nāmaṃ kavisabhāvaṃ yathāvuttaṃ bodhetīti bhāvoyamiti.

330. He illustrates with 'nanu' and so on. The word 'manampi' means 'even slightly'. The word 'mariyādaṃ' means 'one's own boundary of conduct'. 'Saṃvaṭṭepi' means 'even in the time of dissolution'. The rest is easily understood. Here, these are not ordinary oceans and so on, which abandon their boundary, namely, their not transgressing the shore and their unshakeable nature, in the time of dissolution. Rather, the virtuous are these oceans and so on, which, even if the time of dissolution were to arrive, would not relinquish their boundary. When someone, having met with misfortune, makes known their own unsurpassed fortitude, then, through the negation of the other, the spoken name reveals the poet's intention as stated, and thus this is 'bhāva'.

330. Idāni udāharati “nanu”ccādinā. Sāgarā saṃvaṭṭakāle tīramariyādaṃ atikkamentā pakatisamuddā sāgarā na bhavanti. Kulācalā tādisakāle acalasaṅkhātamariyādamatikkamentā satta kulapabbatā kulācalā nāma na bhavanti. Kiñcarahi sāgarādayo. Ye sādhavo saṃvaṭṭepi sabbavatthuvināsakakappavināsakālepi mariyādaṃ attano ācāramariyādaṃ manampi īsakampi no jahanti. Santā eva te sāgarādayo nāma honti nanūti. Koci byasanaṃ patto attano anaññasādhāraṇaṃ dhīrattaṃ pakāsetīti iha sāgarādiatthantarapaṭisedharūpena dassitasāgarādinā vattuno akampanādhippāyaṃ avabodhetīti ayaṃ bhāvālaṅkāro nāma. Mananti appakālavācakamasaṅkhyaṃ. Apīti sambhāvane.

330. Now he illustrates with 'nanu' and so on. At the time of cosmic dissolution, the oceans, by transgressing their shore boundaries, are not true oceans. At such a time, the family mountains, by transgressing their boundary of immovability, the seven family mountains are no longer called family mountains. What then are these oceans and so on? Those virtuous ones who, even at the time of the destruction of the aeon, when all things are destroyed, do not abandon their boundary, the boundary of their own conduct, not even slightly. Indeed, it is the virtuous who are called oceans and so on. When someone who has fallen into misfortune reveals his own incomparable fortitude, here, by means of 'oceans' and so on, shown in the form of negating another meaning of 'oceans' and so on, the speaker makes known the intention of being unshaken—this is called the 'bhāvālaṅkāra'. The word 'manam' is a term for a small, uncountable measure. The word 'api' is used in the sense of possibility.

331.

331.

Aṅgaṅgībhāvā sadisa-balabhāvā ca bandhane;

Saṃsaggo’laṅkatīnaṃ yo, taṃ missanti pavuccati.

From the state of being principal and accessory,

and from the state of equal strength, in a composition;

that association of ornaments

is called 'missa'.

331. Missaṃ dasseti “aṅga”iccādinā. Aṅgamupakārakaṃ, aṅgī upakāriyaṃ, tesaṃ bhāvo aṅgaṅgibhāvo sādhiyasādhanattaṃ, tato ca. Sadisaṃ samaṃ balaṃ yesaṃ te, tesaṃ bhāvo aṅgaṅgibhāvamantarena appadhānabhāvenāvaṭṭhānaṃ tato ca hetuto. Bandhane visaye, yo alaṅkatīnaṃ saṃsaggo ekattha sannidhānaṃ, taṃ missanti pavuccati.

331. He explains 'missa' with 'aṅga' and so on. The 'aṅga' is the helper, the 'aṅgī' is the one helped; their state, 'aṅgaṅgibhāva', is the state of being that which is to be accomplished and the means. And from that, and from the state of those having equal strength—which is the state of existing without a predominant element and without the principal-accessory relationship—and from that cause. In the sphere of composition, the association of ornaments, their being in one place, is called 'missa'.

331. Idāni [M 0.0311] missālaṅkāraṃ dasseti “aṅgaṅgī”ccādinā. Aṅgaṅgībhāvā upakārakaupakāriyasaṅkhātapaṭipādakapaṭipādanīyasabhāvena hetubhūtena sadisabalabhāvā ca sādhiyasādhanabhāvaṃ vinā samānabalavantabhāvena ca bandhane pajjādibandhanavisaye alaṅkatīnaṃ alaṅkārānaṃ yo saṃsaggo sannidhānaṃ, taṃ missanti pavuccatīti. Aṅgaṃ sādhanaṃ assa sādhiyassa atthīti ca, aṅgañca aṅgī ceti ca, tesaṃ bhāvo sādhiyasādhanasaṅkhāto sambandhoti ca, sadisaṃ balaṃ yesamalaṅkārānamiti ca, tesaṃ bhāvo aññamaññanirapekkhatāti ca, missanaṃ missībhavanamiti ca vākyaṃ.

331. Now he explains the 'missālaṅkāra' (mixed ornament) with 'aṅgaṅgī' and so on. By means of the state of being principal and accessory, which is the nature of helper and helped, of that which accomplishes and that which is to be accomplished, acting as a cause; and by means of the state of equal strength, which is the state of having equal power without the state of being that which is to be accomplished and the means; in the sphere of composition, such as the composition of verses and so on, that association or proximity of ornaments is called 'missa'. The phrase 'aṅgaṃ sādhanaṃ assa sādhiyassa atthīti' means 'the accessory is a means for that which is to be accomplished', and 'aṅgañca aṅgī ceti' means 'both accessory and principal'; their state, 'sādhiyasādhanasaṅkhāto sambandho', is the relationship described as 'that which is to be accomplished and the means'. The phrase 'sadisaṃ balaṃ yesamalaṅkārānaṃ' means 'of which ornaments the power is equal'; their state is 'aññamaññanirapekkhatā', mutual independence. The phrase 'missanaṃ missībhavanaṃ' means 'mixing is the act of becoming mixed'.

Aṅgaṅgibhāvamissa

Mixed [Ornament] of the Principal-Accessory Relationship

332.

332.

Pasatthā munino pāda-nakharaṃsimahānadī;

Aho gāḷhaṃ nimuggepi, sukhayatye’va te jane.

Praised is the great river of the rays from the Sage’s toenails;

Ah! Even when one is deeply submerged, it still gladdens those people.

332. Udāharati “pasatthā muni”ccādi. Munino pādesu nakhā tesaṃ raṃsi eva mahānadīsadisattā mahānadī, sā pasatthā acchariyappattisabbhāvato gāḷhamaccantaṃ nimuggepi te jane sukhayatyeva, aho acchariyaṃ yato sesanadīvidhuraṃ. “Ayaṃ attani gāḷhaṃ nimuggepi sukhayatī”ti ettha “nimuggepī”ti samādhino sādhiyattenaṅgitāyāvaṭṭhitassa “pādanakharaṃsimahānadī”ti rūpakaṃ sādhanattenaṅgatāyāvaṭṭhitanti missamidamalaṅkaraṇaṃ.

332. He exemplifies with 'praised, the Sage,' etc. The rays from the nails on the Sage's feet are a great river, due to being like a great river; it is praised because of its astonishing nature. Even when one is deeply submerged, it gladdens those people—how marvelous, since it is unlike other rivers. Here, in 'This gladdens even when one is deeply submerged in it,' the phrase 'even when submerged' (nimuggepi) stands as the principal element (aṅgin) by virtue of being that which is to be accomplished (sādhiya) for the ornament of composure (samādhi). The metaphor 'the great river of toenail rays' (pādanakharaṃsimahānadī) stands as the accessory element (aṅga) by virtue of being the means of accomplishment (sādhana). Thus, this is a mixed ornament.

332. Idāni udāharati “pasatthā” iccādinā. Munino pasatthā acchariyattā pasaṃsanīyā pādanakharaṃsimahānadī caraṇanakhakiraṇasaṅkhātamahāgaṅgā gāḷhaṃ atisayena nimuggepi te jane sādhusappurise sukhayati eva sukhite kato eva. Aho acchariyaṃ sesanadīnamesā pavatti viruddhāti. Ettha sādhanīyabhāvena aṅgino “nimugge”ti samādhialaṅkārassa [M 0.0312] “pādanakharaṃsimahānadī”ti rūpakālaṅkāro sādhanabhāvena aṅganti katvā aṅgāaṅgībhāvena imesaṃ alaṅkārānaṃ missitā. Pādesu nakhāti ca, tesaṃ raṃsīti ca, mahatī ca sā nadī ceti ca, mahānadī viya mahānadī pādanakharaṃsiyo eva mahānadīti ca vākyaṃ. Gāḷhanti kriyāvisesanaṃ. Gāḷhaṃ nimujjanaṃ ye akaṃsu, tepīti yojanā. Sukhasamaṅgino janā sukhite sukhe karotīti vākyaṃ.

332. Now, he exemplifies with 'praised,' etc. The great river of the rays from the Sage's toenails—the great Ganges, which is the multitude of rays from his feet-nails—is praised and worthy of praise because of its astonishing nature. Even when those good and virtuous people are deeply submerged, it gladdens them, indeed makes them happy. How astonishing, for this behavior is contrary to that of other rivers. Here, for the ornament of composure (samādhi), 'even when submerged' (nimugge), being the principal element (aṅgin) by virtue of being that which is to be accomplished (sādhanīya), the metaphor 'the great river of toenail rays' (pādanakharaṃsimahānadī) is the accessory element (aṅga) by virtue of being the means of accomplishment (sādhana). Thus, these ornaments are mixed by way of the principal-accessory relationship. The phrases are: 'nails on the feet,' 'their rays,' 'that great river,' 'a great river like a great river,' and 'the rays from the toenails are themselves the great river.' 'Deeply' (gāḷhaṃ) is an adverb. The connection is: 'even those who have deeply submerged.' The sentence means: 'It makes happy the people who are endowed with happiness.'

Sadisabalabhāvamissa

Mixed [Ornament] of the State of Equal Strength

333.

333.

Veso sabhāvamadhuro, rūpaṃ nettarasāyanaṃ;

Madhūvamunino vācā, na sampīṇeti kaṃ janaṃ.

The appearance is naturally sweet, the form an elixir for the eyes;

the speech of the Sage, like honey—what person does it not gladden?

333. “Veso”iccādi subodhaṃ. Idaṃ pana samādhirūpakopamāmissasadisabalanti.

333. 'Appearance,' etc., is easily understood. This, however, is a mixed ornament of equal strength, comprising composure (samādhi), metaphor (rūpaka), and simile (upamā).

333. “Veso”iccādi. Munino sabhāvamadhuro pakatimadhuro veso jināveṇiko buddhaveso ca nettarasāyanaṃ rūpaṃ lakkhaṇānubyañjanasampannaṃ rūpañca madhūva madhurattena madhusamānā vācā bhāratī ca kaṃ janaṃ na sampīṇetīti. “Sabhāvamadhuro”ti samādhialaṅkāro ca, “nettarasāyana”nti rūpakālaṅkāro ca, “madhūvā”ti upamālaṅkāro cāti ime tayo pīṇane aññamaññāpekkharahitattā tulyabalāti imesaṃ missattaṃ hoti. Sabhāvena madhuroti ca, rasīyati assādīyatīti ca, raso rasabhūto āyanaṃ gati pavatti assāti rasāyanaṃ, rasavatthu. Rasāyanamiva rūpaṃ rasāyanaṃ, nettānaṃ rasāyananti ca vākyaṃ.

333. 'Appearance,' etc. The Sage's appearance, naturally sweet, the unique appearance of the Buddha, and his form, endowed with the major and minor marks, an elixir for the eyes; and his speech, like honey, similar to honey in its sweetness—what person does it not gladden? Here, 'naturally sweet' (sabhāvamadhuro) is the ornament of composure (samādhi), 'an elixir for the eyes' (nettarasāyana) is the metaphor (rūpaka), and 'like honey' (madhūvā) is the simile (upamā). These three, being without mutual dependence in their capacity to gladden, are of equal strength, hence their mixed nature. The phrases are: 'naturally sweet,' 'it is savored, it is tasted,' and 'rasāyana' means that which has rasa as its essence, its going, its course, its occurrence, or it is an object of rasa. 'Form like an elixir is an elixir,' and 'an elixir for the eyes'—thus the sentence.

334.

334.

Āsī nāma siyā’tthassa,

Iṭṭhassā’sīsanaṃ yathā;

Tilokekagatī nātho,

Pātu loka’mapāyato.

Āsī, by name, is the wishing for a desired object. For example:

May the Lord, the sole refuge of the three worlds,

protect the world from states of woe.

334. Āsiṃ [M 0.0313] dasseti “āsi”ccādinā. Iṭṭhassa abhimatassa vatthuno āsīsanaṃ patthanamityanuvaditvā āsī nāma siyāti vidhīyate. “Yathe”tyudāharati. Tilokassa lokattayavattino janassa ekagati asahāyagati paṭisaraṇabhūto nātho lokaṃ sattalokaṃ apāyato pātu pāletūti. Etthātilasitaṃ pālanamāsīsitanti.

334. He explains the aspiration (āsī) with 'āsī,' etc. After glossing 'āsīsana' as the wishing or longing for a desired and agreeable object, it is defined that it may be called 'āsī'. He exemplifies with 'yathā,' etc. May the Lord, the sole refuge (ekagati, asahāyagati, paṭisaraṇa) for the people dwelling in the three worlds, protect the world of beings from states of woe. Here, excellent protection is wished for.

334. Idāni āsīalaṅkāraṃ dasseti “āsī” iccādinā. Iṭṭhassa atthassa icchitavatthuno āsīsanā patthanā āsī nāma siyā. Yathā tatthodāharaṇamevaṃ. Tilokekagati tibhavassa asahāyasaraṇabhūto nātho lokasāmi lokaṃ sattalokaṃ apāyato pātu rakkhatūti. Āsī nāma patthanā, taddīpikāpi utti tannāmikāva hoti. “Tilokekagatī”ti imasmiṃ udāharaṇe pālanaṃ āsīsitaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ lokānaṃ samāhāroti ca, ekoyeva gati paṭisaraṇanti ca, tilokassa ekagatīti ca vākyaṃ.

334. Now, the ornament of aspiration (āsī) is shown with 'āsī,' etc. The wishing or longing for a desired object, a desired thing, may be called āsī. As in the example given there, so it is. May the Lord, the master of the world, who is the sole refuge without equal for the three existences, protect the world of beings from states of woe. Āsī is indeed aspiration, and the utterance that illuminates it also bears that name. In this example, 'the sole refuge of the three worlds' (Tilokekagatī), protection is aspired for. The phrases are: 'a gathering of the three worlds,' 'the one and only refuge,' and 'the sole refuge of the three worlds.'

335.

335.

Rasappatītijanakaṃ, jāyate yaṃ vibhūsanaṃ;

Rasavantanti taṃ ñeyyaṃ, rasavantavidhānato.

That embellishment which arises generating the delight of rasa, that should be known as rasavant, by the definition of rasavant.

335. Rasavantamudāharati “rasa”iccādinā. Yaṃ vibhūsanamalaṅkaraṇaṃ rasābhāsādino patītijanakaṃ avagamasampādakaṃ jāyate, taṃ vibhūsanaṃ rasavantavidhānato sampādanato “rasavanta”nti viññeyyaṃ yathā atthappatīti janako saddo “atthavā”ti.

335. It exemplifies rasavant with 'rasa,' etc. Whatever embellishment or ornament arises generating the delight of a semblance of rasa, etc., producing understanding, that embellishment should be understood as 'rasavant' by its accomplishment, according to the definition of rasavant. Just as a word that generates understanding of meaning is called 'meaningful.'

335. Uddese rasīti uddiṭṭharasālaṅkāraṃ dasseti “rasa”iccādinā. Yaṃ vibhūsanaṃ vuttālaṅkārānamantare yo koci alaṅkāro rasappatītijanakaṃ siṅgārādinavavidharasesu ekassa rasassa vā tasseva rasābhāsassa vā [M 0.0314] avabodhanaṃ sampādento jāyate, taṃ vibhūsanaṃ rasavantavidhānato attano rasasahitabhāvassa pakāsanato rasavantanti rasīti ñeyyanti. Yathā atthappatītijanako saddo “atthavā”ti vuccati, evaṃ rasappatītijanako alaṅkāro rasavanto “rasī”ti ca vuccati. Rasassa patīti ca, taṃ janetīti ca, raso assa atthīti ca, rasavato bhāvoti ca, tassa vidhānaṃ sampādananti ca vākyaṃ.

335. In the exposition, the ornament of rasa, designated as 'rasī,' is shown with 'rasa,' etc. Whatever embellishment, whichever ornament among the stated ornaments, arises generating the delight of rasa, producing the understanding of one of the nine rasas such as the erotic, or even a semblance of that rasa, that embellishment is to be understood as 'rasavant' or 'rasī' by the definition of rasavant, by revealing its own state of being endowed with rasa. Just as a word that generates understanding of meaning is called 'meaningful' (atthavā), so too an ornament that generates delight in rasa is called 'rasavant' or 'rasī'. The phrases are: 'the delight of rasa,' 'it generates that,' 'it has rasa,' 'the state of being endowed with rasa,' and 'its definition is its accomplishment.'

336.

336.

Rāgānatabbhutasarojamukhaṃ dharāya,

Pādā tilokaguruno’dhikabaddharāgā;

Ādāya niccasarasena karena gāḷhaṃ,

Sañcumbayanti satatāhitasambhamena.

The earth, with her face like a marvelous lotus, bent by passion; the feet of the Teacher of the three worlds, bound with exceeding love; taking them firmly with a hand ever moist with savor, they constantly kiss them with continuous, established reverence.

336. Udāharati “rāga”iccādi. Dharāya pathavīaṅganāya rāgena ānataṃ, mukhaṃ. Rāgaṃ rattavaṇṇaṃ ānataṃ ninnamitaṃ, sarojaṃ. Paṭhame abbhutasarojasadisatāya mukhaṃ, tena samānādhikaraṇanti rāgānatena samāso. Dutiye tu rāgānatañca taṃ abbhutasarojaṃ pathaviṃ bhinditvā sirīpādasampaṭiggahaṇatthaṃ uṭṭhahamacchariyapadumañca, tameva tassā mukhasadisattā mukhanti rāgānatabbhutasarojamukhaṃ. Tilokaguruno sammāsambuddhassa pādā. Kīdisā? Adhikabandho rāgo anurāgo, rattavaṇṇo vā yesaṃ te, tathāvidhā. Niccamanavarataṃ sarasena rasavatā karena hatthena, raṃsinā vā gāḷhaṃ ādāya gahetvā satataṃ niccaṃ āhito sambhamo ādaro, tadabhimukhatā vā, tena sañcumbayanti, nikkhipanti vā. Ettha silesarūpakehi sambhogasiṅgārarasābhāso janyate. Siṅgāro duvidho vippalambho, sambhogo ceti. Tesu vippalambhova samaggavaṇṇanādhārattā manoharo, nediso sambhogo. Sambhogābhāse tu vattabbameva natthi. Tathāpi’hā’dhigataṃ sambhogābhāsodāharaṇaṃ bālappabodhanatthaṃ kiñci vicāressāma. Tatra pādānaṃ kāmukattaṃ [M 0.0315] dharāya kāminittañca vākyasāmatthiyā viññāyate. Saddena vuccamānaṃ puna vuttaṃ siyā. Atra pādānaṃ taṃ viññeyyaṃ, ratyukkaṃsābhāso yadi kavinā paṭipādetabbo na bhaveyya, tadā gāthāyamananupapannaṃ siyāti evaṃvidhavacanatova pādā ratyābhāsavantoti gamyate. Ratiyā ālambaṇavibhāvābhāso dharākāmini, rammadesādivisesābhāve acchariyapadumuggamanābhāvato abbhutasarojasaddasavanena gammamānā rammadesādayo uddīpanavibhāvābhāsā, byabhicārībhāvābhāsabodhakāni kavivacanāni anubhāvābhāso. Tathā hi “niccasarasena karena gāḷhaṃ ādāyā”ti karassa sarasatāgāḷhaggahaṇakathanena harisādayo gamyante. “Satatāhitasambhamenā”ti iminā ussukkattādayo pahīyantīti evaṃ bandhavuttīti vibhāvādīhi bandhatthābhāsānaṃ manasi yo uppajjati ānandābhāso, so rasābhāso sambhogarasābhāso vuttoti.

336. It exemplifies with 'passion,' etc. The face of the earth-maiden is bent by passion. 'Passion' (rāga) means 'red color,' 'bent' (ānata) means 'lowered,' and 'lotus' (saroja). In the first interpretation, the face is like a marvelous lotus, hence the compound 'rāgānata' (bent by passion/redness) is in apposition with it. In the second interpretation, 'rāgānatabbhutasarojamukhaṃ' refers to the marvelous lotus, bent by passion/redness, which, breaking through the earth, rises as a wondrous lotus to receive the auspicious feet, and that very lotus is like her face, hence 'face.' The feet of the Teacher of the three worlds, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. What are they like? They are those for whom there is excessive attachment or affection (rāga/anurāga), or they are red in color; such are they. Taking them firmly with a hand (kara) that is ever moist with savor (rasavatā), or with rays (raṃsinā), and with continuous reverence (sambhamo), respect (ādaro), or facing towards them (tadabhimukhatā), they constantly kiss them, or place them. Here, the semblance of the erotic rasa of union (sambhogasiṅgārarasābhāsa) is generated through wordplay (silesa) and metaphor (rūpaka). Erotic rasa (siṅgāra) is of two kinds: separation (vippalambha) and union (sambhoga). Among these, separation is charming because it is the basis for complete description; union is not so. In the semblance of union, there is nothing to be said. Nevertheless, for the sake of awakening the foolish, we shall consider some examples of the semblance of union found here. Here, the feet as the lover and the earth as the beloved are understood by the force of the statement. To state it explicitly would be redundant. Here, this should be understood regarding the feet: if the semblance of intense passion were not to be presented by the poet, then the verse would be inappropriate. Thus, from such words, it is understood that the feet possess the semblance of passion. The semblance of the objective stimulus (ālambaṇavibhāva) of passion is the earth as the beloved. In the absence of specific delightful regions, etc., due to the absence of the emergence of a marvelous lotus, delightful regions, etc., suggested by the mention of a marvelous lotus, are the semblance of excitants (uddīpanavibhāva). The poet’s words, indicating the semblance of transient emotions (byabhicārībhāva), are the semblance of consequents (anubhāva). For instance, by mentioning the hand’s moisture and firm grasp in 'taking firmly with a hand ever moist with savor,' things like joy (harisādayo) are suggested. By 'with continuous, established reverence,' eagerness (ussukkattādayo), etc., are suggested—thus, the expression is connected. The semblance of bliss that arises in the mind from the semblance of the meaning of the composition through the stimuli and so forth, is called the semblance of rasa, the semblance of the erotic rasa of union.

336. Idāni udāharaṇaṃ dassento uttaripi dassetabbasiṅgārahassakaruṇādirasuddesassa anurūpato siṅgārarasayuttameva dasseti “rāgā”iccādinā. Dharāya mahīaṅganāya rāgānatabbhutasarojamukhaṃ rāgena anurāgena abhimukhaṃ katvā namitaṃ acchariyaguṇopetapadumasadisānanaṃ no ce, rattavaṇṇaṃ ānataṃ abbhutasarojasaṅkhatamukhaṃ tilokaguruno bhuvanattayānusāsakassa sammāsambuddhassa pādā adhikabaddharāgā adhikabaddhānurāgavantā no ce, pubbakammena kataadhikarattavaṇṇā niccasarasena karena satatānurāgayuttena hatthena no ce, avikalattā satatasampattisahitena kiraṇena gāḷhaṃ ādāya gāḷhaṃ gahetvā no ce, phusitvā satatāhitasambhamena niccaṃ katādarena no ce, nirantarāhitaabhimukhabhāvena sañcumbayanti [M 0.0316] cumbanti no ce, ṭhitikriyāsādhanattena phusantīti.

336. Now, giving an example, and in accordance with the exposition of sentiments such as the erotic, comic, compassionate, etc., to be shown further, it illustrates specifically the erotic sentiment with 'passion,' etc. The wondrous lotus-face of the earth-maiden is bowed down with passion, made to face with passion and affection, a face like a wondrous lotus endowed with qualities—or rather, a reddish, bowed, wondrous lotus-like face. The feet of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, the teacher of the three worlds, the instructor of the three realms, are bound with excessive passion, possessing excessive affection—or rather, made excessively reddish by past kamma. With a hand constantly endowed with affection—or rather, with an unbroken, constantly prosperous ray—taking them firmly—or rather, touching them—with constant, established reverence—or rather, with an uninterrupted, established facing—they kiss them—or rather, they touch them as a means of achieving stability.

Rāgena anurāgena ānataṃ abhimukhīkatamiti ca, abbhutañca taṃ sarojañceti ca, tena sadisatāya abbhutasarojañca taṃ mukhañceti ca, rāgānatañca taṃ abbhutasarojamukhañceti ca, rāgaṃ rattavaṇṇaṃ ānataṃ ninnamiti ca, tañca taṃ abbhutasarojañceti ca, tameva tādisamukhasadisattā mukhamiti ca, tilokassa gurūti ca, adhikaṃ katvā baddho, attano pubbakammena vā kato, rāgo anurāgo rattavaṇṇo vā yesamiti ca, rasena anurāgena sampattiyā vā saha vattamānoti ca, āhito vihito ca so sambhamo ādaro tadabhimukhabhāvo vā ceti ca viggaho.

Bent by passion, inclined by affection, and made to face towards it; and it is wonderful and that lotus too; and by its similarity to it, the wonderful lotus and that face too; and bent by passion, that wonderful lotus-face too; and passion is red-colored, bent, inclined downwards; and that wonderful lotus too; and that very thing is the face, due to its similarity to such a face; and the teacher of the three worlds too; exceedingly bound, or made by one's own past kamma, passion, affection, or red-colored for those; and existing with taste, affection, or prosperity; and that reverence, respect, or facing towards it, which is established and arranged—this is the analysis.

Ettha “rāgānatā”tiādikena silesālaṅkārena ca “abbhutasarojamukha”nti rūpakālaṅkārena ca sambhogasiṅgārarasābhāso uppādīyati. Tādisaṃ itthipurisānaṃ sambhogābhāvena, tadākārena ca kappitattā rasābhāso nāmāti daṭṭhabbo. Siṅgārassa āyogavippayogasambhogavasena tividhattepi āyogavippayogadvayaṃ vippalambhamevāti vippalambho, sambhogo ceti duvidho hoti. Tesu vippalambhova anūnavaṇṇanāya bhūmittā manoharo. Sambhogo pana tādiso na hoti. Sambhogābhāsopi hīno hoti. Evaṃ sante payogaṃ katvā kurumānāya vaṇṇanāya ucitabhāvena ihādhigatasambhogasiṅgārarasābhāsena rasibhūtālaṅkārassa udāharaṇe rasābhāso evaṃ veditabbo. Pādānaṃ kāmukabhāvābhāse ca dharāya kāminībhāvābhāse ca vācakapadena avuttepi “dharāya pādā tilokaguruno”ti idaṃ ṭhapetvā pāṇidhammapakāsakehi avasesapadehi ñāyate.

Here, the semblance of the erotic sentiment of union (sambhogasiṅgārarasābhāsa) is produced by the rhetorical device of paronomasia (silesālaṅkāra) with phrases such as ‘rāgānatā,’ and by the rhetorical device of metaphor (rūpakālaṅkāra) with phrases such as ‘abbhutasarojamukha.’ Because such a union is absent between this man and woman, and it is merely conceived in that form, it should be understood as a semblance of sentiment (rasābhāsa). Although the erotic sentiment (siṅgāra) is threefold—by way of connection (āyoga), separation (vippayoga), and union (sambhoga)—the two, connection and separation, are indeed love-in-separation (vippalambha). Thus, it is twofold: love-in-separation and union. Of these, love-in-separation is more delightful, as it provides the ground for a full description. Union, however, is not so. Even the semblance of union is inferior. This being the case, in this example of a sentiment-based ornament (rasibhūtālaṅkāra), the semblance of sentiment should be understood thus: through the semblance of the erotic sentiment of union achieved here, which is appropriate to the description being made by this application. Although the semblance of the lover's state in the feet and the semblance of the beloved's state in the earth are not explicitly stated, setting aside the phrase ‘the feet of the Teacher of the Three Worlds on the earth,’ it is understood from the remaining words that reveal the nature of the hand.

Dvinnaṃ [M 0.0317] aññamaññaṃ ratiābhāso “adhikabaddharāgā rāgānata”nti imehi vutto. Ayaṃ ratiābhāso idha ṭhāyībhāvo purisaratiyā itthiyā ca, itthiratiyā purisassa ca ālambaṇattā pādakāmukadharākāminiyo dve aññamaññaṃ ālambaṇavibhāvābhāsā honti. Rammadesādivisesaṃ vinā acchariyapadumodayassa abhāvato abbhutasarojasaddassa uccāraṇena gammamānā rammadesādayo ratiṃ uddīpayantīti uddīpanavibhāvābhāsā nāma. “Niccasarasena karena gāḷhamādāyā”ti iminā karassa sarasabhāvassa ca gāḷhaṃ gahaṇassa ca vuttattā harisādayo ñāyante. “Satatāhitasambhamenā”ti iminā ussāhādayo ñāyanti. Tattha harisaussāhādayo byabhicārībhāvābhāsā nāma honti. Te byabhicārībhāvābhāse pakāsentāni yathāvuttakavivacanāni anubhāvābhāsā nāmāti evaṃ bandhe dissamānaṭhāyībhāvabyabhicārībhāvavibhāvaanubhāvehi atthāvabodhaṃ karontānaṃ paṇḍitānaṃ uppajjamāno yo santosābhāsasaṅkhāto rasābhāso atthi, so idha sambhogarasābhāsoti kathitoti. Ṭhāyībhāvādayo upari āvibhavissanti.

The semblance of mutual delight between the two is expressed by these words: ‘excessively bound by passion, inclined to passion.’ This semblance of delight is here the permanent mood. Because a man's delight has a woman as its object, and a woman's delight has a man as its object, the two—the feet as lover and the earth as beloved—are mutual semblances of the supporting determinant. Since there is no arising of a wondrous lotus without a special charming place, and so on, the charming places and the like, which are understood by the utterance of the word ‘wondrous lotus,’ stimulate delight; thus, they are called semblances of the excitant determinant. By the phrase, ‘taking a firm hold with the ever-moist hand,’ the moist nature of the hand and the firm grasp are stated, whereby joy and so forth are understood. By the phrase, ‘with constant, attentive haste,’ energy and so forth are understood. Therein, joy, energy, and the like are called semblances of transitory moods. Those aforementioned phrases that reveal these semblances of transitory moods are called semblances of ensuants. Thus, for the learned who comprehend the meaning through the permanent mood, transitory moods, determinants, and ensuants—all seen as semblances in the composition—there arises a semblance of sentiment, known as a semblance of contentment, which is here called the semblance of the sentiment of union. The permanent mood and the rest will be made clear later.

337.

337.

Iccā’nugamma purimācariyānubhāvaṃ,

Saṅkhepato nigadito’ya’malaṅkatīnaṃ;

Bhedo’parūpari kavīhi vikappiyānaṃ,

Ko nāma passitu’malaṃ khalu tāsa’mantaṃ.

Thus, following the influence of the ancient teachers, this distinction of ornaments has been briefly declared; for those conceived again and again by poets, who indeed is capable of seeing their end?

Iti saṅgharakkhitamahāsāmipādaviracite

Thus, in the work composed by the venerable Mahāsāmi Saṅgharakkhita,

Subodhālaṅkāre

in the Subodhālaṅkāra,

Atthālaṅkārāvabodho nāma

the chapter named the Comprehension of Ornaments of Meaning,

Catuttho paricchedo.

the fourth chapter.

337. Evamuddesānukkamena yathāpaṭiññātaṃ niṭṭhapetvā idāni nigamanapubbakaṃ bahuttamesaṃ niddisitumāha “icci”ccādi. Iti [M 0.0318] iminā vuttappakārena purimānaṃ daṇḍīādīnaṃ ācariyānaṃ ānubhāvaṃ bandhalakkhaṇāni anugamma anugantvā alaṅkatīnamalaṅkārānaṃ ayaṃ bhedo saṅkhepato nigadito kathito. Saṅkhepatoti vutto, kasmāti āha “uparūparī”tiādi. Uparūpari dīghakālamārabbha yāvedāni matthakamatthake kavīhi vikappiyānaṃ pabhediyamānānaṃ tāsamalaṅkatīnaṃ antaṃ pariyantaṃ passituṃ khalu ekantena ko nāma jano alaṃ samattho.

337. Having thus completed what was promised, in order according to the headings, now, to indicate their multitude by way of conclusion, he says, ‘Thus,’ etc. In this way, following the influence of the earlier teachers like Daṇḍī and others, and adhering to the characteristics of composition, this distinction of ornaments has been concisely declared, that is, spoken. Why is it said concisely? He says, ‘Again and again,’ etc. For a long time, again and again, up to the present, who indeed is capable of seeing the end, the limit, of these ornaments that have been differentiated and divided by poets to the very highest degree?

Iti mahāsāmināmikāyaṃ subodhālaṅkāraṭīkāyaṃ

Thus, in the sub-commentary on the Subodhālaṅkāra, named after the Mahāsāmi,

Catuttho paricchedo.

the fourth chapter.

337. Evaṃ uddesakkamena yathāpaṭiññāte atthālaṅkāre niṭṭhapetvā idāni nigamanamukhena esaṃ atthālaṅkārānaṃ bahubhāvaṃ dasseti “iccānugamma”iccādinā. Iti yathāvuttanayena purimācariyānubhāvaṃ pubbakālikānaṃ daṇḍībhaddapāṇādīnaṃ alaṅkārasatthasaṅkhātānubhāvaṃ anugamma alaṅkatīnaṃ ayaṃ bhedo saṅkhepato nigadito mayā vutto saṅgahito. Kasmāti ce? Uparūpari dīghakālato paṭṭhāya yāvajjatanā kavīhi racanākattārehi vikappiyānaṃ anekappakārato kappiyamānattā puthakkariyamānānaṃ tāsamalaṅkatīnaṃ antaṃ pariyantaṃ passituṃ khalu ekantena ko nāma puggalo alaṃ samatthoti. Saṅgahamanādiyitvā kenāpi pariyantaṃ adhigantuṃ na sakkāti adhippāyo. Pure bhavāti ca, purimā ca te ācariyā ceti ca, tesamānubhāvoti ca, visesato asaṅkarato kappiyanti ca vākyaṃ.

337. Thus, having completed the ornaments of meaning as promised, in order according to the headings, now, by way of conclusion, he shows the abundance of these ornaments of meaning with ‘thus following,’ etc. In this way, following the method as stated, in accordance with the influence of the former teachers, the ancient ones like Daṇḍī, Bhaddapāṇa, and others, whose influence is known as the treatise on ornaments, this classification of ornaments has been briefly stated, spoken, and compiled by me. Why is this? Because, from a long time ago, again and again, up to the present, poets and composers have conceived and diversified them in many ways, making them distinct. Indeed, who is capable of seeing the end, the limit, of those ornaments in every respect? The meaning is that without undertaking a compilation, no one can fully comprehend their limits. And ‘existing in the past,’ and ‘those former teachers,’ and ‘their influence,’ and ‘they are conceived especially without confusion’—these are the phrases.

Iti subodhālaṅkāranissaye

Thus, in the Subodhālaṅkāra-nissaya,

Catuttho paricchedo.

the fourth chapter.

5. Bhāvāvabodhapariccheda

5. The Chapter on the Comprehension of Moods

338.

338.

Paṭibhānavatā [M 0.0319] loka-vohāra’manusārinā;

Tato’cityasamullāsa-vedinā kavinā paraṃ.

By one possessing ready wit, following worldly convention; and furthermore, by the poet who perceives the blossoming of propriety.

338. Tadeva yathāpaṭiññātamalaṅkāravibhāgaṃ bodhetvā sampati rasavantālaṅkārappasaṅgenādhigataṃ rasaṃ sakala saṃsāradukkhanissa raṇekanimittavimuttirasekarasavisuddhasaddhammāgamaviggāhasappīṇanoṇatamatīnaṃ paramasaddhālūnamanadhigatattepi lakkhaṇamattena lokavohārakosallamattapariggahāya kiñcimattamupadisituṃ na sākallena “paṭibhānavatā”tiādimāha. Paṭibhānaṃ taṃtaṃṭhānānurūpappavattā paññā. Sā hi sarasaracanāyaccantopakārikā, tatova kabbaṃ “paṭibhāna”nti vuccati. Tenāha “paṭibhānavatā”ti. Kavinā lokavohārānugantabbo. Yo hi sakalaṃ lokavohāraṃ nānusarati, so kaviyeva na hoti. Tenāha “lokavohāramanusārinā”ti. Yato ocityaṃ nāma kavīnaṃ paramaṃ rahassaṃ lokavohārepi ucitaññūyeva pasaṃsīyate, samucitalokavohārānusāreneva ca vakkhamānānukkamena viracitā racanā sacetanānaṃ rasassādāya sampajjate, tasmā ocitye samullasattaṃ dittaṃ phuṭameva bandhanaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Tatovaccantamocityasamullāsavedinā kavinā bhavitabbaṃ. Tenāha “paraṃ ocityasamullāsavedinā”ti. Sabbañcetaṃ “kavinā”ti ettha visesanaṃ, “kavinā”ti cetaṃ “nibandhā”ti ettha avutto kattā.

338. Having thus explained the divisions of embellishment as previously declared, now, in connection with the discussion of flavorful embellishments, he says ‘by one possessing ready wit,’ etc., in order to teach something, not exhaustively, about the sentiment that has been attained. This is for the mere acquisition of skill in worldly usage, even for those of supreme faith who have not yet grasped, merely by its characteristics, the sentiment of liberation, which is the sole cause for release from all the suffering of saṃsāra, the single taste of liberation, the pure, true Dhamma, for those whose minds are delighted and inclined by plunging into its scriptures. Ready wit is wisdom that arises appropriately in each particular situation. It is exceedingly helpful for creating a delightful composition; hence, poetry is called ‘ready wit.’ Therefore, he says, ‘by one possessing ready wit.’ A poet must follow worldly conventions. For one who does not follow all worldly conventions is not a poet at all. Therefore, he says, ‘by one who follows worldly conventions.’ Since propriety is the highest secret of poets, and even in worldly discourse, only one who knows what is fitting is praised, and since a composition arranged in the sequence to be described, in accordance with appropriate worldly conventions, leads to the tasting of sentiment for the discerning, it is therefore fitting to create a work that is brilliant and clear, shining with propriety. Hence, a poet must be one who perceives the supreme blossoming of propriety. Therefore, he says, ‘furthermore, by one who perceives the blossoming of propriety.’ All this is a qualification of ‘by a poet,’ and ‘by a poet’ here refers to the unstated agent of ‘should compose.’

338. Evaṃ yathāpaṭiññātānamalaṅkārānaṃ dassanāvasare rasavantālaṅkārappasaṅgenādhigatanavavidhasiṅgārādirase sakalasaṃsāradukkhanissaraṇaasahāyakaraṇabhūtavimuttirasena ekarasabhūte atipaṇīte saddhammāmataraseyeva luddhānaṃ saddhābāhullasuddhasaṃyamānaṃ vimukhepi [M 0.0320] lakkhaṇamattapariññāṇena lokavohāresu asammohatthaṃ saṅkhepena dassetukāmo idāni “paṭibhānavatā”iccādimāha. Paṭibhānavatā sarasaracanāya accantopakāraṭṭhānocitapaññāvisesavatā lokavohāramanusārinā sakalaloke vohārānurūpamanugatena tato yasmā ocityaṃ nāma hadayato abahi kātabbaṃ, rahassamiva bandhato viyojanīyaṃ na hoti. Tasmā paramatisayena ocityasamullāsavedinā ucitabhāvena vattumicchitatthassa uddīpanasseva anurūpappakārena iṭṭhatthassa samullāsanaṃ dittiṃ jānantena kavinā bandhakārakena nibandhāti sambandho. Paṭibhā paṭibhānanti paññāyetaṃ nāmaṃ, tato jātakabbassapi paṭibhāti vuccamānattā ayaṃ paññāviseso racanāya accantopakāroti ñātabbo. Paṭibhānamassatthīti ca, lokassa vohāroti ca, taṃ anugacchati sīlenāti ca, ocityena samullāsoti ca, taṃ vijānāti sīlenāti ca viggaho.

338. Thus, on the occasion of showing the embellishments as previously declared, in the context of delightful embellishments, the ninefold flavors of love and so on are attained. With the flavor of liberation—which alone is capable of rescuing one from all the suffering of existence—being utterly refined and unified in the supreme taste of the true Dhamma, even for those who are eager for it, whose faith is abundant and purely restrained, though they may be averse, by merely recognizing the characteristics, in order to avoid confusion in worldly conventions, now wishing to explain briefly, he says, 'endowed with ready wit,' and so on. Endowed with ready wit—that is, possessing the excellence of wisdom suited to the occasion, which is exceedingly helpful for a delightful composition; following worldly conventions—that is, having followed in a manner appropriate to all worldly dealings; and then, since what is called 'propriety' must not be excluded from the heart, like a secret, it cannot be separated from the composition—therefore, by the poet, the composer, who knows the supreme blossoming of propriety, who knows the shining forth of the desired meaning in a manner appropriate to the stimulation of the intended meaning, desiring to speak appropriately, the connection is with 'composes.' 'Ready wit' (paṭibhāna) is indeed a name for wisdom. Hence, even in the Jātaka, since it is said to 'shine forth' (paṭibhāti), this special wisdom should be understood as supremely beneficial in composition. And 'he possesses ready wit,' and 'the world's convention,' and 'he follows it by nature,' and 'blossoming through propriety,' and 'he understands it by nature'—these are the analyses.

339.

339.

Ṭhāyīsambandhino bhāva-vibhāvā sānubhāvakā;

Sampajjanti nibandhā te, rasassādāya sādhunaṃ.

The emotions and determinants, connected to the abiding states and accompanied by their consequents, are accomplished in those compositions for the tasting of relish by the discerning.

339. “Ṭhāyi”ccādi. Ṭhāyino vakkhamānaratyādayo tehi saha sambandho vibhāvādīhi yoge ratyādīnamassādiyattamānīyamānattā etesamatthīti ṭhāyīsambandhino. Saha anubhāvehi vakkhamānalakkhaṇehīti sānubhāvakā, bhāvo vibhāvo ca, vakkhamāno bhāvena bhāvābhāsopi imināva saṅgahito, rasassādāya sampajjantīti sambandho.

339. 'Abiding' and so on. The abiding states (ṭhāyino) are love (rati) and so on, which will be described. Because love and so on are brought to a state of being relishable through their connection with determinants and so on, a connection with those abiding states exists for these emotions and determinants; hence, they are called 'related to the abiding states' (ṭhāyīsambandhino). 'With consequents' (sānubhāvakā) means with the consequents (anubhāvehi) that have the characteristics to be described. Emotion (bhāva) and determinant (vibhāva); the semblance of emotion (bhāvābhāsa), which will be described, is also included by this very term 'emotion.' The connection is 'they are accomplished for the tasting of relish'.

339. “Ṭhāyi”ccādi. Ṭhāyīsambandhino ṭhāyīpadena, tena vāccaratihāsādiatthena vā sambandhupagatā sānubhāvakā vakkhamānānubhāvehi saha pavattā bhāvavibhāvā vakkhamānabhāvavibhāvā nibandhā vuttaguṇopetakavinā bandhitā ekattha āharitvā dassitā sādhunaṃ issādidosarahitānaṃ sajjanānaṃ rasassādāya siṅgārādivakkhamānarasassa assādanatthaṃ sampajjanti pavattantīti. Imāya gāthāya ṭhāyībhāvo byabhicārībhāvo kevalabhāvo vibhāvo anubhāvo raso ceti ime uddiṭṭhā bhavanti, kathanti ce? Bhāvavibhāvānaṃ “ṭhāyīsambandhino”ti visesanaṃ bhavati, tena bhāvassa ṭhāyī ca so bhāvo ceti ca ṭhāyīpadena sambandhattā ṭhāyībhāvo ca, puna byabhicārībhāve sati “ṭhāyībhāvo”ti imassa sādhakattā imasseva ṭhāyībhāvapadassa payogasāmatthiyena gammamāno byabhicārībhāvo ca, puna ṭhāyīpadena samāsamakatvā visuṃ dassitabhāvasaddasutiyā ṭhāyībhāvabyabhicārībhāvehi añño bhāvo ca, tathā eva ṭhāyīpadena vāccaratihāsādiatthassa uppattiuddīpanadvayaṃ vibhūtaṃ katvā sajjetvā ṭhitattā tehi ratihāsādīhi atthehi sambandhino ālambaṇauddīpanasaṅkhatavividhavibhāvā ca, evameva sānubhāvakapadena samāyogena dassitānubhāvo ca, “rasassādāyā”ti iminā niddiṭṭharaso cāti evamime ṭhāyībhāvādayo uddiṭṭhā honti. Ṭhāyinā saha sambandhoti ca, so etesamatthīti ca, bhāvo ca vibhāvo ceti ca, saha anubhāvehi vattantīti ca, rasassa assādoti ca vākyaṃ.

339. 'Abiding' and so on. The emotions and determinants to be described, which are related to the abiding states—by the term 'abiding,' or by being connected with its expressed meaning of love, mirth, etc.—and which occur together with the consequents to be described; these compositions, composed by a poet endowed with the stated qualities, brought together and presented in one place, are accomplished for the discerning, for good people free from faults like envy, for the tasting of the relish, such as the erotic, etc., which will be described. By this verse, the abiding state, the transitory state, the simple state, the determinant, the consequent, and the relish are indicated. How so? The qualification 'related to the abiding states' belongs to the emotions and determinants. Thus, because of the connection of 'emotion' with the term 'abiding' (as in 'abiding' and 'that emotion'), it is the abiding state (ṭhāyībhāva). Further, when the transitory state (byabhicārībhāva) exists, this 'abiding state' is established, and by the power of the usage of this very term 'abiding state,' the transitory state is also implied. Again, by not compounding with the term 'abiding,' and by the distinct hearing of the word 'emotion,' another emotion (bhāva) distinct from the abiding state and transitory state is indicated. Similarly, because the two aspects—basis (ālambaṇa) and excitant (uddīpana)—of the meanings expressed by the term 'abiding,' such as love, mirth, etc., are made manifest and prepared, therefore, those connected with these meanings of love, mirth, etc., are the various determinants (vibhāva) characterized as basis and excitant. And similarly, by the association with the term 'sānubhāvaka,' the consequent (anubhāva) is shown. And by 'for the tasting of relish,' the relish is indicated. Thus, these, the abiding states etc., are indicated. The analytical phrases are: 'connection with the abiding,' 'this exists for them,' 'the emotion and the determinant,' 'occurring together with the consequents,' and 'tasting of relish.'

Bhāvaadhippāya

The Meaning of 'Emotion'.

340.

340.

Cittavuttivisesā tu, bhāvayanti rase yato;

Ratyādayo tato bhāva-saddena parikittitā.

The particular mental states, however, since they produce the relishes, therefore love and the like are designated by the term 'bhāva'.

340. Idāni yathāuddiṭṭhesu ṭhāyādīhi bhāvavibhāvānubhāvarasesu paṭhamaṃ bhāvaṃ vibhāvetuṃ bhāvasaddamanvatthayati “citta”iccādinā. Cittassa vuttiyo ramaṇahasanādiākārena pavattiyo, tāva visesā visiṭṭhasabhāvatthāti cittavuttivisesā. [M 0.0322] Ratyādayo ṭhāyībyabhicārīsāttikā. Tusaddo visese. Yato rase siṅgārādayo bhāvayanti nipphādenti. Tato bhāvasaddena parikittitā bharatādīhi kathitā. Ettha hi ṇyanto bhūdhātu karaṇe vattate. Yato cāyaṃ na kevalaṃ karaṇeyeva vattate, atha kho byāpane, paṭipādane ca, tasmāssa paṭibhānaṃ cittaṃ bhāvayanti byāpenti. Atha vā kavino lokaṭṭhitiñāṇalakkhaṇaṃ adhippāyaṃ bhāvayanti paṭipādentīti bhāvāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

340. Now, to explain the first aspect, 'bhāva,' among the previously mentioned abiding states and so on—namely emotion, determinant, consequent, and relish—he explains the etymology of the term 'bhāva' with 'citta' and so on. The functions of the mind are its activities in the form of delighting, laughing, and so on; these very distinctions, being of a distinct nature, are 'particular mental states' (cittavuttivisesā). Love and the like are the abiding, transitory, and involuntary states. The word 'tu' indicates distinction. Because they produce, they bring forth, relishes like the erotic, therefore they are described by the term 'bhāva,' as stated by Bharata and others. Here, the root 'bhū' with the causative suffix is used in the sense of causing. And since this is used not only in the sense of causing but also in the sense of pervading and accomplishing, therefore 'they cause the mind to be' means 'they pervade the mind with inspiration.' Alternatively, 'they accomplish' the poet's intention, which is characterized by knowledge of the state of the world; hence they are 'emotions' (bhāvā). Thus the meaning here should be understood.

340. Idāni uddiṭṭhesu ṭhāyībhāvādīsu ṭhāyīādīnaṃ ṭhāyībhāvādīnaṃ (ka.) tiṇṇaṃ sādhāraṇo bhāvo nāma esoti dassento anvatthavasena dasseti “citta”iccādi. Cittavuttivisesā tu cittassa uttari vakkhamānārammaṇahasanasocanādīhi, nibbedādīhi, thambhādīhi ca ākārehi pavattisaṅkhātā aññamaññaṃ asaṅkarākārasaṅkhātā visesā pana ṭhāyībyabhicārīsāttikā yato yasmā rase siṅgārādirase bhāvayanti nipphādenti karonti. No ce, rase siṅgārādirasavisaye paṇḍitānaṃ cittaṃ bhāvayanti byāpanaṃ karonti. No ce, tasmiṃyeva rasavisaye kavino lokasabhāvaṃ visayaṃ katvā pavattañāṇalakkhaṇaṃ adhippāyaṃ bhāvayanti paṭipādanaṃ karonti. Tato bhāvasaddena hetukattari nipphannena ratyādayo ratihāsādayo parikittitā bharatādīhi vuttā hontīti. “Ratyādayo”ti ettha ādisaddena hāsādayo ṭhāyībhāvā ca, nibbedādayo byabhicārībhāvā ca, thambhapalayādayo sāttikabhāvā ca saṅgahitāti daṭṭhabbā. Cittassa vuttiyoti ca, tā eva visesāti ca, bhāvo iti saddoti ca vākyaṃ.

340. Now, among the previously mentioned abiding states and so on, to show that 'bhāva' is the common aspect of the three, beginning with the abiding states, he shows this by way of its etymological meaning, beginning with 'citta.' The distinct functions of the mind—which are called modes of operation by means of delighting, laughing, grieving, and so on, which will be spoken of later, and by means of disenchantment, stupor, and so on, and which are called non-overlapping characteristics—are indeed the abiding, transitory, and involuntary states. Because they produce and bring about relishes like the erotic relish. Or else, they pervade the minds of the wise in the realm of relish, the experience of the erotic, and so on. Or else, in that very realm of relish, having made the nature of the world their object, they accomplish the poet's intention, which is characterized by knowledge of the world's nature. Therefore, by the word 'bhāva,' derived from the root here, love, mirth, and so on are described by Bharata and others. Here, it should be understood that by the word 'ādi' (etc.), mirth and so on as abiding states, disenchantment and so on as transitory states, and stupor, paralysis, and so on as involuntary states are included. The analytical phrases are 'the functions of the mind,' 'these are indeed the distinctions,' and 'the word is bhāva.'

Ṭhāyībhāvaadhippāya

The Meaning of 'Abiding State'.

341.

341.

Virodhinā’ññabhāvena,

[M 0.0323] Yo bhāvo na tirohito;

Sīlena tiṭṭhati’cce’so,

Ṭhāyībhāvoti saddito.

That state which is not obscured by another, opposing state, and which remains steadfast by its own nature—this is called the abiding state (ṭhāyībhāva).

341. Ṭhāyādike tividhe bhāve kamenāha “virodhinā”iccādinā. Virodhinā aññena jigucchādinā bhāvena yo bhāvo ratyādiko na tirohito nacchādito, eso bhāvo anucchijjamānattā eva tiṭṭhati sīlenāti, ṭhāyī eva bhāvoti ṭhāyībhāvoti saddito kathito. Yo bhāvādīhi ālokitassādaṃ nīto samānīto, so sāmājikehi assādiyamānattā rasoti vuccati. Vakkhati hi “savibhāva”iccādi.

341. Regarding the three kinds of states, beginning with the abiding, he speaks in order, beginning with 'by an opposing.' That state, such as love, which is not concealed or obscured by another, opposing state, such as disgust, that state remains unbroken and stands by its own nature; thus, it is an abiding emotion, and is called the abiding state (ṭhāyībhāva). That which is brought to a state of illuminated relish by means of determinants and others, being relished by the connoisseurs, is called relish (rasa). For he will say, 'with its determinant,' and so on.

341. Idāni ṭhāyīādike tividhabhāve kamena niddisati “virodhi”iccādinā. Virodhinā aññabhāvena ratihāsādīnaṃ viruddhena jigucchādinā aññabhāvena yo bhāvo ratihāsādiko tirohito na byavahito na hoti, eso viruddhabhāvena abyavahito bhāvo tiṭṭhati sīlenāti iminā atthena ṭhāyī nāma hotīti katvā ṭhāyībhāvoti saddito kathitoti. Yo vibhāvānubhāvādīhi assādanīyattaṃ pāpito sabbhehi assādanīyattā rasoti vuccati, so ṭhāyī nāmāti vuccati. Añño ca so bhāvo ceti ca, tiro kayiritthāti ca, ṭhāyī ca so bhāvo ceti ca viggaho.

341. Now, he indicates in order the three kinds of states, beginning with the enduring, with the words starting 'opposing.' That state, such as love and laughter, which is not concealed or separated by another opposing state, such as disgust, which is contrary to love and laughter; that state, being unseparated by an opposing state, stands by its nature. By this meaning, it is called 'ṭhāyī,' and thus it is referred to as the enduring state (ṭhāyībhāva). That which is brought to a state of being relishable by means of vibhāva, anubhāva, and so on, and is called rasa because it is relishable by all, is also called the enduring (ṭhāyī). The analysis (viggaha) is: 'and that is another state,' 'it is concealed,' and 'that is an enduring state.'

Ṭhāyībhāvappabhedauddesa

Enumeration of the Distinctions of Enduring States.

342.

342.

Ratihāsā ca soko ca,

Kodhussāhabhaya’mpi ca;

Jigucchāvimhayā ceva,

Samo ca nava ṭhāyino.

Love and laughter and sorrow, Anger, energy, and fear, Disgust and astonishment, And equanimity—these nine are the enduring states.

342. Ratyādīnaṃ [M 0.0324] navannameva ṭhāyitvaṃ sambhavatītyāha “rati”ccādi. Samo ceti evaṃ ṭhāyino navāti yojanā. Navevete sakasakavibhāvānubhāvehi samullāsitā visumpi bandhitabbā kavinā, abhinetabbā ca naṭena, tathā sesabhāvāpi. Tattha yadi panāyaṃ rati asesaitthipurisaguṇayuttānaṃ itthipurisānaṃ aññamaññaṃ janitā, candādīhi uddīpanavibhāvehi uddīpitā, ussukkatādibādhakehi anubhāvehi paripositā, sakasakānubhāvasāmatthiyā patīyamānehi anekarūpehi byabhicārīhi cittatā siyā, tadā tu ṭhāyī rati naṭābhinayena, subandhasavanena vā sabbhehi assādiyamānā siṅgārarasattamāpajjate. Evaṃ yathāyogaṃ hāsādiṭhāyībhāvānaṃ hassarasādibhāvāpajjane yuttiṃ samanneyya.

342. He says, with the words beginning 'rati,' that enduringness is possible only for these nine states. The construction is: 'and equanimity,' thus there are nine enduring states. These very nine, being illuminated by their respective causes (vibhāva) and effects (anubhāva), should be composed separately by the poet and enacted by the actor, and likewise the remaining states. In this regard, if this love (rati) is generated mutually between men and women endowed with all excellent qualities, is kindled by stimulating causes (uddīpanavibhāva) such as the moon, is nourished by afflicting effects (anubhāva) such as eagerness, and becomes a state of mind through various transient states (byabhicārī) which are understood by the power of their respective effects, then that enduring love, when enacted by an actor or heard in a well-composed work, attains the state of the erotic sentiment (siṅgārarasa), being enjoyed by all. Similarly, one should understand the logic of how the enduring states such as laughter (hāsa) attain the state of the comic sentiment (hāsyarasa) and so forth, as is appropriate.

342. Ṭhāyībhāvo nāma ratyādayo naveveti dassetuṃ “ratihāsā”tiādimāha. Ratihāsā ca soko ca kodhussāhabhayampi ca jigucchāvimhayā ceva samo santaguṇo cāti evaṃ ṭhāyino nava honti. Imesaṃ ratyādīnaṃ navannaṃ sarūpakathanaṃ “siṅgārahassakaruṇā”tiādikāya uddesagāthāya anantare niddese pākaṭo hoti. Rati ca hāso cāti ca, kodho ca ussāho ca bhayañceti ca, jigucchā ca vimhayā ceti ca vākyaṃ. Ime nava ca evaṃ byabhicārībhāvasāttikābhāvo ceti ime yathāsakamanurūpavibhāvānubhāvehi dittaṃ katvā paccekaṃ kavinā bandhitabbā, naṭena gahetvā dassitabbā ca. Imesu tividhabhāvesu ayaṃ rati asesapumitthiguṇehi yuttehi naranārīhi aññamaññaṃ uppāditā, candādīhi uddīpanavibhāvehi uddīpitā, ussāhādipakāsakakāyikavācasikapayogasaṅkhātānubhāvena positā, sakasakānubhāvasāmatthiyehi gammamānānekappakārabyabhicārībhāvehi vicittakatā [M 0.0325] hoti. Īdisā’yaṃ rati naṭassa abhinayena ca pasatthabandhasavanena ca sabbhehi assādiyamānasiṅgārādirasattaṃ pāpuṇātīti viññātabbā. Hāsādīnaṃ sesaṭhāyībhāvānaṃ hassarasādibhāvāpattiyaṃ yutti evaṃ yathārahaṃ veditabbāti.

342. To show that the enduring states (ṭhāyībhāva) are indeed these nine, beginning with 'rati,' he says 'ratihāsā' and so on. These nine enduring states are: love, laughter, sorrow, anger, energy, fear, disgust, astonishment, and equanimity (samo), the quality of serenity. The explanation of the nature of these nine, beginning with love, will become clear in the subsequent exposition following the summary verse beginning 'siṅgārahassakaruṇā.' The phrases are: 'rati and hāsa,' 'anger and energy and fear,' and 'disgust and astonishment.' These nine, and likewise the transient states (byabhicārībhāva) and the involuntary states (sāttikābhāva), should each be composed by the poet, having made them vivid with their own appropriate causes (vibhāva) and effects (anubhāva), and they should be taken up and shown by the actor. Among these three kinds of states, this love (rati) is produced mutually by men and women endowed with all excellent qualities; it is stimulated by stimulating causes (uddīpanavibhāva) such as the moon; it is nourished by the effects (anubhāva) consisting of bodily and verbal expressions which manifest energy and so on; and it is made diverse by the many kinds of transient states (byabhicārībhāva) that are perceived through the capacity of their own effects. Such love, when enacted by an actor and through listening to well-composed works, is to be understood as attaining the state of the erotic (siṅgāra) and other sentiments, being enjoyed by all. The logic by which laughter (hāsa) and the other enduring states attain the state of the comic sentiment (hāsya) and others should be understood thus, as is appropriate.

Byabhicārībhāvaadhippāya

The Meaning of the Transitory States.

343.

343.

Tirobhāvāvibhāvādi-

Visesenā’bhimukhyato;

Yete caranti sīlena,

Te honti byabhicārino.

By the distinction of concealment, manifestation, and so forth, and by prominence, those that proceed by nature are the transitory states.

343. Byabhicārino āha “tirobhāva”iccādinā. Tirobhāvo ṭhāyīnaṃ ekassāpi bhāvassa nibbedādino aciraṭṭhāyitā ca āvibhāvo pākaṭatā ca nānārasanissayattā te ādayo yassa. Ādisaddena ṭhāyīdhammassa sukhadukkhādirūpassa gahaṇaṃ, sova viseso, tena. Ṭhāyīdhammassa sukhadukkharūpassa gahaṇaṃ, attano dhammassa sukhadukkharūpassa ṭhāyini samāropanañcābhimukhyaṃ. Tathā hi ratiyaṃ parisamo sukhānuviddho bhavati, soke dukkhānuviddho. Ratiyaṃ sukhasabhāvāpi gilānippabhutayo byabhicārino sakammaṃ dukkhamimaṃ samāropayanteva. Tato tena abhimukhabhāvena ye ete bhāvā sīlena caranti pavattanti, te byabhicārino hontīti.

343. He speaks of the transitory states with the words beginning 'concealment.' Concealment (tirobhāva) is the brief duration of a state such as disenchantment in relation to the enduring states, and manifestation (āvibhāva) is its becoming evident; these and others are meant because of their dependence on various sentiments (rasa). By the term 'and so forth' (ādi) is meant the apprehension of the nature of the enduring phenomenon, such as pleasure and pain; that itself is the distinction, and it is by that. Prominence (abhimukhyaṃ) is the apprehension of the nature of pleasure and pain of the enduring phenomenon, and the superimposition of one's own nature of pleasure and pain onto the enduring state. Thus, in love, weariness is pervaded by pleasure; in sorrow, it is pervaded by pain. Even in love, which has a nature of pleasure, transitory states like illness and so forth superimpose their own suffering. Therefore, by that prominence, those states that proceed or occur by nature are the transitory states.

343. Idāni uddesakkamena byabhicārībhāve lakkhaṇato dasseti “tirobhāvā”iccādinā. Tirobhāvāvibhāvādivisesena byabhicārībhāvānaṃ attano anekarasaṃ nissāya pavattattā, lokassa bhinnarucikattā ca kismiñci ṭhāyībhāve byabhicārībhāvānamattano guṇassa līnattañca kismiñci tasseva guṇassa pākaṭattañcātiādikena visesena [M 0.0326] abhimukhyato ṭhāyībhāvānaṃ sukhadukkharūpaṃ attani ca attano sukhadukkharūpaṃ ṭhāyībhāvesu ca āropanasaṅkhātena abhimukhabhāvena yete bhāvā sīlena caranti pakatiyā pavattanti, te bhāvā byabhicārino nāma hontīti. Evameva evarūpā (ka.) pīḷā sarūpena eko parisamasaṅkhatabyabhicārībhāvo ratiyaṃ saguṇena līno sukhānuviddho hutvā, soke saguṇena pākaṭo dukkhānuviddho ca hutvā pavattate. Evameva sukhasabhāvaratiyaṃ gilānādayo byabhicārino sakiyaṃ dukkhasarūpaṃ āropentīti katvā tirobhāvavibhāvādivisesena abhimukhaṃ pavattanti. Tirobhavanamiti ca, āvibhavanamiti ca, tirobhāvo ca āvibhāvo ceti ca, te ādayo yassa ṭhāyībhāvesu vijjamānānaṃ sukhadukkhasabhāvānaṃ attani āropanasseti ca, soyeva visesoti ca, abhimukhānaṃ bhāvoti ca viggaho. Byabhicārīpade visaddo visesatthe abhisaddo abhimukhabhāve vattati.

343. Now, in the order of exposition, he shows the characteristic of the transitory states with the words beginning 'concealment.' Because the transitory states operate based on their own many sentiments (rasa), and because the world has diverse tastes, by the distinction of concealment, manifestation, and so forth—that is, by the distinction whereby in some enduring state (ṭhāyībhāva) the quality of the transitory states becomes hidden, and in some, that same quality becomes evident—and by prominence (abhimukhya), which is designated as the superimposition of the nature of pleasure and pain of the enduring states onto oneself, and of one's own nature of pleasure and pain onto the enduring states, those states that proceed and operate by nature are called transitory states. Just so, the transitory state known as weariness (parisama), which is suffering (pīḷā) in nature, operates by being hidden with its own quality and pervaded by pleasure in love, and by being manifest with its own quality and pervaded by suffering in sorrow. Likewise, in love, which has a nature of pleasure, transitory states like illness and so forth, by superimposing their own nature of suffering, operate prominently through the distinction of concealment, manifestation, and so forth. The analysis is: 'a state of concealment' (tirobhavanam), 'a state of manifestation' (āvibhavanam), 'concealment and manifestation' (tirobhāvo ca āvibhāvo ca), 'that which has these and so forth' (te ādayo yassa), 'of the superimposition onto oneself of the natures of pleasure and pain existing in the enduring states' (ṭhāyībhāvesu vijjamānānaṃ sukhadukkhasabhāvānaṃ attani āropanassa), 'that itself is the distinction' (soyeva viseso), and 'the state of being prominent' (abhimukhānaṃ bhāvo). In the word 'byabhicārī,' the prefix 'vi' is in the sense of 'distinction,' and the prefix 'abhi' is in the sense of 'prominence.'

Byabhicārībhāvappabheda

The Classification of Transitory States.

344.

344.

Nibbedo takkasaṅkā sama-

Dhitijaḷatā dīnatuggālasattaṃ,

Suttaṃ tāso gilānu’ssukaharisa-

Satissāvisādābahitthā.

Disenchantment, Deliberation, Apprehension, Weariness, Steadfastness, Stupor, Wretchedness, Arrogance, Laziness, Drowsiness, Terror, Illness, Eagerness, Joy, Mindfulness, Envy, Despondency, Dissimulation.

Cintā gabbā’pamāro’marisamada-

Matummādamohā vibodho,

Niddāvegā sabiḷaṃ maraṇa-

Sacapalābyādhi tettiṃsame’te.

Anxiety, Conceit, Loss of Memory, Impatience, Intoxication, Thought, Madness, Delusion, Awakening, Sleep, Agitation, Shame, Death, Fickleness, Sickness—these are the thirty-three.

344. Te dasseti “nibbedo”iccādinā. Dīnatuggālasattanti dīnatā ca uggatañca ālasattañca, gilāni ussukaiti [M 0.0327] ussukkaṃ. Capalaiti cāpallaṃ, saha capalena sacapalo, so cāyaṃ byādhi ca, maraṇañca sacapalabyādhi ca samāhāre. Tañca saha biḷāya vattatīti sabiḷanti ete yathāvuttabyabhicārībhāvā tettiṃsa hontīti. Ussāhavatā vīraraso taṃvaseneva assādīyati. Bhīrunā tu sova bhayānakarasavaseneti lokasabhāvassa anekattā tadatthamete byabhicārino ekekassarasassa bahavo vaṇṇanīyā, yato taṃvaṇṇanādvārena sabbopi tesu kiñci assādetīti. Tattha yasmā pana māraṇopagataveridassanamekameva taṅkhaṇeyeva bhinnaṃ pakativasena bhīruno bhayassa hetu, saṅgāmalolassa tu ussāhanimittaṃ siyā. Tathā naṭena kataṃ vikatamābharaṇaṃ kriyāvā nīcapakatīnaṃ ṭhāyino hāsassa hetu, gambhīrapakatīnaṃ byabhicārino hāsassa, tasmā bhāve vaṇṇayatā kavinā bhāvā tathā vaṇṇanīyā, yathocityapariposo siyā. Ocityabhaṅgo tu mahatā vāyāmena pariharitabbo.

344. He shows them with 'disenchantment' and so forth. 'Dīnatuggālasattaṃ' means wretchedness, arrogance, and laziness; 'gilāni' is illness, 'ussukkaṃ' is eagerness. 'Capala' means fickleness; 'sacapalo' means with fickleness. And this, disease and death, are combined as 'sacapalabyādhi'. And that which occurs with shame is 'sabiḷa'. Thus, these aforementioned transitory states are thirty-three. The heroic sentiment (vīrarasa) is relished by the courageous through that very means. But for the timid, that same thing is relished as the terrifying sentiment (bhayānakarasa). Because the nature of the world is diverse, these many transitory states for each single sentiment should be described, since through such descriptions, everyone may relish something in them. Here, for instance, the sight of an enemy approaching death is, at that very moment, a cause of fear for the timid due to their inherent nature; but for the battle-eager, it could be a cause of exertion. Similarly, the exaggerated ornaments or actions of an actor are a cause of stable laughter for those of base character, but of transitory laughter for those of profound character. Therefore, a poet describing states should depict them in such a way that the proper appropriateness is fully developed. The disruption of appropriateness, however, must be avoided with great effort.

Tesu nibbedo attāvamānanaṃ. Tassa ca itthīnañca nīcānañca dāliddiyaṃ vibhāvo, yogīnaṃ tu tatvasaṃvedanaṃ vibhāvo, assupatanacintādayo ettha anubhāvā.

Among these, disenchantment is self-abasement. Its determinant for women and the lowly is poverty. But for yogis, the realization of truth is the determinant. Here, shedding tears, anxiety, and so forth, are the consequents.

Takko vitakkanaṃ. Tassa sandeho vibhāvo, sirokampādi anubhāvo.

Deliberation is thinking. Its determinant is doubt; head-shaking and so forth are its consequents.

Saṅkāya viruddhacaraṇaṃ vibhāvo, kampādayo anubhāvo.

For apprehension, hostile conduct is the determinant; trembling and so forth are the consequents.

Samo khedo. Tattha gatyādi vibhāvo, sedādi anubhāvo.

Weariness is exhaustion. Therein, gait and so forth are the determinants; sweat and so forth are the consequents.

Dhiti santoso. Ñāṇādi vibhāvo, anubhāvo bhogālolatādi.

Steadfastness is contentment. Wisdom and so forth are its determinants; absence of craving for enjoyments and so forth are its consequents.

Jaḷatā [M 0.0328] appaṭipatti. Tassā iṭṭhāniṭṭhadassanādi vibhāvo, animisanayanālocanādi anubhāvo.

Stupor is non-response. Its determinant is the sight of desirable and undesirable things and so forth; the unblinking gaze, fixed looking, and so forth, are its consequents.

Dīnatā cetaso anojatā. Tassā vibhāvo duggatatādi, anubhāvo malinavatthatādi.

Wretchedness is lack of vigor of mind. Its determinant is destitution and so forth; its consequent is wearing dirty clothes and so forth.

Uggatā dāruṇattaṃ. Tassā vibhāvo balavāparādhādi, tassa anubhāvo tajjanādi.

Arrogance is harshness. Its determinant is a grave offense and so forth; its consequent is threatening and so forth.

Ālasattassa parisamādi vibhāvo, jimhatādi anubhāvo.

For laziness, weariness and so forth are the determinants; crookedness and so forth are the consequents.

Suttassa niddā vibhāvo, tassādādayo anubhāvo.

For sleep, drowsiness is the determinant; yawning and so forth are its consequents.

Tāso cittakkhobho. Vibhāvo assa gajjitādi, kampanādi anubhāvo.

Terror is mental agitation. Its determinant is roaring and so forth; trembling and so forth are its consequents.

Āyāsapipāsādi vibhāvo gilāniyā, vivaṇṇatādayo anubhāvo.

For illness, fatigue, thirst, and so forth are the determinants; paleness and so forth are the consequents.

Kālakkhamatā ussukaṃ. Vibhāvo tassa ramaṇīyadassanicchādi, anubhāvo turitatādi.

Eagerness is impatience with time. Its determinant is the desire to see pleasant things and so forth; its consequent is quickness and so forth.

Cetopasādo harito. Tatra ussavādi vibhāvo, assusedādayo anubhāvo.

Joy is mental clarity. Therein, festivity and so forth are the determinants; tears, perspiration, and so forth are the consequents.

Sadisadassanādi vibhāvo satiyā, anubhāvo bhamusamunnamanādi.

For mindfulness, seeing the similar and so forth is the determinant; the raising of the eyebrows and so forth are the consequents.

Paresamukkaṃsāsahanatā issā. Tassā dujjanattagabbādayo vibhāvo, dosakathanāvajānanādayo anubhāvo.

Envy is the inability to tolerate others' excellence. Its determinant is wickedness, conceit, and so forth; fault-finding, contempt, and so forth are its consequents.

Visādo khedo. Vibhāvo tassa āraddhakāriyāsiddhādi, bādhayatāpādi anubhāvo.

Despondency is dejection. Its determinant is the failure of an undertaken task and so forth; distress, torment, and so forth are its consequents.

Abahitthā kāyasaṃvaraṇaṃ. Tassā vibhāvo lajjādi, anubhāvo’ññavikriyā.

Dissimulation is concealment of the body. Its determinant is shame and so forth; its consequent is an altered demeanor.

Cintā [M 0.0329] iṭṭhālābhādīhi, anubhāvo mukulitanayanādi.

Anxiety arises from not obtaining desirable things and so forth; its consequent is half-closed eyes and so forth.

Gabbo abhimāno. Vibhāvossa issariyādi, anubhāvo avajānanādi.

Conceit is arrogance. Its determinant is power and so forth; its consequent is contempt and so forth.

Apamāro gāharukkhādīhi gāharukkhapatanādīhi (?), bhūpātādayo ettha anubhāvo.

Epilepsy arises from seizures, trees, and so forth; here, falling to the ground and so forth are its consequents.

Amariso akkhamatā. Vibhāvo assāvamānanādi, sirokampanatajjanādayo anubhāvo.

Indignation is intolerance. Its determinant is disrespect and so forth; head-shaking, threatening, and so forth are its consequents.

Mado pamādukkaṃso. Tassa vibhāvo pānaṃ, calamānaṅgavacogatihāsādayo anubhāvo.

Intoxication is the height of heedlessness. Its determinant is drinking; unsteady limbs, speech, gait, laughter, and so forth are its consequents.

Mati kaṅkhacchedo. Upadesādi vibhāvo, mukhavikāsādi ettha anubhāvo.

Wisdom is the cutting off of doubt. Instruction and so forth are the determinants; here, a brightening of the face and so forth are the consequents.

Asamekkhitakāritā ummādo. Tassa vibhāvo sannipātagahaṇādi, aṭṭhānaruditagītahāsādayo anubhāvo.

Madness is acting without reflection. Its determinant is seizures due to humoral imbalance and so forth; inappropriate weeping, singing, laughter, and so forth are its consequents.

Moho bhayādīhi, anubhāvo thambhakampādi.

Delusion arises from fear and so forth; its consequent is stiffness, trembling, and so forth.

Durācārādīhi biḷaṃ, adhomukhatādi anubhāvo.

Shame arises from misconduct and so forth; its consequent is a downcast face and so forth.

Maraṇaṃ vibhāvaanubhāvehi supasiddhaṃ.

Death is well-known through its determinants and consequents.

Capalatā rāgadosādīhi, sacchandacaraṇādi anubhāvo. Byādhi pākaṭo.

Fickleness arises from lust, hatred, and so forth; its consequent is acting according to one's own inclinations and so forth. Disease is evident.

Ye vā panaññe idha niddiṭṭhā cittavuttivisesāpi saṃvijjanti sukhumabhedā, tesu keci vuttesvantogadhā honti. Yathā hi icchāsabhāvā sabbe kāmā ratiyaṃ antogadhā, tathā dosappakārā kodhā marisaissādīsvantogadhā, dukkhasabhāvā sokasamabyādhigilāni visādādīsvantogadhā. Pītyādayo sukhasabhāvā hariseti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tesu [M 0.0330] bhayā tāso añño, saṅkā tathā amariso. Tasmā issā, tathā gilānito samo, niddāya suttaṃ, ussukā capalatā, tathā mohā palayo vakkhamāno aññoti mantabbaṃ.

Or if other subtle distinctions of mental states are found here, some of them are included within those already mentioned. Just as all desires, being of the nature of wanting, are included in delight, so too the various kinds of aversion are included in anger, impatience, envy, and so forth; and states of the nature of suffering are included in sorrow, weariness, disease, illness, despondency, and so forth. Joy and similar states, being of the nature of pleasure, should be understood as included in gladness. Among these, terror is distinct from fear; likewise apprehension and impatience. Therefore, it should be considered that envy is distinct, as is weariness from illness, sleep from drowsiness, fickleness from eagerness, and also the forthcoming 'dissolution' from delusion.

344. Idāni te byabhicārībhāve sarūpena dasseti “nibbedo”iccādinā.
