Patāpavikkamādīhi aññarājūnaṃ daṇḍajatejasaṅkhatapatāpo, tesameva paramaṇḍalakkamanasaṅkhātavikkamo phalabhedo cetiādīhi uppanno ussāho vīroti vīrarasoti saññito kavīhi ñāto, ayaṃ vīraraso raṇadānadayāyogā yuddhacāgakaruṇāyogena hetubhūtena tividho bhave. Te eva raṇadānadayā eva imā anubhāvā nāma honti. Dhitimatyādayo dhitimatiuggatagabbādayo byabhicārino bhāvā hontīti. Yuddhavīradānavīradayāvīravasena vīraraso tividho hoti. Patāpo ca vikkamo ceti ca, te ādi yesamiti ca, raṇo ca dānañca dayā ceti ca, tāhi yogoti ca, tayo vidhā pakārā assāti ca, dhiti ca mati ceti ca, tā ādi yesamiti ca vākyaṃ.

363. Now, the division of the heroic sentiment and its process of development are shown by "splendor," and so on. The splendor, which is the power consisting of the majesty and might of other kings, and the valor, consisting of the advance upon the territories of those same kings, and the distinction of results, and so forth—the enthusiasm born from these is known as the heroic sentiment by poets. This heroic sentiment is threefold, due to its causal association with battle, giving, and compassion. These very battle, giving, and compassion are called the consequents. Steadfastness, intelligence, haughtiness, pride, and so forth, are the transitory states. The heroic sentiment is threefold by way of the hero of battle, the hero of giving, and the hero of compassion. The phrases are: "splendor and valor," and "those which begin with these"; "battle, giving, and compassion," and "association with these"; "three kinds are its divisions"; "steadfastness and intelligence," and "those which begin with these."

Vīrarasassa udāharaṇamevaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ –

The example of the heroic sentiment should be understood thus:

Viññāpetvā kuveraṃ sumahati-

Mapi ce’kovakumbhaṇḍasenaṃ,

Uttāsetvā gahetvā maṇiratanavaraṃ

Lakkhamādhāya jūte;

Jetvā korabyarājaṃ sacivaratana-

Muddhacca raññaṃ satamhā,

Etthānetvā’diyissaṃ suyuvatiratanaṃ

Ko mame’ttha’tthi bhāroti.

Having informed Kuvera, and I alone having terrified even a very great army of Kumbhaṇḍas, having taken the excellent jewel-gem, having set a hundred thousand as the stake in gambling; having conquered the king of the Korabyas, having lifted up the counselor-jewel from among a hundred kings, having brought them here, I will take the excellent young woman-jewel. What burden is there for me in this?

Kuveraṃ [M 0.0355] vessavaṇamahārājaṃ viññāpetvā bodhetvā sumahatimapi kumbhaṇḍasenaṃ atimahantiṃ kumbhaṇḍasenaṃ ekova uttāsetvā bhayaṃ janetvā maṇiratanavaraṃ gahetvā jūte akkhakīḷāyaṃ lakkhaṃ ādhāya ṭhapetvā korabyarājaṃ jetvā raññaṃ satamhā rājasambandhinā satena sacivaratanaṃ amaccaratanaṃ uddhacca uddharitvā etthānetvā suyuvatiratanaṃ sobhanaitthiratanaṃ ādiyissaṃ gaṇhissāmi, ettha yathāvuttesu mama ko bhāro atthīti. Ettha “ko mametthatthi bhāro”ti iminā ussāhasaṅkhāto ṭhāyībhāvo pakāsito. Etassa uppattiuddīpanesu kāraṇabhūtassa itthiratanassa ādānakhyātanāgarājagatapatāpavikkamādivibhāvo ca, taṃtaṃrūpappakāsakakavivacanasaṅkhātānubhāvo ca “viññāpetvā”iccādinā vākyasāmatthiyena paṭipādanīyā honti. “Sumahatimapi kumbhaṇḍasenaṃ eko”ti ca, “raññaṃ satamhā sacivaratanamuddhaccā”ti ca imehi dhitiuggatagabbādayo ca, “viññāpetvā kuvera”nti ca, “uttāsetvā korabyarāja”nti ca, “etthānetvā iccādayo”ti ca imehi matyādayo ca byabhicārino bhāvā vibhāvitā honti. Imehi vibhāvānubhāvabyabhicārībhāvehi yuddhavīraraso positoti daṭṭhabbo. Imināyeva nayena dānavīrādayo viññātabbā.

Having informed and enlightened Kuvera, the great king Vessavana, and having terrified even the immensely powerful Kumbhaṇḍa army—the exceedingly great Kumbhaṇḍa army—alone he instilled fear, seized the excellent jewel, and in the game of dice, having set a hundred thousand as the stake, having defeated King Korabya, and having lifted up the excellent counselor-jewel, the minister-jewel, from among a hundred kings, he brought them here. "I will take the beautiful young woman jewel, the lovely woman jewel. In this matter, what burden is there for me?" Here, by "What burden is there for me in this?" the stable state, which is enthusiasm, is revealed. And the determinants, such as the splendor and valor residing in the Naga king, declared by the taking of the woman jewel, which is the cause of its arising and inspiration, and the consequents, known as the words of a poet expressing those various forms, should be presented through the power of the sentence starting with "having informed." And by "Alone, even the immensely powerful Kumbhaṇḍa army," and by "having lifted up the counselor-jewel from among a hundred kings," these show steadfastness, haughtiness, pride, and so forth. And by "having informed Kuvera," and "having terrified King Korabya," and "having brought here," etc., these show intelligence, and so forth, which are transitory states. It should be seen that with these determinants, consequents, and transitory states, the heroic sentiment in battle is nourished. In this very way, the heroic sentiments in giving, and so forth, should be understood.

Bhayaṭhāyībhāva

The Stable State of Fear

364.

364.

Vikārisanasattādi-

Bhayukkaṃso bhayānako;

Sedādayo’nubhāve’ttha,

Tāsādī byabhicārino.

The intensification of fear, caused by distorted sounds, beings, and so forth, is called the fearful sentiment. Sweat and so forth are its consequents here, while terror and so forth are the transitory states.

364. “Vikāri”ccādi. Vikāri asabhāvappavatto viruddho sano saddo satto ca, te ādayo yesaṃ suññāraññādīnaṃ [M 0.0356] itthinīcappakatisambhavantānaṃ, vibhāvānaṃ, guruādīnaṃ vā uttamānaṃ, tehi jātassa bhayassa, kittimassa vā ukkaṃso bhayānako nāma raso. Ettha sedakampanapādacalanādayo anubhāvā, tāsādayo byabhicārino.

364. "Vikāri," etc. "Vikāri" means a distorted, unnatural, hostile sound or being. These are the determinants for those of feminine or inferior nature, such as empty forests, etc., or for superior beings, such as weighty matters, etc. The intensification of fear born from these, whether natural or artificial, is called the fearful sentiment. Here, sweating, trembling, shaking of the feet, and so forth, are the consequents, while terror, and so forth, are the transitory states.

364. Idāni bhayānakarasassa posanakkamaṃ dasseti “vikāri”ccādinā. Vikārisanasattādibhayukkaṃso pakativirahena vikāravantehi viruddhehi asanisaddādisaddehi, rakkhasādisattehi vā vibhāvehi hetubhūtehi sañjāto sābhāviko, kittimo vā bhayapaṭibandho ukkaṃso bhayānakaraso nāma hoti. Ettha bhayānakarasavisaye sedādayo dāhasarīrakampanādayo anubhāvā kāyikavācasikappayogasaṅkhatā anubhāvā honti. Tāsādī byabhicārino tāsasaṅkādayo iha byabhicārībhāvā hontīti. Sano ca satto ceti ca, vikāro etesaṃ atthīti ca, vikārino ca te sanasattā ceti ca, te ādayo yesaṃ suññāraññādīnamiti ca, tehi jātaṃ bhayamiti ca, majjhe padalopo, tassa ukkaṃsoti ca, sedo ādi yesaṃ kampanādīnamiti ca, tāso ādi yesaṃ saṅkādīnamiti ca vākyaṃ. Itthinīcappakatikānaṃ bhayahetu vikārisanasattādi, uttamānaṃ guruādi.

364. Now, the method of developing the fearful sentiment is shown beginning with "vikāri," etc. The intensification of fear, whether natural or artificial, which is fear-inducing, arises from determinants that are distorted and hostile due to the absence of their natural state, such as thunderclaps and other sounds, or beings like demons, etc., which are the causes, is called the fearful sentiment. Here, regarding the fearful sentiment, consequents such as sweating, burning sensations, trembling of the body, and so forth, are the consequents consisting of bodily and verbal actions. Terror, doubt, and so forth, are the transitory states here. The phrases are: "sound and being"; and "that they have distortion"; and "that those sounds and beings are distorted"; and "those which begin with empty forests, etc."; and "fear born from these"; there is an elision of a word in the middle; and "its intensification"; and "sweat, etc.," which means those which begin with trembling, etc.; and "terror, etc.," which means those which begin with doubt, etc. For those of feminine or inferior nature, the causes of fear are distorted sounds, beings, etc.; for superior beings, they are weighty matters, etc.

Ettha lakkhiyamevaṃ veditabbaṃ –

Here, the example should be understood thus:

Yaṃ diṭṭhisatthapatanena paripphurantī,

Kumbhaṇḍarakkhasacamū gamitā samantā;

Ācakkavāḷanaga’massagataṃ purīva,

Bhoto muhuṃ muhu’mapassi sa puṇṇako’hanti.

The army of Kumbhaṇḍas and Rakkhasas, trembling from the striking of the weapon of views, was driven away in all directions up to the world-encircling mountain. O Lord, I, Puṇṇaka, saw you again and again, mounted on a horse, like a city.

Diṭṭhisatthapatanena diṭṭhisallasampātanena paripphurantī kampamānā samantā parisamantato ācakkavāḷanagaṃ cakkavāḷapabbatāvadhi gamitā palāpitā kumbhaṇḍarakkhasacamū kumbhaṇḍarakkhasānaṃ [M 0.0357] senā yaṃ assagataṃ assapiṭṭhe nisinnakaṃ bhoto bhavataṃ tumhākaṃ purī iva puriyā dassanamiva muhuṃ muhuṃ apassi khaṇe khaṇe apassittha, so ahaṃ puṇṇako nāma yakkhoti. Ettha “diṭṭhisatthapatanenā”ti diṭṭhisatthāropanena ca “sa puṇṇako aha”nti iminā ca bhayajananassa hetubhūtaviruddhasattasaṅkhātā vibhāvā niddiṭṭhā, “muhuṃ muhu’mapassī”ti rasāvatthasampattabhayukkaṃsasaṅkhato ṭhāyībhāvo vibhāvito, “kumbhaṇḍarakkhasacamū gamitā samantā ācakkavāḷanaga”nti tāsasaṅkādikā byabhicārino bhāvā jotitā. “Paripphurantī”ti sedakampādayo anubhāvā dassitā honti.

By the striking of the weapon of views, by the piercing of the dart of views, trembling, they were driven away in all directions, all around, up to the world-mountain, up to the boundary of the world-mountain—the army of Kumbhaṇḍas and Rakkhasas, the host of Kumbhaṇḍas and Rakkhasas. That which was mounted on a horse, seated on a horse's back, of you, sir, like a city, like the sight of a city, again and again, moment by moment, I saw. I am Puṇṇaka, the Yakkha. Here, by 'by the striking of the weapon of views' and by 'I am Puṇṇaka,' the determinants, consisting of hostile beings that are the cause of generating fear, are indicated. By 'again and again I saw,' the abiding state, consisting of the intensification of fear that has attained the state of a sentiment, is revealed. By 'the army of Kumbhaṇḍas and Rakkhasas was driven away in all directions up to the world-mountain,' the transitory states, such as terror, doubt, and so forth, are illuminated. By 'trembling,' the consequents, such as sweating, trembling, and so forth, are shown.

Jigucchāṭhāyībhāva

The Abiding State of Disgust

365.

365.

Jigucchā rudhirādīhi,

Pūtyādīhi virāgato;

Bībhaccho khobhanu’bbegī,

Kamena karuṇāyuto;

Nāsāvikunanādīhi,

Saṅkādīhi’ssa posanaṃ.

Disgust arises from blood and the like, from putrid things and the like, and from revulsion. The repulsive sentiment is disturbing, alarming, and gradually accompanied by compassion. Its nourishment comes from wrinkling the nose and the like, and from doubt and the like.

365. “Jigucchā”iccādi. Rudhirantādīhi pūtikimiādīhi virāgato ca jātā jigucchā garahā kamena khobhano ubbegī karuṇāyuto ca bībhaccho bhavati, nāsāvikunanamukhacchadanādīhi anubhāvehi, saṅkāvegādīhi byabhicārīhi ca assa posanaṃ bhavatīti.

365. 'Disgust,' and so on. Disgust, which is reproach, arises from blood, entrails, and the like; from putrid worms and the like; and from revulsion. In due course, the repulsive sentiment becomes disturbing, alarming, and accompanied by compassion. It is fostered by consequents such as wrinkling the nose, covering the mouth, and the like, and by concomitant states such as apprehension, agitation, and the like.

365. Idāni bībhaccharasassa posanakkamaṃ dasseti “jigucchā”iccādinā. Rudhirādīhi rattantaguṇādīhi ca, pūtyādīhi pūtikimiādīhi ca, virāgato virattabhāvena cāti imehi tīhi vibhāvehi hetubhūtehi uppajjamānā jigucchā kamena rudhirādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vibhāvānaṃ paṭipāṭiyā khobhano [M 0.0358] anavaṭṭhāno asamāhito ubbegī ubbegavā karuṇāyuto sokarūpena sahito cāti evaṃ bībhaccho raso nāma hoti. Nāsāvikunanādīhi nāsasaṅkocanamukhapidahanādīhi anubhāvehi ca saṅkādīhi ca saṅkāāvegādīhi byabhicārībhāvehi ca karaṇabhūtehi assa bībhaccharasassa posanaṃ hotīti. Rudhirādīsu tīsu padesu, khobhanādīsu tīsu ca gamyamānattā avuttopi casaddo yojetabbo, tasmā khobhanādīhi tīhi yuttova bībhaccharaso nāmāti daṭṭhabbo. Rudhiraṃ ādi yesaṃ antādīnamiti ca, pūtiādi yesaṃ kimiādīnamiti ca, ubbego assa bībhacchassa atthīti ca, karuṇena āyutoti ca, nāsāya vikunanaṃ saṅkocanamiti ca, taṃ ādi yesaṃ mukhacchādanādīnamiti ca, saṅkā ādi yesaṃ āvegādīnamiti ca vākyaṃ.

365. Now, the process of fostering the repulsive sentiment is shown with 'disgust,' and so on. Disgust arises from three determinants which are its cause: from blood and the like (such as entrails, etc.), from putrid things and the like (such as putrid worms, etc.), and from revulsion (in the sense of being dispassionate). Gradually, in sequence with these three determinants—blood and the like—the repulsive sentiment becomes disturbing, unstable, unsettled; alarming, possessed of alarm; and accompanied by compassion, together with the form of sorrow. Its fostering occurs through the instrumental consequents, such as wrinkling the nose (contraction of the nostrils), covering the mouth, and the like, and through the concomitant states, such as doubt, agitation, and the like. Although the word 'ca' is not stated, it is to be supplied as it is understood in the three instances of 'blood and the like' and in the three instances of 'disturbing and the like.' Therefore, the repulsive sentiment should be understood as being conjoined with these three: 'disturbing,' and so on. The phrases are: 'blood is the beginning of which are entrails, etc.'; 'putrid is the beginning of which are worms, etc.'; 'alarm belongs to this repulsive'; 'accompanied by compassion'; 'wrinkling of the nose is contraction'; 'that is the beginning of which are covering the mouth, etc.'; and 'doubt is the beginning of which are agitation, etc.'

Imassa bībhacchassodāharaṇamevaṃ veditabbaṃ –

An example of this repulsive sentiment should be understood as follows:

Yakkhā maccakaraṅkakaṅkanadharā ye nimmitā puṇṇake-

Nu’ttaṃsīkatapāṇipallavadharā hārīkatantoragā;

Littā lohitakuṅkumehi vidhurene’te pivantā vasā-

Majjaṃ sīsakapālapātihi pure dhuttā viyo’pekkhitāti.

The demons created by Puṇṇaka, wearing bracelets of dead men's bones, wearing hands like tender leaf-buds as head-ornaments, and entrails made into garlands like snakes; smeared with blood-saffron, drinking fat-liquor from skull-bowls—these were regarded by Vidhura as mere drunkards in the city.

Puṇṇakena yakkhena nimmitā maccakaraṅkakaṅkanadharā manussaṭṭhisaṅkhātakarabhūsanadhārino uttaṃsīkatapāṇipallavadharā matthakamālikatahatthatalasaṅkhatapallavadhārino hārīkatantoragā muttāhārīkatamanussantasaṅkhātauragasampayuttā lohitakuṅkumehi rudhirasaṅkhātakuṅkumakakkehi littā sīsakapālapātihi sīsakapālasaṅkhātehi sarāvehi vasāmajjaṃ vasāsaṅkhātasuraṃ pure abhimukhe pivantā ye yakkhā siyuṃ, ete yakkhā vidhurena paṇḍitena dhuttā viya nagare surādhuttā viya upekkhitā hontīti. Iha “littā lohitakuṅkumehī”ti ca “uttaṃsīkatapāṇipallavadharā”ti ca [M 0.0359] “hārīkatantoragā”ti ca imehi cittakkhobhakāraṇabhūto rudhirādivibhāvo ca, “maccakaraṅkakaṅkanaro”ti ca “sīsakapālapātihi vasāmajjaṃ pivantā”ti ca imehi ubbegavantasabhāvassa hetubhūto pūtyādivibhāvo ca pakāsito. Karuṇāyutasabhāvassa kāraṇabhūtavirajjanavibhāvo ca nāsāvikunanādianubhāvo ca saṅkāvegādibyabhicārībhāvo ca bībhacchasaṅkhātaṭhāyībhāvo cāti ime sabbe vākyasāmatthiyena gammāti veditabbā.

Created by the yakkha Puṇṇaka, wearing bracelets of dead men's bones (ornaments for the wrist made of human bones); wearing hands like tender leaf-buds as head-ornaments (wearers of tender leaf-buds in the form of palms made into head-garlands); conjoined with snakes in the form of human entrails made into pearl-garlands; smeared with blood-saffron (a paste of saffron in the form of blood); drinking fat-liquor (liquor in the form of fat) from skull-bowls (cups in the form of skull-caps) in front—whatever yakkhā there might be, these yakkhā were regarded by the wise Vidhura like drunkards, like liquor-drunkards in the city. Here, by the phrases 'smeared with blood-saffron,' 'wearing hands like tender leaf-buds as head-ornaments,' and 'conjoined with snakes in the form of entrails,' the determinant of blood and the like, which is the cause of mental agitation, is revealed. By 'wearing bracelets of dead men's bones' and 'drinking fat-liquor from skull-bowls,' the determinant of putrid things and the like, which is the cause of the state of being alarmed, is revealed. The determinant of revulsion, which is the cause of the state of being accompanied by compassion; the consequents, such as wrinkling the nose and the like; the concomitant states, such as doubt, agitation, and the like; and the abiding state called the repulsive—all these are to be understood by the power of the sentence.

Vimhayaṭhāyībhāva

The Abiding State of Astonishment

366.

366.

Atilokapadatthehi,

Vimhayo’yaṃ raso’bbhuto;

Tassā’nubhāvā sedassu-

Sādhuvādādayo siyuṃ;

Tāsāvegadhitippaññā,

Honte’ttha byabhicārino.

From things beyond the world, this astonishment, the wondrous sentiment, arises. Its consequents are sweat, tears, expressions of approval, and the like. Fear, agitation, resolve, and wisdom are, in this context, the concomitant states.

366. “Ati”ccādi. Atilokehi lokātivuttīhi māyādibbagehārāmādīhi padatthehi jāto ayaṃ vimhayo cittavikārasaṅkhāto ṭhāyībhāvo abbhuto raso nāma. Sedaassusādhuvādaromañcādayo tassa anubhāvā siyuṃ, tāsādayo byabhicārino hontīti.

366. 'Beyond,' etc. This astonishment—an abiding state known as a transformation of mind, born from things beyond the world which surpass worldly existence, such as the illusions of magicians, divine pleasure groves, and the like—is called the wondrous sentiment. Sweat, tears, expressions of approval, goosebumps, and the like are its consequents, while fear and the like are its concomitant states.

366. Idāni vimhayarasassa posanakkamaṃ dasseti “ati”iccādinā. Atilokapadatthehi lokaṭṭhitimatikkamma pavattehi māyādibbabhavanaārāmavimānādipadatthehi hetubhūtehi uppajjamāno ayaṃ vimhayo cittabyāpanasaṅkhāto ṭhāyībhāvo abbhuto raso abbhutaraso nāma bhave, sedassusādhuvādādayo tassa abbhutarasassa anubhāvā siyuṃ, tāsāvegadhitippaññā ettha [M 0.0360] abbhutarasavisaye byabhicārino bhāvā hontīti. Atikkantā lokamiti ca, te ca te padatthā ceti ca, sādhuiti vādoti ca, sedo ca assu ca sādhuvādo ceti ca, te ādi yesaṃ romañcādīnamiti ca, tāso ca āvego ca dhiti ca paññā ceti ca vākyaṃ.

366. Now, the manner of fostering the sentiment of astonishment is shown with 'beyond,' etc. This astonishment—an abiding state known as an expansion of mind, which arises from things that are its cause and are beyond the sphere of the world, that surpass worldly existence, such as the illusions of magicians, celestial abodes, pleasure groves, celestial mansions, and the like—is called the wondrous sentiment, the sentiment of wonder. Sweat, tears, expressions of approval, and the like are the consequents of that wondrous sentiment, while fear, agitation, steadfastness, and wisdom are the concomitant states in the context of this wondrous sentiment. The phrases are: 'surpassing the world'; 'and those things'; 'Sadhu is the expression'; 'sweat and tears and expression of approval'; 'those beginning with goosebumps'; and 'fear and agitation and steadfastness and wisdom'.

Imassa abbhutarasassodāharaṇamevaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ –

An example of this wondrous sentiment should be seen as follows:

Sa puṇṇakenā’haṭanekabhiṃsane-

Sva’ho naṭeneva suniccalo’calā;

Nipātito tena avaṃsiropataṃ,

Asantasaṃ taṃ mini diṭṭhiyaṭṭhiyāti.

When many terrifying things were brought forth by Puṇṇaka, ah! He, like an actor, remained perfectly still and unmoving. Thrown down by him, falling headfirst, unfrightened, he measured it with the measuring stick of his sight.

So vidhurapaṇḍito puṇṇakena yakkhena naṭena iva anekavikāradassanakena nāṭakena viya āhaṭanekabhiṃsanesu bhayattamānītānekavidhabhiṃsanesu vattamānesu suniccalo tena puṇṇakena acalā saṭṭhiyojanubbedhakāḷāgiripabbatamatthakato nipātito avaṃsiropataṃ adhosīsaṃ patanto asantasaṃ evaṃ appatiṭṭhepi anuttasanto taṃ pabbataṃ diṭṭhiyaṭṭhiyā mini pamāṇamakāsi, aho acchariyanti. Ettha bhayahetumhi sati bhītiyā ca tattha parijānanābhāvassa ca lokasabhāvattā tamatikkamma bhayakaraṇe asantāsassa ca diṭṭhiyā pabbataminanassa ca pavattabhāvakathanena lokātikkantapadatthasaṅkhāto vibhāvo “asantasaṃ taṃ mini diṭṭhiyaṭṭhiyā”ti iminā pakāsito. “Aho”ti vacanena, tassa sāmatthiyena ca sādhuvādasedaassuādayo anubhāvā vibhāvitā. Tāsaāvegadhiticcādibyabhicārībhāvā, vimhayasaṅkhātaṭhāyībhāvo ca samuditavākyasāmatthiyena jotito.

That wise Vidhura remained perfectly still, even while many terrifying things that cause fear were occurring, brought forth by the yakkha Puṇṇaka, who was like an actor displaying various transformations in a play. Though thrown down headfirst by that Puṇṇaka from the summit of the sixty-yojana-high Black Mountain, falling head-down, he was not terrified. Even in such an unsupported state, untrembling, he measured that mountain with the measuring stick of his sight, thinking, “Ah, how marvelous!” Here, since fear in the presence of a cause for fear and a lack of comprehension thereof is the nature of the world, by narrating the occurrence of fearlessness in the face of a terrifying cause and the measuring of the mountain with his sight—which transcend that worldly nature—the determinant known as ‘that which transcends the world’ is revealed by the phrase, “untrembling, he measured it with the measuring stick of his sight.” By the word “Ah!” and by his capability, the consequents—such as praise, sweat, and tears—are made manifest. The transitory states—such as terror, agitation, and steadfastness—and the abiding state known as astonishment are illuminated by the power of the entire sentence.

Samaṭhāyībhāva

The Abiding State of Tranquility

367.

367.

Ṭhāyībhāvo [M 0.0361] samo mettā-

Dayāmodādisambhavo;

Bhāvādīhi tadu’kkaṃso,

Santo santanisevito.

The abiding state is tranquility, arising from loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and the like. Its excellence is due to the accompanying states and so forth, and it is the peaceful sentiment, cultivated by the peaceful.

Iti saṅgharakkhitamahāsāmipādaviracite

Thus, in the work composed by the venerable great Elder Saṅgharakkhita,

Subodhālaṅkāre

in the Subodhālaṅkāra,

Rasabhāvāvabodho nāma pañcamo paricchedo.

is the fifth chapter, called 'The Understanding of Sentiments and States'.

Subodhālaṅkāro samatto.

The Subodhālaṅkāra is concluded.

367. “Ṭhāyi”ccādi. Mettādisambhavo samo upasamasaṅkhāto ṭhāyībhāvo bhavati, tadanurūpehi bhāvānubhāvehi tassa ukkaṃso yassa, so santo nāma raso bhavati, so ca santanisevitoti.

367. 'Abiding,' and so forth. The tranquility, reckoned as calm, which arises from loving-kindness and the like, becomes the abiding state. That sentiment whose excellence is due to the corresponding transitory states and consequents is called the peaceful sentiment, and it is cultivated by the peaceful.

Iti subodhālaṅkāre mahāsāmināmikāyaṃ ṭīkāyaṃ

Thus, in the commentary to the Subodhālaṅkāra, called the Mahāsāmināmikā,

Rasabhāvāvabodho pañcamo paricchedo.

is the fifth chapter, 'The Understanding of Sentiments and States'.

367. Idāni santarasassa posanakkamaṃ dasseti “ṭhāyi”ccādinā. Mettādayāmodādisambhavo mettākaruṇāpītiādivibhāvehi sambhūto samo kāyacittopasamo ṭhāyībhāvo nāma hoti, bhāvādīhi byabhicārībhāvādīhi karaṇabhūtehi, apica tassa samassa anurūpehi byabhicārībhāvānubhāvehi tadukkaṃso tassa ṭhāyībhāvassa ukkaṃsayutto santanisevito sādhūhi sevito santo santaraso nāma hotīti. Mettā ca dayā ca modo ceti ca, te ādayo yesamiti ca, tehi sambhavo yasseti ca, tassa ukkaṃso assa santasseti ca, sataṃ nisevitoti ca vākyaṃ.

367. Now, the process of nurturing the peaceful sentiment is shown with 'abiding,' and so forth. The tranquility, which is physical and mental calm, arising from loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and the like, and produced by the determinants such as loving-kindness, compassion, and joy, is called the abiding state. Endowed with excellence on account of the causal transitory states and so forth, and also on account of the corresponding transitory states and consequents of that tranquility, this peaceful sentiment, cultivated by the peaceful and by the good, is so called. The analysis of the verse is: 'loving-kindness, compassion, and joy'; 'these are the beginning of which'; 'from them is its arising'; 'its excellence belongs to this peaceful one'; and 'cultivated by the good'.

Assa [M 0.0362] santarasassodāharaṇamevaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ –

An example of this peaceful sentiment should be seen thus:

Entesu kesarikarīsva’pi veṭhayante,

Nāge nagaṃ madagaje viya veḷugumbaṃ;

Yakkhe vicālayati nocali īsakampi,

Santiṃ gatova vidhuro madhurāpi bhāvoti.

Even when lions and elephants approach, and snakes entwine; even when the Yaksha shakes the mountain as a drunken elephant a bamboo clump, Vidhura, as if having attained peace, did not stir in the slightest, nor from his sweet disposition.

Kesarikarīsu sīhahatthīsu entesu api bhiṃsanākārena samīpamāgacchantesupi nāge veṭhayantepi nāgesu sarīraṃ veṭhayantesupi. Jātyāpekkhāyekavacanaṃ, veḷugumbaṃ madagaje viya vicālayati madagaḷitahatthimhi cālente iva yakkhe puṇṇake nagaṃ kāḷāgiripabbataṃ vicālayatipi anekappakāre cālentepi vidhuro paṇḍito santiṃ gatova nibbānaṃ ālambaṇakaraṇavasena sampatto viya phalasamāpattisamāpanno iva atha vā diṭṭhadhammanibbānasaṅkhatanirodhasamāpattisamāpanno viya īsakampi appakampi madhurā bhāvā api madhurasabhāvatopi no cali, nisinnaṭṭhānato pagevāti adhippāyo. Ettha dhāvanarodanakampanādīnaṃ karaṇabhūtaṃ sīhādīnamāgamanaṃ nāgaveṭhanaṃ pabbatakampanantiādīsu vattamānesupi nibbikārattena santiṃ gatoti iminā santarasassa pakatibhūte uddese dassito navamo ṭhāyībhāvo dassito hoti, etassa uppattiuddīpanānaṃ kāraṇabhūtā mettādayāmodādivibhāvā sāmatthiyā dassitā hontīti. Dhitimatisatiādayo tadanurūpabyabhicārībhāvā ca tādisānubhāvā ca “entesu veṭhayante vicālayatī”ti iminā, sakalavākyasāmatthiyena ca pakāsitāti daṭṭhabbā.

Regarding 'lions and elephants': even when lions and elephants approach in a terrifying manner; regarding 'snakes entwine': even when snakes entwine his body. The singular 'nāge' is used with reference to the class. Even when the Yaksha Puṇṇaka shakes Mount Kāḷāgiri in various ways, just as a drunken elephant with oozing temples shakes a bamboo clump, the wise Vidhura, as if having attained peace—that is, as if he had attained Nibbāna by making it his object, or as if he had entered the fruition of attainment, or as if he had entered the attainment of cessation, called Nibbāna in this very life—did not stir in the slightest, not even from his sweet disposition or from his sweet nature. The intention is, how much less from his seated position. Here, although the approach of lions, the entwining of snakes, the shaking of the mountain, and so forth—which are causes for running, crying, and trembling—were occurring, the ninth abiding state, shown in the section which is the natural basis of the peaceful sentiment, is demonstrated by the phrase 'as if having attained peace' through his imperturbability. The determinants, such as loving-kindness, compassion, and joy, which are the cause of its arising and stimulation, are shown by implication. And the corresponding transitory states, such as steadfastness, wisdom, and mindfulness, and such consequents, are revealed by the phrases 'when they approach, when they entwine, when he shakes,' and by the power of the entire passage. Thus it should be understood.

Iti subodhālaṅkāranissaye

Thus, in the Subodhālaṅkāra Nissaya,

Rasabhāvāvabodho nāma pañcamo paricchedo.

ends the fifth chapter, called 'The Understanding of Sentiments and States'.

Subodhālaṅkāraṭīkā samattā.

The Sub-commentary on the Subodhālaṅkāra is concluded.
